Reactor core plant upgrades for Dreadnought delivered
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
21:50:56 GMT
06:50:56 KST

The major facility upgrades needed to produce reactor cores for the Dreadnought submarines have been delivered, with work now focused on final commissioning and on manufacturing the cores themselves, according to an answer given in Parliament.
James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat member for Lewes, asked what progress has been made on the Core Production Capability programme in the context of the delivery confidence assessments for Government Major Project Portfolio defence projects.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence, said: “Delivery confidence assessments for Government Major Project Portfolio Defence projects published by National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority confirm that the Core Production Capability continues to make progress in delivering the infrastructure, workforce and manufacturing capabilities required to support our submarine programmes.
“The major facility upgrades required to support Dreadnought reactor core production have been delivered, with activity now focused on completing final commissioning, manufacturing and delivering the reactor cores required.
“The Ministry of Defence continues to work with Rolls-Royce Submarines to ensure delivery of reactor components in time to support Dreadnought entering service in the early 2030s as planned.
“Work is also underway to modernise and expand the manufacturing capability and capacity required to produce reactor cores and nuclear steam raising plant for future SSN-AUKUS submarines, supporting both the UK and Australian submarine production programmes.”
Core Production Capability is the programme rebuilding the facilities at Rolls-Royce Submarines in Raynesway, Derby, where Britain manufactures the reactor cores for every nuclear submarine it operates. The site is the single point through which the entire submarine force passes, and the plant it replaced dated from the Cold War.
Expanding that capacity to serve Australia as well as Britain is one of the practical commitments inside AUKUS, since Australian boats built at Osborne will run on the same reactor design. Rolls-Royce has been recruiting on a large scale in Derby and has said the site will roughly double its workforce over the programme.
Steel will be cut on the first SSN-AUKUS submarine next year, and the detailed design and long lead phase completes in 2028. The Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise.

Eisenkot vows to build broad coalition to avert fresh Israeli election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
21:34:34 UTC
06:34:34 KST

Israeli opposition Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot has pledged to establish a broad new governing coalition to avert the prospect of another snap election, following consultations with opposition leader Yair Lapid in the wake of Tuesday's inconclusive parliamentary poll.
In a formal statement issued following the meeting, Eisenkot outlined his coalition conditions and governing priorities, reporting that his goal is to establish a "broad Zionist government committed to the national interest".
Eisenkot established four mandatory principles for any prospective coalition partner: recognition of Israel as a "Jewish, democratic, liberal and egalitarian state"; dedication to the values of Israel's Declaration of Independence; universal military, national, or civilian service for all citizens; and recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organisation whose military and administrative capabilities in Gaza must be eradicated.
"The door to the government we establish will be open to any elected official who accepts these principles and is prepared to rise to the occasion," Eisenkot said.
Legislative priorities and security policy
Insisting that high voter participation mandated decisive action to prevent further ballots, Eisenkot declared: "On October 27, the public had its say. The composition of Israel's next government must be determined solely by Israeli citizens, without outside interference or manipulation".
His immediate legislative programme includes creating a state commission of inquiry, enacting universal service, bolstering armed forces recruitment, enhancing veteran welfare, and repealing legislation passed under the current government's judicial overhaul.
"Don't let anyone mislead you: In Israel, it is the Knesset that gives the government its vote of confidence, not the other way around," he added.
Regarding prospective strikes against Iran prior to a new administration taking office, Eisenkot stated his backing would remain tightly circumscribed.
"Until the new government is formed, I will support military action only in response to direct and immediate threats against Israel that cannot wait until the government is sworn in," he noted.
His declarations follow certified Knesset returns awarding Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing bloc 53 seats, Eisenkot's opposition camp 48 seats, and Arab lists 19 seats in the 120-member parliament, leaving both primary coalitions short of the 61-seat threshold required for an outright majority.

Some 320,000 demonstrators take part in largely peaceful protests across France

Some 320,000 demonstrators take part in largely peaceful protests across France
Around 320,000 protesters took part in a third mass protest over living costs across France on Saturday, the interior ministry estimated, while organizers counted nearly half a million. Tensions flared at the end of marches in some cities but authorities reported that most demonstrations were largely peaceful.
Scuffles broke out in Paris and other French cities on Saturday evening at the end of nationwide demonstrations driven by anger over living costs and strained public services, while authorities warned of possible further violence overnight with Halloween celebrations under way.
The protests, which were largely peaceful through the afternoon, continued for a third weekend after riots and looting on October 17 that caught security forces off guard, leaving a trail of damage to shops, public buildings and businesses across the country.
Read more'Deeply regressive': How the French government plans to make protesters pay for riots and looting
Riot police charged to disperse small groups of rioters at the end of the Paris march, and fired tear gas in Lyon, France's third-largest city, and in Toulouse in the southwest. There were also tensions at the end of unauthorised protests in Marseille, but calm had returned as night fell.
"Security forces held their ground and protected city centres. Public order was maintained," Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told reporters after the marches, adding that police had faced "a great deal of violence". He said authorities were now bracing for scattered unrest later in the evening, amid what he said were calls for insurrection on Halloween night.
"The day is not over. We are ready for those looking for a fight tonight, and we will respond firmly," Nuñez added.
The protests in France have inspired youth-led "Gen-Z" protests across Europe, with demonstrations in several German cities on Saturday. There were also protests in Italy.
Read more'Gen Z' demonstrations across Germany demand more education funding
The marches brought together students – who began mobilising in September – with trade unions and a smaller contingent of anti-establishment Yellow Vest protesters, united by complaints over the cost of living, high fuel prices, rising inflation and President Emmanuel Macron's government.
"The French economy is doing badly no matter what happens, because today we're being run by a group of incompetents who juggle billions, while families are struggling with a few cents," protester Jerome Rodriguez said during the Paris march.
"That's why we're here, to keep shouting our demands louder and louder and hopefully get a response from the government, although that seems very unlikely."
Far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, whose ratings have risen in recent weeks ahead of next April's presidential election, marched at the head of the Paris demonstration. France's top administrative court had upheld a ban on a march between the landmark Paris squares of Nation and Bastille, rejecting a challenge from unions. Authorities instead authorised a route along boulevards on the eastern edge of the capital, away from central shopping districts.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Turnout was lower than for the previous two Saturdays of protests, with 320,000 protesters nationwide, including 70,000 in Paris, the interior ministry said, while organizer's turnout estimates are nearly half a million. That compares with 410,000 the week before and 550,000 on October 17.
The interior ministry said in a statement that "radical elements" intent on damage and looting had attempted to break away from marches in cities including Bordeaux, Toulouse, Lyon and Marseille, but were thwarted by security forces.
It added that security checks at railway stations and roads had uncovered people carrying objects that could be used as weapons.
Authorities have warned that Halloween masks could be used to conceal the identities of rioters. Nuñez has vowed to prevent a repeat of the October 17 violence, noting that existing laws allow police to prohibit face coverings when public order is threatened.
The unrest comes at a delicate moment for the government. On Friday, ratings agency Fitch unexpectedly revised the outlook on French debt to negative, underscoring investor concerns over the country's finances. With public debt nearing 120 percent of economic output and borrowing costs rising, Macron's government faces mounting pressure to curb spending, limiting its room for manoeuvre.
The US Embassy advised travellers to avoid areas where demonstrations or large gatherings were planned.
Protests began with students
The protests gathered momentum in late September as Macron's minority government opened talks on its 2027 budget. Students angered by the deteriorating state of schools, overcrowded classrooms and a university admissions system widely viewed as unfair have since been joined by trade unions and a resurgent Yellow Vests movement demanding action on living costs.
The French government's promises to reform education and ease fuel costs have failed to calm discontent.
Read moreFrench students vow to continue protests despite concessions from Macron govt
"When I was little, I was told young people were the future," said Aaron Berthier de Grandry, a 15-year-old high school student in the Paris suburb of Nogent-sur-Marne, who was planning to join his third consecutive weekend of protests.
"Well, if we, as the future of France, lack resources, that means France will end up collapsing."
The unrest has handed a political boost to far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who leads opinion polls ahead of April's presidential election, while potential centrist successors to Macron remain divided.
Read moreFrench far-right leader Le Pen seeks to leverage unrest in presidential campaign kick-off
The troubles are the latest blow to an economy which data on Friday showed was already shrinking in the third quarter.
The Chamber of Commerce estimates that losses to retailers during the three weeks of unrest has exceeded €1 billion ($1.1 billion). Other estimates put the total at double that when including uninsured damage and lost revenue.
Along Paris' main shopping boulevards, early Christmas lights glowed around boarded-up windows and security grilles.
Among the shops targeted in the unrest of previous weekends were outlets belonging to luxury brands including Hermes, Louis Vuitton and Burberry.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

AI generated
FRANKFURT - German police and protesters clashed across the country on Oct 31 following massive youth-led protests, with authorities using water cannon and pepper spray as masked demonstrators hurled fireworks, stones and bottles.
Several police officers were injured in the violence after tens of thousands joined protests nationwide that were organised by the group “GenZ regelt!” (Gen Z has got this!).
The demonstrations, inspired by similar movements in France and Italy calling for political elites to heed the concerns of the younger generation, were largely peaceful during the day.
But tensions peaked in the evening as some groups of protesters refused to disperse.
Police were pelted with projectiles in the western city of Frankfurt, and responded by using water cannon and pepper spray as they sought to clear protesters.
“Incidents of stones and fireworks being thrown at the emergency services continue to occur,” police said on X. “We are taking action against these troublemakers.”
Police also used water cannon in the cities of Hamburg and Cologne after they said demonstrators targeted emergency service workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.
‘Boiling point’
In Berlin, a protest that was not organised by the “GenZ regelt!” movement took place in the evening, with police reporting they were pelted with eggs and bottles.
Police in the eastern city of Leipzig also used pepper spray after protests turned violent while a police officer in Bonn suffered minor injuries during a confrontation with a group.
Police were reported to have made several arrests.
The youth-led protests earlier in the day took place in a mostly peaceful and festive atmosphere, with some dressed in outfits ranging from dinosaurs to Batman as the demonstrations coincided with Halloween.
They waved signs that read “Time for resistance”, and “Merz must go”, in reference to conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
“I think it’s really important to show solidarity with all the other protests currently happening across Europe, including in France,” Milla, a 20-year-old student who only gave her first name, told AFP in Berlin.
“I’ve been waiting for a long time for something to finally really happen, and for people to tackle this with a bit more force. I believe that today here is the first step.”
Marius, a 23-year-old care worker, added that “politicians need to know about this... the situation is slowly reaching boiling point.”
“I think we can all feel that this just isn’t working anymore,” he added.
The movement’s complaints range from the high cost of living to poorly maintained schools, government spending cuts and, more broadly, what it sees as politicians making decisions with apparently little regard for the younger generation.
They are also unhappy with sharply increased military spending and a new voluntary service model aimed at boosting troop numbers, fearing it is a step towards bringing back conscription.
Europe-wide protests
“GenZ regelt!” said some 120,000 people took part in the demonstrations.
Police said the main protests themselves had been “very peaceful”.
When violence broke out in the evening, police “intervened very decisively and also forcefully”, Andreas Rosskopf, an official from the police union, told the Rheinische Post daily.
He also noted that major property damage had so far been avoided. Some jewellery stores and luxury clothing shops boarded up their windows ahead of the protests to ward off looters.
Protests also took place in France Saturday for a third straight weekend, with clashes erupting in Paris and elsewhere.
Nationwide demonstrations there on Oct 17 degenerated into some of the country’s worst rioting in years.
Berlin has been in contact with officials in France and Italy amid fears that radicals from overseas could seek to join the German protests.
The “GenZ regelt!” movement explicitly rejected violence.
It said that “extremist groups, anti-constitutional symbols, racism and hate speech have no place with us – no matter from which side.” AFP

Hongkongers need more than 4 walls and a roof to make a home

Opinion
Hongkongers need more than 4 walls and a roof to make a home
When people stop worrying about stability and feel they belong, they go beyond being recipients of services to become part of the community
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Paul Yip is the founding director of the Centre for Suicide Research and Prevention at the University of Hong Kong, and a professor at the university's Department of Social Work and Social Administration. 
What kind of living space can truly be called a “home”? That was the question on my mind when I visited United Court, a transitional housing estate in Tung Tau, Yuen Long, run by the Hong Kong Sheng Kung Hui Welfare Council. While there, I shared my thoughts on building a mental health-friendly community.
Nine years ago, I took part in a community-based poverty study and interviewed residents in inadequate housing. I still remember families describing their living space as little more than a bed. Some people shared kitchens and toilets; interiors were dim and cramped.
When life is compressed into limited space over the long term, what suffers is rest, study, family time and the mental health we so often overlook. The mental health problems of many residents, especially young children, are closely tied to poor living environments.

Preparations underway at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan for the INDIA bloc's anti-CEC rally
NEW DELHI: Delhi is gearing up for INDIA bloc rally at Ramlila Maidan on Sunday, with opposition parties expecting a turnout of up to 10 lakh people and police deploying more than 4,000 personnel to manage security and crowds.The rally is being organised to protest against alleged electoral irregularities and demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.The mobilisation comes amid the Opposition's allegations of 'vote chori' and large-scale voter deletions during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
'Chalo Dilli' march to precede rally
The programme will begin with a march, called 'Chalo Dilli', from the Minto Road-Connaught Place junction to Ramlila Maidan at noon. The rally at the venue is scheduled to continue from 10am to 5pm.INDIA bloc leaders are expected to travel in open buses from Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge's residence to the march's starting point.The protest is expected to bring together leaders and supporters of opposition parties, along with student groups and civil society organisations.The INDIA bloc has appealed to students, youth, women and workers to participate.
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), founded by Abhijeet Dipke, and several student organisations have also extended support to the mobilisation.
4,000 cops, 200 CCTV cameras for security
While INDIA bloc leaders have projected a turnout of up to 10 lakh, Delhi Police expects around 50,000 people. Officials estimate that the ground can accommodate 45,000 to 50,000 people when empty, news agency PTI reported. With chairs, enclosures and passageways in place, its capacity is expected to fall to around 30,000 to 40,000. Additional space will be kept outside to manage any spillover.More than 4,000 police personnel, along with Central Armed Police Forces companies, will be deployed along the march route and at the venue. Ramlila Maidan has been divided into 14 security zones, each supervised by an assistant commissioner of police-rank officer.More than 200 CCTV cameras, drones and body-worn cameras will be used for surveillance. A control room has also been set up inside the ground to monitor the arrangements.
Traffic curbs across key Delhi roads
Traffic restrictions will remain in force across parts of Delhi between 10am and 5pm. Diversions are planned at major intersections, including ITO, Delhi Gate, Rajghat, Ajmeri Gate and Turkman Gate. Commuters have been advised to avoid Bahadur Shah Zafar Marg, Jawaharlal Nehru Marg, Minto Road and Desh Bandhu Gupta Road.Special arrangements will be made to ensure that ambulances and emergency vehicles can reach LNJP and GB Pant hospitals. Passengers travelling to New Delhi Railway Station have also been advised to plan their journeys in advance.Delhi Police has said permission has been granted for the rally at Ramlila Maidan, but it has not received an application for the proposed procession from the Minto Road-Connaught Place junction.
Rally follows symbolic 'public impeachment' of CEC
The rally follows a symbolic 'public impeachment' of Kumar organised by the INDIA bloc at Kharge's residence on Saturday. Former Lok Sabha Speaker Meira Kumar presided over the proceedings, while Kharge moved a resolution listing the opposition's allegations against the CEC. Rahul Gandhi delivered the concluding remarks before the resolution was adopted.Leaders of opposition parties, civil society representatives and people affected by the SIR exercise participated in the proceedings, which were modelled on parliamentary debates.The resolution accused Kumar of facilitating alleged electoral manipulation, large-scale deletion of voters and undermining the Election Commission's independence, and called for his removal.

Shared scares may bring people closer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
21:18:26 UTC
06:18:26 KST

Shared scares may bring people closer
Researchers led by Jane K. Wiley from the University of Florida conducted five studies exploring whether recreational fear strengthens relationships. Their findings suggest that feeling closer after a frightening experience does not necessarily translate into an immediate, measurable change in interpersonal closeness.
The research took place at the Gainesville Fear Garden in Florida during three Halloween seasons. Visitors experienced different attraction formats, including sensory deprivation and encounters with scare actors, according to the original paper.
Across the first four studies, participants who reported greater fear and physical contact with companions were more likely to say the attraction had brought them together. However, when researchers compared closeness ratings collected before and after the experience, the changes were consistently small or absent.
“Postexperience processing … may be critical to bonding,” the authors of the study wrote.
To investigate this gap, the team conducted a final study based on interviews. Participants’ accounts pointed to the importance of what happened after leaving the attraction, particularly retelling frightening moments, comparing reactions and laughing together.
The research team explained that collective storytelling appeared to help consolidate the social effects of shared fear.
“This collective reflection seemed to solidify and deepen the relational effects of shared fear,” the team said.
The findings help explain why visitors reported feeling closer despite little immediate change in their relationship ratings. A stronger sense of connection may develop later, as companions discuss the scares and share their reactions.
Although the study does not prove that these conversations improve relationships, it suggests that talking and laughing afterward could be an important part of what makes a shared Halloween outing a bonding experience.

Toyota and Waymo to test autonomous vehicles in Japan in 2027

Toyota and Waymo to test autonomous vehicles in Japan in 2027
Toyota Motor Corporation and autonomous driving technology company Waymo will begin testing a fleet of autonomous Toyota bZ4X vehicles in Japan in 2027 as part of their expanded partnership, the companies announced on Friday, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The initiative builds on a preliminary agreement announced in April 2025. Following the initial testing phase in Japan, the companies plan to introduce the vehicles in the United Kingdom and other markets served by Waymo in the coming years.
The partnership marks a major step towards expanding autonomous ride-hailing services in Japan using high-volume, domestically manufactured vehicles.
Toyota will manufacture the vehicles at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture. The entire process, from assembling the base vehicles to integrating Waymo’s autonomous driving hardware, will be carried out at the facility.
By combining Toyota's global manufacturing and vehicle development expertise with Waymo's fully autonomous technology, the companies aim to accelerate the global deployment of safety-validated Level 4 autonomous vehicles.
The initiative is intended to improve road safety by reducing accidents caused by human error and expanding mobility options for people who have difficulty getting around.
The specially equipped bZ4X vehicles will also feature enhanced comfort and accessibility. These include generous rear legroom, automatic doors, a power liftgate, and ambient lighting to make entering and exiting the vehicles easier for passengers.
Toyota and Waymo will also explore the application of autonomous driving technology to privately owned Toyota vehicles. Together with Woven by Toyota, they will consider further initiatives to improve road safety by applying insights from Waymo’s real-world operations, data analysis and technology to benefit other road users.

A new wave of protests has swept across France and Germany: what is known about Generation Z
Kyiv • UNN
Protests took place in France and Germany over the rising cost of living and the quality of public services. Participants are demanding more funding for education and healthcare.
On Saturday, October 31, new protests broke out in France and Germany over the rising cost of living and dissatisfaction with the quality of public services. This was reported by Reuters, according to UNN.
Details
According to media reports, French authorities deployed 70,000 security personnel to maintain order, while demonstrations in Germany were organized in 34 cities.
The protesters are demanding that their governments increase funding for education and healthcare, reduce the cost of living, ensure a fairer distribution of public spending, and abandon compulsory military service.
Some journalists have already dubbed the protests spreading across European countries the "Generation Z protests." This generation includes people born between the mid-1990s and 2012.
What is known about Generation Z
This is the first generation to grow up with constant access to the internet, smartphones, and social media from childhood. These people easily adapt to new technologies and actively set their own rules in the modern world.
Context
In a number of European countries, mass protests erupted over the rising cost of living, high energy prices, unaffordable housing, and insufficient funding for public services. Demonstrations took place in France, Italy, Spain, Belgium, Portugal, and other countries. Some of the protests escalated into clashes with police, while trade unions have already announced new strikes for November.

CGHS cover for dependent widowed, divorced daughters after parents' death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
21:02:47 UTC
06:02:47 KST

Widowed and divorced daughters returning to live with parents can now be added to their parents' Central Govt Health Scheme (CGHS) cards, even after the death of the govt employee or pensioner in whose name the original card was issued. Health ministry has allowed eligible daughters to be added or reinstated in cards held by family pensioners.
The move will help parents supporting daughters with no independent income who need medical care. Earlier, once the original cardholder died and the spouse began receiving family pension, there was no provision to add or reinstate dependent family members.
The ministry said it had received representations from pensioners facing difficulties supporting such daughters, particularly those with serious medical conditions requiring continued treatment. The benefit will not be automatic: authorities will verify daughter's marital status, income and dependency.
All other CGHS eligibility conditions will continue to apply, the Oct 28 order said. It has been circulated to all central govt ministries and departments and DG of CGHS.

Addressing the Rashtriya Ekta Diwas parade - organised annually on the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel - Modi recalled how Sardar Patel and BR Ambedkar had, while framing the Constitution, clearly laid down duties and roles of govt and opposition.
"Opposition is exercising politics of 'obstruction', in complete disregard of constitutional boundaries and propriety," he added.Warning against divisive forces that have come out in the open after more than a decade of political frustration to plot conspiracies, pit citizens against one another, and weaponise social media to spread rumours and tarnish India's image, the PM urged citizens to recognise the patterns of such forces conducting secret foreign meetings, their external backing by anti-India elements, and their rhetoric echoing the nation's enemies. "We have ended Naxalism in remote areas, but the threat from ideological extremists (dimagi Naxals) is not yet over, and the country has to remain ever vigilant against such entities," he cautioned.Stressing that the grand mission of national unity and the journey toward a strong and capable India must continue regardless of difficulties, the PM outlined the next major national priorities of fully securing India's borders, putting an end to infiltration and resulting demographic changes, and advancing toward a secular civil code. Acknowledging that major resolutions and bold decisions will inevitably face roadblocks and storms, he declared that the nation will not be deterred from the unwavering resolves of 'Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat' and a 'Viksit Bharat', working tirelessly with every breath and heartbeat toward the 2047 goal of a strong and capable India.
Bharti Jain is senior editor with The Times of India, New Delhi. She has been writing on security matters since 1996. Having covered the Union home ministry, security agencies, Election Commission and the ‘prime’ political beat, the Congress, for The Economic Times all these years, she moved to TOI in August 2012. Her repertoire of news stories delves into the whole gamut of issues related to terrorism and internal strife, besides probing strategic affairs in India’s neighbourhood.

Strategy, succession planning needed for Australia after Cape Town collapse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
20:46:49 UTC
05:46:49 KST

Fans of cricketing omens were treated to a masterful piece of psychological theatre before play on the final day of the Cape Town Test.
A week shy of 15 years since he rolled Australia for 47 at the same venue, former South African fast bowling genius Vernon Philander accompanied Proteas coach Shukri Conrad to the middle of Newlands and helped choose the ball to be used on the final day of this thrilling Test series.
Barely half an hour into play, Philander's most gifted successor, Kagiso Rabada, had used it to remove three of Australia's top order. With that, the game and Australia's fading hopes of winning the series were already dead and buried.
Chasing 288, which was always a huge ask, Australia buckled to be all out for 111, having earlier looked like securing its second sub-100 score in as many Tests.
The last Australian team to suffer that indignity at least had the good sense of doing it before the invention of television.
Whatever meagre sense of respectability Nathan Lyon and Pat Cummins restored with a 45-run partnership for the ninth wicket was cancelled out by the emphatic confirmation that Cummins had erred unaccountably by electing to bowl on day one and setting the stage for the impossible chase this one proved to be.
Proteas off-spinner Simon Harmer, who had quite boldly put Cummins on notice before this Test, spun his side to victory with 6-16 from 22 overs of wizardry.
Yet for all the bravado and posturing in this series, it was Harmer's lack of words, and his fighting back of tears when he picked up the man-of-the-match award, that best explained what this triumph means to South Africa.
There will be earnest post-mortems conducted to figure out where else Australia went wrong on this tour. The national selection panel should be interrogated first, and at length, yet so should several experienced batsmen who batted brainlessly at the critical moments that consigned Australia to a 2-1 series loss.
As most astute judges foretold, poor Marnus Labuschagne flubbed what will surely be his final chance at Test level. From the sixth delivery of a frantic day, the dejected Queenslander was trapped in front by Rabada and burned one final DRS review before trudging off with the weight of the world on his shoulders.
Still, we should not flatter Australia so much as to think of their miscalculations and mistakes as the most decisive factors in the resolution of this brilliant Test series.
Brimming with world-beating talent and self-belief, South Africa was simply better organised and better performed in almost every facet of the game.
So many of its players — Marco Jansen and Temba Bavuma in the second Test, Harmer, Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder in this one — can now say they produced career-defining performances when it mattered most. Would a single Australian?
Perhaps it was inevitable that Rabada would do something special after missing out in the first innings, when illness shrunk his powers.
But Harmer, whose performance was the most anticipated factor in the final day of the series, was the one who really played out of his skin.
His spell of 3-5 from eight spellbinding overs before lunch left Australia a Philander-esque 7-60, and the other wicket to have fallen at that point was also his in spirit: desperate to get off strike, Cameron Green called for a quick single that was not there and barbecued Josh Inglis.
Green hung around for 110 deliveries either side of lunch, but Harmer got him too with a raging turner that zipped through the gate.
Some tough and maybe unpopular decisions now await Australian cricket — not knee-jerk reactions to public outcry, and not wholesale personnel changes for now.
But there are matters of strategy and succession planning far more complicated than Marnus's sad slump into redundancy.
The world-class bowling attack which has papered over the cracks in Australia's batting line-up for several years will be, by the end of the coming Australian Test summer, aged 39, 37, 36, and 33, with a 37-year-old its best backup.
No matter how entitled each feels to his spot, and no matter how much career statistics and public sentiment justify that entitlement, some form of attrition is inevitable. Longer-term replacements urgently require game time in Tests, not cordial-mixing duties.
Cummins, who has the most left in the tank, and Lyon, perhaps the least, will be the unhappiest with their returns in this series — just six wickets each, at a cost of 54 apiece for Cummins and 43 for Lyon.
And it is hard to imagine South Africa picking someone to bowl a combined total of 25 overs in two Tests and bat at seven, as Australia did with Beau Webster.
It is not all doom and gloom, of course, and even in this game there were some positive glimpses into the post-Labuschagne, post-Smith era.
Matt Renshaw, streets ahead as the batsman of the series with 369 runs at 61.50, is a lock at the top of the order beside Travis Head. Proven performers now, Green and Inglis should be backed to succeed.
That leaves the number three and six slots to fill, with common sense suggesting Alex Carey needs to return to batting at seven.
That three has been made to appear such a fiendish problem is at odds with the solutions staring selectors in the face. Even in the era of "false threes", it is anathema to the history of the Australian Test team to pick anyone other than a top-order specialist in that crucial slot.
Steve Smith, if his appetite for a big finale remains, may need to be told it is his duty. If he or Australia decide it is time to move on, Kurtis Patterson is a mature and proven option who makes as much sense as Renshaw did for this tour.
As for six, it is a little early to tell exactly what, and how good, Cooper Connolly will be. But for generations it has been a spot that tends to be filled by a youthful player of promise and Connolly is both of those things.
Whichever way Australia goes with the above decisions, it is probably time that a coherent rationale for Test selection is more clearly communicated to contenders and even the public, because nobody who emotionally invests in Australian cricket is buying the strange stories George Bailey has been telling in recent times.
With all that, Australia now drops to third in the ICC Test rankings and New Zealand, who it faces in a Test series starting in 38 days, rises to the top.
If the Black Caps have prepared themselves for their challenge as diligently as South Africa did in this series, there will be plenty more difficult days ahead for Australia.

NEW DELHI: Paying rich tributes to Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel on his 151st birth anniversary, defence minister Rajnath Singh on Saturday recalled how the ‘Iron Man of India’ firmly dealt with the Nizam and Razakars, who sought to challenge India’s sovereignty and “laid the foundation of a strong and united India”. On the issue of Kashmir, Rajnath said, “Sardar Patel himself had said that if Pandit Nehru had not intervened, he would have integrated Kashmir as easily as Hyderabad.”Addressing a gathering, the defence minister said, “Sardar Patel was the architect of India’s political and territorial unity, whose extraordinary leadership, courage and unwavering commitment to national interest laid the foundation of a strong and united India”.He further said, “In democracy, govts are formed by winning the trust of the people and on the basis of public opinion, not through violence and anarchy. The path to change of power is elections, not coups. Those who challenge the unity and integrity of India should not forget the history of Sardar Patel.” “Those who dream of weakening India or creating disorder must remember that the land which gave birth to Sardar Patel has also given birth to Narendra Modi,” the minister said.

He emphasised that ‘regime change’ essentially implies a coup, violence, anarchy and civil war.Rajnath said that Sardar Patel firmly believed that India should never seek what does not belong to it, but should never give up what rightfully belongs to it, under any circumstances. He said that India continues to move forward guided by this very principle. “India does not seek to occupy anyone else's territory, nor does it initiate conflict. However, it remains resolute in securing what rightfully belongs to it and safeguarding its national interests.”He further asserted that whether it is avenging terrorist attacks or reclaiming Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (POK), India remains firmly committed to defending its rights and sovereignty.Recalling the events surrounding the Congress presidential election of 1946, the minister said that despite overwhelming support from provincial Congress committees, Sardar Patel withdrew his candidature in deference to Mahatma Gandhi's wishes. “For Sardar Patel, the country was always bigger than the chair. He also referred to the contrast between the celebrations of Jawaharlal Nehru's birth centenary in 1989 and the relatively subdued observance of Sardar Patel's birth centenary in 1975. He credited PM Modi with restoring national recognition to Patel's legacy through the Statue of Unity, Rashtriya Ekta Diwas, Run for Unity and Ekta March. “Sardar Patel was a great leader in his own right. Honouring him has not made him any greater; rather, it has brought greater honour to India.”
Highlighting Sardar Patel's emphasis on military modernisation and indigenous production of weapons and ammunition, Rajnath said that India's growing defence manufacturing capabilities reflect the spirit of self-reliance that Patel advocated. He said that Sardar Patel's legacy extends far beyond the integration of princely states. It is reflected in India's strong administrative institutions, national security, social harmony and commitment to national interest. He said that the vision of 'Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat' and the mission of building a Viksit Bharat are inspired by the ideals that Sardar Patel upheld throughout his life.“India's greatest strength lies in its unity. We must never allow internal differences to weaken our national resolve. Preserving India's unity and integrity is the responsibility of every citizen,” he said.

Trump has not decided on new Iran strikes – Rubio
US President Donald Trump has made no decision whether to strike Iran again, even though peace talks remain stalled, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday.
“We can achieve military objectives if we seek to,” Rubio told reporters at a press conference in Atlanta, Georgia, where he was hosting G20 foreign ministers for a two-day meeting.
However, he stressed that Trump “hasn’t made a decision” on further military action, amid reports that Washington could resume strikes after Tuesday’s US midterm elections.
“I have no announcement in that regard with you today, and nor do we take any of it lightly,” Rubio said.
The secretary accused Tehran of “actively and openly” targeting commercial vessels but emphasized that Trump preferred a diplomatic solution. He declined to assess the progress of negotiations or provide a timeline for a possible agreement.
“I’m not going to characterize neither the progress on those talks nor any time frame on it, other than to tell you that if there is a diplomatic solution, we would be open to it,” Rubio said.
His remarks came as Iranian negotiators held talks with Qatari mediators in Doha on Saturday in an effort to prevent renewed hostilities, Reuters reported, citing a source familiar with the discussions.
The meeting followed more than 12 hours of negotiations between Iranian and Qatari officials in Tehran on Friday. According to the source, the diplomatic efforts were being coordinated through regular contacts with Washington.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al Jazeera on Saturday that Tehran had reviewed a letter from US Vice President J.D. Vance, and described Washington’s attempt to reopen dialogue as a “positive step.”
“My aide is currently in Qatar to continue consultations,” Araghchi said, confirming that an Iranian delegation was participating in the mediation efforts.

According to Reuters, Qatar has proposed a seven-day plan involving reciprocal confidence-building measures by Washington and Tehran ahead of broader peace negotiations. Iranian officials reportedly find the proposal unsatisfactory.
Tehran has instead advocated its own plan, which would require Washington to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, unfreeze assets, and approve an Iranian-backed shipping arrangement through the Strait of Hormuz before the strategic waterway can be reopened.
Meanwhile, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned Washington and Israel against launching further attacks, ordering the country’s armed forces to prepare for an immediate response.
In a statement published on Saturday by his office, Khamenei required “maximum deterrence” through preparedness for “an immediate and effective response, without geographical restriction” if the country is attacked again.
Trump, who alongside Israel launched the military campaign against Iran in February, has repeatedly suggested that Washington could resume strikes. He recently said he was considering whether to “finish them off,” fueling speculation about renewed military action after the US midterm elections.

Judge dismisses Trump lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein birthday letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
20:31:39 UTC
05:31:39 KST

A US judge dismissed Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal with prejudice on Saturday, according to a court filing, bringing an end to his legal challenge over the newspaper’s reporting on his alleged birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein.
The decision follows an earlier dismissal in April that had allowed Trump to revise his complaint. As of Saturday, the case is dismissed with prejudice, meaning the lawsuit cannot be amended or refiled.
The case stemmed from a Wall Street Journal article alleging that Trump had sent a “bawdy” letter to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein in 2003. Trump denied the letter was real, insisting instead it had been fabricated.
Throughout the proceedings, the court repeatedly pointed to the newspaper’s efforts to obtain Trump’s response before publication and its inclusion of his direct denials as evidence that it had followed appropriate reporting standards.
Judge Darrin P Gayles issued the final dismissal on Saturday after determining that Trump’s amended complaint still failed to establish “actual malice”, the high legal threshold public figures must meet when pursuing defamation claims.
“As President Trump has not plausibly alleged that each Defendant made defamatory statements with actual malice, the Amended Complaint must be dismissed,” the ruling said. “And because this is President Trump’s second attempt to allege his claims, the Court finds that dismissal with prejudice is appropriate.”
Trump, who has frequently pursued legal action against media organizations both during and outside his time in the White House, has maintained that the lewd drawing described in the Journal’s report was fake.
A spokesperson for Trump’s legal team shared a statement following the ruling: “President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants. The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions.”
A Dow Jones spokesperson said: “We’re pleased with the court’s decision.”
Representatives for the Journal had asked the judge to dismiss the claim, arguing that the story was accurate and that it did not meet the bar for defamation. They argued that the reporters had neither knowingly published false information nor proceeded with the belief that the material was likely to be false.
The lawsuit attracted particular attention because it named Rupert Murdoch, one of Trump’s most prominent media allies, among the defendants. Murdoch’s News Corporation media empire owns the Journal. Before the article was published on 17 July 2025, Trump personally contacted Murdoch in an effort to stop its publication.
The report was published under the headline “Jeffrey Epstein’s Friends Sent Him Bawdy Letters for a 50th Birthday Album. One Was From Donald Trump.”
The Journal did not originally publish the image, though it was released by the House oversight committee in September after it was provided by Epstein’s estate.

The Suns started their rebuild when half their roster were just kids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
20:27:22 UTC
05:27:22 KST

Fri, 30 Oct, 7:15 pm, Final score, Cats 88, Bulldogs 20
analysis
Gold Coast Suns had headstart on AFLW rebuild before half of their players even turned 18
Gold Coast finished on the bottom of the AFLW ladder in 2025.
It was the first season under new head coach Rhyce Shaw and it could have seemed like a terrible place for him to start.
The club was giving up the most points per game in history, 64.3, and losing by a record 37.8 points across the course of the season.
But this was all by design, for the Suns knew exactly what sort of talent was going to land on their doorstep via the draft in December, with a third of the list transformed in just one night.
So, the shift in game plan started before they even arrived, fast-tracking their impact in a big way.
The shift bore some startlingly poor results, but it was all for the greater good of propelling the Suns to their third-ever finals series just 12 months later.
Moving away from the contest
For the bulk of their time in the AFLW, the Suns have been synonymous with hard, contested footy, rolling mauls and dour games. Picture Charlie Rowbottom with ball in hand with three players hanging off her.
It bore low-scoring, scrappy affairs where the side relied on resetting games by creating repeat stoppages.
For this reason, the average score the Suns were conceding from turnover in 2024, their last season under Cam Joyce, seemed reasonable at 27.2 points per game, but they were also giving up nearly four goals per game from stoppage.
Essentially, by minimising the opposition's chance to score from live play, they created more opportunities for teams to get busy out of stoppage.
In an effort to shift away from a stoppage-heavy, contested game style, Shaw needed to be willing to go backwards on the scoreboard to benefit in the long run.
They moved to a more controlled game style in 2025, to varying effect on the given day, and focused more on a kick-mark game and valued uncontested possession.
Teaching those who were going to be around for the long haul how to effectively move from inside the contest to outside transition was always going to be crucial when integrating the likes of Sunny Lappin, Mikayla Nurse, Ava Usher and Dekota Baron in 2026.
To get the most out of these star teenagers, existing players needed to know how to best engage them.
But the growing pains of establishing this change meant they were badly hurt when they turned the ball over, giving up an average of 42.1 points from the source throughout 2025. This is what saw their points against balloon out to record numbers.
Throughout that 2025 season, the Suns also gave up 40.7 inside 50s per game, as well as 9.6 marks inside 50, and 23.2 shots on goal, all unwanted club records. But it all came from that desire to be productive in attack themselves.
Their contested possession rate was dropping, their average metres gained were up, and it might have been small flashes of evidence that they were tracking the right way, but Shaw stuck fat because he knew that a host of talented kids were going to take this game plan and run with it.
Learning to score
Although Gold Coast's average score dropped from 28.3 to 26.6 from 2024 to 2025, the side actually kicked scores of 30 or more points five times last year, compared to just three the year prior. So, it was becoming marginally less consistent, but those stronger attacking performances, helped along by the addition of Havana Harris, were popping up more regularly.
There have been six occurrences in AFLW history of a club averaging a losing margin of 30 or more points, but of those six occurrences, the Suns last year averaged the highest score themselves. Another piece of evidence that the focus on attack was in fact working, it was just about improving that movement through the middle of the ground to really get things going their way.
In 2024, just two Suns, Tara Bohanna (nine goals) and Jac Dupuy (eight), kicked five or more goals across the season. Last year, there were three: Harris in her first season (11 goals), Dupuy (seven) and Jamie Stanton (six).
Of those players, just one has played games for the club this year: Harris. Bohanna moved to Carlton for the 2025 season, Dupuy arrived at Hawthorn this year, and Stanton has been unable to break into the side, and has since announced her retirement.
This year, six Suns have kicked five or more goals, while 11 different players have kicked multiple goals. Harris still leads the way with 18, but Usher (11), Anne Hatchard, Alannah Welsh, Lappin (all eight), and Baron (six) have been busy up forward. Harris is the only one who was at the club last year.
But without the clear intention to move into more of a live-play style of footy, which creates greater opportunity to score, it's unlikely these players would have had so many chances to get busy in attack.
Now, Gold Coast is averaging the highest score in its history (49.7 points per game), from the most inside 50s it has ever generated (37.9).
Attacking is the best defence
By way of controlling the ball more effectively once outside of stoppage, and retaining the ball inside 50 once in the zone, Gold Coast's defensive performance has tightened up significantly. The return of classy halfback Daisy D'Arcy and addition of key defender Georja Davies has also contributed to the strengthening line.
This year the Suns are giving up the third fewest inside 50s in the AFLW, and conceding the fifth-fewest points. A far cry from the record-breaking points teams were putting on them last year.
It has been a masterclass in redeveloping a side at speed. Granted, Gold Coast had an advantage very few sides across history have had: the knowledge and understanding of who is going to be added to their list in the coming year.
But it required the bravery for things to get worse before they were going to get better. They survived the worse, and now celebrate the better with a final on the horizon, and a chance of reaching the top four still live depending on results across the last round of the home-and-away season.

Nandan Nilekani-led task force gets extension till January 2027 as exam reforms, including a possible hybrid NEET-UG format, are reviewed
NEW DELHI: Centre has extended the tenure of the Nandan Nilekani-led task force on examination reforms till Jan 2027, with the prime minister's office (PMO) seeking consultations with chief ministers and chief secretaries before the panel finalises its recommendations, TOI has learnt from govt officials. During consultations, some stakeholders and experts have also suggested a hybrid format for NEET-UG 2027, allowing time to expand infrastructure for a complete shift to computer-based testing (CBT) in 2028.A govt official said the PMO wants the task force, earlier expected to submit its report by Oct-end, to seek views from state leadership on challenges particular to different regions. The aim, the source said, is to better understand disparities in testing infrastructure, connectivity and administrative preparedness, and reflect these state-specific concerns in a more comprehensive examination reform roadmap.Another proposal likely to feature in the task force's recommendations is a nationwide network of CBT centres developed by Centre and state govts with private investment, sources said. Such a model could expand govt oversight of testing facilities while mobilising private capital to build infrastructure, particularly in districts that lack secure, adequately equipped centres. The funding, ownership and operating arrangements would need to be worked out.
Such centres could support common security standards, reliable connectivity and better access for candidates outside metros.TOI had earlier reported that the task force is prioritising "debundling" examination responsibilities. Under the proposed restructuring, question-paper setting, conduct of exams, management of test centres and security would be assigned to separate agencies instead of being concentrated with a single operator.The objective is to create clearer lines of accountability and limit the risk of a lapse in one part of the examination process affecting the entire exercise. The approach would, however, require coordination between the agencies handling different stages.
The panel is also considering exam centres in every district and a common calendar for National Testing Agency (NTA), Staff Selection Commission (SSC), Institute of Banking Personnel Selection (IBPS) and Railway Recruitment Boards (RRBs). Coordinated schedules could help students and job applicants avoid exam-date clashes and allow testing infrastructure to be used more efficiently.The six-member task force was constituted in July following the NEET-UG 2026 controversy, which led to the cancellation of the original exam and a retest. It has held 18 internal meetings and around 40 consultations, in addition to seeking public suggestions.An Oct parliamentary committee report also recommended secure govt-controlled testing centres across districts and a phased transition to CBT for NEET-UG. The extension gives the task force more time to assess the feasibility of its proposals with states.

Poland crisis: Donald Tusk strikes defiant tone vowing ‘no compromise’ on rule of law after Tribunal clash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
20:14:46 UTC
05:14:46 KST

Tusk addressed the nation as tensions over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal escalated, accusing PiS and President Nawrocki of undermining the rule of law and pledging support for the newly elected judges and the court’s work.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk addressed Poland’s deepening Constitutional Tribunal crisis in a televised speech on Saturday evening, vowing that the rule of law would prevail over violence as tensions over the country's judiciary reach boiling point.
The dispute over the composition of Poland’s top court has fuelled an open confrontation with President Karol Nawrocki, who attempted to enter the Tribunal building amid a deadlock over the appointment of new judges on Friday night.
Police surrounded the building as the confrontation unfolded live on television, drawing attention to the crisis beyond Poland and into the wider European political debate.
The opposition has accused Tusk’s government of attempting a coup, while the government says it is pushing ahead with long-needed reforms to restore the rule of law after years of PiS interference in the judiciary.
In his address to the nation, Tusk described Friday’s events as “scandalous incidents” and said he hoped such scenes would never be repeated in Poland. He added that restoring calm could not mean accepting lawlessness or violence.
“A democratic state has to be strong and capable of enforcing justice,” he said.
The dispute over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal dates back to 2015, when the governing Civic Platform and opposition Law and Justice parties clashed over the appointment of five judges. It has since developed into a wider conflict over judicial independence, the Tribunal’s composition and the authority of its rulings.
Dispute over control of the judiciary
Tusk said his government had tried to resolve the crisis, but its proposals were blocked by PiS and the president, further deepening the dispute.
He said the parliamentary majority then waited for the terms of judges appointed under the previous PiS-led government to expire in an effort to avoid a confrontation.
“We waited calmly for new judges to be chosen, until the terms of their predecessors appointed by PiS expired. The Sejm made its choice, the judges took the oath, but the president did not deign to receive that oath,” Tusk said.
The Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, elected the new judges, who took their oaths of office. Nawrocki did not formally receive the oaths, while Tribunal President Bogdan Święczkowski refused to allow the new judges to take up their duties.
Tusk described the newly elected judges as legally appointed and said they had been attacked. He also criticised politicians and activists linked to PiS and the far-right Confederation party over their conduct during the confrontation.
He compared the dispute to a thief stealing an elderly woman’s handbag and then accusing others of violence when they try to recover it.
“In certain matters there can be no compromise,” he said, adding that lawlessness could not be negotiated away.
Physical force, aggression and party interests must not determine who is right in a state governed by the rule of law, he added.
Tusk also said no politician, including the president, had the right to enter a court or tribunal, issue instructions to judges or intimidate them. He was referring to Nawrocki’s visit to the Tribunal building after turning his plane around while travelling to Senegal.
Tusk warns against playing into Russia’s hands
Tusk warned that pro-Russian groups could exploit the political conflict.
He pointed to Russian bots operating online which, in his assessment, were supporting opponents of Poland’s current constitutional order.
He said the Constitutional Tribunal would operate in accordance with the constitution and independently of the executive.
As head of government, Tusk pledged to provide the institution with the security and conditions needed to carry out its duties.
“And I intend to fulfil this task,” he said.
However, the speech offered no concrete agreement with Nawrocki or detailed plan to resolve the dispute.

Ukraine’s military leadership shake-up: two new Donbas and Center commands, fewer reports — but gaps remain, commander says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
20:07:09 UTC
05:07:09 KST

Ukraine's army is loosening the reins, with its new commander-in-chief thinning the stream of reports he demands, though the general overhaul is still only partial. That is how Yurii Butusov, a front-line drone-company commander, describes the changes under Mykhailo Drapatyi in an interview with Apostrophe TV.
In July 2026, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy replaced former Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi with Drapatyi. Butusov says the new arrangement has improved control on Donbas but has not yet reached other hard-pressed sectors.
From "manual mode" to a divided chain of command
Under Syrskyi, Butusov said, the command system was centralized, with the commander-in-chief holding full authority and serving as the sole decision-making authority.
"A manual mode of controlling every unit," he called it.
Syrskyi, by his account, followed the front down to individual companies, battalions and brigades, and could hand tasks directly to small units. Under Drapatyi, Butusov said, that has begun to change.
"For now Mykhailo Drapatyi does not yet have the full scope of authority. Perhaps this is just temporary. The command system now consists of the following: Ihor Skybiuk, the commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces and the chief of the General Staff," Butusov said.
They have their own spheres of authority and their own views on various problems.
He suggested the arrangement could be temporary or could become the basis of the army's future command structure.
Fewer reports, two new Donbas commands, and the gaps left behind
Among the concrete changes, Butusov pointed to the scrapping of the twice-daily reports that corps and other large-formation commanders had been required to make to the commander-in-chief.
Drapatyi has also created two troop groupings on Donbas, "Center" and "Azov," which Butusov said have markedly improved control of the force and the division of responsibility there. The redesign, though, is uneven.
"But these changes are fragmentary. For example, in the Kharkiv Oblast a troop grouping has still not been created," Butusov added.

What Counts as Evidence for AI Consciousness?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
20:05:54 UTC
05:05:54 KST

Thanks to for taking the time to read my work. I’ll just write a short response to the key areas of disagreement, including clarifications to my position.
My use of the word ‘organic’ was problematic and that article could have been better written. Here is the core of my view on AI consciousness:
My view is a methodological position. I am not arguing that biology is necessary for consciousness. I am arguing that extending an account of consciousness that was developed for a biological system to a non-biological system requires justification.
My reasons for this are two-fold. First, when we explain consciousness in biological systems, we are assuming that consciousness exists in those systems and then offering our best description of that system in an effort to explain it. It does not follow from this that establishing a similarly adequate description in a non-biological system allows us to assume that consciousness exists in that system. The very thing we assume in the case of human consciousness —namely, that humans are conscious— is precisely what’s at issue in the non-biological case.
Second, regarding today’s theories of consciousness, an account of consciousness may successfully describe (assuming the accounts are correct for the sake of argument) processes involved in human consciousness, without establishing that those processes, described at a computational level of description, are sufficient for consciousness in any system that implements those processes. That’s a further claim requiring justification. That’s one way of describing my core objection.
Assuming this stance of mine, let’s look at some of ’s arguments for AI consciousness. He appeals to leading theories of consciousness and successful computational explanations as evidence for AI consciousness.
My question is: which theories and what justifies their application to AI systems?
Evidence from theories of consciousness supporting predictions about human consciousness is not, by itself, justification for extending those to non-biological systems. The same applies for computational explanation more broadly — and this is something I’ve written about across several articles — we need to distinguish the usefulness of computational approaches generally, from the further claim that implementing this organisation in non-biological systems is sufficient to suggest AI consciousness.
Re my other minds essay: this essay dealt with a particular argument from one particular paper. The argument was that refusing to attribute consciousness to AIs that have indistinguishable behaviours from humans undermines our ability to attribute consciousness to humans. I offered reasons for rejecting that particular claim. is right that the paper does not establish that AI isnt conscious. That was not the purpose of the article.
Re the point about uncertainty around AI consciousness, argues that if the reasons for supporting biological naturalism and computational functionalism are equal, then our confidence for both views should be the same.
Even granting the conditional, he hasn’t established that the reasons are equal (I don’t think that they are).
Separately, he claims that the uncertainty around AI consciousness coupled with the sophisticated behavior of LLMs suggests consciousness is reasonably likely.
I don’t agree. Uncertainty alone doesn’t establish that likelihood, and I don’t agree with the evidential weight assigned to LLM ‘behaviour. We need to ask what the term ‘behaviour’ is really tracking and whether it does in fact count as evidence towards AI consciousness.
A relevant point is raised by Yunze Xiao and colleagues who argue that proposed welfare indicators for LLMs are heavily shaped by the systems training: we can suppress or amplify apparent signs of distress or other potential AI-welfare signals, without those indicators tracking whether the outputs reflect experience. This gives us reason to question the weight we can assign to LLM outputs as significant evidence for consciousness in LLMs.
Re my newsletter’s name, I am confident that present AI systems aren’t conscious, without being certain, nor should it be confused with the claim that I have disproved that AI is conscious.

"Monthly rainfall for Nov over the south Peninsular India, consisting of Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Karaikkal, coastal Andhra Pradesh and Rayalaseema region, Kerala, Mahe and south interior Karnataka, is most likely to be 'below normal' (less than 77% of the long period average)," said IMD chief Mrutyunjay Mohapatra while releasing the monthly outlook for rainfall and temperature for Nov.The long period average of rainfall over south Peninsular India during Nov, based on data from 1971 to 2020, is 118.7 mm. Quick hits: Marnus's career on the brink, Warner aims cutting lunch-time spray
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

05:03:11 KST

David Warner labels his former teammates "disgraceful" and Marnus Labuschagne's career crisis continues to spiral as Australia endures a horror end to its tour of South Africa.
Here are the quick hits from day five of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. Marnus on the brink after horror start for Aussies
It was the first over from hell for the Aussies, and one in which Marnus Labuschagne must have surely seen his Test career flash before his eyes.
All it took was three balls, and the tourists, chasing 288 at the beginning of day five, were one down.
Matt Renshaw, the hero from Durban, was out for a golden duck after a leg-side strangulation, with Proteas spearhead Kagiso Rabada only just beginning to find his groove.
Walking to the middle with his place in the team long under the microscope, the stage was set for Labuschagne's long-awaited innings of redemption.
He found his way off a pair courtesy of a streaky boundary through gully, but a massive lapse in judgement spelled disaster for the Queenslander.
Labuschagne was given out LBW after shouldering arms to a ball that nipped back and thudded into pad, with his review futile in providing life support to a Test career so desperately struggling for air.
It has now been 49 innings and well over three years since his last Test ton.
Australia, remarkably, was 2-5 after six balls.
2. Green barbecues Inglis
Just when it felt like it could not get any worse for Australia, it did.
Having joined Cam Green in the middle after Travis Head had become Rabada's third victim, Josh Inglis, fresh from his century on day three, was 4 from 17 deliveries when Green called him through for a single that was never there.
The towering all-rounder had set off after doing little more than pat the ball into the off-side, meaning Marques Ackerman could race around from silly point, collect the ball, and fire it into Ryan Rickelton behind the stumps.
The bails were dislodged with Inglis helplessly short of his ground, the horror mix-up only appropriate after the first hour that was.
3. Reverse does for Carey in Harmer double strike
Alex Carey has a complicated relationship with the reverse sweep. He clearly likes playing it, but it has often been his downfall.
So, with his side 4-42 on the deciding day of the series, and with the Newlands pitch turning sideways, it perhaps wasn't the time to bring out the cross-bat special.
But facing finger spinner Simon Harmer, Carey just couldn't help himself.
Down on his haunches, his top edge was gobbled up by a diving Marco Jansen, and the wicketkeeper-batter was out for 2.
In at No.7 and playing his second Test, Cooper Connolly never stood a chance.
The 23-year-old was dismissed just two balls later, done by flight and spin, edging behind to Rickelton while attempting a booming drive, leaving the Aussies deep in the mire.
4. Ex-players fume at day five disaster
As Australia went to lunch at 6-70, the recriminations were already in full swing.
On commentary for ABC Sport, former Australia fast bowler Jason Gillespie was close to speechless.
In the Fox Cricket Studio, former Australia opener David Warner wasn't.
"It's un-Australian. There is no fight whatsoever, it's disgraceful," said a fuming Warner.
"The batters have let the bowlers down all series.
"Yes, Matt Renshaw showed fight in that first Test, but I think the batters have been disgraceful, utterly disgraceful."
As we returned for the second session, ex-Australia batter Phil Jaques was still attempting to come to terms with what he had witnessed.
"Words can't describe how disappointing it is for Test cricket today," Jaques said on commentary for ABC Sport.
"I bounced out of bed this morning hoping for a really good day of cricket … and then Australia today just didn't show up.
"They've been found wanting on numerous occasions … it's just been pretty poor from Australia, to be honest, and really deflating as a cricket fan."
5. Aussies go 78 deliveries without scoring
With the result no longer in doubt heading into the second session, Australia changed tact.
Pat Cummins came out alongside Green following the lunch break and was determined to bat time, rather than score runs.
After Green had farmed the strike earlier in the day with Mitchell Starc, protecting him from the pace of Gerald Coetzee, he did the same with Cummins.
They turned the Test into a waiting game and had some success until Harmer, in the middle of a miserly spell, switched ends and threw a spanner in the works by ripping an off break through Green's defences and into his off stump.
Cummins was then joined by Nathan Lyon and finally scored his first run, ending a streak of 78 dot balls and receiving Bronx cheers from those in the stands at Newlands.
It was an embarrassing final nail in the Australian coffin near the end of an embarrassing day for a proud team.
