A policy-focused TikTok improved opinions of Kamala Harris, but trendier campaign clips did not, experiment finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
20:00:05 UTC
05:00:05 KST

A recent study evaluating political TikTok videos found that traditional, policy-focused campaign ads improved voter favorability toward Vice President Kamala Harris, while trendy, short-form clips had a more limited impact. The research, published in Political Research Quarterly, highlights how short-form video platforms influence political attitudes but struggle to overcome entrenched biases. These findings suggest that while social media can mobilize certain voters, it may not easily persuade those outside a candidate’s existing base.
In the months leading up to the 2024 presidential election, political campaigns heavily invested in digital spaces to reach younger audiences. The Harris campaign notably focused on TikTok, a platform where users share short-form videos that generally run around 60 to 90 seconds. Social media allows candidates to bypass traditional news outlets and speak directly to voters. However, political scientists are still working to understand exactly how these short, algorithmic video feeds affect voter opinions.
Past research has established that voters often evaluate Black women politicians differently than other candidates. Black women in public office frequently navigate overlapping layers of racial and gender biases. Some voters hold negative views rooted in racial resentment or modern sexism. These biases can shape how people interpret a candidate’s tone, sometimes causing them to view a Black woman as aggressive when she uses standard political attacks.
Other psychological and behavioral concepts also play a role in how voters consume political media. Negative partisanship occurs when a voter’s behavior is driven more by a strong dislike of the opposing political party than by an affection for their own party. Attack advertisements frequently rely on this dynamic by tearing down an opponent rather than offering positive solutions. Outrage discourse involves speech that is inflammatory or misleading, often aimed at stoking fear or anger in its audience.
Campaigns also sometimes use implicit or explicit racial language to mobilize specific voting blocs. While this can activate support among targeted groups, political scientists debate whether explicit appeals risk alienating moderate voters. The concept of intersectionality helps explain how overlapping identities, such as race and gender, create unique political environments for candidates.
To investigate how different types of short-form videos perform in this environment, political scientists Sydney Carr-Glenn of the College of the Holy Cross, Chaya Crowder of Loyola Marymount University, and Christine Slaughter of Boston University designed a targeted experiment. They aimed to test whether exposure to specific messaging frames on TikTok could alter a voter’s opinion of Harris. The researchers focused on the abbreviated timeline of the 2024 race to capture immediate digital reactions.
The researchers recruited approximately 1,200 participants through an online survey platform during the early voting period in November 2024. The sample was matched to national demographics, though the researchers included extra Black participants to ensure they could properly analyze responses within that demographic group. Each participant was randomly assigned to watch one of five short videos. They viewed the content outside of the actual TikTok application, simulating the experience of having a video texted to them by a friend.
One group served as a control and watched a 13-second, nonpolitical video of teenagers dancing to an Eminem song. The other participants viewed actual TikToks posted by the official Harris campaign account. These four political videos represented different messaging strategies.
The first campaign video focused on policy, running for over a minute. It featured Harris discussing freedom and her platform over a popular Beyoncé song, accompanied by a montage of American citizens. The second video relied on an identity appeal. This 11-second clip mixed audio of Michelle Obama discussing “Black jobs” over a montage of Harris’s career.
The third video featured a campaign rally where Harris challenged Donald Trump to a face-to-face debate. This 30-second clip represented a form of political incivility or outrage discourse. The final video highlighted negative partisanship by attacking J.D. Vance’s stance on a national abortion ban. It featured headlines about abortion restrictions layered over a popular pop song.
After viewing their assigned video, participants answered questions about their favorability toward Harris, their likelihood to share the video, and their voting intentions. The researchers utilized statistical models to isolate the effect of each video from other demographic variables. They found that the traditional, policy-oriented video was the only piece of content that meaningfully increased overall favorability toward Harris compared to the control group. The other three videos did not produce a similar boost in average favorability across the entire participant pool.
While the trendy videos did not elevate overall favorability, all four political videos increased the likelihood that participants would share the content with their own social media followers. This dynamic indicates that provocative content can still achieve viral spread even if it does not improve a politician’s overall image. The policy and debate videos also made participants more likely to believe that social media is an effective tool for generating enthusiasm about an election. None of the videos significantly shifted overall voting intentions for the entire participant group, which the researchers said provides limited evidence that the videos affected votes for Harris.
The researchers noted several nuances when breaking down the data by demographic groups. Black participants reported higher favorability toward Harris after watching the videos focused on identity and abortion rights compared to non-Black participants. Democratic voters naturally showed high levels of support across all categories. Female participants expressed greater favorability toward Harris than male participants after viewing the policy and debate videos.
Racial resentment and modern sexism are academic scales used to measure subtle or institutional prejudices rather than overt bigotry. Participants who scored high on these standard psychological measures showed lower favorability toward Harris after watching the videos. This was particularly evident when they viewed the debate clip, which featured direct confrontation. The authors noted that short-form social media content does not erase preexisting prejudicial attitudes, as these biases continue to act as strong deterrents to positive evaluations.
Age and social media habits also influenced the results in unexpected ways. Older voters sometimes displayed more favorable attitudes than younger participants after viewing specific clips. Participants who reported being frequent TikTok users actually exhibited lower favorability toward Harris in some conditions. The researchers suggested this may indicate that TikTok-using audiences are less engaged by traditional campaign or debate messaging.
The study involves specific design choices that provide context for the results. Participants watched a single isolated video during the survey rather than scrolling through an algorithmic feed. In a natural setting, TikTok users encounter multiple related videos tailored to their interests in a single session. Viewing a single clip may not fully capture the cumulative effect of sustained social media engagement.
Future research could explore how voters respond to seeing a volume of political content natively within an application’s interface. Political scientists could also investigate how user-generated internet memes compare to official campaign content. As campaigns increasingly rely on digital outreach, understanding the exact mechanisms of online persuasion will remain an important area of study.
The study, “Social Media and Candidate Favorability: TikTok and Support for Harris During the 2024 Presidential Election,” was authored by Sydney Carr-Glenn, Chaya Crowder, and Christine Slaughter.

US, Canada see growing interest in limited ceasefire in Black Sea
ATLANTA, Oct 31 - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Saturday said there was growing interest by the international community in facilitating a limited ceasefire in the Black Sea to ensure unfettered energy and grain shipments by Russia and Ukraine.
Rubio told a news conference that the US is reviewing proposals by Turkey and India to get grain shipments moving, even as the US continues to press for a broader, negotiated settlement of the war, which is now in its fifth year.
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine took center stage at a two-day meeting of foreign ministers from the Group of 20, in part due to the participation of Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov over the objections of European and Canadian leaders, who argued that including him normalized Russia's aggression.
The meeting ended without a joint statement or agreement on the myriad issues facing the world's largest economies.
Rubio defended the invitation of Lavrov, saying it would be impossible to end the war diplomatically without talking with Russia, but admitting that such a deal was not on the immediate horizon. He said the US spoke frequently with Ukrainian leaders, although Ukraine's foreign minister was not invited.
He said there was growing interest - if not momentum - in partial deals such as halting attacks on ships carrying grain and, in some cases, energy, in the Black Sea.
"This is threatening the world for food security and some energy security as well," Rubio told reporters after a two-day meeting of foreign ministers from the world's 20 largest economies, which revealed big rifts over the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
"We'd like to achieve it. It doesn't solve the war, but at least it solves a unique aspect of it," Rubio said, adding that a negotiated settlement remained a top priority for US officials, despite the failure to get there yet.
"There's a very nasty war going on, a very destructive war," Rubio said, adding that the war was already threatening to escalate to other countries given irregular efforts at sabotage and drone strikes that wandered into NATO airspace.
Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand told Reuters in an interview that she would not have chosen to invite Lavrov, but she used the occasion to confront him directly about Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"I stared him in the eye and called out Russia's further illegal invasion of Ukraine, the stealing of Ukrainian children, the targeting of Ukrainian ships in the Black Sea, all of which are reprehensible, all of which are contrary to international law and international humanitarian law," Anand said, citing her remarks during a closed-door plenary session on Friday.
Anand said she had spoken with Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, as well as her counterpart from India, about enacting a limited ceasefire in the Black Sea and putting a moratorium on attacks on Ukraine's electrical infrastructure.
Anand said a number of interlocutors were pushing for some kind of ceasefire, with a huge focus on shoring up food supply chains and brokering an end to attacks on Ukraine's electrical grid and energy infrastructure before the coming winter.
"We have to address these issues now as Ukraine approaches the winter," she said, noting that Canada had been engaged in significant and specific talks about a Black Sea ceasefire since the United Nations General Assembly in September.
India and Egypt were two countries that were heavily affected, and wanted to ensure that their own ships - and sailors - remained safe. Ukraine was fully engaged on the issue, but Russia had not shown it was willing to move ahead, she said.
Lavrov on Friday told reporters that Moscow's position on the Ukraine conflict was unchanged, and Russia could not accept Ukraine as a "military threat to the lawful security interests of the Russian Federation," according to Russian news agencies.
Rubio urged G20 participants on Friday to cooperate where possible given the complex web of economic and geopolitical challenges facing nearly every country.
"Because we all face these challenges, we must all work together to address them," he said. "The future of our nations depends on our willingness to understand that while our interests may not always align, we should always seek to work together to advance them when and where they do align."
Rubio told reporters that he spoke briefly with Lavrov on the sidelines of the meeting about the opportunity for US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to meet at the APEC meeting next month and the G20 leaders summit to be held at Trump's Doral golf resort in Miami in December.
Rubio said there was no firm commitment for Putin to attend the G20 summit. He said he wouldn't rule out the possibility that Trump would invite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, especially "if something positive could happen as a result of him attending." REUTERS

Albanese flies to Caribbean for summit as households brace for rate pain

Cricket, climate and colonialism on agenda as Commonwealth leaders meet in Caribbean
In short:
Anthony Albanese is travelling to Antigua and Barbuda for the 28th Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting.
Mr Albanese will advance Australia's bid for a seat on the UN Security Council in 2029.
What's next?
Climate, AI regulation, trade and reparations for slavery will also feature in talks.
The prime minister will advance Australia's campaign for a seat on the United Nations Security Council when he meets Commonwealth leaders in Antigua and Barbuda this week, leaving colleagues to face the fallout of a widely anticipated interest rate rise on Tuesday.
As Coalition figures accuse Anthony Albanese of "jetting off" to the Caribbean while Australians struggle with the cost of living, the prime minister said his attendance at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) came at the personal request of King Charles.
"[CHOGM] provides Australia an opportunity to work with some of our closest partners on shared challenges, including climate change, the preservation of our oceans, trade and investment, and the rise of AI," Mr Albanese said.
"It's also an important opportunity for Australia to advance our campaign for a seat on the United Nations Security Council in 2029-30."
The availability of leaders from 56 nations will also give Mr Albanese an opportunity to speak to key negotiating blocs ahead of summit season, with COP 31, APEC, G20, and the East Asia Summit all in November.
PM to discuss trade, backpackers with UK
Mr Albanese will hold sideline talks with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney, and is expected to meet several Pacific and African leaders.
While Mr Albanese and Mr Burnham briefly met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in September, their first official meeting is set to focus on AI, fuel security amid war in the Middle East, and ballooning British backpacker numbers.
Under a 2021 Morrison-era free trade deal, a rule forcing British backpackers to work in rural and regional Australia was scrapped, leading to a near doubling of UK working holiday-makers.
The government has already directed a "go slow" on processing UK working holiday visas, sitting at about 80,000 per year, but will still allow UK citizens to bypass rural and regional work.
Labor has also introduced a backpacker visa lottery, capping second-year visas at 45,000 and third-year visas at 5,000.
The agreement has been partly blamed for worsening labour shortages in rural Australia and persistently high Net Overseas Migration levels.
'Untapped potential' of Commonwealth
CHOGM is one of the few multilateral forums without the presence of the US or China, but geopolitics will still loom large over the summit.
Over the past two decades, China has poured billions into the region, funding major infrastructure projects across the Caribbean, including Antigua's main port, airport and cricket stadium where CHOGM events will tee off.
Last week, the Trump administration announced it would invest more than $US340 million ($484 million) across 15 Caribbean nations, focusing on digital infrastructure, health care and regional security.
In a pre-CHOGM speech, Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey called for far greater trade cooperation and social mobility among Commonwealth nations, whose combined economies are worth nearly $30 trillion.
"I believe passionately in the Commonwealth's potential to benefit its members and their people today and in the future. And that full potential is still untapped," she said.
Ms Botchwey also called for "bold and urgent change" in the international system amid "a new era of fracture".
"What's clear is that business as usual in international affairs will no longer cut it," she said.
Cricket, climate, and colonialism
Despite Antigua's distance from the region, there are many intersecting issues that Caribbean and Pacific leaders want to discuss this week, including climate change, the legacy of colonisation, and to a lesser extent for the Pacific, the impacts of slavery.
Rising sea levels pose an existential threat to low-lying Caribbean nations, which are more susceptible to natural disasters, and whose economies rely heavily on tourism.
Australian mining magnate Andrew "Twiggy" Forrest is also planning to sail into Antigua's port on the "Fortescue Green Pioneer", the world's first dual-fuel vessel capable of running on green ammonia.
During the 2024 CHOGM in Samoa, leaders acknowledged the "common historical experiences" of colonisation, dispossession of Indigenous peoples, and slavery and committed to '"inclusive conversations" to address the harms of those legacies.
Mr Albanese described the practice of black birding (which saw tens of thousands of Pacific Islanders coerced or kidnapped into indentured labour) as "a sorry chapter in Australia’s history" but said his focus was on the future.
The current Burnham UK government, like the Starmer government before it, has ruled out paying reparations for slavery.
Caribbean and African leaders will, however, want to continue discussions on reparatory justice this week.
CHOGM is expected to tee off on Sunday with a leader's cricket match at the Viv Richards Stadium in St John's, named after the legendary Antiguan cricketer who is the summit's official envoy.
The prime minister won't be playing, but will attend the match.

Serbia after Vucic: The winners are losing patience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
19:49:00 UTC
04:49:00 KST

Serbia after Vucic: The winners are losing patience
October 31, 2026
Aleksandar Vucic is accustomed to the spotlight. As Serbia's all-powerful president, loyal media outlets followed his every move for years. His TikTok outbursts led the evening news. But on October 25 he lost the election to the Student List, and since then, a lot has changed.
Vucic complained at a press conference, before fewer microphones than usual, that the winners were practising "revolutionary terror." He threatened: "If they continue to terrorize those who think differently – beatings, destruction and all the rest – and the state authorities do nothing, we will be forced to organize ourselves."
Vucic regards the immediate resignation of the general director of the Serbian state broadcaster RTS as an example of this "terror." Senior RTS editors have also been dismissed.
On Monday, a small group of protesters invaded the Informer TV station. Thousands of complaints have been lodged against Informer over the years for its demonization of Vucic critics. Now, journalists' associations are calling for its license to be revoked.
Tabloid media outlets loyal to Vucic have already changed their tone. Unlike Informer, they no longer refer to the Student List as "terrorists" and "mercenaries."
Old accusations against Vucic
The List, which emerged from the student revolt, is made up of professors, activists and artists. In the election on October 25, it won 53% of the vote, leaving Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) trailing with just 39%.
Since then, things have moved fast. In many cities, citizens peacefully removed portraits of Vucic from municipal buildings. The public prosecutor's office for organized crime has launched investigations, including into electoral fraud. A special commission is examining the work of the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade, which critics say did Vucic's bidding, and persecuted his opponents.
The accusations against him are old ones: that he and his system kept the media under tight control; that state contracts were only awarded to companies loyal to the regime; and that Vucic, his party, and the Serbian state had links to organized crime.
The catalyst for the revolt was the collapse, two years ago, of the concrete canopy on the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad. Sixteen people died. The accident is believed to have happened as a result of poor workmanship and corruption in the awarding and execution of the renovation contract.
Those who were celebrating in the streets a few days ago are already growing impatient. The new parliament has not yet been convened, and the SNS still controls many levers of power.
"A society that was oppressed for so long by a party that acted like a feudal lord now, understandably, expects justice," Dejan Bursac from the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory at Belgrade University told DW. "In this power vacuum, people are getting impatient."
Vucic and leading officials promise to be a strong opposition, and expect to make a quick comeback once "this lot" have ruined the country. But the majority of critics are calling for Vucic to be investigated and charged. "The SNS people are acting as if they had lost a local election somewhere in democratic Scandinavia, not as if they were part of a deeply corrupt and criminal regime," said Bursac.
How much damage can the old government do to the new one?
It's very common in Serbia for politicians to switch allegiance from one camp to another. They go where the power is. Even Vucic has admitted that many of his former comrades-in-arms are turning their backs on him. "We are going to see cases of people resigning or staying in the shadows, even putting themselves forward as informants for the next government," said Zlatko Minic from Transparency Serbia, an organization that monitors the work of governments.
The million-dollar question is: How much damage can the old government do to the new one? "There's still time for many officials to award contracts and create financial obligations for the agencies they run without necessarily committing a criminal offense," Minic warned.
However, those familiar with the situation said that for some time now the Student List has had contacts with officials in the police and administration opposed to Vucic's style of government. The winners of the election may now be able to prevent certain actions. On Wednesday, the List again demanded the resignations of leading officials in the police and judiciary. Whistleblowers were also asked to come forward if the outgoing government should try to "destroy documents."
In a symbolic move, Student List representatives held their first press conference in Pioneers Park in front of the parliament building. Vucic's followers fenced off the park in 2025, turning it into a pro-government encampment. According to investigative journalists, it also became a base for thugs and criminals who attacked anti-government demonstrators. The morning after the Student List's election win, its supporters went out with binbags and cleaned up the park.
No change in foreign policy
The victorious Student List unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focussed on making changes in domestic politics, and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.
"Our plan is to stabilize and develop the country, not to destabilize it with some abrupt change of course on foreign policy," Oliver Toskovic, a psychology professor and future member of parliament, told DW.
Toskovic said that, unlike under Vucic, the EU will not be misused as a "cover." Serbia's EU accession process recently stalled, with Vucic accusing "the West" of inciting a "color revolution" in Serbia.
"We are very dependent on Russia for energy. This is really a mistake of the previous government," Toskovic said. "But for that reason, sanctions right now would destabilize the country. And that would not be good for us or for the EU." How energy policy will develop under a Student List government is still unclear.
Where Vucic would frequently take aim at Kosovo, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading representatives of the new List have promised better relationships with Serbia's neighbors and a reduction in tensions. On Kosovo, Ilija Srdanovic, the Student List's lead candidate, has said the party is open to dialog with the government in the Kosovar capital, Pristina. He has already spoken by phone with the prime minister of Croatia.
The electoral process is not yet over. On Sunday, November 1, the vote will be repeated in some 50 polling stations because there were irregularities first time around. Once these votes are counted, parliament can be convened. The formation of a government is expected to be quick, but for now the names of the prospective members have not been disclosed.

"DGCA itself had expressed concern that UCADA lacked adequately trained and competent manpower for such high-density operations, yet a specific training mandate for these unique conditions was not in place.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said that Ankara put forward practical proposals to address global crises and strengthen international cooperation during a G20 foreign ministers' meeting in the US city of Atlanta, highlighting Ankara's commitment to a constructive, problem-solving foreign policy.
Speaking to Anadolu and TRT on the sidelines of the gathering on Saturday, Fidan described this year's meeting as particularly timely given the growing number of global crises, including energy disruptions and mounting pressure on international supply chains.
He said the discussions and contributions from participating countries could help advance efforts to address some of the world's most pressing challenges.
The two-day meeting, hosted by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, served as part of preparations for a G20 leaders' summit set to take place in Miami in December.
Global crises, energy, and supply chains
Fidan said the foreign ministers held three main sessions focusing on global crises, energy security, and disruptions to supply chains.
He pointed to growing bottlenecks in the Black Sea, Gulf, and Red Sea, warning that disruptions in these strategically important waterways are seriously affecting global trade and supply networks.
"Global supply chains have been severely disrupted. Discussions have taken place over how we might remedy or resolve these issues, and what the international community should do in this regard."
Fidan acknowledged that discussions involving Russia and countries supporting Ukraine are "not always easy," particularly when addressing the Black Sea situation and the energy consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war.
However, he stressed that such discussions are necessary to allow countries to clearly communicate their positions and explore potential solutions.
Türkiye seeks constructive role in international crises
Fidan said Türkiye seeks to distinguish itself through meaningful contributions rather than simply taking a different position from other countries.
"Türkiye certainly attaches importance not only to our role as a mediator but also—and more importantly—to taking a stance that is distinct from that of other countries: one that is more constructive and focused on problem-solving.
"In other words, when it comes to international and regional crises, we prioritise taking a stance not for the sake of being different, but for the sake of being genuinely useful," he said.
He added that Ankara presents substantive proposals aimed not only at resolving existing problems but also at addressing structural weaknesses in the international system to prevent similar crises from recurring.
"Although there were heated debates at times, the discussions that took place were substantive. Türkiye puts forward truly serious proposals—both regarding practical solutions to existing problems and concerning the steps that need to be taken in a systemic sense to prevent such issues from recurring. This was significant."
Extensive bilateral diplomatic contacts
Alongside the main sessions, Fidan held bilateral meetings with representatives from more than half of the participating countries, according to his account.
His meetings included Rubio, as well as officials from Russia, the UK, France, Mexico, Germany, the European Union, and Saudi Arabia.
He said the discussions covered both global challenges and regional developments, calling the meetings an important opportunity to exchange views and explore ways to address ongoing crises.
Fidan also credited Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's leadership and Türkiye's diplomatic engagement with strengthening the country's international standing.
"Türkiye is an actor whose voice is needed on the international stage," he said.
Fidan said several urgent issues remain at the forefront of international discussions, particularly the ongoing diplomatic engagement between the US and Iran.
He said countries are closely watching how the negotiations progress and whether another military confrontation can be avoided.
According to Fidan, participating countries broadly share the view that renewed conflict should be prevented and that diplomacy must continue to be given an opportunity.
"Almost all countries are at the negotiating table. They have reached a consensus on preventing further conflict and ensuring that diplomacy is consistently given a chance. This is, of course, a significant point."
He stressed that the same diplomatic approach should be maintained in addressing tensions in the Black Sea and efforts to prevent Israeli "expansionism."

Iranian envoys meet Qatari mediators as threat looms of US strikes after midterms

Saturday's talks in the Qatari capital followed more than 12 hours of discussions on Friday between Iranian and Qatari envoys in Tehran, said the source, who was briefed on the negotiations and spoke on condition of anonymity. Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei issued a statement on Saturday ordering the armed forces to be prepared to respond to any attacks. The Iranian military later announced it was taking steps to improve its readiness.
"Any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response," Khamenei, who has not appeared in public since replacing his father, slain at the war's outset, said on Saturday in the statement posted on his official Telegram account.
Khamenei said that senior commanders had reported high readiness along the Gulf coast, in and around the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman, and on Iran's northwestern and southeastern borders.
Rubio, hosting foreign ministers of the G20 major economies in Atlanta, declined to set a timeframe for the talks in Qatar, but said direct and indirect contacts with Iran were under way.
"There are multiple talks. Talks have actually never stopped," he said.

DIPLOMACY CONTINUES DESPITE GAPS

Reuters reported on Friday, citing an senior Iranian official, that this proposal was not deemed satisfactory by Tehran.

For the past three months, Rebecca Williams has been living in a storage yard without power on the fringes of Far North Queensland.
A broad tarp covers her belongings, and at night she sleeps in a pink swag, which she says offers little shelter from the weather and the noise of trucks hurtling down the nearby highway.
The site also has no toilet.
"None of this is secured, so some nights I feel very unsafe," she tells SBS News.
Her makeshift home sits on the outskirts of Seisia, a small coastal town of around 300 people on the Cape York Peninsula. Rising costs and encroaching seas have created a perfect storm for residents, who are struggling to access affordable and climate-resilient housing.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Williams, 35, is a proud Angkamuthi Seven Rivers woman and works full-time in environmental protection. She says she has been living in "survival mode" for far longer than she’s called the compound home.
She's been waiting for a rental for more than 11 years.
"I've been told it's based on not having kids. I'm not a priority," she says.
A chronic housing shortage has gripped the community for more than a decade, driven by undersupply, prohibitively high construction costs and overcrowding. Many in the community have no choice but to rely on government-funded housing stock.
While the Queensland Department of Housing is ultimately responsible for social housing across the state, Seisia's local applications are processed by the Northern Peninsula Area Regional Council (NPARC), which also delivers and maintains government-supported homes. But the waitlist is long, forcing some community members to consider leaving their ancestral homeland.
After a decade of couch surfing, living in overcrowded family homes and even taking jobs on boats for two years, Williams moved into her family’s storage yard in June.
As SBS News was preparing to publish this story, Williams received confirmation from the Department of Housing that it would provide her with emergency accommodation. She expects to move into a government-supported two-bedroom rental with her younger sister in the coming weeks.
She estimates around 100 people in Cape York's Indigenous community are currently waiting for a house — that’s around one in three residents.
"There's a whole heap of us. We're being told to move down to Cairns, but people who are from here, we haven't imagined ourselves living anywhere else," she says.
I see it as structural violence. Maybe a bit of racial, but more structural violence, with not just my generation, but many generations of my family.
A housing crisis on two fronts
Across the Cape York Peninsula, communities like Seisia face similar housing challenges.
As the climate warms and sea levels rise, they are contending with another major threat to their way of life.
Roughly 1,000km north of Cairns, Cape York is bordered by the Coral Sea to the east, the Gulf of Carpentaria to the west and the Torres Strait to the north. Its low-lying, tropical landscape is carved by 21 major river systems, making it home to one of the largest freshwater networks in the country.
Much like the broader Torres Strait region, its topography makes it particularly vulnerable to coastal erosion.
It's difficult to predict exactly how much sea-level rise will inundate low-lying areas around the Torres Strait, but the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has identified the region as among the most vulnerable places in the world.
A sea-level rise of just 50cm could make flooding across Australia 300 times more likely, according to the Australian government. By this estimate, a flood that once struck every hundred years would be expected several times a year.
This is a source of deep concern for residents of Cape York, who have witnessed the long-term impacts of flood events and seen First Nations communities displaced.
Sitting on the shores of Seisia Beach, Torres Strait Islander Elders Leonora Adidi and Jenson Warusam recall the "difficult decision" their grandparents made to leave their home in Saibai, a low-lying island in the Torres Strait just a few kilometres off the Papua New Guinea mainland, to establish a new community on the northernmost tip of Australia.
"This was a community that was built by the blood, sweat and tears of our people," Adidi tells SBS News.
The catalyst was a major flooding event, explains Adidi, who is also a linguist and cultural educator from the Suy-Baydham Clan of Bamaga and Saibai.
In 1947, unnatural king tides and heavy monsoon rains struck Saibai, flooding the entire village.
"There wasn't enough fresh water and also fresh food from the gardens to sustain the population," says Adidi, a linguist and cultural educator from the Suy-Baydham Clan of Bamaga and Saibai.
Sabai's chief, Bamaga Ginau, proposed a bold relocation idea.
"He put forward his plans that we should all move out and abandon the island," Warusam says.
The community was split: some wanted to leave, while others chose to stay.
Seven families representing seven clan groups sailed south to Cape York in pearl luggers, the M.V. Millard and M.V. Macoy, and established a temporary settlement in the abandoned army camps at Muttee Heads, on Cape York’s west coast. In 1948, the Queensland Government gazetted 44,500 acres (18,008 hectares) as a reserve for Torres Strait Islanders.
More families followed, clearing land and building new houses, until the settlements were renamed Seisia and Bamaga.
"When my grandparents moved here, there was a freak tide, probably due to some underwater event," Adidi says.
In The World's News, a discontinued newspaper formerly published in Sydney, a 1952 headline reads: "Disappearing Island Defies Science", referencing the unnatural tides that inundated Saibai.
But Adidi fears that a one-off event is becoming alarmingly regular.
"It's now getting closer and going into areas where they've never been affected by salt water," she adds.
History repeating itself
While the term climate migration is often associated with people moving from disappearing Pacific islands — such as the recent relocation of Tuvalu citizens to Australia — some historians, climate advocates and members of the Cape York community view Saibai's displaced community as Australia's first internal climate migrants.
Today, the Northern Peninsula Area (NPA) of Cape York remains a gateway to the Torres Strait. Residents are deeply connected to their Saibai roots, sharing the same clan groups, cultural knowledge and totemic systems of the crocodile, or Koedal.
But nearly eight decades after the catastrophic floods that displaced several Saibai families, some NPA residents fear history is repeating itself.
As sea levels rise globally and threaten to submerge the island, Cape York’s chronic housing shortage may not support another generation of migrants from Saibai. Now, both NPARC (the local council) and NPA residents are calling for more government funding to accommodate a future wave of families displaced by rising tides.
Some are taking matters into their own hands.
In 2021, two Torres Strait Islander elders, Uncle Pabai Pabai and Uncle Paul Kabai, filed a first-of-its-kind negligence case against the federal government, known as the Australian Climate Case. Kabai, who is based in Saibai, argued the government had failed to protect residents against the threat posed by climate change.
Adidi worked as an interpreter for the Federal Court during the case. The hearings took her back to Saibai for the first time in 25 years.
"Going on Country and being shown the stark, very drastic changes on Saibai was very shocking. I was in tears," she says.
Her grandmother's garden was unrecognisable. The wide beach she remembered from childhood had been whittled down to a narrow strip. The towering coconut and almond trees had disappeared, replaced by mangroves in the saltwater.
It was like I went to a place I'd never been before.
Scientific evidence heard at the Australian Climate Case suggested that islands such as Saibai, which are only 1.5m above sea level in places, could be unlivable by 2050 if global warming continues on its current trajectory.
"It's going to be underwater if nothing is done, and when that happens, the families have got to move somewhere," Adidi says.
"We established these two communities, Bamaga and Seisia, for our people. In the future, if they want to move, there's always going to be a place for them here."
Pressures on the system
However, the community is already buckling under the demand for new homes. In remote Indigenous communities, government housing can be critical in bridging supply gaps, where private development is extremely limited because remote construction is so expensive.
Frances Elu, a former NPARC councillor, has witnessed Cape York’s overcrowding crisis unfold over many years.
"[The area has become] overpopulated, I guess — well, I don't guess, I see it. You put more people in an environment that will create a crisis for housing," he says.
But with limited government funding and the need for location-specific infrastructure, there are no simple solutions, he says.
"We've got to somehow assist not only Saibai but Torres Strait Islanders and land is another issue," he says.
There's always room for adapting. At the end of the day, we all related if we're talking about Torres Strait [Islanders].
Although Williams looks set to secure housing now, it took numerous applications over more than a decade. Just before her approval, she had appealed to the NPARC by sending letters and photos documenting her living situation.
She worries for other community members still on the waitlist. Relocation is not an option for many who, like Williams, have deep cultural and kinship ties to the region. Saibai is the Country of her ancestors, and her grandparents were among the first wave of climate-displaced migrants to leave the island for the NPA.
"My grandmother was one of the pioneers coming over looking for fresh water. They've worked really hard building these communities," she says.
She believes the government owes the community "a basic duty of care".
According to NPARC’s analysis of Census data from 2021, 44 per cent of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in the NPA lacked access to appropriately sized housing, and at least 1,385 additional bedrooms were required to relieve overcrowding. According to the council, this would equate to 462 three-bedroom houses.
NPARC has appealed to the federal government for $137 million to reduce chronic overcrowding. Last month, councillors and NPA community leaders travelled to Canberra to urge the government to fund at least 120 new dwellings across the five NPA communities, as well as maintenance for existing houses.
But building houses in a remote area like Cape York is not easy.
Construction materials and skilled contractors are disproportionately costly. According to NPARC's 2024-2025 budget, 15 new homes cost $15 million to build – roughly $1 million each.
A compounding crisis
For now, both councillors and community members alike are awaiting the federal government’s response.
According to a spokesperson for NPARC, there has been no dedicated federal funding to deliver housing for Queensland Indigenous Communities since 2019.
Council has a role in advocating for investments and to work together with the state government to deliver housing on the ground in our community.
Acknowledging the funding "shortfall", NPARC is calling on the federal government to commit $1 billion from the Housing Australia Future Fund to support Queensland's Indigenous communities.
"Overcrowding has measurable consequences for health and education, including transmission of infectious diseases and acute rheumatic fever," the spokesperson says.
SBS News contacted the Queensland Department of Housing and Public Works for comment but did not receive a response before deadline.
Tess Lea, an anthropologist and Head of Macquarie University’s School of Communication, Society and Culture, says funding social housing is particularly challenging in Indigenous communities.
"The who's responsible question at the moment is kind of everyone and no one. There's no single minister or agency with the responsibility for Indigenous housing," Lea tells SBS News.
"You've got many more Indigenous people dependent on social housing than any other population group in Australia."
While nationally, social housing represents a small minority of total housing stock (in 2025, it accounted for just 4 per cent according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare), much of this problem is structural, Lea explains.
"We've got greater vulnerability [among First Nations communities] just on the basis of the histories of geolocation," she says.
"That's a colonial story – where did water theft start first, where was the most arable land, where was the rich soil."
As Indigenous communities have been displaced and forcibly resettled, their vulnerability to climatic and extreme weather events has increased, she explains.
"Australia's at the front lines of climate change," Lea says.
"We're in the age of fire. There's potentially less water or more intense heat events and flooding events."
First Nations communities, she says, are "the collateral … of dragging our feet".
Williams says if another wave of climate migration comes from the Torres Strait islands, she hopes history will not repeat itself, leaving those already displaced from their homelands without access to basic housing.
"We're the people already here, and we're not being looked after," she says.
We're the children of NPA, and we're the homeless children of NPA.

The invisible war threatening democracy — and why Australia should be worried
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
19:35:13 UTC
04:35:13 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
On the eve of one of the most contentious United States midterm elections in history, allegations of Russian hacking have once again emerged.
Last week US magazine Vanity Fair published excerpts from a book alleging financial links involving US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and bank accounts in Israel, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.
The claims are based on hacked phone information obtained through a cyber operation involving Dutch spies, who allegedly gained access to Kushner’s iPhone after a Russian operative revealed the country's intelligence agency — the Main Directorate of the General Staff of the Armed forces of the Russian Federation (GRU) — had screenshots from Kushner's iPhone on its server in 2017.
Kushner has denied the claims, describing them as "completely insane" in a post on X.
Most in the security community would be unsurprised to hear allegations the GRU accessed Kushner's phone.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Ciaran Martin, the former CEO of the United Kingdom's National Cyber Security Centre, the country's technical authority on cyber security, says Russian cyber operations, including misinformation and disinformation campaigns have been targeting Western democracies since 2016, although there had been a handful of incidents before that.
Among the most prominent examples, several Russian intelligence officers were charged in the US with allegedly hacking into Democratic Party systems with the intent of interfering with the 2016 presidential election, in which Trump defeated Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton. The hacking was accompanied by a separate online influence campaign, in which Russian-backed operatives sought to undermine Clinton and deepen political divisions through targeted advertisements and social media activity.
This month UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham again drew attention to Russian interference after telling The Rest is Politics podcast it was "clear" that Russia interfered with the Brexit referendum, also held in 2016.
Most experts SBS News spoke to said countries, including Australia, are not doing enough to counter the threats posed by cyber operations, not just from Russia but also from countries such as China, Iran and North Korea.
A new front in geopolitical conflict
Some believe Russia has been escalating its cyber activities as part of a "hybrid warfare" campaign that blends military capability with other tactics such as cyberattacks, misinformation, economic pressure, sabotage and political interference.
This month, the director general of the UK national security agency MI5, Ken McCallum, revealed the agency is devoting more resources to countering state threats in 2026 than during the Cold War.
In his annual threat update on 13 October, McCallum noted there had been charges, prosecutions and convictions connected to Russia, Iran and China.
"We've seen hackers attacking energy and water infrastructure, including in the US. European defence companies targeted by arson attacks and even violent intent. Here in the UK, a destructive cyber attack on an energy generator," he said in his address.
This year Germany blamed Russia for a drone attack on one of its airports as well as suspected sabotage attempts on its power grid, and a suspected arson attack on a defence manufacturer.
Poland has also linked Russia to an explosion on its train network last year and a shopping centre fire in 2024.
Nathan Gill, a former politician and ally of Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, was jailed last year for accepting bribes to make pro-Russian statements in the European parliament.
Martin believes there's a "high tempo of risky and difficult behaviour" from Russia.
The University of Oxford professor says Russia's appetite for provocation is much greater than that of any other adversary in recent years, adding that cyber and digital provide the opportunity to do things without the same level of physical risk.
He notes hybrid warfare activities are attractive because they sit below the threshold that would generally trigger an armed response.
You’re not going to send your young men to die over … some sneaky stuff on the internet [or] a cyber attack on an energy grid.
"That's the cleverness of it."
Professor Matthew Warren, director of the RMIT Centre for Cyber Security Research and Innovation, says information warfare is "poison" to democracies as people make decisions based on false information and can be manipulated into outcomes that benefit adversaries.
He says he wouldn't be surprised to see Russian efforts ramp up, especially with the French presidential elections scheduled for early next year, as well as state elections in some parts of Germany.
Last month the far-right party Alternative für Deutschland, a party whose members have faced scrutiny over alleged links to Russia, came first in elections in two German states.
Warren says the rise of populist parties has the potential to destabilise countries, which could serve Russia's interests.
While Russian influence campaigns could also emerge around the US midterms next week, Warren points out that Trump appears to be very unpopular and that this could be difficult for foreign actors to turn around.
Threat to democracy
Strategic analyst and co-founder of policy intelligence platform Statekraft, Lesley Seebeck, who has worked for Australian government departments including the Bureau of Meteorology, says Russian operatives generally look for activities with the potential to tip votes towards a certain outcome.
"They will do so for the left or the right, [using] whichever tool comes to hand … for the general purpose of causing disruption, tumult [and] uncertainty in societies," she tells SBS News.
Seebeck says tactics such as the use of social media as an echo chamber and the harassment of individuals online are also being exported as a form of "techno- authoritarianism" that helps regimes to suppress their populations.
She points to the online harassment of certain communities, including India's alleged targeting of Sikh activists and minorities in Canada, and the targeting of Iranian and Chinese diaspora communities by their governments.
Because governments are less able to respond [to these types of activities], people get more dissatisfied in democracies [and] get more dissatisfied with existing governments.
But Martin says it's important to remember that while hostile powers can amplify social tensions "this only works … if there's existing divisions to exploit".
While authorities should be "realistically concerned" about future Russian interference, he’s hopeful that work to strengthen social resilience may dull its impact.
Martin points to a 2023 deepfake audio recording that purported to show London mayor Sadiq Khan saying a pro-Palestinian march should take priority over Armistice Day commemorations. The recording was widely debunked, and he says it had "no real impact" because people were warned it was fake by Conservative politician Tom Tugendhat.
He contrasts this with the response to the 2016 US presidential election when media reported the Clinton hack that saw around 150,000 Democrat emails published on sites like WikiLeaks. Martin argues there was insufficient consideration of the fact that the material had been obtained through hacking by a hostile foreign power. Trump even encouraged Russia to release more emails, turning it into a "partisan football", he says.
The impact of interference
All the experts SBS News spoke to agree it's difficult to say with certainty whether misinformation or cyber warfare has changed electoral outcomes.
"Even the successes, you can’t unambiguously and incontrovertibly link them to Russian interference because at the end of the day, you don’t know why people voted as they did," Martin says.
But Martin believes Russia was able to sow discontent during the 2016 US presidential election.
I think the measure of success for the Russians in America in 2016 is the fact that America’s still arguing about it.
He notes a candidate considered more sympathetic to Russia, Robert Fico, was returned to power as Slovakia's prime minister in 2023 after his opponent was featured in a deepfake audio clip circulated during an electoral silence period, although its influence on the result has not been established.
Russian influence operations were also alleged to have impacted the presidential elections in Romania in 2024, which were later annulled.
Martin, who was head of cyber security for the UK during the Brexit referendum, says he doesn't believe the Russians succeeded in interfering in the 2016 vote, which saw the UK vote to leave the European Union, despite "rudimentary attempts" at disinformation campaigns.
An intelligence and security committee report into Russian interference in UK elections and referendums, published in 2020, did not make any conclusions on whether Russian activity had influenced the Brexit referendum. However, it criticised the government for a lack of assessment of the attempts after the vote.
How to make communities more resilient
Sven Herpig, lead for cybersecurity and emerging threats at European technology policy think tank interface, says Australia has a long way to go in securing its digital infrastructure against cyber operations but adds so do most other countries in the world.
He says it’s very difficult to apprehend the criminals and intelligence agents behind operations but authorities should keep an eye on influence campaigns and ensure misinformation and disinformation is debunked. He also notes the importance of maintaining back-ups and non-electronic voting records, so election results can be independently checked and recounted if necessary.
"When you cannot guarantee anymore to your public … that your elections are secure and safe, you have a real problem," Herpig tells SBS News.
Warren says information warfare often aims to discourage voters away from the democratic process and this makes it potentially less effective in Australia, which has a compulsory voting system.
Australia's geographic isolation has also protected it from being drawn into wars historically, but Warren says this won't shield it from information warfare.
Certainly Australia has the potential to be very vulnerable.
He doesn't think Australia has yet accepted the need to take the risks seriously, pointing out that other countries have launched national awareness campaigns.
The UK has launched the National Protective Security Authority to help businesses and organisations protect themselves against national security threats; while Lithuania, Latvia and Finland are investing in initiatives to help people recognise disinformation.
"Countries are actually taking the view of preparing their whole populations to deal with information warfare as a threat, the same way [as] kinetic warfare's being dealt with, or propaganda," Warren says.
Martin agrees and says the need for critical thinking is even more crucial with the rise of AI, which can boost the capabilities of operators who may not have been particularly effective in the past, making it more difficult to recognise content that is fake.
Technical measures such as watermarking information so people can see its origin could also be helpful, he says, as well as cracking down on organised troll farms.
'Make the costs higher'
Herpig says Australia must pay closer attention to China's activities, pointing to a statement from Japan's National Police Agency in January 2025 that said it had linked more than 200 cyberattacks over five years (between 2019 to 2024) to a Chinese hacking group called MirrorFace. It said the attacks were aimed at stealing data on national security and advanced technology.
If I was in Australia, I would be zero worried about Russia and I would be very worried about China when it comes [cyberactivity and] election interference.
" We're worried right now about Russian cyber operations for good reasons, but what we're overlooking is how much China has built a huge ecosystem that enables it to run countless parallel campaigns against targets in the entire world … with different levels of control."
Herpig expects there will be more cyber operations, including disinformation and influence campaigns, ahead of election events, not just from foreign intelligence agencies but also from lobbyists and interest groups based in the country.
"Where I think we're falling short is not the lack of policies or regulation, not even the lack of budget [most of the time], but the lack of implementation [of basic IT security measures]," he says.
Seebeck would like to see stronger safe harbour provisions in Australian cyber legislation allowing businesses to share information about cyber breaches with government agencies without fear of prosecution.
She would also like to see more people trained in cyber security, potentially through more government subsidies for training courses.
She says civilian cyber infrastructure should be bolstered to make it more resilient and ensure operations can continue if parts of the system are impacted.
The US has pioneered tools and platforms to debunk misinformation campaigns since 2016, and Herpig stresses governments must continually develop responses to those carrying out attacks.
"You will not convince [countries like] Russia to stop cyber operations … but you can make the costs higher for them, and that's the least we should do."

NASA’s Hubble and Webb capture ghostly Cat’s Head Nebula

NASA’s Hubble and Webb capture ghostly Cat’s Head Nebula
NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have captured detailed images of the Cat’s Head Nebula, a dynamic star-forming scene located about 7,500 light-years away from Earth in the Carina Nebula, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing NASA.
The region earned its nickname because its shape resembles a cat sitting with its back to the viewer, its head turned to the right, and a glowing feature resembling an eye.
The nebula’s distinctive "cat's head" shape was likely sculpted over time by intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from massive stars in the Carina Nebula. Radiation and winds gradually erode the surrounding gas and dust, while denser material within the cat-shaped pillar remains intact for now.
Hubble’s visible-light images show a dense, dark brown pillar of dust, with a glowing red feature resembling the cat’s eye that may be a young star still partially obscured by dust. A hazy yellow ridge traces the filament’s right edge. This bright rim is consistent with gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars, potentially triggering a process known as photoevaporation.
Webb’s near- and mid-infrared observations provide complementary insights into the structure and composition of the Cat’s Head Nebula. Although its overall shape resembles the one captured by Hubble in visible light, Webb’s near-infrared images reveal a more transparent filament and intricate details of its surface. On the cat’s left are ghostly wisps of dust and gas, delicate structures exposed to radiation from nearby massive stars.
The near-infrared images show numerous stars scattered across the region in shades of blue and yellow, some of which remain partially obscured by dust. The glowing feature resembling the cat’s eye is still clearly visible. Webb’s high-resolution images also capture faint background galaxies, offering a glimpse through our Milky Way galaxy and beyond.
Beware… space cat! 🐱 Something spooky lurks about 7,500 light-years away. The watchful eyes of Hubble and @NASAWebb captured the Cat’s Head Nebula, just in time for Halloween Eve. This cosmic cat is in the process of forming new stars: https://t.co/tMFguEFALR https://t.co/rFsK5bK9xC
— Hubble (@NASAHubble) October 30, 2026
Although the Cat’s Head Nebula is a temporary structure that will gradually disperse as stars form and evolve, it offers valuable insights into the processes taking place within star-forming regions. By combining observations from Hubble and Webb, astronomers are gaining a better understanding of the complex and turbulent processes that govern star formation.
Earlier, it was reported that the Vera Rubin Observatory had detected a possible new dwarf planet orbiting the Sun beyond Neptune, marking a potentially significant discovery in the outer Solar System.

UN demands probe into death of its employee in Houthi custody
GENEVA - The United Nations on Oct 31 condemned the “heartbreaking” death of one of its employees in Yemen under custody of the Houthis and demanded an urgent inquiry.
Mohammad al-Shami, a staff member of the UN Human Rights Office in Yemen, had been “arbitrarily held” by the Houthis since June 2024, the organisation said in a statement.
It cited his family as saying he had died more than a month ago, but that his relatives had only been recently informed.
The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Turk, said in the statement that no explanation had been given for the “heartbreaking loss”.
The Iran-aligned Houthis are fighting against Yemen’s internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.
The statement said Turk “demanded full transparency from the Houthi authorities and an urgent, independent and thorough investigation” into al-Shami’s death.
It quoted Turk as saying he was also “gravely concerned for the safety and well-being of the other UN personnel who remain detained”, demanding their release.
“By detaining our colleagues, the de facto authorities are gravely undermining our ability to support the people of Yemen during a most serious humanitarian and human rights crisis,” he said.
“I urge them to change course.”
On Oct 14, UN spokesman Farhan Haq told reporters in New York that 71 UN personnel were being held by the Houthis.
Yemen’s Information Minister Muammar al-Eryani also condemned al-Shami’s death in a statement cited by Yemeni news agency SABA.
“He stressed that the still-mysterious circumstances of his death raise serious questions about the safety of the remaining abductees,” it said.
He demanded “an independent and transparent international investigation to uncover the circumstances of the death, determine responsibilities, and hold those involved to account”.
Yemen slid back into war in July after four years of relative calm, amid fallout from the wider Middle East conflict, and hostilities intensified in September.
Saudi Arabia has carried out air strikes against Houthi positions and the group has stepped up attacks inside Saudi territory. AFP

Regional agreement and threat of a joint response
Donya-e-Eqtesad discussed the unexpected visit of Khalid bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s defense minister, to Tehran. As concerns grow over a possible renewal of war between Iran and the United States, Saudi Arabia is trying to influence Tehran’s calculations through a mix of economic incentives, political proposals, and security warnings.
Riyadh’s message was that if Iran accepts certain concessions that could facilitate an agreement with Washington, Saudi Arabia and other regional states would be willing to discuss a broader regional security arrangement with Tehran. At the same time, Saudi officials reportedly warned that if Iran rejects this path and attacks against Arab Persian Gulf countries resume, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan would be prepared to respond within the framework of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. The importance of the message lies less in any direct military threat and more in Riyadh’s attempt to combine incentives with deterrence. In this view, Tehran faces a choice between greater participation in regional security structures and the possibility of stronger pressure from neighboring countries.
Jam-e-Jam: Cost of the illusion of victory
Jam-e-Jam analyzed what it described as Trump’s strategic deadlock and continued rhetoric. Trump still relies on telling fake stories to support his political position and divert attention from setbacks. However, evidence suggests that military and political leaders in the United States, Europe, and the region have concluded that any new conflict could have very different dimensions and unpredictable consequences. The paper notes that Iranian officials have warned that a future response would not necessarily be limited to military targets and could extend to critical infrastructure, communication cables, and data networks. It also points to calls for diplomacy, including proposals for regional meetings and European interest in renewed negotiations with Iran. These developments indicate a growing recognition that threats and displays of power may reflect concern rather than strength. The future political and security order of the region cannot be shaped without considering Iran’s role and influence.
Arman-e-Melli: Oman’s warning to US and Israel

Iranian officials have repeatedly stated that tensions surrounding the strait emerged as a consequence of attacks against Iran. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi previously warned that any military escalation encouraged by Israel could have serious consequences for international energy markets and remain a major concern for both energy exporters and consumers. Some observers believe that Netanyahu could seek greater regional pressure following domestic political developments, possibly with support from Washington. Against this backdrop, Badr Al Busaidi, Oman’s foreign minister, publicly warned against any new military adventure in the region and urged the United States and Israel to avoid further escalation. The article concludes by questioning whether such warnings and diplomatic efforts by regional states can help reduce tensions and prevent another crisis.
Hamshahri: Iran damaged Trump’s popularity
Hamshahri examined significant decline in Trump’s popularity both inside the United States and internationally. The conflict involving Iran has been one of the major factors contributing to a worsening perception of America over recent months. Public confidence in both the United States and its president has weakened noticeably. Increasing criticism of Washington’s policies, dissatisfaction with unilateral decision-making, and continued interventionist approaches are presented as evidence of a widening gap between America’s claims of global leadership and the way its actions are perceived. According to the newspaper, this decline reflects a broader loss of credibility for the image the United States has long promoted, namely that of a defender of freedom, democracy, and international order.
Ettelaat: US elections and their impact on war with Iran
Ettelaat discussed the possible impact of tensions with Iran on American politics and the midterm elections which will be held on Nov. 3. The newspaper argued that one major difference between these elections and many previous contests is the direct influence of the conflict on the domestic political environment. The first effect identified is increased economic pressure on voters. The second is growing public debate about the necessity and objectives of military intervention. Many Americans remain skeptical about becoming involved in another prolonged conflict in the Middle East. A third consequence, according to the paper, is the more challenging political position facing Trump. If Democrats gain stronger representation in Congress, pressure on the administration to explain the costs, objectives, and long-term strategy of the conflict could increase. Nevertheless, the article notes that the president retains significant authority in foreign affairs. Therefore, even changes in congressional control would not automatically lead to the end of tensions or an immediate shift in Washington’s policy toward Iran.

PM Modi hailed Isro’s successful NVS-03 launch as a boost to NavIC, while the space agency plans two more navigation satellite launches in the coming months
NEW DELHI: With Isro successfully launching navigation satellite NVS-03, which carries an indigenously manufactured atomic clock, on Friday night from Sriharikota, PM Narendra Modi on Saturday called the GSLV-F18 mission “an important step in strengthening NavIC, our indigenous satellite navigation system”.Lauding Isro and its scientists, Modi said the “dedication and ingenuity of our space scientists continue to make our nation proud”. “Equipped with enhanced capabilities, NVS-03 will further our pursuit of self-reliance in critical technologies and support navigation services that benefit our people,” he further said on X on Saturday.Space minister Jitendra Singh said that “this remarkable achievement reflects India’s growing prowess in space technology and our unwavering commitment to strengthening sovereign indigenous navigation capabilities”.The success of the NVS-03 satellite mission will not only get India’s navigation system up and running again but also give a big boost to strategic forces as they have until now been dependent on foreign navigation systems like American GPS and Russian GLONASS for weapon and missile navigation.The advanced satellite has an indigenously developed atomic clock, which is the most accurate timekeeping device in the world.
India has mastered this sophisticated technology and the desi atomic clock is now ticking in NVS-03 satellite in space.NavIC was until now not being used by the armed forces for the purposes of missile navigation, precise positioning and coordination of warships at sea, and indigenous navigation support for troop movement and combat aircraft. This is because four operational satellites were required for a standalone GPS-style position tracking system to work. The strategic forces were, therefore, dependent on foreign navigation systems. But the successful launch of NVS-03 has changed everything. It will make the NavIC constellation operational not only for strategic use but also for civilian purposes across India and up to 1,500 km (930 miles) beyond the country’s geographical borders.Indian security forces need an operational NavIC to maintain strategic autonomy and secure tactical advantage without relying on foreign-controlled networks. The four-satellite constellation will ensure secure, uncompromised communication, mobility and targeting data. Modern military hardware such as ballistic missiles and precision-guided munitions require highly accurate Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) signals to function effectively.Learning from past mistakes, Isro made an important change in the satellite system to make the launch successful. Isro chairman V Narayanan on Saturday revealed that in order to ensure mission reliability and bypass previous technical hurdles, the NVS-03 satellite was operated with “three pyro valves open”.Addressing the media at Sriharikota soon after the launch, Narayanan said that this bold technical decision was validated after rigorous vibration and shock testing by a national-level committee chaired by former Isro chief Kiran Kumar.
Pyro valves are crucial in spacecraft propulsion. However, the NVS-02 satellite launched in 2025, the second spacecraft in the NVS series, was a failure due to a pryo valve-related problem. A high-level panel, after thorough analysis of the 2025 satellite failure, concluded that “the drive signal did not reach the pyro valve of the oxidiser line of the engine meant for orbit raising”.The Isro chief also informed that with four satellites, including NVS-01 now active in India's navigation satellite system, Isro plans to launch NVS-04 in five months, and NVS-05 in 10 months to further bolster the navigation satellite constellation.
