D.C. and Virginia Join the Fight to Block Trump’s Triumphal Arch. What Happens Next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
19:28:26 UTC
04:28:26 KST

Washington, D.C., and Virginia sued the National Park Service and Interior Department on Saturday in a last-minute bid to stop construction on President Donald Trump’s proposed 250-foot triumphal arch. The Trump Administration has said that construction could begin as early as next week.
The new challenge joins two existing lawsuits against the arch, adding to a series of legal battles testing the limits of Trump’s authority to remake Washington.
Calling the project “flagrantly unlawful,” the lawsuit points to the Commemorative Works Act, which requires Congressional authorization for memorials on federal land in Washington and its environs. The lawsuit also alleges violations of the Administrative Procedure Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act, arguing that the Administration failed to adequately assess the project’s effects and consult as required.
“In their rush to break ground on the Arch, Defendants have made only half-hearted gestures at complying with these requirements,” the lawsuit filed Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and D.C. Attorney General Brian L. Schwalb, claims. “Perhaps recognizing that the project is legally indefensible, Defendants have made clear that they will attempt to outrun judicial review.”
“The Commonwealth has a solemn duty and a profound interest in preserving the dignity of this sacred place,” Jones said in a statement to the Washington Post. “We will vigorously litigate to protect its sanctity and honor the legacy of those who made the ultimate sacrifice.”
The Administration argued in a June 17 filing for Lemmon v. Trump—a separate suit filed in February—that Congress already authorized construction at the site in 1925, when it approved plans for Arlington Memorial Bridge that included two monumental columns. Those columns were never built.
In Lemmon, three Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian argue that the arch would “block historically significant reciprocal views between” the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. The plaintiffs have also argued that the plan requires congressional authorization.
The Arlington County Board then filed its own suit Oct. 8 arguing that the construction would disrupt roads important to emergency services and “significantly and detrimentally” affect Arlington National Cemetery.
In response to those suits, and defending the urgency of the project, Trump announced last month that he had agreed, at the Defense Department’s request, to incorporate a military complex into the planned arch, including facilities for drones and snipers.
In sworn declarations filed Oct. 28, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin reiterated the claim that the arch is central to national security.
“The arch is a generational national defense opportunity to mitigate these evolving threats,” Hegseth wrote in his declaration.
The National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC), a federal review panel, is scheduled to consider final approval of the arch’s site and building plans on Nov. 5. The commission includes several Trump appointees, and its chairman has said he plans to support the project, according to the Washington Post.
Interior must also issue its final authorization and publish the required notice. The Administration has told the court that those steps could be completed on Nov. 5, as well, allowing construction to begin that same day.
The Justice Department told the court on Friday that construction could begin immediately once those steps were complete.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan, however, seemed skeptical of the rush.
“What’s the harm to the government to wait 3 or 4 months? What’s the rush to put this arch up?” the judge asked at the hearing for Lemmon v. Trump on Friday.
Chutkan observed that the issue was complex. She said that she would consider the plaintiffs' standing over the weekend and rule expeditiously.
TIME has reached out to the White House about the new lawsuit.
What Could These Lawsuits Mean for Trump's Other Renovation Projects?
The triumphal arch is just one of several projects that Trump has introduced in his second term to remake Washington in his image, including the demolition of the White House East Wing and construction of a White House ballroom, the planned 15-month closure and massive overhaul of the historic East Potomac golf course, and plans to restore and rename the Kennedy Center.
In Friday’s hearing, Deputy Assistant Attorney General Robert Stander cited the Supreme Court’s 5-4 decision in August allowing ballroom construction to continue while litigation proceeded. The majority said the Administration was likely to prevail in arguing that the preservation group had not demonstrated the concrete harm needed to sue.
“It’s the same thing,” Stander said.
Chutkan, however, said that the two legal battles remain distinct in nature.
“The ballroom case differs in significant respects,” she said, pointing to traffic and public safety concerns from plaintiffs in the case.
Chutkan also raised skepticism around the Administration’s justification of national security and pointed out how when Trump announced the arch, its purpose was initially posited as celebrating the country’s 250th anniversary. “This is the first time the government has proffered a national security aspect to this case,” she said.
The arch dispute adds to a broader debate over the Administration’s frequent use of national security to justify its policies.
Beyond defending the White House ballroom and triumphal arch on national security grounds, the Trump Administration has invoked national security to justify pausing offshore wind development, barring journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House, and exempting oil and gas activities in the Gulf of Mexico from certain Endangered Species Act requirements.
The golf-course litigation raises a related question about congressional authority: Plaintiffs there have also argued that federal law requires Congress’s express authorization to erect structures on federal public grounds in Washington.
For now, the immediate question is whether a court will intervene before construction can begin as early as the coming week.

Major Iranian singers, orchestras take stage across country this week

According to information published on official ticket sales platforms, the performances are taking place at concert halls, cultural venues and large stadiums, with further events scheduled throughout the coming days.

Iranian team makes IDFA 2026 trailer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
19:24:09 UTC
04:24:09 KST

Iranian team makes IDFA 2026 trailer
TEHRAN – The official campaign trailer for the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA) 2026 has been made by an Iranian team.
Following the success of the film “A Fox Under a Pink Moon” co-directed by Mehrdad Oskouei and Soraya Akhlaghi at IDFA 2025, its makers were invited to create this year’s festival campaign trailer, ISNA reported.
In the making of the trailer, the filmmakers are accompanied by editor Mohammad Babaee and composer Afshin Azizi.
“From our first conversations with the IDFA team, we shared a vision of creating something beyond a festival trailer — a piece reflecting the urgent concerns of our time: peace, women, children, and hope for a better future,” Azizi wrote in a post on social media.
“At a time when war and violence continue to affect millions of lives around the world, we wanted to create something that speaks of humanity, compassion, and hope through images, animation, music, and sound,” he added. “Collaborating with IDFA, a festival we have always considered a home for documentary filmmakers worldwide, has been a truly special experience”.
Since 2022, IDFA has invited artists from its community to develop the festival’s visual campaign, offering their personal interpretation of IDFA and exploring the relationship between art, documentary, and the world.
For the 2026 edition, this artistic dialogue continues with director Mehrdad Oskouei and co-director Soraya Akhlaghi of “A Fox Under a Pink Moon,” winner of the IDFA Award for Best Film in the International Competition of 2025. Their collaboration extends the conversation that began with the film, in which Soraya’s drawings became a way of navigating memory, displacement, and conflict.
A joint production of Iran, France, the UK, Denmark, and the US, the 76-minute documentary had its world premiere at the festival and won its first international award.
The movie shows 16-year-old Soraya, who is already creating stunning drawings and sculptures that are as beautiful as they are dark. This strong-willed Afghan sculptor and illustrator has been trying for five years to leave Iran and join her mother in Austria.
At the heart of this year’s festival campaign is a visual transformation. The trailer brings together fragments from documentaries previously screened at IDFA: images that bear witness to destruction, migration, and the lasting impact of conflict. But these images do not remain unchanged. Soraya draws directly on them, transforming scenes of violence and devastation through her own visual language. Her illustrations do not attempt to conceal or erase reality. Instead, they respond to it, creating space for another way of looking.
An image of destruction can give rise to an unexpected gesture of beauty. Through drawing and animation, documentary images become canvases for imagination, connecting memory and the present, destruction and hope. This approach echoes a central idea in A Fox Under a Pink Moon: that art can reshape our relationship to the world without denying its realities. Soraya’s work acknowledges violence and suffering while insisting that beauty, tenderness and hope can exist alongside them.
The making of the campaign itself reflects the realities at its heart. It became a patchwork of international collaborations, created across borders, time zones and vastly different circumstances.
Soraya worked on the campaign from the refugee accommodation where she currently lives in Berlin, while Mehrdad coordinated the project from France. Composer Afshin Azizi created the score from the Netherlands, while editor Mohammad Babaee assembled the trailer from Iran. Soraya’s drawings were brought to life by Ukrainian animator Alina Milkina, working from Kyiv as the city continued to endure Russian bombardments.
The campaign is therefore not simply a work about war, displacement, and resilience – it is also shaped by these realities. Its creators bring their own experiences of migration, conflict, and distance into the process. Together, they demonstrate the connections that art can create, even when physical borders make connection difficult.
Emotionally, the trailer moves through four interconnected states: war, devastation, migration, and hope. Rather than presenting them as a linear journey, the campaign allows these experiences to overlap and coexist, reflecting the complexity of contemporary life. Documentary images become starting points for imagination. Drawings interrupt and transform them. Animation gives them movement and new meaning. The result is not an attempt to make difficult realities more palatable, but an invitation to look at them differently.
According to the IDFA website, in many ways, this reflects what IDFA strives to be. Documentary cinema confronts us with reality, while also creating a space in which images can be questioned, shared, and transformed through dialogue. This year’s campaign embodies that belief. Art cannot undo violence, but it can change the way we look at it. And by changing how we look, it can help us imagine what might come next.
IDFA is a leading international documentary institute that provides a space for exchange, collaboration, and inspiration—bringing together filmmakers, artists, audiences, and professionals from around the world.
Its broad scope includes a public festival of films and new media, funding initiatives, markets, talent development, and education programs—alongside a year-round documentary hub in Amsterdam’s Vondelpark.

Iranian strikes damage 274 structures at 24 US-linked military sites
TEHRAN- Iran’s retaliatory missile and drone strikes have damaged at least 274 structures at 24 US-linked military installations across the Middle East, with estimated repair costs reaching as high as $15 billion, according to a report based on satellite imagery and US officials.
The Wall Street Journal analysis documents extensive damage to American military facilities, including buildings, radar systems, missile defenses and communications infrastructure. The attacks have also forced the evacuation and relocation of US personnel, exposing vulnerabilities in Washington’s regional military network.
The Pentagon has estimated the damage to American military facilities at a minimum of $5 billion, while a separate assessment has placed the figure as high as $15 billion. The Center for Strategic and International Studies has estimated that rebuilding damaged buildings alone would cost more than $4 billion, excluding the replacement of military equipment and internal systems.
The scale of the destruction underscores the impact of Iran’s sustained retaliatory campaign, launched after the US-Israeli aggression against Iran began on February 28.
During the first two weeks of the war, Iranian strikes damaged at least 119 buildings at 13 US military installations, mostly in Kuwait, according to satellite imagery reviewed by the Journal.
 
Naval Support Activity Bahrain, which serves as the headquarters of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, was among the most heavily damaged facilities. The attacks forced the evacuation of most personnel stationed there.
Iranian strikes also damaged more than 15 components of critical infrastructure protecting American military installations, including radar, missile-defense, and communications systems.
The attacks inflicted casualties on US forces as well. More than 20 American service members were killed in incidents related to the war, while more than 400 were wounded before the US military suspended conflict-specific casualty reporting following a temporary ceasefire.
Targeting of troop accommodation
After the ceasefire collapsed on July 7, Iran’s targeting strategy increasingly focused on facilities housing American troops.
On July 17, an Iranian strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan killed three US service members and damaged at least 19 buildings used to accommodate military personnel.
Satellite imagery also revealed damage to smaller buildings at several other installations, suggesting a growing focus on troop accommodation and other facilities associated with the presence of American forces.
The sustained attacks have compelled Washington to relocate additional personnel, including through large-scale evacuations from Camp Buehring and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait.
US officials have also considered relocating military infrastructure farther from Iran’s reach and reducing the American military presence at installations in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia.
Pentagon faces scrutiny over damage estimates
The extent of the destruction has prompted criticism of the Pentagon’s limited disclosure of damage to US military facilities.
Lawmakers have demanded public estimates of the financial costs, as the scale of the damage raises questions about the vulnerability of American military infrastructure across the region.
Meanwhile, Iran has continued restoring damaged military infrastructure and recovering buried missile stockpiles, developments that have heightened concerns in Washington about Tehran’s ability to sustain its strike capabilities.
The reported damage across 24 installations highlights the challenges facing US forces in maintaining their regional military network amid Iran’s continued missile and drone operations.

'We came back from hell', say Ukrainians after years in Russia-occupied front-line city
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
19:22:26 GMT
04:22:26 KST

'We came back from hell', say Ukrainians after years in Russia-occupied front-line city
- Published
- Warning: This story contains graphic content.
Olha has one word to describe what life has been like in the front-line city of Oleshky over the past few years: "Horror".
Disembarking alongside her from a coach in the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv with their immediate family and dog, her husband Viacheslav put it this way: "We came back from hell."
The couple were among hundreds of residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city who crossed into northern Ukraine via Belarus on Saturday, many reuniting with loved ones they had not seen for years.
Oleshky, seized by Russia during the first few days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River and on the other side by Russian forces.
Olha and Viacheslav had lived there with their son and daughter, both in their 30s. Even as the shelling around them intensified, they feared that trying to escape could be even more dangerous, with routes mined and subject to drone attack.
As supplies dwindled, the couple said they made an attempt to find food by crossing through minefields earlier this month. "People were stepping on mines, dying and being maimed, all just to survive," Olha told the BBC.
Those who were too afraid to go out in the city had resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive.
"We saw that the situation wasn't getting any better, so we realised we had to get out," Olha said.
That opportunity came earlier this week when a humanitarian ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, took effect in the Kherson region, providing the first few days of peace in the area for four years and allowing Oleshky residents to evacuate.
Up to 6,000 people, including 200 children, were believed to still be living in Oleshky and its surrounding areas, with 1,700 in the city itself.
Residents had a four-hour window on Friday to leave, with a convoy of 25 buses brought in for up to 750 evacuees, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
After travelling through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, then flying to Belarus, evacuees arrived on buses to a military facility in Chernihiv on Saturday.
On the tarmac, where evacuees were processed before travelling onwards, some elderly residents were so weak they had to be carried on stretchers.
For many, there were emotional reunions.
As Mykhailo Palii arrived, his daughters Dasha and Anya, who thought they might never see him again, sprinted across the tarmac screaming and crying.
After an emotional embrace, Palii described a glimpse of life in Oleshky, although he said he had, until then, kept many of the details from his family.
"A hole was blown into the bathroom," he said. "There were drone attacks and missile strikes. It happened, but I didn't tell them about it because I knew they would worry."
Tetiana and Volodymyr, a couple carrying a cat when they arrived in Chernihiv, said their entire home was burned down three years ago, and they had been living in the abandoned house of a neighbour since.
For them, leaving as soon as it was safe to do so was an easy decision. "There's nothing for us to regret leaving. We don't have relatives there. Our children are married and don't live with us in the city," said Tetiana.
But those who managed to escape also worry about those left behind. "There are still a lot of people left there, living under those conditions," said Olha.
Now that the evacuees have left Oleshky, they will also face a new challenge - working out where to go next and how to rebuild their lives.
Palii said he would look for a job so he can provide for his family: "There's no job I can't handle. Digging, hoeing, planting, building. I can even do demolition work."
Olha said she and her family have no relatives elsewhere in Ukraine, and they will stay with some acquaintances for an extended period while they get back on their feet.
"If we managed to survive in hell, we'll survive here too."

Canada’s support for UAE claim to Iranian islands violates UN Charter, Tehran says
TEHRAN — Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei has condemned Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s support for the United Arab Emirates’ claim to three Iranian islands in the Persian Gulf, describing Ottawa’s position as a blatant contradiction and a violation of the principles enshrined in the United Nations Charter.

On October 29, Baqaei also issued a statement condemning Ottawa’s interference, albeit in different terms.

“The UAE was established in 1971. Baqaei said Canada, more than most countries, should understand the importance of respecting national sovereignty and territorial integrity, given its own historical experience.
He cited the US invasion of Canada during the War of 1812, the Montreal Annexation Manifesto of 1849, and, more recently, US President Donald Trump’s remarks about making Canada the “51st state” of the United States.
Against that backdrop, the Iranian spokesman questioned the consistency of Ottawa’s position, asking whether respect for territorial integrity and historical and legal facts was a fundamental principle for Canada or one it upheld only when its own sovereignty was at stake.
He described Canada’s support for the UAE position as deeply contradictory, arguing that a country that has defended its territorial integrity for centuries should not endorse an 'unfounded territorial claim' against another nation.
Such a stance, Baqaei warned, amounted to “sawing off the very branch on which it sits.”

Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky have been reunited with their families after crossing into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday.

Relatives and volunteers with the Red Cross, Médecins Sans Frontières and World Central Kitchen welcomed the evacuees as they arrived at the border, ready to provide aid and food, including for their pets.
Holding a cigarette between shaking fingers, 48-year-old Ivan Yevhenovych described his last months in Oleshky. “It was very difficult. There were a lot of drones. It was hard to move around the streets,” he said. “Since spring, there hasn’t really been any staple food left. People had a little bit of their own reserves. We are thrifty people.”
He said landmines or drone strikes were killing residents every day.
An estimated 2,000 people remained in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of being evacuated to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
“Many people stayed behind and didn’t want to leave,” Yevhenovych said. “Some for their houses, some for their animals.”
Ukrainian authorities, seeking to protect those who remained and safeguard future humanitarian missions, have not said how many residents evacuated Oleshky and have restricted details of their route. Melania Trump posted on social media on Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
Liza Paliy, 19, waited at the border for her father, whom she last saw more than two and a half years earlier when she fled the occupied city with her mother and sister. “We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately two years have already passed,” she said.
Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, hailed the humanitarian mission as a win.
“This is an extremely important moment. Behind us are difficult negotiations, agreements, preparations, and an enormous amount of work. But most importantly, the people who waited so long to be rescued are finally safe,” he said in an online post.
Lubinets said evacuees ranged in age from just over one year old to 94, and they brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon. He said he hoped the Oleshky truce could be replicated elsewhere, saying it “could form the basis of a new mechanism for responding to the most difficult humanitarian crises”.
Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner, said both sides have agreed to conduct regular humanitarian missions in and around Oleshky. Lubinets did not mention this development.
“The mission has concluded, but, unfortunately, living conditions in Oleshky remain extremely difficult,” she said. “We will make every effort to support those residents who have made the decision to stay.”
Some Oleshky evacuees who chose to move to Russian-occupied territory were taken to a temporary shelter in Simferopol, Lantratova said. The city is in Ukraine’s Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
“After everything they have endured and a long journey, it is essential for these people to rest, recover and feel cared for. However, support should not be limited to just a roof over their heads and a hot meal,” she said in a social media post.
A Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia’s western Bryansk region, the local governor, Yegor Kovalchuk, said on Saturday. Five others were wounded, he said.
Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region’s capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.
The Russian defence ministry said on Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.

Finland’s Stubb defends calling Putin
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has defended the phone conversation he and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store had with Russian leader Vladimir Putin earlier this week following criticism from some Moscow hawks in Europe.
The two Nordic leaders made the rare phone call on Tuesday, with discussions focusing mainly on the Ukraine conflict, as well as security in Northern Europe and the Baltic Sea. The conversation followed US special envoy Steve Witkoff’s meeting with Putin in St. Petersburg last week and subsequent consultations in Oslo involving Stubb, Store, and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky.
Both Moscow and Kiev have since agreed to take part in a fourth round of US-mediated trilateral talks that is expected to take place in Abu Dhabi in November, with European countries excluded from the peace process, according to the Kremlin.
Appearing on Yle’s Ykkosaamu (Morning One) program on Saturday, Stubb noted that Tuesday’s call was the first time since becoming Finland’s president that he had spoken with Putin. Stubb emphasized the importance of hearing firsthand the Russian leader’s view of the root causes of the Ukraine conflict, describing the direct exchange of opinions as a “turning point.”
Stubb said he and Store reopened the “channel of communication” with Moscow at Kiev’s request and relayed Zelensky’s messages to Putin after consultations with US and Ukrainian representatives.
He emphasized, however, that Helsinki was “not acting as any kind of peace mediator here.”
Both Nordic leaders earlier specifically pointed out that they were not speaking on behalf of Europe.
The Finnish president clarified that aside from the Ukraine conflict, he and Store brought up the security of their respective countries, which both share an extensive border with Russia.
Among other things, the two Nordic leaders used the opportunity to “clear up some misunderstandings” regarding the Baltic Sea, reaffirming their adherence to international maritime law and the principle of freedom of navigation.
Stubb defended what he described as the “first confidence-building measure” by noting that “Russia is our neighbor now and will remain our neighbor in the future,” with bilateral relations liable to resume at one point.
In the wake of their call with Putin, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen accused the two Nordic leaders of breaking European ranks, claiming the conversation had “not been coordinated with the rest of us” – an objection echoed by Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson.
Responding to these criticisms, Stubb stressed that he and Store extensively briefed Zelensky and multiple EU leaders afterward.
Most Western European leaders shunned direct contact with Moscow after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022 in an attempt to diplomatically isolate Russia. However, in recent weeks they have mounted an effort to secure a seat at the negotiation table as Moscow and Washington ramp up diplomatic work aimed at resolving the conflict.
Commenting on his phone conversation with the two Nordic leaders, Putin stated on Thursday that Russia supported “any steps aimed at restoring full-fledged and comprehensive relations” with European countries.
“After all, there are people in Europe who, unlike some others, do not want to inflict a ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia but instead want to establish some kind of constructive dialogue,” the Russian president explained.
He also reiterated that Moscow is not seeking a broader conflict with the EU or NATO.

VP orders formation of five specialized committees to prepare for ECO summit in Tehran
TEHRAN — First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref has ordered the formation of five specialized committees, covering cultural, tourism, diplomatic, economic, and political affairs, to coordinate preparations for hosting the upcoming summit of the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) in Tehran at the highest possible level.
Aref issued the directive on Saturday, October 31, during a meeting on preparations for the summit, emphasizing that the gathering should serve as an opportunity to strengthen regional cooperation and restore the ECO to its appropriate position among regional organizations.
He said expanding engagement and relations with neighboring and regional countries was a key strategy of the administration, particularly President Masoud Pezeshkian, adding that Iran had made considerable progress in this regard.
According to Aref, Iran's growing engagement with regional countries reflects both the president's approach to foreign relations and the performance of government institutions, as well as the readiness of regional nations to expand cooperation with the Islamic Republic.
Referring to Iran's participation in regional organizations and economic groupings, the first vice president said the country had established an active and effective presence in institutions such as the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU).
He noted that Iran's position within these organizations had improved considerably compared with previous years, with more substantive engagement and cooperation taking shape among member states.
Aref also stressed the importance of hosting the ECO summit in Tehran, saying Iran's experience in organizing regional and international gatherings had demonstrated that the country achieved significant diplomatic successes when serving as host. Officials from participating countries, he added, had generally left such meetings with a positive impression of Iran, with the benefits of the country's hosting efforts continuing to be reflected in subsequent regional gatherings.
ECO summit an opportunity to revive regional cooperation
Addressing the organization's performance, Aref expressed concern that the ECO, initially established through the cooperation of Iran, Pakistan and Türkiye, had not fulfilled its regional potential despite expanding to 10 member states.
He said leaders of member countries also emphasized the need to broaden the organization's activities and strengthen cooperation so that the ECO could regain its appropriate standing in the region.
The first vice president pointed to the growing bilateral relations among ECO members and their cooperation through other regional organizations, saying these developments had created favorable conditions for deeper collaboration within the ECO framework.
He emphasized that the member countries share extensive historical, cultural, and civilizational ties with Iran, providing a strong foundation for expanding regional partnerships.
Aref described the upcoming summit as an important opportunity to make up for shortcomings in the organization's performance over the past four decades and establish a clearer vision for its future.
He also noted that regional conditions had become more conducive to cooperation, with countries in Central Asia, the Caucasus and regions east of Iran showing greater readiness to expand relations with Tehran.
Five committees to coordinate summit preparations
Emphasizing the need for comprehensive and well-coordinated preparations, Aref said the summit's agenda and organizational arrangements should be developed according to clearly defined priorities.
He identified tourism, science and technology, cybersecurity and trade as important areas of cooperation among ECO member states, calling for particular attention to these sectors in the summit's planning and agenda.
The first vice president stressed that the gathering should go beyond a formal diplomatic event and provide a practical framework for upgrading relations and strengthening regional cooperation among member countries.
Following the presentations, Aref ordered the establishment of five specialized committees on cultural, tourism, diplomatic, economic and political affairs, each to be chaired by the relevant minister, to oversee and coordinate the necessary preparations.
The Economic Cooperation Organization is a regional intergovernmental organization established in 1985 by Iran, Pakistan and Türkiye, succeeding the Regional Cooperation for Development (RCD) framework founded in 1964.
Its membership subsequently expanded to 10 countries with the accession of Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan in 1992.
The organization seeks to promote sustainable economic development, facilitate trade by gradually removing barriers, strengthen transport and communications networks, and advance cooperation in human resource development among its member states. Its headquarters are in Tehran, and English is its official language.
The ECO brings together Iran, Pakistan, Türkiye, Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

Ukrainian marines have shown off a Turkish automatic grenade launcher that was rebuilt in response to soldiers' complaints about older models, from a simpler sight to a smoother ammunition feed. The 42nd Separate Marine Brigade released a video of its crews preparing and firing the 40mm RDS40-AGL, made by the Turkish company REPKON Defence.
The launcher is one of the less common foreign systems in Ukrainian hands, first shown in 2022 and designed with the weak points of earlier grenade launchers in mind. Its value here is less as a new piece of kit than as the brigade's own reminder that hardware is only as good as the crew trained to run it.
The flaws the designers set out to fix
Turkish engineers have built the weapon after studying how earlier grenade-launcher systems had fallen short in the field, the brigade said.
They simplified the mechanical sight, reducing the number of small parts that are easy to damage or misalign.
They reworked the ammunition feed to reduce the risk of stoppages while firing and moving, and redesigned the controls to fit better under the gunner's hands.
The aim, according to the maker, is a launcher that is easier to use and service right where it is fired.
Why the brigade says what matters more than the weapon
The 42nd brigade framed the demonstration as the opposite of a sales pitch. Even the most refined weapon, it says, is no substitute for a trained crew, which is why its marines are drilling not only the launcher itself but the coordination that decides whether it works in a fight.
Earlier, the Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps upgraded its kamikaze ground drones with grenade launchers during Operation Vivaldi in Donetsk Oblast. The Bullspikes, used in the offensive, were developed from the Soviet RPG-22 anti-tank grenade launcher, which was previously manufactured under license by a Bulgarian defense company.

Senegal kicks off Africa's first ever Olympics with Youth Games
The 2026 Youth Olympic Games opened on Saturday in the Senegalese capital Dakar in the first ever Olympics to be held on African soil. It comes as the continent seeks a bigger role in international sporting competitions.

The 2026 Youth Olympic Games opened in Senegal on Saturday, the first Olympic event in Africa as the continent seeks a bigger role in international sports competitions.
Tens of thousands of spectators cheered on the opening ceremony in the Diamniadio Olympic Stadium near the capital Dakar. Hundreds of drummers and dancers celebrated Senegalese and African culture in line with the Games motto, “Africa welcomes, Dakar celebrates".
Watch moreOlympic fever grips Senegal as Dakar hosts Youth Olympic Games
A giant map of Africa was created by performers dressed in yellow, black and white traditional Senegalese gowns, dancing in unison, in a grandiose ceremony that saw West African oral storytelling, a concert by Senegalese singer Obree Daman and athletes parading.
Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye declared the Games open.
“This is a historic event and it was so important for me to be here,” said Aby Diouf, 25, a Senegalese spectator at the stadium. “It’s a marvellous celebration and we are all here to bring the energy and get people hyped."
About 2,700 athletes aged 14 to 17 will compete through November 13 in the Dakar, the nearby city of Diamniadio and the beach resort of Saly.
Watch moreFirst Youth Olympic Games in Africa
Russia’s delegation of 13 athletes is competing under its national flag for the first time at an Olympic event since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 led to its suspension.
The first refugee team at a Youth Olympics will field six athletes based in Kenya and Uganda in track and field, judo and taekwondo.
Athletes overall will compete in 153 medal events across 25 sports.
Singapore hosted the first summer Youth Games in 2010. Dakar was initially due to host in 2022 but the coronavirus pandemic delayed the Games.
Watch moreKenya's female athletes make their mark as Youth Olympic Games approach
“This is a historic moment for Senegal, for Africa and for our entire Olympic family” IOC President Kirsty Coventry said at the opening ceremony. Coventry, a former swimming gold medalist from Zimbabwe, became the first female and African boss of the International Olympic Committee last year.
The Games come as African countries increasingly see sports as a tool for diplomacy and development, analysts say.
South Africa hosted the continent’s first soccer FIFA World Cup in 2010. Morocco will co-host the 2030 tournament with Spain and Portugal. Rwanda hosted Africa’s first road cycling world championships last year and Formula 1 is returning to Africa with a grand prix in Rwanda early next decade. Botswana also staged the World Athletics Relays in May.

International artists and intellectuals call for protection of Iranian civilians
TEHRAN — A group of artists, writers, academics and cultural figures from various countries has called for the protection of Iranian civilians and unrestricted access to humanitarian assistance, stressing that ordinary people must not bear the cost of political and military objectives.
In a collective opinion article published by the French newspaper Le Monde on October 27, the signatories expressed deep concern over the consequences of the war in Iran, which resumed in September, and its growing impact on civilian populations.
“Whatever our political views, we believe that civilians must not be the ones to bear the heaviest burden of war,” the statement said.
The signatories urged all parties involved in the conflict to respect international humanitarian law and ensure that military and political measures do not deprive civilians of food, medicine, fuel and other essential supplies.
They also stressed that humanitarian assistance must remain accessible to those in need.
The appeal, which brings together prominent figures from the worlds of literature, cinema, philosophy, academia and the arts, explicitly distinguishes its humanitarian message from political or military endorsements.
“This appeal does not constitute support for any government, political movement or military force,” the statement said, describing its purpose as the protection of human life and the dignity of ordinary people.
The signatories emphasized that the Iranian people, like all civilians affected by armed conflict, must not be made to pay the price for political and military objectives.
They called for the protection of civilians, the prevention of further suffering, and respect for the fundamental value of human life.
Among the signatories are Iranian-American historian Ervand Abrahamian, Iranian scholar Arshin Adib-Moghaddam, Nobel laureates Annie Ernaux and J. M. Coetzee, German filmmaker Fatih Akin, American writer Jonathan Franzen, Indian-born American author Jhumpa Lahiri and Indian artist Anish Kapoor.
The statement also bears the signatures of Iranian journalist and writer Rozhin Hosseini, Iranian writer Karim Nikoonazar and Iranian-American historian Golnar Nikpour.
The collective appeal comes amid renewed hostilities between Iran and the United States, highlighting the importance of safeguarding civilian lives and ensuring that humanitarian needs remain separate from political and military considerations.

America’s next battlefield innovation: Preparing the graves before the war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
19:05:42 UTC
04:05:42 KST

America’s next battlefield innovation: Preparing the graves before the war
TEHRAN - America's military supremacy apparently comes with a new logistical priority: making sure there are enough graves when the bombs stop falling. As Washington continues to promise victory in its next great confrontation, the US Army is busy rehearsing how to bury the casualties. One wonders whether Americans were ever told this was part of the plan.
Washington has spent years assuring the world that the United States possesses the most powerful military on earth. Its aircraft carriers, stealth bombers, precision missiles and global network of bases are routinely presented as proof that no adversary could seriously challenge American power. Now, however, the US Army is rehearsing a rather less glamorous capability: digging temporary graves for large numbers of its own dead.
According to an October 26 report by Army Times, American soldiers recently took part in an exercise in North Carolina to test how quickly battlefield burial trenches could be excavated and filled while preserving remains for later identification and repatriation. The exercise, known as Phase II of Operation Dragon Covenant, brought together engineers, medical personnel, chaplains and specialists in fatality management. It was not a routine lesson in cemetery maintenance. It was preparation for a future high-intensity conflict in which the United States might be unable to retrieve its fallen.
The figures are especially difficult to ignore. Army doctrine envisages temporary interment plots consisting of five parallel trenches, each designed to accommodate 100 bodies. During the latest exercise, D6 bulldozers were used to excavate a trench for 20 remains in an average of one hour and 15 minutes. Based on the results, the Army said an appropriately equipped engineer company could dig and cover trenches for as many as 2,400 bodies in 24 hours—provided it operated nonstop.
Two thousand four hundred. In a single day. One hopes the Pentagon's public-relations department will forgive the observation that this is an unusually grim performance metric for an institution supposedly dedicated to winning wars.
The Army says air superiority in Iraq and Afghanistan allowed fallen personnel to be transported home through established channels. A future conflict against a capable adversary may look different: airfields, transport routes and evacuation networks could be contested or destroyed, making temporary burial unavoidable until the dead can be recovered.
That is a sober logistical assessment, but it exposes the gap between Washington's rhetoric of power and the realities its military is preparing to face. The question is not only whether the United States can strike thousands of miles away, but whether it can protect its forces and bring them home when the other side fights back.
American interventions have often been sold through images of technological superiority and promises of swift outcomes. Their human costs have fallen on service members, their families and civilians in the countries where wars were fought. A large-scale conflict with a peer adversary, however, could mean sustained fighting, disrupted logistics and casualties on a scale unseen in the post-2001 American experience.
The Army Times report does not predict that 2,400 Americans will die in a day, nor does the exercise prove that such a war is imminent. The number is a planning capacity, not a casualty forecast. But planning for a contingency is itself revealing: military institutions devote resources to scenarios they consider serious enough to prepare for. And the Army is not merely discussing how to evacuate the wounded. It is testing how to bury the dead when evacuation is impossible.
Even the details are chilling. Existing guidance on the spacing between trenches proved too narrow for bulldozers to pass without disturbing them, requiring changes to doctrine. Chaplains also considered how to consecrate a site when individual services cannot be provided and the dead people's identities or faiths may be unknown. Ensuring dignity is humane; the conditions being anticipated are not.
American families should ask how their country arrived at a point where the Army is refining the geometry and operating speed of temporary mass burial sites. What political decisions could produce a war in which air superiority is no longer assured, evacuation routes are vulnerable and thousands of casualties must be managed near the battlefield? Who would explain to parents, spouses and children that the return of a loved one has been postponed because the war planners failed to anticipate the enemy's ability to strike back?
The bitter irony is that a political culture treating military force as an instrument of limitless influence can be casual about its limits. A powerful military can destroy infrastructure and project power across oceans; it cannot guarantee victory against an adversary able to impose costs or deny it freedom of action. Superior weapons do not abolish geography, logistics or human vulnerability.
Perhaps the most important message of Operation Dragon Covenant is not about bulldozers or burial procedures. It is that the Pentagon is planning for a future in which the United States may not control the skies, the routes or the pace of escalation. Before Washington contemplates another confrontation, Americans might reasonably ask their leaders a simple question: if the Army is already calculating how to bury thousands, what exactly are the politicians calculating about the cost of the war?

Breadcrumb
Israel's restrictions on reporters shielding settler violence, activist says
Russian activist Adele Shoko has warned that a ban preventing her and fellow campaigner Andrey X and US journalist Jasper Nathaniel from reporting in the occupied West Bank raises serious concerns over press freedom and the documentation of abuses against Palestinians.
The restrictions were imposed by Israeli authorities following an attack by armed settlers on Shoko, Andrey X and Nathaniel in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair, in the Masafer Yatta area of the occupied West Bank, on Wednesday.
Organisations such as Peace Now have repeatedly raised concerns about the safety of residents in Umm al-Khair, a Palestinian community in the southern occupied West Bank surrounded by Israeli settlements and military bases.
They have warned that residents face settler violence and harassment, while accusing Israeli authorities of failing to provide even basic protection and allowing such actions to continue.
Speaking to The New Arab on Saturday, Shoko said the trio had been beaten and verbally threatened by settlers, including Tomer Liani, an Israeli settler from the Havat Maon outpost.
She also said that equipment and personal belongings were stolen during the attack, which she documented on social media.
Following a court hearing attended by Andrey X and Nathaniel, both of whom had been arrested and accused by Israeli forces of assaulting the settlers, Shoko said the activists had been barred from entering the West Bank for two months.
She warned that the restrictions could significantly affect their ability to document abuses against Palestinians.
"[Liani] basically almost killed Andrey, threatened to shoot him multiple times," Shoko told The New Arab. "He injured me and I still have an injury. I can't use my left hand. He stole my phone, he stole my glasses, and I was basically blind throughout the attack."
She continued: "So all of that happened and the settler wasn't punished. But for some reason we were punished and now we can't do our work."
Shoko said she and her colleagues remained uncertain about what would happen next, despite Andrey X and Nathaniel reportedly having been cleared of all charges following their brief detention.
"I want to say that we still don't know what will happen to us because not only we were banned, but also we have another interrogation [on Sunday]. We're still being interrogated," she told The New Arab.
Shoko believes the visibility she and her colleagues have gained through their social media reporting on escalating settler violence since the start of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza has made them targets for Israeli authorities.
She warned that restrictions on their ability to enter the West Bank and report on Palestinian communities could have wider consequences.
"We genuinely believe that Israel is after us, and I'll explain why," she said. "Andrey was arrested before that, and it was also very widely reported incident where Israel brought 12 soldiers and seven police officers to arrest one person."
Shoko added: "If not for the amount of attention that the world is giving to us and what is happening to us, we would be in Israeli jail."
She argued that international attention had helped protect them from further targeting, saying: "The reason why they don't want to do this to us, because there will be protests around the world. Because people right now are getting information about the occupation from us, and they know that we're in essential to this fight."
But Shoko stressed that Palestinian journalists continue to face threats and detention for documenting abuses in the occupied West Bank.
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) has condemned attacks against Palestinian and foreign journalists in the territory, including incidents involving Israeli settlers during the olive harvest season.
"It's getting scary to do our work, especially during the olive harvest, because it's becoming a big problem that we are showing this escalation of violence that was happening before the [Israeli] elections and actually continues to happen," Shoko told The New Arab.
"There are multiple job Palestinian journalists who are in jail right now on administrative detention," she said.
She continued: "And administrative detention means that they don't have any charges and they can [detain] them for as long as they want."
"And we need to put pressure on that. I have also at least three friends that were targeted by [Israeli forces] in the past month and were also taken away and their houses were raided."
With the future of her reporting work uncertain following Wednesday's attack, Shoko urged the international community to maintain its attention on the occupied West Bank.
She said she hoped to return to what she considers an essential part of her work as an activist: documenting abuses and standing alongside Palestinian communities.
She insisted that the focus should remain on the Palestinians affected by settler violence, rather than solely on the activists who were attacked.
"What happened in Umm al-Khair isn't just about us. It's way more about what Palestinians in this village is where it happened and going through," Shoko said.
"The settler violence and what Palestinians in this village are going through such control over their freedom and their basic rights is what we should talk about."
Shoko added that greater international solidarity on the ground could provide both protection and reassurance to Palestinian communities.
"Palestinians will be happy to see more people on the ground who will stand with them," she told The New Arab.
"This solidarity is not only a protective presence because we are staying with communities and using our privilege to stand between the occupation and Palestinian citizens. But it also gives them hope."

Immediate, effective, with no geographical limitation
Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei outlines Iran’s response strategy to a possible next enemy attack in a meeting with senior military commanders.
TEHRAN — Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, the Leader and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, held a meeting with senior commanders of the Iranian Armed Forces, in which he laid out Iran’s doctrine for responding to any renewed military or terrorist aggression.
During the meeting, the Commander-in-Chief emphasized that intelligent combat readiness for a powerful confrontation with enemies is a fundamental prerequisite for achieving maximum deterrence. He decreed that any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response.
Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei stated that should Iran’s enemies resume military or terrorist attacks, it will be the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine when and under what conditions those attacks will end.
The Commander-in-Chief further underscored the need to strengthen military intelligence architecture, deepen indigenous defense capabilities in both “doctrine” and “tactics,” and enhance modernized defense and security capacities through the utilization of emerging technologies. He also highlighted the importance of strengthening spiritual foundations and the spirit of jihad, alongside unremitting efforts to meet the livelihood needs of Armed Forces personnel and provide them with the necessary support.
All US-Zionist assets within reach
In another directive, the Commander-in-Chief ordered the comprehensive updating of the military target database to ensure that all kinds of physical and non-physical assets of the US-Zionist enemy are brought within the reach of the Armed Forces.
He described nationwide support for the Armed Forces as one of the pillars of deterrence against anti-Iranian foreign powers and their domestic mercenaries. He added that the eight-month presence of a nation that has risen up in Iran’s public squares is a continuation of the Eight-Year Sacred Defense, which, alongside the steadfastness of the military, police, and Basij forces, has protected, and will continue to protect, the territorial integrity of Iran and the Islamic system.
The Leader of the Islamic Revolution expressed his appreciation for the intelligent steadfastness of the Resistance Front in various countries. He described the “unity of fronts” as a decisive factor with a strategic impact on shaping the new political and security order in West Asia. He further expressed hope that this new order will increasingly lay the groundwork for unity among Muslim nations and governments and the formation of the New Islamic Civilization.
During the meeting with the Commander-in-Chief, Major General Abdollahi, Chief of the Joint Staff of Iran’s Armed Forces, Major General Hatami, Commander-in-Chief of the Army, and Major General Vahidi, Commander-in-Chief of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), presented reports on the high readiness status of the country’s defenders along the Persian Gulf coast, in the operational areas of the Strait of Hormuz and the Sea of Oman, and along the country’s northwestern and southeastern borders. They also briefed the Leader of the Islamic Revolution on the multi-fold increase in the production of various types of key munitions and reconnaissance, support, and combat weapons.
Expressing his satisfaction with the measures taken, the Commander-in-Chief asked the senior military commanders to convey his gratitude and profound appreciation to all military, police, and Basij forces, the personnel of these organizations, and the dedicated staff of the Ministry of Defense and their esteemed families.
NATO’s admitted role and Iran’s recorded protest
The doctrine of an unrestricted response comes against a documented record of direct and indirect foreign participation in the US-Israeli war against Iran launched on Feb. 28.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has twice openly acknowledged the alliance’s role in supporting the American operation, saying the United States would not have been able to carry out the operation without NATO and without Europe as a platform for projecting US power. Rutte said thousands of US military planes — up to 5,000 sorties — operated from bases in Europe during the war.
Iran reacted at the time through legal and diplomatic channels. Iran’s ambassador and charge d’affaires to the United Nations, in a letter to the UN Secretary General and the Security Council, described Rutte’s remarks as contrary to international law and the UN Charter. The Foreign Ministry spokesman stressed that NATO and its member states, including Italy and Romania — whose roles in the illegal attacks were explicitly acknowledged by the NATO chief — must be held accountable for complicity in US-Israeli crimes against Iran. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also called on European governments to clarify their role in the war.
The analytical conclusion in Tehran today is clear: there is no reason that when certain countries accompany the aggressors against Iran — by providing bases, airspace, fuel, intelligence, or political cover — they should remain immune from its military consequences. Responding to them is Iran’s natural and legal right under the inherent right of self-defense. Any base or facility used to attack Iran is by definition a legitimate military target, and its geographic location does not grant it immunity.
Europe counts €100 billion cost of cheering the war
The price of that accompaniment is now being counted in Europe itself. Germany’s Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Friday in Seoul:
“We now have costs exceeding €100 billion for Europe alone over the last eight months, solely because of the increase in energy prices caused by this conflict. More than €100 billion extra has been paid by businesses and consumers in Europe because energy has become more expensive as a result of this conflict. We have an economic interest in bringing this conflict to an end as quickly as possible.”
Merz added that the conflict cannot be resolved militarily and that Berlin was intensifying diplomatic efforts.
 
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi responded on X:
“When Israel-US bombings of Iran began last year, Mr. Merz hailed them. ‘Doing Europe's dirty work’ 100bn Euro is nothing compared to the Earth-shattering blow Iran's Powerful Armed Forces will deal against those who dare harm our people. Red lines are a thing of the past.”
Merz had hailed the Israeli aggression in June 2025 as “the dirty work Israel is doing for all of us.”
Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei also wrote on X:
“Just yesterday, Europe took pride in the dirty work of the Zionist regime. Today, it’s whining about billions the war with Iran is costing it. When you cheered on war crimes, did you think the fallout wouldn’t hit you, too? War and terror come at a price. Now it’s your turn to pay.”
Updated response plan ready for implementation
In a related development, Al-Mayadeen, citing a senior regional security official, reported that Iran’s updated military response plan to potential attacks has been completed and is ready for implementation.
According to the report: “The decision to deliver a comprehensive and very extensive response is final; a response that could also include the enemy’s installations, centers and political headquarters.”
Taken together — the Commander-in-Chief’s order for an immediate, effective response with no geographical limitation, the completed target bank covering all physical and non-physical assets of the enemy, the documented admission of NATO-European facilitation, and the mounting economic and military costs acknowledged even in Berlin — Tehran’s message is that the next folly will not be answered within the previous limits, nor only within the previous geography.

Submarine berth programme being recovered at Devonport
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
19:01:20 GMT
04:01:20 KST

Ministers have said there are still challenges to delivering the programme rebuilding the submarine berths at Devonport and that the delivery team is working with the assurance authority and the contractor to recover it, according to an answer given in Parliament.
James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat member for Lewes, asked what progress has been made on the Submarine Waterfront Infrastructure Future programme in the context of the delivery confidence assessments for Government Major Project Portfolio defence projects.
Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence, said: “The delivery confidence assessment for the Submarine Waterfront Infrastructure Future (SWIF) programme reflects the likelihood of successful delivery at a specific point in time and the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority (NISTA) Gate Review process is an integral part of the Assurance Framework that the Ministry of Defence has in place to support project delivery.
“Despite positive progress, there are still challenges to the delivery of the SWIF programme. The delivery team is working closely with NISTA and the contractor to recover the programme. The current focus is on the completion of design work, where we have increased the pace of design decisions and streamlined approvals, to enable the start of construction. We have used the principles set out in the Nuclear Regulatory Review as part of these reviews, to identify new opportunities to accelerate work.”
Devonport is the only dockyard in Britain licensed to refit nuclear submarines, and the waterfront infrastructure there handles the Astute class, the decommissioned boats still laid up in the basin, and the deep maintenance periods that keep the attack submarine flotilla available.
Availability in that flotilla has been the subject of repeated criticism, and the Defence Committee reported this month that availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines raises questions about whether Britain can meet its commitments in the High North, and the refit of HMS Vanguard at Devonport ran to seven and a half years against an original plan of three and a half.
The Nuclear Regulatory Review was commissioned to reduce the time regulatory approvals add to nuclear programmes, and its principles are now being applied to the design decisions on the waterfront. Defence has committed more than £2 billion to Devonport infrastructure over the coming decade.
Work at the dockyard runs alongside the Clyde Infrastructure programme at Faslane and Coulport, where ministers declined to give an updated assessment and said the next set of delivery confidence figures will come from information captured on 31 March 2027.

The moment I knew: He loved to travel, I had a fear of flying. I expected him to skol his beer and wish me well
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
19:00:50 UTC
04:00:50 KST

In September 2023 I’d been divorced for about a year. At 59 I thought to myself, “surely there’s got to be a little bit more love that I could give in my life”. But I was also keenly aware that not many people find romance organically these days.
I gave Bumble a go, had some pretty average dates and thought it wasn’t for me, but I decided to give it one last shot. It was Kev’s smile and his eyes that caught my attention. His profile said travel was really important to him, which gave me a bit of a laugh because I have huge anxiety issues around holidaying of any sort. We exchanged a few texts and decided to arrange a date. It was nothing fancy, just a few drinks at a bar in a bayside suburb of Melbourne.
It was all very easy between us, so about half an hour in, not wanting to waste our time, I thought I should make a few disclosures. Firstly I told him that as a divorcee twice over, I obviously wasn’t very good at relationships. He surprised me by saying we were on par there. Then I went on to explain my pathological fear of flying, and that I wouldn’t be a great travel buddy.
I fully expected him to skol his beer and wish me well but instead he asked lots of questions about my anxiety and listened intently before saying: “Well, you don’t need to get on a plane to experience Australia!” I thought that was so nice of him and a little spark lit up in me – if he’s willing to compromise on something so important to him, maybe this could go somewhere.
We caught up the next week, and then he returned home to Newcastle. We stayed in touch and I started to realise you really can learn a lot about a person over the phone. He had a great sense of humour and we were getting along so well, but about six weeks later he told me he didn’t think a long-distance relationship could work. I was sad but wished him all the best and left the door open for him to reach out if he was ever back in Melbourne.
It felt brazen, but a few weeks later, I sent him a text. He replied immediately and said he would love to catch up while visiting family for Christmas. When he arrived at my door on Boxing Day, his smile had me swooning. We talked and laughed and the chemistry was palpable. We met again the next day and, thinking it would be the last I’d see of him. I wrote him a card thanking him for giving me hope and saying had circumstances been different, I would have given a relationship between us 100%.
By New Year’s Eve he’d messaged to say he missed me. A few weeks later he came back to Melbourne, where we both now live, and we went on our first road trip together.
Three and a half years later Kev has never put pressure on me to fly. Instead he’s helped me, by letting me be and warming me up for bigger and bigger jaunts. It’s all still totally anxiety-inducing for me, but it gets a little bit easier every time because he’s there encouraging me. I’m sure he thinks I’m completely neurotic, but he never lets on. Instead he makes considerations for the most problematic triggers, like elevators or staying up high in hotels, while helping me extend myself and see places I never would have without him. We’ve just returned from Jervis Bay, and a trip to Canberra.
I’ve never been in a relationship with anyone who could help me through my anxiety. I’ve always felt very alone in those experiences, but Kev’s way of dealing with it is a balm. Not only does it show me that he’s willing to accept me as I am, but he shows such compassion and patience that it reduces the anxiety itself.
I don’t think I’ll ever get on a plane, but Kev’s gentle, flexible attitude to my anxieties has helped me spread my wings. We plan to set off to central Australia in 2027.

Court orders Russia to pay door factory US$3.6m for destroying business in Chernihiv Oblast
Chernihiv Oblast Commercial Court has ordered Russia to pay UAH 161.31 million (about US$3.54 million) in damages to Korfad LLC due to the destruction or significant damage of its production buildings in the city of Koriukivka.
Source: the court ruling
Details: On 25 November 2025, during a large-scale Russian drone attack on Chernihiv Oblast, Russian drones struck an interior door manufacturing plant in Koriukivka.
According to an assessment by Expert Consulting Firm Desna-Expert LLC, the company sustained UAH 161.31 million (US$3.59 million) in damage after its buildings were struck directly by drones or hit by drone debris. Most of the buildings are now unusable. Specifically:
- UAH 143.84 million (US$3.16 million) – damage to a production building spanning 12,815 sq m on Zavodska Street
- UAH 5.81 million (US$127,610) – damage to a carpentry and turning shop spanning 481 sq m on Sadova Street
- UAH 6.44 million (US$141,445) – damage to a logistics warehouse spanning 532 sq m on Sadova Street
- UAH 5.2 million (US$114,790) – damage to a maintenance station spanning 465 sq m at 4 Sadova Street.
The court upheld the claims and ordered the full amount to be recovered from Russia, represented by the Russian Prosecutor General's Office, along with UAH 225,000 (US$5,000) in expenses for the technical inspection of the buildings and UAH 162,500 (US$3,600) for the independent damage assessment.
The founders of Korfad LLC (Koriukivka Door Factory) are Oleksandr Mysnyk, who also heads the company, Mykola Mysnyk, and Lidiia Mysnyk.
The Korfad website says the company produces panelled and flush interior doors and mouldings, using Italian Sincropan protective and decorative coatings. Its production facilities occupy an area of 15,000 sq m.
Background: Odesa Oblast Commercial Court has ordered Russia to pay UAH 291.59 million (US$6.49 million) in damages to Expansion Retail PrJSC after a missile strike destroyed the Fozzy shopping centre in Odesa.

'Nearly half a million' flood French streets as protests turn violent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
18:53:32 UTC
03:53:32 KST

Nearly half a million people have demonstrated across France, including 200,000 in Paris, according to a coalition of youth organisations and unions representing high school and university students.
Authorities put Saturday’s nationwide turnout at 320,000, including 70,000 in the French capital. A week earlier, officials counted 410,000 protesters across France, including 110,000 in Paris.
The third consecutive weekend of nationwide protests focused on high living costs and police violence. Demonstrations were largely peaceful before tensions flared at the end of marches in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities.
Some demonstrators wore Halloween costumes and carried placards reading: “No need for tear gas to make our future look bleak” and “Dressed up as an angry citizen for Halloween.”
Clashes in several cities
In Lyon, tensions emerged after some demonstrators tried to leave the authorised route near Place Jean Mace and move towards the city centre, prompting police to use tear gas, according to Franceinfo. Projectiles were also thrown at officers.
In Grenoble, southeastern France, police used tear gas after initial tensions near Place Gustave Rivet, where a march split into two.
In Marseille, clashes broke out at the front of an unauthorised march, with protesters throwing paving stones at riot police blocking Boulevard Chave. Officers responded by charging the crowd, while the march continued towards Saint-Charles railway station.
Police used water cannon against an unauthorised protest involving several thousand people in Toulouse. Scuffles were also reported in Rennes and Nantes.
In Paris, a march that began at Porte de Bagnolet reached Porte de Charenton, the endpoint of the authorised route, where clashes broke out.
Dozens of masked people dressed in black used hammers to pry up paving stones and hurl them at police. At least one incendiary device was also thrown. Officers responded with tear gas and several baton charges.
The Paris police prefecture said “a hard core of several hundred rioters” at the rear of the march attacked officers with projectiles, including a Molotov cocktail.
Arrests decline
Earlier in the afternoon, the Interior Ministry described the situation nationwide as “generally calm, with no notable incidents”.
The number of arrests fell sharply compared with the 217 recorded at the equivalent reporting point on October 24.
The ministry said security arrangements remained adapted to the situation and warned that police would show “the greatest firmness” towards anyone responsible for violence or damage.
Fresh school blockades planned
The protest movement, bringing together Yellow Vest activists, trade unions, and high school and university students, initially focused on rising living costs, inequality and deteriorating learning conditions.
Following a security crackdown and serious injuries to some protesters, its demands broadened to include greater protection of civil liberties and the right to protest.
Student unions vowed to stage fresh blockades of high schools and universities next week, while criticising the decision not to authorise a march through central Paris.
“Starting this Tuesday, we will blockade our universities and high schools, and we will do so again on Thursday before joining the demonstration on November 5 called by workers and trade unions,” said Sabrine Kharbach, spokeswoman for Union Etudiante.
