Youth Olympic Games open in Senegal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:46 UTC
01:43:46 KST

The Youth Olympic Games opened in Senegal yesterday, bringing an Olympic event to Africa for the first time as the continent seeks a bigger role in international sporting competitions.
About 2,700 young athletes aged 14 to 17 are competing through Nov. 13 in the capital, Dakar, the nearby city of Diamniadio and the beach resort of Saly.
Hundreds of dancers were to join a spectacle at the opening ceremony — which was to start after press time last night — celebrating Senegalese and African culture, in line with the Games motto: “Africa welcomes, Dakar celebrates.”
Photo courtesy of Taiwan’s delegation to the Youth Olympic Games
“This is a first opportunity for Senegal and, by extension, for Africa, to discover new sports,” Thomas Dieme, a Senegalese student said as Dakar prepared to host the Games. “It is only natural that we should all be happy to welcome other people, other cultures.”
Among the celebrities expected at the opening ceremony was French actor Omar Sy, who has Senegalese roots and stars in the Netflix series Lupin, as well as Senegalese Italian TikTok star Khaby Lame, both ambassadors for the Games.
The mascot, Ayo, is a young lion wearing a traditional Fulani hat. Its name means “joy” in Yoruba, a language spoken in Nigeria and neighboring west African countries.
Photo: AFP
Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye was expected to declare the Games open at 6:30pm at the Diamniadio Stadium, with International Olympic Committee (IOC) president Kirsty Coventry and some heads of state in attendance.
The Youth Olympics are a smaller competition than the Summer Olympics. Singapore hosted the first summer edition in 2010. Dakar was initially due to host in 2022, but the COVID-19 pandemic delayed the event by four years.
Athletes are competing in 153 medal events across 25 sports, including athletics, swimming, 3x3 basketball and for the first time baseball5, with Taiwan starting their campaign in the compact baseball variant on Friday.
Photo: AP
Taiwan scored a commanding victory over hosts Senegal, winning 2-0 in their Group A opener.
Taiwan took the first game 11-1 and the second 10-0 to earn the nation’s first Youth Olympic victory in baseball5.
Hsu Tzu-yi collected four hits in each game, while Chen Wan-zih contributed six hits and eight RBIs across the two contests.
“I think I was a little too excited in the first game and my legs went a bit weak, but once I got into the rhythm, I played smoothly,” Hsu told Top Sporting News Agency.
Chen said that her World Cup experience had prepared her well for Senegal.
“I prepared myself before the game, so I just played freely,” she said.
Coach Feng Wei-kuo said the players had experienced opening nerves and identified details to improve despite the convincing win.
Taiwan were to play Turkey yesterday, with Cuba the other team in the group.
Taiwan’s full delegation includes 37 athletes competing across 17 sports.
Baseball5 is a five-on-five version of baseball played by mixed-gender teams without a bat or gloves on a compact field.
Other sports making their Youth Olympic debut include Wushu, a Chinese martial art, and coastal rowing beach sprint, which combines beach runs with a head-to-head rowing race.
Beach wrestling is also at the Youth Olympics for the first time, a nod to Senegalese wrestling, the country’s national sport also performed on sand.
The first refugee team at a Youth Olympics have six athletes based in Kenya and Uganda in track and field, judo and taekwondo.
The Games arrive 130 years after the modern Olympics began in Athens.
Coventry, a Zimbabwean swimming champion, became the IOC’s first African and first female president last year.
“It is time for Africa, time for Senegal,” Coventry told media upon arriving in Senegal on Tuesday.
South Africa hosted the continent’s first soccer FIFA World Cup in 2010. Morocco is to cohost the 2030 tournament with Spain and Portugal. Rwanda hosted Africa’s first road cycling world championships last year and Formula 1 is returning to Africa with a grand prix in Rwanda starting early next decade. Botswana staged the World Athletics Relays in May.
African countries increasingly see sport as “a weapon in diplomacy and a tool for development,” Dakar-based sports analyst Frederic Sohounde said.
He pointed to Morocco’s investment in sports facilities and its ability to attract repeated competitions.
However, Senegal needs reliable maintenance funding and regular events after the Games to prevent its venues from becoming expensive, unused facilities, he said.
Russia’s delegation of 13 athletes is competing under its national flag for the first time at an Olympic event since restrictions imposed following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Russians at the Paris Olympics of 2024 and this year’s Winter Olympics competed as neutral athletes without national symbols.
That follows a shift in the IOC’s approach under Coventry, who has said the Olympics should not “hold athletes accountable for the actions of their governments.”
It could be a trial run for a full Russian return at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.

Dachshunds at the center of exhibition in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:46 UTC
01:43:46 KST

The humble dachshund is taking center stage in a new exhibition in Germany that explores the history of the sausage dog in art — and visitors are welcome to bring their four-legged friends along.
“The Dachshund: An Icon off the Leash” opened at the Kunsthalle Bremen yesterday, showcasing artwork by dachshund owners and fans including Pablo Picasso, David Hockney and Andy Warhol.
In addition to painting, drawing, photography and video, visitors can admire delights such as a wealth of stuffed toy dogs and many other dachshund-themed objects.
Photo: AP
Museum director Christoph Grunenberg believes it is the world’s first exhibition dedicated to the dachshund in art, rather than dogs in general.
“There are many artists who owned dachshunds, who were inspired by the dachshund, loved the dachshund,” Grunenberg said. “It was like a muse and there is an incredible wealth of representation of the dachshund in very different styles by significant artists.”
“We wanted to take the dachshund as an object, as an inspiration to artists, and trace it through history in all its different forms and important works of art by Picasso, Warhol and Hockney and also ephemera,” he added.
German artist Thorsten Brinkmann honored the compact dogs’ reputation as a “handbag dog” with a bronze sculpture that features a handbag on dachshund legs. He also provided the colorful “Toxie Love” installation in the exhibition’s first room, which sets a playful tone for the show.
The dachshund has “a very curious, very special form, very long — kind of too long, actually, with the short legs — and it looks already surrealistic to me,” he said.
He was helped by objects loaned by the Dachshund Museum in Regensburg, Germany.
For several hours on Thursdays and Saturdays, the museum will let dachshunds and other small dogs into three of its eight rooms for a look and a sniff.
Among the conditions: They must have a maximum shoulder height of 30cm and an online time-slot ticket. A “Dachshund Lounge” will be offered as a waiting area.
“We want to take the dog seriously as a personality and the dog can walk around, can interact, will be able to watch videos, look outside the window, smell — and of course that’s what the dog really is interested in,” Grunenberg said.
Finnish photographer Elina Brotherus’ dachshund, Marcello, already checked out the wares ahead of the opening of the exhibition, which features Brotherus’ pictures of the 13-year-old dog.
Marcello has been her model since 2013, Brotherus said.
“I did not manage to have children, so then we got him and he’s my baby,” she said. “There’s something so, like, cute and philosophical and special about these dogs.”
Business developer Kelsey Crossman explored the show with her dachshund, Leonidas, or Leo for short.
The dogs’ appeal is in “their attitudes — they’re small, but they’re very strong and a little stubborn, probably like myself,” she said.

====================================================================================================

Once opportunity, chokepoints are now a threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:44 UTC
01:43:44 KST

Stand on a clear day atop Singapore’s Marina Bay Sands hotel, and you can see the city-state’s promise and peril in a single glance.
In the foreground, a flotilla of ships lies at anchor, a physical reminder of how Singapore grew rich servicing the immense volume of global trade squeezed through the chokepoint of its narrow strait. On the horizon, you can just make out the coastline of Indonesia, a country with almost 50 times Singapore’s population and 2,500 times as much land. Its proximity is a reminder of how dependent that prosperity remains on good relations with Singapore’s much larger neighbors.
Such issues are top of mind right now. For weeks, the view has been obscured by a pall of haze drifting across the water from wildfires on the Indonesian islands of Borneo and Sumatra. Singapore passed laws a decade ago to combat this recurring public-health catastrophe, but has struggled to enforce them amid intransigence from its neighbor. Just days after the city announced measures against 10 Indonesian companies over the blazes this month, Jakarta started cutting pipeline supplies of natural gas to Singapore.
The decision might have a perfectly innocent explanation. Singapore has shifted aggressively toward liquefied natural gas (LNG) and away from Malaysian and Indonesian piped energy in the past few years, anticipating that its neighbors would use more of their own supplies as their economies expand. A key link allowing Indonesia to divert gas locally was completed just weeks ago, and the affected exports represent less than 2 percent of daily demand.
However, comments from Jakarta’s energy distribution minister do not inspire confidence. He warned neighboring countries to “be careful” about annoying Indonesia if they do not want their exports cut off.
The whole episode is another unpleasant reminder of the vulnerability underlying Singapore’s prosperity. For more than two centuries, it has thrived as a free port, in a world where chokepoints to trade have been progressively dismantled. The city was established by the British to bypass the Dutch stronghold in Java, and its most important nation building projects in the 1960s and 1970s repeated the model by making it a key node of emerging commercial networks, from oil refining, to container shipping, to long-haul aviation.
However, throughout all that Singapore has remained acutely aware of the chokeholds its larger neighbors control. Political separation from Malaysia in 1965 raised fears of water supplies being cut off. A costly program of desalination, recycling, harvesting and reservoir-building would allow near-self-sufficiency in a crisis.
The same cannot be said for energy. Even LNG supplies could be severed easily by a naval blockade. Nuclear power has been considered on and off for years, but comes with its own challenges: You could fit almost the entire nation inside the 20km mandatory-evacuation zone established after the Fukushima Daiichi disaster. Plans underway to install 4 gigawatts of solar panels by 2035 could leave about 5 percent of the country under silicon, and still meet barely a tenth of electricity demand.
Separate plans to develop renewable projects and transmission lines stretching to Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia, Indonesia and even Australia would at least diversify electricity suppliers. However, those connections could, in theory, be cut off with the flick of a switch. Singapore’s driving role in establishing the power grid taking shape across the Association of Southeast Asian Nations can best be seen as an attempt to spread the risk across a web of mutual dependencies.
That is the hopeful vision. In a world of multilateralism, peace and trade, small maritime republics can grow fabulously wealthy as nodes for global commerce and capital. Venice, an inspiration to Singapore’s founding generation, followed that model for centuries.
The worrying part is what came afterwards. As Europe’s commercial order gave way to an age of revolution, mass armies and nationalism, Venice’s wealth proved little protection against the larger powers surrounding it. Napoleon extinguished the thousand-year republic in 1797, and it was traded back and forth like a bargaining chip between France and Austria for decades before being subsumed into the modern Italian state in 1866.
We could be entering a similar moment. The rising force in international relations is the chokepoint maximizer, looking for leverage over computer chips, critical minerals, intellectual property and trade flows to subdue its rivals. This year’s conflict over the Strait of Hormuz is a prime example. With barriers rising to commerce, migration, and capital, free ports such as Singapore are in lonely waters.
“If there were no international law and order, and big fish eat small fish and small fish eat shrimps, we wouldn’t exist,” founding father Lee Kuan Yew (李光耀) mused in a 2007 interview. “A siege? ... Control of sea lanes? We’ll just starve.”
Lee’s successors must hope the great-power conflict brewing today is a passing storm, rather than a permanent shift in the global climate.
David Fickling is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering climate change and energy. Previously, he worked for Bloomberg News, The Wall Street Journa and the Financial Times. Brazil’s chapter in the  anti-authoritarian playbook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:38 UTC
01:43:38 KST

Until Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva staged a remarkable comeback to win re-election, no Brazilian presidential candidate had overturned a first-round defeat in a runoff. Lula did so with nearly 52 percent of the vote, against Flavio Bolsonaro’s 48 percent. More than 128 million Brazilians turned out — nearly three million more than in the first round.
The result matters far beyond Brazil. US President Donald Trump would be unhappy, and not just because his favored candidate lost. The outcome might also send a signal ahead of the US midterms.
It is not the first. After years in which nationalist and illiberal movements appeared ascendant, their opponents are finding ways to fight back. Former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orban was defeated in April after 16 consecutive years in power. On the same day as Brazil’s vote, former Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in a snap election held after nearly two years of protests.
Illustration: Tania Chou
Hungary’s opposition was led by a former conservative insider and Serbia’s by a student-led movement. Yet their experiences suggest an emerging anti-authoritarian playbook. And Brazil, where democracy has been repeatedly tested in the past few years, might have written its most instructive chapter.
It begins in the streets. In the weeks before Brazil’s runoff, enormous crowds gathered in cities across the country. Students marched alongside workers. Artists and indigenous leaders joined pensioners, farmers and entrepreneurs. Many were motivated less by loyalty to a political party than by concern about what another Bolsonaro presidency might mean for democratic institutions and civil liberties.
There was something strikingly spontaneous about the mobilization. Lula acknowledged that he had never seen anything quite like it in five decades of political life. Much of the energy came from outside the machinery of parties and unions. Jolted into action by the first-round defeat to Bolsonaro, civil society had rediscovered its capacity to mobilize.
Brazil’s political earthquake was also digital. For much of the past decade, the far right dominated social media, exploiting its appetite for outrage and confrontation. Supporters of Bolsonaro’s father, former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, were particularly adept at turning WhatsApp groups and online personalities into political infrastructure. The left, with its dependence on televised speeches and conventional party structures, often appeared hapless.
The turning point came partly through Andre Janones, a federal deputy with a flair for digital spectacle, and Rafael Fonteles, the 41-year-old governor of Piaui, who helped pull Lula into a world he had long resisted, even refusing to own a cellphone. On Wednesday last week, he received one from Fonteles and joined Janones’s rapidly expanding WhatsApp operation. A politician whose career began in the factories and union halls of the 1970s was introduced to memes, livestreams and algorithmic engagement.
Janones’s WhatsApp channel, dubbed Lula’s Army, attracted more than 10 million followers. Participants were encouraged to share videos, promote hashtags and generate an avalanche of online content. Each was also given a simple mission: mobilize at least three more voters.
Political humor proved especially potent. The campaign discovered that ridicule could be more effective than another earnest denunciation. In a televised debate, when Bolsonaro, arguing that crime had risen on Lula’s watch, demanded to know why 73 percent of prisoners had supposedly voted for him, Lula shot back: “I want 100 percent of them to vote for me, even your father.” (Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election.)
The attention economy cannot be conceded to those most willing to exploit it. Digital platforms reward speed and emotional intensity. Democratic movements must understand those incentives, even as they resist the temptation to reproduce the disinformation and intimidation that corrupt so much online political debate.
Brazil’s experience also exposed and challenged the power of the digital platforms themselves. Lula’s campaign accused Meta of favoring his opponent through its algorithms and artificial intelligence tools. Meta acknowledged technical failures, but denied political bias. Brazil’s electoral court ordered the company to apply the same criteria to both campaigns. The court’s scrutiny cut both ways: at one point it briefly suspended Lula’s Army itself.
Companies such as Meta and X wield enormous influence over the world’s political conversation, yet their recommendation systems remain opaque. Democratic competition requires transparent rules that are enforced fairly by courts that also protect legitimate speech.
There was another, more symbolic shift, as the left increasingly challenged the far right’s claim to Brazil’s national colors. For years, the green-and-yellow flag had become closely associated with Bolsonaro’s movement. During the runoff, Lula posed in the national soccer team’s yellow jersey as part of a campaign called “The green and yellow is ours,” insisting that patriotism belonged to no party. His army of online supporters followed suit.
Of course, a WhatsApp channel alone does not explain the exceptional turnout that won the election. Lula also benefited from voter dissatisfaction with his opponent, a forceful performance in the campaign’s final debate, a huge late surge of social spending, and concern about democracy. His government offered concrete economic proposals. The campaign’s digital resurgence coincided with its political recovery, but the precise contribution of each is hard to measure.
Nor should the result be mistaken for a wholesale rejection of Brazil’s right. Nearly 60 million people voted for Bolsonaro. His Partido Liberal (PL) party and its allies retain considerable influence in Congress and across state governments.
Although the PL has recognized Lula’s victory, Bolsonaro remains defiant. Like his father, he responded to electoral defeat by challenging the legitimacy of the contest, pledging to organize the opposition and seek disqualification of Lula’s ticket. He also faces a money-laundering investigation, raising the personal stakes of his political survival.
The next four years might prove considerably harder than Lula’s come-from-behind victory. The Brazilian left, heavily reliant on Lula’s extraordinary personal appeal for decades, has struggled to cultivate new leaders. The country needs a politics capable of reaching people who feel alienated from government, including those whose anxiety about crime and economic insecurity make them receptive to authoritarian candidates.
Brazil’s renewed democratic confidence must be matched by institutional and structural reforms and a willingness to build coalitions beyond the left. Its leaders need to recover some of the civic spirit that animated the campaign without assuming that an election has resolved the country’s divisions.
This is where the lessons from Hungary and Serbia become relevant. Their experiences show that resistance to concentrated power can emerge from different ideological traditions. The common denominator is a public willing to organize and institutions capable of translating mobilization into political change. As more of the world looks to the Global South for political direction, Lula’s campaign might prove even more influential than the European examples.
Robert Muggah, cofounder of the Igarape Institute and the SecDev Group, is a member of the World Economic Forum’s Global Future Council on Cities of Tomorrow and an adviser to the Global Risks Report. Ilona Szabo de Carvalho is cofounder and president of the Igarape Institute and founder of the Green Bridge Facility.

The good news is that the US is engaged in both races, which will also benefit US allies and partners in Asia, including Taiwan. On Sept. 14, US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink disclosed, “...the US now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action.” No details about these “space control weapons” have yet been disclosed. However, a graphic apparently issued by French Space Command and posted

People enter cages, animals seem free at Art Zoo museum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:33 UTC
01:43:33 KST

Look up as you enter Amsterdam’s new Art Zoo museum, and a 3.66m crocodile stares down at you, mouth open, ready to chomp.
The taxidermic reptile is one of hundreds of preserved creatures on display, alongside artfully arranged piles of bones, illuminated tulips encased in apothecary jars and a cabinet of grotesque fish.
While it is not a Halloween-themed museum, the show should appeal to anybody looking for something a little dark this spooky season.
Photo: AP
“It was a little creepy,” Tomas Vasko, a Slovak living in the Dutch capital, said after touring the museum.
Art Zoo is the creation of Dutch artists Jaap Sinke and Ferry van Tongeren, who draw inspiration from “wunderkammers,” or curiosity cabinets collected by wealthy Europeans in the 16th and 17th centuries to showcase objects from the natural world.
“The main thing is that we like storytelling with the animals,” Van Tongeren said. “We like to add drama. We add an attitude to the animals, where traditional taxidermists just want to mimic nature.”
Behind him, a cheetah slouched in an alcove under the watchful eye of a cassowary.
In natural history museums, animals are posed as they could be seen in the wild. At the Art Zoo, a Japanese giant spider crab stretches its 1.83m legs above a doorway beside the leg bones of a mastodon that nearly reaches the ceiling.
The duo rose to fame in 2015 after shark-pickling artist Damien Hirst purchased their entire exhibition from a London art show.
Unlike at a traditional zoo, the human visitors are confined, not the animals. The display rooms in the 17th-century canal house where the Art Zoo is located are enclosed by brooding, black metal cages.
“We really like the concept of having all the people in a cage and then all the animals free,” Van Tongeren said. “In that way, the whole building becomes one artwork.”
None of the animals in the eclectic collection were taken from the wild.
“All our animals come from zoos where they died of natural causes,” Sinke said.
However, the paperwork can be challenging, he said.
The pair primarily obtained specimens from Europe to ensure they know the history of the animals.
Sinke and Van Tongeren consider themselves an artistic trio, crediting naturalist Charles Darwin as the third contributor to their work. They pitched the concept of the museum as the return of Darwin’s wonder.
In a nod to the man who developed the first scientific theory of evolution, one wall display contains a series of Darwin busts. Sinke and Van Tongeren see an amusing irony in honoring Darwin inside a building that once housed the Biblical Museum.
Not everything in the collection is a real animal. Underneath the crocodile suspended from the ceiling is a wall of Jenny Hanivers, ray carcasses modified into grotesque creatures by 16th-century sailors who presented the macabre beasts as real sea monsters to gullible collectors.
Their misshapen faces appear to keep an eye on guests as they move from room to room.

Taiwan in Time: How five concubines became legends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:33 UTC
01:43:33 KST

Nov. 2 to Nov. 8
After 41 years in exile and the enemy closing in, the Ming Dynasty’s Prince of Ningjing (寧靖王) decided to meet his end in Taiwan. So did the five women who accompanied him.
The Qing had captured Penghu in July 1683, and the Tainan-based Kingdom of Tungning appeared doomed.
Photo courtesy of Academia Sinica
According to the Taiwan Prefecture Annals (台灣府志), compiled in 1696, the prince announced his intention to his five concubines, telling them they were free to remarry or become nuns. Lady Yuan (袁氏), Lady Wang (王氏), Xiugu (秀姑), Sister Mei (梅姐) and Sister He (荷姐) replied, “If our lord lives, we live; if our lord dies, we die with him. We beg you to grant us silk cords so that we may die alongside our lord. In this way, we may at least remain faithful to one man until death.”
The prince personally buried the women. The next day, he put on his royal robes and headgear, handed his imperial seal to Kingdom of Tungning’s boy ruler, Cheng Ke-shuang (鄭克塽), and hung himself after composing a farewell poem.
A ninth-generation descendant of the Ming Dynasty’s founding emperor, Chu Shu-kui (朱術桂) was the only Ming prince-in-exile in Taiwan to choose death over surrender. The other 16 were sent back to China along with Cheng and his officials.
Photo courtesy of National Central Library
Over the centuries, the suicides of the five concubines became the focus of poems and stories lauding their loyalty and chastity far more than the prince’s own death. The Temple of the Five Concubines was built over their grave in 1746 and renovated and expanded several times, with the latest repairs starting last month and slated for completion in 2028.
In “The unbearable heaviness of widowhood: A reconsideration of the deaths of Prince Ningjing’s five concubines in the perspectives of gender and social history” (妾身敢作未亡人？明寧靖王從死五妃史事的性別與社會史分析), however, Lei Chin-hau (雷晉豪) argues that their deaths may have been romanticized over time to glorify traditional ideals of female virtue. Without discounting their sacrifice and dedication, he notes that in a patriarchal society where women had few means of supporting themselves independently, they might not have had much of a choice.
FALLEN PRINCE
Photo courtesy of Wikimedia Commons
According to the Taiwan Prefecture Annals (台灣府志), compiled in 1696, the prince, Chu Shu-kui (朱術桂), was born in 1617 in today’s Hubei Province. The invading Qing army captured his hometown in 1642, beginning his life on the run. The Ming Dynasty collapsed two years later, and Chu joined other royals in the resisting Southern Ming. Emperor Longwu bestowed him the title Prince of Ningjing and assigned him the role of military supervisor.
The Qing continued to push south, and by 1650 Chu had fled to Kinmen where he sought the protection of warlord Cheng Cheng-kung (鄭成功, Koxinga).
Koxinga drove out the Dutch from Tainan in 1662 and established the Kingdom of Tungning. His son, Cheng Ching (鄭經), invited Chu to Tainan in 1663 and built him a residence. Chu arrived with his principal wife, Lady Lo (羅氏), as well as the five concubines. His biological son died young, so he adopted a relative, Chu Yen-chen (朱儼?), as his heir. Lo died before Chu and the five concubines.
Photo courtesy of National Museum of Taiwan History
According to the Taiwan Prefecture Annals, Cheng Ching eventually discontinued the living stipend for Chu’s household. Chu turned to cultivating land in present-day Lujhu District (路竹), Kaohsiung, but the Cheng regime imposed taxes on the land as it was waging a campaign to retake China, adding to the prince’s financial difficulties.
It’s said that before Chu’s death, he gave his land to the tenant farmers. To thank him, they buried him in Lujhu along with Lady Lo and his son, and built 100 fake tombs in the area to spare it from Qing destruction. It wasn’t identified until 1937. Chu’s residence in Tainan was later converted into the Tainan Grand Matsu Temple (大天后宮).
LITERARY EVOLUTION
Most early literary works focused on Chu’s death, writes Wang Chien-kuo (王建國) in “Political narratives and historical divergence: Poems about Prince Ningjing and the Five Concubines in Qing-era Taiwan” (政治書寫與歷史衍異─清代臺灣寧靖王與五妃題詠現象及其詩作論析).
The earliest known poem dedicated solely to the five concubines appeared in the 1720 Taiwan County Annals (台灣縣誌) by Lin Chung-kui (林中桂). Lin described seeing lingering haze and glow surrounding their grave in Kuishan (魁山), just outside Tainan and much more accessible to visitors than Chu’s unmarked tomb in the countryside. Many other poems mention the grave, which had become a temple site marked by official steles commemorating the women’s deed.
In the same volume, Shih Shih-pang (施世榜) wrote, “Ordinary women know only to share a pillow in life; the Five Concubines alone were seen to share death as one.”
This idea of their act transcending gender norms continued in other poems: “Do not say that women who follow their men are merely concubines; their righteous deaths deserve the praise given to men,” wrote Ho Chieh-yi (何借宜).
Chang Mei (張湄) took it further: “Their loyalty is comparable to Tien Heng’s 500 followers,” referring to the men who committed suicide after learning of their lord’s death rather than submit to the Han Dynasty.
After the 1720s, Wang noted that works praising or mourning the five concubines greatly surpassed those of the prince. A possible factor was the 1721 Chu Yi-kuei (朱一貴) rebellion. Since Chu shared a surname with the Ming royal house, he revolted under the banner of “reviving the Ming Dynasty.”
PRACTICAL CONCERNS
Not much is known about the concubines’ backgrounds, but many modern sources describe them as “young beauties” and add expressions of affection and sorrow absent from the original text, heightening the tragedy of their deaths, Lei writes.
However, according to Chu’s biography in the Annals of the Southwest (西南記事), he married Lady Yuan and Lady Wang in 1644, which would put them at least in their mid-to-late 50s by 1683.
The fact that the family’s heir, Chu Yen-chen, was adopted also complicated matters. Under Ming custom, concubines could not manage or dispose of family property on behalf of an adopted heir, leaving their economic future uncertain amid the imminent collapse of the Kingdom of Tungning. Sources indicate that the family was already in financial difficulty, while women in their position had few ways to support themselves independently. Chu Yan-chen eventually surrendered to the Qing and was taken to China.
As for remarrying, they would have had to wait until the three-year mourning period was over. Remarriage was also frowned upon, as widows were expected to remain chaste. Becoming nuns was another unlikely option: Lei notes that there were few monks in Taiwan at the time and apparently no nunnery in the area.
These circumstances raise questions about how much freedom they had to choose another future.
Taiwan in Time, a column about Taiwan’s history that is published every Sunday, spotlights important or interesting events around the nation that either have anniversaries this week or are tied to current events.
Much attention is being paid to increasing security ties between Taiwan and the Philippines, and rightfully so. The stakes are potentially existential, as explored in “ Donovan’s Deep Dives: Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines need to face the common threat from Beijing” (Sept. 12, page 12). Getting less attention is that across the board the relationship is growing stronger, and both sides appear to be planning to put more of their eggs in each other’s baskets. Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) in August last year confirmed plans to open a second Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) representative

As a result, the next group for that nation got sent to Nepal, and we got bumped to Kenya. The

A televised debate for the main Kaohsiung mayoral candidates, Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) candidate Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆) and Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) candidate Ko Chih-en (柯志恩), was held on Friday evening, followed at noon yesterday by a debate in Taipei between Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the KMT and the DPP’s candidate, Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋).
Chiang and Lai have had local government experience to rely on: Shen and Ko needed to demonstrate that they have the vision and the leadership skills needed for the job.
In Taipei, Chiang has the advantage of seeking a second term in a KMT stronghold, but the underdog Shen has been snapping at his heels, and has even overtaken him in recent polls. Chiang is a major KMT figure whose plain delivery and avoidance of providing satisfactory answers in recent interviews has damaged his campaign, especially when compared with Shen’s social media-savvy “Ocean Wave” (洋流).
Chiang’s performance yesterday failed to address his body-language issues: His team had obviously worked hard on that and positive facial expressions, but he spent a large part of his time, especially during the media questions section, referring to his notes, at times reading from them.
On the other hand, Shen was clearly the better prepared with his answers, and on several occasions pointed out that Chiang had failed to answer the question put to him.
Compare that with Friday’s debate in Kaohsiung, where the DPP is historically stronger than the KMT. Lai was well-prepared, but, like Chiang, came off as wooden in his delivery. He focused on the length of his experience in Kaohsiung’s local governance and attacking Ko over her support for the KMT’s amendments to the Act Governing the Allocation of Government Revenues and Expenditures (財政收支劃分法), which he said disproportionally favored Taipei over Kaohsiung. Ko failed to show how she could deliver on the ambitious vision she offered, but wiped the floor with Lai in terms of her presentation and debating skills.
Lai and Ko referred to previous mayors: Lai spoke of former DPP mayors Frank Hsieh (謝長廷) and Chen Chu (陳菊), as well as and incumbent Kaohsiung Mayor Chen Chi-mai (陳其邁). Hsieh and Chen Chu enjoyed high approval ratings; Chen Chi-mai is polling at 71.9 percent approval. Ko said that Lai had not mentioned former Kaohsiung mayor Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) of the KMT, although he probably did her a favor with the omission: Kaohsiung voters recalled Han before he had served two years of his first term.
As the natural successor of these high approval ratings for DPP leadership, one would expect Lai to win handily on Nov. 28.

Lai has a support rating of 43.2 percent, compared with Ko’s 43.1. The race is neck-and-neck. Crucially, 12.7 percent of voters remain undecided and, while 38.8 percent of independent voters said they would vote for Ko, compared with 20.6 percent for Lai, 38.5 percent were undecided. The outcome of the Kaohsiung mayoral race appears to be in the hands of a small group of swing voters.

Sri Lanka’s Tamil farmers fight to reclaim land after civil war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:31 UTC
01:43:31 KST

Tired but resolute, dozens of Tamil cattle farmers have held a round-the-clock vigil for almost three years in eastern Sri Lanka, protesting what they call land “theft.”
At shift change, farmers exchange news before settling beneath a tarpaulin beside photographs of the bloodied bodies of their dead cows.
“They have been shooting our cattle, threatening us, assaulting us and spraying pesticides or poison on the pasture lands where our cattle graze,” said Seenithamby Thiyagarajah, president of the local farmers’ association, detailing the push his community felt from recipients of a state-funded program that was driving them off their land.
Photo: AFP
“Over 5,700 cows have been destroyed like this. Even after complaining numerous times to the police and all relevant places, we received no resolution,” he said.
The alleged perpetrators are farmers who have benefited from the state-funded Mahaweli development scheme. Most are Sinhalese, the country’s majority ethnic group, settling on land claimed by the largely Hindu Tamil minority, which makes up about 12 percent of the population.
The government denied any forcible attempts to remove people from their land.
Sri Lanka’s 1983 to 2009 civil war between government forces and Tamil separatists killed more than 100,000 people, according to UN data.
Nearly two decades later, land disputes continue to fuel ethnic grievances.
Thiyagarajah said that settlers aided by the scheme have encroached on grazing land used by the roughly 1,000 cattle farmers he represents.
Courts have repeatedly ordered the eviction of the scheme-backed settler farmers, he said.
“Things are peaceful, for a while, but then the illegal cultivators entered again, ruining our land and destroying our cattle,” he said.
Other communities are also fighting to reclaim land.
Ambalavar Nallathambi Velayutham, 64, an indigenous community leader, wants his rice fields back.
Armed with renewed land deeds renewed with local authorities, Velayutham and neighbors in Kunjankulam returned to farming fields they had abandoned during the war.
Sri Lankan Forest Department officials told them the land was a reserve, Velayutham said.
“We said: ‘This land belonged to our ancestors.’ They replied: ‘That won’t do. You must leave,’” he added.
Fearing reprisals, most villagers abandoned their efforts.
One night, a villager spotted forestry officials’ mobile phones glowing in the darkness.
“They dug there and planted boundary stones,” Velayutham said, pointing to the markers.
Repeated appeals to local authorities, the prime minister and president have brought no result, he said.
“This land has neither been freed nor handed back to us,” he said. “If they release this farmland and we get it back from the Forest Department, I believe this will provide a great opportunity.”
Land disputes have multiplied across Sri Lanka’s Eastern Province, where Tamils are a major ethnic group.
Examples include an army barracks encroaching on a school, while government departments responsible for archeology, wildlife or forests claim farmland, temples and private property.
Officials designate land cultivated by Tamils as forest or wildlife reserves, “obstructing development or agricultural activities for them,” said Sabarathinam Sivayoganathan, 57, president of the Eastern Province Civil Society Activists Union.
The scale of these occupations is unclear, with no public statistics and residents risking intimidation by asking questions, he said.
Opposition Member of Parliament Rasamanickam R. Shanakiyan said that population figures point to a deliberate effort to change the region’s demographics.
“In the Eastern Province, the Sinhala population has increased by 700 percent since independence in 1948,” he said, compared with 200 percent nationally.
“This has happened through state-sponsored colonization,” he said, accusing the government of altering the ethnic balance of the north and east through land settlements.
Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s election in 2024 has brought little change, Shanakiyan said, despite campaign promises to the contrary.
He accused the government of failing to honor commitments in the lead up to the election that it would release land, protect minority rights and deliver wider political reforms.
“On these promises, nothing’s been delivered,” he said. “You feel a growing sense of frustration, maybe anger in the population.”
Land ownership disputes continue to fuel tensions, resentment and accusations online and on the ground between Sinhalese and Tamils across eastern Sri Lanka.
The Sri Lankan government said it has commissioned a report on changes to land records since the civil war and whether they should be corrected.
“We will never forcibly acquire people’s land,” Sri Lankan Minister of Environment Dhammika Patabendi told reporters in an e-mail.
“Based on the recommendations of this report, we believe that these issues can be resolved promptly and fairly,” he said.
However, as torrential rain drums on the tarpaulin sheltering the angry farmers, Thiyagarajah remains unconvinced.
“For 1,010 days, alongside this road and under this tent, we have been taking part day and night. Justice has still not been granted to our people,” he said. “Today, our people live in constant fear that today or tomorrow our cattle will be destroyed.”

China’s military purge reduces war risk: experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:29 UTC
01:43:29 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) military purge has reduced the risks of a planned war against Taiwan, yet increased the danger of a conflict sparked by a miscalculation or accident, Taiwanese experts said yesterday.
They made the comments at a seminar on the Fifth Plenary Session of the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) 20th Central Committee held by the research group Secure Taiwan Associate Corp (STA) in Taipei.
The wholesale sacking of Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) officers and managers of the aerospace and defense industry is sure to set back Xi’s timetable to prepare the PLA to launch an invasion of Taiwan by next year, they said.
Photo: AP
The Chinese armed forces’ attention would most likely be fully absorbed by efforts to rebuild their organization and leadership in the next one to four years in a welcome development for Taiwan, they said.
Yet the lack of experience in the Chinese military’s most senior command levels is also a warning sign, as amateurs and sycophants are far more likely to make missteps that inadvertently lead to war, they added.
Association for Strategic Foresight researcher Chieh Chung (揭仲) said that 96 CCP Central Committee members, or 26 percent of the total membership, have departed under a cloud.
This figure is more than double the number of Central Committee officials ousted for corruption or improprieties in the 18th iteration of the Central Committee, he said.
The dismissal of Ma Xingrui (馬興瑞), Jin Zhuanglong (金壯龍), Zhao Xiaozhe (趙曉哲) and Lei Fanpei (雷凡培), among 28 formerly high-ranking defense and aerospace industry officials, would force a comprehensive re-examination of China’s defense procurement plans, he said.
The drastic changes would derail the military reform targets Xi originally planned to achieve by the 100th anniversary of the PLA’s founding next year, he said.
Xi had rolled back the theater commands’ autonomy and ability to conduct operations independently, which runs contrary to recognized principles of modern joint warfare, he said.
The disruption to PLA leadership and its cumbersome command arrangements are likely to cripple the capability of the Chinese military to project force or respond to a contingency for the next three to four years, he said.
Yet, Xi’s willingness to put ideology and politics over professionalism also means Chinese generals would be fearful of voicing disagreements or appearing weak, he said.
These flaws would make it significantly more difficult for Beijing to exercise sound judgement or de-escalate dangerous situations, increasing the risks of sparking an unwanted conflict, he said.
The most recently dismissed members and alternate members of the Central Committee included 16 PLA brass and seven high-ranking managers of China’s defense industry, National Taiwan University political science professor Chen Shih-min (陳世民) said.
The PLA’s organizational table calls for more than 40 full generals and admirals to staff the armed forces, but only six such officers are left at the helm, he said.
The arrest of former vice chairman and PLA general Zhang Youxia (張又俠) nine months ago has all but eliminated the Central Military Commission, where he previously served as one of its two vice chairmen, Chen said.
The only members left in the Chinese military’s high command are Xi and General Zhang Shengmin (張升民), a commissar with no professional training in commanding troops, he said.
National Defense University Chinese military studies professor Ma Chen-kun (馬振坤) said the PLA would be absorbed by efforts to recuperate and reorganize its internal organization for up to two years.
The Central Committee meeting elevated Zhang Shengmin, the Central Military Commission’s last remaining general, to the Politburo, without filling vacancies in the high command, he said.
The prominence of Zhang Shengmin contravened the PLA’s long-standing policy of maintaining separate tracks for commissars and professional soldiers, he said.
Zhang Shengmin’s lack of qualifications have compromised the Chinese military’s crisis management, increasing the chances of dangerous miscalculations and mishaps, Ma said.

FEATURE: The unsung heroes of snake antivenom production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:27 UTC
01:43:27 KST

Taiwan is home to a rich diversity of snake species, and nearly 1,000 people are bitten by snakes each year. In emergency rooms, where every second counts, administering the right antivenom in time can mean the difference between life and death. Behind this lifesaving treatment is an unlikely group of contributors: immunized horses.
The National Immunized Horse Farm at National Pingtung University of Science and Technology covers 2.91 hectares and houses 57 horses in six stables, with four outdoor exercise fields and two horse walkers. Of the horses, 44 are involved in antivenom production, and 13 have retired.
“People often ask us if we get to ride the horses when we travel for work. We always joke, ‘No, the horses outrank us,’” Centers for Disease Control (CDC) Center for Diagnostics and Vaccine Development animal technology specialist Lee Chia-jung (李佳蓉) said with a laugh.
Photo: CNA
Unlike horses at recreational riding stables, which are trained for activities such as riding and running, immunized horses have a very different role, Lee said, adding that the horses’ primary job is to stay healthy and undergo immunization, providing the plasma needed to produce antivenom.
Temperament is the top priority when selecting horses. Neither a spirited racehorse, which might bolt at the prick of a needle, nor a massive draft horse weighing more than a tonne, which could be difficult to restrain if something went wrong, would be suitable, deputy director Hsieh Wen-chin (謝文欽) said.
Only horses with a calm, gentle temperament are suited to the work, he said.
Antivenom must be produced using venom from locally occurring snake species, Hsieh said.
The CDC supplies four types covering Taiwan’s six major venomous snake species.
Each horse produces only one type of antivenom during its lifetime, Hsieh said.
Laboratory staff inject it with one type of venom and wait to see whether it develops antibodies. If none appear within a certain period, they try another type, repeating the process until antibodies develop. Horses that fail to respond to any available type must be retired early.
Once sufficient antibodies have developed, researchers collect the horse’s plasma and separate and purify the antibodies to make antivenom, he said.
Immunization must proceed gradually to allow the horse’s immune system to build a response. Early side effects can include wounds, abscesses and granulomas, but improved formulations have reduced these risks. The farm takes precautions to protect the horses’ health, he said.
Sheep and alpacas can also produce antivenom, but horses remain the most widely used animals because of their size, relatively docile temperament and greater plasma yield, Vaccine Manufacturing Division chief Chen Chao-hung (陳昭宏) said.
Taiwan’s immunized horses mainly come from the US and the Netherlands, Hsieh said.
Imports from New Zealand were discontinued after some horses developed anhidrosis, a condition that prevents sweating and can cause their body temperatures to rise in hot weather.
After quarantine and health checks, horses undergo training to familiarize them with their surroundings and working conditions, Hsieh said.
They learn to wear a halter, follow handlers, enter and leave restraint stocks, and tolerate the smell of alcohol, protruding objects, and pressure on their necks and skin, he said, adding that this preparation reduces stress and injury risks during immunization and blood collection.
Horses typically serve for eight to 12 years, giving blood nearly 100 times over their working lives. Each kilogram of plasma can produce about 30 doses of antivenom, meaning one horse can help save thousands of snakebite victims, Hsieh said.
Taiwan began producing antivenom during the Japanese colonial period, when the mortality rate from venomous snakebites exceeded 6 percent. Today, it has fallen to 0.18 percent, and no one has died from an allergic reaction to antivenom.
A total of 195 medical institutions across Taiwan stock antivenom, while the CDC maintains 6,000 doses across four types, enough for at least 18 months.
National Health Insurance data from 2017 to 2021 show that an average of 979 people in Taiwan are bitten by snakes each year.
“Antivenom cannot wait until someone is bitten before production begins,” Hsieh said.
Finished-product stocks cover 1.5 to two years of demand, while reserve plasma typically covers more than three years, providing a double safety net.

Worthwhile policies, not partisan politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:26 UTC
01:43:26 KST

On Thursday last week, Democratic Progressive Party Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) proposed an urban stitching initiative designed to revitalize and pedestrianize the area surrounding the elevated Civic Boulevard highway, creating a cultural and arts corridor that links with commercial districts. Former Taipei mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) leaped to mock the proposal as foolish to the point of being unworthy of a serious response, and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) dismissed it as wishful thinking.
On Monday, Shen responded by presenting documents from the Taipei Department of Urban Development of a similar “stitching” proposal by the Ko administration in 2020 to create a pedestrian-friendly corridor along the city’s north-south axis. When the same urban design considerations made by the previous administration are ridiculed when put forward by their political opponent, one has to wonder whether this is really a policy issue, or a political point-scoring exercise.
The Taipei Department of Urban Development’s 2020 project to improve the pedestrian environment around Jianguo Brewery and Zhongshan Girls’ High School also proposed using Civic Boulevard as an east-west axis to reconnect the areas to its north and south. It said that existing land use around the elevated highway had fragmented and under-utilized the pedestrian environment, and that landscape and connectivity improvements were needed. The findings were also included in a work report submitted to the Taipei City Council in August 2021.
Shen’s proposal for a cultural and arts corridor linked to commercial districts is not identical to the 2020 plan, and its engineering requirements, traffic impacts and costs need to be assessed. However, the idea of reconnecting fragmented urban spaces is clearly not something that has been plucked from thin air. Politicians are entitled to question its feasibility, but they should not ignore that the administration they once led looked into the same question.
KMT New Taipei City mayoral candidate Lee Shu-chuan (李四川) said that railway undergrounding has already improved the north-south divide, and that the elevated Civic Boulevard has shrunk east-west travel times. That perspective accounts for traffic engineering, but not urban design considerations. Undergrounding the railway removes a physical barrier, but how local governments design pedestrian routes and promote spatial quality activity beneath the elevated road is another matter. That vehicles can pass through quickly does not mean pedestrians can cross safely and conveniently.
As the Ko administration had already identified a direction, the immediate questions should concern what improvements have already been completed and where more work is needed.
Taipei needs continuity in governance, not the wholesale rejection of past policies each time an election rolls around. Shen should offer a comprehensive plan covering spatial design, traffic impacts, construction costs and phased implementation. Meanwhile, Chiang and Ko should explain what has already been achieved and what still needs improvement.
Urban development is a long-term undertaking, and problems do not disappear when a new mayor takes office. Political rivals might have different visions, but policy judgements must not be reduced to partisan squabbles. If the need for a pedestrian-friendly environment was recognized in 2020, today evidence-based discussions are needed around improvements. It is not the idea of reconnecting fragmented urban spaces itself that is disorientating, but how a policy line suddenly becomes unfathomable when it is proposed by someone else.
Elliot Yao is a reviewer.

European soccer’s apology to China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:23 UTC
01:43:23 KST

Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe has never been shy about politics. In June 2024, ahead of France’s snap parliamentary elections, the France captain warned that “the extremes are at the gates of power.” During this year’s FIFA World Cup, fans dressed him up online as a dictator. Last month, he told France Football the memes were less funny once you remembered “the damage that people like that have caused throughout history.” Some of them, he said, showed “a lack of political and human awareness.”
This month, a meme cost him more than any of his political statements ever had. A video from the French show The Bridge showed Mbappe laughing at a meme that pasted his face onto the body of Mao Zedong (毛澤東). He was not making a political point. He was laughing at a meme. Beijing turned it into a diplomatic affair.
On Tuesday, three Chinese companies ended their deals with him with immediate effect, with one citing “a zero-tolerance policy toward any behavior that offends national sentiments.” State broadcaster China Central Television (CCTV) dropped Spanish La Liga.
Then came the apologies. Mbappe said sorry in three languages, Mandarin included, and spoke of his deep respect for Chinese and their history. La Liga apologized. Real Madrid apologized to Chinese. On, the Swiss sportswear brand that signed him last month, welcomed his apology and spoke of its “deep respect” for China. Hublot and Dior removed posts featuring him from their Chinese social media accounts. The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Guo Jiakun (郭嘉昆) said Beijing took the apology “seriously.” He did not say that Beijing accepted it.
Between 1959 and 1961, Mao’s Great Leap Forward caused a famine that killed tens of millions of people. Calling him a dictator is what textbooks do. Apologizing to Beijing for a meme turns a fact into an offense.
Taiwanese have seen this movie before. On Jan. 15, 2016, the eve of the presidential election, Chou Tzu-yu (周子瑜) read a statement on camera. The Taiwanese singer, 16 years old at the time, was a member of the South Korean band Twice. She said there was “only one China.” Her offense had been to hold the Republic of China flag on South Korean television, and she had just lost a Huawei advertising deal. Many Taiwanese compared the video to a hostage tape. Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) won the presidential election the next day.
In May, Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Francois Wu (吳志中) spoke at the European Parliament. Wu described how Chinese vessels harass ships crossing the Taiwan Strait. He said that, their message can be interpreted as: “If you don’t want to be harassed, you must first get my consent.”
That rule now covers soccer players and running shoes as well.
Companies usually bend. In 2018, China told foreign airlines to list Taiwan as part of China on their Web sites. The White House called it “Orwellian nonsense.” By the July deadline, most airlines had complied.
US sport was an exception. In 2019, Daryl Morey, then-general manager of the Houston Rockets, tweeted his support for Hong Kong protesters. CCTV pulled NBA broadcasts. NBA commissioner Adam Silver later said Beijing had asked him to fire Morey, and that there was “no chance” of that happening. The league admitted “substantial” losses, but it survived them.
European soccer picked the other script. Real Madrid did not need to apologize to keep playing soccer. Neither did a Swiss shoe company that has not yet sold a single soccer boot.
Taiwan cannot pay clubs to be brave, but it can make bravery cheaper. It has a decade of case files, from pop singers to airlines. Taiwan’s representative offices in Europe could share them with players’ unions such as FIFPRO, while no case is running. The message would be simple: An opinion about a dead dictator is not a breach of contract.
Taiwanese companies could add a lighter touch. A Taiwanese brand willing to sign a soccer player who laughs at Mao would buy more goodwill in Europe than a year of tourism campaigns.
In Brussels, Wu also told European lawmakers that Taiwan must become a core interest of Europe. On last week’s evidence, Europe’s clubs already have a core interest — the Chinese market.

Prized Voatsiperifery pepper at risk as forests in Madagascar face destruction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:21 UTC
01:43:21 KST

A rare wild pepper endemic to Madagascar and prized by international chefs is facing an uncertain future, victim of its own success and the destruction of its forest habitat.
With its subtle, aromatic flavor, Voatsiperifery pepper grows on vines that reach into the canopy of the island’s natural forests, which shrank 27 percent between 1990 and last year, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization said.
To reach the peppercorns without having to climb, harvesters often tear down the vine and, in many cases, the trees supporting them, contributing to the relentless retreat of Madagascar’s forests.
Photo: AFP
“At times, I tell myself I should never have made it known,” said French chef Olivier Roellinger, who first encountered the spice 30 years ago.
“This pepper blew me away right from the start with that piperine punch that brings out a note of peat, resin, even citrus; it’s incomparable,” he said. “On a fruit salad, it’s absolutely delicious.”
Madagascar pepper sells for 150 to 200 euros (US$167 to US$223) per kilogram in France, its main export market.
Roellinger, the founder of the Epices Roellinger spice boutique, is collaborating with efforts to certify authentic pepper based on strictly regulated harvesting zones in Madagascar.
However, he said he was “under no illusions” about the risk these rules could be circumvented.
The village of Ambongamarina, Madagascar, was at the center of a rush two decades ago for the pepper, which has a characteristic woody tail, a remnant of its stem.
From a ridge on which the village sits, farmer Maminiaina Rabearison pointed into the distance.
“Until 2010 to 2012, it was still covered in natural forest,” he said. “People used to go into the forest and, for 10 to 20 weeks a year, at least 100 kilograms were sold every week at the market to a trader.”
That trader has not visited in a long time. Harvests have dropped as the forest has been consumed by bush fires, charcoal production and slash-and-burn agriculture, or torched in protests against the distant central government.
The destruction of the vines has also forced harvesters to go deeper into the forest to find the plant, which in Malagasy is called “tsiperifery,” meaning “that makes wounds not exist,” a reference to its medicinal use for generations.
Now, “you have to walk almost a full day to find pepper in the forest,” farmer Herinaina Randrianarimanga said.
There is no national system to track the distribution, harvesting and export of this precious pepper, Jacarandas cofounder Mima Chateauneuf said.
“Today, we have no idea whether the resource is becoming scarce,” she said, calling for “traceability” to determine export volumes.
In the absence of a regulatory framework, Jacarandas is turning toward organic pepper, which has grown to make up one-third of its exports.
“For organic products, traceability is mandatory,” Chateauneuf said.
As research into the Voatsiperifery plant advances, French-Malagasy entrepreneur Olivier Ramaherison has been experimenting with domestic cultivation on land inherited from his father.
Between 500 and 1,000 vines — the result of thousands of trials — grew in terraces carved into the Mandraka forest.
There are no support trees here: The plants, laden with fruit just a few weeks from maturity, cluster close to the ground.
“The idea was to try to find a solution to make it easier to pick,” said Ramaherison, head of Essentialys, a company that produces aromatic plants, essential oils, coffee and pepper.
By chance, his team discovered that cuttings taken from the horizontal branches of the vine no longer tried to climb.
“If, like at the Piper nigrum [black pepper] plantations in Vietnam or Brazil, we manage to produce hundreds of tonnes of wild pepper, it would be a real economic boon for the country,” he said.

The US, South Korea and Japan yesterday reaffirmed their commitment to the “complete denuclearization” of North Korea as Pyongyang continues to reject disarmament ahead of possible talks with Washington.
Speculation is mounting over a potential meeting between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un at next month’s APEC summit in China, with Trump making repeated overtures to Pyongyang for nuclear talks.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, South Korean Minister of Foreign Affairs Cho Hyun and his Japanese counterpart Toshimitsu Motegi “reaffirmed their resolute commitment to the complete denuclearization” of North Korea during talks on Friday on the sidelines of a G20 meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, the US Department of State said.
Photo: Reuters
They also pledged “full implementation” of UN Security Council resolutions, including a ban on supporting revenue for North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programs.
Despite long-running UN sanctions, North Korea, which is backed by Russia and China, has enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state in law, with its regime repeatedly declaring its atomic arsenal permanent and irreversible.
Trump has made repeated overtures to Pyongyang for nuclear talks, while scaling back joint military drills with ally South Korea.
He even bucked long-held US policy last year by saying that North Korea was already “sort of a nuclear power,” while reaching out to Pyongyang for talks, saying he was “100 percent” open to a meeting — a suggestion that apparently went unanswered.
Analysts and South Korea’s spy agency said Kim might have conveyed Pyongyang’s position on potential talks with Trump to Beijing during a recent visit to the Chinese border city of Dandong.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung — who has repeatedly offered Pyongyang talks without preconditions — suggested in September that Washington seek a freeze, rather than the immediate elimination, of the North’s nuclear program in return for sanctions relief.
Critics have said such an approach risks tacitly accepts North Korea as a nuclear-armed state while allowing Pyongyang to win sanctions relief without giving up its arsenal.
Analysts said China might also be moving toward tacit acceptance, pointing to the omission of North Korean denuclearization from statements after Kim and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) met in June.
Pyongyang denounced a joint statement yesterday by a group of nations monitoring sanctions implementations against it, vowing that “the stereotyped sanctions racket of the US and the West can neither influence the position of the DPRK [North Korea] as a nuclear weapons state.”

Photo: AFP

Police also barred entry to the Place de la Republique and Les Halles, both hit by rioting and looting on Oct. 17, from 11pm to 6am on Saturday and Sunday nights.

A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.
The movement began with high-school students protesting school conditions and broadened into anger over living costs.

Taipei still feels like home
After half a century of ties to Taiwan, I still find myself looking at a Taipei streetscape and wishing it were more appealing. Yet if asked whether I would rather live here or in beautifully landscaped Singapore, I would choose Taipei.
I first lived in Taiwan from 1975 to 1977, teaching and studying at what was then Chinese Culture College, now Chinese Culture University. I returned from 1982 to 1984 with Irving Trust Co, later acquired by the Bank of New York. My Taiwan-born wife, Joyce, and I have family and friends here that make returning personal.
I have long admired the work ethic I encountered, the importance people placed on education and family, and their determination to improve their lives. As a banker, I followed Taiwan’s economic development with particular interest. Its democratic transformation has been equally impressive.
However, my fondest memories often involve smaller encounters. People have always been quick to compliment my Mandarin, sometimes generously. However, say a few words in Taiwanese, and the enthusiasm rises another notch. An ordinary transaction becomes a friendly conversation, and a foreigner feels welcome.
The food has also held up remarkably well against memory. Nostalgia can be an unfair restaurant critic, but the rolled egg crepes I bought at a roadside stall near my old college were every bit as good as I remembered.
The urban scenery prompted a more mixed response. Driving toward Keelung to visit Joyce’s brother, I noticed old, weathered housing, densely packed buildings and little greenery between them. Modern high-rises provided occasional relief. Persistent drizzle did the older buildings no favors.
These were impressions of particular stretches, not a verdict on Taiwan. A highway view cannot tell the whole story, nor does a weathered facade reveal how people live inside. Still, I wondered why such extraordinary economic progress had not brought more improvement to everyday urban surroundings.
Housing, jobs and transport understandably took priority during rapid growth. Renewing established neighborhoods is difficult. Yet more attention to older buildings, trees and ordinary streets would make a difference. Taipei has parks and attractive places; I wish more of that care extended along the routes connecting them.
Singapore’s greenery and carefully maintained public spaces deserve admiration, but family, familiarity, wonderful food and the easy friendliness I encounter keep drawing me back to Taipei.
Affection sustained over 50 years leaves room for disappointment. I want Taipei to look more appealing, because I care about it. I would welcome more trees and better-kept buildings, and happily return tomorrow for another rolled egg crepe and a conversation in Mandarin, with a few words of Taiwanese thrown in.
Michael J. Ranieri
Bonita Springs, Florida
Responsible policies needed
On Oct. 16, the opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan passed the third reading of amendments to the Senior Citizens Welfare Act (老人福利法), which would require the central government to subsidize the National Health Insurance (NHI) premiums for all people age 65 or older who meet specific income eligibility criteria. The policy appears to offer greater support for elderly people, but why expand blanket subsidies rather than prioritize resources for those with a genuine need for assistance?
The Ministry of Health and Welfare estimates that about 4.03 million elderly people across Taiwan would qualify for the subsidies, amounting to an annual cost of about NT$40 billion (US$1.23 billion). Whether funding through NHI resources or central government tax revenues, someone would have to bear the cost. Taiwan faces a declining birthrate and an aging population. The working-age population is gradually shrinking, while healthcare and long-term care expenditures continue to rise.
The income eligibility threshold is the most important issue to reconsider. Does having an income tax rate below 20 percent mean that someone lacks the means to support themselves? Some elderly people own property, have savings and receive a steady retirement income while others struggle to make ends meet. Do these two groups really need the same subsidies? If the government is committed to supporting the disadvantaged, it should take income, assets and actual living needs into account to ensure that limited public funds first go to elderly people facing financial hardship and to young families in need of support.
Older people need security, but younger generations also need a future. Young people must shoulder mortgage payments, the costs of raising children, and various taxes and fees, all while facing an increasingly heavy burden of social spending. It is easy for political parties to win applause by championing welfare policies, but having the courage to explain the long-term funding of these policies is another matter. Supporting older people is a worthy goal, but every welfare policy must take fiscal capacity and intergenerational equity into account. Today’s political gains must not become a bill young people must pay tomorrow.
Tao Huo
Taipei

The Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall in Taipei on Tuesday held a plaque-unveiling ceremony for the Reading Boy bronze sculpture by artist Wang Hsiu-chi (王秀杞) on the western side of the hall’s grounds.
The Taipei Capitol Lions Club and its Japanese sister Aomori Mahoroba Lions Club had jointly commissioned the statue as a companion to Reading Girl, which the former donated to the museum a decade ago.
The statues celebrate the joy and intellectual benefits of reading as electronic devices increasingly compete for the attention of their users, the hall’s director-general Wang Lan-sheng (王蘭生) said.
Photo courtesy of the Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hall
The pair of bronze statues are also part of the memorial hall’s project to beautify its surroundings to become a more cultured space that art enjoyers can appreciate, he said.
The hall hopes that gathering such creations would make the garden around it a landmark for people in the city, Wang said.
Taipei Capitol Lions Club president Kuo Su-mei (郭素梅) said that the group hopes the new sculpture would encourage a passion for reading in Taiwanese youth amid distractions from phones, the Internet and television.
The group hopes the memorial’s visitors would to rest and read on the three granite benches placed near the statutes, which the club also donated to show its concern for the public good, she said.
Together, the club’s gifts of the Reading Boy and Reading Girl set an example that urges people to rediscover the pleasure of reading, Wang Hsiu-chi told the event.
Wang Hsiu-chi grew up in poverty, having had to walk an hour to school and help his father tend to the family orchard after returning home, with little time left for reading, the sculptor said.
“Although my father used to tell me all the time that I must have an education if I wanted to have a future, I did not study well and chose to create sculptures,” he said. “I am thankful that the organizations involved gave me the chance to contribute to the future generation by creating something beautiful.”

Patriot missiles are among the most important weapons Ukraine has to intercept Russian drones and missiles.

Average taxi income rises: survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:16 UTC
01:43:16 KST

The Ministry of Transportation and Communications’ (MOTC) latest Taxi Business Survey showed that full-time taxi drivers’ average monthly net income rose 20.4 percent last year to NT$32,465, while multi-purpose taxis expanded to 40 percent of the nation’s taxi fleet.
The survey showed that full-time taxi drivers earned an average monthly gross income of NT$55,788, up NT$7,022, or 14.4 percent, from 2023. After deducting operating expenses, their average monthly net income was NT$32,465, an increase of NT$5,508, or 20.4 percent.
More than 76 percent of full-time taxi drivers, defined as those whose principal source of income is operating a taxi, were affiliated with taxi dispatch fleets, up 7.4 percentage points from the previous survey.
Photo: CNA
Nearly 80 percent of taxi rides were arranged through online booking platforms, radio or satellite dispatch services, while the proportion of drivers picking up passengers by cruising the streets fell to 40 percent for the first time, reflecting a shift toward digital operations in the industry.
Full-time drivers who worked at least eight hours a day earned an average monthly gross income of NT$62,822 and net income of NT$37,403, NT$7,034 and NT$4,938 more respectively than the average for all full-time taxi drivers.
Multi-purpose taxi drivers took more days off on average than other full-time drivers, but made more trips and drove longer distances on days they worked. Their average monthly gross income was NT$59,528, higher than the average for all full-time taxi drivers.
The MOTC conducts the survey every two years. From March to June, it sampled taxi operators active at the end of last year and received 9,861 valid responses, a response rate of 33 percent.
Taiwan had 92,768 taxis at the end of last year, up 1,114, or about 1.2 percent, from the previous survey. Of those, 36,023 were multi-purpose taxis, accounting for nearly 40 percent of the fleet, the survey showed.
The ministry also released the results of its Tour Bus Business Survey, which found the industry had contracted slightly as operators diversified their services. Labor shortages among companies specializing in shuttle services and tourism had eased, while overall revenue had recovered to pre-COVID-19 pandemic levels. Tour bus drivers earned an average monthly salary of NT$48,000 last year, up NT$3,686, or 8.3 percent, from the previous survey.
