How is the  US-China tech war going? Ask AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:15 UTC
01:43:15 KST

An unmistakable moment in the US-China tech war arrived in early 2024 — via the Netherlands.
“We do not expect to get export licenses for our most advanced immersion systems — the NXT:2000 and up — for China in 2024,” executives at ASML Holding NV, the Dutch lithography giant at the heart of the global semiconductor supply chain, said on their earnings call in January that year, warning that the curbs, a result of years of US pressure, would knock 10 to 15 percent off the company’s core China equipment sales.
For global investors, this was Washington flexing its hegemonic muscle to delay a key rival’s race to the frontier of artificial intelligence (AI), just as it was becoming the defining general-purpose technology of our era. However, the disclosure raised more questions than it answered: What does a warning like ASML’s mean for investment portfolios? Who would bear the costs and reap the profits — the US, which designed the restrictions, or China, their intended target? And how are risks and returns being rewritten for companies caught in the crossfire across the world?
The investment community has some answers in Geoeconomic Pressure, a paper written by Yale School of Management finance professor Christopher Clayton and other economists. They fed more than 600,000 corporate earnings calls — spanning two decades and 22,000 listed firms worldwide, including China — to open-source large language models running on Stanford University’s computing systems. The algorithm listened for genuine causality: not merely whether CEOs mentioned flashpoints, but if state coercion actually forced them to alter prices, divert investments, or redraw supply chains.
That nuance matters because traditional keyword searches stumble over context. Even sophisticated statistical tools unleashed on a bag of words fail to do the job: A routine maintenance shutdown can get flagged as business disruption and ascribed to a tariff action. A pre-trained language model, by contrast, grasps sentence-level intent, weeding out such false positives.
Language models are just as effective against false negatives. On public calls, corporate executives are notoriously reticent, loath to linger on the fallout of government diktats — particularly those from their own political leaders. To look past this hesitation, the researchers ran the same models over equity analysts’ reports. The AI’s reading of C-suite disclosures matched independent sell-side assessments almost in lockstep.
By latching on to what corporate bosses prefer to downplay, AI captured a nuanced account of pains and gains. In the US, firms subjected to Washington’s restrictions faced lost volumes and compressed margins. Across the Pacific, the shock worked like an adrenaline shot. In about 40 percent of Chinese earnings calls flagged for export curbs, management reported ramping up research and development. Among calls detailing higher spending, two-thirds aligned with a category that AI labeled as “Core Technology Indigenization” — pouring money into homegrown chip gear to escape the US chokehold. (The algorithm did not just sort transcripts into pre-assigned slots; it coined the category names.)
Other geopolitical shocks produced similar ironies. When Western sanctions hit Russia after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, firms in Europe and the US shouldered write-downs, asset forfeitures and higher logistics bills. The real winners were non-aligned bystanders in China and India. Freed from Western competition, they rushed into the vacuum and scooped up heavily discounted Urals crude.
Nor did US President Donald Trump’s tariff offensive last year go as intended. Foreign exporters did not “eat” the duties, as the US president had predicted. In nearly three-quarters of instances where management disclosed an effect, the impact was negative. Among those reporting outright harm, close to 60 percent pointed to inflated input bills. The rare domestic winners were those insulated from foreign supply chains. Without being saddled with the extra costs paid by their import-reliant rivals, they could still raise prices. Meanwhile, foreign producers absorbed the pressure not by slashing export prices, but by moving factories to Vietnam and Mexico.
Whether the weapon is a tariff, a sanction or a chip ban, economic statecraft is rarely a surgical strike. More often than not, it is a messy carpet bomb that leaves substantial collateral damage in its wake. Investors profit from being able to spot unintended consequences before they appear in the price. Machines reading corporate chatter might just give them the edge to bet on geopolitics before the rest of the market catches on.
Andy Mukherjee is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering industrial companies and financial services in Asia. Previously, he worked for Reuters, The Straits Times and Bloomberg News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

MOE sets teacher protection guides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:15 UTC
01:43:15 KST

The Ministry of Education (MOE) has issued guidelines to help schools prevent and handle workplace violence and harassment against teachers, including psychological abuse, online attacks and malicious complaints.
Department of Information and Technology Education official Lien Shan-li (連杉利) on Friday said that the term covers more than physical assaults, and also includes verbal abuse, psychological violence, persistent harassment and being assigned duties outside one’s job responsibilities.
The Guidelines on Preventing Workplace Violence and Harassment in Schools and Early Childhood Education and Care Facilities (各級學校及教保服務機構職場不法侵害預防指引) cover teachers at all school levels, early childhood education and care personnel, and other school staff, Lien said.
Photo: Rachel Lin, Taipei Times
The guidelines identify guardhouses, student affairs and counseling offices, meeting rooms and school entrances as places where incidents involving outsiders are more likely to occur.
High-risk periods include students’ arrival and departure times, meetings between parents and school staff, discussions over serious student misconduct or disputes, and after-school study periods.
Schools are advised to install surveillance cameras and emergency contact equipment at these locations, while avoiding excessive monitoring. Surveillance footage should not be arbitrarily made public or shared, the guidelines state.
Schools must reject anonymous complaints, those lacking specific details and cases that have already received a final decision, it added.
Complaints involving only ordinary disciplinary matters should be handled under teacher performance assessment rules, rather than triggering investigations that could lead to dismissal or non-renewal of contracts, it said.
The guidelines also advise schools not to assign work or contact teachers about parent-teacher matters outside working hours, except in cases involving campus safety, major emergencies or urgent official duties.
A task force to investigate the issues should be formed within three days of receiving a complaint and complete investigations within one month, it said.
If a principal or preschool director is implicated, an impartial third party should conduct the investigation, it said, adding that whistle-blowers or complainants must be protected against retaliation.
The guidelines also protect teachers’ right to legally discipline students, stipulating that necessary disciplinary measures in line with legal requirements should not result in punishment or adverse performance assessments.
Schools and early childhood education and care institutions with at least 100 employees must also draw up prevention plans and retain records for three years, the guidelines state.
The ministry said that the guidelines constitute administrative guidance. Cases involving workplace bullying or sexual harassment should continue to be handled primarily under relevant laws.
The National Teachers’ Association (NTA) in a statement welcomed the guidelines, but said that they lacked concrete accountability mechanisms, calling for clearer employer responsibilities.
NTA chairman Yeh Ching-chi (葉青?) said vague provisions could allow school administrators to avoid taking action.
Schools should help teachers establish the facts and provide legal and administrative support when they face pressure or retaliatory complaints from parents over lawful student discipline, rather than demanding apologies or imposing unreasonable measures, Yeh said.
The association urged the ministry to set clear criteria for identifying repeated or malicious complaints and harassment, and to include teacher representatives in workplace risk assessments and reviews of prevention measures.

Amendments to combat illegal land use pass legislature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:15 UTC
01:43:15 KST

Newly passed amendments to regulations on the utilization of farmland and slopeland are aimed to combat illegal land development, the Ministry of Agriculture said on Friday.
The Legislative Yuan on Friday passed the third reading of amendments to the Agricultural Development Act (農業發展條例), the Soil and Water Conservation Act (水土保持法), and the Act for the Utilization and Transfer of Reserved Mountainous Land (山坡地保育利用條例).
The ministry said that the amendments increased penalties for illegal agricultural land filling and illegal hillside development, as well as including wildlife-related crop losses in the scope of government relief.
Photo copied by Peng Chien-li, Taipei Times
According to amendments to articles 10 and 69 of the Agricultural Development Act, illegal filling or dumping on farmland could be fined up to NT$3 million (US$92,370), it said.
Amendments to Article 60 include crop damage caused by wildlife in the scope of cash relief, subsidies or low-interest loans from the government, the ministry said, adding that it would further formulate relief measures.
According to amendments to the Soil and Water Conservation Act, unauthorized hillside land use or development that causes soil erosion or damage to soil and water conservation could be given a maximum jail term of five years with a fine of NT$25 million.
In scenarios where the violation resulted in death or severe injury, the maximum fines have been raised to NT$100 million from NT$1 million and to NT$80 million from NT$800,000.
Those who fail to make improvements for their violation of soil and water conservation regulations could be fined up to NT$3 million, up from NT$60,000.
The amendments are expected to enhance law enforcement efficiency, the ministry said.
Additional reporting by CNA

Drone firm raided over Chinese chips
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:12 UTC
01:43:12 KST

Three government agencies had purchased a total of 32 drones made by or linked to Align Corp (亞拓科技), the Ministry of the Interior said yesterday, after the company’s director was detained for allegedly using Chinese-made chips in military drones.
The ministry said it would act in accordance with the Government Procurement Act (政府採購法) and contractual provisions, adding that it would not rule out seeking compensation if any contraventions were found.
A preliminary review found that the National Park Service and Central Police University each purchased one drone manufactured by the company last year, the ministry said, adding that it would verify the details and handle the matter in accordance with procurement regulations.
Photo: Taipei Times
Separately, the National Immigration Agency (NIA) this year completed a public tender under the Government Procurement Act to purchase 30 drones from Suyuan Technology Co (速源科技) at a total cost of NT$2.75 million (US$84,673), the ministry said.
While Suyuan Technology had planned to supply the drones manufactured by Align, delivery has not yet taken place, it said.
The NIA would strictly enforce contractual requirements prohibiting the delivery of drones containing Chinese-made components, it said.
As government procurement standards mandate compliance with “non-red supply chain” requirements, the ministry would continue to strictly require government agencies and suppliers to follow the regulations in procurement processes, it said.
Compensation would be sought in accordance with contractual terms if contraventions were found, it added.
The ministry’s review came as the Taichung Prosecutors’ Office on Friday said that it raided Align Corp and the company’s director Tu Ta-sen (杜大森) was ordered detained and held incommunicado.
The company’s drones were purchased by the army for educational and training purposes, it said
To ensure the equipment met procurement specifications, the military conducted inspections that included dismantling the drones and discovered that chips inside the aircraft bore the letters “CN,” it said.
The procurement contracts explicitly prohibit the use of products from China, Hong Kong and Macau, it said.
The case was reported to prosecutors who found the same issue in another batch of drones purchased by the army.
Prosecutors searched locations connected to the company and summoned six people for questioning, including Tu and his wife, they said.
Investigators found that Tu allegedly used chips manufactured by Chinese companies in at least two batches of military drone procurement contracts and directed Align Corp to assemble the drones before delivering them to the military, they said.
The contracts were worth more than NT$8 million in total, they added.
Tu and others were suspected of misrepresenting the country of origin of products supplied under the contracts, they said.
They were suspected of contravening the National Security Act (國家安全法), which prohibits the delivery of products for military procurement when the supplier knows they originate in China, and also face fraud charges under the Criminal Code, they said.
Align Corp, founded in 1984, is headquartered in Taichung’s Fengyuan District (豐原), the company’s Web site showed.
The company has long secured government contracts to supply drones to the military, police and fire departments.
The Changhua County Police Department, which established a drone unit in June, purchased two M490 drones and nine M3 drones from the company.

2026 Elections: Chiang, Shen clash in first televised mayoral debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:09 UTC
01:43:09 KST

Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and his main rival, Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋), traded barbs over public safety, city governance and food safety in their first televised debate yesterday.
One of the sharpest exchanges concerned tougher penalties for drug-impaired driving. Chiang criticized Shen for not taking part in a legislative vote on a related amendment on Friday, accusing him of placing the interests of offenders ahead of victims and their families.
Chiang said Shen’s emphasis on his expertise in criminology showed “professional arrogance,” and questioned whether he understood the suffering of families affected by impaired driving.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
Shen said that while he supported tougher penalties for drunk and drug-impaired driving, he considered the amendment disproportionate, adding that preventing such offenses was a more direct responsibility of local governments through police checks, drug-prevention education in schools and efforts to curb drug supplies.
Drawing attention to his previous work with the Association for Victims Support and recovering drug addicts, Shen said his efforts had been misrepresented.
“It now seems as though I’m being made out to be Taipei’s biggest drug dealer,” he said.
The candidates also clashed over city administration, including the accidental felling of a 40-year-old tree near Dongmen Market and the implementation of a free school-lunch program.
The two also criticized each other’s positions on child protection legislation and food safety, each accusing the other of applying double standards.
Shen questioned whether the city government had responded consistently to cases involving school food safety and alleged child abuse, while Chiang said the city government had taken action in the cases and introduced measures to improve oversight and protect children.
The two also clashed over urban renewal, with Chiang touting his record and Shen calling for greater support to overcome hurdles.
“A mayor’s job is to solve problems by addressing their root causes,” Chiang said, highlighting progress on urban renewal projects at Xinwei public housing, Nanjichang Night Market (南機場夜市), and Hulin Street since he became mayor in 2022.
During the past four years, Taipei has approved 2.4 times more urban renewal projects than before, and 1.3 times as many as the other five municipalities combined, he said.
Chiang pressed Shen on why projects in Datong (大同) and Neihu (內湖) districts had been difficult to advance in the legislature, asking him to identify the obstacles to urban renewal.
Shen did not directly address the two cases, saying that the number of approved projects actually moving forward to construction and completion was what mattered most, “rather than simply showcasing favorable statistics.”
The city government has made it easier to launch urban renewal projects, but issues such as property rights, review times, developers’ estimates and implementation can still hold up projects, Shen said.
About 70 percent of residential buildings in Taipei are more than 30 years old, so the city naturally has more urban renewal projects, but also more that have yet to be approved, he said.
The two-hour debate, held from noon to 2pm at the TVBS studio and cohosted by TVBS and SET News, was the only one that Chiang and Shen, the two frontrunners in a six-candidate field, had agreed to so far.

Cruise ship suspends global voyage due to fuel costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:43:09 UTC
01:43:09 KST

A US cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year journey in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to “make the Odyssey your permanent home,” with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting at about US$230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
Photo: Reuters
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials.
It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged US$1,800 have reached an estimated US$6,000 to US$8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran.
The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on Tuesday. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees” while it tries to restructure.
“The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements,” it said.
However, some passengers said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising, but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable.
While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling.
Changes to the itinerary, unreliable Internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in the past few months, he said.
Lynn said that residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia.
She said the crew members were also not paid.
“We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything,” she said.
“We had hopes, but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement,” she added.
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil could not outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
“I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it’s a dream to live on the ship and I don’t want it to end,” Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship and that she did not need to use a cane to walk anymore.
“You come to this ship to live ... it’s just sad that it’s all over,” she said.
Larson bought her cabin for US$120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years.
She blamed US President Donald Trump for the ship’s woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management.
However, she said she did not regret her investment.
“Because it was a start-up company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money’s worth... I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising,” she said.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville on Oct. 23 and was scheduled to depart on Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk.
The ship’s operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date of departure.
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines before being becalmed by the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last three-and-a-half years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China.
It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them US citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, then-Cambodian prime minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons.
Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.

Thousands of young Germans rally over living costs, spending cuts as police make arrests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:42:54 UTC
01:42:54 KST

Thousands of young Germans have taken to the streets nationwide to protest against political leaders they accuse of ignoring their concerns, with police reporting arrests in Hamburg and unrest in Stuttgart.
Protesters gathered in Berlin, Frankfurt, Cologne and dozens of other cities on Saturday for rallies organised by “GenZ regelt!”, or “Gen Z has got this”.
Demonstrators carried signs reading “Time for resistance” and “Merz must go”, referring to conservative Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
“We’re taking to the streets for a life that everyone can afford,” said movement spokeswoman Veronika Dinter.
“Hardly anyone still believes in a better future if everything just continues as it is.”
The movement’s grievances include high living costs, poorly maintained schools, government spending cuts and insufficient climate action, alongside a broader belief that politicians disregard the younger generation.
Protesters also oppose sharply increased military spending and fear a new voluntary military service model intended to boost troop numbers could pave the way for conscription.
Arrests in Hamburg, unrest in Stuttgart
More than 10,000 people joined the march in Hamburg, where police said at least two men were arrested on Saturday afternoon.
One was apparently carrying a fake firearm in the upscale Jungfernstieg neighbourhood. Officers overpowered both men, with no immediate reports of injuries or information about their motives.
Police used tear gas and pepper spray to disperse protesters. Drones and water cannons were also deployed as part of a large-scale security operation.
In Stuttgart, police said pyrotechnics were apparently fired at officers from within the march. They also reported scattered vandalism along the route, including graffiti and burning litter bins, which officers extinguished.
The march was halted several times over masked participants and the use of pyrotechnics. At least 3,000 people took part, according to police.
Despite these incidents, demonstrations nationwide appeared mostly peaceful by early evening.
Turnout below expectations
Attendance in several cities appeared lower than organisers had hoped, after more than 170,000 people registered to participate nationwide.
Police in Cologne said turnout was significantly below the 15,000 who had registered, without providing a precise figure.
Around 2,700 people attended in Berlin, 1,800 in Munich and 1,000 in Frankfurt.
Thousands of police officers were deployed across Germany, while some shops boarded up their windows amid fears of unrest.
The German movement has drawn inspiration from similar protests in France and Italy. Demonstrations were also taking place in France for a third consecutive weekend, following some of the country’s worst rioting in years on October 17.
German authorities had feared the protests, coinciding with Halloween, could see similar violence. Berlin has been in contact with French and Italian officials amid concerns that radicals from abroad could join the demonstrations.
Before the rallies, however, authorities said they had found no evidence of concrete plans for violence.
“GenZ regelt!” explicitly rejects violence, saying extremist groups, anti-constitutional symbols, racism and hate speech have no place in its movement.
Christian Volk, a protest researcher at Berlin’s Humboldt University, said Germany had the potential for a major protest movement.
But he told AFP that France had a “completely different tradition when it comes to confrontational forms of protest”.

A minority in their homeland who have been facing discrimination and state violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:29:02 UTC
01:29:02 KST

A minority in their homeland who have been facing discrimination and state violence
TEHRAN - “Palestinian citizens of Israel,” also known as the “Palestinians of 1948” or “Palestinians inside Israel” have been subjected to discrimination and violence at the hands of successive Israeli governments.
Making up approximately one-fifth of Israel’s population, their votes in the October 27 Knesset election could play a decisive role in determining the composition of the next Israeli government.
Envious of the 19 seats they have won in the 120-seat Knesset, Israeli Prime Minister Netanayahu, his Likud Party, and his extremist allies have launched a campaign against them, linking their high turnout in the election to Qatar, Turkey and some other countries, a claim which seems ridiculous.
The following text, published by Middle East Eye, provides a brief story of these original inhabitants of Palestine. The text, headlined “Who Are the Palestinian Citizens of Israel?”, reads below:
A minority in their homeland, Palestinian citizens of Israel have faced decades of discrimination, marginalization and violence.
They are descendants of Palestinians who survived the Nakba and remained within the de facto borders of Israel after its establishment in 1948.
Today, they number around two million, making up roughly a fifth of Israel’s population.
Although they hold Israeli citizenship, they continue to face discrimination and state repression.
Deep-rooted inequalities persist in housing, land rights, education and public services, while they struggle with high levels of violent crime and inadequate police protection.
They have also faced deadly police violence and arrests during protests in solidarity with Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip.
Despite these challenges, Palestinian citizens have organized politically and contested elections in their struggle for equal civil and political rights.
So who are Palestinian citizens of Israel? What challenges do they face, and how much influence could they wield over the country’s political future?
Minority in their homeland
Palestinian Arabs made up the majority of the population of historic Palestine before 1947. The territory now comprises Israel, the occupied West Bank and the Gaza Strip.
Between 1947 and 1948, Zionist militias, and later Israeli forces, carried out the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians to make way for the creation of Israel. Palestinians call this the Nakba, or catastrophe.
In a premeditated military campaign, Zionist forces killed thousands of Palestinians, destroyed hundreds of villages and forcibly expelled 80 percent of the Palestinian population from their homeland.
The violence was formally ended in 1949, with Israel signing armistice agreements with neighboring Arab states, whose forces had entered the war to stop the takeover of Palestine.
Israel had captured 78 percent of historic Palestine. Around 150,000 Palestinians remained within the territory that became Israel.
Some survived because Israeli forces had not yet reached their areas, while others resisted attempts to expel them.
Nearly a quarter of those who remained were internally displaced.
They were barred from returning to their homes, many of which were in villages that had been destroyed.
Overnight, Palestinians who remained found themselves a minority in their own homeland.
Today, they make up around 20 percent of Israel’s population of approximately 10 million.
They live mainly in Palestinian-majority towns and cities across the Galilee in the north, the Triangle region in central Israel and the Naqab desert in the south.
Around 80 percent are Muslim, 10 percent Christian and 10 percent Druze.
Israel and much of its society commonly refer to them as “Israeli Arabs” or “Arab citizens of Israel”.
Many, however, identify as “Palestinian citizens of Israel”, “Palestinians of 1948” or “Palestinians inside Israel”.
These terms affirm their Palestinian identity alongside their status as Israeli citizens.
Military rule and resistance
Although Palestinian citizens were granted Israeli citizenship after 1948, early Israeli governments viewed them with suspicion and subjected them to state violence.
From 1948 to 1966, they lived under a military regime imposed exclusively on them, while Jewish citizens were governed by civilian law.
During this period, they faced movement restrictions, curfews, state repression and limits on their political activity.
One of the darkest episodes was the Kafr Qasim massacre.
On 29 October 1956, Israeli forces abruptly brought forward a curfew in the Palestinian village of Kafr Qasim. Hundreds of residents working outside the village were unaware of the change.
Soldiers had been given orders to shoot those who violated the curfew.
As workers returned home, troops stopped them at the village entrance and shot them at close range.
Within hours, 49 Palestinian citizens had been killed, including women and children.
Military rule finally ended in 1966.
In the years that followed, Palestinian citizens increasingly reconnected with the wider Palestinian population, particularly after Israel occupied the West Bank and Gaza Strip in 1967.
One of the most significant protests came on 30 March 1976, in response to Israeli plans to confiscate Palestinian land in the Galilee.
Israeli police violently suppressed the demonstrations, killing six Palestinian citizens and injuring hundreds.
The events became known as Land Day, commemorated annually on 30 March as a symbol of the struggle for Palestinian land and rights.
During the Second Palestinian Intifada, which began in 2000, Palestinian citizens of Israel staged mass protests against Israel’s occupation and in solidarity with Palestinians in the occupied territories.
Police responded with deadly force, killing 13 Palestinian demonstrators and arresting hundreds more.
Discrimination and crime
Beyond state violence, Palestinian citizens have faced decades of discriminatory laws and policies under successive Israeli governments.
According to Adalah, a Haifa-based legal center defending Palestinian rights, more than 65 Israeli laws enacted since 1948 explicitly or implicitly discriminate against Palestinians in Israel and the occupied territories.
These laws cover areas including land ownership, housing, public funding and family reunification.
One of the earliest examples was the Absentees’ Property Law, passed in 1950.
It classified Palestinians who had left, fled or been expelled from their homes during the 1948 Nakba as “absentees”. Their land, homes and other property were placed under state control, including assets belonging to some Palestinians who later became Israeli citizens.
In 2003, Israel passed a law restricting family reunification between Israeli citizens and spouses from the occupied West Bank and Gaza Strip.
A 2011 law empowered admissions committees in certain agricultural and community towns to assess applicants seeking to live there. Critics say the law enables discrimination against Palestinian citizens by allowing committees to reject candidates deemed incompatible with a community’s "Zionist-Jewish character”.
One of the most controversial measures came in 2018, when the Knesset passed the Basic Law: Israel as the Nation-State of the Jewish People.
The law reserves the right to national self-determination in Israel exclusively for the Jewish people. It also downgrades Arabic from an official language to one with a “special status” and declares Jewish settlement a national value that the state should promote.
Alongside legal discrimination, Palestinian communities face a deepening crisis of organized crime and violent killings.
The Abraham Initiatives, an Israeli civil society organization, has linked the crisis to what it describes as “under-policing and tense relations with the Israeli police”.
In 2023, the NGO said that 50 percent of overall violent crime in the country affects Palestinians, even though they make up only 20 percent of Israel's population.
Palestinian community representatives have accused Israeli police of turning a blind eye to the illegal arms trade, and in some cases of indirectly enabling it.
Israel denies responsibility for the crime crisis.
The Palestinian death toll has risen sharply in recent years. A total of 116 people were killed in 2022, rising to 244 in 2023. Most victims were not involved in criminal activity.
In 2025, the number of fatalities reached 252, making it the deadliest year on record.
The Abraham Initiatives’ 2024 report also highlighted a stark gap in homicide investigations. Israeli police solved fewer than 15 percent of killings in Palestinian communities, compared with a clearance rate of around 65 percent for cases in which the victims were Jewish.
Political parties
To challenge discrimination, state violence and Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territories, Palestinian citizens of Israel have long used political organization.
Political activity began as early as the 1950s, but military rule and state repression severely restricted their ability to organize and participate in public life.
By the 1970s, Palestinian citizens were building stronger parliamentary and grassroots movements.
In 1977, Hadash - the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality - was established. It remains one of the most prominent political forces among Palestinian citizens.
Other influential parties emerged in the following decades, including Balad, the National Democratic Assembly; Ta’al, the Arab Movement for Renewal; and Ra’am, the United Arab List.
In 1982, the High Follow-Up Committee for Arab Citizens of Israel was formed. It became a key umbrella body representing Palestinian citizens across political parties and local authorities.
The committee serves as a leading voice for the Palestinian minority outside parliament, linking local municipalities with national political movements.
Palestinian-led parties have contested Knesset elections since those parties began to emerge, but have largely remained outside governing coalitions.
In 2015, Hadash, Balad, Ta’al and Ra’am joined forces to form the Joint List. The alliance followed a 2014 decision to raise the electoral threshold from 2 percent to 3.25 percent, prompting concerns that smaller parties would struggle to enter parliament independently.
The Joint List won 15 seats in the March 2020 election, becoming the Knesset’s third-largest parliamentary bloc. Internal disagreements later fractured the alliance, weakening its collective influence.
For decades, cooperation with Palestinian-led parties was widely treated as a political taboo. Many Jewish Israeli voters opposed such partnerships, while Palestinian citizens themselves remained divided over whether joining a government could deliver meaningful change.
That barrier was broken in 2021, when Ra’am joined the governing coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. Its four seats helped secure the narrow parliamentary majority that ended Benjamin Netanyahu’s 12-year run as prime minister.
Ahead of the 2026 election, Hadash, Balad and Ta’al reunited under the Joint List, while Ra’am remained a separate party.
Together, the two electoral alliances are projected to win 19 seats, potentially giving Palestinian-led parties renewed leverage over coalition negotiations and the formation of Israel’s next government.
Their influence could prove decisive in determining who governs - and whether Palestinian citizens can translate parliamentary representation into meaningful political change.

Binance said Saturday that it has covered up to 90% of the roughly $6.3 billion in token assets stolen from its hot wallets in a record crypto theft announced Thursday.

"All BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC are fully backed 100%," Binance said in a statement. "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users."
The exchange said the outstanding 10% consists of tokens outside its top 10 that are "less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts."
Binance said it is tapping its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a portion of its Futures insurance fund, and its corporate treasury to replenish the assets.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident. We will continue to demonstrate this commitment through measurable progress, transparent reporting, and concrete actions," Binance said.
Its "next milestone" will be resuming withdrawal services for users by Sunday, subject to security checks, while the exchange continues its investigation into the attack, it said.
Binance declined to discuss additional details or updates on its investigation to CNBC, referring questions to its latest statement.
It still isn't clear how the attack — the largest crypto theft on record — took place.
The world's largest crypto exchange initially said the hack may involve "a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions." However, Co-CEO Richard Teng later said the attack involved a more complex process rather than the misuse of a single engineer's permissions.
It also wasn't clear who was responsible for the breach. But TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence and AI investigations company, pointed to North Korean hackers as the potential culprits.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack and the KelpDAO hack in April 2026: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet, staging that began well before the theft, and signatures obtained in advance then executed in one burst," the company said.
— CNBC's Jenny Lee, Liz Napolitano and Davis Giangiulio contributed to this report.

Animal testing in India: Why proposed new rules have sparked a fight over safeguards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:01:25 UTC
01:01:25 KST

The rules propose a differentiated approval system based on the severity of experiments.
NEW DELHI: Animal testing remains an important part of pharmaceutical research, vaccine development and medical science in India. But a proposed overhaul of the rules governing laboratory experiments has triggered a debate over a fundamental question: Can India streamline scientific research without weakening safeguards for animals?The draft Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (Control and Supervision of Experiment, Breeding and Trading of Laboratory Animals) Rules, 2026, issued by the Committee for Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CCSEA), proposes changes to how experiments are classified and approved. While it introduces a severity-based system for assessing animal suffering, animal welfare groups have raised concerns about reduced regulatory scrutiny, the use of certain animals and potential conflicts of interest in institutional approvals.The debate also comes at a time when advances in science are opening up alternatives to animal testing, including human cell-based studies, organoids, organ-on-chip technology and computer modelling. The question is whether India's regulatory framework is keeping pace with these developments.What are the proposed rules1. Severity-Based Classification: Experiments are categorized into four levels based on expected pain or distress: Mild, Moderate, Severe, Non-recovery2. Decentralized Approvals: An establishment's internal Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC) can directly approve mild and moderate experiments on any species.
The central Committee for Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CCSEA) retains approval authority for severe and non-recovery procedures, specifically for animals positioned above rodents and rabbits.3. Three Rs: Replacement, Reduction and Refinement. These involve using alternatives wherever possible, limiting the number of animals to what is scientifically necessary and improving procedures and care to minimise suffering.The proposed framework also lays down requirements for the registration of establishments, institutional ethics committees, veterinary supervision, trained personnel and animal-care facilities. Experiments may be undertaken for specified purposes, including basic and applied research, drug and food safety testing, disease research, environmental protection and species conservationThe sectors that use animals for researchAnimal experimentation is not limited to pharmaceutical companies. Dr Surat, Senior Program Director, Research and Toxicology Department, Humane World for Animals India, said it is carried out across pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies, medical research institutions, universities, veterinary colleges and government laboratories.Animals are used in vaccine development and batch testing, food and feed safety assessments, disease research and studies evaluating the effectiveness of potential treatments. Tests may assess short-term and long-term toxicity, skin and eye irritation, carcinogenicity and reproductive toxicity.
Mice and rats are among the most commonly used laboratory animals, followed by rabbits, guinea pigs, fish and birds. Non-human primates are also used in certain areas of research.However, the scale of animal experimentation in India remains difficult to establish. Dr Surat said that although an estimated 100 million to more than 115 million animals are used in experiments and research worldwide every year, India does not have an official national figure or a transparent public database recording annual animal use, deaths and reported violations.Dr Ramanuj Panda, founder and managing director of Gocarin, has called for a centralised reporting system that records the species used, severity of experiments, animal deaths and welfare complaints.What existing law saysAnimal experimentation in India is governed by the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960. The law provides for the CCSEA to regulate experiments and ensure that animals are not subjected to unnecessary pain or suffering.Section 17 requires the committee to ensure that animals are not subjected to unnecessary pain or suffering before, during or after experiments. Section 18 authorises inspections of facilities and examination of relevant records. Section 19 allows the committee to prohibit experiments where the rules are not being followed, subject to the prescribed process.The proposed rules would change how approval responsibilities are distributed, particularly for experiments involving mild and moderate levels of suffering.Why are animal welfare groups concerned?One of the major concerns raised by animal welfare organisations relates to provisions allowing certain experiments involving protected wild animals, wild-caught animals and stray or feral domestic animals, subject to specified conditions and permissions.PETA India has flagged these provisions, arguing that capturing, handling, transporting and confining animals not bred for laboratory use can cause distress and disrupt their natural behaviour. It has also questioned the scientific reliability of using animals whose health, genetic background and environmental histories may be unknown.The organisation has raised concerns about the possibility of community dogs and cats being exposed to laboratory use. It has also referred to a CCSEA circular issued in 2022 that allowed the use of stray dogs in certain vaccine trials. The circular was withdrawn in 2023.Dr Noopur Jain, Science and Research Policy Advisor at PETA India, said: "India should be moving towards modern, human-relevant non-animal science, not making animal experimentation easier."PETA has also argued that the severity of an experiment, rather than the size or species of the animal, should determine the level of regulatory scrutiny.Could changes to approvals weaken oversight?Beyond the use of animals, the proposed shift towards institutional approvals has raised questions about independence and potential conflicts of interest.Dr Surat said five of the nine members of an IAEC belong to the same establishment seeking approval for an experiment, raising concerns about how independent research proposals may be assessed.The concern is that institutions could approve mild and moderate experiments involving a wider range of species without prior CCSEA clearance. This makes the role of independent members, veterinary supervision and clear scientific justification particularly important.Panda said streamlining approvals should not come at the cost of animal welfare. He called for meaningful participation by independent members in IAEC decisions, mandatory veterinary supervision, documented scientific justification and external reviews for experiments involving greater levels of suffering.The draft provides for inspections by designated nominees, including a socially aware member, at least twice a year. Separately, CCSEA inspection teams can inspect facilities to verify compliance.Dr Surat said facilities also undergo physical inspections for fresh registration and five-year renewals, while yearly mid-term inspections are mandated for large-animal research facilities.Another issue is whether India could become a destination for outsourced animal research.Dr Rukmini Jonnalagadda, founder and chief scientific officer of ULQA Scientific, Hyderabad, referred to an October 2026 investigation by Irish publication The Journal, which found that Irish universities had commissioned animal experiments at overseas laboratories, including in India.The University of Galway disclosed payments of €102,174 to an Indian organisation, Presude Lifesciences, for overseas studies.Ireland's Health Products Regulatory Authority confirmed that it has no regulatory role over animal experiments conducted abroad. The investigation does not establish that the Indian studies violated local rules, but it raises questions about how institutions commissioning research overseas assess and monitor animal welfare standards.Are animal experiments always reliable predictors of human safety?Animal models can provide useful scientific information, but differences between species can limit how accurately they predict human responses. Animals and humans may process chemicals differently and have distinct genetic, metabolic, immune and physiological characteristics.Panda said animal research should not be treated as proof that a drug or treatment will be safe for people.One frequently cited example is the 2006 clinical trial of TGN1412, an antibody that had appeared safe in preclinical testing involving non-human primates. During the first human trial, all six healthy volunteers who received the antibody developed severe immune reactions.Dr Surat also pointed to gene therapy research for X-linked myotubular myopathy. Although the treatment showed promise in dog models, clinical trials in humans were associated with severe liver complications and deaths.He also cited safety concerns surrounding Sarepta Therapeutics' Elevidys gene therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which received a boxed warning from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) over serious liver injury.These cases do not mean animal research has no scientific value. They highlight the limitations of relying on animal studies as the sole predictor of human safety, particularly in complex diseases and therapies.What alternatives are availableNew Approach Methodologies (NAMs) include cell-based tests, three-dimensional tissue cultures, organoids, organ-on-chip systems and computer-based models. These methods allow researchers to study aspects of human biology without relying on live animals at every stage of testing.Organoids are miniature structures grown from cells that mimic certain features of human organs, while organ-on-chip systems reproduce selected functions of organs. Computer models can also help predict how substances may behave in the human body.However, these methods cannot yet replicate every interaction between organs, the immune system and other biological processes in a whole organism. They are therefore being used alongside animal models in areas where complex biological interactions remain difficult to reproduce.India has taken some steps towards recognising alternatives. The New Drugs and Clinical Trials (Amendment) Rules, 2023, recognised methods such as cell-based assays, organ chips, microphysiological systems and computer modelling for relevant regulatory purposes.A government response to Parliament in 2026 highlighted support for 109 non-animal testing projects by the Indian Council of Medical Research across 71 institutions and laboratories.However, experts say wider adoption requires investment in infrastructure, training, validation and collaboration between researchers and regulators.What needs to change?Dr Surat argued that the draft rules should do more than classify experiments according to severity. India should consider stronger provisions to promote the development and validation of alternatives, including a requirement that animal procedures should not be undertaken where a recognised non-animal method is available.The proposed framework could be strengthened by requiring researchers to document their search for alternatives before seeking approval, publishing annual statistics on animal use and establishing a national centre to validate non-animal testing methods.Dr Surat also flagged ambiguity in the draft's definition of a "humane endpoint", the point at which an experiment should be stopped to prevent further suffering. The rules, the expert said, need to establish a clear and actionable response when an animal reaches that stage.
Panda said experiments involving prolonged suffering should face strict scrutiny, with veterinary monitoring, appropriate pain relief and clearly defined humane endpoints. He added that a transition away from routine animal experimentation was possible in an increasing number of applications, but would require rigorous scientific validation and a clear regulatory pathway.Dr Surat also pointed to policy initiatives in the US, UK, European Union and China to advance human biology-based testing methods. India, the expert argued, would risk falling behind without comparable policy support and investment.
The challenge is not simply to reduce the number of animals used in laboratories. It is to ensure that research is scientifically justified, animals are protected wherever experiments continue, and credible alternatives are developed and adopted wherever possible.As the government considers feedback on the draft rules, the central question remains whether the proposed framework can balance scientific research with stronger safeguards while creating a clearer path towards methods that are more relevant to human health.
Priyanka Jaiswal has four years of experience in digital journalism, news agency reporting and video production. Currently with The Times of India, she covers public policy, politics and global affairs. She is particularly drawn to human-interest stories that put people at the heart of an issue, spark awareness , and contribute to meaningful conversations.

What permanent daylight saving time could mean for sleep, mood, and mental health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
16:00:51 UTC
01:00:51 KST

As lawmakers across North America move to end the twice-yearly ritual of changing the clocks, three new papers highlight a complex debate over how clock shifts and permanent time systems affect health. A policy analysis published in CMAJ argues that permanent standard time would better support winter sleep, mood, and biological rhythms than permanent daylight saving time, and a review focused on people with mental illness reaches the same conclusion. A large review of studies tracking health patterns across whole populations, however, finds that seasonal clock changes and summer daylight saving time carry a mix of harms and benefits rather than being uniformly harmful.
Although major sleep societies have recommended adopting permanent standard time, North American governments eliminating the clock switch have largely chosen permanent daylight saving time instead. Yukon adopted permanent daylight saving time in 2020, followed by British Columbia in March 2026 and Alberta and the Northwest Territories in April 2026, while the United States House of Representatives passed a bill in July 2026 to make daylight saving time permanent nationwide. Public opinion does not necessarily match that legislative push: in a 2025 Gallup poll, only 19% of Americans wanted to keep switching the clocks, while 48% preferred permanent standard time and 24% favored permanent daylight saving time.
How clock time interacts with the body’s internal clock
Standard time is a timekeeping system designed so that 12:00 noon on the local clock roughly matches solar noon, the moment when the sun reaches its highest point in the sky along a time zone’s central line of longitude. Daylight saving time shifts local clocks forward by one hour in the spring and returns them to standard time in the autumn, which does not create extra daylight but moves an hour of sunlight from the morning to the evening.
Both schedules interact directly with circadian rhythms, the internal 24-hour biological cycles that regulate sleep, alertness, hormone production, and cellular activity throughout the body. These daily rhythms are coordinated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, a tiny cluster of nerve cells in the hypothalamus at the base of the brain that acts as the body’s master pacemaker.
Because the human master clock naturally runs slightly slower than a 24-hour day, averaging about 24.2 hours per cycle, it relies on natural daylight hitting the eyes to reset itself each morning. Bright morning sunlight speeds the internal clock up so people feel alert during the day and sleepy at night, whereas evening light slows the clock down and pushes sleepiness later. Modern habits like working indoors and looking at illuminated screens at night already weaken morning light cues and strengthen evening ones, creating a mismatch known as social jet lag, where work or school schedules force people to wake up before their delayed biological clocks are ready.
Public frustration with biannual clock shifts has grown alongside evidence that changing the schedule disrupts well-being; for instance, a study covered by PsyPost earlier this year found that both seasonal transitions triggered drops in public mood, with the autumn return to standard time producing a more lasting dip than the spring shift. Beyond temporary mood dips, the authors of a 2015 review argued that chronically disrupted or shortened sleep can contribute to the development of depression.
Canada’s choice between two permanent time systems
To evaluate what happens after a jurisdiction abolishes seasonal clock changes, Raymond W. Lam of the University of British Columbia and colleagues at Simon Fraser University and Vancouver Coastal Health conducted the public health policy analysis in CMAJ. Rather than debating whether twice-yearly transitions should end, the authors examined the chronic, year-round consequences of adopting either permanent standard time or permanent daylight saving time across Canada. They calculated winter and summer sunrise and sunset times across six major Canadian cities, synthesized evidence from biological rhythm research, disease-modeling simulations, and economic border studies, and reviewed lessons from countries that previously enacted permanent daylight saving time.
Lam and colleagues showed that under permanent daylight saving time, winter sunrises would occur around or after the start of many school days across much of Canada. By early January, switching from standard time to permanent daylight saving time shifts the latest winter sunrise from 7:51 a.m. to 8:51 a.m. in Toronto, from 8:08 a.m. to 9:08 a.m. in Vancouver, from 8:27 a.m. to 9:27 a.m. in Winnipeg, and from 8:40 a.m. to 9:40 a.m. in Calgary.
The authors also noted that political time zone boundaries often distort local solar time, pointing out that while Saskatchewan officially observes year-round Central Standard Time, much of the province sits geographically closer to Mountain Time and actually experiences light schedules resembling permanent daylight saving time. Similarly, clock policies have the greatest impact in mid-latitude regions where most Canadians live, whereas high-latitude territories like Yukon have such brief winter daylight that a one-hour shift makes little practical difference.
What darker winter mornings could mean for health
According to Lam and colleagues, prolonged winter morning darkness under permanent daylight saving time would likely worsen social jet lag and seasonal mood vulnerability. Winter dips in sleep, concentration, and energy are already most prominent among youth aged 12 to 17. An estimated 1% to 3% of Canadians experience seasonal affective disorder, a form of winter depression thought to involve a delay in the body clock linked to later morning light, while up to 15% experience milder winter slumps in mood, sleep, and energy.
Geographic patterns point in the same direction, with global prevalence of seasonal affective disorder rising by 0.2 percentage points for every 1-degree increase in northern latitude. In United States county-level analyses, residents on the western edges of time zones, who experience later clock sunrises and sunsets similar to permanent daylight saving time, averaged up to 2 additional suicide deaths per 100,000 people annually compared to those on the eastern edges (the epidemiological review described below rated this study as low quality).
In addition, a 2025 modeling study simulating chronic disease prevalence across the United States indicated that while both permanent policies improved health over twice-yearly switching, the health benefits of permanent daylight saving time were one-third smaller than those of permanent standard time, especially at northern latitudes comparable to Canada.
Comparisons of places with different sunset times indicate that an hour of later sunset is associated with nearly one hour less sleep per week and about 5% lower long-run earnings, and a time-zone border study found that workers on the late-sunset side earn about 3.5% less. In Florida, an extra hour of morning sunlight before school was linked to higher adolescent math and reading scores by 0.08 and 0.06 standard deviations, a gain comparable to reducing class sizes.
Trade-offs and lessons from other countries
Although permanent daylight saving time provides brighter evenings that can support outdoor recreation and retail spending for people with flexible schedules, its dark winter mornings could disproportionately affect teenagers, shift workers, and lower-income or rural commuters traveling on poorly lit roads.
Permanent standard time has trade-offs of its own: summer sunrises would come as early as about 4 a.m. in cities such as Vancouver and Montréal, which the authors note could wake some people too early, and winter sunsets would arrive as early as about 4:10 p.m. International experience shows how these trade-offs can play out: the United States enacted permanent daylight saving time in 1974 but repealed it within a year after widespread public backlash over dark winter school commutes; Russia, which adopted permanent daylight saving time in 2011, reversed it in 2014, and Chile reversed its 2015 move after complaints.
Lam and colleagues concluded that health evidence favors permanent standard time, and that provinces choosing permanent daylight saving time should pair it with later school start times, morning indoor light interventions, pedestrian safety upgrades, and ongoing public health monitoring.
A review of 157 studies finds a more mixed picture
While the Canadian analysis examined which permanent clock system is healthier once seasonal transitions end, a systematic review published in the European Journal of Epidemiology questioned whether the existing epidemiological evidence truly justifies abolishing the twice-yearly clock shifts in the first place. Led by first author Aiste Steponenaite of the University of Kent and the University of Greenwich and senior author Philip Lewis of the University of Cologne, the researchers searched five databases through June 2025 and identified 157 human epidemiological studies across 36 countries.
Two independent reviewers rated each study’s methodological quality as low, medium, or high, giving greater weight to large registry analyses, which draw on national health records, and to studies that included placebo tests, which check whether similar health changes happen in years, dates, or neighboring regions without a clock shift.
Across the 157 studies, roughly one in five of which met high-quality standards, the researchers found that neither the seasonal transitions nor summer daylight saving time were uniformly harmful. Among 17 studies of acute myocardial infarction, commonly known as a heart attack (6 rated high quality and 10 medium quality), the evidence pointed to an elevated risk during the first one to four weeks after the spring shift, corresponding to a relative risk increase of about 4% in a 2024 meta-analysis by two of the review’s authors. Among 16 studies of fatal traffic crashes, the evidence pointed to an increase after the spring shift in some places, mainly the United States. At the same time, a high-quality nationwide United States study found that changes in all-cause mortality, or deaths from any cause, after the spring shift were not statistically significant.
Crimes involving physical harm, such as robberies and assaults, tended to drop briefly after the spring shift and rise after the autumn shift. The autumn transition back to standard time was also linked to a roughly 2.5% relative decrease in all-cause mortality and fewer workplace accidents, each based on a single high-quality study. Living under daylight saving time during the summer months was associated with an approximately 4.5% relative reduction in all-cause mortality in one high-quality United States study and with fewer traffic accidents in Chile.
Across 22 sleep duration studies, 6 circadian rhythm studies, and 15 psychiatric outcome studies, Steponenaite and colleagues found no consistent population-wide changes in sleep duration after the spring shift or in psychiatric hospital admissions and suicides after either transition, although two low-quality studies from Russia did indicate that maintaining daylight saving time through the winter shortened sleep duration. Because summer daylight saving time and the autumn shift were associated with mortality and safety benefits, the authors suggested that retaining seasonal clock transitions while using targeted preventive measures around the spring shift, such as gradual schedule adjustments for heart patients and enhanced road safety enforcement, remains a reasonable option.
Notably, the review also concluded that if transitions were abolished, the limited sleep evidence and circadian theory would favor permanent standard time over permanent daylight saving time, the same choice the CMAJ authors recommend. Where the papers part ways is on whether ending the twice-yearly changes should be the priority, a split visible in the CMAJ analysis itself, which counts the mental-health review among papers supporting an end to clock changes and the epidemiological review among those questioning that consensus.
Why people with mental illness may be especially sensitive
Why did the epidemiological review by Steponenaite and colleagues find no consistent population-level spike in psychiatric emergencies after clock changes, even though sleep loss is closely tied to mental illness? A comprehensive review published in Brain Sciences, led by Liahm Blank, Joshua Khorsandi, Jagdish Khubchandani, and Kavita Batra at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, and New Mexico State University, offers one possible explanation for this discrepancy by focusing specifically on individuals with chronic mental illness.
The authors searched four databases through February 2026 and synthesized 66 peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2026, grouping them into 12 epidemiological studies that directly evaluated daylight saving time transitions, 36 observational studies linking sleep or circadian disruption to mental health symptoms, and 18 experimental studies examining biological pathways across depression, anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder, PTSD, ADHD, and psychotic disorders.
Blank and colleagues noted that while most healthy adults adjust to a one-hour clock change within two to seven days, individuals with pre-existing psychiatric conditions often have fragile circadian timing systems that may adapt slowly or incompletely. They argue that large hospital and emergency department registries mainly capture severe crises and may miss everyday symptom flare-ups, anxiety, and mood instability. For example, a Finnish nationwide analysis and a United States emergency department study found no statistically significant increase in hospital-treated manic or psychotic episodes in the two weeks after clock transitions.
Even in population registries, some specific mental health risks have emerged, including an 11% relative increase in depressive episodes after the autumn transition and a 6.25% relative increase in United States suicide rates following the spring transition. The epidemiological review rated those same depression and suicide studies as medium quality, and its psychiatric conclusion leaned more heavily on a high-quality study from Austria, Switzerland, and Sweden that found no change in suicide rates around clock changes.
Blank and colleagues also explained that because rapid eye movement sleep, the dreaming stage essential for processing emotions and consolidating memories, occurs mostly in the final hours before waking, losing an hour of morning sleep after the spring transition may selectively cut off rapid eye movement sleep even when total sleep loss seems minor.
Across specific psychiatric conditions, modest clock disruptions may interact with baseline sleep difficulties, as sleep disturbances are reported in up to 90% of people with PTSD, and wearable-tracker research in schizophrenia has found severe circadian misalignment in roughly half of clinically stable patients. Similarly, an estimated 73% to 78% of individuals with ADHD have a delayed sleep-wake cycle, and one experiment in children with ADHD found that losing one hour of nightly sleep for a week pushed attention scores from below the clinical cutoff into clinically impaired ranges.
Blank and colleagues proposed three biological pathways that may underlie this sensitivity. First, delayed morning light may alter signals from the eyes to the hypothalamus and disrupt the nighttime release of melatonin, a hormone that promotes sleep. Second, sleep loss may activate the body’s main stress-response system, raising levels of the stress hormone cortisol and of inflammatory proteins. Third, variations in clock genes, which keep time inside individual cells, may make it harder for cells in people with bipolar disorder or schizophrenia to adjust to an abrupt time shift.
Converging with the CMAJ policy analysis, Blank and colleagues favored adopting permanent standard time to protect vulnerable psychiatric populations and recommended that clinicians help high-risk patients shift their sleep schedules by 15 to 20 minutes per day over the three to four days before a transition.
Caveats and next steps
As with all research, there are some caveats to keep in mind when interpreting these three papers. Nearly all population-level findings on daylight saving time rely on observational or quasi-experimental data, which take advantage of natural events such as clock changes, rather than on randomized trials. That means researchers cannot establish direct cause and effect, and studies comparing opposite edges of time zones must assume that neighboring communities do not differ in other lifestyle or economic ways.
Each paper also has its own limitations. The CMAJ paper is a solicited policy analysis rather than a systematic review and relies partly on unpublished data for its claims about evening leisure benefits. In the systematic review of 157 epidemiological studies, roughly four out of five papers were rated as low or medium quality, and placebo tests using non-transition dates or regions made some previously publicized effects disappear, such as supposed clock-shift impacts on stock market decisions.
The mental-health paper was a narrative review, which summarizes studies without the strict search and selection rules of a systematic review, and a single author screened studies for inclusion. Only 12 of its 66 included papers directly measured outcomes during daylight saving time transitions; the rest inferred risk from broader sleep and circadian research that often relied on small clinical samples or self-reported sleep questionnaires. Because sleep disruption and mental illness influence each other in both directions, it remains difficult to separate how much the clock shift itself drives symptom changes.
Looking ahead, the CMAJ authors urged provinces such as British Columbia and Alberta to treat their policy changes as an opportunity to monitor school attendance, traffic injuries, cardiovascular events, and mental health visits over time, while the other two teams called for longer-term studies with objective sleep measures and placebo tests.
The paper, “Analysis of health impacts associated with adopting permanent standard time or permanent daylight saving time to inform policy in Canada,” was authored by Raymond W. Lam, Ralph Mistlberger, Patrick Baylis, and Alexandra Choi.
The paper, “A systematic review of epidemiological studies into daylight-saving time & health identifying beneficial & adverse effects,” was authored by Aiste Steponenaite, Jonas P. Wallraff, Ursula Wild, Lorna Brown, Ben Bullock, Gurprit S. Lall, Sally Ferguson, Russell G. Foster, Jennifer Walsh, Greg Murray, Thomas C. Erren, and Philip Lewis.
The paper, “When the Clock Shifts: A Comprehensive Review of Daylight-Saving Time (DST), Circadian Disruption, and Neuropsychological Risk in Chronic Mental Illness,” was authored by Liahm Blank, Joshua Khorsandi, Elizabeth England-Kennedy, Srikanta Banerjee, Karen Kopera-Frye, Roberto Sagaribay, Jagdish Khubchandani, and Kavita Batra.
