- Organizers said 120,000 took part, though the number has not been officially confirmed
- Demonstrators demand better-funded schools, action on living costs, greater social justice and stronger climate protection, while opposing a possible return to military conscription
- In Cologne, police canceled the planned march over covered faces and pyrotechnics; the gathering continued as a stationary rally on the Rhine riverbank
- In Stuttgart, police repeatedly halted the march, citing covered faces, pyrotechnics and participants leaving the agreed route
This is a round-up of events at the youth protests across Germany on October 31, 2026:
READ: More than 290 arrested in France as protests turn violent
The German protests on Saturday are a part of a wider trend that has seen members of Gen Z, born between 1997 and 2012, protest in several European nations.
The wave of protest was triggered by students seeking education reform in France, with the standoff erupting in violence and looting two weeks ago.
For our standalone story on protests in France today, click here.
Gen Z protests 'very peaceful,' says police union official
After a day of youth protests in Germany, senior police union representative Andreas Rosskopf said that there was no widespread property damage "so far."
"The Gen Z protests have turned out to be very peaceful," Rosskopf told the daily Rhenische Post.
While confrontations were reported after the marches ended in multiple cities, the people driving the clashes were "individuals acting independently, some of whom were masked."
Rosskopf, who represents Germany's federal police, said security forces acted very decisively and forcefully when such response was appropriate.
"Security forces remain absolutely ready to prevent any further clashes in the late evening of overnight," he said.
Minor scuffles reported as German protests wrap up
German security forces reported minor violent incidents in several cites in the wake of the Gen Z demonstrations.
In Hamburg, protesters at the city's Steintor square pelted the police with fireworks . Police used "immediate force" to clear the area, including using a water cannon.
Several police officers were injured during a similar incident in Frankfurt, according to a state interior minister.
Police also used a water cannon in Cologne, where the march was halted and turned into a stationary rally after some protesters covered their faces and used pyrotechnics.
A police officers sustained light injuries in nearby Bonn during a confrontation with a group of protesters.
In Berlin, the authorities noted a rally separate from the official event organized by the Gen Z movement. Police initially reported "isolated instances of throwing eggs and bottles" from a crowd of around 500 people. The authorities later also reported "illegal burning of pyrotechnics" and said the crowd has grown to around 3,000 participants.
Police officers injured in Frankfurt
Several police officers were injured in a clash with a group of protesters following the Gen Z demonstration in Frankfurt, authorities said.
"One officers could be injured more seriously, but this will need some more looking into," said Hesse Interior Minister Roman Poseck.
"We assume there were about 100 attackers motivated by extreme leftist ideology," the state minister said.
"They have staged a massive attack against the police by throwing bottles, stones and fireworks."
Police responded with water cannons and have the situation in hand, he said
IN PICTURES: Germany's Gen Z take to the streets
Thousands of young people took part in protests in 34 German cities on Saturday.
German Gen Z protesters called out rising living expenses, remilitarization of Germany, and declining education.
Some of the protesters also called for Germany's current chancellor, center-right Friedrich Merz, to step down.
The protests were held under the slogan Gen Z regelt (Gen Z sorts it).
Police were out in force after many politicians warned that Germany will not tolerate the kind of violence seen in France in mid-October.
Police reported incidents in which pepper spray and water cannon were used to keep crowds under control, with protesters setting off fireworks and lighting fires.
Most of the demonstrations ended peacefully.
But tensions remained high in some German cities with reports of several police officers injured.
Hamburg: Protesters set fire to barriers
In Germany's second-biggest city, Hamburg, police estimated 6,700 people taking part in the demonstration.
They reported some groups of black-clad protesters, some of whom also wore face masks, pulling apart construction site barriers and throwing them on the street. Some of the barriers were later set on fire.
Police said they pushed the crowd back and used pepper spray to break them apart. The fire was eventually put out.
Police say some 5,000 now gathered at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate
Following an initial estimate of several hundred people attending the rally in central Berlin, police said that some 5,000 people were now gathered at the Brandenburg Gate. The organizers, "Gen Z regelt" (Gen Z sorts it) gave a much higher number, saying 10,000 people were in attendance.
One of the speakers in Berlin, Kaja Schwab, decried false promises made by politicians.
The youth is being told that "we will do well if we work hard enough." In reality, the life is getting unaffordable and the young are "forced into military service," she said, in reference to Germany's renewed recruitment drive.
Youth protests draw crowds across Germany
Thousands of young people have joined the demonstrations in over 30 German cities, with police reporting largely peaceful protests.
Early police estimates included:
- Berlin: Around 650 people gathered at the historic Brandenburg Gate
- Frankfurt: More than 1,500 attended a rally near the European Central Bank.
- Munich: Around 1,000 people attending the march
- Mainz: Police counted around 1,200 participants, situation "peaceful"
- Freiburg: Around 2,500 people attended, according to police.
Hundreds also gathered in Hamburg, Erfurt, Magdeburg, Dresden, Leipzig, Nuremberg, and elsehwere.
Retailers in several city centers had boarded up shop windows, particularly along luxury shopping streets, fearing unrest. Some shops were already closed for the Reformation Day public holiday.
No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available. More than 182,100 people had expressed interest in attending the events online.
Cologne police call off march over masks and pyrotechnics
Police in Cologne called off the planned "Gen Z regelt" procession after some participants covered their faces and used pyrotechnics.
"The demonstration will continue as a stationary rally," a police spokeswoman told the DPA news agency. Participants would remain on the Rhine riverbank, she said, appealing for restraint.
Attendance remained below the 15,000 people registered for the demonstration. Based on advance registrations, Cologne's protest was expected to be the largest in North Rhine-Westphalia.
Police respond to Stuttgart protesters trying to leave route
Police repeatedly stopped a youth protest march in Stuttgart, citing participants covering their faces and leaving the agreed route.
Officers also reported smoke devices and firecrackers before the procession began. "Be loud, but remain peaceful," a police spokeswoman urged in a video.
In other German cities, police reported a largely peaceful start to demonstrations. Authorities estimated included 2,500 participants in Freiburg, more than 1,500 in Frankfurt, 1,200 in Mainz, 1,000 in Munich and 650 in Berlin.
No nationwide turnout figure was immediately available.
Researcher warns against ignoring young protesters
Politicians must involve young people in decision-making or risk the youth turning away from political institutions, education researcher Nina Kolleck warned.
Their exclusion "creates the impression that there is a policy for the old, but not for the young," the University of Potsdam professor told Germany's RBB Inforadio.
Kolleck pointed to decades of underinvestment in schools and the disproportionate impact of climate change on younger generations.
She warned that populist parties could exploit the resulting political vacuum if young people's frustrations continued to go unanswered.
Youth protest organizers reject focus on violence warnings
Organizers of Germany's nationwide youth protests have accused the media of stoking fears of violence and distracting from their demands.
A "narrative of violence" was being used "to divert attention from our core demands," spokeswoman Veronika Dinter told the German broadcaster Deutschlandfunk.
She stressed that "GenZ regelt" — roughly meaning "Gen Z takes charge" — called for peaceful demonstrations, pointing to its published principles. Anyone who shared those principles was welcome, she said.
Dinter also regretted the decision by Germany's national school student representative body to distance itself from the protests. It had cited concerns including unclear organizational structures.
The initiative is holding rallies in Berlin, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich, with local groups organizing protests in another 30 cities. Nearly 180,000 people had pledged online to attend, although actual turnout remained unclear.
Security authorities had warned that extremist groups could try to infiltrate the demonstrations.
What are the rules governing protests in Germany?
People in Germany have the fundamental right, enshrined in the constitution or Basic Law, to assemble in public provided they remains peaceful and are unarmed.
However, several states have adopted their own assembly acts, which means some of them have additional restrictions, such as a ban on protesting on highways in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
Notification generally necessary
Federal law itself imposes the obligation on organizers of protests to notify the local authority entrusted with approving public assemblies at least 48 hours before they invite people publicly to take part.
This aims to allow authorities to put in place security measures and to lessen the impact of any assembly on others by, for example, instigating traffic control measures.
Spontaneous assemblies are, however, also allowed in cases where a topical issue of urgent importance is at stake, and there is no notification requirement for indoor assemblies.
Protests or other assemblies can be banned beforehand or dispersed while they are underway, but this is considered a means of last resort.
Some locations are also subject to restrictions on protests, such as the area around the Reichstag building in Berlin where the German parliament sits, and around the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe.
Demonstrations around the Reichstag are, for example, permitted only when the parliament is not in session.
Germany no stranger to big protests
Post-war Germany has seen several massive demonstrations, including one in 1983, when 250,000 people — according to police estimates — gathered in the then West German capital, Bonn, to protest against the decision by NATO to station American nuclear missiles on German territory.
That was, however, surpassed in size by a protest in Berlin in 2003 against the invasion of Iraq by US-led forces, which drew a crowd of around half a million people.
There is some more detail on the law regarding the right of assembly in this DW article.
German 'Gen Z' protests set for cities across the country
Young people are to take part in demonstrations across Germany on Saturday, following the example of their peers in France and other countries who have been calling for better educational prospects and future opportunities.
In Germany, organizers said there is also to be a focus on rejecting military conscription and on demanding more protection for the climate as the Earth warms, with potentially catastrophic effects.
Saturday's protests are being called for by the youth initiative "Gen Z regelt" ("Gen Z sorts it") through a social media campaign
The group itself will directly organize four of the protests — in Berlin, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich —, with associated demonstrations to take place in some 30 other cities.
It has explicitly called for peaceful protests without the violence that marred recent demonstrations in France.
Focus on security fears
This has not stopped several conservative politicians, notably from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), from warning that similar scenes could occur.
"Gen Z regelt" has, however, criticized what it sees as a wrong focus on the possibility of violence at the protests.
"It shows that our point about not being taken seriously or being heard is right. No one wants to work with us on the issues at stake but instead always put the topic of violence on the agenda," an organizer of the Munich protest told a press conference in Cologne.
However, other lawmakers have come out in support of the protests.
The leader of the parliamentary party of the Greens, Katharina Dröge, told the DPA news agency: "Young people are rightly furious because the federal government does not take their wishes seriously enough."
The Left Party leader, Luigi Pantisano, also said it was the right time for protests as the government mulls reforms of the nursing care and pensions systems, calling them "social cruelties."
"Gen Z" broadly refers to the generation born between 1997 and 2012.
France to see fresh cost-of-living protests
As Germany gears up for a day of mass youth protests, authorities in neighboring France are also bracing for new demonstrations on Saturday amid fears that the violence seen at October 17 rallies could repeat itself.
Some 70,000 police officers have been deployed to monitor around 150 protests across the country.
In recent weeks, protests by school pupils complaining about poor school conditions morphed into wider demonstrations on multiple issues, including the rising cost of living and social inequality.
On October 17 in particular, considerable violence occurred on the sidelines of mostly peaceful protests as extremists took the opportunity to plunder, riot and damage public property.

In the southern city of Toulouse, police used water cannon against an unauthorised protest that drew several thousand people.

In France, rallies that began in September with students demanding lower education costs, more teachers, and better school facilities have since escalated into broader anti-government protests across the continent. 
The German youth-led movement ‘Gen Z regelt’ (‘Gen Z has got this!’) scheduled its nationwide day of action for Halloween to maximize turnout and visibility.

Protests have already begun in Cologne, where demonstrators are marching through the streets. Some are carrying placards reading ‘Stop financing Ukraine’.
Additional police have been deployed across the country ahead of the protests. In Berlin, luxury shops along the upscale Kurfuerstendamm boulevard have boarded up their windows as a precaution.

Elsewhere in Europe, police are on alert for possible weekend unrest, including protests in central Madrid and Barcelona in Spain, and in Rome, Italy.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said last week that the recent wave of protests across Western Europe stemmed from the EU’s own mistakes. He added that European countries were struggling to manage the migration crisis.

Finnish president says he conveyed two messages from Zelenskyy to Putin
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has said he conveyed two messages from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Vladimir Putin during a phone call with the Russian leader on 27 October.
Source: Stubb in a programme on the Finnish broadcaster Yle, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Stubb said he had relayed two messages from Zelenskyy to Putin. The first concerned Zelenskyy's willingness to hold direct talks with Putin, particularly on territorial and security issues. The second outlined Kyiv's proposals for de-escalation: possible ceasefires covering energy facilities, food security, prisoner-of-war exchanges and infrastructure more broadly.
The Finnish president added that he and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre had also been able to ask Putin about Russia's preparations for the trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi. He said the call had been useful because it gave them a chance to find out how Putin planned to approach the talks.
Asked whether the call with Putin had brought peace closer, the Finnish president said it was more of a confidence-building step. Stubb added that they had made no backward steps, but the first call was primarily about establishing trust.
The president was also asked what would come next in terms of restoring contact and relations with Russia after the phone call. Stubb said there is no need to rush and that things should be taken step by step. He added that relations between Finland and Russia, for example, would be completely different from what they had been in the past.
Stubb said Finland and Norway had also told Putin that they oppose the Russian shadow fleet's activities in the Baltic Sea.
Background:
- Stubb has also refuted media reports that Putin lectured him and Jonas Gahr Støre on history during the phone call.
- On Tuesday 27 October, Stubb and Jonas Gahr Støre held a phone call with Putin on their own initiative. Stubb said the discussion was "frank and substantive".
- Zelenskyy said Stubb and Støre had made it clear to Putin that real de-escalatory steps are needed regarding Ukrainian energy and infrastructure.
- Following the conversation between the European leaders and Putin, Zelenskyy said there are indications that Russia is serious about a meeting of the negotiating teams in Abu Dhabi.

Syria mulls joining Mecca defence pact: Shaibani

Breadcrumb
Syria mulls joining Mecca defence pact, foreign minister says
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani confirmed on Saturday that discussions are underway to assess Syria's potential membership of the Mecca Joint Defence Pact.
The Mecca pact, signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan in the Muslim holy city on 7 August, outlines a joint defence agreement which stipulates that an attack on one member state will be considered an attack on all three.
Speaking at the Pillars of Regional Security event at the IISS Manama Dialogue 2026, Shaibani emphasised that the security of the Gulf is an "integral part of Syrian regional security", and that Damascus stands with the Gulf states and their people in confronting cross-border militias.
He added that Syria has experience in confronting militias that intervened in the country and contributed to plunging it into a devastating 14-year war, expressing the possibility of transferring this experience and strengthening regional cooperation and achieving stability.
The minister provided no further details about the ongoing talks to join the Mecca pact.
Shaibani also used his speech to condemn recent missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, affirming Damascus' solidarity with its partners in confronting these attacks, while also rejecting the use of Syrian territory to threaten neighbouring states.
He also affirmed Syria's support for Yemen's internationally recognised government in restoring its sovereignty over the country.
On Israel, Shaibani said that Damascus' position on the occupied Golan Heights remains firm, pointing to UN Security Council Resolution 497, which rejects Israel's Golan Heights law and deems the annexation of the territory to be null and void under international law.
He highlighted that Syria has been subjected to more than a thousand Israeli attacks in less than two years, resulting in dozens of deaths, asking: "How can the demand for border control and weapons confiscation be reconciled with the fact that Syrian sovereignty is violated and targeted daily?", referring to Israel's stated justification for the attacks.
Since the signing of the Mecca pact, Saudi Arabia has come under attack from Yemen's Houthi rebels, which it has resumed fighting against in Yemen, and has reignited the civil war.
Pakistan and Turkey have not announced any attacks on the Iran-backed Houthis.

Ukraine news: Oleshky evacuees reach Kyiv-held territory

What you need to know

- Kyiv also reports strikes on military depots in occupied Ukrainian territory

Here is a roundup of events from Russia's war in Ukraine on Saturday, October 31:
Wadephul says Europe and US are "on the same side" on Russia
At a news conference after the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta, DW correspondent Benjamin Alvarez Gruber asked German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul whether Sergey Lavrov's presence and the possibility of Russian President Vladimir Putin attending the G20 summit in Doral, Florida, in December signaled a normalization of relations with Russia.
Wadephul said the US and European countries were "on the same side."
"Speaking to the Russian Foreign Minister is not a concession we're making to Russia, but it is normal to speak," he said, adding that foreign ministers must be prepared to engage even with adversaries.
"You don't have to negotiate with partners, but you have to negotiate with somebody who has a different position and who's somehow also an adversary to freedom and to security in Europe. So it is necessary that we speak, and for that reason I think it was useful," Wadephul added.
The G20 foreign ministers skipped their traditional family photo at a meeting in Atlanta on Friday, amid objections from several European countries, Australia and Canada to appearing alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
Wadephul said: "We are not in a position that it was necessary or useful or a good idea to have a family photo because in the very situation we are in, Russia does not really show an interest to share our values and to share our interests."
The US State Department removed the photo from the agenda to prevent it from becoming a distraction or a spectacle.
Zelenskyy in Istanbul for talks on Black Sea shipping
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has arrived in Istanbul for talks with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, with Black Sea shipping among the issues on the agenda.
"We're working to strengthen the protection of our people, our bilateral partnership with Türkiye, and real diplomatic prospects," Zelenskyy wrote on X, using the alternative spelling for Turkey.
The Ukrainian president also plans to meet Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew, the Istanbul-based Orthodox Christian leader.
US warns Russia of a 'mass casualty' plot to attack Moscow
The US embassy in Russia warned there was "a credible threat of a mass casualty event" at a historical site in southern Moscow.
"The US government is coordinating with appropriate Russian authorities on a response," the US embassy in Moscow said in a post on X.
The alleged plot would target the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve, a sprawling complex of palaces and gardens built under the orders of Empress Cathrine the Great in the late 18th century.
Russia's federal law enforcement agency, the FSB, said it received the warning and was doing "appropriate work" in response to it, according to Russian news agencies.
Ukraine says it hit Russian rocket fuel factory
Ukraine's military said it struck a factory producing solid rocket fuel in Russia's Rostov region, setting a warehouse ablaze and damaging four production workshops.
The attack on the Kamensky plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky involved drones and Neptune missiles, according to the Ukrainian account.
The military said the plant supplies fuel for ammunition used by Russia's Uragan, Smerch and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, as well as other missiles and air-launched weapons.
Ukraine also reported strikes on four Russian military supply depots in occupied parts of the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Luhansk regions.
The claims have not been independently verified.
Ukraine welcomes civilians from Oleshky after complex evacuation effort
First evacuees from the Russian-occupied Oleshky have reached Ukrainian-controlled territory amid a localized ceasefire.
Oleshky, near the front line in the southern Kherson region, has been occupied by Russia since 2022. In recent weeks, the town has faced a severe humanitarian crisis.
Both sides have recently agreed to a localized ceasefire to extract the estimated 2,000 civilians still in Oleshky, down from its pre-invasion population of 24,000.
Moscow and Kyiv credited the US first lady, Melania Trump, with brokering the truce.
Residents were given a choice to go to Russia or travel via Belarus to the part of Ukraine controlled by Kyiv.
 Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the initiative required "an enormous amount of work."
He said evacuees included a one-year-old baby and a 94-year-old resident of Oleshky. The evacuees brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon, according to Lubinets.
He expressed hope that the Oleshky arrangement can be replicated elsewhere.
The truce started on Tuesday and is due to end on Sunday night.

Poland's top court general assembly planned for Nov. 3
Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who is now in charge of Poland's Constitutional Tribunal (TK), called a general assembly of TK judges for November 3.
Korwin-Piotrowska told TVP Info public broadcaster on Friday evening that the general assembly had to adopt TK's budget for 2027.
She appealed to politicians, including President Karol Nawrocki, "to tone down the current escalation".
Korwin-Piotrowska, who gave the interview at the TK's headquarters, said that "by preventing judges from adjudicating, Bogdan Swieczkowski had made it impossible to adopt the TK's revenue and expenditure plan for 2027".
She added that, given the ongoing parliamentary work on the budget bill, "this is the last moment to convene a general assembly of TK judges and adopt a budget".
Asked how to convince the other side of the political stage that the actions being taken regarding the TK are in accordance with the law, Korwin-Piotrowska said that "we are in a state of constitutional necessity".
"In a modern Europe, a democratic state cannot function without a constitutional court, which... serves as a safeguard of citizens' rights and freedoms," she continued, adding that cases dating back to 2013 were still awaiting review by the TK.
"We will restore the TK to the citizens," she said.
Earlier in the day, information appeared on the TK's website regarding the suspension of TK President Bogdan Swieczkowski and Vice-Prsident Bartlomiej Sochanski from official duties.
According to the TK's website, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who was elected as TK judge by the Sejm, lower house of parliament, is now heading the TK.
The current situation follows President Karol Nawrocki's refusal to swear in five of the eight TK judges elected by the current parliamentary majority.
They bypassed the presidential block by taking their oath directly in parliament and submitting a notarised copy to the President's Office. But they were prevented from assuming office by Swieczkowski. (PAP)

World Insights: Lagarde's early exit raises questions over ECB independence, policy outlook
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
23:34:22 CST
00:34:22 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde's decision to step down nearly nine months before the end of her term has sparked debate over the implications of her early departure and raised questions about the outlook for eurozone monetary policy.
The move comes as the eurozone faces renewed inflationary pressures, mounting fiscal strains and growing political uncertainty ahead of France's 2027 presidential election.
AN EARLY FAREWELL
The ECB announced Thursday that Lagarde, 70, would leave office on Feb. 7, 2027, ahead of the scheduled end of her eight-year term in late October.
A former French finance minister and head of the International Monetary Fund, Lagarde took over the ECB presidency from Mario Draghi in November 2019.
Her tenure has spanned a succession of crises, from the COVID-19 pandemic and the energy shock following the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to record-high inflation and, more recently, renewed price pressures stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.
Under her leadership, the ECB launched an emergency asset purchase programme to stabilize financial markets during the pandemic. It later embarked on an aggressive tightening cycle, raising its deposit rate from minus 0.5 percent to a record 4 percent in just over a year to curb soaring inflation.
As inflation eased, the bank began cutting rates in June 2024, bringing the deposit rate down to 2 percent by June 2025. Lagarde also oversaw a review of the ECB's monetary policy strategy and advanced work on a digital euro.
French President Emmanuel Macron praised her leadership on Thursday and called for an orderly and balanced process to choose her successor.
THE POLITICS OF TIMING
Lagarde told a news conference Thursday that she wanted greater freedom to speak and engage on public issues beyond monetary policy. While the ECB's independence required its president to remain politically neutral, she said she no longer felt able to stay silent on broader international issues.
Much of the attention, however, has fallen on the timing of her departure and its political implications.
France is due to hold its presidential election in spring 2027. German public broadcaster ARD reported that Lagarde's early exit would allow Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and other European leaders to agree on her successor before the vote, amid concerns that gains by France's far right or other eurosceptic forces could complicate the appointment process.
Marcel Fratzscher, head of the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), welcomed the decision, saying that Lagarde had shown a strong sense of responsibility towards Europe and the ECB.
Clemens Fuest, president of the Munich-based ifo Institute, also said her departure would allow the ECB's top post to be filled before the French election, warning of a significant risk that radical candidates could win the vote.
However, Markus Ferber, a German member of the European Parliament, questioned whether the ECB was making itself dependent on election dates in member states despite its longstanding emphasis on independence, according to ARD.
Lagarde has not said that her decision was intended to influence the choice of her successor. Her early departure has nevertheless brought questions about the ECB's independence to the forefront of the succession debate.
AN OPEN RACE
Lagarde's announcement has brought forward the contest for one of Europe's most influential economic posts.
Former Dutch central bank governor Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, the former Spanish central bank chief who now heads the Bank for International Settlements, are widely seen as leading contenders. European Investment Bank President Nadia Calvino, a former Spanish economy minister, has also been mentioned as a possible candidate.
Knot, a longtime participant in ECB policymaking, has traditionally been regarded as a monetary policy hawk, while Hernandez de Cos is seen as more moderate, with extensive experience in international financial cooperation.
Lagarde's departure also comes as several other senior ECB positions, including those of an Executive Board member and the bank's chief economist, are due to become vacant in the coming months. According to the Financial Times, European leaders may seek to negotiate the appointments as a package, taking into account national representation and differences over monetary policy.
The next ECB president will also inherit a difficult economic environment.
At its latest policy meeting Thursday, the ECB kept its three key interest rates unchanged, leaving the deposit rate at 2.5 percent after two increases this year. The bank warned that rising energy prices were adding to inflation risks while weighing on the outlook for economic growth.
The renewed energy shock from the Middle East conflict has left policymakers facing a difficult trade-off. If higher energy costs feed through into broader consumer prices and wages, the ECB may have to tighten monetary policy further. But weak growth and tighter financing conditions could make additional rate increases more costly for the economy.
Fiscal pressures in some member states add another challenge. In France, the eurozone's second-largest economy, a heavy public debt burden and rising government bond yields have heightened concerns about borrowing costs and the potential for financial market strains to spread across the currency bloc.
Despite these challenges, Holger Schmieding, chief economist at German private bank Berenberg, said the leadership change itself is unlikely to bring major shifts in ECB monetary policy. He noted that key decisions were typically reached by consensus in the Governing Council rather than made by the president alone.
Lagarde's successor will nevertheless have to contain renewed inflationary pressures without further weakening growth, while safeguarding the ECB's independence amid Europe's shifting political landscape. ■

DOHA, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said that Tehran currently has no plans to meet with U.S. officials, while consultations with Qatari and Pakistani mediators continue over Iran's conditions for resolving the crisis, Qatar's Al Jazeera reported Saturday.
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Araghchi dismissed reports of possible meetings as media speculation, saying Iran saw no need to meet with American officials at present.
He said Tehran would decide whether to hold direct or indirect negotiations after Washington accepted Iran's conditions.
Araghchi said an Iranian delegation had traveled to Qatar for further discussions, adding that his aide was there to continue consultations with mediators.
According to Araghchi, Iran's conditions include recognition of a new shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz that Tehran had worked out with Oman, and the closure of other routes.
He said Tehran also sought the lifting of sanctions imposed after the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), a reduction in U.S. military forces in the region, the restoration of sanctions waivers for Iranian oil exports, and the release of all frozen Iranian funds, including those held in Qatar.
Iran also demanded an end to hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon, he said.
Araghchi said mediators had presented proposals concerning Iran's nuclear program, which Tehran was reviewing as part of what he described as a second phase.
The Iranian foreign minister also said a letter from U.S. Vice President JD Vance had been reviewed at high-level meetings, describing the American effort to open the door to broader dialogue and understanding as a "positive step."
On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz.
A ceasefire was achieved between the warring parties on April 8. On June 18, Iran and the United States signed the MoU on ending the war in the region on all fronts.
Under the MoU, the two countries were scheduled to hold negotiations within 60 days, ending on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement on Iran's nuclear program and the removal of sanctions. However, they failed to make sufficient progress toward a deal. ■

China's Su Super League finale caps season of grassroots football fever
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
23:34:13 CST
00:34:13 KST

NANJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Amid deafening cheers and a sea of waving flags, China's Su Super League brought its second season to a close on Saturday, with Wuxi edging Changzhou 2-1 in the final before a crowd of 62,356 at Nanjing Olympic Sports Center.
Wuxi, unbeaten throughout the regular season, capped its dominant campaign by lifting the championship trophy, while the attendance set a new record for the tournament's final at the venue, surpassing the 62,329 spectators who watched last year's inaugural-season decider.
"The atmosphere was incredible. We chartered buses and traveled all the way from Wuxi to Nanjing to cheer for our home team," said Li Tao, a Wuxi supporter.
Fans from both Wuxi and Changzhou organized bus trips to the provincial capital, turning the final into a vibrant showcase of local pride and football fervor.
Drawing playful inspiration from both the English Premier League and the Chinese Super League, the Su Super League pits teams representing Jiangsu's 13 cities against one another. What began as a grassroots competition has evolved into a regional sporting phenomenon, fueled by fierce city rivalries, dramatic matches and packed stadiums.
The league kicked off in April and featured 91 matches this season. According to official figures, the 78 regular-season games attracted a cumulative 2.59 million spectators, up 22.17 percent from the previous year.
Demand for tickets remained intense throughout the campaign. The average success rate for ticket applications stood at just 9.6 percent, falling to 2.7 percent for the final.
The championship match also drew a star-studded supporting cast, with Olympic champions Zhang Yufei and Hao Ting, Asian Games champion Wu Mengjie, along with singers and celebrities, adding to the festive atmosphere.
Beyond the competition itself, the league has become a platform for grassroots football development and a catalyst for integrating sports with culture and tourism, helping local cities turn matchday excitement into economic activity.
Host cities have rolled out a range of incentives, including free admission to scenic attractions and discounts on accommodation and dining for fans presenting match tickets.
In Wuxi, the eight home matches this season generated 19.2 billion yuan (about 2.88 billion U.S. dollars) in total consumption across the city, up 5.9 percent year-on-year, according to local authorities.
For fans unable to secure a seat in the stadium, Jiangsu established more than 600 public viewing zones, transforming plazas and shopping malls into fan venues complete with giant screens, food stalls and crowds cheering every goal.
The Su Super League's success has also inspired a wave of grassroots football competitions across China, with more than a dozen regional amateur leagues emerging nationwide.
Earlier this month, the inaugural Northeast Super League final drew 63,259 spectators, setting a new attendance record for an amateur football match in China. ■

INDIA bloc 'impeaches' CEC in mock Parliament, but what will it take to remove him for real?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
15:26:54 UTC
00:26:54 KST

NEW DELHI: The opposition on Saturday unanimously passed a "resolution" to remove Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls during a "mock Parliament" organised at Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge's residence.Former Lok Sabha Speaker Meira Kumar presided over the proceedings, with several MPs and activists supporting the demand for the CEC's removal.Kharge moved the resolution seeking Kumar's removal, accusing him of centralising control over electoral rolls and acting at the behest of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah. Kharge also said that SIR was initiated to remove voters opposed to Bharatiya Janata Party."The proposal we are bringing today is to safeguard the dignity of a constitutional institution. We have no personal enmity with the CEC. Our intention is that the Election Commission should function impartially in keeping with the spirit of the Constitution," Kharge said."The trust of the common man in it should remain intact. No one sitting in Delhi should be able to wrongly delete the voting rights of weaker sections, women, and youth using a computer," he added.
Meanwhile, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi delivered the closing remarks of the proceedings, describing the event as the opposition's political weapon targeting CEC Gyanesh Kumar, PM Modi and Amit Shah."This looks like a meeting of Lok Sabha MPs, Rajya Sabha MPs, and common citizens. But actually, this is a political weapon," Rahul said.In the "mock Parliament" at Kharge's residence, the opposition sailed through the resolution with a voice vote. But while the numbers may have been on its side there, would the same motion stand a chance in the real Parliament?
What will it take to remove CEC Gyanesh Kumar for real
The removal of a CEC is deliberately difficult.Article 324(5) of the Constitution states that the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed from office only "in like manner and on the like grounds as a judge of the Supreme Court.""The other Election Commissioners shall not be removed from office except on the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner," it further says.
The CEC can be removed by the same procedure as a Supreme Court judge and requires a majority vote from both the Houses.
Article 124(4) of the Constitution, which lays down the procedure for removing a Supreme Court judge, states that a judge can be removed only by an order of the President following an address by each House of Parliament.Such an address must be supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a majority of at least two-thirds of members present and voting, in the same session, on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.The process begins with a notice of motion in either House of Parliament alleging misbehaviour or incapacity. The notice must be signed by at least 100 MPs in the Lok Sabha or 50 MPs in the Rajya Sabha.The presiding officer of the concerned House can admit or refuse the motion after considering the material and information available. If the motion is admitted, an inquiry is conducted into the charges by a committee constituted for the purpose.
If the charges are established, the motion must be passed by a majority of the total membership of each House and by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting in both Houses.Once both Houses pass the motion in accordance with these requirements, an address is made to the President, who then issues the order removing the CEC.The President's role at this stage is constitutional and formal once Parliament has passed the required address.Interestingly, this is not the first time when the opposition is gearing up for introducing a resolution seeking CEC's removal.On April 7, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Rajya Sabha Chairperson CP Radhakrishnan had rejected opposition notice, which was signed by 130 Lok Sabha members, 63 Rajya Sabha members, seeking the CEC's removal over alleged partisanship and arbitrariness in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
Rohitashwa Ranjan is a digital journalist with The Times of India, where he decodes Indian politics as a carefully staged production with scripts, subtext and everything behind. His stories track elections, party dynamics and the things that often are buried beneath the headlines. When not parsing vote shares or alliances, he is usually reading between the lines, where the real story tends to reside.

Report: Polymarket probes suspicious last-minute bets on Netanyahu election win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
15:25:51 UTC
00:25:51 KST

The Polymarket betting website is investigating dozens of suspicious bets made this week wagering that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party would win Israel's election, The New York Times reported Thursday, citing a spokesman for the company.
Hundreds of new accounts reportedly placed the bets just before the polls in Israel closed on Tuesday in what appears to be an attempt to manipulate prediction markets. According to The Times, data analysis company Polysights said its tools flagged "massive inflows of YES buys on fresh wallets" within 24 hours, adding that the spike is "definitely worth investigating."
In the months leading to Israel's election, shifts in the betting odds on Netanyahu or on the leading candidate to replace him, Gadi Eisenkot, drew extensive attention and news coverage. After right-wing pundit Amit Segal wrote in Israel Hayom in April that he felt like betting on Avigdor Lieberman, Lieberman's share price on the betting website jumped fivefold.
Polymarket is one of the most prominent platforms in the digital gambling industry today. Its users are required to bet "yes" or "no" on the team's question about whether a certain event will occur in the future. These can be security incidents, political, sports-related, cultural or environmental events, and more. The platforms match buyers and sellers and hold the money until the event occurs.
On Tuesday, Polymarket reportedly announced surveillance efforts to "detect potential attempts to manipulate election markets, distort probabilities or manufacture apparent market consensus." According to The New York Times, one wallet, created 18 minutes before the polls closed, placed a $14,000 bet and cashed out for $42,000 after the odds had risen.
In July, a Haaretz analysis found that one gambler going by the username 25xp, who had previously only made one bet on Polymarket on Iran, held the largest chip stack in the bet on Netanyahu winning the election. At 4:59 P.M. Israel time on April 7, the user began buying "yes" shares in a bet on whether the U.S. and Iran would reach a cease-fire by the end of that day.
At the time, the market put the odds at just 4 percent, meaning the share traded at around four cents. In under an hour, 25xp had put $18,000 into the bet. A few hours later, CNN reported that a Middle Eastern source said Washington and Tehran were reaching a deal.
In February of this year, the Shin Bet security service and Israel Police said an Israeli reservist and a civilian were charged with using classified information to place bets on Polymarket, while other reservists are suspected of the offense. The authorities made the statement after an Israeli court partially lifted the gag order on the investigation following Haaretz's request.
The charges came a month after Kan public television reported that an anonymous user on Polymarket bet tens of thousands of dollars that Israel would strike Iran in June 2025, resulting in over $152,000 in return. The two men charged in February were indicted on security offenses and bribery charges.

Residents and local officials have gathered in the Spanish village of Urda for a memorial Mass honouring at least 69 people killed in a nearby high-speed train collision.
The pews of San Juan Bautista church in the central province of Toledo were packed on Saturday, while dozens more people gathered outside to listen to the service. Some wiped away tears.
Investigators are looking into the cause of one of Europe's deadliest rail disasters this century, which occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into a stationary train on Wednesday.
‘You are not alone’
The Archbishop of Toledo, Francisco Cerro, told mourners that the days since the disaster had been like a "Good Friday for us all", acknowledging that "there are no words that can offer comfort" to those who had lost loved ones.
"Dear families affected by the train accident, you are not alone. Society is with you, the best of society is with you," he said, urging the public not to forget the tragedy and calling for such disasters never to happen again.
He also paid tribute to emergency workers and volunteers, thanking healthcare staff, firefighters, police and rescue teams for their efforts, and praising what he described as "a genuine wave of solidarity".
The president of the Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano Garcia-Page, and Urda mayor Manuel Galan were among the officials who attended the service.
Residents of Urda, which has a population of around 2,500, "are very badly affected, in great pain and with a great need for support", Galan told Spanish public television ahead of the Mass.
Families await identification of loved ones
Relatives of the victims, who have been providing DNA samples to help identify the dead, face an agonising wait for news as rescue teams continue to sift through the wreckage and forensic experts work to identify the bodies.
Authorities overseeing the process have completed autopsies on all 69 people killed in the crash, with 36 identified so far.

On Friday, the US State Department announced that Washington had green-lit a package of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptors worth $2.1 billion for Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has continued to plead with US and European allies for more interceptors for its forces as Ukraine continues to weather Russian missile and drone attacks.
And while he welcomed the new package and thanked the US for its "strong decision," he warned that delivery could take years.
"Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X.
"However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS," he added. "We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Lavrov on the sidelines of the G20 in Atlanta.

Israel's Palestinian 'ghosts' make voices heard at the polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
15:17:01 UTC
00:17:01 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's Palestinian 'ghosts' make voices heard in historic election result
On Tuesday, as Israelis headed to the polls to choose a new government, pollsters noted record participation, resulting in the highest turnout in an Israeli election since 1999.
Though many of these voters were Jewish Israelis, pollsters also took note of high participation among Israel's Palestinian citizens in the election, with queues reported outside polling stations in Palestinian-majority areas.
As results poured in through the night, the turnout of Palestinian citizens of Israel, at around 80% and higher than the 77.9% national average, resulted in a record seat distribution for Palestinian parties in the Knesset, with 19 seats held collectively by the Joint-List - made up of Hadash, Ta'al and Balad - as well as Ra'am.
The 'existential threat' posed by a Netanyahu government
For Israel's Palestinian citizens, the last four years of Benjamin Netanyahu's government, the most far-right in Israel's history, have made their position in Israeli society more precarious.
Among the host of issues are a clampdown on freedom of speech, in particular in opposition to Israel's war on Gaza, an uptick in house demolitions in the Naqab [Negev] desert, and rampant organised crime in the community that’s neglected by the state.
Miriam Azem, International Advocacy Coordinator at The Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel (Adalah), told The New Arab that ahead of the election, "there was a sentiment, at least amongst some of the public, that if we see another Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich, [Itamar] Ben-Gvir government, that's going to be an existential threat, and nothing less than that".
More recently, Azem noted an increasing rhetoric of removing Palestinian citizens from within Israel's international boundaries by members of a government that belong to the settler community and support settler attacks in the occupied West Bank.
"The fact that there is a big settlement movement that is actually a part of the governing coalition, I think, scares a lot of people," she said.
Yet, though surprising for many pundits in Israel, the turnout was expected by the Palestinian parties, who urged their voters to reach a record turnout and put an end to Netanyahu's government.
"We expected a very high percentage of voting within our community because we live within our community," Sami Abou Shehadeh, the head of Balad, told The New Arab.
"A very important thing was the extreme policies, the right-wing, fascist, extreme policies of Netanyahu and his gang. These were the main reason why people voted more."
Abou Shehadeh said that there was a feeling of success in the community because the list had kept its primary election promise, blocking the formation of a Netanyahu government.
"We were telling the people if they will go out and vote in high numbers, Netanyahu will not be able to form a government again with his coalition," he said, adding, "this is clear in [the] numbers. Because of this Arab participation, Netanyahu and his coalition lost the majority in the Israeli Knesset."
Coalition troubles and 'racist' reactions
Despite the inability of Netanyahu to form a government - holding 53 seats, his bloc is eight short of a majority of 61 - Gadi Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc is also hamstrung, falling short with 48 seats.
With campaign pledges not to work with Netanyahu's Likud party, the Ultra-Orthodox parties, and the Palestinian parties, Eisenkot's bloc is at a deadlock.
The campaign promises and continued reluctance to work with Palestinian parties, despite their vocal willingness to oust Netanyahu, were labelled by Abou Shehadeh as racism.
"Can you imagine, in any different state, someone who lost the majority and there's a majority against him in the parliament; it clearly means he lost the election.
"What is preventing Eisenkot from forming the next coalition? It is his racist views regarding the legitimacy of Arab parties."
"Those who won the elections in numbers must put aside a little bit [of] their racism and start thinking cleverly as serious politicians who want to do change," Abou Shehadeh said, doubling down on the Joint-Lists efforts to work with Eisenkot and prevent another Netanyahu government.
"If they will do that, we will be happy to do all that is needed in order to prevent Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, and Smotrich from forming the next government in Israel. But if the racism wins, we will all lose together."
The Joint-List and Ra'am have struggled during the elections to defend the legitimacy of their parties within Israeli politics, both before and since polling day.
Before the election, Israel's Central Election Committee voted to bar the Palestinian parties, alongside Hadash MK Ofer Casif and Abou Shehadeh.
The Supreme Court overturned the ban, but recommended Abou Shehadeh drop out, as it was likely to uphold the decision and set a legal precedent.
Azem, whose organisation Adalah represented the parties and candidates at the Supreme Court, said the move was an effort to delegitimise Palestinian participation in the political process - one that continued on election day and after the results.
In the aftermath, Netanyahu's Likud has called for an investigation into allegations of election fraud by Palestinian parties, a move disputed by Palestinian parties, the election panel director, and some Jewish opposition parties.
The rhetoric from Netanyahu's bloc that the election was 'stolen' by Palestinian parties is evidence that "the right to vote for Palestinians is seen as a threat to the State", Azem said.
The stakes are high. If Eisenkot and his bloc choose not to work with the Palestinian parties, it could mean he blocks himself from forming a government, handing over the political initiative to Netanyahu, according to Beth Oppenheim, a Policy Fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations.
"By refusing to cooperate with the Palestinian citizens, the opposition parties may in fact be blocking their own path to governing, and handing over to Netanyahu," she told The New Arab.
The allegations, rhetoric of a stolen election, and reluctance to work with Palestinian parties are part of a broader movement within Israeli society putting it on a downward spiral regarding the country's democratic norms, norms which only pertain to its citizens, and not to Palestinians in the occupied territories.
"Israel has been for several decades now in a situation where illiberal forces are on the rise and liberal forces are declining, and we've seen in this election how difficult it is for Israel's opposition to really advance a kind of meaningful alternative to what’s been offered by Netanyahu and the far right."
"I think we are looking at a more illiberal future for the country unless we have an opposition that is able to offer something compelling, and that also is able to incorporate Palestinians as equal partners," she added.
Partnership between Israeli governments and Palestinian parties isn't new, however, with the government of Yair Lapid and Naftali Bennett entering into coalition with Ra'am in 2021, and Yitzhak Rabin's government relying on Palestinian Knesset votes to pass through the Oslo Accords.
"In 1995, there was a government that relied on five votes of Arab parties… and the prime minister defended this position unapologetically. It was Yitzhak Rabin. He said, absolutely, I have no problem; I do not need what they call a Jewish majority. [He] even explicitly called it a racist position,” Tamir Sorek, professor of Jewish Studies at Pennsylvania State University, told The New Arab.
"And shortly after he declared that he was assassinated, I believe to a large extent because he dared to make that move, and I think the leaders of the opposition are aware of this precedent," he added.
Despite the precedent, and the unwillingness of much of the Eisenkot bloc to work alongside Palestinian parties, except for The Democrats leader Yair Golan, whose column published in the left-wing daily Haaretz on Friday called for an agreement with Palestinian parties, Sorek said many opposition voters want their leaders to work with Palestinian parties.
"They are so antagonistic to Netanyahu that they are ready to do that, and it included even [a] majority of voters for [Avigdor] Lieberman", Sorek said. In the immediate aftermath of the election, Lieberman, head of Yisrael Beiteinu, reaffirmed his unwillingness to work with Netanyahu, the Ultra-Orthodox, and the Palestinian parties.
"I think because of that, I'm saying that there is still a likelihood that it will happen because Eisenkot is under pressure from different sides… but a significant portion of his constituency [is] expecting [him] to do whatever is needed to oust Netanyahu."
Palestinian 'ghosts' emerge to the fore
The optimism that Eisenkot will be forced to work with the Palestinian parties is not shared, however, as hostility to Palestinian parties has consistently emerged in past elections, with previous attempts to block their electoral participation.
According to Adalah, attempts to ban Palestinian participation from Knesset elections occurred in 2003, 2013, 2015, 2020 and 2022, with the Supreme Court overruling all previous attempts.
"I'm afraid I kind of know the ending, which is that they [Eisenkot's bloc] would much rather cling to their Jewish supremacy than actually confront Netanyahu," Diana Buttu, a Palestinian, Haifa-based lawyer, political analyst and commentator, told The New Arab.
Buttu has previously described Israel's Palestinian citizens as "Ghosts" in how they're perceived within Israeli society: "You're not seen, you're not heard, you're not felt, but they're all afraid of you all the time.”
Following the election, however, "now we're either a monster or we're still a ghost. For the Netanyahus we're a monster, right? We're now here, the ghost is now seen. We're there, and so you're supposed to be afraid of it, and that's why he's [Netanyahu] trying to discount the vote… for the others who are in the opposition, we're still ghosts."
Despite this, for Buttu, the outcome of the elections has changed Israeli politics forever, especially as voters were galvanised to turn up, despite many of the well-known names in Palestinian politics in the Knesset stepping down in this election.
"These people are voting on the basis of confidence, and so has it changed? Yes, it has. The Israelis are now forever going to be thinking about this [Palestinian] segment, and they have to."
For Balad leader Sami Abou Shehadeh, the election victory is merely the first step for Palestinian parties to ensure their recognition in Israeli political life.
"Our struggle against racism will not finish with a knockout. We need to score points step by step," he said, noting that Joint-List's next efforts will be to replace the Likud Knesset speaker alongside opposition parties in a move expected next month.
"It's going to take a lot of time. We have a very long struggle."
As for efforts to oust Netanyahu, he said that despite disagreements, there are common interests with Eisenkot's bloc.
"He [Eisenkot] wants to be prime minister. We don't want Netanyahu as a prime minister. We can work this out if he is able to put his racism aside a little bit, that's all."

WOLOLOW REINTERPRETS 1968 FUTURO HOUSE AS TABLETOP LAMP
Designed by Arthur Koshatahyan and Kostya Trunov, WOLOLOW Night Lamp Ver 2.0 is a compact luminaire that translates the Space Age architectural language of Matti Suuronen’s 1968 Futuro House into an everyday tabletop object. Directly scaling down the iconic portable chalet typology, the second version of the lamp features an elliptical disc-shaped hull punctuated by a ring of oval portholes, elevated on a slender, angled steel tripod base.
ELLIPTICAL HOUSING LAUNCHES ACROSS FIVE CHROMED FINISHES
Currently launched on Kickstarter, the updated 2.0 edition retains the original fiberglass-inspired silhouette while upgrading the internal illumination hardware. Replacing the previous generation’s integrated battery, the revised model incorporates a hardwired power connection and a standard, user-replaceable 12V MR16 LED bulb with a GU5.3 base. The fixture accommodates standard warm-white modules as well as aftermarket smart LED bulbs, allowing integration with wireless home automation protocols for dimming and RGB color adjustments. The lamp is manufactured in five distinct shell finishes: white, yellow, orange, sky blue, and mirror chrome.

Hassan Yazdani makes wrestling history
TEHRAN - Eleven years. Four different weight classes. Eleven World and Olympic medals. As he approaches his 32nd birthday, Hassan Yazdani has achieved a milestone that stands alone in the history of international wrestling.
By claiming bronze at the 2026 World Wrestling Championships in Astana, Yazdani completed an extraordinary record, becoming the first wrestler in history to win World or Olympic medals across four different weight categories.
From 70kg in Las Vegas to 97kg in Astana, the Iranian wrestling superstar has carved out a remarkable legacy, adding another historic chapter to an already glittering career.
Yazdani made his debut at 97kg at the 2026 World Championships. Although he suffered a defeat against Arash Yoshida, he bounced back to secure the bronze medal.
While the color of this medal may not match the Olympic gold he won in Rio or his multiple World Championship titles, its historical significance is undeniable.
The bronze was the 11th World and Olympic medal of Yazdani's career, completing his remarkable achievement across four weight classes: 70kg, 74kg, 86kg and 97kg.
It is a testament to his longevity, adaptability and ability to compete at the highest level across different stages of his career.
Hassan Yazdani's World and Olympic Medal Record
- 2015 World Championships – Las Vegas: Silver, 70kg
- 2016 Olympic Games – Rio: Gold, 74kg
- 2017 World Championships – Paris: Gold, 86kg
- 2018 World Championships – Budapest: Bronze, 86kg
- 2019 World Championships – Nur-Sultan: Gold, 86kg
- 2020 Olympic Games – Tokyo: Silver, 86kg
- 2021 World Championships – Oslo: Gold, 86kg
- 2022 World Championships – Belgrade: Silver, 86kg
- 2023 World Championships – Belgrade: Silver, 86kg
- 2024 Olympic Games – Paris: Silver, 86kg
- 2026 World Championships – Astana: Bronze, 97kg
Eleven medals across eleven years. From his first World Championship silver in Las Vegas to his historic bronze in Astana, Yazdani has experienced the very best of international wrestling.
An Olympic champion, a four-time world champion and now a history-maker across four different weight categories, Hassan Yazdani continues to push the boundaries of what is possible in the sport.
A true legend of Iranian wrestling — and a name firmly etched in the history of the sport.

Iran envoys meet Qatar mediators as threat looms of US strikes after midterm elections
- Iranian and Qatari mediators met in Doha as diplomats tried to stop fresh fighting after the US midterm elections. Talks are linked to regular contacts with Washington.
- Marco Rubio said Trump has not decided on new strikes against Iran and prefers diplomacy, though he still has military options. Trump has delayed action while Republicans seek to keep Congress.

AI generated
DUBAI/ATLANTA - Iranian negotiators held talks in Doha with Qatari mediators on Oct 31 to discuss paths out of war in the Gulf, a source told Reuters, as diplomats try to avert a new outbreak of fighting after the US midterm elections this week.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Oct 31 that President Donald Trump has not decided whether to launch new strikes against Iran, but would prefer to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Trump has held off on strikes on Iran, in recent weeks, ahead of elections at which his Republicans are trying to retain control of Congress.
The Oct 31 talks in the Qatari capital followed more than 12 hours of discussions on Oct 30 between Iranian and Qatari envoys in Tehran, said the source, who was briefed on the negotiations and spoke on condition of anonymity.
The source said the talks were being coordinated in regular contacts with Washington.
Countries in the region have been anticipating that Trump could restart attacks once the voting is over. Iran has repeatedly said it would respond to any new attacks by striking at US and Israeli targets in neighbouring countries.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei issued a statement on Oct 31 ordering the armed forces to be prepared to respond to any attacks.
The Iranian military later announced it was taking steps to improve its readiness.
“Any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response,” Khamenei, who has not appeared in public since replacing his father, slain at the war’s outset, said on Oct 31 in the statement posted on his official Telegram account.
Khamenei said that senior commanders had reported high readiness along the Gulf coast, in and around the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman, and on Iran’s northwestern and southeastern borders.
Rubio, hosting foreign ministers of the Group of 20 major economies in Atlanta, declined to set a timeframe for the talks in Qatar, but said direct and indirect contacts with Iran were under way.
“There are multiple talks. Talks have actually never stopped,” he said.
Trump would “prefer to solve it diplomatically. But I think what the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it,” Rubio said.
Diplomacy continues, despite gaps
Trump, who launched the war alongside Israel in February, has repeatedly hinted at plans to restart strikes on Iran. Last week, he called on Israelis ahead of their own election to keep his wartime ally Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in power, so the two leaders can “finish the job”.
But Washington has also lately taken steps to indicate it is open to diplomacy. Earlier this week, Vice-President J.D. Vance, who led the US delegation at previous rounds of talks with Iran, wrote a letter to a hardline senior Iranian security official, which the New York Times and Wall Street Journal described as an initiative to see if it was possible to restart talks.
Trump has played the letter down, saying he approved it only to discuss the possibility of letting more medical supplies into Iran: “I said if you want to do that, that’s OK. Basically, it’s getting supplies in to help people that are not well.”
In the latest Qatari-mediated discussions, the Qataris brought a proposal to Tehran a week ago for a seven-day plan, under which the US and Iran would take daily steps to build trust ahead of broader peace talks, the source briefed on the negotiations said. A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Oct 30 that this proposal was not deemed satisfactory by Tehran.
Iran has been proposing its own seven-day plan since September, so far rejected by Trump. That calls for Washington to lift a blockade of Iranian ports, unfreeze assets and approve an Iranian-backed route through the Strait of Hormuz, after which the contested strait would be reopened.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said in remarks reported by Al Jazeera on Oct 31 that Iran was studying Vance’s letter. He said the Iranian plan was the only proposal on the table to reopen the strait. REUTERS
