Narcissistic employees will work harder for a title than for a raise, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
15:00:30 UTC
00:00:30 KST

Most employees prefer to receive workplace recognition and bonuses behind closed doors, yet individuals with more pronounced narcissistic traits show a much stronger appetite for public accolades and impressive job titles. New research published in Social Psychological and Personality Science suggests that this preference is tied to a strong desire for social status and a lack of worry about making coworkers envious. The findings indicate that common management tactics like handing out flashy job titles in place of raises may disproportionately appeal to more narcissistic workers.
In the workplace, managers frequently use rewards to recognize strong performance and keep staff motivated. These incentives generally fall into two categories: public rewards, such as an employee-of-the-month award or praise during a company-wide meeting, and private rewards, such as a quiet salary bump or a complimentary email from a supervisor. Choosing the right approach depends heavily on personality, particularly a trait psychologists call grandiose narcissism. Grandiose narcissism is a personality dimension characterized by an inflated sense of self-importance, feelings of entitlement, social dominance, and a belief that one is superior to others.
Past research indicates that people with elevated narcissistic traits often calibrate their effort based on how visible their success will be to an audience. For instance, a 2002 study found that individuals high in narcissism performed much better on challenging tasks when there was an opportunity to win admiration, compared with conditions offering little chance to stand out.
This selective effort stems from a deep craving for social status, defined as respect, admiration, and deference from peers. Supporting this connection, a 2018 study of community members and college students indicated that both the charming, self-promoting side of narcissism and its hostile, competitive side share a comparable desire for status, even though they pursue it through different strategies.
To explain how this drive operates in daily life, the authors of a 2019 theoretical review argued that people high in grandiose narcissism constantly scan their surroundings for opportunities to boost their rank, pursuing status either by showing off to win admiration or by putting others down to defeat rivals. Public workplace rewards offer an ideal stage for both strategies, making it obvious to everyone who won and who lost. By contrast, people with lower levels of narcissism often shy away from the spotlight because they worry about sparking envy, an uncomfortable emotion marked by resentment and feelings of inferiority that can lead jealous coworkers to undermine high performers.
Because narcissism is typically linked to lower empathy, study author Emily M. Zitek, an associate professor of organizational behavior at the School of Industrial and Labor Relations at Cornell University, and her colleagues hypothesized that more narcissistic employees would be less deterred by peer envy. They expected these workers to be much more drawn to public rewards, including the workplace practice of handing out impressive-sounding job titles without added pay or authority, known as title inflation.
“We had two goals,” Zitek told PsyPost. “My colleagues and I do research on entitlement and narcissism in the workplace, so we wanted to continue to explore this topic. And then we were also interested in the phenomenon of title inflation in the workplace and whether inflated titles are indeed appealing. Therefore, we put these two ideas together.”
To test this idea across four main studies and three supplemental replications, with a combined final sample of 1,069 full-time U.S. employees in the main studies, the researchers recruited participants through the online platform CloudResearch Connect. All studies were preregistered with publicly posted materials, data, and code, and sensitivity power analyses showed that the observed effects in every study exceeded the minimum size the designs could reliably detect.
In the first study, 249 participants wrote down one public reward and one private reward actually offered at their jobs, rated how motivating they found each on a seven-point scale, and completed a 16-item questionnaire measuring grandiose narcissism. Overall, workers rated private rewards like raises and one-on-one praise as more motivating than public ones, with average scores of 5.63 versus 4.43 out of 7. While employees across the narcissism spectrum were equally motivated by private rewards, those with higher narcissism scores reported noticeably greater motivation to earn public rewards than their less narcissistic peers.
Because the real-world rewards listed in the first study differed in practical value, such as comparing a private pay raise to a public compliment, a second study held the reward itself constant. A group of 244 full-time employees evaluated seven specific workplace incentives, including a 10 percent year-end bonus, a promotion, and a fancy lunch, rating whether they preferred a private or public version of each on a scale from 1 (definitely private) to 7 (definitely public). As a group, participants leaned toward privacy, averaging 3.23 out of 7 across the seven scenarios, below the neutral midpoint of 4. Even so, higher narcissism scores consistently predicted a stronger preference for public recognition across six of the seven reward types.
In the third study, the authors examined why narcissism predicts a taste for public recognition by asking 294 employees to choose between a private or company-wide announcement for a 10 percent bonus. Participants then rated how much their choice was guided by a desire for social status among peers and a concern about making colleagues feel envious. While the sample as a whole strongly favored the private bonus announcement with an average score of 2.01 out of 7, more narcissistic workers were much more inclined toward the public announcement.
A mediation analysis, which tests whether a relationship can be accounted for by intervening factors, found that people higher in narcissism reported a stronger desire for status and less concern about triggering envy, and that both of these were in turn related to preferring the public bonus. The authors caution that this type of analysis cannot establish that status desire and envy concern are the actual reasons for the preference, and that other untested explanations remain possible. The scale measuring concern about coworker envy also had relatively low internal consistency, which the authors noted could have affected their statistical estimates. Two supplemental studies that varied the measures produced the same general pattern.
The fourth study pitted a visible marker of prestige directly against private financial gain by asking 282 participants to choose between two hypothetical job offers that both required harder work. One job offered a prestigious new title that friends and family would find impressive without increasing pay, while the other offered a higher salary that outsiders would not know about while keeping the old title. To rule out the possibility that people simply wanted more workplace authority, the researchers specified that both positions carried the exact same level of company power, influence, and number of direct reports. Participants also completed an expanded questionnaire that measured overall grandiose narcissism alongside its two distinct sub-traits: narcissistic admiration (self-promotion) and narcissistic rivalry (antagonism toward competitors).
Across the entire sample, workers overwhelmingly favored the higher-paying job over the impressive title, averaging 1.72 on a seven-point scale where 1 favored pay and 7 favored the title. Participants also expressed a much greater willingness to work harder for a pay raise alone (averaging 6.17 out of 7) than for a prestigious title alone (averaging 2.79 out of 7).
However, overall narcissism, as well as both its admiration and rivalry components, positively predicted a greater likelihood of accepting the prestigious title over higher pay and a greater willingness to work harder just for a title upgrade. Higher overall narcissism and rivalry scores were even slightly associated with a reduced willingness to work harder for a private pay increase, and a third supplemental study replicated this link between narcissism and title preference.
“Employees would rather be praised in a 1-on-1 meeting than in front of their colleagues,” Zitek explained. “Narcissists, however, like public rewards much better than non-narcissists do. They are willing to work harder just to get a title increase in a way that others are not. Thus, when a company offers a public award, they should be aware that it might be more appealing to people higher in narcissism and less appealing to people lower in narcissism.”
These results align with a longitudinal study of grandiose narcissism and social status, which found that the two reinforce each other over time. That study tracked general status motives rather than specific workplace incentives, but both indicate that a drive for social rank sits at the core of grandiose narcissism. The new findings also echo a study of public versus anonymous charitable acts, which found that people higher in narcissism are primarily motivated by visible recognition in front of an audience.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Even among participants with relatively high narcissism scores, private rewards and higher pay appear to have remained more popular on an absolute basis than public praise or unpaid title changes; their preference for privacy and money was simply less pronounced than that of people lower in narcissism.
In addition, the questionnaires measured grandiose narcissism as a continuous personality trait found in the everyday workforce rather than diagnosing clinical narcissistic personality disorder. Because the studies relied on cross-sectional surveys and mostly hypothetical choices, the data cannot establish cause and effect, and how employees think they would react to a public award might differ from how they feel when actually receiving one on the job.
Cultural context may play a role as well, since all participants were full-time workers in the United States, and public rewards might be viewed differently in more collectivistic societies that emphasize modesty. In the future, longitudinal workplace studies could test whether offering public recognition actually improves real-world job performance among more narcissistic employees. The research was funded by Cornell University’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations, and the authors declared no conflicts of interest.
“We think our research shows that title inflation probably isn’t the most effective strategy to attract or motivate employees since most people prefer private rewards over public rewards,” Zitek noted. “Instead, the practice of title inflation might primarily attract a disproportionate number of narcissists.”
“My collaborators and I will continue to study the effects of entitlement and narcissism in the workplace,” Zitek added. “Workers often complain about having to interact with narcissistic and entitled bosses, coworkers, and subordinates, and we want to be able to give recommendations for how to deal with these personalities in the workplace. There are both pros and cons of these personality characteristics that are important to study. In our current research, we found that narcissists might work harder than others when offered a public reward, for example.”
The study, “Inflated Titles, Inflated Egos: Narcissism Predicts the Desire for Public Rewards,” was authored by Emily M. Zitek, Verena Krause, and Alexander H. Jordan.

Why the Texas race is a high-stakes test for both Republicans and Democrats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
15:00:28 UTC
00:00:28 KST

Washington DC — Hours before record early voting in the 2026 midterm elections ended in Texas state, Senator Ted Cruz sounded the alarm.
On his podcast, Cruz, one of the top Trump allies, became the most prominent Republican to publicly warn that the Grand Old Party (or GOP) could face major losses in the US state.
He cautioned Texas is "excruciatingly close", "we could lose Texas", and Republicans "could lose every single statewide race in Texas" – including the Senate contest between Republican Ken Paxton — who is endorsed by US President Donald Trump — and Democrat James Talarico, as well as the gubernatorial race involving Greg Abbott.
Cruz, who has represented Texas in the Senate since 2013, did not stop there.
Urging turnout on election day, he described a potential "bloodbath" in which Republicans could lose as many as eight Senate seats nationally if Democratic turnout is high and Republican voters stay at home.
The warning from Cruz came less than four days from the November 3 election and follows a flurry of alarming polls for Republican candidates and similar observations by other Republicans or Trump allies such as former White House adviser Steve Bannon, Lieutenant Governor Dan Patrick, and State Representative Briscoe Cain, who remarked in early October that "if the election were held tomorrow, all statewide races go blue".
The midterm elections present a crucial test for Texas Republicans, offering Democrats their best opportunity in decades to win a key Senate seat.
No Democrat has won statewide office in in the Lone Star State since 1994. That’s when Talarico was in kindergarten.
Thirty-two years later, Talarico, 37, is running neck and neck with Republican Attorney General Paxton, according to multiple polls, in what is being billed as the most expensive US Senate race in the country, with advertising spending in the contest already exceeding $563 million.
Despite troubling polling numbers for the GOP, Republican strategists such as Beau Rothschild remain optimistic that the crown jewel of the Republican national base will stay red in the November 3 elections.
"I have always been skeptical of polling, particularly in Texas. While I believe this race is competitive, I still expect Ken Paxton to win. That said, I anticipate a much closer race than his campaign would prefer," Rothschild tells TRT World.
"Texas remains a Republican state, but Republicans cannot afford to take anything for granted, particularly in the current political environment."
The 2026 US midterm elections will determine the balance of power in Congress, as Democrats seek control of both chambers to challenge President Trump's legislative agenda.
Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers of the Congress, with 53 seats in the Senate and 218 in the House of Representatives.
All 435 House seats, contested every two years, are on the ballot alongside 35 Senate seats carrying six-year terms.
History shows that the president's party often loses political power in midterm elections. The Democrats must gain four additional seats and retain key battleground states such as Michigan, Georgia, and New Hampshire to secure a majority.
Why Democrats are targeting the Texas is because public backlash against rising inflation, tensions surrounding US war on Iran, and Republican immigration policies —combined with a strong Democratic candidate — have created the best opportunity for them to win the seat.
Rothschild says inflation and the rising cost of living are challenges facing Republican candidates across the country and that voters are feeling the economic pressure "which is certainly creating political headwinds."
"However, Democrats have yet to articulate a convincing or responsible plan to address these challenges. Instead, much of their strategy appears focused on voter dissatisfaction with President Trump. While that approach may resonate in certain parts of the country, I do not believe it will be enough to win statewide in Texas," he argues.
Diverse urban centres and rural voters
Texas has grown substantially more diverse over recent decades, creating new electoral opportunities for Democrats.
Suburbs around Dallas, Houston, and Austin are rapidly diversifying, with growing minority populations flipping local offices and narrowing Republican margins.
Texas's rural areas, however, remain predominantly white and consistently deliver substantial support to conservative candidates.
"Voter turnout will be absolutely critical, particularly in the suburbs and rural communities that have historically been essential to Republican victories in Texas," says the Republican strategist Rothschild.
What is encouraging for Republicans, he says, is that early voting numbers suggest stronger participation in several of these key areas compared to previous elections.
"Republicans appear to be making a more concerted effort to turn out their voters early, which could prove decisive in a close race."
Ultimately, Rothschild says, the key will be maintaining strong rural turnout while remaining competitive in the suburbs, where independent and swing voters could determine the margin of victory.
Democrats, meanwhile, point to several key drivers behind their optimism in Texas.
They say the massive population growth, which they claim has heavily diluted the traditional Republican advantage, Trump's immigration policies in an area where Hispanic and Latino residents comprise over 40 percent of the total population, discontent over rising costs of living and Talarico's performance combine to make the Senate seat flippable.
"Texas is changing demographically. During Covid there were people moving in from other parts of the country, including California. Those people bring their politics in with them. Also, Trump did surprisingly well in 2024 with Hispanic voters all the polling show that he has lost a lot of that support partly for the same reasons as other Americans, the economy but also many Hispanics think the Trump immigration policies have gone overboard," Chris Lapetina, a Democratic strategist tells TRT World.
Lapetina says if the Democrats take power, a lot of their legislative effort will be helping Americans who can’t afford healthcare get healthcare.
"Trump cut off federal funding to millions of Americans who couldn’t afford healthcare. And the Democrats will try to get that funding back," says the Democratic strategist.
'Political earthquake'
Texas Senate race between Paxton and Talarico has become a bitter race and a multi-million-dollar showdown. Both have been trying to woo voters on issues such as character, political corruption, culture wars, economy, affordability, immigration and infrastructure.
With voters making the economy their top priority this midterm cycle, and most US polls ranking it above every other issue, Lapetina says there is an affordability issue, which is unusual because it is tied to foreign policy — the US-Iran war.
"A majority of Americans think that higher gas prices aren't particularly tied to the Iran war. Even though the Democrats will have a hard time stopping Trump from prosecuting that war if he chooses to go forward, it will make a big effort to rally Americans against the war saying it’s causing prices to go up," argues Lapetina.
If Republicans fail to hold their traditional bastion in these midterms, it would mark one of the most consequential political shifts in modern US history.
Most forecasts predicting a Democratic win in Texas also project overall Senate control, with probabilities between 60 and 75 per cent ahead of Tuesday's election.
"I do not believe Texas will flip, but if it does, it would represent a significant political earthquake for the Republican Party," says Rothschild.
Losing a statewide Senate race in Texas would force Republicans to seriously reevaluate their messaging, candidate selection, voter outreach, and overall electoral strategy, he adds.
"It would also raise broader questions about the party's ability to maintain its traditional coalition, particularly among suburban and independent voters," says the Republican strategist.
"Texas has been a cornerstone of Republican strength for decades. A Democratic victory would send a clear warning to Republicans nationwide that even their most reliable strongholds can no longer be taken for granted."

Text description provided by the architects. At the Alaska Airlines Flagship Lounge in SeaTac International Airport, the door is always open. Travelers seek lounges as an escape from the anxiety, noise, and commotion of the concourse. Traditionally, airport lounges catered to this desire by emphasizing exclusivity: sleek, business-oriented safe havens that prioritized the needs of a privileged swath of travelers. Alaska Airlines sought to transform the lounge typology by providing a warm, welcoming space where all guests could find refuge – to relax, work, refuel and connect – a home-away-from-home with a sense of place deeply rooted in the Pacific Northwest. Programmatically, the lounge is conceived in four zones: Come In, an approachable entry; Help Yourself, a casual bistro; Take a Breath, a haven for peaceful relaxation; and Cut Loose, a cozy bar atmosphere. Lightly separated with an array of oak and twisted metal screens, the spaces flow together.

Washington's Shrinking Room for Maneuver in West Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:57:12 UTC
23:57:12 KST

Washington's shrinking room for maneuver in West Asia
LONDON -- The current situation is too complex to be summarized in a few brief points, as what is unfolding goes far beyond a direct military confrontation between the United States and Israel on one side, and Iran and its allies on the other.
We are witnessing shifts in the balance of power, the instruments of pressure, the future of the American presence in West Asia, and the nature of the regional order that may emerge once the war on Iran comes to an end.
When referring to the Axis of Resistance at this stage, the focus is primarily on the forces actively engaged in the confrontation, foremost among them the Islamic Republic of Iran, alongside Yemen. Judging by the course of the war, the performance of these forces has exceeded expectations, and the axis is now in a position to secure additional gains. Such gains do not necessarily depend on achieving a swift military victory, but rather on managing the confrontation in a way that exhausts the enemy's options and progressively narrows its room for maneuver.
A battle can also be won on points; it does not necessarily require a single decisive blow to bring everything to an end. Whenever the enemy opens a new front of pressure or takes measures aimed at besieging Iran and forcing it to retreat, the axis finds an opportunity to activate another instrument of pressure, one that has either not been used before or has yet to be deployed to its full potential.
The axis is thus opening new fronts of pressure and changing the rules of confrontation. The significance of this approach lies in the fact that the enemy is no longer facing a fixed set of instruments whose capabilities and limits it already understands. Instead, it is confronting a range of capabilities that can be activated in response to developments on the battlefield.
This highlights the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz, which represents a powerful lever of pressure linked to energy supplies, trade, and the global economy. Alongside it is the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which could also affect maritime traffic and international trade routes if the instruments of pressure associated with it were activated.
The central point is that when the United States and the Israeli occupation entity open a new avenue of pressure, this does not necessarily mean they are expanding their options at Iran's expense. On the contrary, such moves may prompt the axis to activate countermeasures that shift the pressure toward areas far more sensitive to its adversaries.
This is the point that deserves particular attention: the ability to shift the confrontation from one arena to another, and from the military sphere to the geopolitical and economic domains. Such flexibility gives the Axis of Resistance considerable leverage over international calculations and decisions.
Instruments of power are not limited to missiles, aircraft, or land and naval confrontations. They also encompass geographical positioning, maritime corridors, energy resources, regional relations, the ability to withstand attrition, the reorganization of decision-making centers, and the availability of economic and military alternatives. For this reason, the axis's latent power remains greater than many realize, including U.S. President Donald Trump and some political leaders both inside and outside Iran.
The issue is not simply a matter of possessing instruments of pressure, but of being able to deploy them at the right moment and in a gradual manner. This approach ensures that all available leverage is not exhausted at once and that the enemy is not given an opportunity to address every instrument simultaneously. The axis has reached an advanced stage in its ability to influence the course of the war, while a portion of its actual capabilities may not yet have been fully revealed.
Beyond strategic analysis, there is also the dimension of faith and divine providence. Alongside political and military calculations, there is a sense that what is unfolding cannot be fully explained through human calculations alone, and that Almighty God is directing and guiding events according to His will.
This feeling is rooted in the way new capabilities have emerged at different stages of the confrontation.
It is also reflected in the transformations that have compelled forces previously considered unlikely to engage in direct confrontation to confront a reality vastly different from the one that existed before. For example, who could have imagined that the Strait of Hormuz would become an instrument of strategic leverage, followed by the Strait of Bab al-Mandab, to the point that, according to this assessment, 40 percent of global energy flows would come under the scrutiny and potential control of the Axis of Resistance?
This sense of faith does not eliminate the need for political and military analysis. Rather, it forms part of a broader perspective that connects the patience exercised in earlier stages, the building of institutions, and the accumulation of capabilities with the eventual emergence of their results at a decisive moment of confrontation.

Iran's economy has capacity to overcome war pressures: economic analyst
TEHRAN- An economic analyst, emphasizing Iran's economic capacity to overcome the pressures caused by war and to revive production and employment, stated: "Erosive bureaucracy and delays in decision-making have prevented the utilization of the country's economic power."
Economic resilience under wartime conditions does not depend solely on the extent of natural resources, production capacity, or foreign trade power. What ultimately determines how much an economy can withstand external pressures is the quality of decision-making, the speed of response by executive institutions, and the ability to convert potential capacities into actual performance.
In such circumstances, comparing the experience of countries that have been involved in war and sanctions provides an opportunity to evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of economic policymaking. Despite foreign restrictions and war-induced damages, Iran's economy possesses extensive production, agricultural, industrial, and geographical capacities; capacities that require coordination among responsible agencies, a reduction in administrative barriers, and timely decision-making. The fundamental question is how to utilize existing power to curb inflation, maintain production, reconstruct damaged activities, and strengthen employment, and how to prevent the slow pace of decision-making from increasing the cost of external pressures on the economy and people's livelihoods.
Saeed Leylaz, an economic analyst, believes in an interview with IRNA's economic correspondent that Iran's economy cannot only overcome current obstacles and problems but also implement certain reform processes.
Referring to Russia's experience in the Ukraine war and the possibility of Iran benefiting from this country's experience in the current situation, Laylaz stated: "Replicating Russia's experience in Iran's economy to prevent inflation and maintain the level of domestic production is feasible; in some instances and in some areas, we can even perform better than Russia."
He continued: "Most or all of the problems facing Iran's economy have no connection to the war; these problems existed before the war and are not even limited to sanctions, because we faced them before the sanctions as well. Sanctions and war make all these issues and problems more severe, but as our past experiences have shown, we have been able to overcome these problems.
Referring to the economic blockade and its excessive pressure on the body of the economy, the economic analyst stated: "I accept that the current economic blockade is the greatest pressure ever exerted on the country's economy in Iran's history. We have never experienced a higher pressure or blockade than this. I accept this and by no means underestimate it. But the reality is that Iran, apart from its southern water borders, has about 35 other crossings and borders with neighboring countries. As the Prime Minister of Iraq correctly pointed out, many of these countries need Iran for their imports and exports, and in some cases, this dependency can even be greater than Iran's need for them."
He pointed to Turkey and Turkmenistan as two of Iran's neighbors and said: "Perhaps only the Republic of Azerbaijan, given the small size of its economy, could somewhat block our imports and exports; that too in a situation where such a thing has not happened so far. Even if such a restriction is created, nothing decisive will happen, because we have an independent maritime border with Russia. The reality is that Iran's economy, neither in terms of diversity, nor in terms of stability, nor in terms of dependence on oil revenues, is by any means weaker than Russia's economy."
Leylaz further referred to the nature of the Ukraine war and compared it with Iran's conditions, stating: "The war Russia is facing is not just Russia's war; it is the war of the entire NATO and the Western bloc against this country. Similarly, the war we refer to as America's war against Iran has, in my opinion, involved more than 70 countries worldwide."
The analyst stated: "In the first week of the war, I said that almost all of Europe was behind America's war with Iran. Ultimately, we all realized that this assessment was correct. Therefore, just as we are enduring the greatest pressure in Iran's history, we must note that this is not merely economic pressure, but the continuation of an oppressive war."
He added: "We have not yet fully equipped all our equipment and facilities to confront this situation. This is a reality. When such pressure is exerted on a country, all responsible agencies must act in accordance with the existing conditions; but I do not see any sign of such a change in the performance of many of the country's administrative and executive sectors."
The economic analyst, recalling that the country's economic growth was positive in Tir (July) but might become negative again in Mordad and Shahrivar (August-September), added: "The pace of the decline in Iran's economic growth rate is slowing down, meaning that we are returning to the game in the industrial and agricultural sectors."
Referring to the Central Bank's performance in recent months, Laylaz responded: "The liquidity growth rate reached 0.3 percent in Shahrivar (September); we can continue this trend; so why haven't we continuously done so? This is exactly one of our demands. I believe that even a 0.01 percent reduction can be important in controlling liquidity growth. In my opinion, under normal conditions, a liquidity growth rate of around 2 percent could be appropriate; of course, economic conditions and inflation control requirements must also be considered."
He clarified: "We must be able to overcome the imbalance of banks. This requires a serious and revolutionary action, but no decisive event has occurred in this field so far. We can also reduce many imbalances in various sectors.”
He stated: "Now we can also move more rapidly toward reviving government revenues and return these revenues to the people in the form of subsidies. In this way, we can both improve the economic situation and help the country's political and social stability."
Leylaz said: "In the three months ending in Tir (July) this year, Iran's agricultural sector growth was about 6 percent. This growth has occurred after years of stagnation and, in my opinion, is a significant development. Evidence shows that the decline in production in the industrial sector is also being compensated, and activities are gradually returning to normal conditions. This trend is happening in a situation where all the consequences of past events have not yet been compensated."
The economic analyst, stating that we have compensated for a large part of the physical damages, continued: "Do you remember when I spoke about this in the early days of the war, how much I was criticized and some told me I was underestimating the damages? But now, except in the gas sector, where about 100 to 130 million cubic meters of its capacity was involved, and to some extent in the steel sector, which includes a limited part, as well as in the petrochemical industry, a large part of other damages has been reconstructed."

Residents evacuated from Russia-occupied city back in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:47:44 UTC
23:47:44 KST

Residents evacuated from Russia-occupied Oleshky arrive back in Ukraine amid temporary U.S.-brokered ceasefire
Residents who were evacuated from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky as part of a U.S.-brokered temporary ceasefire crossed into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday.
The civilians traveled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus, following a deal brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump.
Oleshky is a city in Ukraine's southeastern Kherson region occupied by Russia since the first days of the Ukraine-Russia war. It is one of the most dire humanitarian crises of the conflict.
The ceasefire began at 3 a.m. Tuesday and is expected to continue through Sunday evening.
The estimated 2,000 remaining residents of Oleshky were offered the choice of traveling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
Those who chose to return to Ukraine were taken to the Russian city of Anapa, then flown to Homel in Belarus, from where they proceeded back home.
Ukrainian authorities imposed restrictions on disclosing the number of evacuees or the border crossing location. The measures are to safeguard those who chose to remain in Oleshky as well as to protect future humanitarian missions, the organizers said.
Relatives waited on Saturday at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them. Volunteers from organizations including the Red Cross, Doctors Without Borders and the World Central Kitchen were also there.
Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father over 2½ years ago when she, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory while he stayed behind, was among those waiting.
"We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.
Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.
He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbors but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through.
"We realized that, well, there was no (other) way, and he walked us to the road and that was it — that was the last time" they saw him, Pavlyn said.
She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.
Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the U.S. first lady posted on social media Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
Apart from Melania Trump, Pope Leo XIV — the first American pontiff — also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
Fighting has continued elsewhere during the localized ceasefire.
A Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia's western Bryansk region, local Gov. Yegor Kovalchuk said Saturday. Another five people were wounded, he said.
Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region's capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Zelenskyy said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in the Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.
The attacks targeted combined heat and power plants in the Kyiv and Sumy regions, four electricity substations and a gas distribution facility in the Dnipro region and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv, he said, adding that repair crews were working to restore power.

China

Gold medalist Ryan Abiang (C) of the United States, silver medalist Eloan Hitz (L) of France and bronze medalist Fu Kaige of China pose for photos during the awarding ceremony of the men's freestyle competition at the Parkour World Cup Beijing 2026 at Shougang Park in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 31, 2026. (Xinhua/Ju Huanzong)
BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- American teenager Ryan Abiang lifted the men's freestyle trophy at the 2026 Parkour World Cup here on Saturday.
The overall Parkour World Cup champion is the athlete with the highest points total in the relevant ranking after all events in the series have been completed, with points calculated from an athlete's best two results.
The 18-year-old won bronze in Montpellier, France, in May, earning 35 world ranking points.
Abiang faced a strong challenge from 17-year-old Chinese rising star Fu Kaige, who was making his Parkour World Cup debut.
Fu topped qualification with 31.4 points after an impressive display of high-speed spinning skills, while Abiang was 1.4 points behind.
However, Fu struggled with the pressure in the final. Starting last, he competed in front of a packed and enthusiastic crowd after strong performances from Abiang and France's Eloan Hitz.
Despite attempting more difficult skills, Fu stumbled several times and was marked down on execution, taking bronze with 30.3 points on his World Cup debut.
Abiang claimed his first World Cup title with 31.0 points and added 50 points to his world ranking tally. Hitz earned his first World Cup silver medal with 30.5.
"The performance was pretty, pretty crazy at first. I was like actually really scared," said Abiang. "I feel really crazy about winning the season title. It was pretty unexpected. But future goals? I would say go undefeated from this."
World Games freestyle champion Noa Man claimed the women's speed title in the 2026 Parkour World Cup series after sweeping all three World Cup events this season.
Man became the first parkour athlete to win a gold medal in women's freestyle at the World Games in 2022, the first edition of the Games to feature the sport.
The 21-year-old Dutch athlete won both women's speed titles at the World Cups in Montpellier and Istanbul, securing top spot in the world rankings before completing her sweep with a third victory this year in 35.12 seconds.
Shougang Park, where a former steel mill and its blast furnaces were transformed into an urban venue that gained worldwide attention during the 2022 Winter Olympics, will host the final two year-end title deciders in women's freestyle and men's speed. ■

WOLFSBURG, Germany, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Representatives of the German automotive industry have given positive responses as delegates representing China's Hunan province introduced Hunan at an economic and trade collaboration meeting this weekend.
The Hunan-Germany economic and trade collaboration meeting took place here on Friday, coinciding with the Sino-German Automotive Congress which was attended by hundreds of delegates of the auto industries from the two countries.
On the sidelines of the meeting room, Gundula Henkel, a board member of the German-Chinese Association Saxony-Anhalt, leaned in with a candid smile, holding a notebook filled with scribbled notes.
As the presentations unfolded, Henkel found her view shifting fast and was deeply impressed by China's development momentum. People can see "how cleverly (China's) local strengths are paired with the right industries," she remarked. "It's a real eye-opener."
Liu Suyue, deputy director of the Hunan Provincial Department of Commerce, summarized the advantages of Hunan as a favorable destination for German investment as "5C": cost, consumer base, whole supply chain cluster, talent base of colleges and convenient environment.
"We are ready to work with you, and I believe our sincerity can bridge the distance from the Xiang River to the Rhine," Liu said.
Germany is currently home to quite a few well-known companies from Hunan province, including the Sany Group.
As a Chinese multinational heavy equipment manufacturing company, Sany Group in 2012 acquired Putzmeister, one of the world's leading construction equipment companies.
Michael Bose, chairman of the Board at automotive BerlinBrandenburg e.V. was present at the meeting with interest.
"I am pleased that we have the opportunity today to engage with Hunan-and specifically with its representatives, as well as potentially later with Sany Group-to discuss vehicles and automotive technologies," he said.
As the chairman of a German association representing companies from the special-purpose vehicle manufacturing sector, Bose is well aware that the German companies "currently have a very strong interest in, and are actively seeking contacts within, the electric vehicle industry, particularly regarding heavy trucks and heavy machinery in relation to China."
As a major manufacturing province in China, Hunan boasts a solid foundation in the automotive industry. These industrial capabilities not only provide enterprises with supporting supply chains and opportunities for market expansion, but also create ample room for China-Germany cooperation on new technologies and products, said Liu Minqiang, Director-General of the Investment Promotion Agency of the Ministry of Commerce, in a speech at the meeting.
"By aligning Hunan's promotion meeting with the Sino-German Automotive Congress today, our objective is to deepen the German community's understanding of Hunan," Liu Minqiang said.
Uwe Fritsch, member relations specialist of automotiveland.nrw, an automotive industry cluster in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia, also highlighted the importance of closer exchanges between China and Germany.

"This means not only closer economic collaboration between German and Chinese companies, but also, equally importantly in the current climate, greater mutual understanding and dialogue." ■

22:46:54 CST
23:46:54 KST

HANGZHOU, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Chinese tech giant Alibaba Group announced a partnership with Apple on Saturday to integrate its Qwen AI model into Apple Intelligence.
The Qwen-powered feature will be available for testing in the latest iOS developer beta starting Nov. 4 and roll out to Chinese users with the official iOS 27.3 release in December, according to Alibaba.
The partnership brings Qwen's AI capabilities to multiple use cases within Apple's operating system. Through Siri, Writing Tools, and Visual Intelligence, Chinese users will be able to tap Qwen's capabilities for text and image understanding and content generation.
Notably, users can choose whether to enable the Qwen integration and what information to share. Alibaba said it will not use user requests or generated responses for model training.
The feature will be available on iOS to users who purchase an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone in China, or whose device location and Apple Account country or region are both set to China.
Eddie Wu, CEO of Alibaba Group, said Qwen drawing on Alibaba's AI expertise will integrate into Apple's ecosystem and work with Apple to deliver new AI-powered service experiences to Chinese users.
Wang Xiaojie, an AI expert at Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, said this is the first time a top global consumer hardware maker has used a Chinese large model as the primary system-level AI backbone in the Chinese market, a significant step in the commercial application of domestic large models.
Apple Intelligence is the AI system Apple first unveiled at its Worldwide Developers Conference in 2024. In a key regulatory move, China's cyberspace authority completed the filing of seven on-device generative AI services for smartphones in July, including Apple Intelligence. ■

China Focus: A helping hand at hospital: China's burgeoning patient companion services
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
22:46:35 CST
23:46:35 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- For 95-year-old Gu Lanzhi in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, a swollen knee after a fall at home meant more than just a trip to the hospital. With her family unable to accompany her, navigating the process of seeking medical care could be a challenge.
Help came from a nearby community health station, where a nurse registered Gu, arranged examinations, handled payment and called a hospital shuttle. At the hospital, station staff stayed with her through each step.
Gu's experience points to a broader challenge facing China's healthcare system as the population ages and medical services become increasingly digital. In response, a range of patient companion services has emerged in recent years.
As these services expand in various forms, the need for clearer requirements and more consistent practices has come into focus. On Nov. 1, China's first national standard for patient companion services will take effect.
A GROWING NEED
By the end of 2025, China had 323.38 million people aged 60 and above, or 23 percent of the population, a figure projected to exceed 400 million by around 2035. Many will need someone at their side.
But the need extends well beyond older adults. People with limited mobility, those unfamiliar with digital devices, and patients seeking care far from home can also struggle with hospital visits without help.
Ever more specialized departments and ever larger hospitals leave many patients unsure where to register or how to move through a visit, ending up "lost in the hospital," said Song Yu, a researcher at the Institute of Sociology of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. Song said changing family structures and a fast-aging population have intensified the need.
The demand is evident in hospitals themselves. At Beijing Tongren Hospital's Yizhuang campus, 76-year-old volunteer Sun Ying has been helping patients in the ophthalmology department since early morning.
By 10:30 a.m., just two and a half hours into Sun's shift, the counter at her station showed she had assisted more than 100 patients. Her tasks range from helping patients check in to directing them to the right departments.
Many older patients cannot manage smartphones and other digital devices, while others struggle to get around or are unfamiliar with hospital procedures, Sun said. "For them, we serve as their eyes, ears and walking sticks."
A SECTOR TAKING SHAPE
Across China, patient companion services are delivered through a variety of channels. Hospital volunteers, community workers and nursing staff provide them, as do specialized agencies and individual service providers.
At Shanghai's Renji Hospital, 66-year-old Cao booked a patient companion service after experiencing frequent dizziness and headaches. Unwilling to disrupt his children's work, he booked through the hospital's WeChat account.
His companion, Wang Ping, helped him complete every step from registration and consultation to collecting medication. Cao finished the visit in less than half a day.
The public-interest program, launched with local civil affairs authorities in August 2025, has since expanded to all of Renji's campuses and provided nearly 4,000 free sessions.
On the commercial side, specialized agencies and individual providers have been joined by tech giants such as Alibaba, JD.com and Didi, which combine online booking with in-person accompaniment. Some providers also cater to international patients seeking medical care in China.
According to China-based consultancy Intelligence Research Group, patient companion services were used 7.41 million times in China in 2025, up 21.6 percent year on year. The market size reached 1.19 billion yuan (about 177 million U.S. dollars), up 18 percent.
A PUSH FOR STANDARDS
However, the sector's rapid growth has also exposed problems. Inconsistent pricing, unclear responsibilities, and inadequate privacy protection have raised concerns.
To address these problems, the national standard for commercial patient companion services was rolled out, scheduled to take effect on Nov. 1.
It lists 12 things companions can do and seven they cannot, such as giving medical advice or making treatment decisions for patients. It also requires organizations to verify companions' qualifications, train them and answer for their services.
Efforts are also underway to strengthen professional training and assessment. In Chengdu, specialized skills assessments have been introduced for patient companions. By June 2026, five assessment institutions had conducted 26 rounds of assessments, with about 1,100 people qualifying, a pass rate of around 64 percent.
Patient companionship is not an "errand business" but a new service that fills the "last mile" of medical care, said Wang Yue, a professor from Peking University's School of Health Humanities. At its core, Wang said, companions serve as "translators of information" and "emotional anchors" between doctors and patients. ■

Reconstruction of residential units damaged in war to be finished in 1 month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:45:15 UTC
23:45:15 KST

Reconstruction of residential units damaged in war to be finished in 1 month
TEHRAN- The head of the Islamic Revolution Housing Foundation, Manouchehr Khajeh Dalouei, said reconstruction of residential units damaged in the 12-day imposed war has been completed, while repairs and rebuilding of units damaged in the 40-day war have passed 92 percent physical progress and should finish within one month.
In the 12-day war, the foundation oversaw reconstruction of 3,300 residential units nationwide, completed in Azar (November) last year. For the 40-day war, more than 140,000 assessments were conducted across 407 cities and villages, with repair and reconstruction beginning immediately alongside the assessments.
A total of 101,000 residential and commercial units in cities under the foundation’s responsibility were damaged by enemy military aggression. Of these, 1,400 required complete rebuilding; the rest received Type 1, 2, or 3 repairs depending on the damage. As of this week, repairs on 93,000 of the 101,000 units have been completed, and the foundation hopes to finish all 40-day war repair and reconstruction work within the next month, with an exact timetable to be announced.
Of the 1,400 units needing full reconstruction, work is underway on 700, with applicants entering construction after receiving permits and debris removal carried out by the foundation. Some applicants previously had two-story homes and now seek permits for four-story buildings; others have requested relocation, though such cases are few. About 20 fully rebuilt units were handed over last week. The original target for completing the project was the end of 1406, but completion is expected earlier.
In Tehran, statistics show 3,500 buildings were damaged, though property use and value differ from other areas; Tehran Municipality is the responsible authority.

Tusk’s government says it is seeking to restore the rule of law following judicial changes introduced during eight years of PiS rule, which ended in 2023.

South Pars phase 11 development continues with drilling of 13th well on platform B
TEHRAN- The CEO of Petropars Group announced the continuation of drilling operations for the 13th well on Platform B of South Pars Phase 11 and stated: After the completion and commissioning of 12 wells at this location, drilling of the 13th well has also been placed on Petropars’ agenda beyond its contractual commitments, and it is currently at the stage of drilling the 16-inch hole.
According to an IRNA report from Petropars, Hamidreza Saghafi, referring to the continuation of development operations at Phase 11 of the South Pars shared field, said: Drilling of the 13th completion well on Platform B has begun with the aim of maintaining production and helping to compensate for the country’s gas shortage.
He added: Its first two holes, 32-inch and 24-inch, were drilled to depths of 186 and 933 meters, respectively, over 15 days. Currently, drilling of the 16-inch hole continues at a depth of 1,010 meters.
The CEO of Petropars Group, referring to the completion of operations for the 12th well on this platform, explained: This well was drilled to a depth of more than 4,400 meters and at an angle of 65 degrees, and its perforation operations in the reservoir layers K1, K2, K3, and K4 were carried out in two stages (TCP). Given the sensitivity of the operation, petrophysical data from neighboring wells were also used to increase accuracy in carrying out the perforation.
Saghafi continued: After perforation, more than 190,000 gallons of 32% hydrochloric acid (HCl), along with relevant additives, were injected into the well in 20 stages. This operation was carried out at the first suitable opportunity given the weather conditions, and to distribute the acid uniformly across the entire perforated interval, especially the terminal sections of the well, the use of an acid diverting agent (VDA) suited to the temperature and pressure conditions was designed.

The partnership brings Qwen's AI capabilities to multiple use cases within Apple's operating system. Through Siri, Writing Tools, and Visual Intelligence, Chinese users will be able to tap Qwen's capabilities for text and image understanding and content generation.
Notably, users can choose whether to enable the Qwen integration and what information to share. Alibaba said it will not use user requests or generated responses for model training.
The feature will be available on iOS to users who purchase an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone in China, or whose device location and Apple Account country or region are both set to China.
Eddie Wu, CEO of Alibaba Group, said Qwen drawing on Alibaba's AI expertise will integrate into Apple's ecosystem and work with Apple to deliver new AI-powered service experiences to Chinese users.
Wang Xiaojie, an AI expert at Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, said this is the first time a top global consumer hardware maker has used a Chinese large model as the primary system-level AI backbone in the Chinese market, a significant step in the commercial application of domestic large models.
Apple Intelligence is the AI system Apple first unveiled at its Worldwide Developers Conference in 2024. In a key regulatory move, China's cyberspace authority completed the filing of seven on-device generative AI services for smartphones in July, including Apple Intelligence. (Xinhua)

URDA, Spain – Residents and local officials gathered on Oct 31 in a Spanish village near the site of a high-speed train collision that killed at least 69 people for a memorial mass honouring the victims.
The pews inside the San Juan Bautista church in Urda, in the central province of Toledo, were packed, while dozens more people gathered outside to listen to the service. Some wiped away tears.
Investigators are looking into the cause of one of Europe’s deadliest rail disasters this century, which occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into a stationary train on Oct 28.
The Archbishop of Toledo, Francisco Cerro, told mourners that the days since the disaster had been like a “Good Friday for us all”, acknowledging that “there are no words that can offer comfort” to those who had lost loved ones.
“Dear families affected by the train accident, you are not alone. Society is with you, the best of society is with you,” he said, urging the public not to forget the tragedy and calling for such disasters never to happen again.
He also paid tribute to emergency workers and volunteers, thanking healthcare staff, firefighters, police and rescue teams for their efforts, and praising what he described as “a genuine wave of solidarity”.
The president of the Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano Garcia-Page, and Urda Mayor Manuel Galan were among the officials who attended the service.
Residents of Urda, which has a population of around 2,500, “are very badly affected, in great pain and with a great need for support”, Galan told Spanish public television ahead of the mass.
Relatives of the victims, who have been providing DNA samples to help identify the dead, face an agonising wait for news as rescue teams continue to sift through the wreckage and forensic experts work to identify the bodies.
The authorities overseeing the process have completed autopsies on all 69 people killed in the crash, with 36 identified so far. AFP

Haunted, but hardly explored: India's untapped ghost-tourism economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:36:47 UTC
23:36:47 KST

India’s haunted destinations offer an untapped tourism opportunity, with paranormal experiences yet to become a mainstream travel attraction. (AI-generated image)
India's ghosts have a customer service problem.There is almost an abundance of local places which have a reputation of being haunted in each and every state.There are ghost villages where nobody is quite sure why everyone left. Forts with stories of spirits walking through them at night. Abandoned cemeteries as old as the world wars, forgotten ‘havelis’ and stretches of forest that have acquired a mythology of their own.Out of all these only a few have become tourist attractions; others survive largely through word of mouth, local lore and the occasional paranormal investigation.India's haunted places do have an audience but it somehow lacks a concrete machinery that could make ‘dark’ tourism and ‘spectral’ cities central factions of an ever growing tourist economy.
The business of the macabre
The tourism industry has a name for this particular appetite for the unsettling: dark tourism. The term broadly describes travel to places associated with death, tragedy, violence and suffering.Ghost tours, haunted heritage walks and visits to places associated with paranormal folklore occupy a more specialised corner of this spectrum, where history, local legend and the promise of an eerie experience often intersect.
It is an appetite that the tourism industry has increasingly tried to package. Turning a city's darker history into something you can book online. And its most ideal form, the ticket buys you a completely immersive tour full of storytelling with a slight hope of encountering your first paranormal spirit.
The commercial potential of dark tourism is reflected in the market estimates. Grand View Research valued the global dark tourism market at $31.8 billion in 2023 and projects it to reach $34.2 billion in 2026 and $38.6 billion by 2030, growing at a compound annual growth rate of 2.9%. MR puts the market at $32 billion in 2025, forecasting it to reach $46.8 billion by 2036.The market for ghost tourism as a separate entity is estimated to be worth $2.9 billion in 2025 and projects it to grow to $5.7 billion by 2034, at a CAGR of 7.8%, by Dataintelo. Its estimate includes guided ghost walks, cemetery and underground tours, paranormal investigations, haunted stays and virtual experiences.For India, the more immediate question may be less about capturing a share of a global market and more about whether these scattered attractions can be turned into viable profitable local experiences. With a history as rich as ours, the ghosts are not in short supply. The challenge is to turn them into profitable experiences that people can discover, book and pay for, while ensuring that the tragedy is respected and the communities living alongside these places have a stake in the business.
From a haunted reputation to a tourism product
Kuldhara, a site that Rajasthan Tourism itself promotes as a “ghost village shrouded in mystery”, is a good starting point. The official government site describes its history as a prosperous settlement abandoned in the early 19th century. The account recounts the popular legend involving the village headman's daughter and the powerful minister Salim Singh, while also identifying the ruins as a protected monument under the state archaeology department.The village, around 17km from Jaisalmer, already has the ingredients of a tourism attraction, but having a story and having a well-managed visitor experience are two different things.There are multiple accounts of litter around the site, including discarded plastic and food packaging. How can an atmosphere feel haunted when the landscape is strewn with chips and tobacco packets?And cleanliness isn’t the only issue. Talking to two people who visited the site, the common experience has been mismanaged and under researched tour which leaves most customers underwhelmed at the end of the day.
Bhangarh, in Alwar district, is often described as one of India's most haunted places. Rajasthan Tourism itself recounts the two popular legends attached to the site: one involving the ascetic Baba Balu Nath, whose warning about the shadow of the fort was allegedly ignored, and another about a sorcerer whose failed attempt to enchant Princess Ratnavati supposedly led him to curse the town.The legends have become part of the destination's appeal, drawing visitors to its ruined temples, palaces and deserted marketplace. The restriction on entry before sunrise and after sunset, imposed at the site, has only added to its mystique. But tourists who visit the site have also called it unorganised, speaking to TOI they noted that the guide also was not entirely accurate about the historical aspects of the site and the site itself needed to have better management.
The business of making a place come alive
There are already attempts to package India's haunted heritage into guided experiences. Delhi Tourism lists Haunted Heritage Walks at Malcha Mahal and Feroz Shah Kotla Monument, each lasting around 90 minutes and available on weekends on group demand. The official booking page lists a minimum group size of six and a tariff of Rs 800 plus GST per person.The Ministry of Tourism's Utsav portal has also listed a Haunted Walk at Bhuli Bhatiyari, organised by Delhi-based Enroute Indian History. The listing describes a guided heritage walk through the old hunting lodge, combining its history with the legends associated with the site.Enroute Indian History, which has been conducting the experience for around two to three years, says the walks attract a good number of bookings and are designed for adventure seekers as much as for history enthusiasts. The operator says it takes care to keep the historical information accurate, while folklore and supernatural accounts are presented as stories rather than fact-checked historical claims. This distinction is central to the format: visitors are offered a combination of documented history, local legends and the possibility of an unsettling experience.These initiatives complicate the idea that haunted tourism in India is entirely informal or absent. There are government-backed products and private operators working in the space. The question is whether they have developed the consistency, visibility and scale needed to make haunted experiences a dependable part of a destination's tourism economy.
Ghost is only part of the experience
Detailing her experience to TOI, Kriti notes that she remembers the underground setting of the haunted heritage walk she took in Edinburgh as much as the stories themselves. The interactive displays and historical details provided by the guide gave the experience a sense of depth that a conventional ghost walk might not have offered.A ghost tour can take several forms, the attraction lies as much in how visitors encounter the story as in the story itself.A 2020 study published in Cornell Hospitality Quarterly, titled Paranormal Tourism: Market Study of a Novel and Interactive Approach to Space Activation and Monetization, makes this case through examples from the United States and elsewhere. It describes how destinations such as New Orleans combine ghost stories with local histories and cultural associations, while Salem packages its reputation around witches and ghosts. These places do not necessarily sell a standalone encounter with the paranormal; they draw on identities and histories that visitors may already associate with them.The study talks in detail about Eastern State Penitentiary in Philadelphia, a former prison that closed in 1971 and subsequently fell into disuse. Limited group tours began in 1988 as part of efforts to preserve the site. A Halloween fundraiser followed in 1991, eventually developing into the annual attraction Terror Behind the Walls. By 1994, the former prison was also offering daily historical tours to generate income for preservation, followed by museum exhibits and a broader marketing campaign.The study also points to the role of participation in making these experiences engaging. The experience can continue beyond the visit itself, with reviews, photographs and word of mouth helping to draw in new audiences.
Research into British ghost walks suggests that the appeal is not necessarily dependent on visitors believing in ghosts. An ethnographic study of 14 tours across Edinburgh, York, London and Brighton found that guides use a combination of storytelling, performance and the physical environment to make history tangible.For India, that distinction could be important. A haunted experience need not rely on sensational claims. It can be built around the history of a place, the folklore that has accumulated around it and the atmosphere of encountering that story on location.
Local community cannot remain part of the backdrop
The opportunity, however, is not simply to make India's haunted sites more theatrical or commercially attractive. It is also to ensure that the people and places behind the stories are not left out of the value chain.A 2023 qualitative study of local perceptions in Kuldhara, based on 25 interviews with residents and people working in the area, found that respondents saw several economic opportunities in developing mystery and paranormal tourism. Some respondents also pointed to existing livelihood opportunities linked to visitors, including guiding, transport and the sale of local crafts.The study also recorded expectations around the restoration and preservation of the village, alongside concerns about the role of government and private bodies in developing the destination. While it offers a glimpse of how residents view the possibilities of mystery tourism, it does not quantify how much income currently reaches the community or how widely those benefits are distributed.The concerns are not unique to haunted destinations. A 2026 study of tourism in Uttarakhand, while not focused specifically on ghost tourism, raises wider questions about the state's tourism economy. It argues for stronger community participation, local supply chains, training and livelihood diversification.These concerns are relevant when considering how niche tourism experiences might develop in the hills. A haunted walk could create work for local storytellers, drivers, homestays, food vendors and artisans. But those benefits are not automatic. If an outside operator controls the bookings, supplies the guides and takes most of the revenue, the local community may remain little more than a feature of the landscape.The challenge is to move beyond treating local legends as raw material that can be packaged elsewhere. Residents may be the custodians of oral histories, but they should also have a stake in how those histories are interpreted and monetised.
India does not need to manufacture a haunted history. What it needs is a way to bring those stories to visitors without reducing them to cheap thrills or leaving the people who have preserved them out of the business.The real test of India's haunted tourism economy will not be how many people it can convince that a place is haunted, but how many people it can persuade to stay, listen, and explore.The ghosts, after all, have been doing their bit for the tourism industry for years. It is time someone took care of the guests.

‘Opportunities for agricultural cooperation with Africa available’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:35:47 UTC
23:35:47 KST

‘Opportunities for agricultural cooperation with Africa available’
TEHRAN- Iran’s Minister of Agriculture, Gholamreza Nouri Ghezeljeh, addressed the First National Meeting on Iran-Africa Agricultural Cooperation, stressing that opportunities for joint agricultural cooperation with Africa are available and must be converted into concrete, operational, and lasting economic ties.
The meeting was attended by ambassadors, economic counselors, honorary consuls, officials from executive bodies, economic associations, entrepreneurs, investors, and more than 200 economic actors. The minister said this broad participation provided a valuable opportunity to translate the political will for expanding Iran-Africa relations into specific projects and durable economic partnerships.
Nouri Ghezeljeh thanked the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Permanent Secretariat of the Iran-Africa Cooperation Summit, and the Ministry of Agriculture for organizing the event. He said Iran’s approach to international cooperation is based on mutual respect, avoidance of unilateralism, opposition to aggression and political pressure, and recognition of the right of all nations to peace, development, and sustainable access to food. He stressed that food and people’s livelihoods must not become tools of political pressure, and that achieving food security requires cooperation, trust, and constructive interaction among countries. This, he said, should be a foundational principle for developing agricultural relations between Iran and African countries.
The minister outlined a clear message: Iran-Africa agricultural cooperation must move from introducing capacities to defining projects; from memoranda of understanding to executive contracts; and from sporadic exchanges to sustainable partnerships in production, technology, and trade. He emphasized that Iran does not view Africa merely as a market for selling goods or as a source for supplying needed products. Rather, Iran regards African countries as important partners for investment, joint production, and creating mutual economic benefits.
Nouri Ghezeljeh linked agriculture to food security, knowledge, and economic development. He argued that food security is not simply about increasing production, but about ensuring people’s sustainable access to sufficient, healthy, high-quality, and reasonably priced food. He described water and soil, seeds and inputs, production knowledge and technology, storage, transportation, and trade as interconnected links in a single chain. Weakening any link, he warned, can undermine efforts to increase production. He also pointed to complementary capacities between Iran and African countries. Iran has strengths in irrigation and water and soil management, greenhouse production, agricultural machinery, seeds, livestock and poultry breeding, vaccines and veterinary products, fisheries, processing industries, and specialized training. African countries, according to their climatic and economic conditions, have considerable capacities in crop production, tropical products, animal husbandry, fisheries, and expanding markets. Linking these capabilities can increase productivity, create jobs, and raise value added on both sides.
The minister further identified removing executive obstacles and strengthening communication among responsible institutions as a fourth priority. He said economic actors need clear procedures, reliable transportation, practical payment mechanisms, insurance and investment coverage, and predictable regulations to enter sustainable cooperation. On tariffs and trade facilitation, he called for examining the capacity of bilateral agreements and regional mechanisms with the participation of relevant bodies. He also stressed continuous follow-up: the problems of each project must be clearly identified and recorded, a responsible body must be designated, and progress must be assessed within clear time frames.
Nouri Ghezeljeh emphasized that the government should act as a facilitator while the private sector should be the driver of economic cooperation. Embassies and economic counselors, he said, can play an effective role in identifying credible opportunities, introducing reliable partners, explaining market regulations, facilitating communication among enterprises, and following up on executive obstacles. In contrast, the private sector must play a central role in defining projects and assessing them commercially and operationally. Within the Ministry of Agriculture, the Office of International Affairs, together with specialized organizations, deputies, and private-sector associations, is responsible for the secretariat of six joint Iran-Africa cooperation commissions and more than 10 joint agricultural committees with African countries. He said the goal is not to create new and numerous mechanisms, but to use existing capacities effectively, clarify responsibilities, and prevent negotiations from stalling at the stage of administrative correspondence.
The minister asked economic actors to present proposals in the form of specific and executive plans. Each plan, he said, should clearly determine the subject of cooperation, the proposed partner, the target market, required capital, legal requirements, timetable, and evaluation indicators. He urged avoiding scattered programs and suggested starting with a few limited, well-considered, and implementable projects rather than a long list of aspirations. For each project, a clear contact point on both sides, a time schedule, and a follow-up mechanism should be designated so that successful cooperation can be expanded after initial results are evaluated.
Nouri Ghezeljeh announced that the Fourth Iran-Africa Cooperation Summit will be held next month, and that the FIDC event will take place in Senegal. He expressed hope that Iran’s private sector and agricultural economic actors will participate effectively in these programs. He said the Islamic Republic of Iran seeks cooperation based on trust, respect, and mutual interests. In agriculture, these principles should lead to more sustainable production, more balanced trade, more job opportunities, knowledge transfer, and more reliable access by people to healthy and sufficient food. He stressed that success should not be measured by the number of meetings or documents signed, but by implemented contracts, projects that produce results, value added created, and benefits that ultimately reach producers and the people. The meeting, he said, should be the starting point for practical cooperation—a stage in which knowledge becomes production, production reaches markets, and friendly relations become lasting economic ties.
On political and security developments, the minister said that when Iran was attacked by Israel and the United States, some abroad welcomed it and others expected further developments. What occurred instead, he said, was Iran’s resistance, the country’s steadfastness, the people’s courage, and the continuation of government services. Addressing ambassadors, he said that despite wartime conditions, government services in various areas, including food security and the supply of public necessities, continued, and needed goods were supplied abundantly, so that wartime conditions were not felt in meeting basic needs. He criticized US actions internationally, saying the world is heavily affected by US warmongering and that the energy and food sectors face major challenges and crises. According to official statistics in some countries, food prices have risen by up to 23 percent, and poor and vulnerable groups suffer most. He said Iran and other countries have been affected by these consequences and expressed hope that the United States would take a rational path and return to the Islamabad Memorandum to pave the way for ending the war as quickly as possible, given its pressure on economies, nutrition, and global food security, especially in poor countries.
Finally, Nouri Ghezeljeh urged participants to engage actively in the specialized panels on the sidelines of the meeting, saying these panels can move cooperation from speeches and negotiations to the operational stage. He expressed hope that, with the companionship of ambassadors, the efforts of economic actors, the support of responsible institutions, and equal participation of African countries, the ground would be prepared for sustainable agricultural cooperation. He said the hoped-for results include increased food security, economic prosperity, development of shared opportunities, and stronger lasting friendship between the Iranian nation and African countries.
