Single dose of psychedelic nasal spray reduced treatment-resistant depression symptoms for eight weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:00:43 UTC
22:00:43 KST

A single dose of a fast-acting psychedelic nasal spray appears to ease symptoms of hard-to-treat depression within a day, with benefits lasting up to eight weeks, according to a clinical trial published in JAMA. The medication, a synthetic formulation of the psychedelic compound mebufotenin, produced a brief psychoactive experience that allowed most patients to be assessed as ready to leave the clinic within two hours. These findings suggest that short-acting psychedelics may offer a practical way to deliver rapid antidepressant relief without the four- to twelve-hour clinic stays required for compounds like psilocybin.
Major depressive disorder is a mood condition marked by persistent sadness, loss of interest in daily activities, and trouble sleeping or concentrating, affecting about 290 million people worldwide. Roughly one-third of patients have treatment-resistant depression, meaning their symptoms do not adequately respond to at least two antidepressant trials. People with treatment-resistant depression tend to experience greater emotional distress, a lower quality of life, and a higher risk of suicide than those who respond to standard medications.
Existing options for treatment-resistant depression, such as esketamine nasal spray or magnetic brain stimulation, require frequent clinic visits. Psychedelic drugs, which alter perception and mood by activating docking sites for the chemical messenger serotonin in the brain, offer a potential alternative because a single dose can produce lasting relief. For instance, a clinical trial of patients with treatment-resistant depression found that one 25-milligram dose of psilocybin with psychological support reduced depression scores at three weeks compared to a 1-milligram control dose, though it carried side effects including suicidal thoughts.
Because classic psychedelics like psilocybin and LSD require four to twelve hours of in-clinic supervision, scientists have turned to mebufotenin, a psychedelic compound chemically known as 5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine that is naturally found in toad venom and certain plants. Mebufotenin activates both serotonin 1A and 2A receptors in the brain and is rapidly absorbed and eliminated by the body, producing a brief psychedelic experience.
Earlier clinical trials tested mebufotenin by inhalation. In a 2026 randomized controlled trial of 81 patients with treatment-resistant depression, an inhaled formulation of mebufotenin produced a 58 percent remission rate at day 8 compared to 0 percent for placebo, and in an open-label follow-up phase allowing up to four retreatments, 87 percent of those who reached remission were still in remission at six months. Researchers have also developed a dry-powder nasal spray for intranasal absorption, and an earlier study of psychedelic-naive healthy adults showed that intranasal mebufotenin elicited emotional, bodily, and cognitive effects peaking within 8 to 15 minutes and resolving within 45 to 60 minutes.
Joint first authors David Feifel of the Kadima Neuropsychiatry Institute in La Jolla, California, and Mathieu Seynaeve of King’s College London, along with their colleagues, tested the nasal spray in patients with treatment-resistant depression.
The researchers conducted a Phase 2b, double-blind, randomized clinical trial, a mid-stage study designed to test doses and gauge effectiveness, between September 2023 and April 2025 at 38 sites in Australia, Germany, Poland, Spain, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Of 443 adults screened, 193 received treatment. Between 5 and 14 percent of each group did not complete the eight-week core study, with the highest rate in the control group and no withdrawals due to side effects. Participants were aged 18 to 75 (average age 41 years, 59.1 percent female) with moderate to severe major depressive disorder that had not responded to two to five antidepressant trials in their current episode, which had lasted an average of 2.6 years.
To test the spray as a standalone therapy, the two-thirds of participants taking antidepressants at screening tapered off their medications at least two weeks before dosing. Participants were randomly assigned to receive a single spray into one nostril of 8 milligrams of mebufotenin benzoate (46 participants), 12 milligrams (73 participants), or a 0.3-milligram comparator dose low enough that most participants would not feel its effects (74 participants), alongside structured psychological support before, during, and after dosing. Midway through recruitment, the randomization ratio was adjusted from an equal split to prioritize the 12-milligram and 0.3-milligram groups for the primary analysis.
The primary outcome was the change in depression severity from baseline to day 29 between the 12-milligram and 0.3-milligram groups on the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale, which scores symptoms from 0 to 60, with higher scores indicating worse depression. Independent, blinded raters conducted these interviews by video call at baseline and every two weeks after dosing, including days 2, 8, 29, and 57. Staff assessed discharge readiness every 30 minutes starting 90 minutes after dosing, though participants had to stay at least four hours. Statistical models controlled for baseline depression scores, geographic region, and randomization schedule.
Baseline depression scores averaged about 32 across the three groups. The trial was designed with enough participants to detect a 6-point difference; the primary comparison at day 29 found an adjusted mean difference of 5.3 points (confidence interval 1.8 to 8.9), as scores dropped by 11.1 points in the 12-milligram group versus 5.5 points in the control group. The 8-milligram group improved by 12.5 points, an adjusted difference of 6.2 points (confidence interval 2.1 to 10.2). Whether a participant had tapered off antidepressants before the trial was not associated with the primary outcome.
Improvements appeared by day 2, when both active groups had dropped about 9 points versus 3.8 in the control group, and persisted to day 57, where active-group reductions averaged about 11 points versus 5.2. At day 29, response rates (at least a 50 percent score reduction) were about one-third in both active groups versus 12 percent in the control group; remission rates (a score of 10 or less) were 26 and 18 percent for the 8-milligram and 12-milligram groups versus 8 percent for the control group. Response and remission rates were reported descriptively, without confidence intervals or statistical tests.
Both active doses outperformed the control dose across all time points on clinician-rated illness severity and self-reported quality of life. On a self-reported depression scale, the 12-milligram group improved more than the control group at all visits, while the 8-milligram group improved more at days 2 and 8, though differences at days 29 and 57 were not statistically significant.
On day 1, the 8-milligram and 12-milligram doses produced higher scores on a 0-to-5 questionnaire measuring mystical-type experiences such as a sense of unity, transcendence of time and space, and ineffability (averaging 2.4 and 2.6, versus 0.4 in the control group). Those scores did not correlate with day 29 symptom reductions, a finding that runs against evidence from other psychedelics, which the authors note has suggested that the intensity of the subjective experience predicts therapeutic outcomes.
Most participants in the active groups (85 percent for 8 milligrams and 78 percent for 12 milligrams) met discharge readiness criteria within two hours of dosing, with two-thirds ready at 90 minutes. Those criteria required that the acute psychedelic effects had fully subsided and that vital signs, orientation, and coordination had returned to normal. This rapid turnaround is the feature the researchers argue sets the spray apart from psilocybin and LSD.
Side effects were common in all three groups, reported by roughly 73 to 85 percent of participants, and 99.7 percent of events were mild or moderate. The most frequent were headache, nausea, and pain at the spray site. Headache was about as common in the control group as in the active groups (29.5 percent overall), while nausea was far more common with the active doses (33 and 40 percent) than with the control dose (3 percent). Because the 8-milligram dose had comparable efficacy to the 12-milligram dose with fewer side effects like nausea and anxiety, the researchers selected the 8-milligram dose for Phase 3 trials, which will follow patients for longer to test how long the benefits last.
Most side effects in the active groups appeared on the day of dosing and resolved within 24 hours, though one participant in the 12-milligram group had two severe panic attacks related to the drug. Temporary increases in heart rate and blood pressure resolved within an hour. No suicidal behavior occurred during the trial. Eight drug-related reports of suicidal thoughts without intent were recorded: one in the 8-milligram group, four in the 12-milligram group, and three in the control group, all mild or moderate, and those in the active groups all occurred in participants with a history of such thoughts.
These results align with an uncontrolled, open-label study of 10 women with postpartum depression, which tested an inhaled formulation rather than a nasal spray in a different patient group, and similarly found rapid relief of depressive symptoms. The findings also parallel a 2019 observational study in which 42 people who inhaled vapor from dried toad secretion containing mebufotenin reported reduced depression and anxiety four weeks later, though that study had no control group and relied on self-reported symptoms.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The trial was funded by Beckley Psytech, an AtaiBeckley company that is developing the nasal spray, and several authors are company employees or hold stock or patents related to the compound. Employees of the sponsor were involved in the trial’s design, data analysis, and the decision to publish.
Statistical adjustments for multiple comparisons were applied to the primary outcome and three key secondary outcomes; the remaining comparisons were not adjusted. The smaller size of the 8-milligram group after the randomization change may also have limited statistical power to detect differences on the self-reported depression scale at later visits.
Difficulty maintaining blinding is a recognized problem across psychedelic trials, and the authors cite it as an inherent limitation, noting that most participants and on-site clinicians guessed their treatment assignment. Blinding was better preserved among the centralized remote raters who scored the primary measure; that measure is scored through an interview in which participants describe their own symptoms. Pre-treatment expectations did not correlate with day 29 outcomes, though those expectations were measured before the first preparation visit, prior to dosing and to any knowledge of group assignment; post-dose expectancy was not measured.
In addition, the two-hour discharge figure describes an assessment rather than an actual discharge. No one was discharged at two hours because the protocol required a minimum four-hour stay. Average times to readiness were just under two hours in the active groups, with the longest cases running past four.
In an editorial published alongside the trial in JAMA, Chittaranjan Andrade of the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences in Bangalore, India, called two findings striking: that a single dose given on its own kept depression scores roughly a third lower for eight weeks, and that most patients were ready to leave within two hours rather than the four to twelve hours that psilocybin and LSD require.
At the same time, Andrade noted that the average patient improved only about 30 percent, and that the response and remission rates fall below those typically seen with ketamine and electroconvulsive therapy. In his reading, either the 8- to 12-milligram dose or the single-dose approach is insufficient, and he suggests testing higher or escalating doses, or a course of treatments as is standard with ketamine and electroconvulsive therapy.
Both the study authors and Andrade note that the trial population may underrepresent more severely treatment-resistant patients. Participants had failed a median of two antidepressants, which Andrade describes as not markedly refractory depression. The protocol also excluded people with PTSD, bipolar or psychotic disorders, any personality disorder, a first-degree family history of schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, suicidal ideation with intent in the prior year, or prior nonresponse to ketamine or electroconvulsive therapy. Because active suicidal intent was an exclusion, Andrade notes that the trial could not examine whether the drug reduces suicidal thinking, as ketamine and electroconvulsive therapy have been shown to do.
Other constraints affect how the findings might translate to clinical care. Participants had to discontinue antidepressants so the spray could be tested on its own, which the authors note can cause withdrawal symptoms or a return of depression and may not reflect how the drug would be used in practice. Andrade adds that the trial offers no guidance on when or how patients would transition to a conventional antidepressant afterward. In addition, the study did not evaluate how much the structured psychological support contributed to the improvements, and the trial population lacked racial and ethnic diversity, as nearly 90 percent of participants were white.
Andrade argues that psychedelic research points toward a broader rethinking of how depression is treated, not just treatment-resistant depression. He questions whether it is justifiable to put patients in severe distress through antidepressants that take four to eight weeks to work when faster-acting options exist, and notes that current Canadian guidelines do not list ketamine and esketamine as third-line treatments for depression, naming them only as second-line add-ons for difficult-to-treat depression.
He also raises a point about access: in low- and middle-income countries, where newly approved psychedelics are likely to be unavailable or unaffordable, generic ketamine can be given orally at negligible cost, though he notes the evidence base for that approach needs strengthening. Andrade has published several studies on oral ketamine and cites his own work in making this argument.
He adds that psychedelics have not yet been approved by regulators and will need to be evaluated for long-term safety, including the risk of hallucinogen persisting perception disorder, a condition in which visual disturbances continue after the drug has worn off. He also calls for more detail on what the mebufotenin experience is actually like, including difficult experiences, whether patients found it unpleasant or frightening, and whether they would undergo it again.
The study, “Single Intranasal Administration of the Psychedelic Mebufotenin for Treatment-Resistant Depression: A Randomized Clinical Trial,” was authored by David Feifel, Mathieu Seynaeve, Wiesław Jerzy Cubała, Fiona Dunbar, Gerhard Gründer, Rosa María Dueñas Herrero, Chandni Hindocha, Paul Liknaitzky, Sean M. McGuigan, Sejal Mehta, Mimi Pierce, Dimitris Repantis, Claire Roberts, Frank Wiegand, and Robert Conley.
The accompanying editorial, “Treatment Approach to Major Depressive Disorder: It’s Time for a Paradigm Shift,” was authored by Chittaranjan Andrade.

Unmanned Systems Forces could account for 40% of all Russian troops neutralized in October – Colonel Veres
Colonel Kyrylo Veres, commander of the K-2 Brigade, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
"The USF as a branch of the military will probably account for 40% of all enemy personnel neutralized this month [October 2026]. Forty percent is a compelling argument. The most compelling one," Veres said.
He also highlighted the role played in developing the Unmanned Systems Forces by the appointment of Robert Brovdi as their commander in June 2025 and their integration with the Drone Line project.
"After the Drone Line was integrated with the USF and the new USF commander took office, we started achieving huge results. Unit commanders were given the opportunity to purchase whatever they wanted, manage their own budgets, and were simply told: do your job as well as you can. They simply stopped interfering with us and gave us the freedom to do things the way we saw fit," Veres said.
Asked about the latest changes along the line of contact, he highlighted Operation Vivaldi.
"As far as the 3rd Army Corps is concerned, there is Operation Vivaldi, and everyone can see its results. Our brigade also played a significant role in it. Of course, we cannot compare ourselves with the infantry, which did all the work – we did not take part in assault operations. But when it comes to destroying enemy personnel, our contribution to the unmanned component was very significant," the colonel said.
Veres also commented on the record losses suffered by Russian forces, which amounted to 46,230 personnel in September.
"They are sending in more troops, and more are dying. The more they advance, the more they die. And the sooner the critical moment will come when they start thinking about their losses. Sooner or later, it will come – whether at 100,000 killed, 200,000 or 46,000 – but it will come all the same," he said.
At the same time, Veres added: "If they send in even more troops, we will kill them in much greater numbers – in direct proportion. And I am confident that we are capable of not losing a single piece of territory in our area of responsibility."
As Ukrinform reported, Russian forces lost 46,230 personnel in September, the highest monthly figure in 2026. Compared with January, their losses increased by 14,520, or 45.8%.

‘Every case has a story’: Delhi HC judge on why judges are ‘great authors’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:57:49 UTC
21:57:49 KST

NEW DELHI: Delhi high court judge Justice Anish Dayal described judges as “great authors” and courtrooms as a “remarkable theatre”, drawing parallels between the judicial process and storytelling.“Judges are great authors. In our case files, we have real stories, real characters, plots, sometimes real, sometimes fictitious. We have problems and, in our judgments, we have resolutions,” PTI quoted Justice Dayal as saying. He made the remarks during his keynote address at the 11th edition of the Himalayan Echoes Festival in Nainital on Friday.“The classic core of a good story is character, problem, and resolution. So, we do it every day, 60-100 cases a day. I guess I am qualified to be here in the literary festival,” he added.Reflecting on his three worlds — the courtroom, literature and the mountains — Justice Dayal said each offered distinct lessons, governed respectively by “rules”, “imagination” and the “uncluttered” force of nature.
He noted that nearly 80% of court cases involved ordinary people, whose stories were often hidden behind the “antiseptic language” of case files.
“Every single day we read real stories,” he said, highlighting the emotional toll of handling criminal cases and reading accounts of victims' experiences.Justice Dayal described a judge's role as applying “cold, objective reasoning and fairness” while navigating allegations, facts and the law.He also shared amusing examples of mistranslations in court documents. The Hindi expression “mooh boli behan” was once rendered as “mouth spoken sister”, while “somersault” became “the salt that you have in the summer”. Another document used the term “clientess”.“We deal with language in all its corrupted forms and archaic forms also,” he remarked, inviting writers to explore court files for their linguistic curiosities.
Karan Manral is a journalist at the Times of India. He covers politics, social issues, and international affairs, exploring stories that affect people’s everyday lives. He also writes explainers to make these stories easier for readers to follow.

Feature: From hardship to mentorship, Kenya rugby veteran inspires next generation at Dakar 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
20:56:24 CST
21:56:24 KST

by sportswriters Wang Qi and You Huiyuan
DAKAR, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- As a teenager, Sheila Chajira could hardly have imagined that a small break in her routine would set her on a new path.
Now a two-time Olympian and veteran of Kenya's women's rugby team, Chajira remains committed to sport's transformative power, embracing a new mission at Africa's first-ever Olympic event.
"I am not just the Sheila that I know: I am a better Sheila," she said of being named an Athlete Role Model for the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games (YOG).
"It's a path of helping athletes stay on the right path and attain their goals through your example and mentorship."
Orphaned at the age of nine, Chajira and her sisters moved between makeshift homes, often finding themselves back in the slums. Through it all, sport provided an anchor.
"I played football. I ran. Sports kept me going," she said. "It was just uphill. But sports took over."
In high school, Chajira never skipped her mandatory morning run before evening football training. "A friend used to tell me, 'You have a body that can play rugby. You can see what happens.' I was hesitant at first," she said.
One morning, however, she was running late. "That day I was free, I decided to go and see what rugby was all about. Since then, I never went back to football."
Rugby offered a culture that "streamlined" her life. "Coming from the slums in Kenya, you see people get married early, get pregnant, or do drugs," Chajira said. "The moment I joined rugby, I wasn't able to focus on those things. I looked forward to getting out of this place for training."
The sport taught her respect, teamwork and self-reliance while opening doors to new opportunities and connections.
Turning professional after high school seemed a natural next step, even as rugby was still in its infancy locally and making a full-time living from it remained, as Chajira put it, "a maybe thing" for women.
"We used to have two or three tournaments a year," Chajira recalled. At times, the team could not afford to travel, and matches were missed.
Her turning point came at the 2016 Rio Olympics, where rugby sevens made its Games debut and Kenya became the first African women's side to compete. "I had no idea what to expect," Chajira said, recalling a mix of excitement and uncertainty.
Drawn into a tough Pool B, the Kenyans battled through the group stage but scored just 17 points, while a dominant New Zealand topped the group with 109. Even after a 24-0 defeat to Japan, Kenya refused to fold, closing its campaign with a landmark 22-10 win over Colombia.
Although an 11th-place finish was modest on paper, the experience of "playing against the world's best of the best" filled Chajira with immense pride and showed how far the team had come.
During the group stage, Chajira found herself on the same pitch as New Zealand star Portia Woodman, an idol she had long admired.
"She gave us some advice and told us that even they didn't start up there. It was slow for them. Because they trained consistently, they were able to perform the way they did," she said.
The Rio Olympics fueled her confidence in what the Kenyan team could achieve. "If we get more support or better facilities, we can be at the top of the world," she believed.
"We knew the intensity, the consistency, and what we needed to compete at a higher level. To the younger girls, we were able to tell them how incredible it is to play in the Olympics."
Driven by greater ambition, a clearer vision and a transformed mindset, the Kenya Lionesses stepped onto the Tokyo stage, with Chajira wearing the captain's armband. Pandemic disruptions fractured their training schedule, but they climbed one place to a historic 10th-place finish.
For Chajira, being an Olympian is every athlete's dream, regardless of age. "I'm able to get opportunities that I've never expected, to get the drive of being that athlete who's able to train and play among the world's best."
Maintaining peak physical condition in a demanding, high-impact sport has been a relentless challenge.
"When you get injured and get out of this rugby space, it's always hard," she admitted. "I always tell myself: 'It is not going to happen forever; It is a phase.' Hold on to it, learn from the experience, and definitely it will end. Here I am."
Since Tokyo, the road has been marked by near-misses. A 24-7 loss to China in the Paris 2024 Olympic repechage final dashed Kenya's hopes of making a third consecutive Olympic appearance, while a 22-0 defeat to South Africa at the 2025 Africa Women's Sevens in Nairobi marked the team's fourth runner-up finish since winning the title in 2018.
Nevertheless, rugby continues to expand its footprint in Kenya. The national team secured a place on the new HSBC SVNS 2 circuit in February, with Nairobi hosting the inaugural leg. At club level, Mwamba RFC Women claimed a historic fifth consecutive Kenya Cup title in May, beating Kenya Harlequin 30-20.
"We're able to play friendlies, compete in more tournaments, and play a home game, like the HSBC SVNS 2," she noted. "We couldn't have said that rugby was a career; then we were just doing it for fun or just getting out of a dark space. But right now, it's something I'm happy to say that rugby pays."
As the game expanded, so did Chajira's influence.
Off the field, she embraced motherhood, earned her World Rugby strength and conditioning credential, mentored young talent in slum academies and took charge as head coach of the Kenya Harlequin women's side.
"There are some girls from Kibera who I coached nine years ago. They play for the senior teams right now in Harlequins, and also some of them have been called up for the training school of the national team," she said. "Seeing such things happen, I'm so proud of the journey. I'll try my best to keep on doing it."
In April, the 32-year-old veteran was selected as an Athlete Role Model for Dakar 2026. Continuing a tradition established at the inaugural YOG in Singapore in 2010, she will help guide the next generation of athletes as they emerge onto the world stage.
"Most Olympics were held outside Africa. It was a dream far away. But right now, being brought here in Africa, it's reachable," she said. "For the girls and boys who are playing local tournaments, they have something to look forward to."
Following Saturday's opening ceremony, the rugby tournament begins the next day at Complexe Iba Mar Diop. Kenya's women's squad joins Pool A alongside Australia, China, Tunisia and host Senegal.
As the only African rugby personality among the Athlete Role Models for Dakar 2026, Chajira was thrilled by the prospect of welcoming the world's finest young talents to her home continent.
"Put yourself out there. Every opportunity you get, just go with it. Just work hard, focus on what you want and you will achieve," she added. ■

Pope meets Villanova and Notre Dame basketball teams at the Vatican

Pope Leo meets with Villanova and Notre Dame basketball teams at the Vatican
Pope Leo XIV met on Saturday with the basketball teams from Villanova and Notre Dame, along with thousands of U.S. fans in Italy, ahead of the two Catholic universities' season opener later this weekend.
About 7,000 people entered the Paul VI audience hall inside the Vatican on Saturday after a special private Mass in St. Peter's Basilica.
Leo, who is an avid tennis player and sports fan, said sports bring people together and can promote values such as fraternity, solidarity and peace.
"By acting as a concrete means of bringing people together, athletics can teach the values of cooperation and mutual sharing. This is increasingly necessary in an age marked by the distance that can be created by technology," he said, according to Vatican News.
The teams are in Rome for the U.S. college basketball season opener on Sunday — an event dubbed the Eternal City Tip-Off and created to honor the U.S.-born pope. The universities' men's and women's teams will play a doubleheader at the Palazzo Dello Sport, an 11,000-seat arena about a half-hour drive from the Vatican.
Leo, who is currently recovering from lung cancer surgery, graduated from Villanova in 1977 with a Bachelor of Science in mathematics.
"Growing up on the south side of Chicago, we oftentimes heard, 'Go Irish.' But as you all know, Prevost graduated from Villanova! So, the Pope doesn't take sides. Prevost has another opinion, but we won't do that now," Leo joked during the audience, according to Vatican News.
Leo urged the teams and their families to embrace sports as a way to grow in saintliness.
"No one is born a champion, just as no one is born a saint," he said.
He warned against letting sporting rivalries get out of hand and he said he hoped the fans in Rome this weekend would actually get to know one another as they cheer, "even passionately."
"In any competition, the members of two teams, even when they have a competitive rivalry, are certainly not enemies," he said. "I hope, therefore, that despite the competitive nature of college basketball, there will be opportunities for the players and the fans of both teams to get to know each other in your days here in Rome."
Before the audience, the Rev. Robert Dowd, president of Notre Dame, acknowledged Villanova had something of an edge considering it counts the pope as an alumnus. But in an interview Saturday, he said the occasion to bring both teams together with all their fans in Rome for a papal audience and season opener was "amazing."
"That could be a little challenging, but I know that the pope is a pope for all of us, and so I'm grateful," he said. "I know in a particular way the pope talks about the importance of bridge building, and I'm sure he'll be a bridge builder when we play each other."
Philadelphia Archbishop Nelson Perez celebrated a private Mass for traveling fans in St. Peter's Basilica on Saturday morning, and asked the thousands of people in the pews to give a round of applause to the players. The English-language liturgy was unusual in that it had all the trappings of a papal Mass celebrated at the main altar and televised live by Vatican Media.
Asked about the upcoming games on the papal plane during a recent trip to France, Leo said, "They tell me that the people coming to the match, 90% are Villanova and 10% Notre Dame, so the voice of the people of God will be very strong on the Villanova side."
Leo is an avid Chicago White Sox fan and has been known to follow basketball, too.
"He will know who they (the players) are. He's a true, blue Villanovan," said the Rev. Rob Hagan, Villanova's longtime team chaplain. He said Leo used to attend Villanova games at the Palestra, the Philadelphia arena known as "The Cathedral of College Basketball."
Sunday's games coincide with All Saints' Day, a major Catholic holiday.
"Our true goal, beyond emerging victorious in any one event, is to win the prize of everlasting life," Leo said.

Turkey nominates former FM in race for next UN chief

Breadcrumb
Turkey throws its former foreign minister's name into the race for next UN chief
Turkey has officially nominated a former foreign minister and yearslong ambassador to the United Nations for the next UN secretary-general, state-run media reported Saturday.
The next UN chief will succeed António Guterres, who has led the world body for almost 10 years. The organization is under pressure to reform as it finds itself sidelined in wars in Iran, Ukraine and Gaza while also facing a financial crisis that has forced major cuts to humanitarian and development programs.
Feridun Sinirlioglu, a 70-year-old former Turkish foreign minister and UN diplomat, had floated his candidacy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly’s high-level meeting in New York last month.
Sinirlioglu was Turkey's top diplomat for a few months in 2015, an interim period between elections, and its UN ambassador between 2016 and 2023.
He currently serves as the secretary-general of the Vienna-based Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe. His current three-year mandate is scheduled to end in December 2027, but the top UN job would have a Jan. 1 start date.
Ahmet Yildiz, Turkey’s current representative to the UN, told the Anadolu news agency that Sinirlioglu's name was officially submitted with backing from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Erdogan has been vocal in calling for reform of the UN Security Council, especially criticizing the dominance of its five permanent members. Sinirlioglu is likely to reflect the president’s agenda.
The next UN secretary-general will be decided by the 15-nation UN Security Council, especially its five veto-wielding members — the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France. The 193-member General Assembly must give final approval.
Sinirlioglu will likely face obstacles from several corners, including Turkey's neighbor Greece, which is one of the 10 elected members of the Security Council. Pushback also would be expected from Israel, a close ally of the United States.
Seven other candidates are vying to replace Guterres as he finishes his second five-year term. Under an informal regional rotation of the UN’s top job, a candidate from the Latin American and Caribbean region could be selected.

Polish PM Tusk vows support for tribunal amid court crisis
WARSAW, Oct 31 - Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk sought to offer assurances that the country's Constitutional Tribunal will operate in accordance with the law, after President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of the previous hard-right government, accused him of staging a forced takeover of the court.
Late on Friday, the Constitutional Tribunal said its longest-serving judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska had suspended Bogdan Swieczkowski, the tribunal's president and an appointee of Tusk's nationalist predecessor, and was now in charge of the court.
The move escalated a battle between Nawrocki and Tusk's pro-European government over control of the judiciary.
"I am certain that the Constitutional Tribunal will function as it should. Also, independently of me and in line with the constitution," Tusk said in a televised speech.
"The task of the executive branch, and therefore mine, is to ensure its safety and working conditions, and I intend to fulfill my duty."
In a dramatic move, Nawrocki turned back his plane in which he was heading to Senegal late on Friday and headed for the court headquarters in central Warsaw, following Swieczkowski's suspension.
Riot police have been guarding the court since Friday afternoon, with several hundred protesters gathered to demand Swieczkowski's reinstatement.
"Tonight, there was a breach of public order in the Republic of Poland and a forcible takeover of a constitutional body," Nawrocki said in a statement read by an aide outside the court early on Saturday.
Nawrocki held political consultations throughout Saturday.
Tusk, writing on X, said his government was seeking to restore the rule of law, which the European Union had accused his predecessors — the Law and Justice Party — of subverting.
"This process is difficult, at times even painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way," he said.
LONG-RUNNING POLITICAL DISPUTE
A long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralysed the institution, with the pro-European government and the nationalist president refusing to recognise appointees put forward by the other side.
The dispute dates back to 2015, when Law and Justice sought to appoint judges to seats already filled by the previous government.
Its nominees gained a majority on the Constitutional Tribunal, while critics at home and abroad said the court no longer met the standards of an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.
After Tusk's coalition took office in 2023 it pledged to restore the rule of law and reform the court, but Law and Justice ally Nawrocki has acted to thwart those efforts since his election as president in 2025.
Earlier this year, Nawrocki refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, while Swieczkowski, a former deputy justice minister in the Law and Justice administration, declined to seat judges elected by the current parliamentary majority.
Last month, parliament appointed Tusk ally Maciej Berek to the tribunal, which critics said undermined the government's stated goal of restoring checks and balances. REUTERS

Scientists discover metals that defy the deep freeze at -424°F
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:45:59 UTC
21:45:59 KST

Scientists discover metals that defy the deep freeze at -424°F
- Date:
- October 31, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a surprising mechanism that allows certain metals to resist cracking at temperatures as low as -253°C (-424°F), when similar materials typically become dangerously brittle. Instead of breaking, two experimental alloys reorganize their internal structures, creating new ways to absorb stress and remain flexible.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered an unexpected way certain metals can withstand extreme cold without becoming dangerously brittle. The discovery challenges long-standing ideas about how metals behave at extremely low temperatures and could help engineers develop tougher materials for some of the harshest environments imaginable.
The findings, published October 14 in Nature, reveal a previously unknown microscopic process that allows two experimental metal alloys to remain remarkably resistant to damage at just 20 kelvin, or -253°C (-424°F). The research was led by an international team from the University of California, Berkeley, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and the University of Oxford.
Why Extreme Cold Makes Some Metals Brittle
Cooling a metal generally increases its strength, but this improvement can come with a serious drawback. Certain metals become increasingly brittle as temperatures fall, making them more likely to crack or break instead of bending under pressure.
This problem is particularly important for a family of materials known as body-centered cubic metals (such as iron, tungsten, and chromium). Their atoms are arranged in a specific crystal pattern that can make them especially vulnerable to brittle failure in extreme cold. At temperatures approaching absolute zero, a small crack that might ordinarily be accommodated by the metal changing shape can instead spread and cause a fracture.
However, researchers discovered that two experimental alloys made from niobium and titanium behave very differently. Even when cooled to -253°C, both materials maintained an impressive ability to withstand damage. Neither showed a measurable shift toward brittle behavior at the lowest temperature tested.
The explanation lies in a surprising change in how the metals respond to stress. Rather than relying on their usual method of deformation, the alloys activate a different microscopic process that helps prevent cracks from spreading.
A Hidden Mechanism Helps Metals Resist Cracking
Under normal conditions, body-centered cubic metals bend and change shape through the movement of tiny defects within their crystal structures. These defects, called dislocations, allow layers of atoms to shift relative to one another, helping the material absorb stress without breaking.
As temperatures drop, however, these dislocations become increasingly difficult to move. With fewer ways to accommodate the forces concentrated around a crack, the metal becomes more likely to fracture.
The newly studied alloys have another way to respond.
Researchers observed a process called nanoscale 'twinning', in which tiny sections of the metal's crystal structure rearrange into mirror-image patterns. This occurs alongside a localized change in the crystal structure itself.
When these newly formed regions encounter the boundaries separating neighboring crystals, they produce concentrated areas of stress. Those stress concentrations generate additional defects, giving the metal new opportunities to deform rather than crack.
The researchers compare this behavior to a road system finding alternative routes when its usual roads become blocked by ice. As extreme cold makes conventional deformation increasingly difficult, the newly formed crystal structures provide other pathways for the metal to accommodate stress.
By creating these new pathways, the material can continue absorbing forces around potential fractures instead of failing abruptly.
A Breakthrough for Metals Used in Extreme Environments
The findings suggest a new approach to developing structural metals that can withstand exceptionally low temperatures. Such materials could be valuable in energy systems, transportation, and aerospace engineering, where components may encounter severe thermal conditions.
Oxford corresponding author Professor Dong Liu (Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford) said: "For decades, the ductile-to-brittle transition has been viewed as a fundamental limitation of body-centered cubic metals. What surprised us is that these alloys remain remarkably damage tolerant even at 20 kelvin. By uncovering how twinning and phase transformation work together to generate plasticity before conventional dislocation motion, we identified a new pathway for designing structural body-centered cubic metals that can operate in extreme cryogenic environments. This class of materials will be extremely useful for components experiencing extreme hot and cold temperatures in one application."
The discovery also changes how scientists may need to think about what determines whether a metal becomes brittle. Previously, much of the emphasis was placed on how easily existing defects could travel through a material. The new results indicate that generating fresh defects may be just as important.
Lead author Dr. David Cook (University of California, Berkeley at the time of the study, now University of Cambridge) said: "Our results suggest we should change how we think about what governs the transition to brittleness for these metals. Traditionally, the focus was on how readily existing dislocations can move through a metal, but now it appears that the ability to create new dislocations at interfaces may also be critical. Using these insights, we may be able to design underlying microstructural conditions that allow a material to create its own routes to remain ductile at extreme temperatures."
How Scientists Tested Metals at -253°C
To investigate how the alloys performed under such punishing conditions, the team conducted experiments using the Engin-X instrument at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source in Oxfordshire.
The researchers used gaseous helium to cool metal samples to approximately -253°C. While directing a beam of neutrons through the materials, they used a specialized testing machine to stretch the samples by pulling from opposite ends.
This setup allowed the team to measure the forces the metals could withstand and determine how far they could stretch before breaking. The neutron measurements also helped researchers investigate what was happening inside the materials as they were deformed.
Afterward, the scientists examined the tested samples using powerful electron microscopes. These instruments revealed extremely small structural changes within the metal, including those near cracks that helped explain its unusual resistance to damage.
The team also used atom-probe analysis to determine how individual elements were distributed throughout the alloys. Combined with computer modeling, these measurements helped establish how the different microscopic processes worked together to prevent brittle failure.
The results offer more than an explanation for the surprising behavior of two experimental alloys. They identify a potentially useful strategy for designing metals that can remain tough even when conventional methods of deformation stop working, opening new possibilities for technologies that must operate in extreme cold.
The international collaboration included researchers from the University of California, Berkeley; Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory; the University of Oxford; the University of Bristol; the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source, Science and Technology Facilities Council; the University of California, Irvine; Pacific Northwest National Laboratory; Texas A&M University; and Nanyang Technological University in Singapore.

Tabriz Blue Mosque to mark 561st anniversary with focus on Qara Qoyunlu tilework
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:41:34 UTC
21:41:34 KST

Tabriz Blue Mosque to mark 561st anniversary with focus on Qara Qoyunlu tilework
TEHRAN - A specialist meeting marking the 561st anniversary of the establishment of Tabriz’s Blue Mosque will explore the history of the Qara Qoyunlu dynasty and the distinctive tilework associated with its period of rule.
The meeting is scheduled to take place on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at the meeting hall of the Azarbaijan Museum in Tabriz, Miras Aria news agency reported.
The event will feature presentations by Masoumeh Qarehdaghi, associate professor and head of the History Department, and Ali Nemati, associate professor of conservation and restoration of cultural and historical objects.
Two main subjects will be addressed: the political and administrative structure of the Qara Qoyunlu dynasty and the development of tilework during its rule.
Qarehdaghi will discuss the dynasty's system of governance and the historical circumstances surrounding the creation of monuments from that period. Nemati will examine the artistic characteristics and decorative techniques of Qara Qoyunlu tilework, with particular attention to the craftsmanship and ornamental features of surviving works.
The Blue Mosque, also known as the Jahan Shah Mosque and the Mozaffariyeh Edifice, is among Iran's notable architectural monuments dating from the 15th century. Its construction is closely associated with the reign of Jahan Shah, the Qara Qoyunlu ruler who governed much of Iran and neighboring territories during the 15th century.
The Qara Qoyunlu, also known as the Black Sheep Turkomans, were a Turkoman Muslim dynasty that ruled parts of present-day Azerbaijan, Armenia, northwestern Iran, eastern Turkey and northeastern Iraq from approximately 1374 to 1468. Their period of rule was marked by significant architectural and artistic patronage, particularly in northwestern Iran.
An inscription above the Blue Mosque's entrance bears the date 870 AH (1465–66), providing an important historical reference for the monument. The mosque is particularly renowned for its intricate mosaic tilework, dominated by shades of blue and turquoise, which has earned it the celebrated name Turquoise of Islam.
Its architectural significance, however, extends beyond its elaborate decorative surfaces. The building's spatial arrangement and the integration of a mosque with a mausoleum make it an important example of Qara Qoyunlu architecture and provide valuable material for studying the period's religious and funerary traditions.
The monument suffered extensive damage in an earthquake in 1193 AH (1779–80), and parts of the structure were subsequently rebuilt during restoration campaigns. Consequently, an understanding of its architectural history requires consideration of its original design, surviving decorative elements and subsequent conservation interventions.
The Blue Mosque has also been highlighted in Iran's submission to UNESCO, reflecting its architectural and artistic significance. Its distinctive tilework remains one of the most remarkable expressions of decorative craftsmanship in the architectural heritage of northwestern Iran.

South Khorasan’s traditional oil-fried bread added to intangible heritage list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

South Khorasan’s traditional oil-fried bread added to intangible heritage list
TEHRAN - The traditional skill of making Nan-e Roghan-Jushi, an oil-fried bread deeply rooted in the cultural and religious traditions of South Khorasan province, has been inscribed on Iran’s National Intangible Cultural Heritage List.
Fariba Kahani, an official responsible for intangible heritage registration at the provincial Department of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts, said the bread is traditionally prepared on the 14th day of Sha’ban (the 8th lunar month) during the local religious observance known as Barat.
Families who have lost loved ones during the previous year prepare the bread as an act of charity in memory of the deceased and distribute it among relatives, friends and neighbors.
Its preparation involves mixing flour, water, turmeric, aromatic spices such as coriander seeds, and sourdough. After resting for about 90 minutes to two hours, small portions of dough are flattened and fried in hot oil.
Kahani said the tradition reflects religious beliefs, charitable practices and family bonds. The skill has traditionally been passed down from mothers to daughters, with women playing a central role in preserving it.

Flu Vaccine Now Required for Many Airmen, Guardians, and DAF Civilians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:35:00 UTC
21:35:00 KST

Airmen and Guardians in the Active and Reserve component, as well as civilian employees, in “mission critical and high-risk populations” are now required to receive influenza vaccinations annually to “preserve force readiness,” according to a recent Department of the Air Force memo.
The Oct. 20 memo, signed by Assistant Secretary of the Air Force for Manpower and Reserve Affairs Richard Anderson, directs personnel in six population categories get vaccinated for seasonal influenza:
- Recruits, training populations, and congregate living
- Rapid deployment forces and “no-fail” missions
- Deployed forces
- Health care personnel
- Civilian personnel in child development and youth services programs
- Air Mobility Command aircrew supporting U.S. Transportation Command taskings, enroute care personnel, and executive airlift personnel
The guidance memo, which was posted on the unofficial Air Force amn/nco/snco Facebook page, comes more than three months after a flu outbreak at Air Force Basic Military Training left one recruit dead and infected more than 280 others at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas.
An Air Force spokesperson confirmed the memo is authentic. Air Force Times was first to report on the memo.
Airmen and Guardians in deploying units should align their vaccinations with pre-deployment timelines. All other personnel included in the policy must be vaccinated no later than Dec. 15 annually, the memo states.
“For service members in the designated populations, vaccinations are a requirement; failure to comply may result in administrative or disciplinary action under the Uniform Code of Military Justice,” the memo states. The memo, however, adds that “commanders should consider using the lowest level of discipline … when evaluating options to address noncompliance, taking into consideration the circumstances of the noncompliance and previous disciplinary record of the Airman or Guardian.”
For civilian employees in the identified populations, flu vaccinations are considered a condition of employment, the memo states. Supervisors “should not take adverse action indecently” but should but address noncompliance through the “Civilian Personnel Section/Human Resources in coordination with Labor and Employee Relations,” the memo states.
The new guidance partially rolls back Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s April announcement that he was rescinding the mandate for Active-Duty troops and trainees to receive the annual flu vaccine. Hegseth said in a video posted on social media at the time that “the notion that a flu vaccine must be mandatory for every service member, everywhere, in every circumstance at all times is just overly broad and not rational.”
The Pentagon approved the Department of the Air Force exception-to-policy request on June 11, the memo states.
“The DAF requested an exemption to the voluntary policy to protect mission-critical and high-risk populations,” according to the memo. “The mandatory vaccination for these select groups [is] deemed essential to preserve force readiness, prevent illness, minimize lost duty days, and ensure the successful execution of DAF missions.”
Airmen, Guardians, and civilian personnel in the designated populations can submit requests for religious accommodations and medical exemptions for the flu vaccine mandate, the memo states, adding that personnel who have their request denied will have an opportunity to comply with the vaccination requirements.
The memo includes detailed descriptions of each population and in some cases offers examples where some personnel will be exempt from the requirement. For example, personnel that fall under the “recruits, training populations and congregate living” category are “excluded” if they are assigned to single-occupancy dorm rooms—such as permanent party—unless they are “assigned to or routinely perform duties in hig- risk environment.”
Another example in this population applies to Air University and other non-technical training organizations whose “primary mission is professional military education, doctrine, graduate education, and other non-technical instruction will not be included solely because they conduct resident education.”
It’s unclear what percentage of Department of the Air Force military and civilian personnel are now required to take the flu vaccine. After the flu outbreak at Lackland, only around 40 percent of Air Force trainees took the flu shot after Hegseth made it optional, The Associated Press reported. That’s a little lower than the 46.5 percent of American adults who got the shot this past flu season, according to the CDC.
Vaccine “hesitancy” has surged in recent years. A mandate in 2021 that all service members receive COVID-19 vaccinations fueled an intense political debate. Around 8,000 service members ultimately were separated for refusing the Pentagon’s mandate, and the Pentagon has taken steps to allow some members to return.

Americans Lost Nearly $18 Billion Last Year to Cyberscams. Is Washington Doing Enough to Help Them Get It Back?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:30:00 UTC
21:30:00 KST

The United States government’s response to escalating cyberscams is fragmented, leaving victims with limited options to recover lost funds, according to an investigation conducted by Democrats on Congress’s Joint Economic Committee (JEC).
The investigation, led by Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire and Rep. Don Beyer of Virginia, found that federal agencies do not have a consolidated or comprehensive record of how much money has been lost to cyberfraud, how much has been seized from overseas scam compounds, or how much has been returned to victims.
The report, published Tuesday, also concludes that the government does not “incentivize” private sector actors—such as financial institutions and social media companies—to “proactively detect and address abuse of the services that they provide while also protecting user privacy.”
Online scam operations are not new, and neither is the knowledge that the issue is escalating. The FBI released an April report showing that Americans lost nearly $18 billion in 2025, amounting to more than $2 million an hour. Overall reported internet-crime losses—a broader category—reached $20.9 billion, up 26% from 2024 and roughly triple the 2021 total.
While the problem grows worse, the response to these crimes has not scaled along with it. The Congressional investigation demonstrates that only a fraction of the money lost to scams is recovered. It also points to the fact that the government fails to fully report on its existing repatriation measures.
The FBI told the committee that it returned $336 million to scam victims in 2025, and the Secret Service returned more than $770 million in seized assets to fraud victims in fiscal years 2024 and 2025—though that money had come from a range of fraud schemes, not just cyber threats.
Suzanne Sando, a fraud analyst at Javelin Strategy & Research, points out that “fragmentation” in the reporting system—including the differing time periods and fraud categories demonstrated above—complicates the government’s ability to grasp the full extent of the problem.
“Many of the groups and entities that scam victims report their losses to operate on disparate systems,” Sando says. “The fragmented nature of these reporting entities means there’s a lack of true accounting of losses—which also means that our grasp of overall scam losses is likely less than the truth of the situation.”
The Congressional report calls on the federal government to enact new legislation to address the rising issue, including the ReportScams.Gov Act, a bipartisan bill co-sponsored by Hassan and Florida Republican Sen. Rick Scott “to mandate a unified federal strategy to combat scams and establish a central location for Americans to find information and assistance regarding scams.”
A more coordinated reporting system could help researchers and advocates better assess the scale of the problem. Another benefit would be helping the public stay informed about potential schemes, allowing advocacy groups to develop preventive strategies and educational materials for at-risk populations, like senior citizens and minors.
According to the FBI’s 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans ages 60 and older reported losses of about $7.7 billion, a 60% increase from 2024. They reported the highest total losses of any age group, the report showed.
Individuals under 18 reported nearly $13 million in losses across 13,168 internet-crime complaints in 2025, according to the same report.
But the true extent of the losses is hard to estimate, experts say. Cyberscams are underreported because victims feel embarrassed, fear judgment, and believe recovery will be impossible.
The last point is salient, because a stronger and more coordinated response—reaching some of the benchmarks outlined this week by members of the JEC—could give victims the confidence to report crimes in a timely manner, in turn making enforcement efforts more effective.
The report calls for legislation that would “hold accountable” countries that “enable or permit” scam compound operations, and advance federal cooperation with private sector entities like the financial institutions and social media companies at the center of these scams.
Experts note that this is a growing issue whose risk is only increasing as technology improves.
In alignment with the Congressional assessment, they tell TIME that a strategic, coordinated, and well-resourced response will be necessary if the government hopes to better protect Americans and help them recover funds lost to scams.
Online scams are on the rise
Data from the FBI and Congress show that transnational criminal organizations run massive compounds—and their reach is skyrocketing.
According to Sando, the growing use of artificial intelligence has been partly responsible. 
Specifically, she calls out the prevalence of abuse on social media and the increasing sophistication of deepfakes—images, voices, or videos that make people appear to say or do things they did not.
“Criminals use social media to build trust through ongoing conversations and relationships, and AI has become a major part of criminals’ ability to manipulate situations and exploit victims,” she says. “Through AI, criminals can create more convincing and polished messages, fake social media profiles, and deepfake voices and videos with less time and effort.”
The manipulation tactics at the heart of these schemes have been consistent, Sando says, but criminals now have improved tools that allow them to quickly build credibility and “commit scams at scale.”
Jake Braun, the executive director of the Cyber Policy Initiative at the University of Chicago, tells TIME that highly vulnerable populations are more exposed than ever before.
“You've got these, you know, super at-risk populations who just weren't online before, and now they are, and so the bad guys are taking advantage of that,” he says. “The idea that a kid had an iPhone and was on Facebook just wasn’t a reality until a few years ago.”
At the same time, technology gives individuals ready access to funding streams. “They've all got Apple Pay on their phones,” Braun points out.
He explains that many of these scams are run by organized criminal networks operating in Southeast Asia, where scam compounds often use trafficked workers forced to defraud people online.
Why is it so difficult to recover lost funds?
It can be difficult to recover stolen funds because the issue is diffuse and widespread—spanning multiple countries, financial institutions, and criminal enterprises—and it is being addressed by a small group of law enforcement agencies that lack centralized coordination.
Braun says investigations are complicated because they affect “millions of victims across dozens of countries” and include large numbers of cases with relatively small individual losses.
“It's just incredibly complicated,” he says. “Nobody's robbing a bank and stealing $300 million. It's $1,000 bucks from somebody's grandma here, and it's $500 bucks [there], that collectively is billions and billions. That's a really hard problem to get after.”
Braun, who also served in the White House with former President Joe Biden as the acting Principal Deputy National Cyber Director, says that there are just a hundred or so top law enforcement officials working on the issue.
“So they're going to focus on big fish, and try and take down big rings, but that just means that they just don't have the bandwidth to go track down hundreds or thousands of dollars that are stolen from individual people because they're trying to take down groups that are collectively stealing billions,” he explains.
When reporting investigations and recovery efforts are “siloed” into different agencies, there are two immediate consequences: The process is more confusing for the victim to navigate, and it makes it difficult for government entities to coordinate quickly on an investigation and take action.
The U.S. State Department told those involved with the JEC investigation that it has 60 employees in the U.S. and Asia who dedicate significant time to fighting overseas scam compounds and said that it “has the tools it needs to combat the threat internationally.”
TIME reached out to the State Department for comment.
What obstacles stand in the way of providing better protections for Americans?
Sando says that within the private sector, there is “a lack of clear ownership and responsibility,” making it difficult to provide more protection.
“Scams can span multiple platforms,” she says. “Preventing and detecting scams to protect consumers requires a coordinated group effort across multiple industries—including financial services, telcos, and social media.”
In a perfect world, Sando continues, the government would coordinate these efforts and set clear standards for private institutions. She describes its ideal role as “facilitating relevant information-sharing, tracking consistent scam attempts and losses, [reporting] recovery rates for victims, and [adding] measures that are working to reduce the effectiveness of scams.”
Social media companies, in particular, need to be incentivized to address “fraudulent ads and impersonation profiles/accounts,” she says.
Braun agrees, saying that holding the companies accountable is one of the most tangible ways that governments could more aggressively address these scams before they ever happen.
“They know everything about every click that's made on their platform,” Braun says. “This problem wouldn't exist if those platforms didn't exist.”
Braun says meaningful discussions around prevention are often buried in conversations about how to address losses in the U.S.
“We should really think through the [cyber] grants we give to state and local governments from FEMA, [and having them include] a component where they're doing education for these at-risk communities: seniors, minors, migrants,” Braun says. “We’re focused on going after the ‘bad guys,’ when maybe we need to be focused on thinking about: ‘How do you specifically protect minors in this space? How do you specifically protect senior citizens?’”
He believes that these considerations must be part of any comprehensive solution to bring down the rate of cyberscams in the U.S.
Once the government has a better understanding of how specific communities are impacted by these scams, he says, it can start to “tailor” solutions to help protect each vulnerable group.

Israeli attacks on Syria
Shaibani also said Israel had carried out more than 1,000 attacks on Syria in less than two years, killing dozens of people.
“How can calls for border control and placing weapons exclusively under state control be justified while Syrian sovereignty is violated and targeted on a daily basis?” he asked.
Condemning the attacks, Shaibani called for a return to the lines in place before December 8, 2024, and implementation of the 1974 Disengagement Agreement.
He stressed that the Golan Heights is Syrian territory, citing UN Security Council Resolution 497 as the reference on the issue.
Since the fall of the Assad regime on December 8, 2024, Israel has occupied the Syrian buffer zone established under the 1974 agreement and set up military positions inside and outside it. The UN has described the move as a violation of the agreement.

US approves Patriot missiles sale to Ukraine
The US State Department has green-lit a $2.1 billion Patriot missile sale to Ukraine.
The announcement follows a report by CNN earlier this month that Kiev had completely exhausted its stockpile of US-made interceptors used to defend against Russian missile and drone strikes at military-related targets.
The State Department said in a statement on Friday that the Ukrainian government had requested that Washington sell it 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles and spare parts for launchers.
Kiev will pay for the interceptors with funds donated by Canada, Germany, and Norway, the State Department said. “No US funds are involved in this sale,” it added.
The principal contractor for the deal will be Lockheed Martin, according to the statement.
“There will be no adverse impact on US defense readiness as a result of this proposed sale,” the department stressed.
The US depleted much of its Patriot missile stockpile during the war with Iran, which was widely reported by American media and confirmed in a Pentagon inspector general’s report last month. A separate Congressional Budget Office assessment said that the Pentagon had consumed between one-half and two-thirds of its inventory of certain missile-defense interceptors since June 2025.
However, US President Donald Trump has downplayed the shortages, claiming that American stockpiles are virtually unlimited.
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky reacted to the State Department announcement in a post on X, saying that he was grateful to Trump and that 500 Patriot missiles was “a substantial number.”
However, he complained that “it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin only in a few years,” while Kiev needs the interceptors “right now.”
Zelensky claimed US and European countries currently have “sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses,” urging Washington to find a solution that would see them supplied to Ukraine immediately.
“The Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day. In just these past two weeks of October, there have already been more than 30 Russian strikes on critical parts of our power grid,” he said.
On Saturday, the Defense Ministry in Moscow said that Russian forces had conducted more drone attacks against logistics and energy infrastructure supporting Ukraine’s war effort. Among other things, a heating and power plant in Kiev and workshops used for production of UAVs and weapons’ parts in Kharkov were hit, according to the ministry.
Moscow says that the strikes are being carried out in response to Ukrainian terrorist attacks on residential areas and civilian infrastructure inside Russia, to which Kiev resorts in order to compensate for setbacks on the front line.

ICOMOS continues evaluation of Masuleh’s UNESCO World Heritage nomination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:28:15 UTC
21:28:15 KST

ICOMOS continues evaluation of Masuleh’s UNESCO World Heritage nomination
TEHRAN - The evaluation of Masuleh and its cultural landscape for inscription on UNESCO’s World Heritage List is continuing, with an international expert from the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS) conducting field assessments and attending specialist meetings on the Iranian town’s architectural, archaeological, ecological and socio-economic heritage.
The ongoing assessment in Gilan province, northern Iran, examines different aspects of Masuleh and its surrounding landscape, including its physical fabric, ecological characteristics, local livelihoods, social structures and management practices, according to the Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts.
The program includes field inspections and discussions with university professors, researchers and heritage specialists, focusing on safeguarding the town’s Outstanding Universal Value (OUV) while ensuring its long-term conservation and sustainable development.
As part of the assessment, the ICOMOS expert visited the archaeology and anthropology museum of Rasht, where historical collections from across Gilan province, including archaeological discoveries from Old Masuleh, were presented.
Among the notable objects displayed were the Rashi silver-gilt goblet and the Toleh gold goblet from Talesh. The artefacts offer evidence of the region’s ancient history and sophisticated metalworking traditions.
Specialist sessions also examined archaeological excavations and experimental archaeology, particularly research into historical iron-production technologies. Researchers presented findings from a project involving the reconstruction and experimental operation of ancient iron smelting furnaces, shedding light on Masuleh’s industrial history.
Last year, an interdisciplinary research team successfully reconstructed a medieval iron smelting and casting complex at the Old Masuleh archaeological site, demonstrating the technological capabilities of communities that once inhabited the area.
Led by Farzad Asadi, a faculty member at Islamic Azad University, the project involved the experimental reconstruction of a four-stage furnace system documented through approximately two decades of archaeological research.
The experiment went beyond reconstructing the physical structure. Researchers examined its operational characteristics, including airflow, thermal efficiency and the production process from sponge iron to cast iron.
The reconstructed complex featured preheated air channels, permanent stone structures and a dedicated casting installation, distinguishing it from simpler, temporary bloomery furnaces. Laboratory analysis of the resulting slag and iron also indicated high material purity and considerable control over the production process.
Mostafa Pourali, director of the Masuleh World Heritage nomination dossier, has said the second, more detailed reconstruction phase had revealed technological connections with broader Iranian-type furnaces.
The findings point to Old Masuleh's potential role as a permanent iron-production centre and a place of technological exchange along historical trade routes connecting Iran with the Caucasus and Central Asia. The research is expected to be published internationally.
Beyond its archaeological significance, the furnace reconstruction has added an industrial dimension to the understanding of Masuleh's cultural landscape, demonstrating that the settlement's historical importance extends beyond its distinctive architecture and natural setting.
Other discussions during the ICOMOS assessment addressed sustainable destination management and community-based conservation. Participants examined approaches to managing the historic settlement through the active involvement of residents, while protecting its stepped residential fabric and maintaining the relationship between people, the mountainous environment and traditional livelihoods.
Ecological research and archaeobotanical studies also featured in the program. These interdisciplinary investigations aim to improve scientific documentation of the area's historical environmental conditions and the relationship between past communities and their natural surroundings.
The sessions further addressed the physical conservation of Masuleh, including construction regulations, the use of traditional building materials, appropriate restoration techniques and the management of changes in a vulnerable mountain settlement.
According to Iran's nomination dossier, Masuleh is believed to be between 800 and 1,000 years old. Its numerous cemeteries, both within and outside the settlement, are among the archaeological indications of its historical depth.
The town is particularly distinguished by its multi-storey, terraced urban layout, which follows the slope of the surrounding mountain. Its architecture is closely integrated with the natural landscape, while the arrangement of buildings allows the roofs of lower houses to function as pedestrian spaces and courtyards for those above.
The traditional architectural arrangement also reflects the importance of craftsmanship and the visual character of the settlement. With the main facades of houses directly visible to residents and visitors, local builders and artisans paid particular attention to their appearance and architectural details.
The nomination dossier describes the combination of traditional architecture and natural scenery as a potential basis for tourism development, while recognizing tourism and the preservation of local livelihoods as closely interconnected.
The latest round of assessments highlights the need to approach Masuleh as an integrated cultural landscape rather than merely an architectural attraction. Its historic buildings, traditional industries, archaeological remains, ecological setting and living community collectively contribute to its heritage significance.
The continuing ICOMOS evaluation is an important stage in the international assessment of Iran's nomination. ICOMOS serves as an advisory body to UNESCO on cultural heritage nominations, conducting expert evaluations before the World Heritage Committee considers whether a property should be inscribed on the World Heritage List.

Syrian women’s delegation participates in New York UN Security Week in first
An official Syrian women’s delegation attended the UN’s Women, Peace and Security Week in New York, reports said on Saturday, allowing the group to relay their struggles amid over a decade of war and displacement as well as their growing role in decision-making.
This is the first time a women’s delegation from Syria has attended the event, which included several bilateral meetings, events and social gatherings.
The event also included a UN Security Council open debate on women, peace and security.
Nahla Othman, the Director of Expatriate and Refugee Affairs from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, told local media that women in the country have long faced persecution, and that the new government since the fall of the Assad regime has been working to expand the role of women in state institutions.
During the high-level meetings, she called on the international community to support Syrian women in implementing UN Security Council Resolutions, and put a stop to Israeli violations in southern Syria.
“The story of the Syrian woman is not a story of a victim, but a story of extraordinary resilience,” she said, noting that while there are now many pathways for women to take part in parliamentary work, there is still a long road ahead.
The delegation of women was also made up of Nour Jandali, a member of the Syrian People’s Assembly; Zahra Albarazi, Deputy Chair of the National Commission for Transitional Justice; Mayassa al-Sheikh Ahmad, a member of the National Commission for Missing Persons; and Saba Abdul Latif, a representative of the ministry’s International Organisations Department.
During the meeting, Othman also spoke about addressing the legacy of the past as well as continued Israeli attacks.
She presented several case studies, including examples of mothers searching for their children and loved ones while the international community failed to act.
She ended by reiterating calls for Israel to fully respect the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement, withdraw from Syrian territories it entered after December 2024 and completely withdraw from the occupied Syrian Golan, as well as return all those detained and abducted.
Earlier this year, 22 women representatives were selected in the new Syrian parliament, the first to sit since the overthrow of Assad in 2024.
Their appearance at the first session of parliament in August garnered widespread conversation on the increased diversity in Syria, and changes underway.

Humanitarian hub set up to receive participants in mission to temporarily occupied Oleshky
