Humanitarian hub set up to receive participants in mission to temporarily occupied Oleshky
According to an Ukrinform correspondent, the hub is ready to receive those evacuated from the city.
1 / 12
Representatives of the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, medical workers, a psychological support service and volunteer organizations are on site. Mobile heating points have been set up, and hot meals are being provided. Wheelchairs are available for people with limited mobility. An area with water and food has also been prepared for pets. A separate vehicle was allocated to transport animals as part of the humanitarian mission.
A medical mission representative at the humanitarian hub, doctor Bohdan Komlevyi, told reporters that everyone arriving will first undergo a medical examination, and first aid will be provided on site if necessary.
"We have all the specialists, from surgeons to physicians. If anyone needs urgent medical assistance, we will immediately take them to a medical facility," Komlevyi said.
Yuliia Stefaniuk, a representative of World Central Kitchen in Ukraine, told reporters that dietary meals, children's food packages and pet food had been prepared for those leaving Oleshky.
"We have adapted the meals to accommodate possible dietary restrictions, including low-fat broths. We have borshch, a traditional dish associated with home. We want them to feel that they are returning to their family. We have prepared buckwheat with chicken, a dietary meal to help them regain their strength, as they still have a journey ahead. For the children, we have special packages with treats, hematogen, which is important during the autumn-winter period, fruit purees and snacks to lift their spirits. We will also give them fruit and sweet muffins for the road," Stefaniuk said.
She added that, together with the Hachiko Foundation, they had provided food, water and pet carriers for domestic animals.
Hot drinks are also being served to people waiting to welcome their family members from Oleshky.
One of the women, Zhanna, left Oleshky after Russia blew up the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant. She came to the border area after learning about the humanitarian mission to meet her husband. She brought him some salo (cured pork fat).
"He loves salo. He promised to bring me his homemade pickled tomatoes. Kherson-style pickled tomatoes and Kyiv salo – that will make a fantastic dinner. It's emotionally difficult. For three years, we communicated only by phone. Imagine what the people leaving there must be going through – it's a shock, it's grief over everything they've lost. They will need time to recover," she said.
She also said the situation in Oleshky is difficult. The humanitarian mission had now delivered food there, and recently the Ukrainian Armed Forces had also been delivering humanitarian supplies by drone.
"If the road to the villages is demined, perhaps people will be able to bring in food. My husband lived for three years on what he grew himself," Zhanna said.
Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets reported on Telegram that the participants in the humanitarian mission to Oleshky were already in Belarus.
"We'll be home soon! We are now in the Republic of Belarus – together with our people and even their pets!" Lubinets wrote.
As reported, agreements to carry out a humanitarian mission to Oleshky were officially confirmed on October 23, 2026. International humanitarian mediation was provided by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump and her team. The agreements were confirmed on the Ukrainian side by Ukraine's Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and on the Russian side by Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova.
Lubinets headed the Ukrainian negotiating team responsible for implementing the mission, while his Russian counterpart, Lantratova, led the Russian team. As part of the mission, the ombudsmen, acting as heads of the negotiating teams, agreed to establish a ceasefire, clear transport routes to Oleshky of mines, deliver humanitarian aid, and allow anyone wishing to leave to travel either to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government or to the Russian Federation.
To enable the humanitarian mission, Ukraine and Russia agreed to observe a ceasefire in the area around temporarily occupied Oleshky from October 27 until 22:59 on November 1.

UN wraps up 3-decade-long mission in conflict-hit Somalia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:11:00 UTC
21:11:00 KST

The United Nations political mission in Somalia officially ended Saturday following a two-year transition, bringing to a close more than three decades of U.N. political and peacebuilding operations in the East African country.
Established by the U.N. Security Council in 2013, the United Nations Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNSOM) supported Somali authorities in efforts to strengthen democratic governance, uphold the rule of law and rebuild state institutions after more than two decades of conflict involving militias, terrorist groups and criminal gangs.
The mission traces its origins to 1995, when the U.N. established the United Nations Political Office for Somalia (UNPOS).
In May 2024, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud requested the mission's closure ahead of the expiration of its mandate in October that year.
He later revised the request, proposing a two-year transition period to allow for an orderly handover.
During the transition, UNSOM was replaced by the U.N. Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS).
"Today is not an end to the partnership between the United Nations and Somalia. Rather, it marks the conclusion of one chapter and the beginning of another," said Raisedon Zenenga, UNTMIS officer-in-charge and the U.N. secretary-general's deputy special representative for Somalia, in a statement.
"While significant challenges remain, the closure of UNTMIS comes after considerable progress by Somalia since the early years of international efforts to support the country's recovery," he added.
The mission's responsibilities have been transferred to Somali institutions or the U.N. country team.
The transition comes as Al-Qaeda-linked Al-Shabaab, which has fought the Somali government for two decades, continues to control large swaths of central Somalia despite a major international military campaign against the group.
The fight against Al-Shabaab faces growing pressure from international funding cuts, particularly after the United States withdrew all funding for a key U.N. logistics mission, raising questions about the future of military operations.
Somalia is scheduled to hold parliamentary and presidential elections next May, but persistent insecurity and disputes between the government and opposition threaten the electoral process.

Video footage shared on social media by Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, showed some of the evacuated residents stepping off a bus draped in Ukrainian flags and embracing loved ones after crossing the border.
"The moment we had all been waiting for: residents of Oleshky have crossed the border — the humanitarian mission has been successfully completed!" Lubinets wrote alongside the clip, while also thanking US First Lady Melania Trump for her help brokering the deal.

"It includes 25 buses, 50 medical professionals, and ambulances," she said.
The ceasefire is due to last until Sunday evening.

It comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said around 280,000 Ukrainian households had been left without power after Russian strikes overnight.
"Russian strikes have created a difficult situation with electricity supplies across our regions," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on X.

"Repair crews are working to deal with the aftermath of the strikes and doing everything they can to restore electricity supplies," he said, adding that Russian forces had hit a "combined heat and power plant" in Kyiv on Friday night as well as four electrical substations in the eastern Dnipro region, among other targets.

PARIS, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Fitch Ratings said Friday that it has revised France's long-term issuer default ratings (IDRs) outlook to negative from stable while affirming the country's rating at "A+".
The negative outlook reflects weaker economic growth, higher borrowing costs and a wider budget deficit since its August 2026 review, which together have worsened France's debt dynamics from an already weak starting point, it said.
Persistent political fragmentation and a challenging social environment have made it more difficult for France to achieve sustained fiscal consolidation, noted the report, adding that however, the country's rating remains supported by its large, wealthy and diversified economy, strong institutions, membership in the euro area and resilient banking sector.
Fitch forecasts France's public debt-to-GDP ratio to rise from 115.7 percent in 2025 to around 124 percent in 2028, up from its previous forecast of 122.7 percent. It noted that a large share of public spending is politically difficult to reduce, while the already high tax burden leaves little room for further revenue increases.
The agency also noted that the French government projected in late September that the budget deficit would reach 6.4 percent of GDP in 2027 without additional consolidation measures, up from its previous projection of 5.9 percent. The draft 2027 budget targets a deficit of 5.0 percent of GDP and includes politically difficult measures.
Fitch lowered its forecasts for France's real GDP growth to 0.5 percent in 2026 and 0.9 percent in 2027, from previous estimates of 0.8 percent and 1.1 percent, respectively, citing weaker economic data in the first half of 2026.
France's GDP contracted 0.1 percent in the third quarter of 2026, according to preliminary data released Friday by the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies. Fitch said the figure in the third quarter further highlights downside risks to its growth forecast. ■

====================================================================================================

Analysis of FDA reports finds Prozac’s sexual side effects vary widely, with some emerging years into treatment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:00:39 UTC
21:00:39 KST

A recent study published in Progress in Neuropsychopharmacology & Biological Psychiatry suggests that sexual side effects associated with the antidepressant fluoxetine are highly varied, involving severe sensory disruptions alongside changes in libido. Using computer modeling, the researchers found that the drug may interfere with immune and cellular stress proteins, offering clues about the biological mechanisms behind these symptoms.
Fluoxetine is a widely prescribed medication used to treat depression and anxiety. It belongs to a class of drugs called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. These medications work by increasing the availability of serotonin, a chemical messenger in the brain that helps regulate mood. While effective for mental health conditions, these drugs frequently produce unwanted sexual side effects.
Lead authors Jun Li and Xing Wang, along with corresponding author Honglin Hu from Nanchang University in China, initiated the investigation to better understand these adverse reactions. Previous research pointed to serotonin as the primary culprit, as heightened serotonin activity can suppress other brain chemicals like dopamine, which drives sexual arousal. The research team suspected that other biological networks, such as inflammation and cell survival pathways, might also be involved in these side effects. They combined real-world patient reports with advanced computer simulations to explore this hypothesis.
The scientists began by extracting data from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System. This public database collects voluntary reports of adverse drug reactions from patients and healthcare professionals. The team filtered the records from 2004 to 2025 to isolate cases where fluoxetine was listed as the primary suspected drug. They analyzed 997 reports related to sexual dysfunction to see if certain side effects were disproportionately associated with the medication.
The analysis revealed strong statistical signals for a wide range of sexual problems. Common issues like erectile dysfunction and decreased libido appeared frequently in the patient reports. However, the researchers observed the strongest reporting intensities for highly specific conditions. Symptoms such as a total inability to climax, decreased orgasmic sensation, and genital numbness showed unusually high reporting rates compared to traditional measures of sexual dysfunction.
Following the database analysis, the team calculated the time it took for these symptoms to appear after a patient started taking the medication. They only included reports that contained complete date information for both the start of treatment and the onset of the side effect. They used statistical distribution models to map out the timing patterns for different symptoms across the patient population.
The timing of the side effects varied greatly depending on the specific symptom. Some conditions, such as prolonged and painful erections or persistent genital arousal, emerged within the first few days of treatment. Issues related to sexual desire, such as a loss of libido, tended to surface after about four to five months. The most delayed side effects involved sensory and orgasmic disruptions, with reports of genital numbness and an inability to climax often appearing after more than two years of continuous medication use.
To understand the biological roots of these symptoms, the researchers turned to network toxicology. This computational approach maps out how drugs interact with the body by cross-referencing vast genetic and protein databases. The team first compiled a list of human proteins known to interact with fluoxetine. They then created a separate list of proteins and genes associated with human sexual dysfunction.
By comparing the two lists, the scientists identified 56 overlapping genetic targets. These shared targets operate within networks that control brain chemistry, including both serotonin and dopamine pathways. The overlapping targets were also heavily concentrated in biological pathways that regulate inflammation, immune responses, and cellular death.
The researchers built a digital map to visualize how these 56 targets interact with one another inside the body. This mapping process identified two core hub proteins that act like major intersections in a city traffic grid, handling a high volume of biological signals. The first is IL10, a protein that helps regulate the body’s inflammatory and immune responses. The second is TP53, a protein that responds to cellular stress and helps control when a damaged cell undergoes programmed death.
To see if the drug could physically influence these proteins, the team used a technique called molecular docking. This computer simulation predicts how a small drug molecule might fit into the three-dimensional structure of a larger protein. It operates much like a simulation of a key entering a lock.
The simulations showed that the fluoxetine molecule fits neatly into the structural pockets of both the TP53 and IL10 proteins. The binding affinity was notably strong for the IL10 protein. This physical compatibility suggests that the drug might directly attach to and alter the function of these proteins in the human body. The researchers suspect that fluoxetine might contribute to sexual side effects by triggering low-level inflammation or cellular stress in nerve and reproductive tissues.
Because the FDA database relies on voluntary submissions, it cannot capture the true frequency of these side effects in the general population. The reporting system also lacks complete information on drug dosages, the duration of treatment, and the patients’ other medications. These missing details prevent researchers from determining exactly how much of the drug is required to trigger a specific symptom.
The database does not track the severity of a patient’s underlying depression. Since depression itself is associated with bodily inflammation, it is difficult to isolate the medication as the sole driver of the immune system changes observed in the data. The underlying mental health condition may be contributing to the same biological pathways highlighted in the computer models.
The computer models used to predict protein interactions are entirely theoretical. While molecular docking shows that a physical bond is possible, it does not confirm how the drug behaves inside a living human body. Physical laboratory experiments and clinical trials are necessary to verify these biological mechanisms.
The study, “Deciphering the molecular mechanisms of fluoxetine-induced sexual dysfunction: Evidence from pharmacovigilance, network toxicology, and molecular docking,” was authored by Jun Li, Xing Wang, Yunfeng Zhang, Penglin Zhang, Zhenfa Tan, Ruizhen Huang, Zuhuan Xu, Zhiyu Zhou, and Honglin Hu.

Why You Shouldn't Toss Your Old Halloween Pumpkins In The Trash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

The only thing scarier than Halloween? Getting rid of a sad looking jack-o’-lantern when it's over.
When confronted with a rotting, deflating carved pumpkin, your first instinct might be to beeline to the trash as quickly as possible. But experts caution against doing so—warning that trashing pumpkins, and thus sending them to landfill, can release harmful greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.
“Everybody throws them out from Halloween to right after Thanksgiving,” says Kay McKeen, executive director at Scarce, an environmental education non-profit. “It's a huge burst of methane gas that's going into the landfill all at one time.”
Why shouldn’t you trash your pumpkin?
When pumpkins are sent to landfill, they release methane, a potent greenhouse gas that, over a 20 year period, is around 80 times more powerful at trapping heat in the atmosphere when compared to carbon dioxide.
The lack of oxygen in landfills causes pumpkins to rot “anaerobically,” which releases methane. They are also full of water, and when they mix with waste and moisture it creates leachate, a toxic sludge that can pollute the environment.
Though a single pumpkin might not do much damage, if you consider how many pumpkins are trashed each autumn, it adds up.
“Maybe if we had a handful of pumpkins going into that waste stream, that might be one thing,” says Chris Enroth, horticulture educator with the University of of Illinois Extension, which organizes annual “Pumpkin Smash” events to help people recycle and compost old jack-o'-lanterns and pumpkins. “But we have millions of people who buy multiple pumpkins. We're talking about hundreds of millions of pumpkins that need to be disposed of post Halloween, and it's just a massive amount of organic material that goes into the landfill system.”
How do I get rid of my pumpkin?
Composting sidesteps many of the harms that come with sending food waste, like pumpkins, to landfill.
“When we compost something, it's really a whole system that we're creating that introduces both water and oxygen, [and uses] microbes, bacteria, fungi, all the little decomposers,” says Enroth. “When we introduce those things, we get that aerobic composting process, so we don't produce methane, and we're able to turn those pumpkins back into organic matter that has nutrients and can be put back out into the garden.”
What’s the best way to compost? If you have a curbside compost bin or designated compost for your apartment building, you can throw it there. If not, see if there are any drop-off composting sites near you. Some areas even organize dedicated events for residents to drop off old pumpkins. Since starting “pumpkin smashes” in 2014, Scarce and Illinois Extension have saved over 1,600 tons of pumpkins from landfill.
Don’t leave your pumpkin out for animals to eat or dump it in a park—they can be harmful to wildlife. While pumpkins are generally safe for most wildlife to eat, some small animals, like hedgehogs, can become sick, different animal species congregating together could increase the risk of disease, and it can attract predators to residential areas.
As you’re thinking about composting, keep in mind that it’s not just pumpkins that are compostable. Food is the single most common material sent to landfills in the U.S.—and wasted food is responsible for 58% of landfill methane emissions. If you’ve been thinking about starting your own home compost, now is the best time to do it, says Enroth. “We often recommend to folks thinking about starting a compost pile, to try it in the fall because we usually have leaves, grass clippings, things to get that pile started. And you could incorporate that pumpkin into that compost pile,” he says. “It's a really good combination of materials for you to get compost out of it next year.”

====================================================================================================

Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:00:01 UTC
21:00:01 KST

The next time someone's supercharged AI agent attempts to make a phone call to negotiate a cable bill, it could be an actual human who haggles with customer service rather than the software.
That's because AI agents, powered by the bleeding-edge foundation models developed by companies like Meta and OpenAI, still can't reliably take actions across the web, particularly those involving phone calls. Former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer, who now helms agent startup Dazzle AI, says current top-tier AI models excel at surfacing online home renovation services for consumers, but might blow it when they need to book and schedule a rooftop upgrade.
"We're relying on the frontier models to give us good suggestions and a good candidate list, but we're checking that over to make sure that we're really delivering the type of service that we can stand behind," Mayer said, referring to how Dazzle funnels certain tasks to human contractors.
Digital assistants driven by artificial intelligence are currently gaining renewed interest thanks to Meta, OpenAI and others that are pitching the technology as capable of tasks like scouting the internet for shoes.
Meta's Muse, OpenAI's Dots and a host of other agents can accomplish a multitude of web-browsing feats, but it's still early days for the technology, and it often hits digital roadblocks. Those barriers typically involve tasks that would have an AI agent make a phone call, schedule a doctor's appointment on someone's behalf, or reserve a couch scrubbing from a local cleaning service, said Meghan Joyce, CEO of digital agent startup Duckbill.
For tasks that require real-world judgment, Joyce said humans still trump AI, and companies building consumer-grade digital assistants will need to patch in real people to take over. That's why Duckbill recently debuted an application programming interface, or API, intended for companies building personal agents to connect with human contract workers.
"We work on a model that is not dissimilar from Uber, where we boil tasks down into atomic bite-sized pieces," Joyce said, referencing the ride-hailing company where she previously worked.
Companies making agents can use Duckbill's API to delegate the tasks that the agent is likely to fumble. Duckbill translates those tasks into bite-sized pieces that the average adult can do consistently and reliably.
"And then we track what happens," Joyce said.
Confused agents
Mayer said that AI models can still lack common sense. She said a Dazzle AI super user attempted to have the technology simultaneously handle a series of home renovation projects involving a roof replacement, a broken window and the purchase of a glass tabletop.
But the AI agent, Mayer said, confused window glass with tabletop glass, resulting in the digital assistant "trying to figure out if he could make the tabletop fit in the window."
The mishap didn't last long, Mayer said, because Dazzle's technology flagged the task and outsourced it to a person to complete.
"Within a few seconds, the human had things sorted out. Whereas an agent would have burned a ridiculous number of tokens," Mayer said. "Or they may never have gotten to a good solution."
Shivani Poddar, CEO of personal AI agent startup Wajo AI, is also incorporating human workers to handle phone calls and even CAPTCHA tests intended to fend off bots from sites.
"I think AI plus humans, collaborative AI, is what you need to actually get the job done," Poddar said, emphasizing that people will stop using the technology if agents can't complete tasks.
Chatbot and agent interactions can be ultra personal and users have good reason to be concerned about the humans stepping in, particularly if the company didn't tell them how it works.
Meta employees previously raised privacy concerns about the company's internal test using human contractors to handle phone calls on behalf of its Muse AI agent. A Meta spokesperson said in a statement at the time that this kind of testing is "core to the product development process."
Meta currently doesn't use humans to complete users' Muse requests.
Duckbill's Joyce said her startup does "full background checking" into the 1099 contractors it uses, comparing them to drivers for Uber and DoorDash, "people who live here in the United States and want a source of additional income." Duckbill also uses contract workers from businesses that typically offer contact center labor to companies.
Mayer said Dazzle conducts background checks and looks for contractors with the same qualities someone might look for in a human personal assistant.
"We generally are screening for people who we think are extremely discreet and have good taste and good judgment, both in terms of how they interact with our users, but just the ability to kind of forget and compartmentalize that information afterwards," Mayer said. "I understand it's a point of privilege, but I've had personal assistants for some time, and I know how I want them, and I know how I guide them."
Mayer said that while foundation models are still improving, the market is in a "transitionary period" until the technology can perform more involved web tasks and phone calls as efficiently as people.
"We're not even trying to hide it, we think the human in the loop is a benefit," Mayer said.

Automakers like Rivian and Ford are ‘democratizing 3D printing’ to reduce costs and increase speed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:00:01 UTC
21:00:01 KST

DETROIT — Automakers including Ford Motor and Rivian Automotive are leaning into a new type of manufacturing line: 3D printing.
Manufacturers say it's helping them reduce costs and increase speed. The technology has been around for decades, but it's becoming more commoditized in the automotive industry, with 3D printers used to create everything from vehicle parts and accessories to tools for assembly plants and testing units for research and development labs.
"At this point, we don't have a choice but to scale up and begin using it through all factions of Rivian," Jared Beck, head of Rivian's additive manufacturing, told CNBC during a tour of the automaker's expansive 3D-printing operations in suburban Detroit. "We're going to be democratizing 3D printing for the entire company."
The benefits of 3D printing
Also known as additive manufacturing, 3D printing can create three-dimensional objects from digital designs by dispensing material layer by layer, much like a traditional printer does with ink on paper. Instead of ink, the machines use a wide variety of materials such as plastics, composites, ceramics and even metals.
Printers can range from hundreds of dollars for hobby-like devices to hundreds of thousands of dollars for specialty equipment, depending on how big the product being produced is and the material it needs. They can produce individual pieces or hundreds of smaller parts in a batch using powders and resins.
Rivian said it has spent more than $5 million on 3D-printing machines, with the cost of materials for the operations growing to about $1.7 million annually.
Beck said despite the costs, the machines typically pay for themselves within a year. He said the technology helps lower supplier tooling costs, streamline logistics expenses and cut production times for parts from weeks to days, if not hours.
"It's well in the millions [for savings], but the main thing is speed for Rivian," Beck said.
The all-electric vehicle company's latest expansion of 3D printing includes adding new machines that can build flexible silicone parts as well as installing a bay of machines at its plant in Normal, Illinois, for employees to print parts on demand.
"3D prints should be readily available for every engineer so that they can make a part and get it in their hands as soon as possible," Beck said.
Rivian has also used the technology for electric-motor models for fluid testing, creating screw guides for tooling and stamping press inserts and some production parts, including trim pieces to fill gaps in some early builds.
GM, Ford
There's a similar push underway at larger, more-established automakers like Ford and its crosstown rival General Motors, which have used 3D printing for many years, including in their massive assembly plants.
Instead of having a bay of 3D-printing machines like at Rivian, Ford has departments for additive manufacturing at many of its plants to produce and distribute needed parts. That includes a new vending machine for 3D-printed parts for production of F-150 pickup trucks near its Dearborn, Michigan, headquarters.
"By putting the vending machine up, all the team leaders have access," said Gregory Foresi, a Ford mechanical engineer who ran Ford's 3D-printing lab at the plant from 2024 until last month. "We're able to keep that thing stocked rather than have a bunch of parts laying around in the lab. So that's been pretty huge."
Foresi used roughly two dozen machines to print off thousands of tools, some of which have been designed by employees, such as torque bit sockets, hood jackers and hand tools for smoothing adhesive.
Employees can use an app to request that specific auto parts or tools be printed. Ford's 3D-printing teams help develop them or determine what to produce next, as the machining time to build different parts can range from hours to days, if not weeks.
Foresi said creating the tools with 3D printing has allowed the automaker to uniquely design them when needed, get them faster and, in many cases, receive them at a lower cost.
Ford also has used 3D-printed parts to help keep production running. For example, Foresi said a large machining wheel was needed to maintain assembly line production and the company was able to 3D print the part until a permanent replacement from a supplier was available.
"They didn't perform as well, and it's not really a replacement for the ones that we were purchasing, but they kept the plant running," Foresi said.
Ford said it expects to have 3D labs deployed at more than 23 plants by the end of this year. Its current 3D-printing program has more than 200 machines, and there are additional printers outside the official program, the company said.
GM has used 3D-printed parts for some of its low-volume products in addition to research and development and inside plants, including recently expanding its use of industrial Stratasys printers that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars based on use case, training and certification.
The Detroit automaker uses 135 components that are 3D-printed for its bespoke Cadillac Celestiq as well as other components for its performance Cadillac Blackwing sedans, including a unique medallion on the manual shifter knob.
Fadi Abro, senior global director of automotive and mobility at 3D-printing company Stratasys, said GM has been a great example of how companies can "standardize and then scale" 3D printing.
"The material properties improved so significantly that the use cases improved," he said, noting the company works with virtually every major automaker. "From a product perspective, we have to get the technology to become faster and more accessible, in an economic sense."

Spooky New Infostealer Malware Uses AI to ‘Autodox’ Victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.
New research shared exclusively with Kernel Panic shows that hackers have started adding AI functionality into a new strain of infostealer malware, making it possible for the system to automatically profile victims and quickly surface the highest value targets and their information. Dubbed “Volta-Autodoxer” because of how the malware refers to itself internally, the finding by Cisco Talos researchers sheds light on the ways that commercial LLMs are being used to augment and enhance the capabilities of established types of malware.
Often hidden in counterfeit software, infostealers are designed to live up to their name, grabbing usernames, passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, credit card data, and more from infected machines. Many of the biggest data breaches in recent years—from the widespread Snowflake-linked breaches that included AT&T and Ticketmaster to the theft of a terabyte of Disney data—have resulted from hackers accessing targets using login details gathered by infostealers. Overall, the malware has been used to steal hundreds of millions of credentials in recent years.
“Volta is pretty mature as a stealer. It casts a pretty wide net for what it collects,” says Ryan Fetterman, a security researcher at Cisco Talos. “It compiles all of those things together, ultimately producing a serialized dossier that it can send to a couple LLM models. It’s asking the model to act like an intelligence analyst and produce structured citation-backed assessment of the victim. It’s like a prioritization and analysis function.”
Talos flagged the malware using its new CAIRN framework, built to identify hacking tools that incorporate AI capabilities. Fetterman notes that Talos did not track whether Volta has been used in the wild.
Volta’s traditional infostealer capabilities are powerful and seem to be geared toward targeting younger internet users with robust digital lives. It sweeps for passwords stored in browsers, Microsoft OAuth tokens, cookies, payment cards, and crypto wallet seed phrases, but also active Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions. Then the malware does a second, deeper sweep using its first-round findings. By looking through the target’s Gmail or another central account, Volta builds a fuller picture of the victim, their location, and their habits using data like receipts and order history from services including UberEats and DoorDash.
Once all of this is done, the malware feeds its findings into AI tools for analysis using OpenRouter, a service that can send prompts to multiple different AI providers. Volta defaults its requests to Anthropic’s Claude Opus 4.6. But apparently preparing for the possibility that the model’s guardrails could block the activity, Volta is built with fallbacks to the Chinese open weight Moonshot AI Kimi K2 and, if that fails, Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash. Building in fallbacks and relying on cost-effective, older-generation models are common techniques among attackers.
Volta’s creators included a 240-word prompt, including bullet points and a numbered list, as part of their instructions to any LLM analyzing the collected data. “You are a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment from a structured evidence bundle,” the Volta prompt says. It instructs the chatbot to produce an “executive summary” about the person, details of what they do, “what they’re worth,” and a summary of “their opsec.” It adds that the chatbot should “connect dots across fields,” for example, checking whether someone’s Wi-Fi password matches their last name. “Go deep, not wide,” the prompt says.
“The prompt is pretty carefully crafted not to imply anything overtly malicious,” Fetterman says. “But they’re building in the expectation to potentially hit model refusals at first request. And so they plan for failover kind of cascading to more permissible models as they go down the chain. And there’s also the capability to still use the implant without the AI. The AI calls are kind of above and beyond, but the malware will still work without it.”
Some low-level cybercriminals and scammers have complained about AI slop filling up cybercrime forums, but security researchers are increasingly discovering other hackers using LLMs for coding tasks or analyzing troves of stolen information. Researchers at threat intelligence firm Crowdstrike, for example, recently told WIRED they had seen four distinct hacking groups with varying sophistication—operating in Chinese, Spanish and English, Indonesian, and Russian—using AI tools to compromise dozens of targets around the world, including government entities and businesses in health care, retail, and travel.
Cisco’s Fetterman says Volta contains some clues that it may have been built to sell to a range of attackers rather than being developed for one specific actor’s campaigns. And while the malware at its core is still a traditional infostealer, the AI expansion foreshadows even more invasive and sinister activity in the future.
“If you’re able to identify your high-value targets faster, you probably have a better chance of using their credentials or authenticating using stolen tokens more often than maybe you would have if you had to do that triage yourself,” Fetterman says, referencing the fact that authentication tokens expire and passwords can be changed. “We’re seeing more advanced capabilities accessible to lower-level sophistication attackers. It’s really interesting and disturbing.”

- At one point it looked as though Raman had a comfortable lead over Bass.

Late one afternoon, at the intersection of South La Brea Avenue and Obama Boulevard, Shirley Dace cold-called fellow Angelenos and encouraged them to give L.A. Mayor Karen Bass a second term.
“I love Karen Bass because of all the experience she has,” Dace, a retired flight attendant, told me between phone calls. “Karen Bass was raised here. She knows the city. ... I’ve seen her around at different events.”
Meanwhile, roughly 10 miles to the northeast, Christian Perez and Marium Mohiuddin organized a night of door-knocking for Bass challenger Nithya Raman in Boyle Heights.
“I think she’s incredibly intelligent and I want to give her an opportunity,” said Perez.
Given the ICE raids and general denunciations of immigrants, Mohiuddin, a Muslim and Canadian immigrant, said he’s been impressed by Raman’s outreach to minority communities. And Raman is an immigrant, too.
“I want a mayor that’s going to protect me,” said Mohiuddin, who speaks out against Islamophobia and antisemitism, “and I really feel like Nithya would go to bat for us.”
You may have noticed a pattern here. Lots of positivity.
Lopez: Disney built the monorail in a year. LAX’s people mover, almost 8, hasn’t left the station
Years of delays for the SkyLink people mover at LAX have led to finger-pointing, litigation and a grand jury probe into how a $1.9-billion project has become a $3.3-billion boondoggle.
I figured that with just hours to go before election day, you’ve heard plenty from me and others about City Hall dysfunction, about each mayoral candidate’s flaws, and about undecided and uninspired voters here in the land of budget-busting rent, broken sidewalks and blue tarps.
It appeared for a while as if Raman wouldn’t even make it out of the primary, and then it looked as though she had a comfortable lead over Bass in the runoff. But if the latest poll can be trusted, it’s hard to pick a winner. So today I’m going to shed every cynical bone in my body — only temporarily, I promise — and hand the megaphone over to people who unabashedly like either Bass or Raman.
And to be honest, in connecting with these folks on the phone, by text and in person, I was inspired by their interest in civic affairs (if only there were more like them), and their belief that their vote matters.
So here goes, and I’ll start with the incumbent.
::
Shirley Dace, as she worked the phones at Bass headquarters, referred to a five-page list of personal achievements and positive developments during the mayor’s first term. Violent crime is down, solar street lights have been installed by the thousands, Metro rides are free for students, thousands of affordable housing units are on the way and thousands of homeless people have been brought indoors.
“We have a homeless problem, and I realize that,” Dace said, but she believes there’s been progress. “It takes a while to solve these problems.”
One day I happened upon a social media post by Christian Green, who said he was driving by Bass headquarters and popped in to volunteer. I reached him by phone, and the West L.A. College professor told me he volunteered for Bass four years ago, too. Green said he was once in the foster care system, and said Bass has supported foster youth initiatives dating back to her time in Congress.
Bass is the first Black woman, and first female, to be elected mayor of Los Angeles. Given the history of the city’s power structure, economy and racial makeup, Green said, “that is not something we should take lightly.”
One of Green’s students in African American studies, 23-year-old Kioi Shropshire-Maina, also works as a Bass volunteer.
“I’ve heard about her since I was a kid,” said Shropshire-Maina, a communications major.
One of the things he likes about Bass is that her career has followed a long and varied public service trajectory. She first worked in healthcare as a physician assistant at County-USC, then became a social justice activist and co-founder of the Community Coalition, followed by a leadership role in the California Assembly and 12 years in Congress.
“She’s always been kind of like the standard of public service,” said Shropshire-Maina.
He pushed back when I mentioned that Raman seems to be the candidate with more backing among younger and more progressive voters.
“I definitely think Miss Bass has a lot of youth support. I’ve seen it myself. We organize events all the time, and people turn out,” said Shropshire-Maina.
“She’s the most progressive mayor Los Angeles has ever had,” he added, saying he thinks that has played out in her approach to homelessness. She inherited a huge challenge, Shropshire-Maina said, but moved away from policies that criminalized homelessness. “It started with her executive directive ... which made government be more proactive and work across departments, and not just rely on police.”
At Bass headquarters, Shropshire-Maina worked at one phone bank table while Philip Rosen of Hollywood and Christina Schiepe of Westchester worked another table. Rosen said Bass is a pragmatic Democrat who has been dealt a lot, with homelessness and the Palisades fire, “but she’s taken accountability,” and he believes Raman will be accountable primarily to the Democratic Socialists of America.
Schiepe, who had been to Bass headquarters twice previously, is 16.
“I can’t vote, but you know, at least I can do something that could help the cause,” Schiepe said, telling me her parents also support Bass, and one issue in particular stands out for her.
“We really are not happy with the ICE raids going on at the moment,” she said, and Bass “has done a lot to kind of combat that ... and try to get them out of Los Angeles.”
Schiepe said she wants to study political science in college, so who knows. Maybe she and Shropshire-Maina will run for office one day, and I can volunteer for them.
Now on to Raman.
Jane Demian, an Eagle Rock retiree and longtime activist and volunteer, said she would have voted for Bass if the opponent were Pratt, but Raman will get her vote.
Demian thought there were some bumps in the rollout of the mayor’s homelessness plan, but she thinks Raman did a good job as head of the council’s homelessness committee. She noted that Raman was one of the founders of the SELAH neighborhood homeless coalition, which steers people in the direction of housing and case management.
“I’m not put off as others are by her DSA connection. DSA is made up of people who want to provide economic support to working people,” Damian said. The “main focus is affordable housing, healthcare, and good wages for working people.”
Just as the Bass volunteers had their scripts to work with, Raman supporters touted the candidate’s work on renter protections, cleared encampments and a reduction in homelessness in her council district. I met with Mid-City residents Perez and Mohiuddin at La Monarca in Boyle Heights, where they were distributing literature to volunteer door-knockers.
As mayoral election day nears, four people talk about how they escaped homelessness.
Perez, who works in post-production, and Mohiuddin, who works in communications, both like the specificity they hear in Raman’s comments about homelessness, City Hall accountability and greater urgency in problem-solving.
“When I see Nithya Raman speak, I see someone who’s sincere, who’s kind of a wonk,” and isn’t afraid to dive into policy minutiae, said Perez, or to forge a path independent of the political establishment or dependent on endorsements from fellow council members.
Perez and Mohiuddin voted for Bass four years ago, but don’t think she’s earned a second term.
“It’s very hard to find an Angeleno who’s happy with government,” Perez said.
The change Mohiuddin wants to see, she told me, is simple. She wants for a candidate “to say something’s going to happen, and then stick to it.”
As Perez sees it, Bass has attempted to position herself as the candidate of the people.
“But in canvassing and speaking to people throughout the city ... there’s a lot of people who are disappointed with the status quo and perhaps not enough has happened in the last four years to justify them giving [her] another shot,” he said. “So I do think there is an aspect of [voters being hungry for] fresh blood and energy in order to confront the emergencies the city is facing.”
Whatever the outcome on election day, Mohiuddin said, there will be a victory of sorts.
“We’re still going to have a woman leading the city.”

DPR Korea: Isolation deepens even as the country changes, says UN rights official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

DPR Korea: Isolation deepens even as the country changes, says UN rights official
The Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) is building factories and hospitals, rolling out smartphones and mobile banking, and passing new laws at an unprecedented rate. But its people are more cut off from the outside world than at any point in the country’s history.
That is the picture painted by James Heenan, head of the UN human rights office (OHCHR) in the South Korean capital, Seoul. His team monitors the DPRK from beyond its borders because, as he puts it, “almost no one” can get in.
Speaking to UN News in New York, Mr. Heenan described a country where hunger remains a constant, forced labour touches every family and the border with China is so tightly sealed that even illegal crossings have all but stopped.
Yet he warned against seeing the DPRK – more commonly known as North Korea – as frozen in time. “The country is constantly changing, like every country in the world,” he said.
UN News: How does your office monitor human rights in the DPRK without direct access?
James Heenan: Well, it’s a tricky situation because we don’t have direct access to the country. Almost no one does at the moment. It’s very closed. In fact, historically, it’s never been more closed. We monitor, therefore, from outside.
We prioritise information from direct witnesses, so people who have suffered violations themselves, or who have witnessed them, or whose family members have suffered violations.
We also rely increasingly on Government information because the Government of the DPRK publishes more and more information, particularly over the past eight or nine years. We use other sources such as satellite imagery.
UN News: How many people have you interviewed?
James Heenan: Well, we’ve interviewed about a thousand people. That might not sound like much when you’re coming from some other parts of the world, but when you are dealing with what is possibly the most closed country in the world, that’s quite a lot.
UN News: How does the country’s isolation affect ordinary people?
James Heenan: There are very few people coming in or out of the country. There is very little information coming in or out of the country. That has a pretty serious impact on people.
They do not have access to the internet. They don’t know what’s going on outside or even inside the country.
The international humanitarian community, including the UN, has not had access for five or six years now, so when there’s a disaster, they don’t have access to that sort of support.
For average people, I think another impact is that there’s no access to certain types of medicines or treatment. There’s no access to certain types of food and so forth.
UN News: What is daily life like for an average family?
James Heenan: It depends very much on your status in society, your Songbun, as they call it, whether you are – essentially – in the loyal class, a wavering class or a hostile class.
For everyone, there’s a very high level of surveillance from the earliest years, both at home, in the workplace and at school. You have the risk of Government working groups arriving at the house at any time of the day or night to check electronic equipment to see whether there’s any forbidden information.
Food has always been a problem in the DPRK. Every single person we’ve spoken to has talked about hunger at some point.
We’ve had people tell us that one of the ways they realised things were different outside the country was when they escaped to China and saw that everyone was eating white rice. White rice is a luxury in the DPRK.
I think forced labour is also part of everyone’s life. You have mobilisations. They call them shock brigades, where people are essentially required to provide free labour for public works.
You might be sent away for days, weeks, months or even years to work on difficult projects for no pay. It’s classic forced labour, and it affects the whole country.
In many places, schoolchildren are sent to the fields, particularly during harvest, to work. Our information and analysis indicate that it’s a form of forced labour involving children.
UN News: Harvests have reportedly been good. Why is there still concern about food?
James Heenan: There was a drought earlier this year, but the harvests have been okay.
When you add to that an unreformed production and distribution system, you can very quickly end up in a situation that may not be famine but certainly involves widespread nutritional problems across society.
During COVID, we saw starvation. We saw people starving to death. Not as badly as in the 1990s, but it still happened.
UN News: The government has emphasised economic development. Is it bringing relief?
James Heenan: The flagship programmes include things like the 20-by-10 project, which is to construct factories in 20 counties every year for 10 years. You also see a large amount of hospital construction.
This is welcome. Anecdotal evidence suggests that it is creating more jobs for people, and jobs that pay. There have always been jobs, but traditionally they often paid nothing.
The challenge is that we don’t know exactly what impact this is having on people because we can’t get into the country to monitor it.
We are concerned because we know from the weight of historical evidence that many of these large infrastructure projects can involve forced labour during construction.
UN News: What is happening with digital technology?
James Heenan: Our latest report talked about thousands of 3G telephone masts across the country. There are more than 20 types of smartphones available in the DPRK.
But the issue is that it all exists within a restricted environment, meaning there is no access to the internet. It is clearly also being used to, if not increase surveillance, at least make surveillance more efficient. So, technology is a two-sided coin.
At the same time, we know that people are very happy to be able to use their phones for mobile banking, which is now widely used in the DPRK.
UN News: What is your single biggest concern right now?
James Heenan: I think I would have to say that there is a real concern about isolation and the restrictions of people’s ability to move freely.
People cannot move in and out of the country, even illegally, which was always something of a pressure valve that allowed people to go to China, for example, to earn money and come back. That’s not even possible anymore.
If I may add a second concern, it is the issue of separated families. We still have many families separated between DPRK and the Republic of Korea, and to some extent Japan as a result of enforced disappearances by the DPRK in the past.
Those families are getting older and older. Hundreds or thousands of family members have died over the years because this is a long-standing issue.
The survivors are elderly, and we’re pushing for progress among all those countries, if for no other reason than as a confidence-building measure that would allow these families to meet.
It’s something that happened up until 2018, and we’re pushing for it to happen again.
UN News: Is there anything else you want to emphasise?
James Heenan: I think the situation in the DPRK is one where people sometimes think it’s unchanging, but it’s not.
The country engages with the UN. It engages on human rights issues. In that way, the situation there should not be forgotten.
We can’t just talk about the Korean Peninsula in terms of peace and security. We also have to remember the human rights dimension, which is the focus of the United Nations.

Samarkand: A ‘living museum’ on the Silk Road grapples with a tourism boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Samarkand: A ‘living museum’ on the Silk Road grapples with a tourism boom
As the sun sets over Samarkand’s majestic Registan, its last rays glint across the turquoise mosaics. Dusk settles on the ancient square where great trade routes have crossed for centuries.
Tourists linger at the stalls as the lights come on, lending the square an air of mystery.
The Registan is part of historic Samarkand, a UNESCO World Heritage site. But this is more than a city of monuments. People live here; schools, shops and workshops are open, and old neighbourhoods stand alongside new districts.
UN News visited ahead of World Cities Day to ask: how can civil leaders preserve its heritage while it keeps growing?
That question is at the heart of Samarkand’s “Silk Road” International University of Tourism and Cultural Heritage, which trains specialists in both fields from a campus in the city centre.
The university’s rector, Professor Muhsinjon Kholmukhamedov, told UN News that for centuries Samarkand was a crossroads not only for trade, but for ideas, crafts and cultures, flourishing in the eighth and ninth centuries and again in the Timurid era, when it became a centre of science, culture and the arts.
A first for UN Tourism
The university began working with the World Tourism Organization, now UN Tourism, in 2023 and renewed the partnership this year.
“We are the first partner university of this organization. We have established cooperation in several areas,” the rector said.
It is translating courses from the organization’s online academy for residents and preparing to open an INSTO tourism observatory – the first in Central Asia.
The observatory will track not only visitor numbers, but tourism’s impact on jobs, the urban environment and residents’ daily lives, as similar observatories already do from Barcelona and Vienna to Gifu in Japan and Nuevo León in Mexico.
Undoing the repairs of the past
Heritage preservation is another strand of its UN work, through a UNESCO Chair. One challenge, Mr. Kholmukhamedov said, is the legacy of restoration work in the 1990s.
“Unfortunately, gypsum, concrete and rebar were used then. We are now conducting research with experts and providing evidence-based recommendations on the use of modern composite materials that do not damage the historic fabric of the monuments,” he said.
Laser scanning lets researchers build three dimensional models of buildings and spot dangerous deformations in time. “If there is a critical tilt, we try to support the structure,” the rector said.
He calls Samarkand a living museum, where people go to work, meet friends and eat out beside monuments of global significance – a city that teaches its residents to value history.
Visitors feel that energy too. “Visiting Samarkand always reminds me of its special hospitality and energy. It is truly inspiring to see the city grow so vibrant and culturally rich,” UN Resident Coordinator in Uzbekistan Sabine Machl told UN News.
Why Timur chose Samarkand
Legend has it that Amir Timur picked his capital by having meat hung in several cities to see where it would take longest to spoil.
In Samarkand, the rector said, it stayed fresh longest – thanks, he believes, to the climate, the Zarafshan River and the nearby mountains.
Legend or not, Samarkand’s place in a fertile oasis at the crossroads of trade routes shaped its fortunes – and made it a welcome stop for merchants after arduous journeys.
A crossroads once more
Today, according to the rector, new railways are expected to connect Uzbekistan with China and Afghanistan, and on to South Asia, while a planned high speed highway should cut the Samarkand–Tashkent journey to about two and a half hours. Both are due for completion between 2030 and 2032.
The skies are busier too, with direct flights from Samarkand to more than 40 destinations.
A tenfold tourism boom
According to Mr. Kholmukhamedov, about 1.2 million tourists visited Uzbekistan in 2016, compared with nearly 12 million in 2025. He estimates Samarkand alone received around seven million visitors last year; more than 10 million came in the first nine months of 2026, and the city expects around 14 million by year’s end.
Many come for the food – not least Samarkand palov - a rice pilaf – cooked and served in layers with local sesame oil. Uzbek palov culture is on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list.
Homes for the people
Rapid growth is raising urgent questions about housing for Samarkand’s own residents – fitting, as this year’s World Cities Day theme is Urban Renewal: Affordable Housing for All.
More than 1,100 apartment buildings have gone up in Samarkand Region over the past eight years. UN-Habitat is now developing the Samarkand Housing Profile, Uzbekistan’s first, with the national Government.
Our generation’s task is to preserve Samarkand while making it future proof so that it stays liveable for future generations while keeping its identity, through resilient communities — Katja Schaefer
The city’s master plan to 2040 foresees a big expansion of housing, but also looks at the condition, energy efficiency, affordability and upkeep of existing homes – most of them individual houses. The Profile will recommend ways to make adequate housing more affordable, resilient and sustainable for all.
“In Samarkand, heritage is not only the monuments. It is also the mahallas, the traditional neighbourhoods where people live and where community life happens.
“The best approach is to upgrade homes and services in place rather than replace them: better water, heating and energy efficiency, sensitive renovation that respects the historic urban fabric, and new growth steered to areas outside the historic core,” Katja Schaefer, a UN-Habitat representative working on the project with local specialists, told UN News.
“Above all, residents should be involved in decisions about their neighbourhoods. Done this way, heritage and better living conditions support each other,” she said.
“Every era has left its mark,” she added. Much of the Soviet era housing and infrastructure is now outdated, and since independence the city has grown rapidly, at times without a plan, squeezing the green spaces that make it pleasant to live in.
Growing a ‘green city’
Ms. Schaefer hopes the new master plan and the Green City Action Plan will tackle these challenges together.
In August, Samarkand and Tashkent joined the Green Cities Network of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), a group of cities working towards greener, healthier urban environments.
“What struck me most in Samarkand is how much of its greatness came from being a meeting place. Its position on the Silk Road made it a crossroads of trade and cultures for centuries, and it drew scholars from across the region.
“Under Ulugh Beg, it became one of the world’s leading centres of astronomy, mathematics and science. That spirit of exchange and innovation is still part of the city’s identity,” she said.
“Our generation’s task is to preserve Samarkand while making it future proof so that it stays liveable for future generations while keeping its identity, through resilient communities,” Ms. Schaefer said.

‘They deserve to know the truth’: UN rights chief demands probe into staffer’s death in Houthi custody

21:00:00 KST

‘They deserve to know the truth’: UN rights chief demands probe into staffer’s death in Houthi custody
The UN human rights chief on Saturday demanded an independent investigation into the death of a Yemeni colleague held by the Houthis for more than two years, whose family learned of his death only weeks after it happened.
Mohammad el Shami, a staff member of the UN human rights office in Yemen, had been arbitrarily detained by the Houthi de facto authorities since 6 June 2024. His family say he died more than a month ago but were told only recently.
“Mohammad’s family has not received any explanation of the cause or circumstances of his death – they deserve to know the truth,” said High Commissioner Volker Türk, who described the loss as devastating.
Records and accountability
Mr. Türk called on the Houthis to disclose all relevant medical and detention records, preserve evidence and allow independent scrutiny of any stated cause of death. “There must be accountability for wrongdoing,” he said in a statement.
He said he was gravely concerned about the UN personnel still being held, including seven colleagues from his own office, as well as detained humanitarian and civil society workers. He again appealed for their immediate and unconditional release.
Dozens still held
Mr. el Shami was reportedly detained during a wave of Houthi raids in June 2024 in which 13 UN staff were seized.
As of mid-October, the UN said 71 of its personnel were in Houthi detention. In June, the Secretary-General’s office said one UN colleague had already died in detention.
Briefing the Security Council on 9 October, UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg said many detainees had serious health problems, which made their release all the more urgent.
“Under no circumstances can UN personnel be detained, much less charged with crimes, for undertaking their vital work on behalf of the Yemeni people,” Mr. Türk said in March.
Back to full-scale war
Yemen has been at war since 2014. The fighting pits Houthi separatists against the internationally recognised Government based in Aden.
The relative calm that followed a UN-mediated truce in 2022 has broken down. On 9 October, Mr. Grundberg told the Security Council that Yemen had “slid back into full-scale war, with hostilities spreading across multiple frontlines”.
The UN aid coordination office (OCHA) says more than 22 million people need aid this year.
“By detaining our colleagues, the de facto authorities are gravely undermining our ability to support the people of Yemen during a most serious humanitarian and human rights crisis,” Mr. Türk said. “I urge them to change course.”

Bangladesh records deadliest dengue month as deaths reach 418
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:57:00 UTC
20:57:00 KST

Bangladesh recorded its deadliest month of the year for dengue in October, with 173 deaths as health experts warned that the outbreak is likely to persist through November and may not ease significantly until December.
The country reported 418 dengue deaths and more than 133,000 hospital admissions between Jan. 1 and Oct. 30, according to Health Ministry data. October's toll surpassed September's 148 deaths, making it the deadliest month of 2026 so far.
The surge comes as Bangladesh is also struggling with the world's worst measles outbreak, which has killed more than 1,200 people, placing additional pressure on an already overstretched health care system.
Doctors said many dengue patients were arriving at hospitals only after developing serious complications, making treatment more difficult.
At the state-run Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College and Hospital in Dhaka, 279 dengue patients were receiving treatment after 67 new admissions in a single day, hospital director Mirza Golam Sarwar said.
"We are getting many patients in shock. Their blood pressure sometimes is too low to measure, and their oxygen levels are dropping," he said.
Medicine specialist ABM Abdullah said repeat infections, coupled with delays in diagnosis and treatment, were contributing to the rise in severe cases and deaths.
People who have previously contracted dengue face a greater risk of serious illness if infected again, he said, urging residents to eliminate mosquito breeding sites and seek medical attention as soon as symptoms appear.
The danger of repeated infections is a growing concern for residents such as Dhaka's Faisal Ferdous, who has contracted dengue three times, in 2017, 2024 and again earlier this month.
"This time, both my wife and I needed hospital treatment," said Ferdous, who is now recovering at home.
He said the couple fell ill shortly after spending several days at a hospital where their 5-year-old son was receiving treatment for an unrelated illness.
"Every bout has been difficult. After getting it repeatedly, you become increasingly concerned about the risk of severe illness," he said.
Health experts have also warned that the circulation of all four dengue virus serotypes is contributing to more severe infections. People previously infected with one serotype can develop more serious complications when subsequently infected with another.
Bangladesh has yet to introduce a dengue vaccine, although authorities are considering vaccination as a longer-term measure to tackle the disease.
Despite the October surge, entomologist Kabirul Bashar of Jahangirnagar University said the monthly death toll was unlikely to continue rising at the same pace. However, he warned that dengue transmission would probably remain high through November.
"We may see some relief, but dengue is unlikely to disappear in November. Any decline is likely to be modest, with significant improvement unlikely before December," he said.
Bashar said mosquitoes would continue emerging from breeding sites created by earlier rainfall, allowing transmission to persist even as weather conditions become drier.
He also pointed to changing rainfall and humidity patterns, partly linked to climate change, which are extending mosquito breeding seasons and allowing Aedes mosquitoes, the primary carriers of dengue, to remain active for longer.
The prolonged transmission season, combined with repeat infections and mounting pressure on hospitals, means Bangladesh is unlikely to see a substantial improvement in its dengue situation before the end of the year.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – A Chinese coast guard ship entered restricted waters near Dongsha with its Automatic Identification System switched off, the Coast Guard Administration said Saturday.
Dongsha is a disputed coral island in the South China Sea administered as part of Kaohsiung City. The Chinese coast guard has repeatedly sent vessels into restricted waters near Taiwanese islands, including Dongsha and Kinmen, to pretend it holds jurisdiction over the areas.
In the latest incident, the Coast Guard Administration located the Chinese ship northwest of Dongsha early Saturday morning, per CNA. A patrol ship found the Chinese vessel entering restricted waters from the west at 4 a.m.

Saturday’s intrusion was the 13th incident of its kind this year, involving 16 Chinese ships. The Coast Guard called on Beijing to stop its campaign of harassment, while emphasizing its determination to take the necessary measures to defend Taiwan’s sovereignty.

Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal crisis explained: a decade-long dispute over legitimacy of the justice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:52:31 UTC
20:52:31 KST

The dispute over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal began in 2015, when the two main political camps, PO and PiS, clashed over the appointment of five judges. It later escalated into a wider conflict over judicial independence, the Tribunal’s composition and the authority of its rulings.
After taking office in 2023, Donald Tusk’s coalition moved to reverse judicial reforms introduced by PiS.
The dispute entered a new phase in 2026, when President Karol Nawrocki refused to accept the oaths of several judges elected by parliament.
The standoff reached boiling point on Friday outside of the Constitutional Tribunal’s headquarters, with both sides disputing the other’s legitimacy.
Euronews explains the conflict in five key stages.
1. 2015: Five judges, two rival appointments
The crisis began in June 2015, when the outgoing PO-PSL coalition changed the law to allow parliament to elect five Constitutional Tribunal judges before the October elections.
On 8 October, the outgoing Sejm elected Roman Hauser, Andrzej Jakubecki, Krzysztof Ślebzak, Bronisław Sitek and Andrzej Sokala. President Andrzej Duda refused to accept their oaths.
After PiS won the election, the new Sejm declared the previous appointments invalid and elected five alternative candidates on 2 December. Duda accepted their oaths.
A day later, however, the Tribunal ruled that three of the outgoing parliament’s appointments were constitutional, while two were not. It also said the president must accept the oaths of properly elected judges without delay.
This meant three seats had already been lawfully filled. PiS’s subsequent appointments to those seats were therefore challenged. The three disputed appointees — Mariusz Muszyński, Henryk Cioch and Lech Morawski — became known as the Tribunal’s 'stand-in judges'.
While PO-PSL had overstepped its powers by filling two seats prematurely, PiS also challenged three appointments that the Tribunal had deemed valid.
2. 2016–2023: Changes to the Tribunal and questions over independence
After taking power, PiS changed the rules governing the Tribunal, including how cases were heard, the number of judges required and voting thresholds.
In March 2016, the Tribunal ruled that the first set of changes was unconstitutional. Prime Minister Beata Szydło’s government refused to publish the judgment, arguing that it had been issued under the wrong procedures.
The dispute deepened after Julia Przyłębska became Tribunal president in December 2016. The three disputed PiS appointees were also allowed to take part in its work.
Critics said the changes undermined judicial independence and brought the Tribunal under political control. PiS argued that it was restoring the institution and reforming the justice system.
The conflict also reached European courts. In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the Tribunal's composition, including Mariusz Muszyński, did not meet the requirement of a tribunal established by law.
That year, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal also issued rulings challenging the primacy of certain EU law provisions concerning the judiciary.
By 2022–2023, divisions had emerged within the Tribunal itself. Several judges questioned Przyłębska’s continued leadership, arguing that her six-year term as president had expired. She maintained that she could remain in office until the end of her nine-year judicial term.
3. 2024–2025: Tusk’s coalition attempts to reverse the reforms
After the October 2023 election, Donald Tusk’s coalition made restoring the rule of law a central priority.
In March 2024, the Sejm adopted a resolution questioning the status of the three disputed PiS appointees and Przyłębska’s authority to lead the Tribunal.
Two reform bills followed in September. They proposed changes to the appointment of judges and the institution’s functioning. President Andrzej Duda referred both to the Constitutional Tribunal for review, preventing them from taking effect.
In December 2024, Duda appointed Bogdan Święczkowski, a former national prosecutor and close associate of Zbigniew Ziobro, as Tribunal president.
Meanwhile, the government restricted the publication of Tribunal rulings in the Journal of Laws, citing concerns over the institution’s composition. Its leadership said the move was unlawful and that its judgments remained binding.
The result was a deepening institutional standoff: the government questioned the Tribunal’s legitimacy, while the Tribunal challenged the legality of the government’s actions.
4. 2026: Nawrocki refuses to accept four judges’ oaths
The crisis escalated in March 2026, when the Sejm elected six new judges to replace those whose terms were ending: Krystian Markiewicz, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, Maciej Taborowski, Magdalena Bentkowska, Marcin Dziurda and Dariusz Szostek.
President Karol Nawrocki accepted the oaths of Bentkowska and Szostek but refused the remaining four.
His office cited concerns over the appointment procedure, including deadlines and the requirement for individual votes. It also argued that the president was not obliged to accept appointments automatically.
The government maintained that the Sejm had the constitutional authority to elect judges and that the president could not block their appointments.
On 9 April, the four judges took their oaths before a notary in parliament and sent the documents to the presidential office. Nawrocki’s office and Tribunal president Święczkowski rejected the move, arguing that the oath had to be taken in the president’s presence.
The Tribunal added to the dispute on 12 May, ruling in case K 3/26 that the president was not obliged to accept every appointment and had to be physically present for the oath.
The government challenged the ruling, pointing to the disputed status of judges sitting on the panel.
In May, the European Court of Human Rights issued an interim measure requiring Polish authorities not to obstruct the four judges from taking up their duties. The Venice Commission also said the president’s role in the oath should be ceremonial and that a refusal or delay should not prevent a judge from taking office.
5. October 2026: The dispute reaches the Tribunal’s headquarters
The conflict escalated again in October, when Maciej Berek also took his oath in parliament after receiving no invitation from the president.
Święczkowski refused to recognise oaths taken without the president’s presence and prevented some newly elected judges from sitting on cases.
On 30 October, judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska ordered a one-month suspension of duties for Tribunal president Święczkowski and vice-president Bartłomiej Sochański, citing provisions on the temporary suspension of judges. She then took over the management of the institution.
She said the move was necessary to restore the Tribunal’s functioning and allow all judges elected by the Sejm to perform their duties.
The existing leadership rejected the decision as unlawful, arguing that there was no legal basis for suspending the president and that judges sworn in outside the presidential procedure were not full members of the Tribunal.
The confrontation then moved inside the building. After seven judges entered the headquarters accompanied by State Protection Service officers, scuffles broke out. President Nawrocki arrived during the night and described the events as an attempted takeover of a constitutional institution. He called for urgent consultations with political leaders.
On Saturday, Święczkowski said he and the remaining judges would seek to regain control of the Tribunal. Korwin-Piotrowska, meanwhile, announced that she would convene a General Assembly of judges on 3 November.
What is at stake?
Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal crisis is no longer simply about appointments or who runs the institution. It raises fundamental questions about the separation of powers, judicial independence and the authority of constitutional rulings.
The consequences extend beyond the political institutions. When judgments are not published and state bodies disagree over their legal force, uncertainty spreads to laws affecting citizens, businesses, taxation and public services.
More than a decade after the crisis began, successive governments and presidents have failed to agree on a common solution. Instead, each change of power has brought new legal interpretations and further disputes over who has the authority to decide.
