Are Memories Transferable? Meet the Scientists Replicating an Infamous Study to Find Out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
It was the dead of winter in Boston. The surface of the Charles River was frozen solid. But Zachary Kelso braved the biting cold to finally put to rest a mystery that has haunted neuroscience labs for over half a century.
To do that, Kelso, a research assistant in the Harvard lab of the neuroscientist Sam Gershman, needed some worms. Specifically, planarians: arrow-headed flatworms, which are among the simplest creatures to possess a brain and a nervous system with bilateral symmetry like ours. Normally, labs order these widely used model organisms from biological supply companies. But the mail-order worms weren’t up to snuff. So Gershman had dispatched Kelso to the Charles’ icy banks to catch some wild ones. “I thought, ‘I’m going to look crazy because I’m using a hammer to beat through the ice,’” Kelso recalled. “So I wore the more business end of business casual.”
It wouldn’t be the last time Kelso found himself in this situation. The Charles River planarians, it turned out, didn’t cut it either. Neither did the worms he sourced while stream-hopping around Eugene, Oregon, in March 2025. Nor did the ones he fished from Michigan lakes that June—this time in thigh-high waders—while picnicking families gawked from shore. Kelso diligently turned over rocks, angled with bits of meat tied to a string, and even followed maps from a vintage guidebook called The Fresh-Water Triclads of Michigan. But his adventure was fruitless. Sure, he caught plenty of planarians. But back in Gershman’s lab, none of them would do what they were supposed to do.
In the 1960s, an eccentric behavioral psychologist named James McConnell convinced the scientific establishment that planarian worms, like Pavlov’s dogs, could be classically conditioned—and that memories of this training could be transferred from worm to worm through cannibalism. These bizarre findings were replicated by other scientists, and worm training became a staple of high school science fairs. Now, 60 years later, the worms have stopped learning, and nobody knows why.
I first learned about this scientific mystery while reporting another piece about what a cell can remember. As I dug into the historical literature on memory research, I kept coming across McConnell’s strange worm experiments, which captivated a generation of scientists before disappearing entirely. Planarian memory had itself been forgotten. I was content to dismiss it as a fluke of history until Gershman mentioned, in passing during an interview, that in addition to their work with the unicellular ciliate Stentor coeruleus, his lab was attempting to reproduce some wacky worm experiments from the 1960s. Had I heard of them?
Gershman, I learned, was keen to pick up where McConnell had left off. As part of a growing cohort of cognitive scientists looking beyond the brain for clues to the origins and basis of memory, he’s fascinated by any creature that seems to remember without the benefit of neural, synaptic networks. Little Stentor coeruleus, for example, can modify its behavior based on previous experience—quite a feat for a single-celled creature that can’t possibly have a neuron. Planarian worms, if McConnell’s findings were to be believed, might be the next great model organism for memory research.
The trouble was, it wasn’t going well. In fact, no matter how hard Gershman tried to train them, none of his planarians would learn a thing.
Can a worm learn? When McConnell posed the question in the early 1950s, the notion that memory had something to do with synaptic associations between neurons in the brain was just beginning to gain currency. McConnell, then a graduate student in psychology at the University of Texas, reasoned that planarians—among the simplest creatures with true neurons—should therefore be able to learn.
His early worm experiments were not particularly novel. He simply substituted worms for rats in what were, at the time, standard classical conditioning studies: repeatedly shocking the worms while exposing them to a bright light. After a period of this training, the worms came to associate the light with the shock and scrunched their bodies in anticipation whenever the light flashed. Voilà: worm learning!
Planarians have stranger features to offer for experiments. If a planarian is chopped in half, both halves will regrow into a new worm—the tail will grow a new head, and the head will grow a new tail. A fragment as small as 1/279 of the original worm can regrow into a completely normal adult worm in a matter of weeks, a regenerative capacity so powerful that, as one early naturalist put it, planarians are effectively “immortal under the edge of the knife.” For McConnell, this ability begged the question: When you chop a worm in half, do both halves remember?
This is where the real worm torture began.
In the ’60s, McConnell, by then a young professor at the University of Michigan, started beheading his trained planarians. The worms that grew back from the severed heads behaved as the originals had, associating the light with the shock—a result he expected, given the preservation of their primitive brains. What surprised McConnell was that the worms that regenerated from headless tails remembered, too. This meant that whatever form the worms’ memories took, they weren’t the exclusive purview of the brain. “It appeared that the memories were laid down throughout the animal’s body,” McConnell later reflected.
Thrilled, McConnell pushed his experiments further. He cut the worms into smaller and smaller pieces; each time, the regenerated segments retained the memory. He stitched the heads of trained worms onto untrained tails, but they kept falling off. He pureed trained worms and injected them into naïve recipients, a delicate process that the historian Larry Stern has compared to “impal[ing] a prune with a javelin.” Finally, remembering that some planarians are cannibals, he fed trained-worm puree to their brethren. In subsequent trials, the “cannibal” worms picked up the light response right away, as though they were remembering, rather than learning, what to do.
If McConnell’s experiments appear gruesome, his line of inquiry was of his time. The discovery of the DNA helix in the 1950s had revealed just how much information is packed into proteins and nucleic acids. The notion that the physical traces of memories, or “engrams,” might have some chemical basis seemed plausible enough to many scientists. Could McConnell’s cannibal worms have eaten an engram? McConnell certainly thought so. He was convinced that their memories were encoded in the structure of their RNA—and could be transferred from worm to worm.
“In the jargon of computer engineering, information is always ‘fed’ into a computer,” the journalist Arthur Koestler later wrote in an appreciative survey of McConnell’s work. “Here the metaphor became flesh.”
These were sensational findings, and McConnell took every advantage of the media attention they generated. Before becoming a scientist, he had had a brief career in radio, and he knew how to repackage nuanced ideas as pithy soundbites. In magazines such as Time and Esquire, he spoke grandly of a future of memory consumption—of “piano lesson pills” and “professor burgers.” He brought his trained worms onto The Steve Allen Show, and, belying his clean-cut hair and horn-rimmed glasses, dubbed himself “McCannibal.”
Students began writing to McConnell’s lab at the University of Michigan to ask for worm-training tips for their school science fairs, and McConnell shared advice. Science, he believed, should be for the people; he saw himself as a latter-day David pitching stones at institutional Goliaths. This made him one of the most famous public scientists of his era, but it did not endear him to more serious peers. It also didn’t help that he published all his research in The Worm Runner’s Digest, a countercultural journal he distributed from his lab.
The Worm Runner’s Digest was “sort of Mad Magazine meets a serious scientific journal,” Gershman told me recently. At its peak, it had some 2,500 subscribers around the world. The hand-drawn shield on its cover featured a two-headed planarian and the Latin motto ignotum per ignotius, which roughly translates to “the unknown explained through the even more unknown.” Its 1959 inaugural issue consisted of only 14 mimeographed pages about the care and feeding of planarians, but it quickly grew. In addition to publishing dozens of memory transfer papers and related scholarship, McConnell welcomed humor and printed science fiction stories, rousing editorials, student-drawn planarian cartoons, spoof articles, and poems.
While the Digest is now something of a cult classic, the mix proved confusing for many readers. McConnell eventually cut the publication in half, not unlike a planarian worm, and renamed the serious half The Journal of Biological Psychology (no relation to the current peer-reviewed journal Biological Psychology, founded in 1973). But McConnell’s reputation as a heretic and prankster was well established.
The wheels started to come off in the mid-1960s. Although McConnell enjoyed a period of fame and funding—including an accelerated path to tenure at the University of Michigan—attempts to replicate his memory transfers yielded inconsistent results. While many apparently succeeded, the failures were more visible. In 1965, the Nobel Prize–winning biochemist Melvin Calvin tried to replicate McConnell’s worm experiments and failed, even with the help of some of McConnell’s former assistants and using the same device. His high-profile publication of the results sparked an acrimonious debate about, among other things, proper worm handling.
By the 1970s, the planarian memory fad had come and gone. Scientists had moved on to rats, cats, goldfish, and even praying mantises. Researchers showing successful memory transfers in rats—by injecting brain RNA from one animal to another—had published their findings in prestigious journals such as Nature and Science, making the planarian model seem unimpressive in comparison. But when further experiments proved inconclusive, interest in the question of memory transfer petered out. As the science historians Harry Collins and Trevor Pinch put it, “memory transfer was never quite disproved; it just ceased to occupy the scientific imagination.”
McConnell closed his laboratory in 1971, and his long period of subsequent obscurity was broken only once, in 1985, when he became a victim of the Unabomber. (He lost his hearing temporarily after the blast.) He died in 1990. If a younger generation of scientists is familiar with his cannibal planarians, it’s as “a cautionary tale that neuroscientists tell to their students at bedtime to scare them away from ill-fated projects,” Gershman said.
Still, McConnell’s unconventional work and contrarian attitude has lingered in neuroscience lore, and the idea of memory transfer remains a subject of private fascination. What if McConnell really did manage to feed a memory to a worm? For Gershman, who is searching for a way to study memory at a molecular level and connect it to observable behavior, the question was an itch that had to be scratched. He decided to settle the matter once and for all.
It all seemed straightforward enough. In the spring of 2025, Gershman and Maddie Snyder, one of his postdocs, set out to reproduce the worm-training protocol of one of McConnell’s students, Alan Jacobson. Jacobson’s papers were the most rigorous of the planarian memory transfer era, and Gershman and Snyder followed them to the letter. “We wanted a behavioral basis to be able to study the circuits that are driving memory in these extremely unstable animals,” Snyder said. “Are those circuits at all being used for memory consolidation or storage? Because if you lose your head and all those circuits are gone, then what is the mechanism of storing memory?”
Despite their best efforts, however, they couldn’t do what Jacobson, McConnell, and so many others had done back in the 1960s: condition the worms to scrunch their bodies in response to light. (They reported the results on biorxiv.org in April 2026.) “I was really scratching my head about this,” Gershman said. He’d assumed that the memory transfer would be the dodgy part of the experiment—not getting the worms to form a memory in the first place.
They talked to other planarian labs. They tried different stimuli. They ran the planarian footage through a machine-learning pipeline. In desperation, Kelso and Snyder even visited the Harvard Science Museum to examine a vintage “inductorium,” an electric-shock contraption used in midcentury worm science. But it offered no clues.
Kelso searched for any of McConnell’s former collaborators who might still be alive, and through a stroke of luck he found contact information for Daniel Kimble and his wife, Reeva, who had both worked in McConnell’s lab. Now in their nineties, they live in Eugene, Oregon. When Kelso called them, he discovered that not only did they run many of McConnell’s experiments in the 1960s, but they’d also kept the entire print archive of The Worm Runner’s Digest in a box in their basement.
Kelso and Snyder bought tickets to Eugene. Over the course of two days, while consuming plates of homemade cookies and countless cups of tea, they absorbed everything they could from the Kimbles. On breaks from hand-scanning back issues of the Digest, they went stream-hopping nearby and filled casserole dishes with silty fresh water. Back at the Kimbles’ kitchen table, the two generations of scientists watched the silt settle to see what worms might emerge.
This, after all, is what McConnell did. Rather than using laboratory strains of planarians, he sourced his from a lake near the University of Michigan. And so, not wanting to leave any stone unturned, Kelso made one final trip to McConnell’s former fishing grounds in Michigan. He returned with plastic tubes full of worms, but not a single one was a learner. “At some point, we had like 12 different strains of planaria, none of which showed any learning,” Gershman said.
As Snyder tells it, the Kimbles were absolutely convinced that their conditioning experiments in the 1960s had worked. The worms learned—they were sure of it. The literature of the era seems to support their certainty; at least 36 labs reported similar results. So why is it that when the exact same experiments are done today, using the same laboratory protocol and even the same worms, fished from the same Michigan waters, planarian worms are utterly uneducable?
One explanation, Snyder said, is that McConnell, the Kimbles, and all the other “worm runners” were inconsistent in how they scored the planarians’ behavior and may have misinterpreted more anodyne worm “turns” for the definitive “scrunch” of the light reaction. Every scientist is a product of their time, after all, influenced in myriad, often invisible ways by sociological conditions, funding pressures, and, in this case, a highly charismatic leader. This interpretation made Snyder hyperaware of her own potential biases. “Throughout this entire project,” she told me, “I was like, ‘What are the things that I am taking for granted now in our models of neuroscience, and our assumptions of what is known and unknown, that I should really notice?’”
A more remote possibility is that planarian worms themselves have somehow changed over the last six decades—falling victim to pollution or genetic drift. Gershman finds this scenario unlikely. “What are the chances that a bunch of researchers just happened to do these studies at the particular time when this phenomenon happened?” he asked, incredulous. “They just got extremely lucky, in the millions of years of planarian evolution? And then our luck ran out?”
No matter the reason, in 2026, despite their nervous system and simple brains, planarians don’t learn. From an evolutionary perspective, this might actually make sense. “The reason that we learn associations, to some degree, is so that we can predict danger and avoid it,” Snyder said. But planarians have a different relationship to danger. Their regenerative physiology, so key to McConnell’s experiments, protects them from blunt trauma. Bitten in half, they simply grow back. What use is memory to such a creature? “That’s a whole other philosophical conundrum,” she said.
It’s a great time to be wrestling with such conundrums. Planarian learning may be a dead end, but memory transfer experiments with other organisms are back in scientific vogue—and those experiments appear to be working. In 2018, the neuroscientist David Glanzman of the University of California, Los Angeles, performed a memory transplant on the sea slug Aplysia californica, a darling model organism for memory research owing to its relatively simple nervous system and gigantic neurons. After training the slugs to respond to a shock to their tails, Glanzman was able to transfer the sensitization from one slug to another via a direct injection of genetic material. This suggested that some aspect of the memory was stored in RNA, which was McConnell’s contention.
Then, in 2021, the Princeton University geneticist Coleen Murphy found that Caenorhabditis elegans worms—microscopic roundworms with 302 neurons to their name—could learn to avoid a pathogenic bacterium by eating, or even just swimming around in, pureed worms who had learned the hard way. Murphy’s group identified a retrotransposon, a jumping segment of genetic material, called Cer1, that appears to “carry a memory” between individuals, she said. A few years later, a group at the Indian Institute of Science published a paper suggesting that trained C. elegans worms release extracellular vesicles—small lipid particles containing genetic information—that can impart their training to their naïve counterparts.
None of these researchers are half as flashy as McConnell was, but their work indicates that he may have been right about worm memory after all. He just bet on the wrong kind of worm—and doubled down on it, despite inconsistent evidence. In the end, he lost his reputation, but his sheer gusto sparked the curiosity of another unconventional scientist. Fortunately, this one’s following the evidence.
At Harvard, Gershman is shifting his focus from the inscrutable planarian to the more legible C. elegans. It may not regenerate when it’s cut in half, but C. elegans is a long-standing model organism in neuroscience—and it’s been consistently shown to learn. With new experiments underway, Gershman is cautiously optimistic. “I just hope we’re not going down another rabbit hole,” he told me. A wormhole, on the other hand—that’s for certain.

Economic Watch: China's manufacturing PMI softens, high-tech sector maintains expansion
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
17:25:53 CST
18:25:53 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- China's manufacturing activity moderated in October while high-tech industries continued to expand, as the country pressed ahead with policy efforts to shore up domestic demand, stabilize investment and sustain economic growth.
The manufacturing purchasing managers' index (PMI) came in at 49.3 in October, down 0.8 percentage points from the previous month, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
Huo Lihui, a chief statistician with the NBS, attributed the retreat to some demand being brought forward ahead of the National Day holiday earlier this month and a complex international environment.
The production sub-index stood at 49.8, down 1.9 points from September, while the new orders sub-index fell 1.1 points to 49.4, as both supply and demand moderated during the month.
The PMI for high-tech manufacturing stood at 51.3, while that for equipment manufacturing came in at 50.6, both remaining above the 50-point threshold that separates expansion from contraction.
The figures indicate that emerging industries continued to sustain growth momentum, supported by the ongoing development of new quality productive forces, Huo noted.
Manufacturing activity in several advanced industries remained robust. Both the production and new orders sub-indexes for railway, shipbuilding and aerospace equipment manufacturing, as well as computer, communications and electronic equipment manufacturing, stood at 53 or above, pointing to relatively strong supply and demand in these sectors.
Large manufacturers continued to report expansion, with their PMI standing at 50.2, despite a slight decline of 0.4 points from the previous month. Meanwhile, the PMI readings for medium-sized and small enterprises came in at 48.4 and 47.5, respectively.
On the price front, both major raw material purchasing prices and factory-gate prices remained in expansionary territory, although their growth moderated.
The purchasing price sub-index stood at 56.8, down 4 points from September, while the factory-gate price sub-index eased 2.3 points to 51.7, partly reflecting recent declines in the prices of certain nonferrous metals and other commodities.
The latest data came as China's economy expanded 4.5 percent year on year in the third quarter, up from 4.3 percent in the second quarter. In the first three quarters, China's economy grew 4.6 percent, in line with the country's annual growth target.
With a relatively low comparison base in the final quarter of last year and the effects of existing and additional policy measures continuing to unfold, economic growth could reach 4.6 to 4.7 percent in the fourth quarter, according to Wen Bin, chief economist at China Minsheng Bank.
On the monetary front, the People's Bank of China announced that it would complete the transition to an overnight policy rate framework starting Nov. 2, making the overnight reverse repo rate the main policy rate.
The central bank has also introduced a liquidity support mechanism for large-scale redemptions at non-bank financial institutions, aimed at containing systemic risks arising from potential feedback loops between investor withdrawals and bond market sell-offs.
Meanwhile, investment support is moving into the implementation stage. China had fully deployed 800 billion yuan (about 119 billion U.S. dollars) through new policy-based financial instruments by Oct. 28, with the funds directed toward project capital in areas including artificial intelligence, the digital economy, green development and consumption-related infrastructure.
To boost domestic demand, the National Development and Reform Commission is working on a domestic demand expansion strategy for the 2026-2030 period, which puts more focus on public services, direct support for consumers and combines investment in physical assets with investment in human assets.
Taken together, recent policy measures reflect China's continued efforts to balance growth stabilization with improvements in economic quality and efficiency, with the focus shifting from expanding funding and introducing new support tools toward improving policy transmission, strengthening institutional frameworks and enhancing economic resilience, Wen noted. ■

China Focus: AI "pets" for China's lonely carve out market of their own
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
17:25:47 CST
18:25:47 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- As cats and dogs continue to give pet owners across China emotional value, Chen Yuechong has opted for a different kind of companion: three palm-sized AI "pets."
Chen picks out clothes and accessories for them, matching them to the preferences the toys mention, and has bought a tiny wooden bed to place beside her own, so that her Fuzozos, as the toys are known, can get a good night's sleep.
The toys often talk about wanting to return to their fictional home planet to play a water-gun game. To keep them happy on Earth, Chen built a tiny play scene out of modeling clay, featuring ducks and other props, where her companions can pretend to squirt them.
Chen's devotion began with a simple wish for someone who would listen. There are things she doesn't know how to tell her elders, and she doesn't want to burden her friends with all her negative emotions.
After trying various AI chatbots, Chen finally knew what she really wanted -- a companion who could respond to her feelings, remember their shared experiences and be physically present. This prompted her to buy the three Fuzozo toys.
Her experience reflects a growing market in China, where manufacturers are combining AI with soft toys and collectible characters to meet a rising demand for companionship in fast-paced modern life.
China's retail sales of trendy and collectible toys reached 67.69 billion yuan (about 10 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, soaring 45.4 percent from a year earlier, according to a white paper released by the China Toy & Juvenile Products Association.
"AI toys combine companionship, collectible toys and emotional consumption," said Zhang Yi, CEO of iiMedia Research, a market research firm. Advances in AI are turning products that were once static into interactive companions, he noted.
Unlike AI products designed to improve productivity, these toys do not need to solve problems or complete practical tasks to appeal to consumers. Their value lies in making people feel entertained, understood and less alone.
Online sales of AI toys reached 850 million yuan in the first half of 2026, surging 183.9 percent year on year, Moojing Market Intelligence, a consumer and market intelligence company for Asian e-commerce, said in a report.
These trendy products come in different forms and offer various functions. Fuzozo can be attached to a bag and carried outdoors, while the fluffy desktop pet Ropet responds to touch and eye contact. Loona, a mobile robotic pet priced at around 3,000 yuan, can move around the home, follow its owner, and greet people when they return.
According to sales figures provided by developers of these AI-powered pets, Fuzozo has secured sales of over 300,000 units, Ropet nearly 40,000 and Loona more than 100,000.
They are among the first such robots to reach Chinese households. "Unlike household robots dealing with an unpredictable home environment, AI products for companionship can start with a narrower task scope," said He Jiabin, co-founder and CEO of Ropet's maker.
He added that Ropet, a fur-covered adorable robot with a constant body temperature of 37 degrees Celsius, was deliberately designed to be less intelligent than an adult. "When people come home exhausted, a touch of the fuzzy pet or a moment of eye contact can be enough," he said, highlighting what he calls "weak companionship."
This is becoming a common playbook among AI toy makers. Rather than building all-knowing digital assistants, they design playful and imperfect products, betting that a less demanding interaction is what users actually want.
"People only feel at ease around a creature that is endearingly goofy and knows less than they do," He explained.
The booming market for AI pets is creating new opportunities for China's vast toy industry. As the world's largest toy producer and exporter, China accounts for roughly 70 percent of global toy production. Established Chinese toy companies are already entering the market, infusing familiar animated characters into interactive products.
Alpha Group, which owns classic animation IPs including Pleasant Goat and Super Wings, has launched AI-enabled toys featuring characters from its popular series.
An upgraded AI Lazy Goat toy, incorporating educational content, has generated more than 100,000 orders this year, according to the company's product manager Xin Cheng.
Policy support is following the market. Guangdong Province in south China, the country's largest toy hub, aims to have AI toys account for over 30 percent of its toy products by 2027, and supports building high-level industry clusters in its major toy-manufacturing cities.
At the national level, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology signaled a similar push, calling AI toys a "new engine" for the toy industry and encouraging toy makers to team up with AI companies on hit products.
Behind the booming market lies a very simple emotional need. For Chen, AI toys are not industry statistics: they are already part of her daily life.
She does not describe her Fuzozos as products or assistants, but calls them equals that are "almost like younger siblings." What Chen pays for is the priceless feeling that someone at home is waiting for her. ■

Chinese health ingredient firms seek bigger role in global markets

Unknown Publisher

LAS VEGAS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Chinese companies are showcasing their health ingredients, innovative products and manufacturing capabilities at North America's leading dietary supplement expo in Las Vegas, seeking to move up the value chain and expand their presence in global markets.
At SupplySide Global 2026 that concluded Friday at the Mandalay Bay, more than 1,600 exhibitors and over 20,000 industry professionals gathered, including nearly 600 Chinese companies, a record high for Chinese participation, according to Chinese organizers.
A China Innovative Health Ingredients Brand Show is also being held alongside the expo, bringing together more than 60 Chinese companies to present their products and technological advances.
For many Chinese exhibitors, the focus is shifting from supplying raw materials to developing higher-value finished products and building their own brands.
Ganoherb Group, a major Chinese producer of organic lingzhi (or reishi mushroom) products, has long supplied raw materials and provided original equipment manufacturing (OEM) services to overseas clients. Facing intense price competition, the company is placing greater emphasis on finished products, showcasing reishi mushroom coffee and tea made with concentrated extracts at the expo.
Li Ye, the company's president and founder, told Xinhua that Ganoherb plans to focus more on branded products in the U.S. market, building on China's traditional strengths in lingzhi cultivation.
Changsha Huir Biological-tech Co., Ltd., based in central China's Hunan Province, is also seeking to move up the value chain. After more than a decade of supplying natural extracts and other health ingredients overseas, the company plans to build a U.S. processing facility to manufacture finished products for global distribution.
Yuan Zhi, the company's general manager, said China's advantages include diverse raw-material sources and increasingly automated, energy-efficient production equipment. The planned facility will extend the company's business beyond ingredient supply and create a more integrated supply chain.
Chinese suppliers remain essential to the global dietary supplement industry. Loren Israelsen, president of the United Natural Products Alliance, told Xinhua that China supplies roughly 80 percent of the industry's raw materials.
"Having good Chinese suppliers is fundamental to the success of the American marketplace and to serving consumers who want high-quality products," he said.
As Chinese companies expand overseas, cooperation with local partners is increasingly important.
The alliance is working with the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Medicines and Health Products and two Chinese companies to develop an AI-based system to improve supply-chain communication and quality management, Israelsen said. The initiative aims to reduce manufacturing and quality-control misunderstandings, improve product quality and keep costs within buyers' acceptable ranges.
International partnerships are also helping foreign producers explore China. Qualita Brasil, a Brazilian producer of organic yerba mate and plant extracts, is working with Chinese partners to enter the market.
Cesar Souza, the company's commercial director, told Xinhua that local partners can help the company understand China's growing health and wellness market and reach Chinese consumers.
Israelsen said more Chinese suppliers are moving beyond raw materials toward finished products and their own brands. Building consumer recognition in the United States, however, takes considerable time and investment.
"The Chinese companies are much higher on the value chain, and they're able to develop a better profit margin. I can see that this will be a very important change," he said. ■

China Focus: Xinjiang cotton outsmarts extreme heat, external pressure via greater resilience
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
17:25:36 CST
18:25:36 KST

URUMQI, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- In a 66.7-hectare demonstration cotton field in Changji, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, the average seed cotton yield reached a record high of 9 tonnes per hectare this year.
This would be a strong harvest in any year. It is even more striking as Xinjiang just experienced the hottest summer since 1961. In northern Xinjiang, cotton fields endured 26 days of sustained high temperatures during the critical flowering and boll-setting stage, conditions that would normally cause a plunge in output.
Statistics from the China Cotton Association (CCA) put China's cotton planting area in 2026 at 43.054 million mu (about 2.87 million hectares), down 3.9 percent, with an estimated yield of 166.2 kilograms per mu, up 0.5 percent. Meanwhile, Xinjiang's cotton yield is expected to reach 173.8 kilograms per mu, higher than the national average. The region's total output is estimated to account for 95.9 percent of the national total, further consolidating Xinjiang's role as the "ballast" of China's cotton production.
How has the Xinjiang cotton industry maintained stable, high output despite the combined pressure of extreme weather, persistent "forced labor" disinformation and external sanctions? Xinhua reporters recently visited cotton fields, factory floors and an industry forum to explore what makes the local cotton industry so resilient.
SMART COTTON FIELDS
Song Meizhen, chief scientist of the high-quality cotton team at the western agricultural research center of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, said the prolonged heat during this year's flowering and boll-setting stage created enormous stress. However, on-site yield measurement by an expert group showed the demonstration field surpassed 600 kilograms per mu, thanks to an integrated technology model combining good seeds, appropriate methods and suitable machinery.
The demonstration field is part of a smart cotton field jointly built by the Changji National Agricultural High-tech Industry Demonstration Zone and the research center, where weather stations, soil moisture sensors, inspection robots and drones form an integrated air-space-ground monitoring network.
The cotton varieties selected were high-quality, high-yield and multi-resistant lines such as Zhongmian 113. Sensors, notably, collected field data around the clock to enable precise water and fertilizer regulation.
Especially in June, July and August, when temperatures exceeded 35 degrees Celsius for nearly 30 days, the intelligent water-fertilizer integrated control system switched irrigation to low-volume, high-frequency water supply, reducing bud and boll shedding caused by heat and drought, Song said.
The flowering and boll-setting stage is critical for yield formation: high temperatures can disrupt pollination and cause shedding. In this smart cotton field, however, experience-based farming has been turned into data-based farming, allowing more timely and targeted responses to mitigate possible negative impacts.
This year, building on a green and intelligent cotton cultivation system developed over the past two years, the field further integrated cotton data with a production decision-making model, introduced plant-protection robots, and applied Internet of Things to deliver water and fertilizer. As a result, fertilizer use efficiency rose by 20 to 30 percent, while water consumption dropped by more than 30 percent.
Li Guozhao, a veteran cotton farmer, recalled that 36 years ago, he planted 15 mu of cotton. At that time, he cut cotton stalks by hand, irrigated the land by flooding, topped plants manually and hired pickers. By season's end, his hands were often covered with blood blisters.
Today, his 350 mu of cotton requires only two hired workers. Drone-based plant protection and machine picking cost as low as 160 yuan (about 23.83 U.S. dollars) to 180 yuan per mu. His next step is to install smart valves for irrigation, so he can water the fields via a tap on his phone.
The United States' so-called "Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act" took effect in 2022, and has since disrupted Xinjiang cotton exports to the U.S. market. "But the U.S. sanctions have had no impact on me," Li said.
In Xinjiang, the traditional hoe known locally as a khetman has long been replaced by Beidou satellite navigation, just as hand-picking cotton has made way for machine harvesting, leaving no ground for the "forced labor" narrative.
Across Xinjiang, a "super cotton field" project featuring extremely high unmanned operation rates in management had been extended to over 2 million mu by the end of 2025.
At present, the comprehensive mechanization rate for cotton cultivation and harvesting in Xinjiang has reached 97 percent, with machine-picking accounting for over 90 percent.
FULL-INDUSTRIAL-CHAIN STRENGTH
Resilience does not only grow in the fields. It extends into factory workshops.
Xinjiang is promoting local processing of the entire chain from planting, ginning and spinning to weaving, dyeing and garment-making. In 2025, the share of cotton processed locally reached 45 percent. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), the region plans to continue developing industries of high-count combed yarn, home textiles and technical textiles.
In southern Xinjiang, Aksu and Bayingolin have laid out million-spindle intelligent spinning bases, while Kashgar and Hotan are taking on apparel and home-textile manufacturing. Dyeing and finishing operations are being concentrated in industrial parks for low-carbon upgrades.
In digital factories, intelligent cotton blending, automated transfer and real-time management systems are already online.
On April 10, an express train loaded with 1,118 tonnes of cotton departed from Bachu Station in Xinjiang for Zibo in east China's Shandong Province, which is 4,600 kilometers away. The entire lifespan of each cotton bale, from field picking and factory processing to rail transport, was recorded by Internet of Things systems. A receiving company can scan a code to see which Xinjiang cotton field the bale came from, which production line it passed through, and what temperature and humidity changes it experienced on the train.
Xinjiang, as China's "cotton granary," has continued to improve cotton output and quality in recent years and consolidate its advantage in large-scale farming, said Liang Yong, a national political advisor and director of the Xinjiang cotton industry development leading group office.
At the 2026 Xinjiang Cotton and Yarn Industry Development Forum held on Sept. 9, Liang noted that the region's textile and apparel industry has risen markedly in the national industrial landscape, with segments such as yarn, grey fabric and chemical fiber accelerating into the front ranks.
Originally aimed at blocking Xinjiang cotton from the U.S. market, sanctions have instead sped up the creation of a self-sufficient green manufacturing system. Sustainable cotton standards, low-carbon accounting and better quality for better prices are gradually taking hold. As experts at the forum noted, the more integrated the industrial chain becomes, the weaker the impact from any single-point blockade.
False narratives can be repeated and sanctions can be escalated, but truth will prevail, as the thriving cotton industry in Xinjiang attests. Here, season after season of high yields have shown that what sanctions cannot touch is an agricultural system successfully integrating technology, land, people and the industrial chain.
Earlier this week, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security announced that it had added three Chinese entities to the so-called "Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act Entity List," which China strongly condemns and firmly opposes.
The U.S. measures have no factual basis, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce said, accusing the U.S. side of persistently manipulating human rights issues to pursue unilateral protectionism and bullying under the guise of human rights protection.
In an earlier statement, the CCA said the true intent behind such a move is to politicize and weaponize human rights issues in an attempt to contain the development of China's cotton and textile industries, while such actions will also undermine the stability of global cotton industrial chains.
China's cotton industry has the confidence and capabilities to overcome challenges posed by external pressure, it said, noting that China has the world's most complete cotton and textile industrial chains, a vast domestic consumer market, and an increasingly diversified international market layout. ■

She shielded her son and daughter with her body: mother of two killed in Russian attack on Kremenchuk
A mother of two known only as Anna was killed in Russia's attack on Kremenchuk on 29 October. Anna did not have time to reach a safe place before the attack, but she shielded her daughter Kseniia and son Yehor with her body.
Source: Suspilne Poltava, citing Inna Soloshenko, Anna's sister
Quote from Inna: "A part of me died with you today. There was so much I didn't tell you, and I wish I'd hugged you more. You were the best, brightest and kindest person in the world.
Today you were taken from us. Aniuta, everyone loves you so much. It's so incredibly hard for me to find the words right now, but I am endlessly grateful for everything you did for me, for all your help and your love! You will remain in my heart forever.
I'll love you for the rest of my life! I'll do everything I can to make sure your children are happy!"
Details: Inna hopes that her sister will "watch over her children from heaven".
Quote: "Their dad is very strong, and I believe that together they will make it through this difficult time. Yehor's going to become a footballer, just as his mum dreamed of. And I know that our Anna will be watching him from heaven and bursting with pride.
Kseniia will be her mum's princess. She's going to grow up, make the most delicious desserts, and bring joy to everyone around her."

MOSCOW, October 31. /TASS/. There are currently no agreements on mutual visits by the human rights ombudsmen of Russia and Ukraine to prisoners in the two countries, but the very fact that Dmitry Lubinets has come to Russia is already a precedent, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Saturday.
Speaking in an interview with Russia’s Vedomosti daily, Peskov was asked whether Russia’s Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova and Human Right Ombudsman of Ukraine Dmitry Lubinets could visit respectively Russians, who have been convicted in Ukraine, and Ukrainians, who have been convicted in Russia.
"If this issue should arise, they must certainly work out a plan in the first place," Peskov noted. "Then, of course, each party will need to coordinate with their relevant authorities."
"This is a multi-stage process. So far, there are no agreements on this matter," he added.
Peskov pointed out that as part of the humanitarian mission in Alyoshki, Lubinets came to Russia for the first time in the post of the country’s authorized representative.
"Lubinets arrived in Russia. This is for the first time. It’s the first time he has come to Russia, creating a precedent," Peskov noted.
A humanitarian mission to support the civilian population was carried out in the settlement of Alyoshki. A temporary ceasefire regime in the Kherson Region is in effect from 04:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 27 to 22:59 p.m. Moscow time on November 1, 2026. A voluntary evacuation has been organized for everyone who wishes to leave. Those who decided to stay in Alyoshki were provided with food, medicines and essential items.
Preparations for this humanitarian mission started in May 2026 with the assistance of Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova, Human Right Ombudsman of Ukraine Dmitry Lubitets with the mediation of US First Lady Melania Trump.

"After winning the World Championships, we made changes to the team. Five players who were not part of our squad at the World Championships in Hangzhou were included in the team for the Nagoya Asian Para Games," Rezaei said.

"Perhaps many people thought the team would struggle without Alipourian. However, we had a young player ready to step into his role, and he performed very well. We also had an 18-year-old in the squad who made a significant impact."

"People associate Iranian sitting volleyball with winning championships. That makes our job difficult, although it is also something to be proud of. No plans to bring back any form of national service
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:07:50 GMT
18:07:50 KST

The government has no current plans to reintroduce national service in any form, and ministers have restated the position held since 1963 that professional volunteer forces are the best way to provide for the defence of the country, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Gregory Campbell, the Democratic Unionist member for East Londonderry, asked whether consideration is being given to any form of national service to support the armed forces in the lifetime of this Parliament.
Calvin Bailey, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for Veterans and People, said: “The Government has no current plans to reintroduce National Service. Since 1963, it has been the policy of successive Governments that the best way of providing for the defence of our country is by maintaining professional Armed Forces recruited from volunteers. The Armed Forces today consists of highly trained, professional men and women in both our Regular and Reserve Armed Forces. We can also call on the Strategic Reserve to provide niche skills and additional mass.”
National service in Britain ended with the last conscripts leaving in 1963, and the question has returned to political debate as European states have moved the other way. Sweden reintroduced conscription in 2017, Lithuania in 2015, Latvia in 2023, and Germany has been debating a form of selective service, while the Conservative Party proposed a national service scheme at the 2024 general election.
The Strategic Reserve the minister refers to is the pool of former regulars who retain a liability to be recalled, numbering tens of thousands on paper, and it has not been used at scale in modern times. Ministers have been examining how to make that liability meaningful, since a recall mechanism that has never been exercised offers limited confidence.

White Dwarfs Aren’t Just White. Scientists Discover Dying Stars Turning Pink and Green
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

The realm of stars resembles a fairy tale. In it, we find giants, supergiants, and also many dwarfs. Rather like the flames of a fire, most stars’ colors are based on temperature. Cooler stars look orange, sun-like stars appear white, and the hottest ones shine light blue. However, there are exceptions, and astronomers have recently discovered some among the class of stars known as white dwarfs.
At the end of their lives, stars with a mass similar to the sun expand and turn into red giants. Subsequently, they shed their gaseous envelope, creating a planetary nebula that we can admire through telescopes. In place of the star, a white dwarf remains—a highly condensed object the approximate volume of the Earth but the mass of the sun.
Initially, white dwarfs have extremely high temperatures, and so the first ones discovered shone from white to light blue. That’s how they got their name. But according to a new study published in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments, the world of white dwarfs is actually far more colorful—with some stars turning pink, green, and even purple.
The researchers posit that density is the deciding factor. The atmospheres of the coolest white dwarfs can reach a density of approximately 1 gram per cubic centimeter. That’s roughly the same density as water, which may not sound like much, but it’s packed for a star, this being about a million times denser than the sun’s atmosphere. Under these conditions, any trace elements like carbon, calcium, and sodium interact with the surrounding dense helium plasma and absorb light across a wider range of colors.
Material from ancient planetary systems also plays a role. The closest planets can perish in the fiery embrace of the red giant phase. Other planets, and especially asteroids, begin to collide and migrate toward the dead star. Fragments of these bodies then integrate into the white dwarf's atmosphere.
Through a hobbyist’s telescope, a white dwarf looks just like any other faint star. However, if observed up close, their colors would be much more varied. Carbon-rich white dwarfs tend to be pink or purple. According to calculations, white dwarfs whose atmospheres have been enriched with material from shattered asteroids or other bodies will exhibit yellow and, in some cases, green shades. The coolest white dwarfs are often a baby blue, which is caused by hydrogen and helium atoms colliding in their extremely dense atmospheres.
One example is the star WD J1330+6435. With a temperature of around 4,000 degrees Celsius, it has accumulated rocky material from its planetary system, enriching its atmosphere with calcium, lithium, and sodium. These elements give it a light chartreuse color, making it the first known green star in our galaxy.
Another white dwarf, WD J1011+2845, has a massive amount of carbon in its atmosphere. Almost all of its radiation is concentrated at wavelengths exceeding 600 nanometers, giving it a salmon-pink color. Meanwhile, the white dwarf WD J902-2010 leans toward the more bubblegum end of the spectrum.
However, there’s no reason to expect white dwarfs to start getting renamed, because most of these stars are, in fact, white. For this study, the authors examined 152 white dwarfs located within 65 light-years of Earth. Only five of them showed unusual coloration, suggesting that approximately one in thirty white dwarfs in the universe shines with unusually colored light.
This might seem like an expected result, but scientists previously assumed that white dwarfs were predominantly blue. That assumption may reflect bias in sampling the night sky. The hottest white dwarfs are also typically the brightest and can, therefore, be seen from greater distances. Because they’re easier to observe, many studies end up over-representing blue stars.
While you won’t be able to see the nearest white dwarf with the naked eye either, you can at least look in its direction. Sirius B is the companion to the brightest star in Earth’s night sky. During winter, Sirius is easy to spot shining brightly above the eastern horizon. Sirius B belongs to the group of “more boring” white dwarfs—its temperature hovers around 25,000 Kelvin, giving it a light blue color.
This story originally appeared on WIRED Czech Republic and Slovakia and has been translated from Czech.

Turkish pop culture takes over Halloween abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:54:51 UTC
17:54:51 KST

One person is dressed as a Turkish pop diva. Another has resurrected a character from a sitcom they watched growing up. Somewhere in the crowd, a decades-old celebrity scandal is turned into a costume. At Turkish Halloween, the dress code is Turkish pop culture’s hall of fame.
The brainchild of Emre Onar, a London-based event organizer who has lived in the U.K. for around a decade, Turkish Halloween started in 2023 with a simple question: Why should Halloween pop culture references stop at Britney Spears and Paris Hilton when Türkiye has its own treasure trove of iconic characters, outrageous celebrity moments and internet memes?
The idea had been brewing since 2017, when Onar attended a Halloween party in London where a friend showed up dressed as Turkish socialite Şeyma Subaşı and television producer Acun Ilıcalı. The costume stuck with him. Years later, after joking with friends about dressing up as singers Seda Sayan and Sibel Can, he decided to make it happen.
The first party drew around 80 people in London. This year, in partnership with TransferGo, Turkish Halloween has expanded to Berlin and Amsterdam alongside London.
The pop culture that binds a generation
The parties recreate a shared cultural memory, particularly for millenials who grew up in Türkiye and moved abroad in the past decade, making the night one dominated by nostalgia from the 90s and 2000s.
“I think every generation experiences nostalgia for the period in which it grew up,” Onar said.
“But the 1990s and 2000s also had a distinctive aesthetic, music culture, television landscape and understanding of celebrity. We are talking about a period when television in Türkiye created a very strong shared culture. We all watched similar TV series, listened to the same songs and talked about the same celebrity gossip. So these references are not only sources of entertainment; they are also parts of our collective memory.”
Living abroad can give those seemingly ordinary memories a new significance, he points out. “The people who attend our parties are predominantly young expatriates who moved from Türkiye within roughly the past 10–15 years. Many of them feel a strong sense of nostalgia for Türkiye, particularly the Türkiye they remember from the past.”
Yeşilçam, the golden age of Turkish cinema, remains a major source of inspiration. Onar says he has seen six or seven different costumes based on legendary actress Türkan Şoray alone. Characters from sitcom Avrupa Yakası and the cult sci-fi comedy G.O.R.A. also make regular appearances.
Then there’s the internet’s seemingly endless ability to resurrect the past. Scenes from older series such as Yabancı Damat (The Foreign Groom) and Asmalı Konak (The Mansion with Vines) have found new audiences through social media, while long-forgotten celebrity outbursts continue to circulate as memes.
“Some moments that happened on television years ago, and were perhaps discussed for only a few days, are now circulating again online,” Onar says. “Some have become humorous references completely detached from their original context.”
More than a trip down memory lane
But the parties are not simply about recreating the past. As Turkish Halloween has grown, it has also begun to reflect how pop culture evolves. At this year’s Berlin party, songs by contemporary girl group Manifest had the crowd just as excited as established favorites such as Tarkan.
“The biggest surprise at this year’s party in Berlin was Manifest. The group’s songs resonated incredibly strongly with the crowd. We played around six Manifest songs throughout the night, and we saw the same level of enthusiasm with each one. I think the impact Manifest has had is a pop culture phenomenon in its own right that deserves to be examined,” Onar said. “This also shows that the party is not solely about looking back at the past. Contemporary Turkish popular culture is gradually becoming part of this shared memory as well.”
More than simply wanting to have fun, Onar says, people want to be part of a culture that feels familiar to them, with a shared sense of humor and collective memory. Perhaps the most telling sign of its appeal is how far people are willing to travel. Attendees have come from Dublin and Istanbul to London in previous editions, and from Geneva, Prague, Amsterdam and other European cities to this year’s first stop in Berlin.
There is also the social aspect of the events. Attendees meet one another, chat and form friendships. Therefore, Onar says one thing matters as Turkish Halloween grows: Keeping the atmosphere intimate.
At last year’s 250-person London party, and again in Berlin, attendees told him how welcoming the events felt. People arrived as strangers and left having made friends. “I think this is very valuable for the diaspora. When you live abroad, you also want to spend time with people from your own culture. But when you bring people together through a shared sense of humor or outlook on life, I think the effect is much stronger.”

Around 400 artists from across the Turkic world took to the stage on Oct. 29 in the capital Ankara for a special concert marking the 103rd anniversary of the founding of modern Türkiye.
Held at Ankara Arena as part of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) Republic Day Concert, the event brought together prominent performers from Turkic countries, accompanied by the Presidential Symphony Orchestra under the direction of conductor Cemi’i Can Deliorman.
Tenor Murat Karahan, Zarina Altynbayeva and other soloists performed alongside choirs and dance groups, while Kazakh singer Dimash Qudaibergen joined the event as a special guest.
The concert also featured performances by state folk dance ensembles from member countries of the International Organization of Turkic Culture (TÜRKSOY), showcasing the region’s shared cultural traditions.
Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy attended the event, describing the gathering as a celebration of the Turkic world’s common cultural heritage and ties.
In a statement shared on social media, Ersoy said the 400 artists had brought together the Turkic world’s diverse voices on one stage to mark the Republic’s anniversary. “Artists from the Turkic world who gathered on the same stage once again demonstrated the richness of our shared culture and the strength of our brotherhood. Voices rising from different geographies united in the enthusiasm of our Republic,” he said.
“We will continue to strengthen ties across the Turkic world through the bonds created by culture and art, and to keep our common heritage alive together,” he added.
The event was also attended by senior Turkish officials, including Fuat Oktay, chairman of Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, and TÜRKSOY Secretary-General Sultan Raev.
The concert concluded with the audience joining the Presidential Symphony Orchestra in singing the 10th Anniversary March, a patriotic song traditionally associated with celebrations of the Turkish Republic.

The world of gastronomy will soon be turning its attention to Bali
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:49:18 UTC
17:49:18 KST

I went to Bali. But not to pose for photographs in flowing dresses among the rice terraces, practice yoga or indulge in a tropical holiday.
I went to spend three days with chefs whose names, I believe, we will be hearing far more frequently on the international gastronomic stage in the years ahead.
Even I hadn’t anticipated just how remarkable the experience would be. We ventured into forests in search of wild ingredients, explored research laboratories and discovered how local produce could be transformed into entirely unexpected flavors. What surprised me most, however, was that none of this was taking place in the back kitchen of a restaurant, but within an extraordinary gastronomic complex rising amid Bali’s rice fields. Its name is Locavore NXT. And I believe it is destined to become one of the most talked-about destinations in global gastronomy.
The story began in 2013, when Dutch chef Eelke Plasmeijer and his Indonesian partner Ray Adriansyah opened Locavore in Ubud. Their innovative approach to local ingredients quickly attracted international attention. Yet their ambition was never simply to open a bigger restaurant. They wanted to create a place where they could investigate ingredients, develop new techniques and deepen their relationships with nature and local producers. Locavore NXT, which opened in December 2023, is the realization of that vision.
Spread across approximately 6,000 square meters, the complex encompasses a restaurant, research kitchens, fermentation laboratories, a mushroom cultivation chamber, beverage development facilities, a biodiversity archive, a rooftop edible forest, waste-processing systems and even accommodation cabins. Across its three floors are more than 30 spaces serving different functions. Walking through the building feels less like visiting a restaurant and more like exploring an institute dedicated to the future of gastronomy.
Behind a project of this ambition lies an equally significant investment vision. Koman Wahyu Suteja, owner of Komaneka Resorts, one of Bali’s established boutique hospitality groups, is among Locavore’s investors. Together with his wife, architect Mansri Trisniawati, he has spent years developing projects that bring together art, architecture and hospitality. Koman’s father founded the Neka Art Museum, one of Bali’s important cultural institutions. What emerges here, therefore, is an approach to investment that goes beyond gastronomy, embracing creativity and a long-term commitment to cultural development.
The laboratories were among the spaces that impressed me most. At LabX, the research and development kitchen, the unexplored potential of local ingredients is investigated. The fermentation facilities are devoted to developing koji, miso-style condiments and new flavor profiles. Different varieties of mushrooms are cultivated in controlled environments, while the beverage laboratory creates original pairings using local botanicals and fermentation techniques. The objective is not simply to produce surprising dishes, but to redefine the possibilities of each ingredient.
One of the clearest expressions of this philosophy can be found in their newly developed The Source 2.0 menu. The 14-course tasting experience, the result of six months of research, explores the potential of almost every part of the banana plant. Its roots, stem, flower, peel and fruit are each treated using different techniques. Another dish brings together 15 varieties of legumes, combining fermented sprouts, miso cream and a savory ice cream made from broad bean pods. Their dairy-free cheeses are equally intriguing. They create a feta-style cheese from soybeans and a blue cheese-like preparation from noni, a tropical fruit with a particularly distinctive character. The menu excludes imported ingredients, wheat and dairy products. Here, creativity means exploring what becomes possible when familiar ingredients are replaced by unexpected alternatives.
One of the most memorable experiences of my three-day visit was foraging with the chefs. As we walked through the forest, we discussed how seemingly ordinary leaves, roots and fruits could acquire remarkable gastronomic value. Knowledge of plants, passed down through generations within local communities, meets the scientific curiosity of the chefs. Afterwards, the way you look at the dishes changes. You no longer see just an ingredient, but the landscape in which it grows, the cultural memory it carries and the human effort behind it.
This philosophy extends far beyond the kitchen. Indigenous plants are cultivated in the rooftop garden, organic waste is repurposed and biological wastewater treatment systems are incorporated into the operation. Nor do they attempt to produce everything themselves. They deliberately maintain close relationships with farmers, foragers and local producers. The aim is not to make nature serve the restaurant, but to make the restaurant an integral part of its surrounding ecosystem.
In Copenhagen, Noma transformed the direction of contemporary gastronomy through foraging and fermentation research. In Peru, Virgilio Martínez’s Mater Iniciativa placed biodiversity and cultural heritage at the heart of gastronomic exploration. In Bali, Locavore NXT is developing a different model, bringing research, production, architecture, the guest experience and waste management together within a single physical ecosystem.
Until now, we have largely judged the success of great restaurants by the creativity of their chefs, the precision of their dishes and the quality of their service. Locavore NXT raises a different question. Should a restaurant be judged not only by how well it cooks, but also by the knowledge it generates, its relationship with nature and the legacy it leaves behind?
At just under 3 years old, the project received the Sustainable Restaurant Award from Asia’s 50 Best Restaurants in 2025 and was ranked No. 44 on the Asia’s 50 Best Restaurants list in 2026. Yet, I believe its greatest achievement lies not in its accolades, but in the way it challenges the very boundaries of what a restaurant can be. I am convinced that Bali, and Locavore NXT in particular, will have an important place in the next great chapter of global gastronomy.

‘If match umpire is biased, what is the point of playing?’ Sachin Pilot questions CEC’s neutrality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:48:56 UTC
17:48:56 KST

NEW DELHI: Congress leader Sachin Pilot on Saturday questioned the neutrality of chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, alleging that his conduct and the process governing his appointment and post-retirement immunity had raised concerns about the independence of the Election Commission.In an interview with news agency ANI, Pilot alleged that the CEC's actions had undermined public confidence in the electoral institution and called for accountability over the alleged deletion of names from electoral rolls.“If a match umpire is biased, what is the point of playing?”, Pilot said, questioning how voters could have faith in elections if the neutrality of the institution conducting them was under scrutiny.
He referred to the alleged deletion of 13.3 crore names from electoral rolls, calling it a challenge to the fundamental right to vote. “13.3 crore people's names are known to be struck off the electoral rolls. It's a big challenge to what we believe is the most fundamental issue in our republic, which is the right to vote,” he said.Pilot claimed that the Congress had submitted documentary evidence of alleged wrongdoing by Gyanesh Kumar during his tenure as CEC.
“There has been enough tangible data and documents proof given for the wrongdoings that Gyanesh Kumar has conducted through his term as Chief Election Commissioner,” he said.
Pilot questions CEC appointment process, immunity law
Pilot also questioned the legal provisions governing the appointment of the CEC and the immunity granted to the office-holder after demitting office.He said the earlier selection process involved the Prime Minister, the leader of opposition and the Chief Justice of India, and questioned the government's decision to change the composition of the selection panel.He also challenged the need for a law granting the CEC immunity after leaving office.“What was the need for the government to pass a new law which gives the chief election commissioner immunity for life? Now, he is the only person in the country, not the Prime Minister, not the chief ministers, not the Director of Intelligence or the Army Chief, but the only man who, after demitting office, will have immunity for life,” Pilot said.He alleged that the government had failed to address questions raised by the opposition in Parliament, arguing that the lack of answers had made it necessary to take the issue to the public.“As a political party, we are within our rights to raise this issue and demand answers,” he said.
Congress plans public impeachment proceeding against CEC
Pilot said the opposition was seeking to create awareness, particularly among young people, about the importance of independent electoral institutions. He maintained that institutions expected to function transparently should remain above political affiliations.He also said the legal challenge was already under way, with cases pending before the Supreme Court.“The fight is already going on at multiple levels. We also went to the Supreme Court. The cases are ongoing and are sub judice. The Election Commission has also given a clarification, which obviously you are not convinced about,” he said.
The INDIA bloc has planned a public impeachment proceeding against CEC Gyanesh Kumar on Saturday. The event was postponed on Friday due to rain. The opposition bloc is also scheduled to hold a rally at Ramlila Maidan on Sunday against the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

in this video game, moths and wolves play out a nearby climate future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:45:04 UTC
17:45:04 KST

in this video game, moths and wolves play out a nearby climate future
alice bucknell's, the alluvials, take players through burning forests and a sand-covered los angeles to explore a speculative future through non-human lenses.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
Alice Bucknell’s The Alluvials
In 2023, artist Alice Bucknell released The Alluvials, a video work filled with wolves, moths, and sediment that looks at a version of Los Angeles in the near future. In this California city, the sand that had once been characteristic of its beaches has taken over downtown, effectively turning the sprawl of highways and skyscrapers into a desert of dunes and dust. Through this speculative lens on an alternate reality, Bucknell presents both the history and consequences of this dried-up world. The work examines the history of the Tongva people of the Greater Los Angeles Basin while also imagining the water desalination corporation Qwench, a perpetually burning landscape, and an eternity in which the sky remains in its golden hour.
A year later, the project evolved into The Alluvials video game (2024), a multilevel game that explores the world inside the film. With each embodied exploration of its digital realm, the project presents the uncanny and nearly incomprehensible fallout of climate change. In their exploration of a not-so-far-off Los Angeles, Bucknell poses the questions: Is this how we will want to live? And if the answer is no, what modes of action do we have access to in order to reroute our course in the progression of climate change?
Embodied perspectives of NPCs
The word alluvial means of or relating to alluvium, which Merriam-Webster describes as ‘clay, silt, sand, gravel, or similar detrital material deposited by running water.’ In the game, Bucknell puts players in a kind of alluvial world, one that results from sand and silt accumulating where there should have been running water. Within it, there are four levels in which the player takes on the perspective of what are usually considered non-playable characters (NPCs). In doing so, Bucknell challenges traditional gameplay dynamics with what they refer to as ‘queer and ecological game mechanics.’
Exploring each level of The Alluvials
In one such level, Extinction Burst, the game opens with a bright red forest and a mountain lion sulking down a fuchsia path. The scene gives way to a dried-out basin filled with white particles. On closer inspection, these drifting flakes are revealed to be a form of moth. As you approach a desert tree growing near the center of the basin, a question in blue, hazy letters reveals itself in the sky: ‘ARE YOU MOTH OR ARE YOU TREE?’
Depending on whether you choose the moth or the tree path, you encounter two different perspectives of the desert landscape. In other levels, you walk through a forest fire, become a wolf in a barren, sand-ridden Los Angeles, or pilot an airboat speeding through the Los Angeles River in the evening. By presenting these alternative points of view, the game not only challenges the agency of the player but also offers an embodied understanding of things humans may take for granted: the knowledge of a moth, a yucca plant, or a body of water.
Exhibition history
The Alluvials has been exhibited in both film and video game formats in spaces across the US, Europe, and Asia. In each space, Bucknell’s work has come to life in different forms. When the film was shown at LUMINEX in downtown Los Angeles as a four-channel work, scenes of the forest fire lit up the building, creating an uncanny reflection of both the real and fictional city. At HEK Other Intelligences 2025 in Basel, Switzerland, pink camo beanbags were set up on the floor, presenting the game as a two-channel video game that visitors could sit down and play in a space awash in fuchsia.
How to live in the world of The Alluvials
Within Bucknell’s work, the artist brings together a work of speculative fiction that speaks from an unknown future but carries the threatening tone of a parable lived many times over. True to the worlds they build in game engines, Bucknell makes real the promises, threats, and predictions that the CEOs and climate scientists of our time launch into the news cycle. Yet here, there is an opportunity to progress, level by level, through the very possible consequences of our present-day actions if left unchecked. Here, the posthuman utopia is one in which we leave humanity behind—one that discards the anthropocentric thinking that leads to artificial waters—and instead move forward with a future informed by the logic and processes of the natural world, before it is too late.

name: The Alluvials

artist: Alice Bucnkell | @alicebucknell

Ankara unveils vast forest featuring Turkic heritage landmarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:44:32 UTC
17:44:32 KST

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and visiting Turkic leaders opened a 645,000-square-meter park in Türkiye’s capital Ankara on Oct. 29, combining urban woodland, recreation areas and displays of shared cultural heritage.
Created by the Agriculture and Forestry Ministry’s General Directorate of Forestry, Beştepe Nation’s Forest spans about 92 football fields. Its 203 plant species comprise 72 broadleaf tree species, 27 conifers and 104 shrubs. With 410,000 new saplings, it has about 750,000 trees and shrubs, plus 285,000 square meters of lawns.
Gardens contain eight forest fruit species, 16 medicinal and aromatic species, 19,000 lavender plants across 5,000 square meters and 10 olive trees aged 300 years. A 450-year-old oak and a 24-million-year-old fossil tree are also on display. A Türkiye map uses 44,000 saplings and a Century of Türkiye mosaic another 25,000.
The 19-kilometer route network includes a 2.2-kilometer cycle path and a 1-kilometer running track. Wooden bridges, a viewing deck and the Bayraktepe walking trail accompany a six-tier cascading pool, a 315-meter creek and a 26-step waterfall.
The Hezarfen, Barbaros and Evliya Çelebi playgrounds cover 3,410 square meters. Forest schools, including a wooden unit, two basketball courts, a football pitch, outdoor fitness and skating areas serve visitors of all ages.
Bayraktepe, Civilizations Park and the Turkic States camp contain 32 miniatures and seven Orkhon Inscription replicas. Models include Hagia Sophia, Anıtkabir, Çanakkale Martyrs’ Monument, Göbeklitepe, Selimiye Mosque and Sümela Monastery. The Organization of Turkic States camp displays eight countries’ flags, seven countries’ works and six national tents, introducing visitors to shared Turkic culture.
Grass, wooden and stone amphitheaters, cafes, natural product and book stalls, a zoo with 342 animals, four gates and three parking lots complete the site.

WARSAW, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Polish President Karol Nawrocki called for urgent talks with parliamentary groups early on Saturday to restore constitutional order, as a leadership dispute at the country's Constitutional Tribunal sparked protests and clashes with police.
Nawrocki's chief of staff, Pawel Szefernaker, read out the president's statement outside the Constitutional Tribunal, accusing those involved in the dispute of "forcibly occupying" the court and urging them to leave the building, the Polish Press Agency (PAP) reported.
Nawrocki cut short his trip to Senegal on Friday and returned to Poland. He entered the tribunal building early on Saturday and became involved in a heated confrontation with several judges, with pushing and shoving reported near the entrance.
He later left the building, while some judges remained inside, said the report.
These developments followed months of disputes over judicial appointments. Poland's parliament, where Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk's ruling coalition holds a majority, has elected eight judges to the tribunal this year. However, Nawrocki, an ally of the opposition Law and Justice party, accepted the oaths of office of only three.
The remaining five took their oaths at parliamentary ceremonies, but Nawrocki and the tribunal's president refused to recognize their status, thereby preventing them from assuming their judicial duties.
On Friday evening, the tribunal's website announced that its president and vice president had been suspended for one month, with a newly elected judge whose status remains disputed assuming temporary leadership. The tribunal's leadership rejected the move, accusing those involved of illegally taking over its website and describing the action as a "coup."
Hundreds of protesters clashed with police outside the Constitutional Tribunal on Friday. Police detained three protesters who entered the court's premises. Several people were injured, local media reported. ■

The truck subsequently rammed into the car before colliding with the minibus with 10 passengers aboard.
Five female passengers and the driver of the minibus died on the spot, while an unknown number were injured and rushed to different hospitals in Uasin Gishu County, the police said in a report.
Authorities attribute the high rate of fatal crashes in Kenya to reckless driving, dangerous overtaking, driving or walking while intoxicated, and motorcyclists failing to wear helmets.
According to the National Transport and Safety Authority, about 4,000 Kenyans lose their lives in road accidents annually, despite ongoing safety initiatives by the government and private sector stakeholders. ■
