France on edge as Halloween protests threaten to reignite riots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:35:00 UTC
17:35:00 KST

France is deploying 70,000 police officers and gendarmes across the country as authorities brace for another weekend of protests and possible violence over rising living costs, deteriorating public services and growing dissatisfaction with President Emmanuel Macron's government.
The nationwide demonstrations, scheduled for Saturday, coincide with Halloween and come amid fears of renewed rioting after two consecutive weekends of unrest left shops, businesses and public buildings damaged in cities across the country.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has warned that the demonstrations carry a high risk of violence, particularly after dark, and pledged a forceful response to anyone involved in disorder.
"Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble," Nunez said earlier this week, describing the situation as carrying "a very high risk" of unrest.
Authorities are also concerned that protesters could exploit Halloween masks to conceal their identities. Nunez said existing legislation allows police to prohibit face coverings when there is a threat to public order.
The U.S. Embassy in France has advised American travellers to avoid areas where demonstrations and large gatherings are expected.
In Paris, authorities have imposed additional restrictions in an effort to prevent a repeat of the Oct. 17 violence, when rioters looted hundreds of shops and security forces struggled to contain the disorder.
Police have restricted union and Yellow Vest demonstrations to a route along the capital's outer boulevards, running from Porte de Bagnolet to Porte de Charenton, keeping marches away from the city center and major shopping districts.
Unions and student organizations have challenged the restrictions in court, arguing against the limitations on their right to demonstrate. Macron said Monday that marches would be kept away from central shopping areas to protect businesses.
Police have also prohibited access to Place de la Republique and Les Halles, two locations affected by the previous unrest, between 11 p.m. and 6 a.m. on Saturday and Sunday.
A separate 9 p.m. curfew applies to unaccompanied minors around the Champs-Elysees. However, a Paris court suspended an earlier curfew imposed on minors, ruling that it seriously and unlawfully infringed on freedom of movement.
The protests began in late September, initially driven by high school students angered by deteriorating school facilities, overcrowded classrooms and an admissions system they consider unfair. The movement has since expanded into a broader campaign against the rising cost of living, inadequate public services and government policies.
Trade unions and supporters of the resurgent Yellow Vest movement have joined the demonstrations, adding pressure on Macron's minority government as it negotiates the 2027 budget.
With public debt approaching 120% of economic output and borrowing costs rising, the government faces mounting pressure to reduce spending, leaving limited room to accommodate demands for greater investment in education and financial relief for households.
Authorities counted approximately 550,000 demonstrators nationwide on Oct. 17, when widespread looting accompanied the protests. Attendance fell to about 410,000 the following Saturday, when demonstrations were largely peaceful, although police made more than 1,300 arrests.
Government promises to improve education and ease fuel costs have done little to contain public anger.
"When I was little, I was told young people were the future," said Aaron Berthier de Grandry, a 15-year-old high school student from Nogent-sur-Marne, outside Paris, who planned to attend his third consecutive weekend of demonstrations.
"Well, if we, as the future of France, lack resources, that means France will end up collapsing."
The French protests have inspired youth-led demonstrations elsewhere in Europe, with rallies planned in more than 30 German cities on Saturday.
A youth initiative called Gen Z regelt, roughly translated as "Gen Z's got this," has called for demonstrations in Germany to demand improvements in education and health care, climate protection and more affordable living conditions, while opposing any return of compulsory military service.
Organizers said more than 140,000 people had registered their support online. Berlin police expected approximately 10,000 demonstrators to gather near the Brandenburg Gate.
Some businesses along Berlin's Kurfuerstendamm shopping boulevard have boarded up their windows in anticipation of possible unrest, although authorities said they had no specific information indicating planned violence.
In Spain, Catalan police prepared their highest level of alert in Barcelona after an anonymous network on TikTok known as Blocus called for further gatherings. Clashes during demonstrations the previous Saturday resulted in approximately 130 arrests, most involving minors.
Italian police also remained on alert following confrontations in Milan, Turin and Bologna, while calls for demonstrations circulated on social media in Belgium, the Netherlands, Austria, Switzerland and Portugal.
The growing unrest comes as France faces mounting economic and political pressure. Figures released Friday showed the economy contracted in the third quarter, adding to concerns over the impact of prolonged instability.
The Chamber of Commerce estimates that retailers have suffered more than 1 billion euros ($1.1 billion) in losses. Other estimates put the overall economic damage at twice that amount when uninsured property damage and lost business revenue are included.
In Paris, the approaching Christmas shopping season has brought an unusual contrast to the capital's main commercial avenues, where festive lights illuminate streets lined with boarded-up windows and security grilles.
Luxury retailers, including Hermes, Louis Vuitton and Burberry, were among the businesses targeted during previous outbreaks of violence.
The government is also pursuing legislation that would make rioters financially responsible for damage caused either individually or by groups they are considered to belong to, with penalties reaching 10,000 euros.

Delivery of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine will not begin before 2030
The delivery to Ukraine of 500 PAC-3 MSE missiles for Patriot air defence systems worth US$2.1 billion, approved on 30 October by the US Department of State, is not expected before 2030.
Source: Alex Raufoglu, a Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty correspondent in Washington, citing sources familiar with the matter
Details: The journalist noted that this does little to address Ukraine's acute shortage of interceptor missiles ahead of the winter.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for his part, also said on X (Twitter) that deliveries of these interceptors may not begin for several years.
Zelenskyy urged US partners to find a solution to provide PAC-3 interceptors while Ukraine faces an immediate need for them. He noted that Russia was striking Ukraine's energy sector daily, with more than 30 attacks on critical parts of the energy grid in the last two weeks of October alone, and said Ukraine had requested a winter support package of 100 interceptors per month.
Zelenskyy said 500 missiles would help protect Ukrainian skies in the coming months and strengthen Ukraine's position in negotiations. He stressed that the US and other partners had sufficient PAC-3 stocks to supply Ukraine during the winter of 2026-2027 and could replenish their arsenals in subsequent years through already contracted and funded production.
US Senator Richard Blumenthal also said it was a "disappointing catch to the announcement about interceptors going to Ukraine – delivery in a few years".
"Facing a hideously harsh winter & searing hardship from Russian bombs, Ukraine urgently needs air defence. America's green light to immediate aid would be lifesaving," he stressed.
Background:
- On 30 October, the US Department of State approved a potential agreement to sell Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) missiles for Patriot air defence systems to the Ukrainian government.
- Zelenskyy had previously said he was still awaiting approval from US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth for the delivery of additional interceptors.
- According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine has been receiving an average of only 12 Patriot missiles per month this year.
- Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara called on the E5 countries – Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Poland and Italy – to consider supplying 10% of their stocks of Patriot and IRIS-T interceptor missiles to Ukraine in exchange for future deliveries expected by Kyiv.

The Israeli army has intensified its military measures in residential neighbourhoods of Hebron in the occupied West Bank, deploying reinforcements across the city as its offensive enters a ninth consecutive day on Saturday.
The assault, which began on October 23, has displaced thousands of Palestinians and led to dozens of arrests. Troops have also demolished homes and facilities and destroyed infrastructure.
On Friday evening, the army imposed a military closure on the Ein Dir Baha neighbourhood and carried out raids and detentions targeting a number of young men, eyewitnesses told Anadolu Agency.
Witnesses said Israeli military vehicles stormed the area and soldiers announced over loudspeakers that it was a "closed military zone" where presence and movement were banned.
Footage published by local media outlets showed Israeli forces deployed across the neighbourhood and residents being warned against staying in the area.
Other clips shared online, including by Quds News Network, showed soldiers holding a group of Palestinians, forcing them to put their hands on their heads, and leading them away under heavy guard to an unknown location.
In the latest demolitions, local sources and eyewitnesses said the army razed the homes of Hamouda Wael Mohammad al-Jabbah and Ahmad Bassam Mohammad Ashour al-Jabbah in Ein Dir Baha. Israel accused the two men of carrying out a shooting in the Farsh al-Hawa area, west of the city, on October 23.
Illegal settler attacks
The army's operation has coincided with a wave of violence by illegal settlers. Five Palestinians were injured on Friday when settlers attacked a family with sticks, pepper spray and stones as they picked olives in the Tel Rumeida neighbourhood in central Hebron, and stole their harvest, according to the Palestinian Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission.
The commission said settlers also burned down an agricultural room and equipment in the Masafer Yatta area, south of Hebron, while farmers were prevented from working in the towns of Dura and al-Shuyukh.
The army launched its offensive after a shooting attack by two Palestinians on October 23 that killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three others. The army later killed the two attackers.
Since then, the army has sealed off the city and surrounding villages. It has seized homes in the Jalada and Ein Dir Baha neighbourhoods and turned them into military barracks. The early days of the offensive saw forced displacement, the demolition of homes, shops and other structures, the destruction of infrastructure, and Israeli flags raised over homes converted into barracks.
Hebron Municipality said on Tuesday that the offensive had displaced 4,969 Palestinians, representing 780 families.
The Palestinian Prisoners' Society said the army detained 110 Palestinians in the Hebron governorate between Friday and Wednesday.
The siege and closures have also disrupted education in 66 schools, affecting 2,872 students. Some 2,198 of them are under direct siege, while 674 were forcibly displaced and cannot reach their schools.
Displaced Palestinians are demanding an end to the military closure and the lifting of the siege on their neighbourhoods, so they can return home and resume daily life.

‘Bicycle for the mind’: The contentious AI claim disproven by school students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:30:30 UTC
17:30:30 KST

IN BRIEF
- Nearly 80 per cent of Australian children are using AI assistants every day.
- Experts warn an overreliance on AI could lead to cognitive decline and skills loss.
Artificial Intelligence is becoming increasingly common in classrooms and workplaces across Australia. But, could using the technology make us dumber?
The AI assistant, Gemini, said using AI could improve a person's memory and recall, problem-solving skills, and efficiency. It claimed that "cognitive scientists view AI as a bicycle for the mind".
"[It] handles routine cognitive labour, freeing up mental energy for higher-level creativity and strategy, provided users remain actively engaged," Gemini said.
However, former chief scientist of Australia and neuroscientist, Dr Alan Finkel, says otherwise.
"I don't think your brain, or my brain, needs a bicycle to orgment it," he told SBS News, adding that the AI assistant provided a "self-serving comment".
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"[It's trying] to convince us that it is there to help us achieve. Whereas, in this respect, it is there to replace what we do," he said.
Neuroplasticity expert and director at the Wicking Dementia Research and Education Centre, Emeritus Professor James Vickers, likened AI assistants to a "self-driving car".
"You no longer need to think about how you get from Point A to Point B, you just put yourself in the car and it gets you there," he told SBS News.
Vickers said there could be cognitive consequences from the use of AI to solve problems.
"The brain is very much a use it or lose it type of organ," he said.
"If you don't keep using it to tackle problems, then what you'll see is a withering of those functional connections that allow you to respond. The more you offload that capacity to AI or a machine, the less capacity you have to do that."
Almost 80 per cent of Australian children are using AI
In August, the eSafety Commissioner released a report that revealed that 78 per cent of Australian children use an AI assistant.
ChatGPT was the most popular, with 70 per cent of children using the assistant. Gemini and Copilot were each used by 20 per cent of the cohort.
The study found that 20 per cent of children used an AI assistant daily and 28 per cent used it a few times a week.
Over 90 per cent reported using the technology to find information or support their learning, 70 per cent used it for writing or editing and 68 per cent for entertainment.
Half of the surveyed cohort reported using an AI assistant for "personal or social reasons".
There's little research on what daily use of AI assistants does to a child's neurocognitive development. However, Finkel says there is global evidence that children who use it for their homework suffer lower learning capacity and grades.
Collaborative research from the University of Hong Kong and Stockholm University studied 13,500 school students who used AI to assist with their homework and 13,500 school students who didn't.
The two-year study found that while the students who used AI got better results for their homework, they scored 20 per cent lower in in-person classwork, than children who didn't.
It's a reality that's already showing up in Australia's national standardised school test, NAPLAN.
NAPLAN tests the reading, writing and numeracy skills of 1.2 million students across Years 3, 5, 7 and 9.
The latest results from August 2026, found that reading and writing skills were decreasing across every age group — with one in three children failing to meet NAPLAN benchmarks.
Finkel said that students who are turning to AI for help are failing "to really use their brain".
There was increasing tension between on-paper results and learning, he added.
"Somebody who's written a school essay as a draft or in dot points could say, "Listen, Claude or ChatGPT, can you take my dot points and turn it into a 2,000-word essay?". That person has then failed to really use their brain to consolidate their thoughts into an elegant expression," he said.
General practitioner and associate professor at the University of Melbourne's Centre for AI and Digital Ethics, Dr Grant Blashki, said students should use generative AI as a "sparring partner, not a stunt double" and recommended educators focus on processes over outcome.
"The dilemma for us as educators ... is if we are just giving students assignments that they can throw into AI, what are they learning from that? Reading an essay that they've just put into ChatGPT or Claude, what have we learnt there?"
He said he's adjusted his teaching methods to combat this.
"We've changed our assessments now to what we call "assured learning". As well as an essay, students have to do a one-on-one interview with us face-to-face, or on Zoom."
What about educators or professionals?
Blashki uses AI regularly as a doctor. With patient consent, he uses an AI tool to transcribe medical appointments.
While it saves him time and lets him focus on more complex tasks, there's a catch.
"When you've been using AI ... it can make mistakes. It can so-called hallucinate or make errors, or hear something wrong," he said.
"But when it's mostly getting things right, you can get a bit dependent on it."
This can lead to "skill loss" in seasoned doctors.
"For new doctors, if they're already going into the medical system where AI is embedded, or they get reliant on it, they don't learn to read the nonverbal cues and the gut feeling you get from practising medicine," he said.
Blashki, who co-authored the book Artificial Intelligence for Better or Worse, said the AI debate is very complex.
"I don't think it's as simple as AI bad, using your brain good," he said.
"We can be intelligent about the way we use it.
"As our successful young Australians go out into the workforce and the world, if we can make them smart with how they use AI, to my mind, that's a great investment."

Kärcher boss: Less regulation, more action to get Europe and Germany fit again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:30:30 UTC
17:30:30 KST

Kärcher, best known for its pressure washers, recorded €3.5 billion in sales in 2025 and employs 17,000 people worldwide. Its CEO warns of a 'perfect storm' and calls for a fitness plan for Germany and Europe.
For some time now, we in Europe are facing a perfect storm. Geopolitical crises are casting a shadow over the European economy. The unpredictable trade policy of the U.S. keeps threatening, without warning, to raise tariffs and erect trade barriers – a toxic scenario for free global trade and export-oriented companies.
Meanwhile, China is no longer merely a low-cost manufacturer but has become a highly aggressive technological competitor that, with its tremendous speed, threatens to outpace key European industries in future-oriented fields.
What is often perceived as pure technological supremacy or even innovative strength is, however, largely the result of a well-targeted governmental industrial policy. Massive subsidies in key strategic industries, along with a currency policy artificially focused on competitiveness, are leading to noticeable market distortions and overcapacity.
For private companies operating on a market-based basis, this creates an imbalance that makes fair global competition almost impossible.
Europe risks deindustrialisation
The consequences for the industrial heart of Europe are alarming. The loss of tens of thousands of industrial jobs and the decline in production volume show that deindustrialization is not an abstract threat – it is happening right now.
When plant closures and production relocations are being negotiated in key German industries such as the automotive and manufacturing sectors, it must be clear even to the most optimistic observer: We are at a critical turning point.
As a family-owned company with 170 subsidiaries in 87 countries, Kärcher has weathered these turbulent times robustly thanks to its balanced business model – combining B2B (editor's note: Business to Business, i.e. corporate customers) and B2C (editor's note: Business to Consumer, i.e. private customers) – and its unconditional focus on customers. We are investing significantly in research and development, setting new standards in autonomous cleaning robots and battery technologies, and driving digitalization across all areas of the company.
However, even innovation leaders cannot withstand increasingly challenging operating conditions and unfair competition in the long term. Considering the massive rise in structural and employee costs, expanding capacity or increasing headcount in domestic production is no longer economically feasible.
Reform fatigue and regulatory zeal are holding back investment
While the latest economic forecasts – which expect Germany’s growth to return to 1.3 percent this year – seem cautiously optimistic at first glance, we must not be misled by this modest increase. What we are seeing here is largely “borrowed growth,” artificially driven by special government funds, defense contracts, and subsidies.
A short-term boost fueled by debt is no substitute for a real, self-sustaining recovery in private investments. And the causes of the ongoing weakness are largely homegrown: a creeping reform fatigue and a regulatory frenzy on the part of government institutions that hinders rather than facilitates investment. Instead of promoting entrepreneurship, regulations from Brussels to Berlin are suffocating the courage to embrace change.
The ongoing uncertainty among people in Germany is also having an impact on society. The rise of political extremism is a clear sign that many people are calling for greater reliability and noticeable reforms. To regain confidence in our country’s economic strength and future viability, we now need clear direction and bold action.
For me personally, the attitude towards “working hard” has been ingrained in me since childhood on my parents’ family farm. Success doesn’t just fall from the sky; for me, it consists of 97 percent hard work and dedication, 2 percent talent, and 1 percent luck.
If we want to secure our prosperity and our social standards, we must once again recognize that value creation is the precondition for prosperity – and not the other way around. If you rest, you rust – that applies to people just as much as it does to economies.
Germany needs a fitness programme
That is why we need a real fitness program for Germany. Rigid rules, excessive bureaucracy, high energy costs, and steadily rising non-wage labor costs are poison for our business environment. If the total amount of social security contributions consistently far exceeds the historically critical threshold of 40 percent, then tax breaks, selective government subsidies, and special funds will amount to nothing more than ineffective paper measures as long as the business environment itself remains entrenched in its current state.
While the federal government’s political reform efforts are heading in the right direction, they fall far short of what is needed. Instead of tackling the root of the problem, authorities are allowing a flood of regulations to continue – regulations that tie up valuable employee time and cost our companies millions. Money and personnel that are needed for core business operations and innovation are being wasted on documentation requirements alone. This cannot be solved with cosmetic fixes.
We need the courage to provide real relief. A key lever for this would be, for example, a cultural shift within the administrative system: In the future, government departments must see themselves as digital enablers and service-oriented partners to the economy – pragmatic, fast, and AI-supported. If other countries are already moving toward eliminating reporting obligations overall, this must send a clear signal to Germany and all Europe.
More work, less bureaucracy, and a resolute trade policy
Furthermore, we should not avoid necessary debates on the labor market. Demographic trends require an increase in the overall volume of work in the economy. Incentives for overtime, flexible working hours, practical rules regarding continued pay during medical leave, and a noticeable reduction in bureaucracy when employing skilled workers are essential.
Those who reflexively condemn such debates as an attack on workers’ rights are turning a blind eye to reality and putting precisely those jobs at risk that they claim to be protecting. At the same time, we need a resolute trade policy at the European level that guarantees fair competition and consistently punishes rule-breakers – because free trade only works when everyone follows the same rules.
If we truly want to secure our competitiveness in the long term, we don’t need a bureaucratic approach – we need a return to a can-do mentality: less regulation, more personal responsibility, ambitious investment incentives, reliable framework conditions, and, above all, the courage to tackle issues properly and comprehensively once again. Real change begins in the mind – it’s time to act.
Alfred Kärcher SE & Co. KG was founded in 1935 and generated almost 3.5 billion euros in revenue in 2025. The family-owned company based in Winnenden, Germany, earns 86 percent of this abroad. The Kärcher Group operates 170 companies in 87 countries and employs 17,000 people worldwide. Kärcher's portfolio comprises more than 3,000 products for cleaning and care, with Kärcher high-pressure cleaners being particularly well known.

Reading of Bahram Beyzaie’s ‘Arash’ to be held in Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:21:41 UTC
17:21:41 KST

Reading of Bahram Beyzaie’s ‘Arash’ to be held in Tehran
TEHRAN- A staged reading of “Arash,” a play by acclaimed Iranian playwright and filmmaker Bahram Beyzaie, will be held at Neauphle-le-Château Theater Hall in Tehran on Saturday, October 31.
Directed by Morteza Sabahi and produced by Davoud Namvar, the event is organized by the Qalamro theater group and will feature a cast of actors accompanied by a live music ensemble, Mehr reported.
The production draws on Beyzaie’s work, which takes its title from Arash, a legendary archer in Iranian mythology whose sacrifice is associated with the defense of the homeland and the determination of its people.
The staged reading cast includes Mohammad Hossein Navai, Kasra Farahnak, Soheil Semyari, Nastaran Zeynali, Kimia Akbari, Aida Berenji, Maryam Kamali, Shiva Bahrampour, Saba Jafari, Sogand Dadar, and Amir Farazi.
The musical ensemble will be led by Ehsan Samani-Manesh, who will also perform percussion and other musical instruments. Kamancheh player Mehrpad Zahmatkesh will join the group, providing live musical accompaniment to the reading.
Arash, known in Persian mythology as Arash-e Kamangir, is one of the most celebrated heroic figures in Iranian cultural tradition. His story has been preserved in different forms in Persian literature and mythology and has come to symbolize self-sacrifice, courage and devotion to the homeland.
According to the best-known version of the legend, Iran and Turan have been engaged in a devastating war. After years of conflict, the two sides agree to settle their dispute by determining a new boundary. The agreement requires an Iranian archer to shoot an arrow, with the point where the arrow lands becoming the border between the two lands.
Arash is chosen for the task.
The legend presents the challenge as far more than an ordinary feat of archery. Arash is required to put all his strength into a single shot, knowing that the act will cost him his life. He climbs to a high mountain and prepares to release the arrow. In one of the most famous images associated with the legend, Arash's entire strength and vitality are said to enter the arrow as he shoots it toward the horizon.
The arrow travels an extraordinary distance before finally landing, establishing the border and bringing an end to the conflict. Arash, however, dies after completing his mission, having sacrificed himself for the survival and territorial integrity of his homeland.
This element of sacrifice lies at the heart of the legend. Arash does not fight for personal glory or wealth. His heroism comes from accepting a responsibility that requires him to give everything he has for the sake of others.
The story has consequently acquired a symbolic significance far beyond the act of shooting an arrow. Arash has become an embodiment of the idea that the fate of a nation can sometimes depend on the courage and sacrifice of an individual. His story also connects personal choice with collective responsibility, making the ancient legend relevant to later generations.
Arash's story has been particularly influential in Persian poetry and modern Iranian literature. Writers and poets have repeatedly returned to the character, interpreting his sacrifice in different historical and political contexts. The image of the arrow traveling across the land has also become a powerful metaphor for hope, determination and the possibility of shaping the future through individual action.
Unlike some mythological heroes whose stories revolve around conquest, Arash's defining act is one of giving. He wins not by defeating an enemy in combat, but by making the ultimate personal sacrifice to bring an end to war and protect his people.
Beyzaie, who is widely recognized for drawing on Iranian mythology, history and folklore in his dramatic works, has frequently reinterpreted traditional narratives to examine questions of identity, collective memory and the relationship between the past and the present. His writing combines elements of ancient Iranian traditions with modern theatrical language, giving familiar legends new dramatic and intellectual dimensions.

Special dubbed version of ‘East of Eden’ went on screen in Tehran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:21:31 UTC
17:21:31 KST

Special dubbed version of ‘East of Eden’ went on screen in Tehran
TEHRAN- A special version of Elia Kazan’s classic drama “East of Eden,” featuring an Iranian dub from the golden age of film dubbing in the country, was screened at Tehran’s Arasbaran Cultural Center on Wednesday.
The screening was followed by an analytical discussion with Amir Qaderi, editor-in-chief of the Iranian film website Cafe Cinema, offering audiences an opportunity to revisit the 1955 American film and discuss its themes, performances and place in cinema history.
Based on the novel of the same name by American author John Steinbeck, “East of Eden” is one of the best-known works associated with actor James Dean. The film, directed by Kazan and released in 1955, explores family conflict, sibling rivalry and the struggle for parental acceptance against the backdrop of California’s Salinas Valley in the early 20th century.
The program at Arasbaran Cultural Center is part of an initiative to present notable works of world cinema to Iranian audiences. Its emphasis on a high-quality Persian-dubbed version also highlights the country’s longstanding tradition of film dubbing, which has played an important role in introducing international cinema to generations of moviegoers.
“East of Eden” follows Cal Trask, a troubled young man who struggles to win the affection and approval of his father, Adam. Cal feels that his father favors his brother Aron, whose more conventional behavior makes him appear to be the preferred son. The brothers’ contrasting personalities and their competition for their father’s love drive much of the drama.
As the story unfolds, Cal attempts to prove his worth and gain recognition, but his efforts are complicated by family secrets and the emotional distance between him and his father. His relationship with Aron becomes increasingly strained, while the brothers’ encounters with Abra, Aron’s girlfriend, add another dimension to their rivalry.
The film draws on biblical themes, particularly the story of Cain and Abel, to examine jealousy, moral responsibility and the possibility of choosing a different path from the one expected of an individual. Through Cal’s struggle, the narrative raises questions about whether people are defined by their family circumstances and past experiences or can exercise control over their own choices.
Kazan’s adaptation does not simply reproduce the novel’s family saga. Instead, it concentrates on a portion of Steinbeck’s story, bringing the emotional conflict between Cal and Adam to the forefront. This focus allows the film to explore the need for parental recognition and the lasting effects of rejection on a young person’s sense of identity.
The film’s historical significance is also reflected in its awards. It received the Best Dramatic Film award at the 1955 Cannes Film Festival and won the Golden Globe for Best Motion Picture – Drama in 1956. At the Academy Awards ceremony that year, Jo Van Fleet won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actress for her portrayal of Kate, Cal and Aron’s mother. The film also received nominations for Best Actor for Dean, Best Director for Kazan and Best Writing (Screenplay) for Paul Osborn.
Dean’s performance as Cal became a defining moment in his brief career. His emotionally intense portrayal of a young man seeking acceptance helped establish his lasting image as one of the most memorable actors of 1950s Hollywood. “East of Eden” was his first major film role, and his performance brought a distinctive sense of vulnerability and rebellion to the character.
Kazan, meanwhile, was known for directing films that examined personal struggles alongside wider social issues. His approach to performance and character psychology made him one of the influential filmmakers of American cinema, with works such as “A Streetcar Named Desire” and “On the Waterfront” also earning significant critical recognition.

Nations strike deal to revive global nature goals, but progress falls short
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:20:17 UTC
17:20:17 KST

Nearly 200 nations struck hard-fought agreements Friday at a UN biodiversity summit, but the outcome was accompanied by disappointment over missed opportunities to address humanity's destructive toll on nature.
Delegates cheered as crucial texts were approved in overtime but the celebrations were tempered by acrimonious debates and regret over limited progress on some of the most contentious issues.
The COP17 summit in Armenia sought to revive a landmark commitment to halt and reverse the destruction of nature by 2030 after global efforts to meet that goal fell short.
Over two bruising weeks in Yerevan, nations were urged to correct course to keep the pact alive and protect the plants, animals and ecosystems that sustain life on Earth.
The United Nations had warned that progress was insufficient to meet the goals of the 2030 target including protecting 30 percent of Earth's land and oceans, tackling pollution and invasive species, and boosting money for conservation.
"And that's it. Perfect," said COP17 president Hambardzum Matevosyan in Armenia as he brought down the gavel on two major texts, the final versions of which were still not available early on Saturday.
But the outcome was "not commensurate" with the crisis engulfing the natural world, said French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut early Saturday as the summit drew to a close.
"The progress we failed to achieve here is a series of missed opportunities to speed up our response to the loss of biodiversity," Barbut said in a lengthy statement sent to AFP, stressing that "nature will not wait for the pace of our negotiations."
'Step forward'
The final plenary stretched through Friday night and well into the next morning, with negotiations turning sour as the hours dragged on.
Even as some delegates left to catch flights, others stayed behind to argue technical points.
Veteran COP observer Juliette Landry from the IDDRI think tank told AFP "there was a lot of push and pull in every direction" throughout the summit and "in that context, it's hard to get things accepted".
In a draft agreement of one closely watched text, nations were urged to "accelerate" their efforts and warned that "increased action" was needed to tackle the forces driving biodiversity loss.
This "represents a positive outcome... and though there are weaknesses, particularly on harmful subsidies, it does represent a step forward," Guido Broekhoven from WWF International told AFP.
Tackling subsidies and other incentives that encourage activities harmful to nature, such as fossil fuels, intensive agriculture and overfishing, was one of the most politically fraught agenda items at the summit.
"Even though the agreed decision text expresses it in weak terms, COP17 saw important political momentum to address harmful financial incentives, including subsidies," An Lambrechts from Greenpeace International told AFP.
A rare fight over science cast a pall over the summit, with a number of countries accused of undermining efforts to approve key reports in scenes that shocked even seasoned negotiators.
"We regret the increasing instances in which scientific evidence and its uptake has been challenged or constrained" by politics, said Swiss negotiator Gabriela Blatter in a statement on behalf of dozens of countries.
"Our delegations fully respect every state's right to safeguard national interest but science is not negotiable".
Finance feud
A separate row revolved around finding new cash sources to fund conservation efforts, another hot-button issue with public budgets under strain amid an energy crisis and conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.
The European Union led a charge for wealthy emerging economies such as China to contribute to global conservation efforts, a contentious issue at COP17.
In a sign of possible compromise, another draft text that circulated Friday invited countries outside the developed-country donors to voluntarily join the group.
Outstanding questions over the design of the Cali Fund, a UN mechanism that hoped to attract billions of dollars in corporate contributions but is close to empty, were left unresolved.
"By punting essential decisions to two years from now, parties have all but ensured the fund remains empty until then," said Pakhi Das from the nonprofit organisation Plant-for-the-Planet.
The COP17 summit decided early Saturday that Ecuador would host the next biodiversity talks in 2028 after the South American nation defeated rival candidate Panama in a secret vote.

====================================================================================================

The seven days I thought I might have breast cancer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:17:55 UTC
17:17:55 KST

Seven days of uncertainty following a breast biopsy become a deeply personal reckoning with cancer, family history and fear. From that experience, Euronews reporter Monica Pinna explores Europe's persistent inequalities in early detection and care.
Nine o'clock on an ordinary Monday morning. The designated day of an appointment I'd put off for a year, maybe two — too long.
I get undressed and enter the room. It's all just routine — isn't it?
"Madame, don’t move. I have to move you into the right position. Turn slightly. Not like that. Let me do it. Stay still. You're too stiff; relax.” The woman is touching me, moving, flattening and squeezing one of my breasts into the machine. It ends up looking as flat as a slice of the Italian sliced cheese 'Sottilette'.
And then the other one. “Turn around. Let me move it.” The process starts again with my breasts being squeezed sideways, which is unpleasantly painful, something many women are familiar with.
When it's over, I'm left alone in a tiny room — half naked, waiting. In that small barren space, my mind races, hitting highs and lows, thinking of the glimpse I got of the X-ray images of my breasts, of the shapes and shadows, looking like the branches in a stylised painting of a giant oak tree.
Is there cancer hidden in those pictures that I can’t interpret? Don't we all think that after looking at those black-and-white encrypted images?
I’m not even sure how long I've been surrounded by those four claustrophobic walls when the door finally opens and I'm moved to another dark room to wait for a doctor and the next examination. But first the smiling doctor says: “Your mammogram is absolutely fine.” And the frown you didn’t even realise was carved into your forehead disappears. You breathe in deeply and then exhale for a long time.
It's time for the echography. You start talking as the lubricating gel is smeared on one breast and then on the other. The scanner's moving probe sends sound waves bouncing off the tissues in your breast, revealing shadows, white and black stains, waves, darker patches.
There's a whole world in our breasts we totally ignore and that is just impossible for us to read. I'm explaining to the radiologist how much I hate all this, how almost every woman in my family has had breast cancer and how anxious this all makes me, when she starts focusing the probe on the one particular area and stops talking. She pushes the probe down, then moves it and presses down again. There is silence.
“I think you need a little biopsy." All my fears materialise in that one moment and a single sentence. “There is a darker patch there that doesn’t disappear as I move the probe. It’s best to check it.”
Two days later I returned, wanting the follow-up to happen fast and to quickly know the outcome. In other countries, beyond France, my adopted home, I could have had to wait days between a mammography and an echography and for weeks before the biopsy was done.
First a local anaesthetic, then a small cut which I don’t feel; the doctor smiles reassuringly, but I remain tense and at the same time already off somewhere else in my mind. A long cannula goes deeply into my flesh five times. Some bloody flecks of whitish flesh emerge and are placed in tiny glass containers.
That was the beginning of a week I will never forget.
I would wait seven days before finally learning if I had cancer. I entered a sort of parallel world, where everything came through a filter and seemed far away. My body and my life were on hold. Plans suspended. A work trip and meetings with friends were postponed. I had started the process of acceptance, with that taboo word – cancer – becoming a possible option. It was possible that I would enter that same room days later to be told that I had to be operated on and then would need chemo.
Everything every cancer patient goes through. Fear, waiting, uncertainty. A time when friends you wouldn’t have thought of show up and when some of those you would have expected to stick with you might disappear. Deep fears resurface and people around you react differently. I was definitely floating, preparing myself. Bracing. The same feeling you'd have about a flight you're due to take when a storm is hitting.
"I have it, I don’t have it. I don’t know. I must wait."
Spiralling thoughts take you into the depths of your mind and your fears, sometimes a long way down. You recall your mother’s experience, as she went through the same fears, was operated on, had radiotherapy and made it through. You recall your auntie who didn’t. Your cousin who is now a beautiful and bright survivor. You think of her sister, who had to have her stomach removed, but who is always smiling and serene despite the medical checks she will have to endure for the rest of her life.
While you recall the faces and the stories of those who made it and those who didn’t, you float, detached from the world. The student protests, the riots and looting in French cities that I would have run to cover as a journalist are just a faraway noise.
The morning of the results, it's like I'm in a different dimension.
I'm trying to prepare myself for the worst, like bracing for an emergency landing. My appointment is at midday and I start wandering the streets of Lyon at 9.00 am. I walk like a lost soul for kilometre after kilometre. The hilarious part is that all this is happening to me during Pink October, the annual breast cancer awareness month. Launched in the United States in 1985, it's become one of the world’s most recognisable public-health campaigns. So, during my “week off”, I would regularly be seeing pink ribbons and breast symbols all over the place.
Worldwide, millions of euros are raised every year, yet organised breast screening participation in France remains below 50%. And look at me: I’m a journalist. I know the statistics; I’ve seen serious illness in my family. And yet I delayed making an appointment. Pure fear. How could I, or anyone, be ready to be told you have cancer? Still, it happens. And early detection can save your life.
Early detection: not only a question of fear, but of access to care
When breast cancer is detected before it spreads, five-year survival approaches 100%, compared with 38% for women diagnosed at an advanced stage. Despite its importance and the European Commission pouring around €80 million to strengthen screening across the bloc under its ‘Europe’s Beating Cancer Plan’ access to screening remains uneven across Europe, meaning that the chances of an early diagnosis can still depend on where a woman lives, not only on her fears. That’s due to screening organisation, access to appointments, out-of-pocket costs and awareness of the benefits of screening, as well as social inequalities, reveal latest research by the EU and the OECD..
As Luis Seijo, Co-chair of the European Cancer Organisation’s Prevention, Early Detection and Screening Network, has said, “Inequalities in cancer screening are costing lives.”
But disparities in Europe exist not only regarding early screening but how long it takes from screening to getting the diagnosis, ranging from a median of eight days in Denmark to 32 days in Romania.
While in my case it took just over a week, for Maria Assunta who lives in the Italian region of Sardinia, it took seven times longer.
She has been having annual breast checks since the age of 40, around ten years before the age generally recommended for routine screening in the European Union. Four years ago, when she was 46, a routine ultrasound revealed a 4-centimeter lump in one breast. She underwent a biopsy one month later and received her breast cancer diagnosis three weeks after that.
Maria Assunta is now in the follow up phase, with checks every 6 months. She describes the care she received “excellent both from a human and medical point of view” and calls her doctors her “angels”. Since going through this experience, she has become a passionate advocate for prevention and early detection.
Timeline from diagnosis to start of the treatment also differs across countries. In Maria Assunta’s case, there was almost no interval between the diagnosis and the start of the treatment. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) identifies long waits for specialist consultations, imaging and diagnostic tests as a concern in several countries, including Ireland, Greece, Romania and Spain.
Stalled process of screening participation
While early detection has improved over the long term and mortality has declined, according to the OECD and European Commission’s “Health at a Glance: Europe 2020”, progress has stalled in many countries and screening participation continues to vary sharply across Europe.
Compared with 2019, breast cancer screening rates rose in nine EU countries with available data, with the largest increases observed in Slovakia by over 12%, followed by Croatia and Estonia.
Breast cancer on the rise in the EU
As for my own story, the time finally came. I went in and waited for another half an hour till my name was called.
“I can reassure you, there is nothing, but it was best to check,” the doctor said with a smile. All my tension eased; I thanked her and shook her hand like a perfectly polite Italian. But even so, I remain disoriented by everything that has happened.
I was lucky, but every year around 360,000 women in the European Union receive a breast cancer diagnosis, 61,000 in France. Breast cancer is on the rise in Europe due to demographic changes, reproductive patterns — with later and fewer pregnancies — lifestyle habits and metabolic and hormonal factors, with research ongoing on environmental chemicals, pollution and diet impacts too. Statistics show that one in eleven women will develop breast cancer at some point in their life. It doesn’t mean they will die from it, but it doesn’t mean they will have an easy path through it either.
What happens for those who receive a breast cancer diagnosis?
I was lucky enough to walk out of that room with the same life I had before. But for many who receive a different diagnosis, the fear, uncertainty and sense of suspension I experienced for just seven days can become a lasting part of their lives.
So, is the mind cared for as much as the body, whether the journey leads to recovery or, ultimately, the end of life?
OECD’s 2026 European Cancer Inequalities Report found that only sixteen EU countries out of 27, plus Norway and Iceland, include psychological support in the cancer care pathway, and provision remains uneven.
In France, psychological care is part of the official package of supportive cancer care, alongside pain management, nutritional support and social assistance. In Italy access remains limited despite legal requirements and guidelines. A 2024 study of around 3,000 people with cancer found that only 20% reported receiving psychological support, while just 16% said a therapist had helped them throughout their cancer treatment. Much of this support still depends on private initiatives.
Eleonora is now 52 and lives in the Italian city of Genoa: She underwent a mastectomy at the age of 39, after a four-centimetre lump was discovered in her breast during the first ultrasound she had ever had.
In the thirteen years since her diagnosis, she has become a volunteer with the non-profit association Braccialetti Bianchi and a Qigong instructor. Rooted in traditional Chinese medicine, Qigong is one of the complementary practices the association offers to hospitalised patients and those undergoing rehabilitation. Other activities include circle dancing, yoga, empathic support, biodanza* and shiatsu. Eleonora says these therapies “can make the entire cancer journey just more bearable”.
This free support programme was launched around thirty years ago by a group of doctors working at the San Martino Hospital of Genoa. Maria Giuseppina Vidili is one of the oncologists who helped establish the initiative. She specialises in cancer rehabilitation, and she explains doctors and associations do what they can facing limited national budgets and healthcare cuts. She said she has worked tirelessly for years to build friendly spaces for patients at any stage of their cancer pathway.
She retired four years ago and never stopped offering complementary activities, saying that doctors and associations are on the frontline to fill in the gaps of the national healthcare system, at least in terms of psychological support.
According to the Italian Federation of Voluntary Associations in Oncology (FAVO), only around 20% of hospitals provide specialised psycho-oncology support. Such support becomes even less available once cancer treatment has ended. Doctor Vidili says a standardised psycho-oncology service should be available throughout the country. Initiatives like the one she launched are still limited to a reduced number of people. Some Italian hospitals, she says, don’t even have rehabilitation units.
Pink October, every month
The day after I received my all-clear, and I’m supposed to go back to work, answer emails, make calls to set up interviews, plan my next reporting trip. To pick up where I left off, as if nothing had happened.
But something did happen and has left a mark.
I wrote most of this article that morning, between 5 am and 9 am. I just had to get it off my chest – literally – hoping that sharing my experience would help even one single woman face her fears and go for regular screenings. But writing this was also a way to delve into a subject that people still prefer to look away from, including myself. I struggled to research and discuss cancer as if it were any other journalistic topic. It comes with a burden.
Today, my thoughts are with those fighting to live and those working to find new cures. Awareness campaigns matter, but awareness alone is not enough. Women need access to screening, prompt diagnosis and appropriate care. They also need to be encouraged to put their health first, even when fear makes it tempting to look away.
Psychological support and complementary therapies should be accessible to everyone, everywhere, not just to the limited number of people who can currently benefit from them across the EU.
And one thing is for sure: my next screening appointment will be on time.

Hainan’s Sanya expands global network of free trade partners

HAIKOU /China/, October 31. /TASS/. The resort city of Sanya, located on the coast of south China’s Hainan Province, has recently been expanding its network of global partners to develop free trade relations, Sanya Daily newspaper reported.
According to the newspaper, the Sanya Central Business District Administration signed a memorandum of understanding with Italy’s Western Ligurian Sea Port Authority in an online ceremony last week, expressing their intention to strengthen ties through joint projects. The agreement brought the number of Hainan’s global free trade partners to 46, accelerating the island’s efforts to increase its openness to other countries and regions.
The cooperation with Italy will focus on areas including cruise and yacht transportation, maritime logistics, the exchange of corporate expertise, and foreign trade. One of the key objectives is to strengthen and expand Hainan’s supply chains in line with advanced international standards.
According to an official assessment, the southernmost Chinese province’s cooperation network is increasingly extending across Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and European markets. The recently concluded agreements are expected to deepen cooperation between Hainan and Italy in port construction, the development of the cruise and yacht industries, as well as international logistics.
The newspaper’s authors emphasized that such partnerships are “in particularly high demand for the modernization of the maritime industry.” The publication noted that Sanya has more than 1,000 berths and 1,400 registered yachts, with the latter figure continuing to rise, partly thanks to various international exhibitions held on the island and the elimination of import duties on recreational vessels. Another important incentive for the development of this segment of the economy has been an increase in the maximum permitted passenger capacity of yachts to 26 people. Cross-border cruise routes also play an equally important role for the city, the newspaper stressed.
The Sanya Central Business District Administration said local authorities would continue strengthening international ties, expanding channels of cooperation with European countries, and broadening the global partnership network aimed at promoting free trade.

Türkiye takes Turkic bloc chair as Erdoğan urges unity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:17:06 UTC
17:17:06 KST

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan called for greater unity among Turkic states on Oct. 30 as Türkiye took over the Organization of Turkic States’ (OTS) rotating chairmanship from Azerbaijan at a summit in Ankara.
“There is no place for division, discord, or conflict in the family portrait of the Turkic world,” Erdoğan told the gathering at the Presidential Complex.
The 13th summit concluded with the adoption of the Ankara Declaration. Uzbek diplomat Mirvokhid Azimov was named the organization’s next secretary-general, succeeding Kubanychbek Omuraliev.
The gathering was held under the theme “Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed.” Erdoğan said Türkiye would seek closer cultural and linguistic ties, support sporting activities and ease travel between member countries during its chairmanship.
He called for stronger contacts with the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, an OTS observer, and said he hoped Turkmenistan would soon become a full member.
On regional issues, Erdoğan reiterated support for Azerbaijan’s talks with Armenia and urged diplomacy to address renewed tensions involving Iran.
He called on Turkic states to do more to secure a just resolution of the Palestinian issue, deliver humanitarian aid to Gaza and begin reconstruction. He reaffirmed support for an independent Palestinian state based on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
The Ankara Declaration backed a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. On Cyprus, it called for a negotiated, mutually acceptable settlement based on the realities on the island and supported efforts to secure Turkish Cypriots’ equal rights.
Erdoğan also called for closer economic and technological cooperation, citing the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor’s role in trade between Asia and Europe. He proposed a joint digital trade platform linking member countries’ markets.
He urged the early signing of a cybersecurity cooperation agreement, faster progress on a joint satellite project and contributions to an artificial intelligence language model covering the Oghuz, Kipchak and Karluk language groups.
Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev proposed a network of logistics hubs across Turkic states, while Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov called for greater capacity along the Middle Corridor.
The declaration reaffirmed respect for member states’ sovereignty, territorial integrity and noninterference in their internal affairs. It also supported efforts to promote a common 34-letter Turkic alphabet.
Leaders welcomed consultations on classifying footballers from member states as domestic players in one another’s leagues and organizing a Turkic Cup for national teams.

Trump administration clashes with states ahead of midterms

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:15:19 UTC
17:15:19 KST

The Trump administration and state officials are clashing over voting procedures ahead of the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, with disputes over alleged noncitizen voters and an Alaska Senate candidacy reaching the courts.
A federal appeals court on Oct. 30 rejected the Justice Department’s request to set aside California mail ballots from about 20,000 people it alleges may not be U.S. citizens. The 2-1 ruling followed a district judge’s refusal to grant the request.
Separately, a federal judge barred the department through Nov. 16 from threatening election workers to stop processing ballots solely because it alleges a voter is ineligible.
In Washington state, prosecutors sought to separate ballots from more than 400 people they alleged had registered without U.S. citizenship.
Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said the list included U.S. citizens and demanded individual evidence before officials could withhold a registered voter’s ballot from counting.
The Justice Department says preventing noncitizen voting is a federal responsibility and rejects accusations that its actions are politically motivated.
In Alaska, federal prosecutors are investigating allegations that Democratic challenger Mary Peltola’s campaign helped recruit retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. to divert votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Peltola denied knowing about the effort, while Sullivan Jr. denied running at Democrats’ behest. The department has also asked a court to separate ballots ranking Sullivan Jr.
State officials elsewhere are preparing for possible federal intervention. Maryland election administrator Jared DeMarinis said contingency planning with 70 officials included arranging legal representation and bail if he were detained on Election Day.
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel said her lawyers had prepared briefs “for virtually every set of circumstances we could think of, except the zombie apocalypse.”
Both major parties are also preparing legal teams for possible disputes after voting ends.
Nearly 47.9 million Americans had voted early by midday on Oct. 30, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, surpassing the 45.9 million early votes recorded in the 2022 midterms. The Nov. 3 elections will determine control of both chambers of Congress.

Türkiye, Uzbekistan target $5 billion in trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:13:38 UTC
17:13:38 KST

Türkiye and Uzbekistan have signed agreements to expand trade and investment as they seek to raise annual bilateral trade to $5 billion from about $3.1 billion in 2025.
The two countries signed five agreements on trade, social security and business cooperation in Ankara on Oct. 29, following talks between President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev ahead of the Organization of Turkic States summit.
A protocol expanding their preferential trade agreement will add more products to tariff concession lists. It will enter into force once both countries complete domestic approval procedures, the Turkish Trade Ministry said.
The presidents also agreed to establish a high-level business council to promote joint trade and investment projects and strengthen cooperation between public institutions and companies. The council will support a medium-term target of $10 billion in bilateral trade, the ministry said.
A separate customs protocol provides for advance electronic data sharing on goods and vehicles to speed up border procedures.
Türkiye is Uzbekistan’s fourth-largest trading partner. Bilateral trade reached $2.4 billion in the first nine months of 2026, including $1.5 billion in Turkish exports and $917.4 million in imports, according to figures compiled by Anadolu Agency.
Machinery led Turkish exports to Uzbekistan last year, while copper and copper products were the largest import category.
Turkish contractors have undertaken 333 projects in Uzbekistan worth more than $9.5 billion.
Uzbek visitor arrivals in Türkiye reached 649,719 in 2025, more than double the 272,604 recorded in 2021.

Millions embezzled in fraud scheme at Ukrainian defense firm – investigators
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:09:00 UTC
17:09:00 KST

Millions embezzled in fraud scheme at Ukrainian defense firm – investigators
A former head of a state-owned Ukrainian defense company is suspected of embezzling millions of dollars through fake mediation deals, the country’s anti-corruption bodies have said.
Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) announced in a statement on Friday that the scheme had cost the government 1.1 billion hryvnia (around $43 million).
The Western-backed agencies, which frequently target Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s inner-circle, didn’t name the suspect, only saying that he used to lead a subsidiary of Ukrspecexport, a state-run company with exclusive rights to export and import military hardware.
According to the investigators, the former head of the state-run firm signed a deal with a foreign company in 2015 for it to provide mediation during the sales of Ukrainian military products abroad.
However, it had been established that the Ukrainian firm had conducted all of the negotiations with a customer from a Middle Eastern country on its own, and the foreign company wasn’t involved, they said.
Despite this fact, the official signed falsified documents about mediation services being provided by the foreign company and transferred millions to it as payment, the statement read.
The actions of the suspect are being qualified as large-scale embezzlement and forgery of government papers, it added.
Ukrainskaya Pravda reported later in the day that, according to its sources, the official in question is Taras Shiyko, who now holds the positions of the deputy director of Ukroboronprom, a state-run conglomerate comprised of Ukraine’s arms makers. The fraud scheme relates to his time as the head of Progress, a state-run export and import company.
Shiyko became part of an anti-corruption case earlier this year, involving the suspected embezzlement of 32 million hryvnia (around $700,000).
Zelensky’s government has been rocked by a series of corruption scandals involving people close to him since November 2025, when NABU and SAPO accused Timur Mindich, a longtime associate of the Ukrainian leader, of masterminding a $100 million kickback scheme involving state contracts in the energy sector. Other investigations have implicated former Ukrainian ministers, diplomats, and senior officials.
NABU’s latest high-profile case targeted an alleged protection racket involving scam call centers and officials from the Prosecutor General’s Office. Although he was not personally named as a suspect, Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko left Ukraine before being dismissed by parliament last month, according to Ukrainian media.
Critics accuse Zelensky of leading a sprawling corruption network which permeates his government, allegedly helping him maintain power and enriching those involved. A poll issued by the Kiev International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) last month suggested that the Ukrainians consider corruption to be a bigger problem for the country than the conflict with Russia.

When buses stopped running on Brazil election day, 'Lula's Army' grabbed their car keys
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
08:06:41 UTC
17:06:41 KST

When buses stopped running on Brazil election day, 'Lula's Army' grabbed their car keys
SALVADOR, Brazil, Oct 31 - When buses in the northeastern Brazilian city of Salvador inexplicably stopped running last Sunday, history teacher Martins Mafra grabbed his car keys and set off to pick up stranded voters across town.
Mafra's efforts in Salvador, the capital of Bahia state, were part of a massive get-out-the-vote drive across Brazil that helped power leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva to an unprecedented fourth term.
Lula supporters, shocked by right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro's first-round lead, quickly mobilized as the prospect sank in that the Bolsonaro clan could return to power. They used innovative social media initiatives, free taxi rides and grassroots campaigning to secure the incumbent president over 10 million more votes in the runoff.
"I'm a father, and I work in education, so this was an opportunity to teach and show that we can make a difference," said Mafra, who offered rides to supporters of all stripes. "It's one thing to stay home complaining about city hall or posting videos online; it's another thing to get up, walk out the door, and actually do something."
Bolsonaro, son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, fled this week to the US, where he declared himself the legitimate "leader" of Brazil, questioning the credibility of Lula's 10 million-vote leap.
Bolsonaro also questioned a two-hour voting extension, requested by Lula's campaign and granted by a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice, due to the out-of-service buses in Bahia. Bolsonaro's campaign also sought an extension due to rains in conservative-leaning southern states, and the extension had little bearing on the result, the federal electoral court said.
LULA STRONGHOLD
Bahia, a populous Lula stronghold, was the state with the highest fall in abstention rates between both rounds, with nearly 400,000 more people voting in the runoff.
Almost a quarter of those additional voters came from Salvador, a city of over 2.5 million people where Lula won 73% of runoff votes.
Salvador resident Gabriel Mercury, 41, son of Brazilian pop star Daniela Mercury, was one of those who helped orchestrate the turnaround.
The Lula voter watched with concern as the leftist underperformed in the first round, and decided to do something about it. He began by inviting undecided voters to have coffee with him and talk politics. Later, he offered cash rewards of up to 2,400 reais ($445.67) to anyone who could name a single Bolsonaro legislative proposal that had benefited workers.
Nobody took him up on the offer.
LULA OVERHAULS CAMPAIGN
After the underwhelming first round, Lula's team sought to reboot a campaign marred by infighting, mixed messaging and the complacency of incumbency, aides said.
Aware that no presidential candidate had ever been elected after trailing in the initial vote, the 81-year-old Lula bought his first ever smartphone to reach Brazilians on the platforms that increasingly shape Brazil's political debate.
Meanwhile, lawmaker Andre Janones, who helped Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in 2022, rapidly expanded a WhatsApp channel he called "Lula's Army."
By instructing followers to recruit friends and amplify Lula content online, he grew the channel from roughly 50,000 people ahead of the first round to over 10 million by the runoff.
Dharma political risk consultant Creomar de Souza said Lula's team, and particularly Janones, successfully pounced on missteps by Bolsonaro to convince voters he would threaten Brazil's democracy, reverse social advances and slash welfare payments on which millions of Brazilians depend.
As the runoff approached, polls showed Lula closing the gap on Bolsonaro. By election day, they were tied.
In Salvador, Mercury began to believe Lula could win. Then, early on Sunday, Salvador's bus network ground to a halt.
BUS FIASCO
In Brazil, public authorities are required to provide free public transport on election day.
But reports from across Salvador, where Mayor Bruno Reis supported Bolsonaro, suggested many buses were not running.
Inspectors from the Bahia consumer protection agency found 944 buses idling in Salvador depots. Jaime Barreiros Neto, the Bahia electoral court's judicial analyst, estimated at least 30% of the fleet was not operating.
Reis blamed the outage on Lula stickers that had been placed on buses in violation of electoral rules. As soon as city hall realized sticker removal efforts were causing a bottleneck, it immediately ordered the fleet released, he said in a press conference on Sunday.
Reis told Reuters he supported Bolsonaro in the runoff in accordance with his party, União Brasil. He denied detaining public transport or hindering voter mobility, saying the stickering of the buses held up the fleet.
Bahia’s electoral court ordered the arrest of Salvador’s transportation chief, Pablo Souza, over the absent buses. It revoked the order once voting had ended the following day, but demanded a probe into the incident.
Souza, who was in Paris on an official visit during the day of the vote, denied wrongdoing. He told Reuters the number of buses was the same as during the first round, and in line with electoral regulations.
MASS MOBILIZATIONS
As news of idling buses rippled through Salvador, Mercury and five friends asked their social media followers to drive people to voting stations. Some people got behind the wheel; others donated to cover fuel costs. Mercury estimated that his team moved around 600 voters on election day.
"Politics isn't just institutional politics," he said. "We make politics through our actions."
Uber drivers also stepped up, with thousands offering free rides worth up to 50 reais ($9.28) throughout the day, said Adriano de Jesus Braga dos Santos, an Uber driver and content creator, who personally offered 36 rides to passengers.
Nicole Soares, 18, waited 40 minutes for a bus, but never considered giving up. "I had the right to vote," she said, casting her ballot for Lula.
Some residents were still unable to vote.
Grecia de Jesus Nunes, a 54-year-old street vendor, said only two buses passed her hotdog stand between 8 a.m. and 2 p.m. No buses were available during her brief break, and when volunteer drivers eventually reached her, she could no longer leave work.
Though unable to vote, Nunes rejoiced at Lula's victory.
"My life is Lula," she said. "I am Lula until I die." REUTERS

China's manufacturing activity moderated in October, with the purchasing managers' index falling to 49.3 as the high-tech and equipment manufacturing sectors maintained expansion, official data showed on Saturday.
The overall reading was down 0.8 percentage points from September, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.
Chief statistician Huo Lihui attributed the retreat to some demand being brought forward ahead of the National Day holiday this month and a complex international environment.
The production subindex stood at 49.8, down 1.9 points from September, while the new-orders subindex fell 1.1 points to 49.4, as both supply and demand moderated during the month.
The PMI for high-tech manufacturing stood at 51.3 while that for equipment manufacturing came in at 50.6, both remaining above the 50-point threshold that separates expansion from contraction.
The figures indicate that emerging industries continued to sustain growth momentum, supported by the ongoing development of new quality productive forces, Huo noted.
Manufacturing activity in several advanced industries remained robust. 
Both the production and new-orders subindexes for railway, shipbuilding and aerospace equipment manufacturing, as well as computer, communications and electronic equipment manufacturing, stood at 53 or above, pointing to relatively strong supply and demand in these sectors.
Large manufacturers continued to report expansion, with their PMI standing at 50.2, despite a slight decline of 0.4 points from the previous month. 
The PMI readings for medium-sized and small enterprises came in at 48.4 and 47.5, respectively.
On the price front, both major raw material purchasing prices and factory-gate prices remained in expansionary territory, although their growth moderated.
The purchasing price subindex stood at 56.8, down four points from September while the factory-gate price subindex eased 2.3 points to 51.7, partly reflecting recent declines in the prices of certain nonferrous metals and other commodities. (Xinhua)

Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian missile and drone attacks. The rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has praised the US for its "strong decision" to approve the sale of 500 much-coveted Patriot missiles to Ukraine - but he has warned that delivery could take years.
The US State Department announced on Friday that Washington had green-lit a package of Patriot PAC-3 interceptors worth $2.1 billion as Kyiv continues to defend against Russian missile and drone attacks.
"Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defence package," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on social media in response.
"However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS," he continued. "We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors."
Earlier this week, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had been waiting for almost a month for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on a batch of missiles for both the Patriot and NASAMS systems.
Kyiv has long called for more interceptors to help its forces fend off Russian attacks, and the rapidly approaching winter is pressing home that need. Russia has repeatedly sought to target Ukraine's power grid over wartime winter periods as Moscow has looked to break the country's resolve.
Dwindling stocks of interceptors have already encouraged Russia to ramp up missile attacks in recent months, and there are fears this trend could lead to an especially brutal winter for Ukrainians.
"The United States, our European partners, and other partners around the world have sufficient stocks of PAC-3 interceptors in their warehouses," Zelenskyy said overnight. "Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS, through this production already contracted and paid for by Ukraine and our partners would be the right approach."
The Patriot missile platform is one of the world's most advanced air defence systems and can be used to defend against a variety of threats, including incoming aircraft and ballistic missiles.
Ukraine receives the majority of its Patriots through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which facilitates the purchase of military equipment and munitions from the US by allies and partners.
As of June 2026, allies had committed to funding more than $6 billion of defence equipment for Ukraine through the scheme, per NATO.

BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- China's gross ocean product reached 8.5 trillion yuan (about 1.27 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first three quarters of this year, up 4.9 percent year on year, according to data released by the Ministry of Natural Resources.
The marine economy maintained steady growth, with an improved structure, stronger resilience and growing momentum, moving toward innovative and high-quality development, the ministry said.

The seawater desalination and comprehensive utilization industry made new progress, with the combined capacity of newly launched desalination projects this year exceeding 520,000 tonnes per day.
China's marine tourism maintained stable growth in the first three quarters, the ministry said.
Dai Bin, president of the China Tourism Academy, said marine tourism is characterized by strong experiential attributes, high technological content, and extensive industry linkages.
