Denmark, Greenland and Faroe Islands to jointly lead Nordic Council in 2027
Lars-Christian Brask, a member of Denmark’s parliament for Liberal Alliance, has been elected president of the Nordic Council, which brings together parliamentarians from the Nordic countries.
Brask was elected Thursday during the council’s session in Helsinki, Finland, according to a statement from Folketinget, Denmark’s parliament.
Denmark will take over the rotating presidency from Finland in 2027, sharing leadership responsibilities with Greenland and the Faroe Islands for the first time.
Brask has chaired Denmark’s delegation to the Nordic Council since 2023. He said the presidency involves leading parliamentary cooperation between the Nordic countries.
“Just like in the Folketing, we can make proposals that are voted through and then go to the Council of Ministers, which then has to implement them,” Brask told Ritzau, Denmark’s news agency.
Greenland and the Faroe Islands will share the vice presidency. Justus Hansen of Greenland’s Demokraatit party will serve during the first six months, followed by Sunnvá Dahl Høgfeldt of the Faroese Sambandsflokkurin party.
According to Folketinget, the presidency will prioritize removing barriers between Nordic countries to improve regional cooperation and competitiveness.
Children, young people, civil society, culture and understanding of Nordic languages will also feature in its agenda.
Brask said Denmark intends to focus on practical outcomes rather than formalities.
“There will be fewer ceremonial speeches and more focus on delivering concrete results,” he said.
The Nordic Council has 87 parliamentarians, with its presidency rotating annually among five Nordic countries.
Denmark last held the presidency in 2021, when Bertel Haarder of Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, served as president.
Arctic sea ice survives summer with less melting than expected despite record-low winter
Arctic sea ice has retained more of its coverage than expected this summer, thanks to unusually cool weather conditions, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute (DMI).
In a statement Thursday, DMI reported that Arctic sea ice reached a record-low winter extent earlier this year but experienced relatively limited melting during the summer months.
A large low-pressure system over the Arctic helped keep temperatures cooler, slowing the melting process and allowing more ice to survive.
Gorm Dybkjær, a climate researcher at DMI, said the development was surprising but cautioned against interpreting it as a reversal of climate change.
“It is remarkable that the sea ice in the Arctic has retained so much of its winter ice after the winter’s record-low extent. But that does not mean that climate change has released its grip on the ice,” he said.
In September, when Arctic sea ice reached its annual minimum, its extent ranked as the 16th-lowest since records began in 1978.
Despite this year’s relatively favorable conditions, scientists continue to observe a long-term decline in the thickness and volume of Arctic sea ice.
Since 2007, the Arctic’s total sea ice volume has fallen by an estimated 20 percent or more.
Dybkjær warned that thinner ice is increasingly vulnerable to changing weather and ocean conditions, which could trigger sudden, substantial losses.
Researchers also monitor sea ice because of its role in regulating Earth’s temperature through the albedo effect.
This refers to how much incoming sunlight is reflected into space.
Ice and clouds reflect substantial amounts of solar radiation, while darker ocean surfaces absorb more energy, contributing to warming.

Copenhagen Police will introduce a stop-and-search zone around Parken on Sunday, 8 November, when FC Copenhagen face Brøndby IF in a match classified as high risk.
The zone will be in force from 06:00 to 20:00 across parts of Østerbro, including Trianglen, Blegdamsvej, Jagtvej, Østerbrogade, Svanemøllen Station and Strandboulevarden.
Within the zone, police can stop and search people without suspecting them of a criminal offence. The measure is intended to prevent unrest surrounding the derby.

“We will also be present in large numbers so that we can intervene if there should be signs of unrest brewing,” he said.
Police have also instructed FC Copenhagen to keep Brøndby supporters inside Parken for up to an hour after the final whistle. The aim is to separate the two groups of fans and prevent confrontations after the match.
Copenhagen Police warned that penalties for certain offences committed in connection with a football match can be increased by up to 50 percent. These include offences involving drugs, weapons and fireworks.
PET warns Ukrainians in Denmark of Russian sabotage recruitment
Denmark’s Security and Intelligence Service (PET) is distributing information in Ukrainian to warn Ukrainians living in Denmark that Russian intelligence services may try to recruit them for sabotage.
PET has previously warned the wider Danish public. Emil Græsholm, its head of counterintelligence, said the warning must also be accessible in Ukrainian because Ukrainians in Denmark could be targeted.
According to PET, Russia may seek to discredit Ukrainian refugees by making them appear involved in Russian sabotage operations.
Russian intelligence services can hide behind intermediaries, offering paid assignments disguised as journalism, market research or routine documentation. Those carrying out the work may have no idea who is ultimately directing it.
“You can end up helping a Russian intelligence service without knowing who you are actually working for,” Græsholm said.
Recruitment takes place through social media and messaging platforms. PET urges people to be cautious if strangers offer payment for taking photographs or observing locations, particularly if they insist the assignment must remain secret.
Anyone who becomes suspicious should contact the police, even if they have already completed the assignment, Græsholm said.
The warning comes less than a week after two young Ukrainian men were released from custody in an espionage case. They remain charged with allegedly photographing the company MyDefence in Nørresundby and sending the images to a Telegram user, thereby assisting Russian intelligence operations in Denmark.
The court in Aalborg found that the suspicion against them was insufficient to justify keeping them in custody.
PET is working with the Ukrainian embassy and Danish immigration authorities to distribute the warning.

Written Danish exam grades fall across Denmark’s upper secondary programs
Grades in written Danish have fallen across Denmark’s upper secondary education programs, according to the latest exam results released by the Education Ministry on Thursday.
At general upper secondary schools, known as stx, the average grade in A-level Danish, the highest subject level, fell from 6.8 in 2018 to 6.2 in 2026.
Across upper secondary programs, grades declined both compared with last year and over the longer term.
Education Minister Magnus Heunicke of the Social Democrats said the figures worried him and raised concerns about students’ use of artificial intelligence.
“Artificial intelligence has in a very short time changed the students’ everyday lives,” he said in a press release.
“And we cannot ignore what it can mean for their academic proficiency. Because if AI becomes a shortcut around the work of writing, analyzing, and expressing oneself, then we risk that the students learn less,” he said.
The figures follow a PISA international student assessment published in early September that showed declining performance in reading, mathematics and science among 15-year-olds, renewing debate about academic standards in Danish schools.

Rigshospitalet declined 10 donor livers over the past year because of capacity shortages
Rigshospitalet, a major hospital in Copenhagen, declined three donor livers for children and seven for adults over the past year because it lacked capacity, according to health news outlet Sundhedsmonitor.
The outlet reported the figures from a response by the Capital Region of Denmark to regional council member Christoffer Buster Reinhardt of the Conservative People’s Party.
The organs were offered through Scandiatransplant, which coordinates organ distribution between Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Estonia. Rigshospitalet can receive offers from other hospitals when they do not need the organs themselves.
The hospital told Sundhedsmonitor it was “not unusual” to decline livers for children.
“Rigshospitalet has at no point been staffed to be able to perform liver transplants on children 24/7/365,” the hospital said.
Sundhedsmonitor contacted the five other hospitals in the collaboration that perform liver transplants. Three major university hospitals in Sweden and Norway said they had never declined a liver because of capacity constraints.
Rigshospitalet performed between four and 12 liver transplants on children annually from 2021 through 2025. It has performed seven so far this year. The hospital told Ritzau that its number of pediatric liver transplants was at least on par with those in the other Nordic countries.
External review follows doctors’ departures
On Monday, regional politicians announced that external reviewers would examine Rigshospitalet’s transplant department, the only department in Denmark that performs liver transplants.
The announcement followed a meeting between hospital management and the Capital Region’s executive committee. Regional council Chairman Lars Gaardhøj of the Social Democrats and Reinhardt spoke about the review after the meeting.
Hospital managers were asked to explain whether patients could still receive proper treatment after several doctors had resigned or been removed from their positions.
Two surgeons left the department earlier this year. Five senior physicians subsequently wrote to hospital management and the region to express concern about patient safety.
Three of those five were later sent home and are now leaving the hospital entirely, Danish public broadcaster DR reported Monday.
Direct flights from Copenhagen to Ilulissat cleared as Greenland airport opens
Travelers heading to western Greenland will no longer need to change planes in Nuuk after aviation authorities approved the opening of Ilulissat’s expanded airport on Thursday.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority granted final safety approval overnight, following inspections and a test flight.
“Following a long series of inspections and a test flight, we have approved that the airport meets the necessary level of safety required to operate a modern, international airport,” said deputy director Lars Korsholm.
The approval comes with temporary restrictions during the airport’s initial operating period. These will gradually be eased as the airport gains experience.
Korsholm said the restrictions were unlikely to affect scheduled flights, particularly outside the tourist season.
The airport’s runway has been extended from 845 meters to 2,200 meters, allowing larger aircraft to land in Ilulissat, a town on Greenland’s western coast near Disko Bay.
Previously, passengers traveling from Copenhagen had to connect through Nuuk, Greenland’s capital.
The new direct route will take approximately four hours and 40 minutes.
Initially, Air Greenland will generally operate one direct flight between Copenhagen and Ilulissat every Wednesday, with additional weekly departures during busy periods, including Christmas and New Year.
Thursday’s opening will be marked by an inaugural flight from Copenhagen, scheduled to land in Ilulissat at 11:40 a.m. local time, corresponding to 2:40 p.m. Danish time.
The expansion forms part of a multibillion-krone investment in Greenland’s airports, which also includes improvements in Nuuk and a new airport near Qaqortoq in southern Greenland.
The projects aim to improve transport connections and support economic development, particularly through increased tourism.

Five Danish municipalities agree to take additional Ukrainian refugees
Five municipalities in Jutland have volunteered to accommodate more Ukrainian refugees than their allocated share, offering some relief to municipalities facing pressure elsewhere in Denmark.
Haderslev, Horsens, Skive, Struer and Viborg will receive a combined 133 additional refugees, according to the Ministry of Immigration and Integration.
Viborg will take the largest share, with 65 additional arrivals, while Skive will accommodate 18.
Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bødskov, from the Social Democrats, welcomed the decision, noting that Copenhagen and municipalities in its western suburbs are particularly stretched.
“It is a shared task to ensure that the Ukrainians who come to Denmark also gain a proper foothold in our local communities,” Bødskov said.
The announcement comes as the government seeks to restrict residence permits for displaced Ukrainians arriving from 14 areas it considers less affected by the war.
Parliament has already passed legislation excluding Ukrainian men aged 23 to 60 from obtaining residence under a special law, aiming to prevent them from avoiding military mobilization.
Several Jutland municipalities previously offered to accept additional refugees, citing available accommodation and demand for workers.
However, only Skive proceeded among the five municipalities that initially expressed interest.
Brønderslev requested additional funding, which Bødskov rejected, saying municipalities willing to help must operate under existing financial arrangements.
More than 47,000 Ukrainian refugees currently live in Denmark, compared with the 100,000 arrivals authorities prepared for in 2022.
Despite the lower number, Bødskov said pressure on municipalities justified tighter admission rules.
He acknowledged the difficulties involved while emphasizing Denmark’s continued military, civilian and humanitarian assistance to Ukraine.
Most Danish companies want to help during crises but lack emergency contacts
Danish businesses are willing to provide equipment and other resources during emergencies, but many do not know how to offer their assistance, a new analysis shows.
According to Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, 81 percent of companies want to support their local communities during crises. However, two-thirds do not know whom to contact.
Morten Høyer, the organization’s political director, believes this leaves valuable resources unused.
“The business community has a very large capacity, which can help people faster and perhaps even make the effort cheaper,” he said.
“But it is not utilized well enough.”
Høyer cited pumps for storm surges and emergency generators for power outages as examples of equipment businesses could provide.
He urged municipalities to identify available resources and include local companies in emergency preparedness plans.
Civil Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from the Socialist People’s Party (SF), agreed that businesses need clear contact points.
“We must build relationships, clear channels of contact, and a shared understanding of situations and threats before, during, and after crises,” she said in a written statement.
The minister expects to announce further initiatives soon.
Maja Broløs, director of Virksomhedsberedskabet, a business emergency preparedness organization, also stressed the importance of planning ahead.
Her organization, which has more than 200 members, is developing a nationwide overview of companies willing to assist during major emergencies.
“If you only start investigating who can help, and what resources they have, once the crisis has arisen, a quick and effective effort becomes really difficult,” she said.
Broløs noted that businesses without conventional emergency equipment can also contribute, citing Copenhagen Zoo’s fenced areas, kitchens and operational facilities as examples.

Danish tax agency faces further scrutiny over identity theft cases
Denmark’s Parliamentary Ombudsman has demanded further explanations from the Danish Tax Agency over its handling of cases involving citizens who were wrongly pursued for millions in taxes after becoming victims of identity theft.
Ombudsman Christian Britten Lundblad said the agency’s report, submitted on August 31, did not adequately address concerns raised about the cases.
“After reviewing the report and the complaint that I previously received from a lawyer on behalf of a citizen in the complex of cases, I have found reason to ask the Danish Tax Agency for a statement,” Lundblad wrote.
The investigation concerns 126 people involved in tax cases linked to money transfers through five businesses. The agency began examining the transfers in 2021.
In June, TV 2’s investigative programme Operation X highlighted how citizens had faced incorrect tax claims worth millions following suspected identity theft connected to money laundering cases.
The agency’s own report found that it should have acted in 2023, when police provided information suggesting widespread identity theft.
In August, Danish Tax Agency Director Thomas Hjortenberg acknowledged the mistakes and apologised to those affected.
“Our mistakes have had major personal consequences for the affected citizens,” he said.
Hjortenberg also admitted that the agency should have responded much earlier to the police’s warnings.
The ombudsman now wants to establish what information the agency possessed before issuing its tax assessments.
He has also requested clarification on whether evidence in each case supported the information obtained from the money transfer businesses.
The Danish Tax Agency has until November 7 to provide its response.

Alm. Brand to lay off 55 employees as it reports record insurance result
Danish insurance group Alm. Brand has decided to lay off 55 employees and has eliminated 30 other positions as part of efforts to reduce costs, even as it reported its highest quarterly insurance result to date.
The group’s insurance result reached 755 million DKK in the third quarter, according to financial statements released Wednesday. The measure reflects earnings from its core insurance business, taking account of premium income, claims and operating expenses.
Chief Executive Officer Andreas Ruben Madsen said the job cuts were needed to improve efficiency and support the company’s previously announced strategy.
“It is a difficult decision because it affects colleagues, but it is at the same time a necessary step to realize the efficiencies that support the strategic direction we have already announced,” he said in a stock exchange announcement.
Lower claims costs were the main factor behind the record insurance result. Claims expenses fell by 165 million DKK from the same period last year to approximately 1.7 billion DKK. Insurance income rose slightly to more than 3 billion DKK.
The group reported a third-quarter profit after tax of 397 million DKK.
Madsen attributed the insurance result mainly to fewer major claims, fewer weather-related claims and positive run-off results. Run-off results arise when an insurer adjusts its estimates for claims from previous periods.
He cautioned that those factors might not provide the same boost in future quarters.
“This contributes significantly to earnings in the quarter, but at the same time these are conditions that we cannot expect will contribute at the same level going forward.”

Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.

Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.
The coin, associated with Viking king Svend Tveskæg, fetched more than twice its estimated price of 6,000 to 8,000 euros, or roughly 45,000 to 60,000 DKK.
Auction house Stack’s Bowers confirmed the sale on its website following Tuesday’s auction.
The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.

Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.
The Moderates, a centrist party, have changed their position since 2024, when parliament rejected a proposal to ban the production, sale and import of Ross 308 chickens.
At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.
At Rema 1000, the figure is 15 percent.
Social Democratic animal welfare spokesperson Birgitte Vind also told Berlingske that the chickens’ conditions were unacceptable and should be examined.

Denmark moves towards allowing wolf hunting from 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:16:41 UTC
16:16:41 KST

The Danish government hopes to allow wolf hunting as early as 2027. Researchers will now determine how large the country’s wolf population needs to be to remain viable.
Denmark is taking another step towards allowing wolves to be hunted, after EU rules protecting the species were relaxed last year.
The government has commissioned work to determine how many wolves Denmark needs to maintain a stable and viable population in the long term.
At the same time, authorities want to introduce more precise monitoring using DNA to identify individual wolves.
Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen of the Social Democrats said the scientific work could pave the way for hunting as early as 2027.
“We need a population model in place. It is a step towards being able to regulate – that is, hunt wolves in Denmark,” he said.
The Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment (SGAV) will put the development of the population model out to public tender. A separate tender will cover individual monitoring of wolves.
At least 49 adult wolves
Denmark does not currently have an exact count of its wolf population.
In spring 2026, researchers from the Natural History Museum Aarhus and Aarhus University estimated that there were at least 49 adult wolves in Denmark.
The government now wants a more precise assessment based on DNA, making it possible to identify individual animals.
“We need a scientific count of the wolves, and we need a model for a minimum population,” Rabjerg Madsen said.
Once that work has been completed, the government hopes it will provide the scientific basis for introducing regulated hunting.
EU rules on wolves were relaxed in 2025
Wolves remain protected under EU law, but their protection status was changed in 2025.
The species was moved from Annex IV to Annex V of the EU Habitats Directive, changing its status from “strictly protected” to “protected”.
The change gives EU countries greater flexibility to manage their wolf populations, including through hunting.
However, it does not mean Denmark can simply introduce unrestricted wolf hunting.
Any hunting or population management must be compatible with maintaining the wolf at what EU rules call a “favourable conservation status”.
Determining that status involves more than simply counting wolves. Authorities must also consider factors including the population’s geographical range, habitat and long-term prospects.
The population model being commissioned by the Danish authorities is expected to be ready during 2027.
Minister hopes for hunting in 2027
Rabjerg Madsen said his ambition is to allow wolf hunting that same year.
“It is my ambition that we can have wolf hunting in 2027, because that is when we will start getting the numbers,” he said.
“My expectation is that they will show that we have a viable wolf population and that we therefore can have hunting of the wolf.”
Asked whether he was anticipating the researchers’ conclusion before the calculations had been made, the minister said the outcome would have to remain within the scientific and international rules governing Denmark.
“I have been very careful to say that it is my assessment and hope that we have a viable wolf population, so that we can have wolf hunting within the scientific boundaries we are committed to by international rules,” he said.
Individual wolves can already be killed under certain circumstances in Denmark. This can include wolves that repeatedly attack livestock protected by approved wolf-proof fencing or animals that display an abnormal lack of fear of humans.
Sources: Ritzau, European Commission and Agency for Green Land Transformation and Water Environment (SGAV)

Pesticide load rises, derailing targets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:16:20 UTC
16:16:20 KST

Denmark misses pesticide target as concerns grow over groundwater
Denmark’s pesticide load rose by 33 percent in a single year, new figures show. Part of the increase is linked to farmers stocking up on pesticides that can form the PFAS compound TFA and leach into groundwater.
Denmark has missed a key target for reducing the impact of pesticides on human health and the environment, with the country’s pesticide load instead reaching its second-highest level in 12 years.
New figures from the Danish Environmental Protection Agency show that the pesticide load indicator reached 2.29 in 2025.
The target was 1.43.
The indicator is used by Danish authorities to measure the overall impact of pesticides on human health and the environment.
The issue is particularly important in Denmark, where more than 99 percent of drinking water comes from groundwater.
TFA, a highly persistent PFAS compound, was detected in 40 percent of the Danish drinking-water wells tested between 2021 and 2024. However, the Danish Environmental Protection Agency says the concentrations currently found in drinking-water wells do not pose a risk to human health.
“It is completely unsatisfactory and simply not good enough,” Environment Minister Maria Reumert Gjerding of the Socialist People’s Party (SF) said in a statement.
Pesticide load rose 33 percent in one year
The pesticide load increased by 33 percent from 2024 to 2025.
Part of the increase was caused by farmers buying stocks of pesticides before 33 products were banned.
The products contain active substances that can break down into TFA and potentially leach into groundwater.
The European Chemicals Agency has classified TFA as harmful to unborn children and human reproductive health.
The Danish Environmental Protection Agency withdrew the 33 pesticide products as part of efforts to protect groundwater.
But stockpiling does not explain the entire increase in Denmark’s pesticide load.
If purchases of the affected pesticides are excluded, the pesticide load indicator is estimated at around 1.99 – still considerably above the 2025 target of 1.43.
The government is now preparing a new strategy aimed at reducing the impact of pesticides used in Danish agriculture.
“The figures clearly call for a new ambitious pesticide strategy that ensures the necessary initiatives to reduce the load from pesticides,” Gjerding said.
Environmental group calls it a serious setback
The Danish Society for Nature Conservation (Danmarks Naturfredningsforening) described the figures as a serious setback.
“It is a serious setback for a target that we were already far from reaching,” director Lars Midtiby said.
He also criticised farmers for stocking up on pesticides before restrictions came into force.
“When a tightening is on the way, agriculture stockpiles the pesticides affected by it, and then nature, our drinking water and the Danish population risk paying the price,” Midtiby said.
Landbrug & Fødevarer, which represents Denmark’s agriculture and food sector, defended the use of the now-phased-out pesticides.
The organisation said the products had been necessary to combat diseases, weeds and pests in crops and to maintain yields and quality.
Peter Nyegaard Nissen, the organisation’s director of plant production, said a new pesticide strategy needs to balance environmental protection with agricultural production.
“An ambitious pesticide strategy must both protect our groundwater and nature and at the same time ensure that Danish farmers can continue to produce food efficiently and competitively,” he said.

The survey, conducted from October 16 to 19, 2026, found that 54% of Americans believe the military action against Iran was not worth the costs when weighed against its benefits. Only 23% said the operation was worthwhile, while 20% were uncertain.
Opposition to the military campaign was even higher, with 61% of respondents opposing US attacks on Iran, compared with 34% who supported them.
The opposition was particularly strong among Democrats, 88% of whom opposed the attacks. The figure stood at 66% among independents and respondents with other political affiliations. Similarly, 80% of Democrats and 55% of independents said the costs of the military action outweighed its benefits.
The poll also revealed widespread skepticism about the Trump administration's approach to the war. A total of 58% of respondents said the US government does not have a clear strategy for achieving its objectives in the conflict with Iran, while only 16% believed it had one.

Syrian curriculum changes spark debate over removal of images and historical figures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
07:00:17 UTC
16:00:17 KST

Changes were not limited to the texts; images and illustrations were also edited in Photoshop, adding hijabs or long robes to female figures, deleting women's photos, and covering or replacing statues, sculptures and artworks.
A set of changes made to a number of school textbooks in Syria has sparked a wave of criticism and reactions on social media, after they included alterations to pictures and artworks, among them adding the hijab to drawn female figures, removing images of women and children, covering statues and replacing paintings and works of art. The revisions have also affected teaching content dealing with political life, citizenship, democratic participation, local administration and the media.
These changes have reopened the debate over the standards used by the Ministry of Education when it reviews curricula, and how far they take into account Syria's social and cultural diversity, amid questions about the nature and aims of the amendments, and whether they fall simply within a review of content linked to the former regime or go further towards reshaping how society is represented in school books.
Changes to images, illustrations and educational content
Comparisons posted on social media between different editions of school textbooks show amendments to material for several grades, including the early years and seventh grade, as well as the sixth-grade primary textbook "Social Studies".
It emerges that this last book, reissued for the current academic year, originally dates back to the 2012–2013 school year, with changes added that include the removal of material linked to the former regime, alongside lessons on local administration, political life, citizenship, the media and democratic participation.
The changes were not limited to texts; they also extended to images and illustrations using Photoshop. Hijabs were added – and in some cases long robes – to drawn female characters, entire pictures of women were deleted, statues were covered, and sculptures and artworks were removed or replaced with others.
The visual alterations to paintings and expressive illustrations became a main focus of controversy, after committees removed the world-famous painting "Mona Lisa" and deleted a drawing showing a girl skipping rope beside two children in textbooks for early age groups.
The revisions also extended to historical figures and symbols. The Phoenician princess Elissar, founder of Carthage, was affected when a painting depicting her on a hunting trip was dropped and replaced with another portrait that had been digitally modified to cover the chin and neck – a step critics saw as imposing contemporary ideological standards on an ancient historical era.
One of the examples that provoked ridicule and debate was dressing a pharaonic statue in a striped shirt, which many users likened to prison uniforms.
Accusations of "falsifying history" and erasing national symbols
A new batch of visual comparisons circulated on social media documented far-reaching changes introduced to the new Syrian school curricula in particular history books, with the new editions showing the removal of prominent national and pan-Arab figures and the alteration of the content of historical passages, amid sharp questions and concerns about systematic ideological and sectarian exclusion.
Activists highlighted information that caused widespread anger and was described as "a blatant falsification of history". The updated curriculum contains passages portraying the "martyrs" executed on 6 May by the Ottoman governor Jamal Pasha, known as the Butcher, as "agents of Britain and France", instead of their historical description as symbols of the national movement resisting Ottoman colonial rule.
The changes also include deleting the picture of Sultan Pasha al-Atrash and replacing it with that of Sheikh Saleh al-Ali, a move that raised fears of exclusion on sectarian grounds. The alterations further removed a photograph of the late Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser.
The revisions reached school maps too, with the district of Iskenderun and the occupied Syrian Golan omitted from one of the maps, as well as the deletion of a paragraph on the role of Syrian women in resisting the French Mandate. This has raised questions about the motives behind these changes and their impact on the historical narrative presented to pupils.
Artistic inconsistencies and satire on social media
The nature of these changes and how they were carried out unleashed a wave of sarcastic comments on social platforms, where many users felt some of the alterations were random and lacked unified artistic standards to ensure visual coherence within a single textbook.
The most widely shared example in this context is a female doctor character in first-grade books who appears wearing a hijab on one page and without a hijab on another.
The comments did not stop at the artistic side, but also questioned the rationale for removing artworks and illustrated characters from school textbooks, and the criteria used to decide which images should be kept, modified or removed.
Parents criticise the changes and warn of their consequences
Among parents, objections went beyond the quality of the illustrations or the inconsistencies in modifying them, to the implications of these changes and their possible impact on how children view society and diversity.
Speaking to Euronews, Alia, the mother of a lower-secondary pupil, said she had not at first noticed the amendments because of the poor print quality and lack of detail in the drawings, pointing out that the heavy academic content and padding make it difficult for both parents and pupils to focus on visual details.
She argued that editing images of historical figures by adding a hijab raises questions about the purpose of such a step, and felt that replacing the pictures with new drawings would have been a more logical option than tampering with the original works. She warned that imposing a single pattern in the way women are depicted could shape how social diversity is presented to children, instead of promoting values of harmony and coexistence.
She added that priority should be given to developing the curricula and keeping pace with global shifts in education, rather than becoming preoccupied with cosmetic changes that add no clear educational value. In her view, such practices risk deepening divisions and fuelling intolerance instead of reducing it.
Alia went on: "The highest priority in this critical phase should be to fundamentally develop the educational curricula and keep up with the latest global changes in the education sector", considering that focusing on superficial visual adjustments does not serve the learning process or offer pupils any clear educational benefit.
Concluding her remarks to Euronews, she warned that the persistence of such practices within educational institutions could produce the opposite effect, as they help to deepen ideological divisions in society and feed exclusionary and fanatical thinking rather than mitigating it and strengthening shared citizenship values.
In the same vein, Jaber, the father of a primary-school girl, expressed even stronger concerns in his interview with Euronews, arguing that these visual changes cannot be separated from ideological orientations that risk being entrenched in society's consciousness through the education system. Jaber called on international organisations concerned with children's rights to take urgent action to safeguard children's right to receive balanced and neutral education.
He summed up his objection with a stark contrast between global technological progress and the regression of local curricula, saying: "While the world has reached leaps forward in developing artificial intelligence, we in Syria are still drowning in sterile arguments over covering women's images and deleting artworks from school textbooks".
From satire to accusations of trying to impose an ideology
On the other hand, reactions went beyond mockery of how the changes were implemented and raised deeper questions about their cultural and social dimensions. Critics and observers accused the ministry of seeking to impose a specific ideology through the education system, arguing that changing the visual appearance of female characters and removing elements of global artistic heritage reflects a deliberate effort to reshape children's perceptions and build a new social identity.
Some believe these concerns are particularly sensitive in a country such as Syria, marked by religious, cultural and social diversity. Their fear is that, if adopted as a lasting approach, such changes could entrench a one-sided view of Syrian society and sideline its historical pluralism and the natural differences in ways of life that distinguish it.
Part of the controversy centres on the distinction between two separate steps: the first involves removing content linked to the former regime, and the second relates to altering artistic illustrations or deleting educational topics on citizenship, political life and democratic participation.
While some see purging the curricula of the previous era's legacy as part of a normal modernisation process, the other changes raise questions about the educational and cultural foundations that govern how content is selected and directed.
Others argue that the published amendments alone are not enough to conclusively prove the existence of a coherent policy to impose a specific ideology. To reach an objective assessment of this accusation, they say, it is essential to see the official standards adopted, define the real scope of the changes and their causes, and compare them with the broader orientations the new curricula will adopt in the coming phases.
Ministry of Education: curricula respect diversity and do not adopt a single line
For its part, Syria's Ministry of Education on Monday rejected, in an official statement, the reports circulating on social media about new changes to images and content in the school curricula, describing this information as "inaccurate" and asserting that no new changes have been approved to the curricula in force for the current academic year.
The ministry clarified in its statement that the changes carried out since the fall of the former regime were limited to a single amendment that was announced and fully detailed in January 2025. According to the statement, that change focused mainly on removing the symbols and ideological content of the ousted regime and correcting the images and material linked to it, especially in the social studies and Islamic education curricula after they were merged and unified, in order to safeguard the diversity of Syrian society and strengthen the presence of all its components and cultures.
The ministry stressed that its plans to develop the curricula aim first and foremost to meet Syrians' aspirations and to entrench the values of citizenship and belonging, a culture of law and respect for others. In this context, it announced the completion of the "national framework for curricula" and the adoption of modern scientific standards that place the learner at the centre of the educational process, with the aim of fostering critical thinking, analysis and creative problem-solving, as well as enhancing life and digital skills, with the new curricula to be introduced gradually in line with the approved procedures.
The ministry attached to its release original samples and images from school textbooks to demonstrate the visual and social diversity they contain and to counter the circulating claims, calling on the media and the public to verify information carefully, rely on official sources and avoid being drawn into rumours.
The ministry's official statement, however, failed to defuse the crisis. It was met with a broad and fierce wave of criticism from activists and education watchers, some of whom went as far as accusing the ministry of "lying and concealing the truth".
Critics argued that the ministry's denial of any new amendments is completely at odds with the evidence and live visual comparisons taken from the textbooks distributed in schools.
On 17 August 2026, the Syrian Ministry of Education announced the adoption of unified curricula in all provinces for the 2026–2027 academic year, based on the previous year's curricula known as the "Damascus curriculum". It stated that it had completed the preparation of national standards for the new curricula in preparation for moving to the drafting phase.
On 14 September 2026, Syrian Education Minister Mohammad Abdulrahman Turko told a parliamentary hearing that the ministry had removed images and symbols linked to the former regime from the last two editions of schoolbooks.
He indicated that a single curriculum had been adopted across the different provinces, with a two-year transition period granted to pupils who had studied under the previous curricula.
Turko added that the ministry had referred the national standards for building the new curricula to the Higher Council for Education in preparation for starting to write the textbooks once those standards are approved.

Explainer: A journey without pause: how a century-old political party governs itself
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
14:49:22 CST
15:49:22 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- How does a large ruling party that has long enjoyed the people's support keep moving forward without being lulled by its own success?
For the Communist Party of China (CPC), one key to doing so is to stay vigilant and never lose sight of potential risks that come with long-term governance. Faced with the dangers of complacency, inadequate competence, estrangement from the people and corruption, the Party has chosen to confront them head-on.
At the just-concluded fifth plenary session of its 20th Central Committee, the CPC reaffirmed its commitment to persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance.
The session took stock of what has been achieved and set out the fundamental task, guiding principles and plans needed to sustain that effort.
NOT A PASSING GUST
In 2014, when the term "full and rigorous Party self-governance" was first introduced, skeptics asked whether it would be a passing gust. Time has answered. The campaign has neither stopped nor softened.
The numbers show the scale of that sustained effort. From January to September 2026, disciplinary inspection and supervision organs across the country opened 800,000 cases and disciplined 680,000 people -- both figures well above the totals for the whole of 2014.
These increases require context. Broader oversight and stronger enforcement, aided by big data and other information technologies, have helped uncover more violations. The figures also point to an ongoing task: addressing corruption that has already taken root while preventing new abuses. This is no time to let up.
Looking at history, the pattern is evident. Attention to the Party's self-governance has never been an improvised matter. As early as 1926, just five years after the Party's founding, its Central Committee issued its first document aimed at combating corruption.
In recent decades, nearly every Central Committee of the Party has convened a dedicated plenary session on Party building. The emphasis has shifted with changing circumstances, but the issue remains a priority on the core political agenda of the Party, which now has more than 101 million members.
WHY PARTY SELF-GOVERNANCE MATTERS
This year marks the start of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) period, a critical stretch for advancing Chinese modernization. Next year, the Party will hold its pivotal 21st National Congress, a highly important meeting and an event of great political significance for both the Party and the country.
At this juncture, emphasizing the importance of persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance is particularly significant for the CPC, whose capacity to lead bears directly on whether Chinese modernization can ultimately succeed.
Much remains to be done: cultivating high-caliber officials, building a well-knit organizational system characterized by cross-level alignment and effective implementation, taking firm and coordinated action against corruption, and refining Party and state oversight systems.
The implications extend beyond China. As a major contributor to and stabilizer of global economic growth, China offers broad market prospects, stable policy expectations and a sound security environment as it advances Chinese modernization.
Through targeted oversight, disciplinary inspection and supervision organs are helping ensure certainty in development and provide strong guarantees for economic and social progress.
By persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance, and combining Party self-supervision with supervision by the people, the CPC has offered the world new experience in supervising and constraining the exercise of power within a political party. ■

Travelling beyond the borders of Baku through fiction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:45:07 UTC
15:45:07 KST

What connects an Iranian novelist exploring women's lives, a British children's author creating imaginary worlds and an Azerbaijani writer preserving her country's cultural identity? The answer is stories that cross borders, connect continents, and blend cultures through books.
From the poetry of medieval Azerbaijan to contemporary novels reaching readers from across different continents, Baku's relationship with the written word is rooted in centuries of cultural exchange.
Today, that literary heritage is finding new expression as authors, publishers and readers from Europe, Asia and beyond came together in the Azerbaijani capital for the twelfth year running.
The 12th Baku International Book Fair saw 32 countries taking part in an event which was not simply about discovering the latest books.
It was an opportunity to explore how literature connects hearts and minds across languages, generations, and geographical barriers by blending and sharing ideas and stories.
At a time when technology is transforming how tales are told, published, and consumed, the fair also questioned how books will remain an intrinsic and vital part of our futures.
Where history meets the modern word
Azerbaijan's literary traditions stretch back centuries and have been shaped by its position at the crossroads of Europe and Asia.
The 12th-century poet Nizami Ganjavi features heavily.
He was born in what is now Azerbaijan and became one of the most influential literary figures of the Persian-speaking world, with his works travelling the globe. He continues to be celebrated today.
Centuries later, writers and poets include Muhammad Fuzuli, who contributed to a rich literary tradition that developed across different languages and cultural influences.
This heritage provides a historical and rich backdrop to the country's modern relationship with international literature, where translation, publishing partnerships and literary festivals help stories reach audiences far beyond local borders and countries of origin.
For Iranian novelist Parinoush Saniee, literature offers a way of exploring the relationships between individuals and the societies in which they live.
Her internationally recognised novel The Book of Fate follows the life of an Iranian woman through decades of personal and political change, examining themes of identity, family, education and the expectations placed upon women.
Saniee explained that she initially assumed her work would only resonate regionally, but she was quickly surprised by the global reaction.
"The first translation of my book was into Italian," Saniee recalled.
"When I saw all that reception and various journalists came from different places, I asked them what was interesting about the book for you. They said it was close to us. We also had such experiences. It was very relatable."
Although rooted in Iranian society, the questions raised in her writing resonate far beyond its borders. The works have been translated into numerous languages and demonstrate how literature can offer readers an understanding of lives and experiences different from their own.
She observed this same phenomenon when the novel became a bestseller in Norway, proving that universal themes of suffering and endurance translate seamlessly.
"Human suffering, lifestyles, issues, and problems are overall very impactful for humanity, and we all understand it," Saniee stated. "Therefore, it doesn't matter where it is from."
Reaching younger minds
British author Darren Simpson, meanwhile, approaches storytelling through the imagination of younger readers.
He is known for novels such as Scavengers and The Memory Thieves, where he creates unusual worlds and characters exploring friendships, belonging, identity and the challenges of growing up.
Simpson echoed the sentiment that human emotion makes storytelling cross borders effortlessly, noting that children across the globe seek the exact same things from a narrative.
"When I see children from all around different countries connect to my stories in the same way, it speaks to me about the universal nature of a lot of feelings about people's needs and their desire to connect," Simpson explained.
His works reflect the importance of children's literature at a time when arguably young people have an unprecedented choice of digital entertainment and books are not necessarily the most popular choice. Yet, he highlighted that the local reception at the fair had been incredibly inspiring.
"I have been struck in Azerbaijan by how much passion there is here in the young readers," he added.
Championing local voices
Alongside its international offerings, the fair is also celebrating the locals who have helped to shape Azerbaijan's contemporary literary identity.
One of those is Reyhan Yusifgizi, a prominent voice in Azerbaijani children's science fiction who brings a unique academic background in computer science to her writing.
When discussing how to cultivate reading habits in a digital age, Yusifgizi explained that increasing a child's interest requires a two-step approach.
"First, this depends on the author," Yusifgizi noted. "They must write well, write in a modern way. With simple language, they must interest the child."
However, she stressed that the second factor is often the most fundamental.
"The parent directly influences the child. The parent stands between the author, the book, and the child," she said.
"First of all, the parent must demonstrate it through their own experience, their own example. They need to read."
Azerbaijani writer and publicist Elmira Akhundova reflected on the profound emotional weight that physical books carry compared to fleeting digital news. For her, literature's ultimate purpose is to promote peace and multiculturalism.
"What is at the end of the most difficult, the saddest book? It is light," Akhundova said.
"It is a call towards tolerance. We must hear these humanistic calls and instill them in our young generation," she told Euronews.
She challenged the next generation to seek out complex, philosophical narratives rather than settling for easy entertainment, noting that every story should ultimately lead the reader towards hope.
"A book must absolutely be geared toward humanism," she added, asserting that no matter what, a book "must be on the sunny side of the street."
The future of the written word
It is recognised that the relationship between books and their readers is changing.
Digital publishing, audiobooks and new forms of storytelling are reshaping the literary landscape, but rather than replacing traditional physical books entirely, there is an advantage to the technological advancements.
Books can now travel at lightning speed. A touch of a button can transport us to another universe, and perhaps that is what makes an international literary gathering even more relevant today.
Beyond the book stands, authors are choosing to move from the desktop to have those important physical discussions, drawn together by that love of narrative.
And what better place to have those conversations than the gateway between East and West?

Somalia looks to the future as the UN's political mission closes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:41:11 UTC
15:41:11 KST

Somalia looks to the future as the UN's political mission closes
“The story of the UN's political engagement in Somalia has been one of persistence, partnership and adaptation,” Raisedon Zenenga, the UN Secretary-General's Deputy Special Representative for Somalia has said, as three decades of UN political missions in the Horn of Africa country comes to an end on 31 October.
The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia, known as UNTMIS, wraps up its work on Saturday and according to Mr. Zenenga “while significant challenges remain, the closure of UNTMIS comes after considerable progress by Somalia since the early years of international efforts to support the country's recovery.”
Somalia has undergone a profound transformation since the early 1990s, when the collapse of central State institutions and the outbreak of civil war ushered in years of conflict, instability and humanitarian crises.
The conflict sparked a major outflow of refugees and internal displacements, while ongoing insecurity, contested electoral processes and constitutional reform, as well as recurrent climatic shocks – including droughts and floods – compounded humanitarian needs and presented formidable challenges to the country's recovery.
Somalia’s responsibility
Successive political missions accompanied Somalia through critical stages of its peacebuilding and State-building journey, supporting Somali-led efforts to restore governance, rebuild institutions and foster national reconciliation.
With the end of the UNTMIS, it is now Somali institutions which will take on the full responsibility for the country’s recovery with support from UN agencies already working in the country.
“Somalia today possesses national and federal institutions that did not exist when the UN’s political engagement began. Progress has been made in State formation, political inclusion, constitutional processes, human rights frameworks and the development of governance structures that enable Somali-led decision-making,” said Mr. Zenenga.
“However, continued engagement by the international community will remain important to sustaining progress and addressing outstanding priorities,” he added.
Humanitarian and development support
That engagement includes some 25 UN entities that are still working across Somalia on humanitarian and development support.
In September, in the town of Balcad, a run-down vegetable market got a makeover from the UN's migration agency, IOM.
There are now 56 sturdy stalls, running water and solar lighting. About 70 per cent of the stalls went to women-headed households, women-led businesses and small enterprises.
Elsewhere, Somalia's health ministry, working with UNICEF, launched national guidelines on caring for newborns, including babies who are small or sick.
In Puntland, where nearly a million children are out of school, the UN's food agency FAO is backing a school meals programme that links 1,330 local farmers and fisherfolk to schools serving 18,700 children, so kids eat and families earn.
And in Baidoa, mine action experts from UNMAS helped Somali authorities teach hundreds of students and teachers how to spot explosive dangers.
A complex crisis
The UN's humanitarian affairs office, OCHA, calls the situation in Somalia one of the world's most complex crises.
Conflict and climate shocks keep feeding each other, and families who fled drought or fighting have often been uprooted a second or third time by floods or fresh violence.
This year, 4.8 million Somalis, out of a population of just under 20 million, need humanitarian help.
Aid agencies are asking for $852 million to reach 2.4 million people, just half of those in need, and by mid-October only about 35 per cent of that had arrived.
The UN Secretary-General also wants continued support to tackle the threat from the terror group Al-Shabaab and to help Somalia move to a gradual, sustainable security transition.
Looking ahead, one huge challenge for Somalia's leaders after October is poverty.
They'll need to tackle it while steadying an economy that's still fragile. It leans heavily on subsistence farming, livestock, money sent home by relatives abroad and pastoralism.
The country imports more than 90 per cent of its essential goods, according to OCHA.
UN will remain
While UNTMIS is closing down, the United Nations is not leaving. UN humanitarian and development agencies continue to support Somalia and its people.
“Today is not an end to the partnership between the United Nations and Somalia,” Deputy Special Representative Zenenga said. "It marks the conclusion of one chapter and the beginning of another.”

Azmi Bishara: Arab turnout denied Netanyahu a majority in Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:32:22 UTC
15:32:22 KST

Breadcrumb
Azmi Bishara: Arab turnout denied Netanyahu a majority in Israeli election
Record turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel was decisive in denying Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies the parliamentary majority needed to form a government, Arab intellectual Azmi Bishara said in an interview with Al-Araby TV from Lusail, Qatar, on Friday evening.
Bishara, director general of the Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies, analysed the results of the Israeli Knesset elections and responded to what he described as a Zionist campaign against both him and Qatar following the unprecedented Arab turnout.
In Bishara's reading, that turnout prevented Netanyahu's bloc from reaching the 61 seats required to form a government. He described Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the anti-Netanyahu camp, as "less bad than Netanyahu", while arguing that his bloc "does not offer a genuine alternative to the right".
The interview also touched on next Tuesday's US midterm elections. Bishara said a Democratic "blue wave" in the House of Representatives now appeared almost certain, while the contest for the Senate remained extremely tight.
At the same time, he cautioned that any U.S. decision to go to war with Iran would not depend on the outcome of the congressional elections. He reiterated what he had told the same channel the previous Thursday: an agreement with Iran would be better for Iran and the wider region because the current oscillation between war and peace was nearing its end, with relations between Tehran and Washington moving toward either war or an agreement.
Arab turnout defeated Netanyahu
Bishara focused at length on the 80% turnout among Arab citizens in Tuesday's election, arguing that this participation denied Benjamin Netanyahu and his camp the 61 seats required to form a government.
He said the most powerful force driving Arab citizens to vote in such unprecedented numbers was the government of Netanyahu and Itamar Ben-Gvir itself. Palestinian citizens of Israel, he said, had been shocked by the war of genocide in Gaza, by the repression they faced and by attempts to prevent them from expressing their position on the massacre.
This had created fear and deep frustration, Bishara said, and Arab citizens had been waiting for the election as an opportunity to express that anger and sense of grievance.
He added that what Netanyahu's government had done in Gaza and the West Bank, against Palestinian citizens inside Israel, and through its wars and crimes abroad "left no need for anyone to convince Arabs to turn out in large numbers".
Palestinian citizens of Israel had also come to feel that their citizenship and political legitimacy were genuinely under threat, he said. Their turnout therefore became a way of asserting their presence and exercising a form of citizenship that, in his view, stands in contradiction with Zionism.
Asked whether Arab citizens were better served by running on one, two or three electoral lists, Bishara said the priority was to maximise turnout regardless of how many lists contested the election.
He pointed to the fact that Arab parties had secured 19 seats through two separate lists.
Bishara said the result had sent the Israeli right into a frenzy, "to the point that its leading figures are now openly proclaiming apartheid slogans".
He said the most immediate parliamentary issue arising from the election result would be the election of the Knesset speaker.
This mattered to Arab citizens, Bishara said, because "it will be easier for Arab MPs to work in parliament if the Knesset speaker comes from outside Netanyahu's camp", adding that Yair Lapid could potentially take the post.
He again stressed that the main priority was to prevent Netanyahu from forming a coalition.
Bishara expressed regret that some elected Arab representatives, referring to the United Arab List, which won eight seats, were openly saying they would be prepared to work with a government led by Gadi Eisenkot in return for civil and economic services.
He argued that such gains had already been secured over previous decades. Bishara himself, he noted, had been a leading advocate for political and civil rights from within the Knesset over four consecutive terms without joining governments responsible for wars or apartheid.
In this context, Bishara stressed that most Arab votes had gone to the Joint List, "which may negotiate, but does not enter government coalitions".
The campaign against Qatar and me is 'sick fantasy'
Bishara said the unprecedented Arab turnout was driven by an "entirely political" cause.
Claims that American or Jewish organisations had played a role, or that money had been paid to increase turnout, were "nonsense", he said.
He described as "sick fantasy" the campaign being waged against him and Qatar by Israeli ministers, MPs and media figures who accused both him and Doha of playing a decisive role in the election result and in pushing Arab turnout towards the 80% mark.
Although he regarded the allegations as "sick fantasy", Bishara spent several minutes of the television interview responding to them.
What struck him most, he said, was the extent to which leading figures in the campaign, including Israeli Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli, were resorting to conspiracy theories to explain their defeat.
Bishara noted that "any genuinely democratic country, meaning not Israel", regards participation in elections as something fundamentally healthy.
He added that around 22 countries make voting compulsory and fine people who fail to take part, citing Australia and Belgium as examples.
Bishara said the level of what he described as delusion had reached the point where the Israeli magazine Makor Rishon, which is close to Netanyahu, claimed on Friday that Qatar was behind the current protests and unrest in France.
He described the claim as "hallucination, obsession and an outright lie".
Bishara said he simply did not have the time to run electoral campaigns because he was occupied with research, writing and the institutions he had founded.
He summed up his position by saying: "I am, of course, with my people, but I do not have time to run campaigns. A person should not retreat from their positions because of these campaigns. The mistake would be not to take these positions, not the opposite."
Asked why he and Qatar were being grouped together in the same Zionist campaign, Bishara said the idea was a baseless fantasy.
He suggested that the main reason for the campaign against Doha was Qatar's support for the Palestinian cause.
Possible scenarios
Turning to the possible scenarios after Tuesday's election failed to produce a clear winner, Bishara repeated what he had said in his previous interview with Al-Araby TV about US pressure to form a national unity government headed by Netanyahu and joined by Eisenkot and others from his camp.
That arrangement could potentially include Avigdor Lieberman, who previously served as director of Netanyahu's office before the two fell out.
Bishara said this option, aimed at avoiding another election, was also favoured by Israeli President Isaac Herzog.
He noted that Herzog had previously been a senior figure in the Labour Party and was known for signing shells that were later fired at Lebanon and Gaza.
Bishara said both the Netanyahu and Eisenkot camps were now trying to persuade individual politicians and parties to cross over from the opposing bloc.
Another possibility was to bring the opposition into a government headed by Netanyahu, perhaps under an arrangement in which the premiership would rotate after two years.
Netanyahu, he said, was meanwhile trying to persuade individual figures from the opposing camp to join him so that he could avoid the unwelcome prospect of sharing the premiership under a rotation deal.
Bishara cited ongoing contacts with the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party, which holds seven seats, as one example. Efforts were underway to persuade it to leave Netanyahu's camp and join an Eisenkot-led alliance.
If that happened, Bishara said, Eisenkot's bloc would reach 55 seats and achieve what he described as a clear Jewish majority.
Bishara then looked back to the period before the 1999 election to illustrate what he sees as the decline of the Zionist left.
The Labour Party, which won the 1999 election, secured only four seats in 2022, he said.
Now, even after allying with the left-wing Meretz party, it had secured only eight seats.
In Bishara's analysis, aside from those eight representatives of the Zionist left, virtually everyone else in the Knesset belonged to the right.
His conclusion was that the organised Zionist left had effectively disappeared, leaving only individual figures.
"Either the left must be non-Zionist or it will disappear," he said.
Within this context, Bishara described Eisenkot as "less bad than Netanyahu".
But, he argued, like Netanyahu's other rivals on the right, Eisenkot had failed to establish a stable political party or organisational structure.
Bishara cited Benny Gantz as another example. Gantz had once been the strongest opposition leader, yet his party failed to cross the 3.25% electoral threshold in Tuesday's vote.
Bishara argued that liberal right-wing forces, which he said did not fundamentally differ from Likud on Palestine or on the question of a just political settlement, had struggled to establish stable parties or coherent ideological structures precisely because they did not offer a genuine alternative to the right.
The only areas in which they offered a fundamentally different programme, he said, concerned lifestyle issues, personal freedoms and the powers of the judiciary.
"Apart from that, all their criticism of Netanyahu is either security-related or concerns the failure to draft the ultra-Orthodox into the army," Bishara said.
What awaits the region after the election
Addressing the potential regional impact of the election result, Bishara said Netanyahu's opponents did not reject his regional policies in principle, whether towards Iran, Lebanon or Syria.
Instead, he argued, their differences were mainly over the methods and form those policies should take.
On a possible war with Iran, Bishara said there would therefore be little difference between a Netanyahu government and one formed by the camp opposed to him.
He said, however, that some figures within the opposition had criticised Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Some within Eisenkot's camp might also be more willing to engage with the Palestinian Authority, Bishara said, although not to remove settlements, establish a Palestinian state or withdraw to the 1967 borders.
In Bishara's assessment, a government emerging from the anti-Netanyahu camp might take greater account of US alliances in the region than the current Israeli government does.
Life under such a government might also be somewhat less difficult for Palestinian citizens of Israel and for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, he said.
"But at the international level, a government emerging from the anti-Netanyahu camp could be more useful to Israel," Bishara said.
He argued that such a government would present a better international image than Israel's current position of growing isolation under a far-right government containing figures he described as "terrorists", including Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.

This comes days after the French government presented several policies addressing student grievances on Monday, which unions have branded as insufficient.
Authorities are rolling out a ramped-up security operation, as they did on 24 October, in response to the widespread violence and looting that overshadowed otherwise peaceful demonstrations on 17 October.
The source close to the Interior Ministry warned on Friday that "calls for undeclared gatherings in public squares across France have proliferated," along with "plans for unauthorised marches towards places of power and state institutions."
On Thursday, France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez declared that protests in city centres had been banned and that only those "on the outskirts of cities" would be permitted. He added that organisers had been asked to "provide guarantees" that demonstrations would occur in "good conditions."
For their part, trade unions and the yellow vest movement have criticised these measures. In a joint statement issued on Wednesday, major unions said they would explore "all possible avenues of appeal against this general and disproportionate ban on the exercise of a public freedom that is essential in a democracy."
Halloween could heighten unrest
Nuñez also said on Thursday that the fact that protests coincided with Halloween could encourage unrest, which may run into the night. He warned that gatherings seeking to pass off as Halloween celebrations would be banned, while also calling out social media posts from groups including "ultra-left circles" that have urged individuals to back a "revolution" and "insurrection."
The heightened security measures come amid as human rights groups continue to accuse French law enforcement of using excessive force against protesters.
A number of law enforcement officers who were on leave had been called back to duty across France, while others have had their rest days cancelled.
Meanwhile, Paris police imposed a curfew on Saturday and Sunday night in districts that experienced significant unrest on 17 October.
The final route for the march in Paris on Saturday has been set for the eastern outskirts of the capital, from Porte de Bagnolet to Porte de Charenton, after the Council of State (Conseil d'État)overturned an administrative court's decision that had authorised a demonstration between Bastille and Nation.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed party, said on Saturday that he would join protesters at Porte de Bagnolet.
"We want to uphold the right to demonstrate peacefully at a time when Macron’s government is drifting towards authoritarianism and the far right seeks to hold the country to ransom with threats of attacks," he wrote in a post on X.
France's student protest movement began in mid-September, after pupils staged demonstrations against school conditions in the Parisian suburbs. The movement rapidly spread nationwide, leading unions and political forces to join.
The demonstrations - which come around six months before France's presidential elections - have since expanded into a broader social movement against the cost-of-living crisis and rising fuel prices.
