====================================================================================================

France pushes 'responsible' 2027 budget as Fitch cuts debt outlook to 'negative'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:27:11 UTC
15:27:11 KST

The US rating agency doubts France's ability to sustainably restore its public finances after the 2027 presidential election, probably followed by parliamentary elections. The government, for its part, reiterates the "absolute necessity" of having a budget adopted by the end of the year.
Equipping France with a "responsible" budget for 2027 is the goal announced by the French government as bad economic news continues to mount.
Ratings agency Fitch has kept France's sovereign debt rating at A+, but has cut its outlook from "stable" to "negative", citing weaker growth, higher borrowing costs and a bigger deficit than at its previous review last August.
This verdict comes after figures published by Insee on Friday morning showed that French gross domestic product fell by 0.1% in the third quarter, after stagnating in the second quarter and shrinking by 0.2% in the first.
To justify its decision (source in French), Fitch notably highlighted that "the persistence of political fragmentation" and "a difficult social climate", with the mass protests shaking the country, "further complicate the implementation of a lasting fiscal consolidation".
France's rating is nevertheless supported by "the size, wealth and diversification of its economy, the strength of its institutions, its membership of the euro area and the resilience of its banking sector".
"The absolute need to adopt a budget"
In a statement sent to the media on Friday evening, Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure said he "takes note" of the US agency's decision to lower France's outlook.
"This assessment confirms the absolute need to adopt by the end of the year a responsible budget that aims to restore the public finances by reducing our deficit to 5%", he continued, adding that the government was "determined to stay on a path of fiscal consolidation".
"In an uncertain international environment, it is imperative to give economic players visibility", the finance minister concluded.
Earlier in the day, reacting to the fall in GDP on Franceinfo, Roland Lescure had described the French economy as "at a standstill". He had also warned that the country would be heading "into the wall" if the "recovery" budget were not adopted.
"I am saying it, I repeat it and I will repeat it to the end: we need a budget, we need a budget deficit of 5% or less", he hammered home.
But the chances of the text being adopted by a parliamentary vote look more than uncertain, given the lack of a majority in the National Assembly and the approaching presidential election.
49.3, ordinances: Fitch expects a push-through
The political debates taking shape six months before the vote "have not significantly increased Fitch's confidence in the possibility of a lasting reduction in the deficit that could stabilise the debt", the agency notes.
"We believe that the budget should be adopted, thanks to the constitutional mechanisms available to the government despite the lack of a parliamentary majority", the Fitch analysts say.
In the event of deadlock in Parliament, Roland Lescure has indicated that the government does not rule out resorting to article 49.3 of the Constitution, which allows a bill to be passed without a vote unless a motion of no confidence is adopted. Another option would be to use ordinances, a procedure that has never been used to pass a budget since the creation of the Fifth Republic in 1958.
Speaking to Euronews, Jérôme Mathis, professor of economics at Paris-Dauphine University, believes that a budget adopted by ordinance could reduce uncertainty in the short term, but would not restore long-term fiscal credibility.
"Markets generally prefer a contested decision to a prolonged absence of decision. But if a budget adopted by ordinance is seen as fragile, liable to be called into question after the presidential election or as revealing a lasting inability of the political system to build majorities, the positive effect on [investor] confidence could be limited", the researcher explains.

Flavio Bolsonaro posts video, says he fled Brazil due to ‘persecution’

Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday's election runoff to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, gave no details of how he left the country.
Former conservative presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro said Friday that he fled Brazil to the United States because he was a victim of "persecution" in his country.
Bolsonaro, who lost Sunday's election runoff to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, secretly left Brazil on Tuesday and arrived in Florida aboard a private jet on Wednesday after traveling through Argentina and Ecuador.
"The persecution began even sooner than I imagined," the senator said during an Instagram livestream in which he discussed his decision to flee after his Brazilian passports were canceled as part of a money laundering investigation.
In the video, he recounted how police informed him Monday that his passports were being revoked as he left a visit to his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest.
"With tears in his eyes, he told me: 'You know where they're going with this, don't you?'" he said of his father.
"I told him: 'Dad, I know... Now I know what I have to do,'" he recounted.
Although he gave no details of how he left the country, he said he and his wife made the decision "without anyone knowing" and urged people not to "point the finger at anyone."
US President Donald Trump and Argentine President Javier Milei are under pressure to explain the involvement of the United States and Argentina in the senator's escape.
"I didn't leave Brazil, I left for Brazil," Flavio Bolsonaro said, alleging that Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes had made false accusations against him.
He also suggested there had been irregularities in the runoff, comparing them to "handball goals" that were not disallowed by VAR, without detailing what those irregularities might have been.
Read moreFlavio Bolsonaro’s great escape: Is this the beginning of the end for ‘Bolsonarism’?
He also predicted that the economy would "go bust" under Lula and said he was willing to run for president again: "I'm not talking about 2030, I'm talking about before then."
Brazil summons Argentina’s representative
Brazil's government summoned Argentina’s representative in the country after Bolsonaro fled to the US via Argentina, marking the latest episode in tense relations between South America’s two powerhouses.
Brazil’s foreign ministry asked for explanations on Thursday afternoon after the defeated presidential candidate passed through Argentina on his way to Miami, according to a diplomatic source who requested anonymity as they were not allowed to discuss the matter publicly.
Milei backed Bolsonaro in the presidential election won by Lula on Sunday and is yet to acknowledge the leftist’s win, differentiating himself from other Trump allies in the region who quickly congratulated the incumbent.
Bolsonaro, who is under investigation in Brazil over allegations of corruption and money laundering, refused to concede and has called the elections fraudulent, without providing evidence. His father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, also refused to acknowledge his 2022 loss to Lula and is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup.
Under Milei and Lula, Argentina and Brazil have had a rocky relationship, which took a decisive turn for the worse in July when Brazil recalled its ambassador to Argentina after Milei insulted Brazilian officials while in the country.
Milei was in Sao Paulo participating in the event confirming Bolsonaro’s presidential bid when he called Lula a “thief” and “delinquent”, among other things.
Argentina also recalled its ambassador to Brazil. The interests in both countries are represented by a lower diplomatic rank, known as chargés d’affaires.
Brazil’s top diplomat Joao Marcelo, the director of the ministry’s South America department, summoned Argentina’s chargé d’affaires María Emilia Cortés for a brief meeting, the source said.
Milei has not commented on Bolsonaro's journey, but presidential spokesperson Juan Pablo Carreira said on social media that the administration rescued Bolsonaro “from the claws of communism, which seeks to imprison all opposition figures”.

The tension at the Gold Coast did not cool after the two send-offs, with several big shots and a pair of flare-ups between the two sides.

After Louvre heist and string of thefts, Europe’s smaller museums are on guard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:11:41 UTC
15:11:41 KST

After Louvre heist and string of thefts, Europe’s smaller museums are on guard
PARMA, Italy – Two men wearing head torches climbed through a forced-open window at the Fondazione Magnani Rocca museum near Parma on the night of March 22 and calmly lifted artworks by Cezanne, Renoir and Matisse from the walls.
Within three minutes, they had passed the works, valued at about €9 million (S$12.9 million), to an accomplice and fled.
At the museum’s main gate, a fourth man discharged a fire extinguisher when the alarm sounded, distracting the custodian.
“Whatever could go wrong, did,” said Stefano Roffi, director of the private foundation that runs the museum.
The raid was one of a string of museum thefts in France, Italy and Spain since 2025’s heist at the Louvre in Paris, raising concerns that criminals are increasingly targeting smaller institutions with fewer resources to protect valuable collections.
“This is where we see the ‘Louvre effect’,” said Marc Balcells, a Barcelona-based researcher specialising in crimes against cultural heritage.
“If the Louvre was so easy to rob, just imagine a tiny museum in a rural area or a smaller town.”
Works by Antonello da Messina vanished from a museum in his Sicilian hometown in August, while two Renoirs were stolen from Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera the following month.
In Spain, thieves stole hundreds of historic gold coins from museums in Badajoz and Albacete and made off with a Bronze Age treasure in Villena, near Alicante.
A 2024 survey by France’s Culture Ministry found only one in four cultural institutions had an emergency and risk-prevention plan, while nearly half lacked video surveillance.
Who checks when the alarm goes off?
A French parliamentary report in May said museums lacked the resources and preparation to adequately protect artworks and artefacts.
In Italy, the challenge is amplified by the way the country’s cultural heritage is spread across hundreds of towns and institutions, a legacy of centuries of fragmented rule.
“That is also what makes our system distinctive: Works remain in the places where they were created,” said Antonella Pinna, president of the Italian committee of the International Council of Museums. “But we need to make life harder for criminals.”
The council worked with Italy’s Culture Ministry and the Carabinieri on museum security guidelines published in 2015, but Pinna said technology alone was not enough.
“If an alarm goes off, someone has to make sure it is checked,” she said.
In a narrow street in the Tuscan town of Sansepolcro, the civic museum displays four works by Renaissance master Piero della Francesca, born just steps away in the 15th century.
The Louvre theft “affected us deeply because cultural heritage is central to Sansepolcro’s identity. It is our soul”, culture councillor Francesca Mercati told Reuters.
After the Louvre raid, officers from the Carabinieri’s cultural heritage protection unit recommended more cameras, longer retention of CCTV footage and tighter controls on bags and bulky clothing.
“We immediately implemented those recommendations,” Mercati said.
A vast network to protect
The scale of the challenge is daunting.
Italy has more than 4,400 museums and similar institutions, according to national statistics agency ISTAT.
Spain has about 1,500 museums, while France has more than 1,200 institutions carrying the official “Musees de France” designation, alongside hundreds of smaller collections.
Protecting such a broad network is particularly difficult for smaller institutions that depend on local funding.
Florence Imbert, a Paris-based security consultant for cultural institutions, said 85% of small French museums were run by the local authorities with limited financial resources.
“The budget is key to winning the war,” she said.
France’s Culture Ministry announced a 33-point security plan in July, backed by €30 million over three years for local museums.
Recent figures suggest concern is warranted.
The Carabinieri art squad recorded 17 thefts from Italian museums and galleries in 2025, up from 14 a year earlier.
Europol said in an August report that museum thefts were becoming more forceful and increasingly focused on precious metals, gemstones and other high-value artefacts.
A fast buck?
Unlike gold or jewellery, which can be broken up or melted down, a well-known painting is difficult to turn into quick cash.
Celebrated works such as those by Renoir can rarely be sold openly, Pinna said. Instead, stolen art is more likely to be hidden, used as leverage in ransom attempts or offered privately.
Even when works are recovered, museums can face significant costs linked to investigations, recovery efforts and upgraded security.
The recent thefts have also reignited debate about insurance.
Most major state-backed museums in Western Europe rely on government indemnity schemes rather than commercial cover, but some institutions have begun reassessing the risks, said Filippo Guerrini-Maraldi, a private wealth and fine art insurance specialist at broker Howden Specialty.
“And for the first time, really, in my 40-year career, I’ve seen art theft now becoming more of a major, major risk. It was always the minor risk,” he said.
Insurers are also turning to technology.
Beazley is exploring how AI can be used to analyse CCTV footage to identify suspicious behaviour in museums and galleries, helping security staff spot threats sooner, said fine art underwriter Dishni Mahendran.
Security vs access
For museum directors and cultural officials, the challenge is how to tighten security without cutting collections off from local communities or diminishing the visitor experience.
“Ultimately, museums must remain easy to access,” Imbert said. “People should be able to enter without having to pass through 50 security checks.”
Julien Volper, a conservator at Belgium’s Africa Museum, said particularly vulnerable treasures should only be displayed when adequate security measures are in place.
“I’m not saying that’s the ultimate solution, but it seems better than displaying replicas,” he said. “We’re not at Disneyland.”
In August, the Carabinieri recovered the three artworks stolen from the Parma museum from a cardboard box hidden in an apartment. Five Moldovan nationals were arrested in connection with the theft.
Investigators said wiretaps indicated the suspects had unsuccessfully tried to find buyers in Eastern Europe and Russia.
The works have since returned to the museum in what Roffi called a “homecoming party”.
“The theft triggered an outpouring of solidarity in Italy and abroad,” he said. The museum now has round-the-clock guards funded by a local cheese consortium.
“It was seen not simply as a theft from a museum, but as an attack on art as a shared cultural heritage.” REUTERS

The personal data of nearly 17,000 students based in mainland China who applied to take two international exams through the Hong Kong Examinations and Assessment Authority (HKEAA) has been leaked after its information system was compromised.

“The HKEAA apologises to the affected individuals and will take all feasible measures to minimise the impact of the incident on them,” it said.

NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Saturday shared a heartfelt message remembering his grandmother and former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi on her 42nd death anniversary, recalling childhood moments spent with her and sharing a photograph from their time together.In a post on X, Rahul recalled sitting on her lap, holding her hands and repeating Sanskrit verses after her. He described the memory as a beautiful gift from his grandmother.
“Sitting on your lap. Holding both your hands. Listening to your voice say these words. Repeating them after you. asato mā sadgamayatamaso mā jyotirgamaya, mṛtyormā amṛtaṃ gamaya, OM Shanti, shanti, Shanti, What a beautiful gift you gave me Dadi. What a gift. I never imagined.”Rahul also paid homage to Indira Gandhi at Shakti Sthal in New Delhi on Saturday. Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi, Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and other senior party leaders also attended the programme to pay tribute to the former prime minister.Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar also remembered Indira Gandhi, describing her as the 'Iron Lady' and recalling her efforts towards the upliftment of the poor through the slogan 'Garibi Hatao'.
"The Iron Lady who made revolutionary decisions for the progress of the country, making the entire world look towards India. A compassionate leader whose heart beat for the upliftment of the poor and the downtrodden through the slogan 'Garibi Hatao' (Abolish Poverty). On the death anniversary of Smt. Indira Gandhi, the first woman Prime Minister of the country, respectful tributes to the legendary leader," he said.Shivakumar also recalled her role in India's political, economic and institutional development, citing milestones in agricultural production, banking and the country's space and nuclear programmes."Paying my respects to the Iron Lady and former Prime Minister Smt. Indira Gandhi on her death anniversary. She occupies a significant place in India's history as a leader whose tenure witnessed far-reaching political, economic and institutional developments. From strengthening agricultural production and expanding access to banking to supporting India's space and nuclear programmes, her years in office encompassed several important milestones," Shivakumar said."As we remember her journey in public life, we also recognise the mark she left on India's political landscape and its development trajectory. Her contributions remain an important part of India's post-independence history, and her memory will continue to be remembered with respect," he added.
Indira Gandhi, India's first woman prime minister, served from 1966 to 1977 and again from 1980 until her assassination on October 31, 1984. Born on November 19, 1917, she was the daughter of India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru.She was assassinated by two of her bodyguards at her residence in New Delhi on October 31, 1984. Her death anniversary is observed every year in remembrance of her contribution to the country's political history.

Cyclo-cross World Championships return to Ostend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:02:00 UTC
15:02:00 KST

100 days before the Cyclo-cross World Championships in Ostend (West Flanders) the official countdown to the final has begun. From 29 to 31 January, the city will host the World Championships. The World Championships are returning to Ostend after six years. It is also 11 years since Cyclo-cross World Championships with spectators took place in Belgium. The organisers are eager to turn them into a huge public celebration.
In 2021, the seaside resort of Ostend hosted the UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships. At that time, due to the coronavirus pandemic, no junior races were held and no spectators were allowed. Early next year, the atmosphere will be completely different, with a full sporting programme and tens of thousands of spectators lining the route.
“The countdown has now begun,” says Flemish Sports Minister Annick De Ridder (Flemish nationalist N-VA). “The Cyclo-cross World Championships are a highlight for this sport and a celebration of our sporting heritage and cycling DNA. We look forward to welcoming cycling fans from at home and abroad to Ostend.”
“Cyclo-cross is a sport with deep roots in Belgium and enjoys enormous popularity in Belgium,” says Ostend Mayor John Crombez. “Soon we will see the world’s very best competing for the world title in our city, on a unique course that links the sea, the beach, the city and our heritage.”
2 sand hills on the circuit
The countdown clock is located near King Leopold II’s statue and local landmark Drie Gapers, close to the Royal Galleries. Together with the beach and the Wellington Hippodrome racecourse, this site forms the circuit. The circuit is approximately 3.4 kilometres long. Unlike in 2021, there are now 2 bridges over the tram lines. Six years ago, there was just one bridge.
Two hills of sand will be erected on the beach. In front of one of these two, a paved section will be laid out using cycle path slabs. This will allow the riders to build up speed as they approach the hill. There will also be a paved section in the finish area. The riders will cross from the beach to the finish area via a long flight of steps just before the finish line.
‘We’re currently working on two fan zones, but a World Championship calls for something extra,’ says Tomas Van Den Spiegel, CEO of organisers Flanders Classics. "That’s why these zones will be a little more than just the classic, traditional marquees. We’re creating a festival atmosphere where everyone feels at home, from cyclo-cross fans to families. We’re looking into adding extra entertainment around the course and want to showcase Ostend’s culinary delights.”
Programme
On Friday 29 January, the Team Relay is scheduled as a rainbow race. After that, there will be an opportunity for adaptive or disability sports with the Belgian G-cyclo-cross Championships for riders with an intellectual disability or autism.
In Belgium and the Netherlands G-sport (where "G" stands for gehandicapt, meaning disabled) is the term used for adaptive or disability sports.
“The fact that a Belgian G-cyclo-cross Championship is being organised in Ostend on the Friday is a real bonus,” says Tom Van Damme, chair of Belgian Cycling. “It will undoubtedly be a unique experience for the participants to be able to compete for their Belgian title within the context of a World Championship. The combination of these two events is an example of how sport can be inclusive – something we at Belgian Cycling wholeheartedly welcome and are keen to support.”
Schools in Ostend will also play a part. Pupils will take part in various challenges attached to the World Championships. On Friday 29 January, a Schools’ World Championship will take place in a section of the course.

This week Foster + Partners unveiled the replacement for San Siro stadium
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

This week Foster + Partners unveiled the replacement for San Siro stadium
This week on Dezeen, architecture studio Foster + Partners and US studio Manica unveiled their design for Generali Stadium in Milan, which will become home to local football clubs AC Milan and Inter Milan.
The stadium will seat 71,500 people and be built alongside the 99-year-old San Siro stadium, which will eventually be torn down. Generali Stadium will be defined by a structural facade composed of elongated X-framed concrete supports.
Architect Norman Foster told Dezeen that the Generali Stadium’s design draws on his “great personal connection with the city”.
Foster also made the news this week with the launch of his first watch, which the architect designed for Spanish watch brand Lebond.
The watch draws on aviation design and was designed to be customised, in line with Foster’s philosophy that a watch is “intensely personal”.
The public vote winners for Dezeen Awards 2026 were announced this week and included Japanese studio Schemata Architects’ Uchida Shōten head office, above, in the architecture category.
We also revealed the public vote winners in the interiors and design categories. The public vote is separate from the main judging process, with the overall winners of this year’s programme set to be announced on 16 November.
In Abu Dhabi, a new concert hall by the late architect Frank Gehry was revealed. The Youth Orchestra Abu Dhabi will be located in the Mina Zayed port district.
It will be dedicated to young musicians and contain a 600-seat concert hall and 18 rehearsal rooms.
Technology brand Apple unveiled its new MacBook Pro model, which features its first-ever laptop touchscreen. The brand said the display is “a monumental step forward for the Mac”.
Apple Music also showed off a new logo this week. The first rebrand since Apple Music launched in 2015 was made in collaboration with musician Fred Again by passing sound waves through a pool of oil.
KPF completed Texas’s tallest skyscraper, a supertall tower called Waterline that is 1,025 feet tall (312 metres tall).
Its developer described the shape of the skyscraper as a “cowboy boot”. It will have hotel and office programmes at the bottom, with luxury residences at the top.
Popular projects on Dezeen this week include a pink house that brings a “fairytale flamboyance” to London, an arrow-shaped viewpoint in Denmark and a minimalist house in Japan.
Our podcast this week looked at the Oxford Street pedestrianisation and asked: what happens next?

11 ‘extraordinary’ European hotels included on Fodor's Finest list for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

A new list of the 50 most incredible hotels in the world features 11 properties in Europe.
For some people, a hotel may simply be a place to lay their head when travelling. For others, it’s one of the biggest reasons to book a trip in the first place.
If you fall into the latter camp, the Fodor’s Finest list of the most incredible hotels in the world in 2027 is for you.
This latest edition features 50 "extraordinary" properties that offer more than just a stunning room. Impeccable service, luxurious amenities, extravagance and a deep connection to the surroundings are what set these stays apart.
In Europe, 11 hotels made the cut, including the Grand Hotel Tremezzo in Lake Como, the Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo in Monaco, and the Orient Express La Minerva in Rome.
Housed in a 16th century building close to the gates of Edinburgh Castle, The Witchery was also included and offers guests an “immersive experience” with lavish rooms replete with Gothic interiors.
Opened in 2021, Acro Suites Crete combines luxury resort offerings with being a state-of-the-art wellness retreat. A night’s stay can be in a cave suite and by day, guests can take a dip in their private plunge pool.
Meanwhile, the five-star Charlotte Street Hotel in Fitzrovia, London, features rooms that each have a distinct design. It also has its own library, drawing room and screening room for film buffs.
Other European hotels on the list include Airelles La Bastide in Provence, Argos in Cappadocia, Hotel Pigalle in Gothenburg, Maison Souquet in Paris, and Pulitzer Amsterdam.
"An extraordinary hotel stay can mean something different to every traveller,” said Jeremy Tarr, Editorial Director at Fodor’s Travel. “It might be a remarkable sense of place, an unexpected level of personal service, or a setting that makes you see a destination in an entirely new way.
"By focusing on just 50 properties this year, we're spotlighting the hotels that truly stand apart and give travellers a compelling reason to make the journey."
How were the properties chosen?
Curated by Fodor’s editors in collaboration with hundreds of hospitality experts, the compilation features a range of stays from varying price points.
This includes properties that have a character-rich history, are design driven urban retreats to stays that are intimate hideaways. With only 50 places on this year’s list, “every selection has earned its place”, Fodor’s said.
Specifically in Europe, Fodor’s said the continent has been "perfecting the art of hospitality for centuries", with its portfolio of finest hotels having the history, character and occasional eccentricity to prove it.
Beyond price tags and copious marbling, the publication said its European curation is united by “a sense of personality”. It added: “Whether extravagantly opulent or quietly understated, these are places with stories to tell – and plenty of reasons to become part of them.”
Fodor’s ‘finest’ hotels in Europe
Out of the 50 properties on Fodor’s Finest list, 11 are in Europe:
- Acro Suites Crete, Crete, Greece
- Airelles La Bastide, Gordes, Provence, France
- Argos in Cappadocia, Uçhisar, Türkiye
- Charlotte Street Hotel, London, England
- Grand Hotel Tremezzo, Lake Como, Italy
- Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo, Monaco
- Hotel Pigalle, Gothenburg, Sweden
- Maison Souquet, Paris, France
- Orient Express La Minerva, Rome, Italy
- Pulitzer Amsterdam, Amsterdam, Netherlands
- The Witchery, Edinburgh, Scotland

Canada lists Vancouver port expansion as national interest project to curb reliance on U.S. market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:56:03 CST
14:56:03 KST

A container-handling vehicle operates at the Global Container Terminals facility at Roberts Bank in Delta, British Columbia, Canada, on Oct. 30, 2026. The Canadian federal government on Friday announced that it has officially listed the Roberts Bank Terminal 2 project at the Port of Vancouver, Canada's largest port, as a project of national interest to strengthen trade infrastructure and reduce reliance on the U.S. market. (Photo by Liang Sen/Xinhua)
OTTAWA, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- The Canadian federal government on Friday announced that it has officially listed the Roberts Bank Terminal 2 project at the Port of Vancouver, Canada's largest port, as a project of national interest to strengthen trade infrastructure and reduce reliance on the U.S. market.
The move is part of Canada's broader strategy to double its exports to non-U.S. markets by 2035, according to Transport Canada.
With a planned investment of 5.9 billion Canadian dollars (about 4.2 billion U.S. dollars), the project is expected to increase the container capacity at the Port of Vancouver by approximately 50 percent. It will add 2.4 million containers of annual processing capacity and support up to 100 billion Canadian dollars (71.55 billion dollars) in annual trade.
Transport Canada said that the listing decision provides regulatory certainty, accelerating the project's commercial operations to 2035, up to four years ahead of schedule. The project is currently on a viable path to reach a Final Investment Decision by mid-2027. ■

Border with U.S. can not be changed by state-level government: Mexico
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:55:52 CST
14:55:52 KST

MEXICO CITY, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The Mexican Foreign Ministry said Friday that border between Mexico and the United States can not be changed by the decision of a state-level government, and the demarcation of boundary between the two countries must follow standards established by international treaties.
The Texas General Land Office, a U.S. state agency led by Commissioner Dawn Buckingham, has declared nine islands in the Rio Grande (known as the Rio Bravo in Mexico) property of the state of Texas.
In response, the ministry said that under the 1970 Mexico-U.S. Boundary Treaty, the international boundary in the river follows the center line of the normal channel and that line determines sovereignty over the land on either side, regardless of who previously held sovereignty over it.
The International Boundary and Water Commission is the body authorized by the two governments to carry out the treaty and has the power to determine on which side of the boundary each island lies, the ministry said, noting that no state-level government body has the authority to make such determinations.
It stressed that under the treaty, neither side may build works that the International Boundary and Water Commission finds could alter or obstruct the normal flow of the river.
The ministry said Mexico will closely monitor any actions in the area and reiterated that it will abide by the treaty governing the two countries' shared border and continue to pursue dialogue through established mechanisms. ■

Protein may help identify breast cancers resistant to targeted drugs: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:55:33 CST
14:55:33 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Tracking a protein that drives cell division could help doctors tell which breast cancers are likely to respond to CDK4/6 inhibitors, a widely used class of targeted drugs, an Australian study has found.
Researchers at Australia's Garvan Institute of Medical Research found that the activity of a protein called CDK1 in breast cancers is linked to how they respond to a common therapy, an insight that could inform more personalized treatment approaches for patients, according to a statement of the institute released on Friday.
The study focused on estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer, the most common type, fueled by the hormone estrogen. Many people with this cancer now receive drugs called CDK4/6 inhibitors alongside hormone therapy. These drugs stop cancer cells from multiplying, but they don't work for everyone, and in advanced cancer, they eventually stop working for most patients.
In more than 400 patients' breast cancer biopsy samples, the researchers found CDK1 activity rose as the cancer became more aggressive, and higher activity was linked to worse outcomes.
The findings need to be tested in larger groups of patients treated with CDK4/6 inhibitors, and could eventually open the door to new drugs targeting CDK1, according to the study published in Advanced Science. ■

Australia launches new biodiversity restoration method to expand nature repair market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:55:28 CST
14:55:28 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- The Australian government has launched a second method under its national Nature Repair Market, expanding opportunities for landholders to participate in biodiversity conservation and restoration projects.
Minister for the Environment and Water Murray Watt announced on Friday that the new method, known as enhancing native vegetation, would allow landholders to register projects aimed at improving and maintaining existing native vegetation or restoring vegetation in areas where it has been cleared.
The method also enables projects to improve habitats for threatened species and control invasive plants and animals, according to a government statement.
The Nature Repair Market was established to encourage landholders, farmers, Indigenous groups and conservation organisations to invest in activities that restore and protect biodiversity.
Under the market's first method, replanting native forest and woodland ecosystems, four projects have so far been registered, covering a total of 2,656 hectares of land being protected and restored.
The government said the new method would broaden eligibility for participation and allow certain projects to be used for environmental offsets, potentially stimulating demand for biodiversity restoration activities.
"The Nature Repair Market is still in its early stages, but by introducing more methods for use, we're incentivizing and rewarding landholders for protecting and restoring biodiversity on their land, including by controlling invasive species," Watt said.
He added that protecting habitats on private land was essential to improving conservation outcomes for Australia's threatened native species. ■

Dakar hosts Africa's first Olympic event
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
05:53:45 UTC
14:53:45 KST

The 2026 Youth Olympic Games, the first Olympics ever to be held on African soil, open Saturday in the Senegalese capital marking an historic moment for the continent.
Signs proclaiming "Africa welcomes, Dakar celebrates" are abundant across Dakar, which is hosting some 2,665 young competitors aged 14 to 17 from around the world.
The event marks the return of Russian athletes to the Olympics and also includes a refugee team. Overall, the athletes will compete across 25 sports and 153 medal events.
"We've got people from around the world that maybe had a very different idea about Africa and they're going to leave, hopefully, with something really positive in mind", International Olympic Committee (IOC) President Kirsty Coventry, a former Zimbabwean swimmer, said Thursday during a press conference in Dakar.
"I think that is really important for our continent", she said.
Events ranging from athletics to beach wrestling, rugby sevens to breaking, will be held across eight venues in three locations.
Dakar, the nearby suburb of Diamniadio and the beach town of Saly located some 80 kilometres (50 miles) from the capital, will all host events.
Sports culture
An opening ceremony Saturday evening in Diamniadio will kick off the Games.
A total of 136 Senegalese athletes will participate in the Youth Olympics, with some 6,000 volunteers from Senegal helping put on the event.
The west African nation is renowned for its sports culture, including its football team, traditional wrestling and surf scene.
Football enthusiasts and young people often organise impromptu matches in the evenings or weekends on the beach or in village squares.
And as the day cools, hundreds of people flock to Dakar's iconic coastal road, the Corniche, to run, do strength training or take part in group exercise.
While a sense of excitement is beginning to stir in the capital, the fourth summer edition of the Youth Olympics have struggled to stoke wild enthusiasm across Senegal.
Many are more concerned with the high cost of living, unemployment and economic hardship.
"Once the youth Olympic Games in Senegal begin, Dakar will become the capital of African youth," Senegal Prime Minister Ahmadou Al Aminou Lo said in an interview with AFP this week.
"Africa hosting the (Youth) Olympic Games, it's a symbol", he said.
Russian athletes
With the IOC effectively lifting the Russian Olympic Committee's (ROC) suspension in July, the Youth Games will mark the first Olympic competition since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in early 2022 in which Russian athletes are allowed to compete under their own flag and colours.
According to the ROC, 13 Russian athletes will participate and 10 coaches will accompany them to Senegal.
"The kids are excited, it's good news that our legitimate right to participate with the national anthem and Russian flag has been restored", Anzor Gaunov, who coaches Anastasia Dobrovolskaya in judo, told AFP earlier this month in Moscow.
However, it is up to each sport's international federation whether to authorise the Russian athletes' participation.
The Dakar Youth Games will also welcome a refugee Olympic team, composed primarily of athletes based in Africa.
The IOC has called the Dakar Games an important milestone for the continent and an opportunity to showcase Senegal's cultural richness and Africa's growing role within the Olympics.
South Africa could potentially become the first African nation to host the Olympic Games, having already paved the way by hosting the men's FIFA World Cup in 2010. The country is officially in the running for the 2036 Summer Olympics.

Where in Europe do people spend over 40% of their income on housing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
05:46:39 UTC
14:46:39 KST

Housing costs take up more than 40% of disposable income for millions of Europeans. Euronews Business takes a closer look at which countries are hit hardest, with experts explaining the drivers.
House prices in the EU have risen by 69% on average between 2015 and the second quarter of 2026, according to Eurostat. In some member states, prices have more than doubled. Rents and energy costs have also continued to climb.
“Europe faces a crisis driven by rising house prices and increasing housing costs,” the European Council said.
The housing crisis puts particular pressure on people who spend more than 40% of their disposable income on housing. Eurostat calls this the housing cost overburden rate. In the EU, it stood at 7.7% on average in 2025.
“The main drivers of housing cost overburden are rising costs for housing (be it rents or house prices, which are spiking in many cities) in relation to the modest growth in incomes, especially for the lower quantiles of the income distribution,” Dr Hannah Widmer from ETH Zürich told Euronews Business.
So, which countries are hit hardest? Where in Europe is the housing cost overburden rate highest?
What are housing costs?
According to Eurostat, housing costs are the monthly expenses households pay for their homes. They include rent or mortgage interest, utilities such as water, electricity, gas and heating, and regular charges such as insurance, maintenance, repairs and taxes.
Disposable income refers to a household's total income after taxes and social contributions. It also includes social benefits such as pensions.
Greece has the highest housing cost overburden rate in Europe among countries with available data. This includes the 27 EU member states, two EFTA countries and five EU candidate countries.
In 2025, 26.4% of people in Greece lived in households that spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing. This is more than three times the EU average of 7.7%.
Denmark follows among EU countries, with 14.7%. Germany (11.2%) and Sweden (10.8%) are also well above the EU average.
The housing cost overburden rate is also above the EU average in Estonia (8.8%), Czechia (8.2%) and Luxembourg (8.1%).
Outside the EU, the rate is high in Switzerland (15.3%) and Norway (13.5%). Three candidate countries are also above the EU average: Turkey (10%), Montenegro (8.7%) and Serbia (7.9%).
“Given the very different contexts, not least in terms of economy and welfare system, the explanations for the level of the housing cost overburden in Greece, Switzerland and Denmark are not the same. And the consequences are not either,” Rikke Skovgaard Nielsen, senior researcher at Aalborg University, told Euronews Business.
She added that the money people have left after paying rent differs considerably between these three countries, as do living costs. As a result, the impact on households varies too.
Cyprus has the lowest rate. Only 2.4% of people spend more than 40% of their disposable income on housing. Croatia (3.2%), Slovenia (3.5%) and Slovakia (3.5%) also have low rates.
Dr Marietta Haffner from TU Delft noted that when housing costs such as house prices, rents, energy prices, interest rates and inflation rise faster than income, the share of housing costs in income increases. Eventually, the share of those paying more than 40% of their income also increases.
“It is likely that the increasing energy costs will be a main driver in the next year of increasing housing costs,” she said.
Among the EU’s largest economies, Spain (7.2%), France (6.4%) and Italy (5.0%) are all below the EU average, while Germany (11.2%) ranks fifth overall.
Why does the burden differ across countries?
“It's probably the interplay between housing tenure structures (with tenants renting from the private rental market usually having the highest housing cost burden), welfare systems and the broader economic situation that explains higher or lower shares of housing cost overburden,” Widmer said.
However, she cautioned that comparing countries is complex. Experiencing housing cost overburden can mean something very different in Switzerland than in Greece, depending on welfare provisions and the quality of housing.
Over 34 million people in the EU are affected
The actual numbers tell a clearer story. More than 34 million people in the EU live in households that spend more than 40% of their disposable income on housing.
Germany has the highest number of people affected by housing cost overburden, at 9.4 million. Turkey follows with 8.6 million, followed by France (4.4 million), Spain (3.5 million) and Italy (2.9 million).
Despite its relatively small population compared with these countries, Greece ranks sixth, with 2.7 million people living in households affected by housing cost overburden.
Of course, people on low incomes are hit harder. In the EU, the rate rises to 29.1% among people who are at risk of poverty. This group comprisespeople with an equivalised disposable income below the at-risk-of-poverty threshold, which is set at 60% of the national median equivalised disposable income.
In 2025, the EU’s median equivalised disposable income was €22,939 a year, or €1,912 a month. At EU level, 60% of this amounted to €1,147 a month.
Greece again tops the list. In 2025, 82.6% of people at risk of poverty in Greece lived in households that spent more than 40% of their disposable income on housing. This means that more than four in five were affected. Denmark (59.8%) and Switzerland (56.1%) follow, while the rate is also above 40% in Sweden (46.8%), Norway (43.8%) and Czechia (43.4%).
Germany (35.0%) is above the EU average of 29.1%, while Spain (28.3%), France (25.4%) and Italy (21.7%) are below it.
Cyprus has the lowest rate, at 7.6%, followed by Albania (8.2%), Croatia (14.9%) and Slovakia (15.4%).

Taiwan gas demand set to outstrip winter supply capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
05:39:08 UTC
14:39:08 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — State-owned oil company CPC Corp. said Saturday that winter cooking gas demand could exceed its monthly supply capacity of 90,000 tonnes, adding to pressure from government price controls.
CNA reported that CPC Spokesperson Lin Ko-ju (林珂如) said demand for liquefied petroleum gas, widely used for cooking in homes and restaurants, is expected to peak between December and January. She said the company would give priority to domestic supplies and do its best to meet demand.
CPC expanded its facilities in Shenao, New Taipei, last year, raising its maximum monthly supply to 90,000 tonnes. The company sold about 678,000 tonnes of cooking gas from January to September, accounting for more than 90% of the domestic market.
The expected rise in demand comes as the government keeps household cooking gas prices at the same rate until the end of the year. The policy aims to protect consumers from rising fuel costs but has placed financial pressure on suppliers, per Economic Daily News.
CPC has raised cooking gas prices by just NT$3.15 (10 cents) per kilogram since December 2020. Taiwan Petroleum Workers' Union Chair Chen Chia-lin (陳嘉麟) said the company was absorbing NT$23.75 per kilogram in costs to keep its selling price at NT$20.01.
National Federation of Liquefied Gas Fuel Commercial Associations Chair Lai Fang-chuan (賴芳泉) said CPC sold gas for NT$1.80 less per kilogram than private supplier Formosa Petrochemical. The price gap has driven more dealers to CPC, where supplies have struggled to keep pace with demand, per CTS News.
Lai said dealers who buy from Formosa Petrochemical must either absorb the higher cost or risk losing customers by raising prices. The problem is especially serious in central Taiwan, where competition is strong and profit margins are tight.
Taiwan has more than 2,300 gas retailers and 110 plants that fill gas cylinders, Lai said. More than 10 retailers have closed this year, while some filling plants have merged in recent years to cut costs.
Lai warned that the supply gap could widen as winter and year-end holidays drive up demand. He urged CPC to increase supplies and called on the government to bring prices charged by the two producers closer together.
Energy Administration Deputy Director-General Chen Chung-hsien (陳崇憲) said the government would work with suppliers to keep gas supplies stable throughout winter. He said officials would seek to prevent shortages despite pressure on the market, per Rti.

Math Puzzle: Mysterious pyramid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
05:27:38 UTC
14:27:38 KST

The nine cells of the triangle contain nine zeros. Try to change the numbers, with any number of moves, so that they become nine consecutive positive integers, the smallest of which is a. The arrangement of these nine numbers in the triangle is irrelevant. A move is the increase or decrease by 1 of the two numbers occupying two adjacent cells, where adjacent cells share a side. For which values of a is the problem solvable?
A pair of adjacent cells always consists of one orange and one black triangle. Initially, the sum r of the numbers on the orange cells is equal to the sum b of the numbers on the black cells, namely, 0. A move does not change this equilibrium r = b. At the end, the nine numbers of the triangle should be a , a + 1, ..., and a + 8. Thus, because b is the sum of six of the numbers, b ≥ a + (a + 1) + (a + 2) + (a + 3) + (a + 4) + (a + 5) = 6a + 15, and because r is the sum of three of the numbers, r ≤ (a + 6) + (a + 7) + (a + 8) = 3a + 21. Because b = r, 6a + 15 ≤ 3a + 21, or a ≤ 2. Furthermore, r = b means that r + b = 2r, so r + b must be an even number. For a = 1, the sum of the nine numbers 1 + 2 + ... + 9 = 45, which is odd. Therefore, if there is a solution to the problem at all, it is only for a = 2.
Instead of increasing the numbers on the same pair of cells by 1 n times, one can directly increase both numbers by n. This does not change the problem in any way. The order of the individual moves also plays no role. The image shows in three steps that there is indeed a solution for a = 2.

Major water infrastructure project nears completion in N. Australia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:02:06 CST
14:02:06 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- A major water infrastructure project in Australia's Northern Territory has entered its commissioning stage and is expected to boost water supply to the Darwin region by the end of 2026, the territory government said.
The Manton Dam Return to Service project, one of the Northern Territory's most significant water infrastructure developments in the past 50 years, has reached the commissioning stage at 174 million Australian dollars (about 114 million U.S. dollars), coming in 15 million Australian dollars under budget, according to a government statement released Friday.
The project includes the modernization of an existing reservoir intake tower, construction of the new Strauss Water Treatment Plant, a new pump station and 22 kilometers of pipeline.
Once operational, Manton Dam will provide an additional 7,300 megaliters of water annually, strengthening water security for Darwin and surrounding areas.
The government said commissioning of the new water treatment plant was underway, with water from Manton Dam expected to enter the Darwin region's supply network by the end of 2026.
Construction of the project has engaged more than 111 employees and 500 contractors over the past two years, delivering economic benefits to local businesses.
The project forms part of the first stage of the Darwin Region Water Supply Infrastructure Program, jointly funded by the Australian federal and Northern Territory governments. ■

China calls for stronger global cooperation to advance right to development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
13:01:42 CST
14:01:42 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- China on Friday called for stronger international cooperation to advance the right to development, and urged countries to put development at the center of the global agenda amid widening inequalities and mounting challenges facing developing nations.
Speaking at a side event marking the 40th anniversary of the UN Declaration on the Right to Development, Sun Lei, China's deputy permanent representative to the United Nations, said that "only through continuous development can people's aspirations for a better life and social stability be realized."
Development has been politicized and pushed to the margins when it is needed most, while divisions and confrontation are being fueled when solidarity is more critical than ever, he said.
Sun put forward four proposals to advance the right to development: defending the right to development, reinvigorating development partnerships, improving the development environment, and fostering new drivers of growth.
"The rights to subsistence and development are basic human rights of paramount importance," he said, adding that equal importance should be placed on different types of human rights.
"Without development, there would be no human rights to speak of, nor could any enjoyment of rights be sustainable," he said. "Development should be put front and center on the international agenda."
Sun also called for a more just and equitable international economic and financial architecture.
"Unilateral sanctions and long-arm jurisdiction are inimical to development and must be rejected," he said, urging the international community to promote "an inclusive economic globalization that benefits all."
On innovation, Sun called for speeding up technology transfer and knowledge sharing, so as to close the digital divide and artificial intelligence divide, and accelerate the low-carbon transition.
Sun said China's Global Development Initiative (GDI) has mobilized more than 23 billion U.S. dollars in funding and supported over 1,800 "small and beautiful" projects, benefiting local communities in more than 120 countries.
"China stands ready to work with all parties to strengthen international cooperation and create an enabling environment for the realization of the right to development," Sun said.
The event was co-organized by the Permanent Mission of China to the United Nations, the Coordinating Bureau of the Non-Aligned Movement and the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.
Godfrey Kwoba, charge d'affaires of Uganda's UN mission and chair of the Coordinating Bureau of the Non-Aligned Movement, said that the principles contained in the declaration must be translated into practical policies and actions at national, regional and international levels.
Claudia Fuentes Julio, UN assistant secretary-general for human rights, said development is not simply about economic growth; it is also about ensuring that the benefits of development are shared fairly and equitably.
Bjorg Sandkjaer, UN assistant secretary-general for policy coordination, welcomed the GDI as a contribution to global development efforts.
The emphasis on prioritizing development, adopting a people-centered approach and promoting practical cooperation is closely aligned with the right to development and the 2030 Agenda, she said.
Adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1986, the Declaration on the Right to Development recognizes development as an inalienable human right, affirming that every person and all peoples are entitled to participate in, contribute to, and enjoy development. ■

UK historian says Taiwan can learn from Ukraine to defend itself against China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:52:09 UTC
13:52:09 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Royal Historical Society fellow Iain MacGregor said Taiwan could better defend itself against China by learning from Ukraine's use of drones, military training, and civilian preparedness.
In an article titled "Ukraine has shown Taiwan how to fight Goliath and survive," published by The Telegraph on Friday, MacGregor said Ukraine had shown how a smaller country can resist a stronger enemy. He said Taiwan faces a similar threat from China, which has far greater military resources.
Russia's failure to defeat Ukraine quickly showed that military strength alone does not ensure victory, MacGregor said. He credited Ukraine's military reforms, trained troops, and determination to fight for helping it resist Russia's invasion in February 2022.
MacGregor pointed to Ukraine's use of low-cost drones to destroy expensive Russian tanks. He also mentioned unmanned boats that have damaged Russian warships in the Black Sea.
Taipei has sought to apply those lessons by expanding domestic drone production and reducing its reliance on foreign suppliers. Its monthly production capacity reached about 15,000 drones by May 2026, according to government figures.
MacGregor also cited the country's decision to extend mandatory military service from four months to one year. The change took effect in January 2024 and applies to eligible men born in or after 2005.
He said Ukraine's experience showed that weapons alone were not enough to defend a country. Trained reserve troops, civilian volunteers, and reliable supplies were also vital during a long war.
MacGregor warned that Taiwan must prepare for power cuts, cyberattacks, and damage to transport and communications. The country has expanded emergency drills to keep essential services running and ensure people can obtain supplies during a crisis.
He also warned that Taiwan would face greater difficulties receiving foreign aid during a war. Unlike Ukraine, which can receive supplies across its land borders with European neighbors, it could face a Chinese blockade that cuts off sea and air routes.
However, the Taiwan Strait would also make an invasion difficult for China, as troops and equipment would have to cross the water under threat of attack. Taiwan, MacGregor argued, should convince Beijing that any attempt to seize the island would be costly, prolonged, and unlikely to succeed.

The 15 designs for the tableaux, selected through competition, are based on the implications of ‘Vande Mataram’ on nationhood and development.
There will also be a cultural programme curated entirely by people from different states and communities who have made Gujarat their home. Around 5,000 artists will showcase dances and culture of their respective states through this mega-performance.
Bharti Jain is senior editor with The Times of India, New Delhi. She has been writing on security matters since 1996. Having covered the Union home ministry, security agencies, Election Commission and the ‘prime’ political beat, the Congress, for The Economic Times all these years, she moved to TOI in August 2012. Her repertoire of news stories delves into the whole gamut of issues related to terrorism and internal strife, besides probing strategic affairs in India’s neighbourhood.

A surprising vitamin A discovery is changing what scientists know about vision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:31:41 UTC
13:31:41 KST

A surprising vitamin A discovery is changing what scientists know about vision
- Date:
- October 31, 2026
- Source:
- Johns Hopkins University
- Summary:
- Scientists at Johns Hopkins University have uncovered a surprising process that helps humans develop sharp vision before birth, challenging decades of assumptions about how the eye forms. Using miniature human retinas grown in the lab, researchers discovered that a vitamin A derivative and thyroid hormones work together to shape the foveola, the tiny region at the center of the retina responsible for our sharpest vision.
- Share:
Scientists at Johns Hopkins University have uncovered a surprising role for a vitamin A derivative in the development of human vision. Their research reveals how this molecule works alongside thyroid hormones to help form the part of the eye responsible for our sharpest sight, challenging a scientific explanation that has stood for roughly 30 years.
The discovery centers on an unexpected transformation that occurs in the developing retina before birth. Certain cells that initially detect blue light appear to change into cells sensitive to red and green light, helping create the specialized arrangement needed for clear central vision.
Published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the findings could reshape scientists' understanding of how human eyes develop. They may also help advance research into future treatments for macular degeneration, glaucoma, and other conditions that cause vision loss.
"This is a key step toward understanding the inner workings of the center of the retina, a critical part of the eye and the first to fail in people with macular degeneration," said Robert J. Johnston Jr., an associate professor of biology at Johns Hopkins University who led the study. "By better understanding this region and developing organoids that mimic its function, we hope to one day grow and transplant these tissues to restore vision."
How Scientists Recreated the Developing Human Retina
To investigate how human vision forms, Johnston and his colleagues turned to an innovative laboratory technique they have helped develop over the past several years. Instead of relying entirely on animal experiments, they grew miniature versions of human retinal tissue called organoids.
These small clusters of cells, grown from fetal cells, reproduce important features of developing human tissue. By observing the retinal organoids over several months, the scientists could follow changes that would otherwise be extremely difficult to study during pregnancy.
Their attention focused on the foveola, a tiny region at the very center of the retina. The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye that converts incoming light into signals the brain can interpret. Within it, the foveola plays an especially important role in detailed central vision, which allows people to read, recognize faces, and distinguish fine details.
Although the foveola occupies only a small fraction of the retina, it is involved in approximately 50% of human visual perception, according to the researchers.
The Surprising Secret Behind Sharp Human Vision
One of the keys to understanding the foveola is a group of specialized light-detecting cells called cones. Unlike rod cells, which are particularly important for seeing in dim light, cones support daytime vision and allow us to perceive color.
Humans have three types of cone cells, each most sensitive to different wavelengths of light. These are commonly described as blue, green, and red cones. By comparing signals from these different cells, the brain can distinguish a remarkably broad range of colors.
However, the cones are not distributed evenly throughout the retina. The foveola contains red and green cones but lacks blue cones, which are found in other retinal regions. This precise arrangement is essential for the exceptionally sharp vision produced by the center of the eye.
For decades, researchers have struggled to explain how this pattern develops. One major obstacle is that commonly studied animals, including mice and fish, do not share the same retinal organization found in humans. That makes it difficult to use traditional animal models to investigate how these specialized cells develop.
The laboratory-grown human retinas offered a new opportunity to solve this longstanding mystery.
Vitamin A and Thyroid Hormones Trigger a Remarkable Change
The researchers discovered evidence that the arrangement of cones in the foveola develops through two coordinated processes. Together, they determine which types of cells form in the central retina and how some of those cells change as development continues.
During weeks 10 through 12 of fetal development, a small number of blue cones are initially present in the foveola. By week 14, however, these cells appear to have transformed into red and green cones.
The team identified two important chemical influences behind this process.
The first involves retinoic acid, a molecule produced from vitamin A. Retinoic acid helps regulate how cells develop and specialize throughout the body. In the developing retina, the breakdown of this molecule limits the formation of blue cones in the central region.
The second influence comes from thyroid hormones, which are best known for regulating metabolism but also have crucial roles in growth and development. In this case, the hormones appear to encourage the remaining blue cones to change into red and green cones.
"First, retinoic acid helps set the pattern. Then, thyroid hormone plays a role in converting the leftover cells," Johnston said. "That's very important because if you have those blue cones in there, you don't see as well."
Importantly, the discovery concerns how vitamin A signaling helps guide eye development before birth. It does not establish that taking vitamin A supplements can improve sharp vision in adults.
A Discovery That Challenges a 30-Year-Old Theory
The results offer a striking alternative to an explanation that has influenced vision research for decades.
Under the longstanding model, blue cones that initially appear in the foveola were thought to move away as the retina developed. Scientists generally assumed that once these cells became a particular type of cone, their identities remained fixed.
The new findings suggest something different. Rather than simply relocating, at least some blue cones may undergo a change in identity, becoming red or green cones as the eye develops.
"The main model in the field from about 30 years ago was that somehow the few blue cones you get in that region just move out of the way, that these cells decide what they're going to be, and they remain this type of cell forever," Johnston said. "We can't really rule that out yet, but our data supports a different model. These cells actually convert over time, which is really surprising."
The researchers have not completely ruled out the possibility that some cells migrate. Nevertheless, their observations support the idea that developing cone cells have more flexibility than previously recognized.
That possibility could fundamentally change how scientists study the formation of human color vision and the development of the retina's most specialized regions.
Could the Discovery Help Scientists Restore Lost Vision?
Beyond explaining how healthy eyes develop, the findings could have important implications for treating diseases that damage the retina.
One particularly promising application involves macular degeneration, a major cause of central vision loss, especially among older adults. The disease damages the macula, the retinal region responsible for detailed central vision, and can severely interfere with reading, driving, and recognizing faces. Although treatments can slow or manage certain forms of the disease, there is currently no cure.
Understanding how the retina creates its specialized light-sensitive cells could eventually help scientists produce healthy replacements in the laboratory.
Johnston's team is now working to improve its retinal organoids so they more closely reproduce the structure and function of the human eye. The long-term goal is to develop precisely controlled populations of photoreceptors, the cells that detect light, for potential transplantation into damaged retinas.
Katarzyna Hussey, a study author and former doctoral student in Johnston's laboratory, believes this approach could open an important new direction for vision restoration. Hussey is now a molecular and cell biologist at CiRC Biosciences, a cell therapy company in Chicago.
"The goal with using this organoid tech is to eventually make an almost made-to-order population of photoreceptors. A big avenue of potential is cell replacement therapy to introduce healthy cells that can reintegrate into the eye and potentially restore that lost vision," said Hussey.
The idea is to introduce healthy cells that could integrate with existing retinal tissue and potentially replace functions lost to disease. Achieving that goal would require researchers to demonstrate that transplanted cells can survive, connect properly with the eye's existing circuitry, and function safely.
Hussey emphasized that the technology remains far from routine clinical use, with extensive development and testing still necessary.
"These are very long-term experiments, and of course we'd need to do optimizations for safety and efficacy studies prior to moving into the clinic. But it's a viable journey."
For now, the discovery provides something fundamental: a clearer explanation of how the human eye develops its remarkable ability to see fine details. By revealing how vitamin A signaling and thyroid hormones help shape the retina, scientists have taken another step toward understanding vision at its earliest stages and potentially finding ways to restore it when disease strikes.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Johns Hopkins University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Katarzyna A. Hussey, Kiara C. Eldred, Brian Guy, Clayton P. Santiago, Jingliang Simon Zhang, Ian Glass, Thomas A. Reh, Seth Blackshaw, Loyal A. Goff, Robert J. Johnston. A cell fate specification and transition mechanism for human foveolar cone subtype patterning. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2026; 123 (7) DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2510799123

AI generated
MUSCAT, Oman – Oman said on Oct 30 it had rescued 25 sailors from a merchant ship set ablaze in an attack, as Iran reported three oil tankers were halted while crossing the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has restricted maritime traffic through the strait since the Middle East war erupted on Feb 28 with US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic republic.
The narrow waterway, which normally carries about a fifth of global oil, has become a focal point of the conflict, with ships regularly coming under Iranian fire.
Muscat’s navy “carried out an evacuation operation for 25 crew members of the merchant ship RITI, flying the Panamanian flag, after it was targeted, which led to a fire breaking out on board”, Oman’s Maritime Security Centre said in a statement.
The crew members were provided with medical care, the Omani statement said, without giving details.
The Marine Traffic ship-tracking website described the RITI as a crude oil tanker.
US Central Command chief Brad Cooper said in a video released on Oct 30 that US forces had “successfully cleared the strait’s internationally recognised primary transit routes of Iranian sea mines”.
US forces remain “present to ensure that all primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear”, he added.
Cooper said he visited some of the more than 50,000 US service members in the region, repeating earlier statements that Washington has helped Gulf countries export more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude via the strait since summer.
British maritime security agency UKMTO said that a ship 40 nautical miles south of Lavan island in Iran was struck on Oct 30 by an unknown projectile, which caused a fire onboard.
“The crew of the vessel have been reported as safe and there is no reported environmental impact at this time,” the UKMTO said on X.
Blockade
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said earlier that three oil tankers had been halted after encountering unspecified “incidents” or hitting mines.
“Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorised route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait,” the IRGC said in a statement.
Iran has demanded that vessels use a designated route through the strait and coordinate their passage with the country’s armed forces, labelling a southern corridor closer to Oman’s shores as unauthorised.
The tankers had “switched off all their navigation and positioning systems and, with the support of the terrorist US military, were attempting to exit through the unauthorised route”, the Guards’ statement said.
The Guards did not specify the nature of the “incidents” the tankers encountered, which came a day after Iran’s armed forces said at least four tankers had stopped in the area after hitting mines.
They said the incidents on Oct 30 occurred after the vessels received several radio warnings but disregarded them.
The IRGC said in a later statement that a supertanker carrying two million barrels of oil had stopped following an explosion “after striking a naval mine while navigating an unauthorised route through the Strait of Hormuz”.
“This is the third oil tanker to have exploded and caught fire today as a result of attempting to pass through an unauthorised route,” it added.
The United States has responded to Iran’s blockade of the strait with a counterblockade of Iranian ports, further restricting Tehran’s ability to export oil and conduct trade. AFP

Zelensky: 500 Patriot interceptors could provide Ukraine with strong defense this winter

“Five hundred PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number, and very soon – this winter – they COULD make for a highly effective defense package. However, it has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS. We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” he wrote.

Europe has blown its chance to mediate Ukraine conflict – Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:15:00 UTC
13:15:00 KST

Europe has blown its chance to mediate Ukraine conflict – Lavrov
European countries have repeatedly failed to uphold agreements intended to resolve the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, undermining their credibility as potential peace guarantors, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
Moscow previously stated that European officials would not take part in the upcoming US-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi.
Speaking at a press conference on the sidelines of a G20 meeting in Atlanta, Georgia on Friday, Lavrov said “the Europeans want to insert themselves into the negotiation process.”
“What matters is not what the Europeans want, but what added value they can actually bring to the table.”
Lavrov accused European governments of failing to uphold agreements intended to resolve the crisis, beginning with the February 2014 deal between then-Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovich and opposition leaders. France, Germany, and Poland helped broker the agreement, which was intended to end months of protests and deadly clashes in Kiev.
Yanukovich was ousted shortly afterward, an event Moscow maintains prompted Crimea to secede from Ukraine and join Russia, while also triggering a revolt in the largely Russian-speaking Donbass.
According to Lavrov, France, and Germany also failed to ensure that Ukraine implemented political reforms and granted special status to Donbass under the 2014-2015 Minsk agreements which they helped broker.
Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel and former French President Francois Hollande acknowledged in separate interviews in December 2022 that the agreements gave Ukraine time to strengthen its military. Moscow cited their remarks as evidence that Western governments never intended to implement the accords in good faith.
Lavrov also cited the December 2019 summit in Paris, where the leaders of Russia, Ukraine, France, and Germany reaffirmed their commitment to implementing the Minsk agreements. The diplomatic process ultimately failed to produce a lasting settlement.
“Over the past 12 years, they have had more than enough opportunities. Through their actions, they have demonstrated that their track record cannot be ignored the next time they seek to act as ‘guarantors,’” Lavrov stated.
His remarks followed a rare telephone conversation on Tuesday between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store. The 90-minute call, which focused on the Ukraine conflict and upcoming peace negotiations, drew criticism from several European leaders. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the initiative had not been coordinated with other European countries; Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said he was not informed in advance.
Putin welcomed the contact, describing it as a step toward establishing “some kind of constructive dialogue.”
Lavrov attended the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta at the invitation of the US, despite objections from some European governments to Russia’s participation. US President Donald Trump has also invited Putin to the G20 leaders’ summit scheduled for December in Miami.
European opposition to Russia’s participation was evident on Friday when the traditional G20 group photograph was canceled after several European diplomats objected to posing alongside Lavrov.
