More than $3m spent on government merch, including condoms and lollies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
04:10:13 UTC
13:10:13 KST

Millions spent on government merchandise, including condoms, lollies, tote bags
In short:
The Commonwealth has banned federal agencies from using taxpayer funds to buy promotional merchandise "without exemption".
Figures provided to the Senate reveal government entities spent more than $3.4 million on merchandise last financial year.
What's next?
The new rules took effect from July, with departments required to report their expenditure on merchandise in their annual reports.
The Albanese government has launched a clampdown on taxpayer-funded merchandise in a bid to rein in the millions of dollars spent on promotional knick-knacks.
Stress balls, condoms, lollies, tote bags, pens and beanies were among thousands of branded or promotional products bought by federal entities in the past financial year.
The total cost across a range of government departments, agencies, independent statutory authorities, regulators and other entities came in at more than $3.4 million.
But under a new edict that came into effect from July, the government has banned agencies from using taxpayer funds to purchase promotional merchandise unless they seek approval.
There are some exemptions, such as if items are sold for profit or if they are considered critical to the government's policy objectives.
The policy, which was part of this year's budget, mandates that agencies must also publicly report details of their merchandise spend in their annual reports.
"The Department of Finance has issued guidance to agencies to support implementation of the government's policy," a government spokesperson told the ABC.
What the departments spent
The Department of Defence was among the biggest spenders in 2025–26, putting more than $1.4 million towards merchandise, according to figures provided to the Senate.
This included gifts for foreign militaries and dignitaries, as well as items for recruitment activities, employment expos and base open days.
A Defence spokesperson said officials must ensure spending on merchandise represented an efficient, effective, economic and ethical use of public resources.
Another $383,000 was also spent at the health department, which included 40,000 condoms in an initiative aimed at preventing sexually transmitted infections.
It also purchased 7,000 campaign-branded "condom wallets".
Among the other items the department bought were 5,000 stress balls, 5,000 mints packs, and 220 yo-yos — all with anti-vaping messages.
A department spokesperson defended its spend on merchandise, saying it was procured in limited circumstances for public health campaigns or strategies.
"Evaluation of these campaigns consistently show they are highly engaging, are well recognised by their target audiences and meet the campaign objectives," they said.
"Merchandise plays an important role in this.
"When used, merchandise carries important health messages and information, such as vaccine schedules, reminders of the importance of STI testing and scheduling, and strategies to assist in how to quit vaping and smoking."
Fewer 'branded generic keepsakes'
The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) also incurred $176,000 in merchandise costs last financial year, with most of it aimed at spruiking this year's census.
This included census-themed beanies, mini AFL footballs, socks, reusable shopping bags, pencils, pens and "I heart census" button badge pins.
An ABS spokesperson said its agency had not purchased any further promotional material since the government's new merchandise policy came into effect.
"Census merchandise was used at community events, information hubs, during remote community engagement activities and to support the enumeration of people experiencing homelessness," they said.
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) spent more than $251,000, with a spokesperson saying it uses "standardised promotional material" for career expos and fairs.
The spokesperson also said it was "reasonable to expect" some of its reported expenditure on merchandise was used to purchase items from the AFP Legacy Shop.
"The AFP has formal governance on the acquisition of merchandise and has recently tightened this governance further to ensure a greater proportion of our merchandise has an educational element, rather than branded generic keepsakes," they said.

AI generated
WASHINGTON – HKT, a leading Hong Kong telecom carrier and subsidiary of PCCW, agreed on Oct 30 to halt its operations in the United States under pressure from the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC).
The FCC in October 2025 said it was moving to revoke the authority of HKT to operate in the US, citing national security concerns and its affiliation with China Unicom, which is a shareholder in PCCW.
Under a consent decree reviewed by Reuters, HKT has agreed to stop international and domestic telecom services to and within the US.
HKT must file an application with the FCC within 30 days to discontinue services and must discontinue US services by Sept 1, 2027. PCCW declined immediate comment.
The agreement means the FCC will not move forward with the revocation proceeding that could have offered more details on Washington’s national security concerns.
The FCC has previously barred China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom from providing international telecommunications services to the US, citing broad national security concerns.
The Trump administration has continued an extensive crackdown on Chinese telecoms over the past year.
The FCC on Oct 29 voted to ban all Chinese labs from testing US electronics starting from December 2028.
The telecom crackdown has sparked a strong reaction from Beijing.
China said on Oct 30 it firmly opposes the FCC action on labs, warning it would take necessary countermeasures “if the US side persists in acting unilaterally”.
The FCC also announced on Oct 29 it plans to soon ban Chinese telecom firms from direct access to US phone numbers on national security grounds.
The plan would bar Chinese IP network service providers from direct access and those that use equipment from companies on the FCC’s list that pose national security risks, including Huawei and ZTE.
Other measures under consideration by the FCC include barring Chinese telecom firms from connecting to US networks and from operating their data centres in the US.
Concerns about the potential for spying and other harms to arise from Chinese access to US telecom data and infrastructure have grown in recent years.
In late 2024, Washington said a Chinese state-sponsored cyber espionage group known as Salt Typhoon stole consumers’ call records and US call data and infiltrated US telecommunications and telecom infrastructure firms.
China has consistently denied any wrongdoing. REUTERS

China's non-manufacturing PMI dips, services activity remains stable

BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- China's non-manufacturing activity moderated in October, while the services sector remained broadly stable, with holiday-related consumption and certain service industries showing relatively strong growth, official data showed Saturday.
The purchasing managers' index (PMI) for the non-manufacturing sector came in at 49.7 in October, down 0.5 points from September, partly due to weaker activity in some service industries, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
A reading above 50 indicates expansion, while a reading below 50 signifies contraction.
The business activity index for the services sector stood at 50.0, down 0.2 points from the previous month, indicating broadly stable activity.
By industry, business activity picked up in most major service categories. Railway transportation, accommodation, and culture, sports and entertainment services saw notable improvements, with their respective indexes rising into expansionary territory, supported by travel and consumer spending during the National Day holiday.
Meanwhile, business activity indexes for water transportation, postal services, and internet, software and information technology services all remained above 55.0, indicating relatively rapid growth in business activity.
The financial sector was the only major service category to register a decline in its business activity index, with a relatively sharp drop contributing to the overall moderation in services activity.
Business expectations remained positive, with the services sector's business activity expectations index standing at 55.2, suggesting that most surveyed enterprises remained confident about market prospects.
In the construction sector, the business activity index fell 2.3 points from September to 48.0, indicating a slowdown in construction activity.
The sector's business activity expectations index stood at 52.3, down 3.1 points from the previous month.
Saturday's data came as China's service sector has maintained strong growth momentum this year, underpinned by supportive policy expectations, growing market confidence, resilient consumption and opening up.
In the first half of the year, the service sector contributed 66.1 percent to the country's economic growth, up 5.9 percentage points from the same period a year earlier. ■

Interview: CIIE offers "gateway" for shared growth, says Indonesian expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:08:32 CST
13:08:32 KST

by Xinhua writers Zhang Yisheng, Feng Yulin
JAKARTA, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- The upcoming ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) offers a "gateway" for international businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), to tap into China's vast market and build resilient global trade networks, an Indonesian expert has said.
"The good thing is that China gives opportunities to countries all across the globe to come," Humprey Arnaldo Russel, head of the ASEAN-China Research Center at the University of Indonesia, told Xinhua in an interview ahead of the expo, scheduled to be held in Shanghai on Nov. 5-10.
Launched in 2018 as the world's first national-level expo dedicated to imports, the CIIE aims to expand China's opening up and provide businesses worldwide with access to its large market. This year's edition will feature over 200 representative global debuts and first-time exhibits.
For smaller enterprises, entering a foreign market often involves navigating complex regulatory and compliance requirements. The CIIE helps address these challenges by providing a face-to-face platform for Indonesian SMEs to engage directly with Chinese businesses, Humprey said.
Indonesian businesses "can learn how to enter the Chinese market by meeting directly with their Chinese counterparts to discuss regulations," he said. "Sometimes an opportunity exists, but you must first meet the market requirements."
Amid ongoing shifts in global trade dynamics and unilateral tariff pressures, the Shanghai expo provides Indonesian exporters with "timely momentum" to diversify their export markets, build sustainable supply chains and integrate into broader economic ecosystems, Humprey said.
"Beyond accessing the Chinese market, our businesses can connect with international buyers and global distributors who convene in Shanghai. It is an invaluable platform for our export expansion," he said.
Highlighting the participation of companies from around the world, including U.S. firms that have maintained a strong presence at the CIIE over the years, Humprey said, "I think countries across the globe want to see China and the United States cooperate with each other for a better world."
"We need an open system where people with small and medium-sized enterprises, whether in Africa, Indonesia, Vanuatu, or Fiji, have the opportunity to trade across the globe based on WTO rules," he said.
Emphasizing that trade serves as a bridge for cooperation, Humprey noted that stronger economic ties and their positive spillover effects can help narrow differences among nations.
"A shared future is a must, because the future does not belong only to us. It belongs to the next generation," he said. "We have to prepare good things for them." ■

Feature: Mauritius' rare homegrown coffee embarks on aromatic journey to China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:08:26 CST
13:08:26 KST

PORT LOUIS, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Known for its striking multicolored volcanic dunes, southwestern Mauritius is also home to a less familiar attraction: the African island country's only coffee plantation.
Located in the Chamarel 7 Colored Earth Geopark in the Black River District, the plantation produces distinctive beans that remain little known outside Mauritius.
This signature coffee, grown amid the volcanic landscapes of Mauritius, is set to make its debut at this year's China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai.
"We would love the Chinese market to discover a rare coffee specialty from Mauritius," said Thomas Lehoux, development manager of coffee operations at Chamarel Coffee, the sole brand in Mauritius that grows coffee locally and makes products from its own beans.
At the plantation, humid conditions, gentle sunlight and mineral-rich soil provide a favorable environment for coffee trees, helping produce beans with a rich and balanced flavor.
Like wine, coffee derives much of its character from its origin, flavor and quality, Lehoux told Xinhua, adding that Chamarel Coffee uses beans grown on its own plantation and processed entirely by hand, producing flavors that distinguish from comparable products of other origins.
The plantation mainly grows two varieties of coffee, Arabica and Liberica. Lehoux will bring both to this year's CIIE, marking the brand's debut at the event.
Lehoux said coffee consumption in China has grown in recent years, along with increasing interest in bean varieties, flavor profiles and places of origin, creating opportunities for Mauritian coffee.
"I believe there can be a strong link between us as a small producer on a small island and a big market like China," he said.
At this year's CIIE, the brand hopes to connect with Chinese coffee importers, upscale restaurants, specialty coffee shops and roasters. For Lehoux, who has about 20 years of experience in coffee production, the expo will also offer a best chance to better understand Chinese consumers' preferences and explore ways to tailor products to the market.
To prepare for potential business opportunities following the CIIE, the company is expanding its plantation, which currently covers about 16 hectares and produces around one tonne of finished coffee beans for export annually. An additional 4 hectares were planted this year, with output expected to increase in two to three years.
The company has also been developing coffee-scented fragrances, perfumes and coffee cups as part of its efforts to diversify its business beyond coffee.
Walking through the plantation, Lehoux said he hoped the CIIE would help Chamarel Coffee build long-term relationships in China and find partners to support its growth.
Though separated by vast stretches of ocean, Mauritius and China have achieved fruitful results in practical economic and trade cooperation. Mauritius is the first African country to sign a free trade agreement with China. China, for consecutive years, has been Mauritius' largest trading partner and largest source of imports.
Mauritian sugar products, which have appeared at the CIIE for several editions, are a prominent example of the Indian Ocean island's efforts to reach Chinese buyers. With coffee and other new products to be presented at the expo this year, the two countries are poised to deepen trade cooperation and expand Mauritian exports to China. ■

Global wildlife trade involves over 107,000 species: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:08:20 CST
13:08:20 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- More than 107,000 species are used and traded worldwide, more than double previous estimates, according to a new study that warns the true scale could be far greater due to major gaps in global monitoring data.
Published in Science Advances and led by Australia's University of Melbourne, the study identified 107,356 species traded across plants, animals and fungi, compared with previous estimates of about 50,000 species in trade worldwide, according to a university statement released on Saturday.
Wildlife trade was a well-established driver of biodiversity loss, but information on its extent and sustainability remained incomplete and fragmented, said lead researcher Professor Alice Hughes from the university's School of BioSciences.
Wildlife trade extended far beyond the illegal trade of elephants, tigers and pangolins, encompassing timber, seafood, medicinal plants, pets, cut flowers, ornamental fish and fungi, most of which were legal, Hughes said.
"For most of these species we have little to no data. There is no data on quantity and origins, let alone the population level data to assess if trade poses a risk to species survival," she said, adding the global biodiversity framework's existing trade target covered only about 2 to 3 percent of species in trade, missing the remaining 97 percent.
The researchers called for standardized data collection and more comprehensive, transparent and globally coordinated reporting, saying existing customs and animal health inspection processes could be adapted to improve wildlife trade monitoring. ■

China's manufacturing PMI softens, high-tech sector maintains expansion
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
12:08:13 CST
13:08:13 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- China's manufacturing activity moderated in October, with the purchasing managers' index (PMI) falling to 49.3, while high-tech and equipment manufacturing sectors maintained expansion, official data showed Saturday.
The overall reading was down 0.8 percentage points from the previous month, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
Huo Lihui, a chief statistician with the NBS, attributed the retreat to some demand being brought forward ahead of the National Day holiday earlier this month and a complex international environment.
The production sub-index stood at 49.8, down 1.9 points from September, while the new orders sub-index fell 1.1 points to 49.4, as both supply and demand moderated during the month.
The PMI for high-tech manufacturing stood at 51.3, while that for equipment manufacturing came in at 50.6, both remaining above the 50-point threshold that separates expansion from contraction.
The figures indicate that emerging industries continued to sustain growth momentum, supported by the ongoing development of new quality productive forces, Huo noted.
Manufacturing activity in several advanced industries remained robust. Both the production and new orders sub-indexes for railway, shipbuilding and aerospace equipment manufacturing, as well as computer, communications and electronic equipment manufacturing, stood at 53 or above, pointing to relatively strong supply and demand in these sectors.
Large manufacturers continued to report expansion, with their PMI standing at 50.2, despite a slight decline of 0.4 points from the previous month. Meanwhile, the PMI readings for medium-sized and small enterprises came in at 48.4 and 47.5, respectively.
On the price front, both major raw material purchasing prices and factory-gate prices remained in expansionary territory, although their growth moderated.
The purchasing price sub-index stood at 56.8, down 4 points from September, while the factory-gate price sub-index eased 2.3 points to 51.7, partly reflecting recent declines in the prices of certain nonferrous metals and other commodities. ■

====================================================================================================

Courtney Barnett's songs aren't just about Courtney Barnett
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:58:53 UTC
12:58:53 KST

Courtney Barnett is in her late-30s, over a decade into an incredibly successful music career, and past the point of being Australia's next big thing: she arrived a while ago.
Where some artists fear maturity might dull their edge, Barnett recognises how experience works in her favour.
While making her latest album, Creature Of Habit, disjointed recording sessions and writer's block had the singer-songwriter feeling a little unstable. But this wasn't her first time at the big dance.
"There were moments where I thought it would never get finished," she says.
"It kind of comes in waves. I think that's just the creative process for me: it's ups and downs. I said to myself, 'I've been here before. I've made a few albums, and I've felt this feeling. I'm just going to trust that hopefully I'll pass whatever the difficult moment is and just get on with it.'"
Old habits die
Spoiler: it did pass, resulting in yet another remarkable collection of songs in which Barnett captures our insecurities and reflects them with startling clarity.
That's long been one of her great strengths as a songwriter. The details in a Courtney Barnett song often belong to her, but the feelings somehow belong to everybody.
"I know I got a sensitive heart, I'm always picking it apart when I throw it to the vultures. They don't want it either, probably too sincere," she sings on Sugar Plum, a highlight from Creature Of Habit.
Barnett won audiences over from the outset with sharply observed stories about the messy process of trying to figure out life. Her songs often felt intensely personal, but left enough room for listeners to find themselves inside them.
When the young, shy artist was thrust into the spotlight following the success of her early EPs, those innermost thoughts suddenly became open to scrutiny. Seeing her work picked apart by strangers was unsettling.
These days, she's more accustomed to it.
"It kind of adds up, time and experience and all those things … I just feel a little more comfortable doing what I do," Barnett says about her current standing.
While she feels the impact of years in the game, she still finds it a challenge to pinpoint what exactly has changed.
"I feel like I've learned a lot a lot of small but important lessons, but sometimes I don't quite know how to articulate them. One of them is just learning how to trust myself a bit more.
"In the past, I would often spiral into this self-doubt, which just doesn't feel very productive or enjoyable.
"Even just facing a difficult moment and just working through it, something that sounds kind of simple; it was hard to trust in that process.
"Sometimes you got to fake it till you make it. You've got to convince yourself that you 100 per cent know what you're doing."
Start somewhere
While experience helped, Barnett also benefited from coming back to her discipline with fresh eyes.
Making the 2023 instrumental album End of the Day — the soundtrack to the Anonymous Club documentary about her life on the road — gave her a chance to work in a different realm.
"When I started working on it, I was just kind of learning how to write again because I hadn't written a song for a little while," she says. "So, it felt in a way that I was kind of beginning again.
"I was doing a lot of free writing, trying not to go into writing with any kind of intention or idea. I was kind of just trying to understand what was rattling around in my head as unfiltered as humanly possible.
"I guess a lot of my writing is kind of like that. Then it shows me something and then I kind of piece a narrative or an idea together. I guess it was just a thing circling in my head."
Condensing swirling thoughts into compact and compelling cuts of relatable indie rock is not easy on a technical level. Making sense of that flood of thoughts can be just as challenging.
What's worse, there's not really anywhere to hide when you're bleeding onto the page.
"It can be confronting, because you're face to face with yourself and holding a mirror up to yourself and sometimes you see things that you don't like," Barnett says.
"I was exploring parts of my personality or just parts of my world or life. I guess that kind of plays into the album title.
"I was looking at parts of myself that I didn't really like or that I wanted to change or wanted to work on, and kind of gently and kindly doing that work or making those subtle changes."
The You and the I
In many of her best songs, Barnett tells stories about her own life. A medical incident in Avant Gardener, a trip to an open home she can't afford in Depreston, the general suburban malaise of Rae Street. But the inward focus is not always intentional.
"I think that sometimes when I do look out, or write something for someone else, or to someone else, it often makes its way back around to me somehow," she says.
"Whether that's putting myself in someone's shoes or finding some kind of level of connection or empathy or something. I don't know. But I often end up talking to myself in a weird roundabout way."
And if you see yourself in Barnett's songs, you're right. If you reckon she's singing about you, she's not going to argue.
"The 'you' and the 'me' and the 'I'… it's kind of interchangeable," she says.
"In some songs, I might be addressing multiple people or things in my head, but it might sound like it's to just one person."
Of course, the song and its intent don't necessarily belong to its creator. Perhaps music's most magical power is allowing us to interpret it how we feel, and project our own emotions and life onto it.
"It's why I don't like over explaining meanings of songs, I don't always find it necessary," Barnett says.
"I love learning what old songs are about and the story that is behind some old classic song, but also, it's nice that we get to project our own stuff onto music. I think that's really beautiful."
Making connections with those who see themselves in her songs brings the purpose of her endeavours into sharpest focus.
"I was just thinking of moments in my life where someone has come up to me and said exactly that. They've been the moments where I have really truly felt that connection. I'm really grateful for that," she says.
"I think it's sometimes it's so hard to know… you're just sitting in your room making music and then it goes on the internet and there's comments and all that stuff…
"But sometimes it doesn't really connect until a human says that or I play a show and I see people singing along or having an emotional moment. That's extremely powerful. I'm really grateful for those moments."
Courtney Barnett plays Brisbane on Wednesday before shows in Sydney and Melbourne on Friday and Saturday.
Creature Of Habit is out now.

'Credibility rests on even-handedness': India flags politicisation of UNHRC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:35:25 UTC
12:35:25 KST

First secretary at India's Permanent Mission to the UN, Bhavika Mangalanandan
NEW DELHI: India has said the credibility of the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHRC) depends on “even-handedness”, warning that country-specific mandates pursued without the involvement of the concerned nation deepen divisions rather than improve human rights conditions on the ground.Addressing the United Nations General Assembly's debate on the Human Rights Council's report on Friday, First Secretary at India's Permanent Mission to the UN, Bhavika Mangalanandan, called for dialogue, cooperation and equal treatment of all countries in addressing human rights concerns.
She said country-specific mandates pursued without the engagement of the country concerned seldom improve conditions on the ground and instead create divisions within the council.
“Credibility of the council rests on even-handedness. Country-specific mandates pursued without the engagement of the country concerned seldom improve the situation on the ground,” she said.Recalling external affairs minister S Jaishankar's remarks at the high-level segment of the 61st Human Rights Council in February, Mangalanandan said human rights should be advanced through dialogue and genuine partnerships rather than selective approaches.
Jaishankar had said that “human rights are best advanced through dialogue, capacity building and genuine partnerships, and not by politicisation, selectivity, or double standards.”Mangalanandan said such an approach was necessary for the council to speak with one voice and address allegations that human rights were being weaponised.She also identified the Universal Periodic Review (UPR), which involves cooperation and engagement with member states while treating all countries equally, as the appropriate platform for assessing human rights records.
India calls for equal emphasis on all human rights
India also stressed that economic, social and cultural rights, along with the right to development, should receive the same attention as civil and political rights.“Economic, social, and cultural rights and the right to development deserve the same attention as civil and political rights,” Mangalanandan said.She noted that poverty, debt and limited access to financing and technology remained major obstacles to the enjoyment of human rights across much of the developing world.“These call for international cooperation and not coercion,” she said.India also flagged terrorism as one of the gravest threats to human rights, particularly the fundamental right to life, and called on the council to maintain sustained attention to the issue.“We would encourage the council to give this threat the sustained attention it warrants on the basis of zero tolerance,” she said.
India raises concerns over funding and duplication of mandates
Mangalanandan said the Human Rights Council should fulfil its mandate within the resources available to it and called for transparent, member-driven rationalisation of its work.She cautioned against budgetary measures disproportionately affecting mandates dealing with development and economic, social and cultural rights.“Rationalisation should remain member-driven and transparent. It should not fall disproportionately on mandates that address development and economic, social, and cultural rights,” she said.
India also called for adequate and predictable funding for the UN's human rights pillar through the regular budget, arguing that its priorities should not be determined by earmarked voluntary contributions.Mangalanandan further flagged duplication between resolutions and initiatives taken up by the Human Rights Council and the UN General Assembly.“We should consider mechanisms that avoid resolutions and initiatives on the same topic and of similar nature, both in the Council and (General) Assembly."We see an increasing tendency for the Council to dictate reporting to the Third Committee, including reporting by Special Rapporteurs, which further undermines the need for a specialised Council,” she said.The Third Committee of the UN General Assembly deals with social, humanitarian and cultural issues.India returned to the Human Rights Council in 2026 for its seventh term, covering the 2026-28 period.

Union home minister Amit Shah also paid floral tributes to Patel and attended the 'Run for Unity' event at Major Dhyan Chand National Stadium in New Delhi on Friday.Addressing the gathering, he said Patel's birth anniversary has been observed as National Unity Day since Narendra Modi became prime minister in 2014, highlighting his contribution to integrating the country after Independence.Recalling the challenges India faced at the time of Independence, Shah said political observers across the world had predicted that the country would disintegrate.

Yet, in the 1,218 days following independence, Sardar Patel accomplished what everyone had deemed impossible," Shah said.He added that Patel achieved in just 1,218 days what even a group of leaders might not have accomplished in a lifetime, forging a united India.
Priyanka Jaiswal has four years of experience in digital journalism, news agency reporting and video production. Currently with The Times of India, she covers public policy, politics and global affairs. She is particularly drawn to human-interest stories that put people at the heart of an issue, spark awareness , and contribute to meaningful conversations.

Protests erupt outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal amid leadership dispute
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:16:52 CST
12:16:52 KST

Police stand guard outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw, Poland, Oct. 30, 2026. Protesters clashed with police outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw on Friday night after the court's president was suspended amid an escalating dispute between Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government and the opposition over control of the judiciary. (Photo by Neil Milton/Xinhua)
WARSAW, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Protesters clashed with police outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw on Friday night after the court's president was suspended amid an escalating dispute between Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government and the opposition over control of the judiciary.
Police detained three protesters who entered the court's premises. Several people were reportedly injured, according to local media.
Hundreds of demonstrators, including supporters of the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, gathered outside the tribunal, accusing Tusk's government of attempting to seize control of the court. PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki were among those present.
The confrontation followed months of disputes over judicial appointments. Poland's parliament, where Tusk's ruling coalition holds a majority, has elected eight judges to the tribunal this year. However, President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of the opposition PiS party, accepted the oaths of office of only three.
The remaining five took their oaths at parliamentary ceremonies, but Nawrocki and the tribunal's president refused to recognize their status, preventing them from taking up their judicial duties.
On Friday evening, the tribunal's website announced that its president and vice president had been suspended for one month, with a newly elected judge whose status remains disputed assuming temporary leadership. The tribunal's leadership rejected the move, accusing those involved of illegally taking over its website and describing the action as a "coup."
Nawrocki cut short his trip to Senegal and returned to Poland, where he held an emergency meeting with judicial officials late Friday. Shortly after midnight, he visited the Constitutional Tribunal and entered the court building. ■

California governor announces "strike team" to coordinate 2028 Olympics preparations
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
11:16:22 CST
12:16:22 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- California Governor Gavin Newsom announced Friday that he had signed an executive order creating a state coordination team to oversee preparations for the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games in Los Angeles.
The governor appointed Jamie Callahan, his deputy chief of staff and senior counselor on infrastructure, to serve as executive director of the Games' delivery and coordination "strike team."
The team will bring together more than a dozen state agencies and departments to strengthen statewide planning and readiness ahead of the Games, the governor's office said in a statement. The team will also support regional efforts to expand workforce and economic opportunities, it added.
"California knows how to deliver on the world stage," Newsom said. "With the Olympics and Paralympics coming to Los Angeles in 2028, we're making sure our state is ready to meet the moment."
The Games are projected to cost 7.2 billion U.S. dollars, the Los Angeles Times reported, adding that the city is responsible for upgrading its transportation infrastructure to accommodate the influx of visitors.
According to the governor's office, California has already taken steps to support Los Angeles in preparing to host the world, including infrastructure investments to strengthen the region's transportation networks and modernize major venues.
State officials described the projects as investments intended to continue to benefit residents after the competitions end, not solely to accommodate visitors during the Games.
Security planning also involves multiple levels of government. The California Office of Emergency Services will help coordinate police assistance from across California and the western United States, while the U.S. Secret Service has ultimate security authority, the Los Angeles Times reported.
The announcement follows legislation Newsom signed in September to strengthen public safety coordination and address operational needs of the Games.
The Los Angeles Olympics are scheduled for July 14-30, 2028, followed by the Paralympics on Aug. 15-27, according to the Olympics' official website. Los Angeles previously hosted the Olympics twice, in 1932 and 1984. ■

woven bamboo armchair clad in UV-reactive crocheted blooms glows in the dark
peiyang (camille) li designs she blooms in the dark, an intimate woven bamboo armchair clad in hand-crocheted blossoms made from uv-reactive yarn that absorb daylight and emit a soft nocturnal glow.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
WOVEN BAMBOO pairs with CROCHETED TEXTILES IN CHAIR SCULPTURE
Designed by Peiyang (Camille) Li, She Blooms in the Dark is a glowing seating sculpture that examines emotional vulnerability and protective spatial thresholds. The project pairs hand-crocheted textile craft with traditional bent-wood furniture techniques, mounting an array of individual blossoms across the open-lattice framework of an oversized, woven bamboo armchair.
SHE BLOOMS IN THE DARK: Day Time View | all images ©Kexin Liu
UV-REACTIVE YARN BLOOMS STORE DAYLIGHT TO EMIT AMBIENT GLOW
The sculptural seat by designer Peiyang (Camille) Li functions simultaneously as a functional chair and a semi-enclosed personal retreat, utilizing a curved, basket-like silhouette to delineate an intimate interior microclimate for solitary reflection. Each floral element is crocheted by hand using phosphorescent, UV-reactive yarn engineered to absorb daylight and emit a soft, low-intensity glow in dark environments. By forgoing high-output electric fixtures in favor of photoluminescent fibers, the textile piece activates after dark, transforming the structural bamboo envelope into an illuminated shelter where soft woven media counterbalance the rigid natural framework.

Thousands march through Taipei for transgender equality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:03:43 UTC
12:03:43 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Organizers said around 3,800 people took part in Taiwan's eighth transgender pride march in Taipei on Friday.
CNA reported the march began at 228 Peace Memorial Park on Friday and was organized by the Taiwan Tongzhi Hotline Association, a group advocating for sexual and gender minority rights. More than 61 local and international rights groups took part, calling for an end to discrimination against transgender people.
The association's spokesperson, known as Pan (盤), said the march aimed to bring people together across gender and national boundaries. Transgender rights faced growing threats at home and abroad, he warned.
Pan said online debates over transgender issues had become more divided in recent years. Such debates, he said, often reduced the issue to support or opposition, leaving little room for people to learn from one another.
Organizers also drew attention to problems transgender people face at school, work, and in healthcare. They said strict rules on changing legal gender records and social prejudice continued to create barriers, per the association's press release.
The group said the legalization of same-sex marriage in 2019 did not mean the fight for sexual and gender minorities' rights was over. Issues involving transgender rights, people living with HIV, marriage, and family life still needed attention.
The transgender march is held each year ahead of Taiwan's larger gay pride parade, which takes place in Taipei on Saturday. Organizers said the separate event aims to draw greater attention to transgender rights and issues often overlooked by the wider public.

KMT, DPP mayoral candidates cross swords in Kaohsiung televised debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:03:03 UTC
12:03:03 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — KMT Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Ko Chih-en (柯志恩) and her DPP counterpart Lai Jui-lung (賴瑞隆) sparred over party loyalty, government funding, and the city's future during a televised debate Friday.
CNA reported that the two accused each other of putting party interests ahead of Kaohsiung. Ko called for a leadership change, while Lai defended the record of past DPP mayors and pledged to build on their work.
Lai accused Ko of backing changes to the revenue-sharing law that he said had reduced Kaohsiung's share of government funds. The DPP candidate said Ko had followed the KMT's position in the legislature instead of fighting for the city, a claim he had raised earlier in the campaign.
The law determines how tax revenue is shared between the central and local governments. Ko rejected Lai's claim, saying the final version did not include a KMT proposal to give Taipei more funds, and questioned his own record in the legislature.
The candidates also clashed over plans for a former military site in Kaohsiung. Lai questioned Ko's proposal to move City Hall and the city council there, while Ko said the site could become a major business district and criticized Lai's plans as unclear.
Ko accused Lai of having close ties to a powerful faction within the DPP and warned against letting party interests shape city policy. Lai rejected the claim and pledged to oppose any party decision that went against Kaohsiung's interests.
The KMT candidate also said she would not let senior KMT figures control City Hall if elected. She argued that a change in power would strengthen oversight and help uncover problems left unresolved under DPP rule.
Turning to the city's economy, Ko said many residents had yet to benefit from its growing high-tech sector. She said Kaohsiung's population had fallen by 62,000 over six years, while wages and life expectancy remained below those in Taipei.
Ko pledged to set up an office to address bullying in schools and workplaces within her first month as mayor. She also proposed an office to improve healthcare, transport, and tourism in the former Kaohsiung County, which merged with the city in 2010.
Ko said she would help traditional businesses adopt new technology and create better-paid jobs for young people. Her plans also include new roads, metro lines, expanded airport services, and a new business and housing district.
Lai pledged to raise birth grants to NT$50,000 (US$1,600) per child and expand public child care. He also proposed more aid for young families, short-term child care, and better health services for older residents.
Lai said he would expand affordable rental housing and build more homes near metro stations. Ko, meanwhile, has pledged to build 5,000 public housing units and encourage private investment to ease housing costs.
Lai also pledged to help traditional industries adopt new technology and expand Kaohsiung's role in artificial intelligence and chip production. He proposed better transport links and airport upgrades as the city attracts more investment in its semiconductor sector.
Lai credited Mayor Chen Chi-mai (陳其邁) and past DPP mayors with helping turn Kaohsiung into a major industrial and high-tech center. He pledged to build on their work over the next decade, while Ko argued that the city needed stronger oversight and new leadership.

'It's like being in an unlisted war' — Economy turns US midterms into a patience test for voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
03:00:38 UTC
12:00:38 KST

Washington, DC — "It takes $100 a day just to be a human being."
This is how Alfie Murphy, a mid-20s resident of New York, described the economic squeeze driven by high inflation and low wages in the US as the country heads to the midterms.
He says many people of his generation don't want to sacrifice time to work a dead-end job when they have knowledge and know what's going on in the world.
"It makes everything seem finite in the end. We just want to live. The dream of working until a certain retirement age is outdated in our eyes," Murphy tells TRT World.
Murphy, who used to live in Washington, DC, says that the food stamps in the capital used to be close to $300, but "that is now barely enough to cover weeks' worth of groceries."
"For my generation, it's always like being in an unlisted war. We are stressed out of our minds about the future, and most of it has to do with what we're exposed to… It can be a lot, especially when you don't see much change."
Murphy isn't the only one who shares this view.
According to Pew Research Center, the economy is ranked the single highest priority concern for voters, with 84 percent of all registered voters rating it as "very important".
Ongoing financial strains — compounded by high food prices, energy costs, and elevated borrowing rates — have left a strong majority of the electorate seeking substantial political change.
Young Americans, working-class, and retirees
This economic squeeze affects most Americans, though the impact can vary by class.
Working-class families are fearing the worst because jobs, while not falling, are not providing the necessary increase in income to beat or at least match the increase in prices.
Young Americans, however, are arguably suffering the most, as they struggle to secure jobs, which creates additional issues.
According to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, the FRED Youth Unemployment Rate (Ages 16–24) sat at 9.9 percent, which is more than double the national general unemployment rate of 4.2 percent.
While the broader US economy is not experiencing mass layoffs, companies have shifted into a highly competitive "low-hire, low-fire" cycle.
This lack of natural corporate turnover, paired with automated AI screening filters and an ongoing drop in entry-level listings, has made finding work unusually difficult and impersonal for young adults.
The impact on retirees, by contrast, could be starkly different.
Eugenio Aleman, Chief Economist at Raymond James, says retirees — especially those who managed to save for retirement — could see an advantage.
"Retirees, especially if they have saved for retirement, are doing much better because returns on equity have been very strong, and now fixed income is also starting to be a good place to put their savings," Aleman tells TRT World.
"Since baby boomers have accumulated the largest amount of wealth of any generation, their relative position is better than previous generations."
Those who didn't save for retirement could be disadvantaged, he says.
Disillusioned supporters
The economic strain has left a sour taste in President Donald Trump supporters' mouths, with many of them now holding a negative view of the GOP.
"Every poll is showing that trend," Aleman says.
"However, how much that will translate into a defeat for Republicans is not that clear," he adds.
The widespread disillusionment does not necessarily mean all of these voters are switching to Democrats; instead, it is creating a severe voter enthusiasm deficit for Republicans.
As many Americans reel under the pressure of inflation and economic uncertainty, the economy could be the most decisive issue in the midterms.
"Because there are lots of unfulfilled promises and people are upset about higher prices. This is affecting Republicans particularly hard because many of these issues are affecting their constituents the most," Aleman says.
"The economy is going to be the decisive factor in swing districts."
The economic picture, however, is not entirely straightforward.
Figures released just days before the election showed the US economy growing at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter, but consumer prices also accelerated to 3.6 percent year over year in September.
The contrast captures the political problem facing the administration: strong growth figures may offer reassurance, but they do not necessarily translate into relief for households still struggling with high prices, fuel costs and borrowing expenses.
For voters facing expensive groceries, housing and healthcare, national economic statistics can feel distant from the realities of the monthly budget.
For candidates across the country, the challenge is to convince voters that they understand these pressures and have a plan to address them.
They now have only three days to do so.

The four principles outlined by Eisenkot were: recognizing Israel as a Jewish, democratic, liberal and equal state; committing to the values of Israel's Declaration of Independence; requiring all citizens to perform military, national or civilian service; and recognizing Hamas as a terrorist organization whose military and governing capabilities in Gaza must be destroyed.

The shift toward Israel began more than a decade ago, but the latest election marked a milestone, with thousands of residents who acquired Israeli citizenship in the past two years casting ballots for the first time.
Mossad to assist Shin Bet in probe of potential election interference by countries other than Qatar
The Mossad will assist the Shin Bet security service in investigating suspected foreign interference in Israel's election, including the possible involvement of countries other than Qatar.
A source familiar with the investigation told Haaretz on Friday that security agencies are examining suspicions that foreign funds were transferred to political figures in Israel and used to finance voter mobilization efforts through various platforms.
However, the source assessed that the affair was limited in scope and that its impact, if any, was far less significant than some accounts have suggested.
The Shin Bet, which is responsible for identifying and thwarting foreign interference in Israel, is leading the investigation. Until Thursday, the Mossad had maintained that it had no role to play in the probe, but on Friday it agreed to a Shin Bet request to assist with specific aspects of the investigation involving suspected foreign involvement.
If Netanyahu stays, even his voters will feel it in their pockets | Analysis
Tuesday's election cost Netanyahu's coalition its majority, yet the opposition may still be unable to replace him. The frustration of its voters does not augur the demise of the state. But there is a real danger that the decline will continue, even accelerate, a process that began with Netanyahu and Likud's relatively surprising victory in 2015 (then too, contrary to the polls and even the exit polls).
In retrospect, this was the moment the prime minister's self-confidence swelled and when he became more immersed in the three criminal affairs in which he was charged in 2019. His investigation and subsequent prosecution brought on a holy war against the judiciary, a series of closely spaced general elections amid political instability, his close alliance with the far-right parties and, finally, his absolute shirking of responsibility for the failures that made possible the October 7 massacre.
In recent years, Netanyahu resembled a driver who was determined to smash the Zionist project into a wall, indifferent to the outcries of the passengers who were stuck behind him and had no way of extricating themselves.
For many in the change bloc, the hope for an exceptional showing by Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party on Tuesday represented the last off-ramp from the expressway to hell. So far, that hasn't happened. The power of tribal-religious identity politics and fanning the fear of the Arabs played into Netanyahu's hands, even though his bloc is 11 Knesset seats smaller than after the 2022 election. In that one, too, a year before the massacre, he played on the same sentiments.
The Democrats doubled their Knesset seats, but alienated Arab voters along the way
The Democrats ultimately won eight seats: short of expectations, but double the representation of Labor in the outgoing Knesset. In the 2022 election, Labor and Meretz – the two parties that later merged to form the Democrats – ran separately. Labor won only four seats, while Meretz failed to cross the electoral threshold.
Still, the party appears to have fallen short in reaching voters it had neglected, particularly Arab citizens. During the Knesset term, Democrats lawmakers Naama Lazimi, Efrat Rayten and Gilad Kariv stood out for their parliamentary work, while during the campaign the party's candidates traveled extensively around the country. Kariv was particularly active in reaching Arab communities, and the party recruited a large volunteer network.
But Soumaya Bashir, the party's representative from the Arab community, finished only 10th in the primary, and the Democrats won only small shares of the vote in many of Israel's larger Arab localities.
Issawi Frej, a former Meretz minister and lawmaker, does not consider the Democrats' result a significant achievement. "The Democrats were never genuinely interested in partnership with Arab society. It was a pretense," he charged.
At Shin Bet's request, Mossad to assist in probe into suspected foreign election interference
Mossad has agreed to a request from the Shin Bet security service to assist in its investigation into suspected foreign interference in Israel's elections.
The move comes after Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg instructed Shin Bet chief David Zini to investigate what he described as "serious suspicions" of improper foreign influence on the election through foreign funding. Sohlberg clarified in the letter that he could not "attest to the nature of the suspicions."
According to a source on the committee, claims were raised, among others, that Qatar had invested money to increase voter turnout in the Arab community. The Shin Bet said it was conducting an investigation but declined to provide further details.
Qatar, for its part, denies interfering in Israel's elections.

Judge orders Trump administration to cease threats to prosecute election officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:56:35 UTC
11:56:35 KST

US judge orders Trump administration to cease threats to prosecute election officials
WASHINGTON – A US judge ordered the Justice Department on Oct 30 to stop threatening to prosecute state and local election officials who do not comply with the Trump administration’s demands related to voting by alleged non-citizens.
The ruling comes days before the US midterm elections that will determine control of Congress, where Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate.
Although several key races appear closely contested, polls favour Democrats to take control of the House and give them a plausible chance of a Senate majority.
In the months leading up to the midterms, US President Donald Trump’s administration has taken an aggressive approach to election oversight, such as pressing states for voter-registration data, saying stricter measures are needed to ensure election security and public confidence in the vote.
But the Justice Department went too far in October when it threatened to prosecute state and county officials who do not cooperate with the Trump administration’s election-related initiatives, US District Judge Trina Thompson ruled in connection with a lawsuit brought by election workers’ unions and some other groups.
“Because the public has a paramount interest in ensuring that election officials and workers are able to carry out their work in accordance with federal law and election procedure, and the official day of the elections is only a couple of days away, the balance of the equities and public interest weigh in plaintiffs’ favour,” Thompson wrote in her temporary restraining order.
The Justice Department had no immediate comment on the ruling.
Critics, including political experts as well as Democratic and some Republican election officials, have viewed the Trump administration’s moves as federal overreach. Some election officials have told Reuters they were preparing for potential federal interference in the midterm elections.
Thompson, who was appointed by former president Joe Biden, ordered the Trump administration to refrain from demanding that local election officials remove voters from statewide rolls, refuse ballots to specific voters, or segregate ballots cast in the midterm elections, based on a Trump administration list of alleged non-citizen voters.
Trump has made false claims related to elections in the past, including not acknowledging his defeat in the 2020 election. REUTERS

Crypto exchanges call for quick moves to bolster defences after Binance heist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:50:00 UTC
11:50:00 KST

Crypto exchanges call for quick moves to bolster defences after Binance heist
SAN FRANCISCO – Crypto exchanges are taking quick action to bolster their defences and urging greater industry-wide information-sharing after a record US$6.3 billion hack of Binance exposed their vulnerability just as they become more embedded in mainstream finance.
Coinbase said it had made adjustments to its systems that store cryptocurrency keys offline “solely out of an abundance of caution”, while Kraken said it was monitoring industry incidents for lessons it could apply to its defences.
But the industry will need to move urgently, analysts and industry executives said, as US President Donald Trump’s regulators promote deeper integration of digital assets into the financial system, raising the stakes for an industry with a history of big hacks.
“For crypto to reach its full potential, the security situation must be addressed immediately,” said Chris Perkins, Franklin Templeton’s head of crypto.
Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, halted withdrawals after the Oct 29 attack – which analysts blamed on North Korea – and said it would use company funds to cover the losses.
Binance co-chief executive Richard Teng said on X that the “complex attack” may have begun with a compromised software engineer’s laptop, giving hackers access to systems used to process withdrawals.
The company later found additional breaches, while software designed to erase traces of the attack hampered the investigation.
On Oct 30, rival crypto exchanges moved quickly to shore up their own systems and to reassure customers that their tokens were safe
“Full-time teams at Kraken look for potential vulnerabilities every day,” a Kraken spokesperson said.
Still, even as the industry reeled from the biggest cryptocurrency heist of all time, executives expressed confidence that Binance had sufficient resources to cover the losses and that the hack would not have broader financial repercussions.
Bitcoin fell more than 4% on Oct 29 while ether, the second-largest cryptocurrency, fell more than 5%, although both tokens recovered some of that ground on Oct 30.
“Our expectation is the industry writ large will actually not suffer material losses, even though Binance is obviously going to have to deal with the exploit directly,” said Josh Riezman, chief legal and strategy officer at crypto firm GSR.
The bulk of the heist unfolded in around 20 minutes late on Oct 29 and bore similarities to previous attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.
North Korea routinely denies involvement in cryptocurrency thefts, and its mission in Geneva did not respond to requests for comment.
Hack involves social engineering, money laundering
While much remains unclear, social engineering, a common tactic in which hackers trick victims into revealing sensitive information or granting access to systems, may have been involved in compromising the laptop, security experts said.
Harry Donnelly, CEO of Circuit, a crypto risk infrastructure company, said companies are planning more employee training to guard against social engineering attacks.
In such attacks, hackers race to launder the funds before the exchange detects the breach and token issuers freeze assets.
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly US$1.57 billion linked to Binance, while Circle said it froze US$800 million.
Bitcoin and Ether cannot be frozen because no single entity controls the coins.
Chainalysis said the hackers appeared to be using sophisticated laundering patterns it had not seen before.
On Oct 30, some crypto exchange executives called for the industry to develop a coordinated hack detection system.
“We need a real-time alert system that allows participants to share information immediately when a hack occurs, coordinate a rapid response, and temporarily freeze suspected stolen funds,” said Star Xu, CEO of crypto exchange OKX, in a post on X.
GSR’s Riezman added that the Binance hack could spur the industry to act: “As we’re at this kind of confluence moment for traditional finance and digital assets, I think it’s obviously important that we continue to improve, and I think this, if anything, will be a catalyst for that.” REUTERS

NMC invites applications to empanel 17 standing counsels across Supreme Court, 16 High Court positions

The National Medical Commission is seeking applications for standing counsels aimed at bolstering its legal expertise.
New Delhi: The National Medical Commission (NMC) has invited applications from advocates to empanel 17 standing counsels to represent it before the Supreme Court, High Courts and their benches across the country, with preference for lawyers experienced in medical institution and medical negligence cases.According to an Expression of Interest (EOI) issued on October 30, the commission is seeking one standing counsel for the Supreme Court and 16 positions across various High Courts. These include two positions each at the Delhi High Court and Himachal Pradesh High Court, and one each at the Karnataka High Court's Bengaluru, Dharwad and Kalaburagi benches, Uttarakhand High Court at Nainital, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh High Court's Srinagar and Jammu benches, Rajasthan High Court's Jodhpur bench, Bombay High Court's Nagpur and Goa benches, Gauhati High Court's Kohima and Aizawl benches, and Jharkhand High Court at Ranchi.The eligibility criteria require applicants to be between 35 and 70 years of age as on November 1, 2026, registered with the concerned State Bar Council and to have completed at least 100 appearances before the Supreme Court or a High Court in the preceding three years. Applicants must also have a minimum of 10 years' experience handling constitutional, civil, criminal or educational institution matters before High Courts.
For the Supreme Court position, applicants must be Advocates-on-Record with at least 10 years of experience.The NMC has said preference will be given to advocates with experience in medical institution and medical negligence cases, as well as those who have handled cases involving government organisations, institutions, departments and public sector undertakings.The empanelled advocates will represent the commission in court, draft petitions, counter-affidavits and other legal documents, conduct legal research, provide legal opinions and coordinate with government departments. They will also be required to keep the commission updated on important developments and hearing dates and submit monthly and annual statements of cases handled and their outcomes.The empanelment will be for three years or until further orders, whichever is earlier, and may be extended based on performance. There will be no fixed retainer fee, with payments governed by the revised fee structure prescribed by the Department of Legal Affairs, Union law ministry.
Applications must be submitted in the prescribed format by November 30, 2026. The commission will scrutinise applications through a screening committee, followed by interviews of shortlisted candidates, either physically or virtually.

World Bank calls for translating African urbanization into growth, jobs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
10:24:34 CST
11:24:34 KST

ABIDJAN, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- The World Bank (WB) has called on countries in sub-Saharan Africa to turn the region's rapid urbanization into a powerful engine of economic growth and job creation.
The region's urban population grew from 170 million in 1975 to 913 million in 2025 and is projected to reach 1.7 billion by 2050, the international financial institution said in a report, adding that around 15 million young people enter the region's labor market each year.
Sustained population growth in particular underscores the need for creating more jobs correspondingly for youth while expanding access to productive, better-paying employment, according to the report titled "Africa's Urban Awakening: Catalyzing Economic Growth and Job Creation," which was published Wednesday.
The Bank recommends better planning for urban expansion, targeted investment in infrastructure and transport, and stronger regulatory frameworks and land governance. It also calls for greater mobilization of private capital to finance urban facilities and services.
Marie-Chantal Uwanyiligira, WB division director for Cote d'Ivoire, Benin, Guinea and Togo, noted that currently in the region, "productivity gains remain limited, incomes have grown slowly, and too many jobs remain informal and poorly paid."
In Cote d'Ivoire, official data showed it had 17.84 million urban residents out of an estimated total population of 32.8 million last year. The number of localities with more than 100,000 inhabitants increased from eight in 1998 to 17 in 2021.
The West African country has prioritized urban development, mobility and improvements in people's living conditions in its 2026-2030 national development plan. ■

Trump, Milei under pressure to explain Bolsonaro flight from Brazil

Unknown Publisher

Trump, Milei under pressure to explain Bolsonaro flight from Brazil
BRASILIA – US President Donald Trump and Argentina’s Javier Milei faced mounting pressure on Oct 30 to explain the role their countries played in helping Flavio Bolsonaro flee Brazil after he had his passports cancelled.
The 45-year-old Brazilian senator bolted his country two days after being defeated by incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a presidential election on Oct 25.
He had been ordered to surrender all his passports due to an ongoing investigation into him on suspicion of money-laundering.
However, he left the country in a cloak-and-dagger operation via Argentina and Ecuador, and landed in Florida on Oct 28, where he declared himself the rightful “leader” of Brazil.
Bolsonaro refused to concede defeat after his loss, which came as a shock after he won a first-round election and had been seen as the narrow favourite.
According to the Argentine migration authority, Bolsonaro boarded a private plane on the evening of Oct 27 in north-eastern Puerto Iguazu, 40 minutes after entering Argentina by land.
While Bolsonaro’s Brazilian passport and diplomatic passport had been cancelled, he also holds an Italian passport, which he used to board a private jet in Argentina, according to a flight document seen by AFP.
A Brazilian diplomatic source, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that Argentina’s diplomatic representative had been summoned for a “routine meeting” to “provide explanations” on Oct 29.
Brasilia recalled its ambassador and downgraded diplomatic ties with Buenos Aires in August after repeated insults from Milei, who called Lula “a thief” and “corrupt”.
Argentina’s Foreign Minister on Oct 30 denied that Brazil had asked Buenos Aires to explain its role in Bolsonaro’s flight.
“False. There was no request for information,” Pablo Quirno wrote on social media platform X.
Outliers in not accepting result
Bolsonaro thanked Milei and Trump in his first statement after fleeing the country.
Milei has not recognised Lula’s election victory and Trump said the poll was a “disgrace” and “very strange”.
However, Lula’s victory has been recognised by global leaders from across the political spectrum, Brazil’s electoral court, Bolsonaro’s own party – which holds a majority in Congress – and other right-wing allies.
In the United States, Democrat lawmakers wrote a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio to request “an immediate accounting” of his department’s role in helping Bolsonaro leave Brazil.
Luis Grande, head of the Baires Fly airline that carried Bolsonaro, told AFP on Oct 29 that he had been hired by a broker “who lives in the United States”.
Some US media, including The New York Times and the Wall Street Journal, have reported that the plane was chartered by Jason Miller, an adviser to Trump.
The White House has not commented on the matter.
‘Difficult times’
Bolsonaro, who is the son of former far-right leader Jair Bolsonaro, has found himself isolated and the object of ridicule at home, after his departure and proclamation that he would lead the opposition from abroad.
Speculation has switched almost immediately to who would lead the right with Flavio out of the country, and the future of the Bolsonaro movement.
Jair Bolsonaro, 71, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for plotting a coup against Lula after his 2022 election loss.
His wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was just elected senator, released a statement on Instagram on Oct 30 referring to Jair Bolsonaro as “our leader”.
“We are living through difficult times. We need to reflect and only then act,” she wrote.
“My husband stresses that this is a time for unity, not for looking for people to blame,” she said. AFP

Inside fraternities and why they are so important to US colleges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:15:56 UTC
11:15:56 KST

What are frats and why is one at the centre of rape allegations at Cornell University?
New York state police have announced they will take charge of future sexual assault investigations at Cornell University in the latest fallout over the university's handling of an alleged gang rape on campus.
It comes as the university's faculty undertook a vote of no confidence in the school's administration over how it handled the allegation, with the results expected on November 6.
The alleged Cornell University incident in 2024 is not isolated, with the Associated Press reporting police were investigating allegations of sexual assault at a fraternity party at the University of Chicago on October 11.
A female student at the University of Arizona alleged she was sexually assaulted by two men at a fraternity house on August 26, according to AP.
A few weeks later, on October 8, the University of Arizona suspended fraternity activity after reports of hazing and sexual misconduct.
According to the AP, previous hazing at the university's fraternities included forcing new members to consume large quantities of alcohol, as well as live goldfish.
Australian attitudes to fraternities, also known as frats, have been mostly shaped by popular culture, but what are fraternities really? And why are they so ingrained in higher education in the US?
What are fraternities?
Social fraternities or sororities are exclusive clubs for undergraduate students who can live together, socialise together and participate in traditions, usually in a same-sex environment.
Kimberly Davis, data analyst at Pennsylvania State University's Piazza Centre for Fraternity and Sorority Research, said fraternities were "often built around a shared identity" and members could maintain fraternity relationships "long after graduation".
"For some students, that level of connection is especially appealing during a period of life that can feel uncertain and transitional,"
Dr Davis said.
The first fraternity-like organisation was founded in 1776 at the College of William and Mary in Virginia, but they became much more popular across the US by the mid 1800s, according to Dr Davis.
Why are fraternities so important to US universities?
Dr Davis said on a practical level, fraternities provided additional residential options for university campuses.
She said fraternities were also "valuable partners" for universities to foster leadership development, student involvement in community activities, service and philanthropy.
"The friendships and communities that fraternities create also offer benefits for universities," she said.
"Alumni who have favourable fraternity experiences often associate their experiences with the university, which in turn encourages alumni to stay connected to the institution through alumni mentor ship and financial donations."
What are the problems with frats?
Loading...
According to a 2019 survey by the Association of American Universities, 10 per cent of undergraduate women who reported being raped said the incident occurred at a fraternity house, and 20 per cent of women reporting unwanted sexual touching said it occurred in a fraternity house.
6.4 per cent of men and 6.7 per cent of transgender, gender queer or questioning students who reported being raped said the incident occurred in a fraternity house, and just under 10 per cent of men and 12.6 per cent queer students reported unwanted sexual touching.
Dr Davis said fraternities did not contribute to a culture of sexual violence by design, but "that does not mean that fraternity environments cannot contribute to risk".
"Some organisational environments can normalise attitudes and behaviours that increase the risk of sexual violence," she said.
"A chapter that prioritises accountability, healthy relationships, and intervention can create a very different environment from one that normalises excessive alcohol use or tolerates harmful behaviour."
As well as sexual assault allegations, fraternities are also often associated with hazing.
The University of Colorado defines hazing as any activity that humiliates, degrades, abuses, or endangers someone, regardless of consent, as condition for entering an organisation.
The Pennsylvania State University Piazza Centre is named after student Timothy Piazza, who died as the result of a hazing incident at the university's Beta Theta Pi fraternity.
Mr Piazza was given at least 18 drinks in 82 minutes, according to prosecutors, and fell down the fraternity house stairs, becoming unconscious.
He later died from a head injury after a delayed response by bystanders.
"Timothy Piazza was one of four IFC fraternity men who died in hazing incidents in 2017 alone; that was an especially deadly year and the catalyst for many revised state hazing laws,"
Dr Davis said
Hazing prevention organisation HazingInfo's database indicates about five deaths per year have been reported in the US since 2000.
Do we have anything like them in Australia?
In Australia, the frat niche is filled by residential colleges, which provide accommodation, meals, academic support and social activities for residents.
Southern Cross University professor Elizabeth Mackinlay said instances of sexual harassment, assault and violence persisted at Australian residential colleges.
She said under-reporting continued at a concerning level, because students feared potential consequences for them and those responsible.
Professor Mackinlay said what Australian residential colleges and US fraternities had in common was hazing.
Hazing, abuse and misogyny have been reported at some residential colleges, including at Sydney University when, in 2018, allegations emerged of sexual assault, excessive alcohol consumption and other incidents.
In 2024, the City of Sydney council recommended the abolition of the University of Sydney's Residential Colleges after an incident at St Paul's College "where 6 students were expelled and a further 21 suspended after engaging in acts of 'serious humiliation' and sexual violence against a student".
Professor Mackinlay said the issues reported at Cornell University, the University of Arizona and St Paul's College she experienced herself during her time at university in the late 80s and 90s.
"The alcohol abuse, the degradation, rape, everything happened," she said.
"Nobody reported it. Leadership in the student group took part."
Professor Mackinlay said the culture of hazing and alcohol abuse had to change and "cultural norms around respectful relationships have to be in place and reinforced".
"If there's gender-based violence, there's a good chance that you're going to have to sit at the breakfast table in halls the next morning with the perpetrator there," she said.

French economy ‘headed straight for a wall’ – finance minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:15:05 UTC
11:15:05 KST

French economy ‘headed straight for a wall’ – finance minister
France is “headed straight for a wall” unless it reins in its budget deficit, Finance Minister Roland Lescure has warned, as the country’s economy contracts and inflation accelerates.
Gross domestic product fell by 0.1% in the third quarter, following stagnation in the previous three months and a 0.2% decline at the start of the year, the national statistics agency reported on Friday. Annual inflation climbed to 3.4% in October from 3.1% in September, its highest level since January 2024.
Lescure also described the economy as being “at a standstill,” underscoring the mounting financial challenges facing President Emmanuel Macron’s government.
The downturn extended across key sectors. Exports dropped 1.7%, largely due to weaker overseas aerospace sales, while investment fell 0.6%. Manufacturing output declined 1.4%, with automobile production shrinking for the fourth consecutive quarter.
France is also struggling with public debt equivalent to roughly 119% of GDP and a substantial budget deficit. Government borrowing costs climbed following Friday’s figures, with yields on ten-year bonds approaching 5%, raising concerns about the cost of servicing the country’s debt.
The deteriorating outlook has increased pressure on Macron, whose government is pursuing spending cuts while boosting military expenditure and weapons deliveries to Kiev. France increased its 2026 military budget by €6.7 billion ($7.5 billion) despite its mounting debt.
The government’s austerity policies have also fueled nationwide unrest that began in September with protests over staff shortages and deteriorating conditions at a high school near Paris. The demonstrations quickly spread, with thousands of students demanding more education funding and accusing the authorities of prioritizing weapons over schools.
The unrest escalated into violence, with rioters looting shops, setting vehicles ablaze and damaging the historic city hall in Limoges. Thousands were arrested and hundreds injured.
The protests have drawn comparisons with the 2018 Yellow Vest movement, which challenged Macron’s economic policies. Activists, students and trade unions have called for fresh demonstrations on Saturday, prompting authorities to mobilize 70,000 security personnel nationwide. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned of a “very high risk” of disorder.
Macron has blamed the purchasing-power crisis on the US-Israeli war against Iran, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and surging fuel prices. He has also accused social media platforms of “damaging democracy” by circulating footage of protests and riots.
With the 2027 presidential election approaching, the economic downturn and continuing unrest have further weakened Macron’s position, complicating efforts to secure parliamentary approval for a deficit-cutting budget.
