Flesh-eating Buruli ulcer cases are rising. Here's how to protect yourself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:13:29 UTC
11:13:29 KST

Flesh-eating Buruli ulcer cases are rising in Victoria and NSW. Here's how to protect yourself
It starts as a small, painless lump on the skin that is easy to ignore.
But under the seemingly innocuous lump, flesh-eating bacteria are burrowing through fat and muscle.
Warning: Readers are advised that this article includes an image of an open wound.
The skin over the lump then dies, turns black and eventually becomes an open sore that, if untreated, grows.
This is a typical case of Buruli ulcer, a condition that until recently was primarily found in West Africa.
Victoria is now considered the Buruli ulcer centre of the world, with a record 426 confirmed cases last year.
Buruli ulcer is typically acquired in summer and autumn.
It is endemic in the Mornington Peninsula, Bellarine Peninsula, Geelong and some Melbourne suburbs.
It is also found in other parts of Australia: pockets of coastal Queensland, where it is sometimes called Daintree ulcer, and around Darwin.
Most recently, cases have popped up on the New South Wales south coast around Batemans Bay.
Visitors to these popular tourism areas might unknowingly get infected, go home and, months later, develop a Buruli ulcer where local doctors may not be aware of the condition.
So, coming into summer holidays, how can you protect yourself from the disease?
What causes Buruli ulcer?
Buruli ulcer is caused by the microbe Mycobacterium ulcerans.
It can be transmitted to humans via mosquitoes, so ulcers usually appear in areas near bites, such as on arms and legs.
Loading...
Once in the skin, the bacteria secrete a cocktail of molecules that numb the area, slowly kill surrounding tissues and suppress the immune system.
"These things make it quite an impressive pathogen, and often, it's been there for a while before people actually know they've got it," Daniel O'Brien, an infectious diseases physician at Barwon Health in Geelong and Royal Melbourne Hospital, says.
The progression of lump to ulcer happens in about 90 per cent of Buruli ulcer cases he sees.
In less than 1 per cent of cases, the bacteria reach bone.
How is Buruli ulcer diagnosed and treated?
Buruli ulcer advances so slowly that the first symptoms usually are not noticed until five or six months after the infection.
It is diagnosed by sending a swab off for PCR testing to see whether the ulcer contains M. ulcerans bacteria.
Treatment starts with a six-to-eight-week course of antibiotics, but the drugs themselves can be problematic. They interact with many other medications and produce side effects so awful that about 20 per cent of patients cannot finish the whole course.
Dr O'Brien is leading a team trialling a new antibiotic that can be taken over just 10 days, which he says is less harsh on the body, yet still effective against M. ulcerans.
For most people, antibiotics will be enough, but if there is too much tissue damage or the wound is not healing properly, surgery is needed.
Even with treatment and good wound care, it can take months — even a year — for an ulcer to fully heal.
Dr O'Brien says outcomes for patients are generally better if the ulcer is diagnosed early.
For that reason, he recommends getting a health practitioner to look at any suspicious lumps sooner rather than later, especially if you live or holidayed in an area known to have the bacterium, and to specifically ask about Buruli ulcer.
How can I protect myself from Buruli ulcer?
While Buruli ulcer prevalence is rising, Dr O'Brien says it is important to remember that the disease is still uncommon in humans.
"If you protect yourself from the environment … you really minimise your risk of acquisition."
While mosquitoes are a main source of Buruli ulcers, they are not the only one.
Brushtail and ringtail possums are also known to get infected, and can develop nasty ulcers on their paws, face and tail.
A 2025 study found that analysing the poo of possums could help predict regions where Buruli ulcer might crop up next, with human cases usually appearing up to three years after the first positive possum poo test.
That is because possums shed the bacteria in droppings, introducing it to the soil, which can then get into cuts in our skin.
Dr O'Brien's advice is to:
- cover up as much as possible
- wear mosquito repellent on exposed skin
- cover any wounds while handling soil, and if you injure yourself, wash it immediately with soap and water, then apply antiseptic
- avoid handling sick or injured possums
A recent study found reducing mosquito numbers in Buruli ulcer areas also lowered human case numbers, so it is a good idea to tip out standing water where mosquitoes breed and put out mosquito traps.
It is also important to note that research shows not all possums in Buruli-endemic areas carry the bacteria, and it is illegal to trap, relocate or cull possums without a licence.
And, in good news for ringtails and bushies, an edible possum vaccine in the works could help reduce infections and ulcers in the future.
Hear more about Buruli ulcer on Outbreaks, a special series on Science Friction.

Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:09:38 UTC
11:09:38 KST

Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- Brookhaven National Laboratory
- Summary:
- Scientists have recreated a primordial state of matter from the dawn of the universe by colliding oxygen nuclei at nearly the speed of light. The surprising results show that this exotic substance can form in smaller, lower-energy collisions than previously demonstrated, challenging the known boundaries of early-universe physics.
- Share:
New findings from the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) suggest that scientists can recreate an extraordinary form of matter from the earliest moments of the universe using surprisingly small atomic collisions. By smashing oxygen nuclei together at nearly the speed of light, researchers have uncovered strong evidence of quark-gluon plasma (QGP), an extremely hot and dense state of matter that existed shortly after the Big Bang.
The findings, published in Physical Review Letters, reveal that high-energy streams of particles lose energy as they travel through the material created by these collisions. This effect, called jet quenching, provides an important clue that quark-gluon plasma has formed.
Scientists have previously observed jet quenching in collisions involving much larger atomic nuclei at RHIC, a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Science User Facility that operated at Brookhaven National Laboratory from 2000 until 2026. The same effect has also been detected in oxygen collisions at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the European Particle Physics Laboratory.
What makes the new RHIC findings especially significant is that the oxygen collisions occurred at substantially lower energies. The results establish a new lower boundary for the conditions known to produce quark-gluon plasma in this small collision system, helping scientists narrow down what it takes to create matter resembling that of the infant universe.
"The QGP is believed to be the form of matter that filled the early universe -- before the protons and neutrons that make up today's atoms formed. Understanding its properties is essential for uncovering how the early universe evolved in its first microseconds," said Li Yi, a professor of physics at Shandong University who oversaw the STAR analysis.
"One of the most powerful ways scientists study the QGP is by identifying where its signatures appear -- and just as importantly, where these signatures turn off," she said.
Rongrong Ma, a STAR physicist at Brookhaven Lab, explained why investigating smaller collisions is so valuable.
"This analysis is pushing the boundaries to an extreme case to help us learn something about this jet quenching phenomenon and the conditions needed to generate a QGP."
How Scientists Recreate Matter From the Early Universe
RHIC was designed specifically to produce and investigate quark-gluon plasma. Traditionally, researchers have accomplished this by accelerating gold nuclei to enormous speeds and crashing them into one another.
Each gold nucleus contains 79 protons and 118 neutrons. When two such nuclei collide with sufficient energy, the boundaries of their protons and neutrons effectively break down, releasing the quarks and gluons inside them. The tremendous energy of the impact also generates thousands of additional quarks and gluons through the conversion of energy into matter, as described by Einstein's famous equation, E=mc2.
The result is a fleeting droplet of primordial matter. It is smaller than an atomic nucleus and survives for less than a billionth of a billionth of a second. Almost immediately, the quarks and gluons recombine into more familiar particles.
Because this exotic substance disappears so quickly, scientists cannot examine it directly. Instead, they use enormous instruments such as the STAR detector to analyze the particles that emerge from the collision.
One particularly revealing clue comes from particles that escape with less energy than expected. Their reduced energy suggests they interacted with the dense mixture of quarks and gluons before escaping.
Researchers pay special attention to jets, which are narrow sprays of extremely energetic particles. These often originate when a quark or gluon from one nucleus strikes a quark or gluon from another, sending two particle jets traveling in opposite directions.
If these paired jets, known as "di-jets," form near the edge of the collision region, one may have to travel farther through the plasma than the other. Comparing their behavior allows scientists to investigate how the surrounding material drains energy from particles passing through it.
Yi offered a familiar comparison to explain the process.
"You can think of it like shooting a bullet through, say, water," Yi said. "Because of the resistance, the bullet will slow down. It's the same thing with these high-energy particles. When they go through the QGP, they will lose energy."
The Telltale Signs of Quark-Gluon Plasma
For decades, RHIC experiments have provided clear evidence of jet quenching in collisions between gold nuclei. The effect is especially noticeable in jets that travel longer distances through the newly created matter.
Scientists believe these particles lose more energy because they encounter more quarks and gluons before escaping. Jets originating closer to the outer boundary generally pass through less material and experience fewer interactions.
These measurements helped establish that RHIC was successfully producing quark-gluon plasma. Additional evidence came from several other experiments, including an unexpected discovery about how the resulting matter behaves.
Scientists observed that relatively low-energy particles emerging from gold collisions moved collectively, following coordinated patterns. This behavior indicated that the plasma flowed almost like a perfect liquid, with extraordinarily little viscosity or internal resistance.
The discovery was a major surprise when researchers first identified it. Collective flow has since become another important "smoking gun" signature of quark-gluon plasma.
Can Tiny Atomic Collisions Create Primordial Matter?
After establishing these signatures in collisions involving large nuclei, physicists began finding similar collective motion in much smaller systems.
Experiments at the LHC, followed by studies at RHIC, detected collective flow when tiny projectiles such as protons, deuterons, and helium-3 nuclei struck much larger gold or lead nuclei. Researchers at the LHC even observed comparable flow patterns in collisions between individual protons.
These results raised a major question. Did the coordinated particle motion mean that these much smaller collisions were also producing quark-gluon plasma, or could another mechanism explain the observations?
Scientists needed a more definitive sign.
"The next natural question is: Can you see jet quenching, the other key signature that QGP is formed, in these very small collision systems?" asked Brookhaven's Ma. "We haven't seen any unambiguous signal, so it's still kind of under debate in these small systems. We want to search for the smallest system where we can still see an unambiguous jet-quenching signal," he said.
To investigate, researchers turned to collisions between oxygen nuclei.
An oxygen nucleus contains just eight protons and eight neutrons, making it far smaller than the gold nuclei typically used in RHIC experiments. Oxygen nuclei also have a relatively symmetrical, spherical shape, which makes the geometry of their collisions easier to analyze.
"That means we can more easily look for signs of asymmetric quenching of di-jets produced close to the edge of the circular interaction region in head-on collisions," said Maowu Nie, an associate professor at Shandong University who contributed to the research.
The scientists could also examine how the outcome changed depending on whether the oxygen nuclei collided directly or merely grazed one another.
"We can also compare how jets behave in head-on central collisions -- those that produce the most particles and therefore have the highest likelihood of making a QGP -- with collisions where the two oxygen nuclei barely strike each other, which aren't expected to generate a QGP."
Nie explained that these grazing collisions are recognizable because they generate far fewer particles than direct impacts.
Oxygen Collisions Reveal a 20% Suppression
To search for jet quenching, the researchers developed an analysis that identifies concentrated streams of high-energy particles and measures how many emerge above a selected energy threshold.
"Our measurements are essentially counting experiments," said Sijie Zhang, who conducted the research for her master's thesis under Yi and Nie at Shandong University and is now pursuing a Ph.D. at Yale University.
"We have an algorithm that finds the collimated groups of high-energy particles, the jets, and we count how many of these particles above a certain energy threshold come out."
Yang He, a former Ph.D. student at Shandong University who developed the analysis framework and now studies oxygen collisions at the LHC, described how the team used different collision types to identify energy loss.
"We compare what we see in back-to-back jets produced near the edge of the system, and we compare what we see in head-on collisions with the counts in non-central collisions where we don't expect to see quenching."
The team analyzed STAR measurements from oxygen collisions conducted at RHIC in 2021, at a collision energy of 200 billion electron volts (GeV).
The results revealed a 20% suppression of high-energy particles associated with jet quenching.
Although this suppression was smaller than what physicists typically measure in gold collisions, that difference was expected because oxygen collisions generate much smaller systems.
Crucially, the observed effect was still strong enough to provide clear evidence that quark-gluon plasma had formed.
Comparing Big Bang Matter at Different Energies
Oxygen offers scientists another important advantage. Apart from proton-proton collisions, it is the only nuclear species that has been investigated in collisions at both RHIC and the LHC.
That gives researchers an unusual opportunity to make an "apples-to-apples" comparison between two facilities operating at very different collision energies.
The LHC carried out its first oxygen collisions in 2025. According to results reported by CERN, those experiments revealed both collective flow and jet quenching, providing additional indications that quark-gluon plasma can form in relatively small nuclear collisions.
However, the LHC operated at collision energies exceeding 5,000 GeV, far above the 200 GeV used in the RHIC measurements.
"With a higher energy collision, it's more likely to create more and more quarks and gluons and a hotter, denser QGP system," Yi said. "That means the jet quenching signal, if it's there, should be bigger at LHC compared to RHIC."
While higher energies make it easier to create the hot, dense conditions needed for quark-gluon plasma, lower-energy experiments may be more useful for determining precisely when those conditions are no longer sufficient.
By reducing the collision energy and using smaller nuclei, physicists can approach the threshold at which the distinctive signatures of primordial matter disappear.
"We are pushing the boundaries in two ways to explore the minimal conditions for creating a QGP, both in terms of the nucleus size by looking at these small oxygen-oxygen collisions, but also by looking at data from lower collision energies -- and we still see this crucial QGP signature. That's a unique feature of our measurement," Ma said.
New Experiments Could Reveal the Limits of Primordial Matter
Although RHIC has now completed its operations, scientists still have additional oxygen collision data to investigate.
During the collider's final experimental run, researchers collected measurements using both STAR and sPHENIX, RHIC's newest detector. The facility concluded its operations with oxygen collisions recorded by both instruments on February 6, 2026.
These remaining datasets could provide further insights into how small a collision system can become, and how low its energy can fall, before quark-gluon plasma can no longer form.
Understanding those limits may help physicists piece together the behavior of matter during the first microseconds of the universe, when quarks and gluons had not yet combined into the protons and neutrons that make up ordinary atoms today.
The research received financial support from the DOE Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), and additional international agencies and organizations identified in the scientific publication.
The researchers also used the Open Science Grid, which receives direct support from NSF, along with computing resources at Brookhaven Lab's Scientific Data and Computing Facilities and the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC), a DOE Office of Science User Facility located at DOE's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

'Dedication and ingenuity of our space scientists': PM Modi hails ISRO after successful GSLV-F18 launch carrying NVS-03
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
02:04:02 UTC
11:04:02 KST

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday congratulated Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) scientists and engineers following the successful launch of the GSLV-F18 mission carrying the NVS-03 navigation satellite, saying the mission would strengthen India's indigenous satellite navigation system, NavIC.In a post on X, PM Modi said, "Congratulations to our scientists and engineers at ISRO on the successful launch of GSLV-F18 carrying NVS-03.
Also read: Success launch of navigation sat NVS-03 with desi atomic clock will make NaVIC up & running, and give military strategic independenceThis mission marks an important step in strengthening NavIC, our indigenous satellite navigation system. Equipped with enhanced capabilities, NVS-03 will further our pursuit of self-reliance in critical technologies and support navigation services that benefit our people.The dedication and ingenuity of our space scientists continue to make our nation proud."
The successful launch is expected to strengthen India's strategic autonomy by helping restore the operational capabilities of NavIC, India's indigenous alternative to global navigation systems such as the US-operated GPS and Russia's GLONASS.The NVS-03 satellite carries an indigenously developed atomic clock, alongside imported atomic clocks, marking an important step towards reducing India's dependence on foreign technologies for satellite-based navigation.
Atomic clocks provide highly precise time signals that are essential for determining location, navigation and timing.NavIC, which was originally designed around a seven-satellite constellation, had been operating with only three active satellites, below the minimum requirement of four satellites for standalone positioning services. This had limited its use for critical applications, including military navigation, precision positioning and coordination of naval assets.An operational NavIC constellation is particularly important for India's armed forces, which require reliable Position, Navigation and Timing (PNT) signals for missile guidance, precision-guided weapons, troop movement, combat aircraft and naval operations.Dependence on foreign navigation networks can pose strategic vulnerabilities during conflicts, as access to such services could potentially be restricted or disrupted. India experienced the limitations of relying on foreign satellite navigation systems during the 1999 Kargil war.With NVS-03, India aims to strengthen the availability of indigenous navigation services for both civilian and strategic applications. NavIC is designed to provide coverage across India and up to 1,500 km beyond its geographical boundaries.
The original NavIC constellation comprised seven satellites supported by a network of ground stations operating round the clock. Three satellites were placed in geostationary orbit, while four were placed in inclined geosynchronous orbits.However, the constellation's operational strength declined over time as ageing satellites could not be replaced as planned. The launch of NVS-02 on January 29, 2025, also failed to deliver the intended results after a pyro valve signal loss in the engine prevented the satellite from reaching its designated orbit.The successful deployment of NVS-03 is expected to address some of these operational limitations and strengthen India's efforts to establish an independent satellite navigation capability.
Ayush Pandey is a journalist at The Times of India, covering breaking news, politics, defence, and major legal and policy developments across India and the world. His reporting focuses on elections, national security, and institutional affairs, tracking the decisions and conflicts that shape public life. He specialises in sharp explainers and in-depth feature stories that go beyond headlines to decode political shifts, defence strategy, geopolitical flashpoints, and changing public sentiment. His work combines speed, clarity, and depth for a fast-moving digital audience.

Is it legal to recruit spoiler candidates in US elections?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:46:00 UTC
10:46:00 KST

Is it legal to recruit spoiler candidates in US elections?
- The Justice Department is investigating claims that Democrats recruited spoiler candidates in Alaska’s Senate race. The case could affect certification if Republican Senator Daniel S. Sullivan loses narrowly.
- Legal experts say the DOJ faces a weak case because election rules are mainly set by states. A judge may rule soon on whether the lawsuit should be dismissed.
- Possible charges include conspiracy against rights, fraud, dishonesty, civil rights breaches and perjury. Experts say many “dirty tricks” are legal, but tricking voters may be different.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The Justice Department is investigating allegations that Democrats recruited potential spoiler candidates to run in Alaska’s US Senate race, and has asked a US judge to prevent certification of the vote if incumbent Republican Senator Daniel S. Sullivan loses narrowly.
The race, in which Democratic former US representative Mary Peltola is challenging Sullivan, could prove critical for determining the balance of power in the Senate in the Nov 3 midterm elections.
President Donald Trump’s fellow Republicans are battling to maintain majorities in both chambers.
Here is an explanation of the legal issues at play and why the Justice Department will face challenges in its civil lawsuit or any criminal case.
What is the state of the Alaska race?
Alaska’s ranked-choice ballot will feature Sullivan, Peltola, a retired teacher whose name is also Daniel Sullivan, and another long-shot candidate.
Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that Peltola’s aides worked with the campaign’s lawyers and senior staff at Senate Democrats’ campaign arm to recruit the retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan.
Reuters has not verified the report.
Trump has called for Peltola to be prosecuted, and Alaska’s Republican governor Mike Dunleavy has ordered a state law enforcement investigation.
Neither Trump nor Dunleavy specified which laws they believed may have been violated.
A Justice Department official said no charging decision had been made.
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has denied involvement and said Republicans had also propped up other candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns.
Daniel J. Sullivan has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.
Peltola’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
Its lawyers have asked US District Judge Sharon Gleason to dismiss the Justice Department’s lawsuit, arguing the federal government lacks the legal authority to bring the case.
Alaska’s ballot will indicate that Daniel S. Sullivan is the incumbent.
Could the Times report affect the outcome of the DOJ lawsuit?
The Justice Department case seeking to prevent certification of election results if the incumbent Daniel S. Sullivan loses by a slim margin is pending.
The department plans to seek a preliminary injunction, Michael Heyman, the top federal prosecutor in Alaska, told reporters on Oct 30.
Alaska’s elections regulator earlier in 2026 blocked Daniel J. Sullivan from appearing on the ballot, finding that his candidacy was not filed in good faith and was instead an attempt to “confuse or mislead.”
State courts later restored him to the ballot, ruling that there was not enough evidence that he was trying to confuse voters and that there was no requirement under Alaska law that a candidacy be in good faith.
Legal experts have said the Justice Department’s case is weak because the US Constitution clearly assigns the responsibility for administering elections to the states, not the federal government.
Joshua Douglas, a law professor at the University of Kentucky, said the reporting asserting that Democrats helped recruit spoiler candidates was unlikely to help the Justice Department’s case.
“Regardless of who encouraged him to run, the second Dan Sullivan validly qualified for the ballot. And this is a matter of state law,” Douglas said.
Gleason’s decision on Peltola’s motion to dismiss the Justice Department’s lawsuit could come as soon as Oct 31, though it is not certain when she will rule.
What criminal laws could be at play?
Legal experts said the Justice Department could seek to bring a criminal case under a federal statute that makes it illegal for any two people to conspire to deprive anyone of their constitutional rights, including the right to vote.
The law, originally passed in 1871 to combat the Ku Klux Klan, makes it illegal to conspire to “injure, oppress, threaten, or intimidate any person” to prevent them from exercising a right.
In addition, if anyone lied under oath in earlier state-level litigation over whether Dan J. Sullivan could appear on the ballot, they could be prosecuted for perjury, UCLA law professor Rick Hasen wrote in an Oct 8 blog post.
A Justice Department official said the conduct under investigation could implicate statutes prohibiting fraud, dishonesty, and deprivations of civil rights.
Would any prosecution be viable?
Hasen said any federal criminal prosecution under the conspiracy-against-rights statute would likely fail because the free speech guarantees in the First Amendment to the US Constitution would likely protect the right to run for office with “impure motives.”
Michael Fragoso, a former lawyer for Republican Senator Mitch McConnell, said “dirty tricks” – such as one major party trying to help a fringe candidate win over voters from the other major party – were generally legal.
But he said convincing voters they were voting for their preferred candidate when they were not was different.
“It’s suppressing disfavoured votes by tricking voters into thinking that they’re voting one way when in fact, they aren’t,” Fragoso, now a fellow at the Washington-based think tank Ethics and Public Policy Centre, wrote in an Oct 28 blog post in the National Review.
Is there any legal precedent?
In a case brought by the Justice Department under Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration, a social media influencer was convicted in 2023 in Brooklyn federal court of conspiring against civil rights by using social media posts to spread false information about the 2016 election to help Trump win.
The Manhattan-based 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals in 2025 overturned that conviction, finding a lack of evidence he conspired with anyone.
The appeals court’s decision did not address the influencer’s argument that the First Amendment would protect speech deceiving voters. REUTERS

AI giants promise publishers new way to block some scraping

AI giants promise publishers new way to block some scraping
- OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic will offer one standard way for publishers to block content scraping for AI training.
- The change comes after complaints and court cases, including The New York Times' 2023 lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft over unauthorised use of articles.
- The tool will roll out slowly, and it only stops future AI training, not crawling by default; opt-outs may also reduce content visibility in AI apps.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO, California – OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic pledged on Oct 30 to give media outlets and other websites a single way to prevent their content from being scraped to train artificial intelligence models, amid growing criticisms and legal battles from news publishers.
Publishers currently have to implement multiple blocking commands for every bot that crawls the web to collect data, but the new proposed solution will allow them to enter a single, standardised instruction that is recognised and honoured by any AI company that adopts the protocol.
The solution will not fully take effect for months, though.
Microsoft will implement it beginning Feb 1, 2027, and Google sometime in 2027.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it will roll it out “in the coming months”, while Claude-maker Anthropic said it has “already started” rolling it out.
The announcement comes as publishers are facing a surge in bots that scrape their articles to feed AI models. Some, like the New York Times, have taken the matter to court.
In December 2023, the Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft for allegedly using millions of its articles without authorisation or payment to train ChatGPT.
The two tech companies are invoking an exception to copyright law known as fair use.
Meanwhile, internet infrastructure provider Cloudflare has blocked AI bots by default on new customer sites since July 2025, and a standard called Really Simple Licensing already allows publishers to charge bots that visit their pages.
The new setting will apply only to future training of models but does not prevent bots from crawling otherwise, and content scraping will be allowed by default until the setting is changed by a publisher, Microsoft said in a blog post.
Opting out of AI training could reduce the chances that a publisher’s content will surface in AI apps and experiences, Microsoft and Google said in separate blog posts.
“We believe creating a common signal that conveys such preferences to multiple providers at once is an important step. And we look forward to working with other AI companies on the standards and their implementation across the industry,” Meta spokesman Andy Stone wrote on X, conveying his support for the effort. AFP

====================================================================================================

War Is Hell—And The Mosquito Bowl Won’t Let Us Forget It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:33:07 UTC
10:33:07 KST

When you’re a kid, young men going off to war look like men. When you’re a grown-up, you see that they’re really just boys. If The Mosquito Bowl gets close to any essential truth, it’s that one. This is director Peter Berg’s retelling of a true story involving young football stars who went off to fight in the Pacific during World War II, focusing on four real-life figures: Dave Schreiner and Bob Bauman (played by Tom Francis and Bill Skarsgård) were teammates and close friends playing for the University of Wisconsin; Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson, son of Jack) was a fullback for Purdue; and John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine) had graduated from Brown University and been drafted into the NFL by the time the war had started. As Berg presents it, all four of these men went off believing they could win the war the same way you win a football game, with strategy and athleticism, only to learn how far off the mark they were. The film’s title refers to a legendary football game between two Marine regiments at Guadalcanal, on Christmas Eve, 1944. A few months later, three of the four would be dead in Okinawa: Of the 65 men who played in the Mosquito Bowl, 15 were killed on the island.
There’s a lot of drama inherent in that premise, and Berg—director of films like Hancock, The Kingdom, and Friday Night Lights, progenitor of the hit TV series—takes perhaps too much time drawing it out. He introduces the main characters with moderate efficiency: Schreiner is a solid, rather quiet guy who’s given to overthinking everything; as the film opens, his team has just lost to Purdue, and he’s still simmering with resentment toward Butkovich, who appears to be something of a hothead. Bauman is the solid Wisconsin country lad, giving his younger brother instructions on holding the family homestead together. And McLaughry is intelligent and grounded, if somewhat undersketched, though he does anchor the movie’s opening scene, which gives us some sense of what these young men left behind when they went to war, things they could never get back.
After some characteristically dehumanizing basic training, the men are hauled off to Tarawa. (In real life, the four weren’t in the same regiment, though it’s a forgivable dramatic tweak.) This occasions the movie’s first protracted battle sequence, in which these newly minted Marines get a swift education in what war is about. Legs are blown off. Pinwheeling men, having been set ablaze with flamethrowers, scream in agony. Blood burbles through gaping wounds. After we, and they, have made it through this ordeal, there’s a great deal of talking among the men about the grim circumstances they’ve found themselves in. Then there’s some football—the actual Mosquito Bowl—where they get to have some fun. This is the most exhilarating section of the film. It also feels like the shortest.
Because the deadly battle at Okinawa is yet to come, and Berg will spare us no bloody detail. (The script was adapted from the 2022 book of the same name by Buzz Bissinger, who also wrote the book that the 2004 film Friday Night Lights was based on.) More limbs are blasted off, more bullets end lives instantly or with agonizing slowness, more bayonets pierce tender flesh. War is hell, and Berg doesn’t want us to forget it.
In my early film-reviewing days, even before the existence of comments sections, I would sometimes get emails from veterans telling me what I had gotten wrong in writing about this or that war film. Most of those letters had a “Listen here, little lady” tone, but I didn’t mind them. The experience of watching a war movie is hardly the same as being in combat; it’s not supposed to be. Still, these guys had been to places I hadn’t. Even if they clearly didn’t understand my job, I’d have to admit to knowing next to nothing about theirs.
But from watching lots of war films—from the time I was a kid, when my World War II veteran dad would bring me along to see movies like the 1976 Midway, because no one else would go with him—I do know that when it comes to depicting the brutality of war, less is more. You can dramatize, or allude to, some truly horrific stuff—but choose your details wisely. One well-placed depiction of a combat atrocity can be enough to haunt a viewer forever. With The Mosquito Bowl, Berg throws so much violence at us that it comes to feel like padding, while the depiction of the Mosquito Bowl itself, the core of the movie, is pure joy. War doesn’t make a boy a man so much as it knocks the boyhood out of him, fast—which may be why it’s both freeing and poignant to watch these young men escaping, if only briefly, into versions of themselves that no longer exist.

AI generated
WASHINGTON - A US federal judge on Oct 30 pushed back on government assertions that President Donald Trump’s planned massive arch in Washington is needed for national security.
Trump did not mention national security concerns when first announcing plans to build the 76m triumphal white arch, which is modelled after the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.
He said later, however, in a Truth Social post, that it would include a “top grade military complex” that could house drones and snipers.
District Judge Tanya Chutkan noted that the Republican president had also invoked national security in presenting the case for building a White House ballroom to the Supreme Court.
“It doesn’t make the use of national security talismanic in this case,” Chutkan said. “This is the first time the government has proffered a national security aspect to this case.”
Robert Stander, a Justice Department lawyer, said the arch is a “high priority project” for the administration.
The lawsuit being heard by Chutkan was brought by a group of Vietnam War veterans seeking to stop construction of the arch, which could begin as early as next week.
Wendy Liu, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said that given its massive size, the arch would obscure the sight lines between the Lincoln Memorial, one of Washington’s iconic landmarks, and Arlington National Cemetery, the final resting place for hundreds of thousands of American service members.
The arch is one of a number of projects launched by Trump in a bid to put his personal stamp on the capital.
They include the ballroom that is being built at the White House, for which Trump had an entire wing of the presidential mansion demolished.
Another is the laborious renovation of the Reflecting Pool, a massive rectangular water basin on the National Mall.
Trump has also proposed revamping the East Potomac Golf Links, a historic waterfront Washington golf course.
That project is the focus of a bitter legal battle: the judge presiding over the case launched an investigation on Oct 30 into whether lawyers for the Trump administration had lied to the court.
For a time, Trump also had his name placed on the walls of the Kennedy Centre, the culture and arts institute named after assassinated president John F. Kennedy, before a judge reversed the move.
Chutkan did not make an immediate ruling in the arch case but said she would do so “expeditiously.” AFP

Feature: Blind football team from Xinjiang makes mark on China's national stage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
09:27:52 CST
10:27:52 KST

URUMQI, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- At 19, Bilali Yasen has emerged as one of the most promising players in Xinjiang's first blind football team, having gone from years of isolation after losing his sight as a child to becoming a potential candidate for China's national team.
Bilali, who lost his sight aged seven, recently returned to his hometown of Shache County in Kashgar, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, to recover from a recurring foot injury following a training camp in Guangdong Province.
Before losing his sight, Bilali had enjoyed playing football with friends in his village. But afterward, he withdrew from the outside world, afraid to leave his home.
"I always felt that I would spend the rest of my life in darkness," he recalled.
His fortunes changed when he discovered blind football, a sport that has since taken him and his teammates from the edge of the Taklamakan Desert to national competitions across China.
In March, Bilali was identified as a potential candidate for the national team, becoming the first player from Xinjiang's blind football squad to receive such recognition.
Hundreds of kilometers away, at Xinjiang Special Education Vocational Secondary School in Changji Hui Autonomous Prefecture, his teammates continue their training, calling out "wei, wei, wei" to communicate as they move across the pitch.
The team's origins date to 2021, when Su Yiyan, then a senior executive at a Shanghai film and television company, visited Shache County Special Education School to recruit young actors for a film about blind football.
"For the first time, I learned that even blind people can play football," said Abdumijiti Maimaiti, 19, one of Bilali's teammates.
Under the guidance of a coach from Shanghai, the students began learning the fundamentals of the sport, which uses a ball fitted with bells to help players track its movement.
For Bilali, football provided an opportunity to regain the confidence he had lost after becoming blind.
The original film project was suspended shortly after production began, threatening to bring the team's activities to an end.
Su, however, decided to continue supporting the players.
"You don't give people something, then take it back," she said.
She subsequently resigned from her position and, working with filmmakers Li Zhiwei and Liu Xiaoran, who had been involved in short films for the Beijing 2022 Winter Olympics, began financing a documentary about the team.
With support from a physical education teacher at Shache County Special Education School, the players continued training while Su worked to keep the project alive.
The team faced another setback as its members approached graduation because their school did not offer upper secondary education.
The Xinjiang Disabled Persons' Federation intervened, helping establish the region's first blind football team in August 2024.
The following month, the players transferred to Xinjiang Special Education Vocational Secondary School, where they began studying traditional Chinese medicine rehabilitation while continuing their football training.
Their progress in national competition has been rapid.
The team made its national debut at the 2024 National Blind Football Championship in Fuzhou, finishing ninth.
At the 2025 National Games for Persons with Disabilities and National Special Olympics in Guangzhou, the players recorded their first victory in national competition by defeating Henan, eventually finishing seventh.
They improved further at the 2026 National Blind Football Championship in Korla, beating Shanghai 3-2 in a penalty shootout to reach the semifinals.
With an average age of 18, the squad is the youngest blind football team in China.
Its development has been supported by donations, educational opportunities and assistance from organizations and individuals across the country.
Su has raised more than 1 million yuan (140,000 U.S. dollars) to finance the documentary, titled "Wei Wei Wei, Football Team," while remaining closely involved with the players.
Years of training, travel and competition have made her an important figure in their lives.
"Without her, this blind football team as we know it today would never have existed," one player said.
The Xinjiang Disabled Persons' Federation has also played a central role in ensuring that the players can continue their education alongside their sporting development.
"Xinjiang Special Education Vocational Secondary School had never enrolled fully blind students before; we made an exception for this team," said Chen Jin, vice chairman of the federation.
Wang Jingrong, secretary-general of the Xinjiang Disabled Persons' Welfare Foundation, said businesses and organizations had provided equipment, clothing, financial assistance and training facilities.
A Chinese mobile phone manufacturer donated more than 100 accessible phones, while a local biotechnology company supplied clothing, footwear and nutritional supplements.
The Xinjiang branch of a centrally administered state-owned enterprise contributed tens of thousands of yuan, and a sports venue in Guangzhou provided accommodation and training facilities at a reduced cost during a monthlong training camp.
The team's story has also begun reaching audiences beyond the football pitch.
In July 2026, "Wei Wei Wei, Football Team" began limited preview screenings across China, documenting the players' journey from a special education school near the Taklamakan Desert to national-level competition.
For Bilali and his teammates, the ambition now extends beyond their own achievements.
"We cannot see the world with our eyes, but we are determined to make the world see us," the players said. ■

One of the leading international challengers for the Melbourne Cup, Defiantly, has been ruled out of the race after failing a vet's inspection on Saturday.
The Joseph O'Brien-trained horse, which had been a long-time favourite for the race, had won the Group Two Prix Kergorlay race over 3,000m at Deauville in France.
Defiantly was in quarantine at Werribee after arriving in Australia, and had failed an initial inspection on Thursday.
The horse was re-examined on Saturday morning.
"In the opinion of the veterinarians, Defiantly remains unsuitable to accept for the Melbourne Cup and has been withdrawn from the race by order of the stewards acting on veterinary advice," Racing Victoria said in a statement.
Defiantly's absence makes it likely that another Joseph O'Brien-trained horse, Kizlyar, will take its place in the field.
Two other international chances in the race, Enfjaar and Wine Dark Sea, had also failed initial assessments, but they passed inspection on Saturday and are approved to accept their spots in Tuesday's race.
Defiantly is the second international ruled out of this year's Melbourne Cup. Japanese entry Stinger Glass was ruled out after CT and PET scans showed the horse was at heightened risk of injury.
The Ciaron Maher-trained Saint George, who was runner-up in the Caulfield Cup a fortnight ago, before coming fifth in the Cox Plate last weekend, was also removed from the race after CT scans showed he was at heightened risk of injury.
The scans and vet inspections are part of veterinary protocols to ensure each horse is suitable to accept a place in the final field.
The field will be finalised at 4:30pm AEDT, followed by the Melbourne Cup draw an hour later.

Family of real estate CEO wounded in violent Toronto home invasion, officials say; 3 suspects at large

Once inside, police said they went to the second floor of the home and confronted 75-year-old David Morton; his wife, 64-year-old Doriana Morton; and their two adult daughters, Maggie and Cristina.
"There was a demand made for valuables from within the home," Toronto Police Service Inspector Kristy Smith told reporters. "Whether or not they escaped with anything is uncertain at this point."

Police said David Morton, CEO of the MAC Group, and his daughters, ages 28 and 26, tried to fight off the intruders when shots were fired.

David Morton said that he and his two daughters were still hospitalized Friday with gunshot wounds, but he did not provide details on their conditions.
"What should have been the safety and security of our own home became a terrifying and life-threatening experience," David Morton said in his statement. "... It is difficult to put into words the trauma of experiencing something so horrific in the one place where everyone should feel safest: their own home."
The three male suspects, all believed to be in their 20s and wearing dark clothing, fled the scene in an SUV, police said. On Saturday, Smith said one of the suspects they are looking for is 23-year-old Dejon Richards.
Richards is believed to have been accidentally shot in the shoulder by one of his accomplices during the incident, according to Smith. Richards went to the hospital, where he was interviewed by police, but they could not establish a connection to the incident and he was later discharged.
"All these houses have good security," Cecil Hawkins, a former resident of Bridle Path, said. "So I'm kind of surprised. Shooting people in the house, it just seems mind-boggling."

Australia's basket is about to be reweighted. Here's why it matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:08:18 UTC
10:08:18 KST

in brief
- The latest CPI data shows inflation accelerating, with transport, housing and food among key drivers.
- The ABS is about to reweight the CPI basket of goods to produce a better measure of inflation.
Last week, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) reported an unexpected spike in inflation in September, prompting fears of more interest rate hikes.
According to the ABS Consumer Price Index (CPI), Australia's annual inflation rate sits at 4.3 per cent — up from 4 per cent in August.
Amongst the largest contributors to rising inflation were housing, which rose 5.2 per cent; alcohol and tobacco, which rose 4.3 per cent and health, which rose 3.7 per cent.
The ABS will be reweighting the CPI basket of goods in January to better reflect current spending trends and produce a more accurate CPI, a crucial exercise as Australians adjust their spending amid continued rising costs.
According to retail expert at the University of Sydney Business School, Lisa Asher, a reweighting exercise is undertaken to "adequately reflect" what people are "actually spending" their money on.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
While a change usually occurs at the end of each year, the ABS had postponed the 2026 change to January. The last reweight was in late 2025.
"Some of the key changes or movements that we saw last year and this year focus much more on the increase in food and non-alcoholic beverages, as a larger percentage, as well as health costs and transport," Asher said.
While the ABS does not flag early what the new weightings may look like, previous changes offer some clues.
In 2025, the biggest weighting increases were in education, health and food and non-alcoholic beverages and the larger weight decreases were in furnishings, household equipment and services, alcohol and tobacco and housing.
What is the CPI and how is calculated?
The CPI is "really a measure of inflation" or "price changes in the economy" and it is based on a representative basket of goods and services for Australian households, head of price statistics at the ABS, Rachael McCririck, said.
The CPI provides a "sense of the underlying price pressures in the economy" but isn't a good measure for how the cost of living crisis is impacting individual households.
"The CPI is really an aggregate measure that informs policymakers and decision-makers about aggregate trends, it informs things like monetary and fiscal policy settings," she said.
"When we talk about the cost of living, we're really talking about an individual household and what pressures they're facing in their day-to-day lives — so to get a sense of that you have to look at the individual consumption basket."
To calculate the CPI, the ABS collects prices for items grouped into 87 categories and 11 groups. Every month, the ABS calculates the price changes of each item from the previous month and aggregates them to work out the inflation rate for the basket.
Prices are collected from a variety of retailers across the eight capital cities and the ABS uses methods like web-scraping and online and telephone interviews with retailers.
A knitter and an EV owner, McCririck said her basket would differ from the "average household's basket".
"But the weights that we give to the basket for the CPI are based on the average household experience," she said.
How are CPI items and weights chosen?
In deciding which goods and services to include in the CPI basket and what their weights should be, the ABS uses data about how much – and on what – households in Australia spend their income.
If households spend more of their income on one item, that item will have a larger weight in the CPI.
McCririck said reweights are based on the ABS' household expenditure survey.
"We've grown forward the CPI weights by looking ... at how trends in the household expenditure change — we've grown the weight forward each year manually," she said.
Looking at the reweight in 2025, the weight for alcohol and tobacco fell because sales of legal tobacco had fallen as smoking rates decline, although it did not include vapes and illicit tobacco.
The weight for housing also fell because home buying declined amid a shortage in new construction and supply. Dwelling commencements in 2024 were the lowest in over ten years.
In 2024, school fees rose in 2024 and there were more non-government school enrolments forcing the weight for education to go up for 2025.
Due to the rise in airfares, Australian household spending on overseas holidays rose so the weight for international holiday travel and accommodation increased.
Inflationary pressures are 'going to persist'
Regardless of the weights, Asher told SBS News that rising inflation is a trend that is likely to continue.
"The wars will continue, which means that fuel prices will continue to be high and that has a flow-on effect on goods, logistics and transport systems — which flows onto anything that's imported," she said.
"Many materials, even if they are locally produced here, will increase."
She said inflationary pressures have seen Australians reduce their spending — a habit she hopes can continue into the Christmas period.
"As we move into the Christmas period, people are worse off now than they were at the beginning of the year with inflation — wage growth hasn't kept up," Asher said.
"Some people will be inclined to still spend at Christmas because they feel obliged to do so. I really think that people should be okay to pull back and not overdo it or put things on credit.
"As we move into next year, it's still going to be incredibly tough. Many of the challenges we're seeing are going to persist."

A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:59:52 UTC
09:59:52 KST

A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms
- Date:
- October 30, 2026
- Source:
- Mass General Brigham
- Summary:
- A major international study found that a simple blood test could help predict Alzheimer’s-related cognitive decline years before symptoms appear, with the highest-risk individuals facing a 38% chance of impairment within five years and an estimated 78% chance within 10 years. Scientists believe the discovery could pave the way for earlier intervention and future treatments designed to prevent Alzheimer’s before memory problems begin.
- Share:
A simple blood test could help identify people at increased risk of Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline years before they experience any noticeable problems with memory or thinking. In a large international study, researchers found that older adults with very high levels of a particular blood biomarker faced a 38% chance of developing cognitive impairment within five years. Over 10 years, the estimated risk rose to 78%, although the longer-term findings were based on substantially less data.
The findings offer new insight into the potential of blood tests to predict future cognitive problems in people who currently show no signs of impairment. The research was led by scientists at the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute and involved teams working across three continents. The results were presented at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference and simultaneously published in JAMA.
The study focused on phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217), a blood biomarker associated with Alzheimer's disease. A test measuring this marker recently received federal clearance, raising hopes that blood testing could make Alzheimer's detection more accessible. However, an important question has remained: Can these tests reliably predict whether someone with normal cognitive function will eventually develop symptoms?
Blood Test Reveals Cognitive Decline Risk Years in Advance
To investigate, researchers combined information from six observational studies and clinical trials conducted in North America, Japan, and Australia. Together, these studies included 2,684 older adults who showed no signs of cognitive impairment when they entered the research.
At enrollment, participants provided blood samples that were analyzed for p-tau217. They also underwent positron emission tomography (PET) brain scans, allowing researchers to establish baseline measurements of brain health. Annual follow-up assessments were then used to monitor changes in memory, thinking, and other cognitive abilities.
The combined data covered an unusually long period. Some participants entered one of the studies as early as 2004, while the most recent follow-up assessments took place in 2025.
Across the studies, approximately 478 participants eventually developed cognitive impairment. When researchers compared these outcomes with the original blood test results, they found a strong relationship between higher p-tau217 levels and the likelihood of future cognitive problems.
Among people with very high biomarker levels, the estimated probability of developing cognitive impairment reached 38% within five years. By 10 years, that figure increased to 78%. However, the researchers emphasized that substantially fewer observations were available for the 10-year period and beyond, making those longer-term predictions less certain.
A Powerful Alzheimer's Predictor Beyond Genetics and Brain Scans
One of the most important findings was that p-tau217 provided information about future cognitive decline beyond what could be explained by other established risk factors.
The biomarker remained significantly associated with cognitive impairment even after researchers accounted for amyloid-beta plaques, which are abnormal protein deposits in the brain that can be detected with PET imaging. Its predictive value also extended beyond known genetic risk factors (such as APOE4).
This suggests that a relatively simple blood test could eventually provide doctors with additional information when estimating an individual's likelihood of developing cognitive difficulties.
"This is a critical step toward better understanding what p-tau217 can tell us about a person's risk for cognitive impairment," said lead author Rachel F. Buckley, PhD, a cognitive neuroscientist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "What really sets this work apart is that it estimates an individual's level of risk for cognitive impairment. We harmonized data across six cohorts, creating a large and varied data set, and still found consistent results showing how p-tau217 informs risk over time."
Rather than simply identifying biological changes associated with Alzheimer's, the research helps estimate how those changes translate into the probability of developing symptoms over a specific period.
Why Alzheimer's Blood Tests Are Not Yet Recommended for Healthy People
Despite the promising results, the researchers caution that blood tests are not currently recommended for routine Alzheimer's risk screening in people without symptoms.
One major reason is that preventive treatments capable of changing the course of the disease have not yet been established for otherwise healthy individuals identified as being at elevated risk.
"We do not yet have disease-modifying treatments for people who find out they are at high risk for developing cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease, which is why we don't recommend currently available blood tests for asymptomatic individuals. Today, our medical advice would remain the same regardless of test results: exercise regularly, maintain a healthy diet, and prioritize sleep and overall wellness," said senior and corresponding author Reisa Sperling, MD, a neurologist with the Mass General Brigham Neuroscience Institute. "But the preventive care landscape could change rapidly if ongoing trials of disease-modifying therapies prove beneficial. In the future, these tests could help identify those who might benefit most from these treatments. Our long-term goal is to get us to where cholesterol testing is in predicting your risk of a heart attack."
There are also important limitations to the research. Although the investigators brought together data from multiple studies and geographic regions, the participants may not fully represent the broader population. This potential selection bias could affect how well the findings apply to other groups.
In addition, the analysis focused on predicting cognitive impairment over relatively limited periods rather than estimating a person's lifetime risk. Researchers say larger, more representative studies and longer follow-up periods will be needed to confirm the findings and improve the precision of individual risk predictions.
Could Blood Tests Help Prevent Alzheimer's Before Symptoms Begin?
The greatest potential benefit of this approach may emerge as scientists develop treatments designed to slow or prevent Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline before noticeable symptoms develop.
Several clinical trials are already investigating whether disease-modifying therapies can benefit people who have biological signs of Alzheimer's but have not yet experienced cognitive impairment. If those treatments prove effective, blood biomarkers such as p-tau217 could help identify individuals most likely to benefit from early intervention.
Such an approach could eventually make Alzheimer's prevention more similar to cardiovascular prevention, where cholesterol measurements help doctors estimate future heart attack risk and determine who may benefit from treatment.
For now, the blood test offers researchers a way to identify higher-risk individuals who may be suitable candidates for prevention studies.
"Today, p-tau217 can help identify people at high risk for future Alzheimer's dementia for participation in prevention trials," said Sperling. "As these trials move forward, individualized estimates, including the biomarker's prognostic value, could guide earlier treatment and monitoring decisions."

Trump administration accelerates criminal probe into Alaska Senate race
- Trump’s administration has sped up criminal and civil probes into claims that Democrats backed a spoiler candidate in Alaska’s key Senate race, adding uncertainty before the Nov 3 midterm vote.
- The Justice Department says it is investigating “intensely and swiftly” and has asked a judge to block Alaska from certifying results if Dan Sullivan loses to another Daniel Sullivan.
- The administration is also pressing a California case over alleged non-citizen voting, but courts have rejected its bid to stop mail ballots, calling the move a risk to legal voters.
AI generated
WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE - US President Donald Trump’s administration stepped up criminal and civil investigations into allegations that Democrats conspired to recruit a spoiler candidate in a critical Senate race in Alaska, US officials said on Oct 30, injecting fresh uncertainty into Nov 3’s congressional midterm election.
The Justice Department’s top prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a press conference that a New York Times article on Oct 28 about the effort had driven a “surge” of FBI resources, adding that he had assigned several prosecutors to the case and that investigative steps were taking place “intensely and swiftly.”
“Every Alaskan deserves a fair election, and they’re going to get one,” he said. “Anyone who tries to illegally deceive voters and interfere with the election, they’ll answer for it.”
The Alaska contest is widely seen as one of the US Senate races that could sway control of the chamber, now narrowly held by Trump’s Republicans.
The Justice Department’s legal actions in Alaska and California, where the Trump administration is trying to prevent some ballots from being counted, represent an extraordinary federal intervention in state-run elections, which are administered locally under the US Constitution.
When the DOJ filed the civil suit against Alaska a week ago, Trump told reporters, “I’m the one that said do it.”
Heyman declined to offer specifics when asked what possible crimes were being examined, saying he would let the Alaska investigation proceed, although Trump has called for a prosecution of Senate candidate Mary Peltola, a Democrat.
“This is voter fraud at the highest level,” Trump told a Florida rally on Oct 30.
The Department of Justice asked a federal judge on Oct 30 to ensure the preservation of ballots that “may be impacted by voter confusion.”
The court filing requested the judge’s help obtaining documents from the Democratic campaign and others to determine “whether Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy is frivolous or fraudulent.”
The DOJ also has sued Alaska to preemptively block the state from certifying the results of the Senate race if the Republican incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, loses due to the presence of a third candidate, named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.
It is not clear what, if any, laws may have been broken; both parties have engaged in “ballot stacking” by propping up lesser-known candidates to siphon votes from their opponents.
The New York Times this week reported that staffers from the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Party’s Senate campaign arm helped recruit a retired teacher living in a remote fishing village who is named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr to appear on the ballot.
Reuters has not been able to independently confirm the Times’ reporting.
Peltola has denied knowing about any effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan, and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has also denied involvement.
Sullivan, the retired teacher, has denied coordinating with Peltola’s campaign.
Surge of voting nationwide despite uncertainty
Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are bracing for further disruptions from the Trump administration, which has sued about 30 states seeking unredacted voter rolls.
“The new tactic is just to create enough confusion and enough uncertainty and enough doubt through the filing of all these lawsuits to lay the groundwork to ultimately, I think, challenge the results once the dust settles after Tuesday,” said Jonathan Diaz of the non-partisan Campaign Legal Centre.
Trump has long sought to sow distrust of election results, falsely claiming for years that his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden was the result of widespread fraud.
Voter fraud in the US is extremely rare, studies and investigations have found.
Despite any uncertainty, a record 49 million people have cast early ballots, more than any other midterm election in US history, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, with even the American-born Pope Leo casting a ballot by mail.
The DOJ has also pushed forward a legal case in California, issuing subpoenas to election officials as part of a criminal probe into alleged voting by non-citizens, according to copies of documents seen by Reuters.
A US appeals court on Oct 30 rejected the department’s request to temporarily block California from counting any mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters who the Trump administration alleges are likely noncitizens, the second time the court has done so this week.
A lower court judge had already denied the administration’s request, finding it would potentially disenfranchise thousands of legal voters.
Trump said on Oct 30 he would attend weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas after all, a day after cancelling them, telling reporters at the White House that Republicans in those states had called him and asked him to reconsider.
Former Vice-President Kamala Harris, whom Trump defeated in the 2024 election, will rally for Democrats in Atlanta on Oct 30. REUTERS

Russian Red Cross provides assistance to over 133,000 residents of border regions

MOSCOW, October 31. /TASS/. More than 133,000 residents of Russia’s border regions have received assistance worth over 96 million rubles (approximately $1.2 million) from the Russian Red Cross (RRC) since the beginning of the year, the organization’s Chairman Pavel Savchuk told TASS.
"Since the beginning of 2026, the Russian Red Cross has provided assistance worth over 96 million rubles to more than 133,000 residents of border regions. They are residents of the Kursk, Voronezh, Rostov, Belgorod and Bryansk regions, as well as the Republic of Crimea," he said.
Savchuk noted that the RRC supports people affected by emergencies, those forced to leave their homes, and those who find themselves in difficult life circumstances. "We provide food, drinking water, clothing, hygiene products, items for children and school supplies, bedding and household appliances. We also provide cash assistance and vouchers so that families can purchase the necessities themselves," he stressed.

Italian Language Week: Guatemala Speaks Italian, Between Academia and Cinema
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
01:50:48 CET
09:50:48 KST

From university classrooms to the big screen, the Italian language and culture took center stage in Guatemala during the 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World, celebrated from October 22 to 26 with a program of conferences, academic meetings, and film screenings organized by the Italian Embassy and the Italian Cultural Institute in Guatemala City.
                                    
A special guest was Professor Alejandro Patat of the University for Foreigners of Siena, who led the audience in a reflection on the relationship between language, creativity, and cultural identity with his lecture “The Italian Language and the Concept of Genius,” hosted by the Universidad del Istmo.
                                    
The initiatives also involved the University of San Carlos of Guatemala (USAC), the country’s only public university, where approximately 150 students from the translation and interpretation programs at the Escuela de Ciencias Lingüísticas participated in a virtual meeting with the Italian professor, demonstrating the interest in studying the Italian language and culture in Guatemala.
                                    
Professor Patat’s visit also provided an opportunity to strengthen dialogue with the local academic community and explore new avenues for collaboration between Italian and Guatemalan universities.
                                    
There was also a focus on cinema, with public screenings of “Sostiene Pereira” and “Becaària,” which enriched the program by offering the Guatemalan public further opportunities to engage with Italian culture through the language of film.
                                    
The Week concluded in the spirit of cultural exchange and academic collaboration, helping to strengthen ties between Italy and Guatemala and to promote the Italian language as a tool for knowledge, dialogue, and cultural exchange.

McDonald’s must face lawsuit over McRib, US judge rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-31
00:46:00 UTC
09:46:00 KST

McDonald’s must face lawsuit over McRib, US judge rules
CHICAGO - A federal judge on Oct 30 rejected McDonald’s request to dismiss a proposed class action accusing it of defrauding consumers about the content of its McRib sandwich.
The plaintiffs accused McDonald’s of intentionally shaping McRib patties with ridges to resemble pork ribs and make diners believe the sandwich contains rib meat, an expensive cut known for its higher fat content and rich flavour.
Consumers said McDonald’s actual use of lower-grade pork products including shoulder, heart, tripe or stomach caused them to overpay for the McRib, one of its most expensive menu items.
While dismissing some claims, US District Judge April Perry in McDonald’s hometown of Chicago called it premature to accept the company’s argument that no reasonable consumer could expect the McRib to contain rib meat.
She said McDonald’s website describes the sandwich only as containing pork, and reasonable consumers need not do research before buying a US$7 (S$8.95) fast-food sandwich.
The judge also said ads highlighting the meat’s rib-like shape could support a claim of intent to defraud, though further proof was needed.
“Plaintiffs’ proffered understanding of ‘McRib’ is not unreasonable or fanciful,” Perry wrote.
McDonald’s has sold the McRib periodically since 1981.
It contended that distinctive product names do not fool reasonable consumers, and the plaintiffs’ preference for a certain cut of pork “doesn’t turn McDonald’s truthful marketing into consumer fraud.”
In a statement, McDonald’s maintained that it does not use hearts, tripe or stomach in the McRib, and has always been transparent about its ingredients. “This lawsuit distorts the facts and the claims are meritless,” it added.
Thiago Coelho, a lawyer for the plaintiffs, said his clients will continue seeking accountability for deceptive marketing.
Fast-food chains have faced other lawsuits over product depictions in ads and on menu boards.
These include cases accusing McDonald’s, Burger King and Wendy’s of making burgers appear larger than they actually are. REUTERS
